lists.title: 50 Hard-Problem Projects: Search & Systems
lists.author: Arnav Dewan
howToUse: Start with a Starter project in one lane, then grow it into a Hard one rather than jumping between ideas. Good first picks: 1 (recruiter search), 13 (HNSW from scratch), 25 (malloc in C), 33 (crash-safe KV store), 35 (B+tree with a buffer pool).
Levels assume you are learning from scratch: Starter = a few weekends once you know Python or C basics; Intermediate = 1 to 2 months; Hard = open-ended, research-flavored.

Write each one up the way strong systems repos do: (1) one question the project answers; (2) numbers for every claim, with the machine and command that produced them; (3) why the surprising results happened; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.

lanes.name: Search, retrieval & ranking
lanes.intro: Semantic search finds things that sound right but break must-have constraints, and good rerankers are slow and expensive.

lanes.name: Vector search internals
lanes.intro: Keeping recall high while cutting memory, latency and cost, under filters, deletes and constant updates.

lanes.name: Memory & concurrency
lanes.intro: Code that is fast on one thread often collapses on eight, and concurrent code can be wrong in ways tests rarely catch.

lanes.name: Storage & databases
lanes.intro: Data must survive crashes, disks are slow, and every design trades write speed, read speed and space against each other.

lanes.name: I/O, distributed & GPU
lanes.intro: Networks drop and reorder messages, machines fail mid-operation, and GPUs are only fast when memory access is arranged just right.

lanes.name: Bridge: search meets systems
lanes.intro: These combine both lanes, which is where the rarest and best-paid skills sit: making AI and search fast at the systems level.

lists.title: 50 Real-World Projects to Build and Test Outside
lists.author: Arnav Dewan
howToUse: Pick the idea you would actually use this month, then test it outside with real photos, real places and real friends. Your own data is messy in ways public datasets are not, and fixing that is the interesting work.
Start small: a phone camera plus a laptop is enough for most of these; hardware ideas are at the end.
Measure it: accuracy on 100 of your own photos, latency on your phone, or how many friends kept using it after a week.
Privacy rule of thumb: identify things, places, plants and animals, not people. Where people appear, count them anonymously on-device and never store faces.
Safety: for anything about rules or food (fishing limits, allergens), treat the app as a helper and always check the official source.

lanes.name: Hardware & sensors
lanes.intro: These need a Raspberry Pi, an ESP32 or just your phone's sensors, and they exercise the systems lane: small memory, tight latency, unreliable networks.

lists.title: Open Source Contribution Flows
lists.author: Arnav Dewan
howToUse: Pick a repo you already use, or one the role you want names. For LLM infra roles that means projects like vLLM, SGLang, verl, NeMo RL or Megatron Core: a merged PR there is stronger proof of familiarity than a side project.

Climb the ladder: docs or tests first, then a reproduced bug fix, then a benchmark-backed performance change, then a small feature. Each rung teaches more of the codebase and builds trust with maintainers.
Read the repo CONTRIBUTING guide and its policy on AI-assisted contributions before opening a PR. If an agent helps write code, you must understand, test and be able to defend every line.
Comment on an issue before starting larger work, keep each PR small and focused, and do not claim an issue you cannot finish.
Good-first-issue labels go stale fast, so each flow links to the live issue search instead of naming specific issues.

projects.title: Recruiter search engine on a public resume or jobs dataset
projects.problem: Rebuild the interview pipeline: retrieve, filter, rerank
projects.proveIt: NDCG@10, % of top 10 meeting all hard criteria
projects.question: Can a retrieve, filter, verify, rerank pipeline put only fully qualified candidates in the top 10 while ranking them well by NDCG@10?

steps.title: Frame the recruiter search question and its two metrics
steps.learn: The task mirrors a recruiter search interview: a query mixes hard criteria (must hold) and soft criteria (nice to have). Report NDCG@10 and the % of top 10 results meeting every hard criterion. Data: Kaggle Resume Dataset (2400+ livecareer.com resume examples, 24 categories, uploader-labeled CC0).
verify: Download the CSV and confirm the columns ID, Resume_str, Resume_html, Category and the row count yourself
Read 20 resumes and list which hard criteria the text can actually support (titles, years, degrees, skills)
Write 40 recruiter queries (one hard, one soft criterion each) and freeze 15 as a held-out test set you never look at while building

steps.title: Extract structured candidate profiles from resume text
steps.learn: Hard filters need fields, not prose. Extract normalized title, total years of experience (from date ranges, merging overlaps, treating 'current' roles with a fixed reference date), highest degree and skills. Normalize synonyms (e.g. 'Sr.' and 'Senior') so filters match. Keep 'unknown' distinct from 'no'.

decision.choice: Offline LLM extraction to a strict JSON schema, validated with Pydantic, cached per resume ID
decision.why: The corpus is small (a few thousand resumes), so a one-time LLM pass is cheap, and schema validation catches malformed output. Doing it offline keeps query time fast and makes extraction reproducible from the cache.

alternatives.name: Regex and date rules only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and deterministic, but resume layouts vary a lot and rules miss titles and degrees phrased in unusual ways.

alternatives.name: No extraction, embed raw text
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest pipeline, but you cannot enforce hard criteria, so the % meeting hard criteria will suffer.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Write extract.py: read the Kaggle resume CSV, call an LLM with a JSON schema (Pydantic model CandidateProfile: title_normalized, years_experience float|None, degree_level enum, skills list[str], evidence spans). Cache results in a JSONL keyed by ID; skip cached rows. Compute years from date ranges in Python, not the LLM, merging overlaps. Tests: overlap merge, 'present' handling with fixed reference date, schema validation failure path.
verify: Hand-check 30 extracted profiles against the raw text and record field-level accuracy for years and degree
Confirm overlapping jobs are not double counted in years of experience on 3 handpicked resumes
Count how many profiles have 'unknown' for each field; note which hard criteria are risky

steps.title: Parse the recruiter query into hard filters and soft criteria
steps.learn: The query parser decides what is non-negotiable. 'Senior accountant, 5+ years, CPA, ideally healthcare' splits into hard filters (title, years >= 5, certification) and soft text ('healthcare'). Values must map onto the same normalized vocabulary used in extraction, or filters silently match nothing.

decision.choice: LLM call with a strict schema whose enum fields reuse the extraction vocabulary
decision.why: Recruiter phrasing is varied and an LLM handles it well, while the schema forces outputs into values the filters understand. Sharing one vocabulary between extraction and parsing removes a whole class of silent mismatches.

alternatives.name: Hand-written grammar
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and free, but only works if queries follow a template; real phrasing breaks it.

alternatives.name: No parsing, treat the query as text
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to build, but every criterion becomes soft and hard-criteria precision drops.

steps.delegate: Python. parse_query.py with parse(query:str) returning ParsedQuery (Pydantic: hard: list[HardFilter{field, op, value}], soft: str). Use the same enums as extraction. Use tool calling or structured outputs. On validation failure retry once, then fall back to soft-only. Tests: 10 fixture queries with expected hard filters, a fallback test, and an enum-mismatch test.
verify: Hand-label hard vs soft for your 40 queries and measure parser agreement on each field
Feed 5 ambiguous queries ('ideally', 'preferred') and confirm they land in soft criteria
Confirm parser output always validates against the schema, including on a nonsense query

steps.title: Retrieve about 200 candidates with BM25 plus dense vectors
steps.learn: BM25 catches exact skills and certifications (CPA, AutoCAD) that embeddings blur; dense vectors catch paraphrases ('managed payroll' vs 'compensation administration'). Fuse the two ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which uses ranks rather than raw scores, so the two scales never need calibrating.

decision.choice: rank_bm25 BM25Okapi plus a small sentence-transformers model, brute-force cosine in NumPy, fused with RRF
decision.why: A few thousand resumes fit in memory, so exact search is fast enough and removes ANN recall loss as a variable. Two plain libraries keep the pipeline easy to read and ablate.

alternatives.name: Qdrant with prefetch and RRF fusion
alternatives.tradeoff: Built-in hybrid queries and payload filters; worth it at larger scale or when you need a service, but adds infrastructure to a starter.

alternatives.name: Dense only
alternatives.tradeoff: One index and simpler code, but exact terms like certification names get missed.

steps.delegate: Python. retrieve.py: build BM25Okapi over tokenized Resume_str, embed resumes with a sentence-transformers model (chunk long resumes, max-pool chunk scores per resume), cosine via NumPy. rrf(lists, k) returns fused IDs; return top 200. Save embeddings to .npy with the model name. Tests: RRF on toy lists with known output, deterministic ordering on ties, chunk max-pooling.
verify: Hand-judge the top 20 from BM25, dense and fused for 5 dev queries and count relevant resumes in each (full recall comes after labeling)
Find one query where BM25 wins and one where dense wins and explain why
Confirm the same query returns identical results across two runs

steps.title: Apply hard filters to the candidate pool before ranking
steps.learn: Filtering after taking the top 200 can leave fewer than 10 survivors for strict queries; filtering first guarantees every candidate is eligible. With exact search over a small corpus, pre-filtering has no recall cost, which is not true for ANN indexes at scale.

decision.choice: Pre-filter with boolean masks on extracted fields, then retrieve the top 200 inside the eligible set
decision.why: Exact search makes pre-filtering free, and the prove-it metric punishes any top 10 result that breaks a hard criterion. Masks are simple to test and explain.

alternatives.name: Post-filter the top 200
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but strict queries can end with too few results, hurting both metrics.

alternatives.name: Filter inside a vector DB
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales and handles filtered ANN, but you then depend on the engine's filter strategy and its recall behavior.

steps.delegate: Python. filters.py: apply(parsed.hard, profiles) returning bool mask over NumPy arrays (years >= N, degree_level >= X, normalized title in set, skill contains with fuzzy match threshold). Policy flag for unknown values (exclude or keep-and-mark). retrieve.py accepts the mask. Tests: each operator, unknown handling under both policies, empty-mask path returning an explicit 'no eligible candidates'.
verify: For each dev query, log how many resumes pass the filters; flag queries with fewer than 10
Compare survivors in the top 200 with pre-filter vs post-filter and report the difference
Confirm a resume with 'unknown' years is handled the way your policy says

steps.title: Verify hard criteria with a rule-based checker
steps.learn: Extraction can be wrong, so re-check each hard criterion per candidate against the raw resume text (evidence spans, regex for named certifications, dates re-parsed from the span) and return pass, fail or unknown with the text that justifies it. Rechecking extracted fields alone adds nothing.

decision.choice: Deterministic Python rules over extracted fields plus evidence spans; unknown never ranks above a pass
decision.why: Rules are cheap, repeatable and auditable, which matters when a metric is defined as 'meets all hard criteria'. Pushing unknowns below passes keeps the top 10 clean without discarding them.

alternatives.name: LLM verifier per candidate
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles messy phrasing better, but costs a call per candidate and can disagree with itself across runs.

alternatives.name: Trust the filters only
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra code, but every extraction error reaches the top 10 unseen.

steps.delegate: Python. checker.py: check(candidate, hard_filters) returning list[CriterionResult{field, status: pass|fail|unknown, evidence}]. Recheck against raw Resume_str: confirm each evidence span occurs verbatim, re-parse dates inside it, regex-match named certifications and degrees. Ranking key puts all-pass first. Tests: one fixture per operator, a missing-evidence case returning unknown, and a regression test using the 5 injected violators.
verify: Inject 5 known-violating resumes into a candidate list and confirm the checker rejects all 5
Read the evidence for 20 passes and count how many are actually correct
Report how often the checker disagrees with the metadata filter, and why

steps.title: Rerank eligible candidates on soft criteria with a cross-encoder
steps.learn: Retrieval embeds query and resume separately; a cross-encoder reads them together and scores fit, so it judges 'healthcare billing experience' far better. It is slower, so it only sees surviving candidates. It reads at most 512 tokens per query plus chunk pair, so score the best chunks, not the first page.

decision.choice: sentence-transformers CrossEncoder (ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2) over soft text vs top resume chunks, max-pooled
decision.why: It runs locally on a laptop, is a documented retrieve-then-rerank pattern, and has zero per-query cost, so you can iterate on dev queries freely.

alternatives.name: LLM reranker (pointwise or listwise)
alternatives.tradeoff: Better at nuanced criteria and explanations, but adds latency, cost per query and run-to-run variance.

alternatives.name: bge-reranker-v2-m3
alternatives.tradeoff: A larger multilingual reranker; may score better on varied text, at higher compute per pair.

steps.delegate: Python. rerank.py: rerank(soft:str, candidates, top_n=10) using sentence_transformers.CrossEncoder('cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2'); split resumes into chunks, pick top chunks by BM25 against the soft text, predict pairs in batches, max-pool per candidate; final order keeps the checker's all-pass group first. Tests: deterministic order, batching equals unbatched scores, empty soft text skips reranking.
verify: Hand-judge the top 10 with and without the reranker for 5 dev queries now; compute NDCG@10 for both once the judge-labels step exists
Time reranking 200 candidates on your machine and record the hardware
Read the top 3 for 5 queries and check the soft criterion is actually visible in the text

steps.title: Build graded relevance labels with pooling and an LLM judge
steps.learn: NDCG needs graded labels (for example 0 to 3) per query and resume. Pool the top results from every system variant so no system is judged only on its own hits. An LLM judge scales labeling, but measure how often it agrees with you before trusting it. Keep the dev/test split frozen in step 1.

decision.choice: Pool the top 20 from BM25, dense, hybrid and reranked runs; LLM judge on a 0 to 3 rubric; human-check a sample
decision.why: There are no public relevance labels for this dataset, so you create them. Pooling across variants reduces bias toward one system and a human-checked sample tells you how far the judge can be trusted.

alternatives.name: Label everything by hand
alternatives.tradeoff: Most trustworthy, but slow; realistic only for a smaller query set.

alternatives.name: Use Category as relevance
alternatives.tradeoff: Free labels, but a category is far coarser than a recruiter query, so NDCG would measure the wrong thing.

steps.delegate: Python. labels.py: pool top 20 per query from all runs, dedupe, call an LLM judge on the raw resume with a fixed rubric (0 to 3) plus pass/fail per hard criterion, temperature 0 if supported; write TREC-style qrels and a criteria labels file. CLI to sample N pairs for human labeling and agreement. Load the frozen dev/test IDs. Tests: pooling dedupe, qrels round trip, stable split.
verify: Hand-label 100 pooled pairs and report agreement with the LLM judge
Confirm the judge prompt never sees which system produced the result
Confirm the 15+ held-out queries frozen in step 1 were never used while tuning any earlier step

steps.title: Cache LLM calls and handle failures end to end
steps.learn: Two LLM touchpoints (extraction offline, parsing per query) can fail, rate limit or drift. Caching makes runs reproducible and cheap to rerun; fallbacks keep a query answerable when the parser fails. Record latency per stage so you know where time goes.

decision.choice: Disk cache keyed by hash of model, prompt and input; retry with backoff; soft-only fallback
decision.why: Evaluation means rerunning the same queries many times, so caching removes most cost and variance. A fallback is better than an error for a search tool.

alternatives.name: No cache, call live every time
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but slow, costly and results shift between runs, which corrupts comparisons.

alternatives.name: Async batch every call
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster cold runs at the cost of more complex code; useful once the query set grows.

steps.delegate: Python. llm_cache.py: decorator caching responses in SQLite keyed by sha256(model+prompt+input); retry with exponential backoff on rate-limit errors; per-stage timers written to a CSV. Wire it into extract.py and parse_query.py. Tests: cache hit skips the call (mock client), retry count respected, fallback path on persistent failure.
verify: Run the full pipeline twice and confirm the second run makes zero LLM calls
Simulate a parser failure and confirm results still return using the soft-only fallback
Report p50 and p95 latency per stage over all dev queries

steps.title: Measure it: NDCG@10, hard-criteria precision and ablations
steps.learn: Run every variant on dev and held-out test: BM25 only, dense only, hybrid, plus filters, plus checker, plus reranker. Report NDCG@10 and % of top 10 meeting all hard criteria. Tune only on dev. With about 15 test queries, use per-query paired tests before calling a gap overfitting or a win.
steps.delegate: Python. eval.py: for each variant write a run, load qrels with ranx, compute ndcg@10; compute hard-criteria precision@10 from the independent per-criterion labels (judge plus human sample), not the system's checker. Output a Markdown table for dev and test plus per-query JSON. CLI flags --split and --variant. Tests: toy run with hand-computed NDCG, a variant flag that disables each stage.
verify: Report both metrics for all 6 variants on dev and test in one table
Record machine, OS, Python and library versions, model names and the exact command
Check NDCG on 3 queries with sklearn ndcg_score (add unretrieved judged docs with lowest score) vs ranx 'ndcg'

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: Write the 4-part write-up: the one question, numbers for every claim with machine and command, why surprising results happened (for example where the reranker hurt), and what this does not prove (LLM-judged labels, a synthetic query set, one resume source).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2 gives a number, machine and command for every claim, for dev and test
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with an example query
Part 4 lists assumptions, including judge agreement and the dataset's limits

projects.title: Constraint-aware retrieval
projects.problem: Vector search ignores "must have 5+ years" or "must hold a JD"
projects.proveIt: Constraint-violation rate before vs after
projects.question: How often does plain vector search return job postings that break a must-have constraint, and how far do filters cut that rate without hurting NDCG@10?

steps.title: Frame the question, the violation metric and the frozen test set
steps.learn: Prove-it is the constraint-violation rate before vs after: the share of top 10 results that break at least one must-have in the query. Track NDCG@10 too, so returning nothing cannot look like a win. Data: Kaggle LinkedIn Job Postings (124,000+ postings from 2023 and 2024, CC BY-SA 4.0).
verify: Download postings.csv and confirm columns title, description, min_salary, pay_period, remote_allowed and formatted_experience_level exist
Write 60 job-seeker queries, each with 1 to 3 must-haves written as a gold spec by hand (field, op, value) plus soft text
Freeze 20 queries and their gold specs as the test set (record a sha256) before building anything; tune only on the other 40

steps.title: Profile and normalize the constraint fields
steps.learn: A filter is only as good as the field behind it. Salaries come with a pay_period (hourly, monthly, yearly), experience levels are free-ish labels and many rows are missing values. Decide how 'unknown' behaves before any filter exists, because it drives the violation rate directly.

decision.choice: Normalize salary to a yearly figure with a stated hours assumption; keep missing as an explicit 'unknown' state
decision.why: Queries say 'at least 120k a year', so hourly and monthly rows must be comparable. Keeping unknown separate lets you report results two ways (strict: unknown counts as a violation; lenient: unknown is allowed) instead of hiding the choice.

alternatives.name: Drop rows with missing fields
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean filters, but shrinks the corpus and biases it toward postings that publish salary.

alternatives.name: Treat missing as satisfying
alternatives.tradeoff: More results, but the violation rate becomes meaningless for salary queries.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, pandas. normalize.py: load postings.csv, output postings.parquet with job_id, title, description, yearly_min_salary (from min_salary and pay_period, hours-per-year as a named constant), remote (true/false/unknown), experience_level (canonical enum), work_type. Print null rates and value counts per field. Tests: hourly, monthly and yearly conversion, missing pay_period gives unknown, unseen experience label raises.
verify: Report the share of rows with unknown salary, remote and experience level
Spot-check 20 converted salaries against the raw rows by hand
Inspect how remote_allowed encodes 'not remote' vs missing and document what you found

steps.title: Build the plain vector search baseline
steps.learn: The 'before' number needs a fair baseline: embed each posting and return the nearest neighbors of the full query text, constraints and all. Embeddings capture topic well but treat '120k', 'remote' and '5+ years' as fuzzy words, which is the failure this project measures.

decision.choice: sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 on title plus the start of the description, indexed with hnswlib (cosine)
decision.why: A small model keeps embedding 124k postings cheap, and hnswlib exposes a filter argument on knn_query, so the same index serves both the baseline and the filtered variants later. One index removes a confound from the before vs after comparison.

alternatives.name: Exact NumPy brute force
alternatives.tradeoff: No ANN recall loss at all; at this corpus size it is feasible but slower per query, and it skips the filtered-ANN question.

alternatives.name: Larger embedding model
alternatives.tradeoff: Better topical relevance, but slower to embed and it does not fix constraint violations.

steps.delegate: Python. embed.py: encode title plus truncated description with sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2, normalized, save to .npy with model name. index.py: hnswlib Index(space='cosine'), init_index with M and ef_construction as CLI flags, add_items with job row ids, save. search.py: search(query, k) returns ids and scores. Tests: a posting's own text returns itself at rank 1; saved and reloaded index gives identical results after set_ef.
verify: Run 5 dev queries and hand-check whether the top 10 is on topic
Count by hand how many of those top 10 break a must-have; this is your first glimpse of the problem
Measure recall@10 of hnswlib vs exact brute force on 100 random queries

steps.title: Extract text-only constraints from job descriptions
steps.learn: Some must-haves live only in prose: 'requires 5+ years', 'JD required', 'active bar admission'. Extract years required and required credentials into fields with an 'unknown' state. Distinguish 'required' from 'preferred', or a filter will wrongly drop postings that only prefer a credential.

decision.choice: Rule-based extraction (regex for year ranges, keyword lists for credentials) with required vs preferred cue words
decision.why: 124k long descriptions make a full LLM pass slow and costly, and rules are deterministic, so a change in the violation rate comes from the filter, not extraction noise. Measure rule accuracy on a labeled sample.

alternatives.name: LLM extraction to a JSON schema
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles odd phrasing better; worth it on a smaller subset, but costs money and time at this scale and must be cached.

alternatives.name: No extraction, keep these soft
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but text-only must-haves can never be enforced and stay in the violation rate.

steps.delegate: Python. extract_text.py: for each description return years_required (int or None, the lower bound of patterns like '5+ years' or '3-5 years'), credentials_required and credentials_preferred (sets from a keyword map, e.g. JD, bar admission, CPA). Look for 'required', 'must', 'preferred', 'nice to have' near the match. Write to parquet. Tests: 15 fixture sentences covering ranges, 'plus', preferred vs required and no mention.
verify: Hand-label 100 random descriptions and report precision and recall for years_required and each credential
List 5 extraction errors and classify them (pattern missed, preferred read as required, other)

steps.title: Parse each query into must-have filters and soft text
steps.learn: The parser decides what is non-negotiable. 'Remote data engineer, at least 150k, 5+ years, ideally fintech' becomes remote = true, yearly salary >= 150000, years_required <= 5 (the seeker has 5) and soft text. Values must land in the same vocabulary as the normalized fields or filters silently match nothing.

decision.choice: LLM call with a Pydantic schema whose enums reuse the normalized field values, cached per query
decision.why: Query phrasing varies a lot and an LLM handles it, while the schema forces output into values the filter understands. The parser is graded against your hand-written gold specs, never against itself.

alternatives.name: Hand-written grammar
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and deterministic, but only covers phrasings you anticipated.

alternatives.name: No parsing, whole query as text
alternatives.tradeoff: This is the baseline; every constraint stays soft.

steps.delegate: Python. parse_query.py: parse(q) returns ParsedQuery (Pydantic): filters list of {field enum, op in [eq, gte, lte, has], value} and soft_text. Use structured output or tool calling; on validation failure retry once, then fall back to soft only. Disk cache keyed by model and query. Tests: 10 fixture queries with expected filters, 'ideally' kept soft, fallback path, cache hit makes no call.
verify: Compare parser output to your gold specs on the 40 dev queries and report exact-match rate per field
Confirm every 'preferably' or 'ideally' phrase in dev lands in soft text

steps.title: Choose where the filter runs: before, during or after ANN
steps.learn: Post-filtering (fetch k times m, then drop violators) is easy but returns fewer than k when the filter is selective. Pre-filtering (exact search over only eligible rows) is exact but slows with broad filters. Filtering inside the graph walk is fast, but recall falls as the filter gets more selective.

decision.choice: Selectivity-based plan: exact search over eligible ids when few rows pass, hnswlib filter callback otherwise
decision.why: Filter selectivity varies widely across these queries (remote is common, a JD requirement is rare). Counting eligible rows first is cheap, and it lets each query use the plan that keeps recall near exact. Qdrant's docs describe a similar planner switch to full scan.

alternatives.name: Post-filter with overfetch
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest; fine for broad filters, but rare constraints leave short or empty result lists.

alternatives.name: Qdrant payload filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Production-ready filtering and a query planner built in; costs a service and hides the mechanism you are measuring.

alternatives.name: FAISS with an IDSelector
alternatives.tradeoff: Per-query id restriction in FAISS; good if you already use FAISS indexes.

steps.delegate: Python. filtered_search.py: eligible_mask(filters, mode=strict|lenient) as a NumPy bool array over row ids; plan(): if eligible count < threshold run exact cosine over eligible rows, else hnswlib knn_query with filter=lambda i: mask[i], num_threads=1. hnswlib raises when fewer than k results exist, so catch it and fall back to exact. Also implement post_filter(overfetch). Tests: every returned id passes the mask, threshold switch, empty eligible set.
verify: For 10 dev queries compare filtered results to exact filtered search and report recall@10 per plan
Bucket queries by selectivity and record latency per plan; find where post-filtering returns fewer than 10

steps.title: Decide what happens with unknown fields and too few matches
steps.learn: Two edge cases decide the user experience: postings whose field is unknown, and queries where fewer than 10 postings pass. Silently topping up with violators brings the violation rate back; returning a short list honestly is better, with any unknown-field postings shown separately and labeled.

decision.choice: Return only passing postings; then a labeled 'could not verify' tier for unknowns; never pad with known violators
decision.why: The metric counts known violations, and the user asked for must-haves. A separate unknown tier keeps recall for postings that simply omit salary, without pretending they qualify.

alternatives.name: Relax the least important filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Fills the list, but requires a priority order the user never gave and reintroduces violations.

alternatives.name: Treat unknown as pass
alternatives.tradeoff: Longer lists, but the system will confidently show postings that may break the constraint.

steps.delegate: Python. results.py: assemble(query) returns {passing: [...], unverified: [...], short_by: int}; unverified holds rows where every known field passes and at least one is unknown, each with the unknown field names. Tests: query with zero passing rows, query with only unknown rows, ordering within tiers by score.
verify: Find 3 dev queries with fewer than 10 passing postings and check the output explains it
Confirm no known violator appears in either tier on all dev queries

steps.title: Rank eligible postings on the soft part with hybrid search
steps.learn: Once must-haves are enforced, NDCG@10 depends on ranking the eligible set by the soft text ('fintech', 'Spark'). BM25 catches exact skill names that embeddings blur; dense vectors catch paraphrases. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines ranks, so the two score scales never need calibrating.

decision.choice: rank_bm25 BM25Okapi and dense cosine over the eligible set, fused with RRF
decision.why: The eligible set is a subset you already have as a mask, so scoring it with both methods is cheap, and RRF has one knob. It also lets you show that constraint handling and relevance ranking are separate problems.

alternatives.name: Dense only
alternatives.tradeoff: One signal and less code, but exact skill terms get blurred.

alternatives.name: Cross-encoder rerank of the top 50
alternatives.tradeoff: Usually better relevance, at a higher latency per query; add it after the main comparison.

steps.delegate: Python. rank.py: given eligible ids and soft_text, compute BM25Okapi scores (index built once over tokenized title plus description) and dense cosine; rrf(lists, k) returns fused ids. Tests: RRF on toy lists with a hand-computed result, deterministic tie-breaking by job_id, empty soft_text falls back to dense similarity to the full query.
verify: On 5 dev queries hand-judge the top 10 from dense only, BM25 only and fused
Confirm fused results contain no posting outside the eligible mask

steps.title: Label violations and relevance independently of the system
steps.learn: The violation rate must not be graded by the system's own parser or extractor. Check structured must-haves with a separate gold checker driven by your hand-written specs and the raw columns. Text-only must-haves (years, JD) need human labels on pooled results. Relevance for NDCG gets graded labels too.

decision.choice: Pool the top 10 of every variant, label text constraints by hand, relevance by an LLM judge spot-checked by hand
decision.why: Pooling covers every result any variant shows, so no variant is scored on unlabeled postings. Constraint labels drive the main claim, so they stay human; relevance is softer and more numerous, so a judge with a measured agreement rate is acceptable.

alternatives.name: Use the extractor's fields as truth
alternatives.tradeoff: No labeling effort, but it grades the system with its own logic and hides extraction errors.

alternatives.name: Human labels for everything
alternatives.tradeoff: Most trustworthy, but slow; reasonable if your query set is small.

steps.delegate: Python. pool.py: union of top 10 ids across all variants per query. gold_check.py: evaluates the hand-written gold spec against raw CSV columns (not normalize.py output) and returns pass, fail or unknown per constraint. label_cli.py: shows description text and records text-constraint labels to JSONL. judge.py: graded relevance 0 to 2 with cached LLM calls. Tests: gold checker on fixture rows.
verify: Hand-label relevance on 50 pooled pairs and report agreement with the LLM judge
Confirm gold_check.py never imports the system's parser or normalizer
Report how many pooled postings are unknown for each constraint

steps.title: Measure it: violation rate, NDCG@10, recall and latency
steps.learn: Compare baseline vector search, post-filter, and the full plan on dev and the frozen test set: violation rate@10 (strict and lenient), NDCG@10, recall@10 vs exact filtered search, and p50 and p95 latency by selectivity bucket. With 20 test queries, use a paired per-query test before calling a gap real.
steps.delegate: Python. eval.py: per variant write a run, load qrels with ranx, compute ndcg@10; compute violation rate@10 from gold labels only; use ranx compare with stat_test='fisher' across variants. Time each query with time.perf_counter after a warm-up pass. Output a Markdown table for dev and test plus per-query JSON. Flags --split, --variant, --mode strict|lenient.
verify: Table shows violation rate and NDCG@10 for every variant on dev and test, strict and lenient
Record CPU, RAM, OS, Python, library versions, model name and the exact command
Hand-recompute violation rate@10 for 2 queries from the raw labels and match the script

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example a filter that lowered NDCG, or recall loss on rare constraints); what this does not prove (one job site snapshot, rule-based text extraction, your own query set).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives violation rate and NDCG@10 before vs after, with machine and command, on test
Part 3 explains at least one surprise with a concrete query
Part 4 lists assumptions: unknown handling, salary conversion, labeler agreement, dataset scope

projects.title: Query distribution-shift test suite
projects.problem: Systems tuned on 10 queries break on paraphrases, typos, other languages
projects.proveIt: NDCG drop on shifted queries, then recovery
projects.question: How much does NDCG@10 drop when tuned retrieval meets paraphrases, typos and non-English queries, and which fixes recover it without hurting the originals?

steps.title: Frame the question and freeze the test split
steps.learn: Prove-it: NDCG@10 drop on shifted queries, then recovery. Use BEIR SciFact (5,183 abstracts, 300 test claims with relevance judgments, plus a train split). Tune on 10 train queries, pick fixes on a dev set of other train queries; test is only for the final measurement.
verify: Download SciFact via BEIR and confirm 5,183 corpus docs and 300 test queries yourself
Pick 10 train queries for tuning and 100 other train queries as dev; record test query ids and a sha256 of test qrels before anything else
Read 10 test claims and note what makes them hard (numbers, gene names, long phrasing)

steps.title: Generate shifted queries once and freeze them
steps.learn: Each shifted query keeps the original's qrels, so it is only valid if meaning is preserved. Build three families: typos (character edits), paraphrases (same need, different words) and translations. Penha et al. built such generators from a taxonomy of real user variations. Generate once, then freeze before tuning.

decision.choice: Seeded character typos with nlpaug, LLM paraphrases and LLM translations, filtered by a human meaning check
decision.why: SciFact has no natural variants, so you have to generate them. Seeded typos are reproducible; an LLM gives fluent paraphrases and translations. The human check removes variants whose meaning changed, since their old qrels would be wrong.

alternatives.name: Real typo queries (CharacterBERT dataset)
alternatives.tradeoff: Real user typos instead of synthetic ones, but they come with MS MARCO, a far larger corpus than SciFact.

alternatives.name: mMARCO translated queries
alternatives.tradeoff: Ready-made translations with qrels, but again tied to MS MARCO passages.

alternatives.name: Rule-based paraphrase only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and reproducible, but variants are shallow (word order, synonyms).

steps.delegate: Python. shifts.py: typos with nlpaug KeyboardAug and RandomCharAug using a fixed seed (one and two edits per query); paraphrase and translate (Spanish, German, Chinese) with a cached LLM call that returns JSON. Write shifted_dev.jsonl and shifted_test.jsonl {qid, family, variant_text}. Tests: same seed gives identical typos, every qid present per family, cache hit makes no call.
verify: Hand-check 30 variants per family; drop and count those whose meaning changed
Record a sha256 of shifted_test.jsonl and the LLM model name; never regenerate after tuning starts
Note which LLM made paraphrases and translations so recovery can use a different one

steps.title: Build and tune the baseline on 10 queries
steps.learn: Recreate the failure mode: a hybrid English retriever whose knobs were tuned on 10 queries. BM25 depends on exact tokens, so typos and translations remove matches; an English-only embedding model tolerates paraphrase better but is not built for non-English queries.

decision.choice: rank_bm25 BM25Okapi plus bge-small-en-v1.5, fused with RRF; tune BM25 k1, b and fusion weight on the 10 train queries
decision.why: 5,183 abstracts fit in memory, so exact search removes ANN error as a variable. Tuning on exactly 10 queries reproduces the overfitting the project is about. Its model card lists a query instruction for retrieval; get that right before blaming shifts.

alternatives.name: BM25 only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fully interpretable, but one signal makes the shifts less interesting to recover.

alternatives.name: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as the dense leg
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller and widely used, with no query prefix to manage; usually lower retrieval quality.

steps.delegate: Python. retriever.py: BM25Okapi over tokenized title plus text (k1, b as params); bge-small-en-v1.5 via sentence-transformers with the model card's query instruction, normalized embeddings, exact cosine in NumPy; weighted RRF. tune.py: grid search on the 10 train queries only, saving the chosen config to JSON. Tests: RRF toy example, deterministic ties, tune.py refuses test qids.
verify: Report NDCG@10 of the tuned config on the 10 tuning queries and on the dev originals
Compare against default BM25 parameters on the dev originals to see whether tuning on 10 queries helped or hurt

steps.title: Build the paired robustness harness
steps.learn: The fair comparison is per query: the same qid's NDCG@10 on its original vs on each variant. A mean drop can hide a few total failures, so also report the share of queries that lose more than half their NDCG. Relative drop lets you compare families with different baselines.

decision.choice: Paired per-query NDCG@10 deltas per family, ranx for metrics, a paired significance test across variants
decision.why: Variants inherit qrels from the same qid, so pairing removes query difficulty from the comparison. With 300 queries a paired test is meaningful and keeps you from chasing noise.

alternatives.name: Only aggregate NDCG per family
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler table, but cannot tell many small losses from a few collapses.

alternatives.name: Wilcoxon signed-rank in scipy
alternatives.tradeoff: Non-parametric paired test on deltas; a good cross-check if NDCG deltas are far from normal.

steps.delegate: Python. harness.py: for a config and a family, run retrieval for originals and variants, build ranx Run objects keyed by qid, compute ndcg@10, per-query deltas and the share with delta below -50% of the original. Use ranx compare with stat_test='fisher'. Output Markdown plus per-query JSON. Tests: identical runs give zero deltas, a hand-computed NDCG on a toy qrel.
verify: Run the tuned baseline through all dev families and record the drop per family
Hand-inspect the 5 worst dev typo and 5 worst dev translation queries and explain each failure

steps.title: Recover from typos with corpus-aware spelling correction
steps.learn: Typos break BM25 exact matches and change the subword tokens a BERT-style encoder sees, which Zhuang and Zuccon showed hurts dense retrievers. A spelling corrector built from the corpus vocabulary fixes many typos without 'correcting' rare domain terms like gene names into common words.

decision.choice: symspellpy with a dictionary built from the SciFact corpus; correct only tokens not in the corpus vocabulary
decision.why: The corpus vocabulary is exactly what queries need to match, so it is the right dictionary. Leaving known tokens untouched limits damage to original queries, which must not regress.

alternatives.name: Typo-aware training (CharacterBERT, Self-Teaching)
alternatives.tradeoff: Makes the encoder itself robust; much stronger, but needs training data and GPU time.

alternatives.name: Character n-gram BM25
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches through misspellings without a corrector, at a cost of a bigger index and noisier matches.

steps.delegate: Python. spell.py: build a symspellpy SymSpell dictionary from corpus tokens with create_dictionary on a corpus text file; correct(query) uses lookup per out-of-vocabulary token (max edit distance as a param) and keeps in-vocabulary tokens. Tests: known typo of a corpus word is fixed, a rare in-corpus term is untouched, numbers pass through.
verify: Report dev typo-family NDCG@10 before and after correction
Confirm NDCG@10 on the dev originals does not drop after adding the corrector
List 3 corrections that went wrong and why

steps.title: Recover from paraphrases with multi-query retrieval
steps.learn: Paraphrases swap the original's key terms for synonyms, so BM25 loses matches while dense retrieval often holds. Generating a few rewrites and fusing their results raises the chance one rewrite uses the corpus's words. Use a different LLM from the one that made the paraphrases, or recovery can just undo its own edit.

decision.choice: LLM writes 3 rewrites per query; retrieve for each with the hybrid retriever and fuse all lists with RRF
decision.why: Fusion over several phrasings is robust to one bad rewrite, and it reuses the retriever and RRF you already have. Caching rewrites per query keeps evaluation reproducible.

alternatives.name: Shift the fusion weight toward dense
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and fast, but tuned on 10 queries it may overfit again and hurt keyword-heavy queries.

alternatives.name: HyDE (embed a hypothetical answer)
alternatives.tradeoff: Often helps short or vague queries; costs a generation per query and can drift on scientific claims.

steps.delegate: Python. multiquery.py: rewrite(query) returns 3 rewrites as JSON from a cached LLM call (model name in config, different from shifts.py's); search_multi(query) runs the hybrid retriever on the original plus rewrites and RRF-fuses them. Tests: cache hit makes no call, original query is always included, fusion of identical lists equals the single list.
verify: Report dev paraphrase-family NDCG@10 before and after, and on the dev originals
Record extra latency and LLM calls per query

steps.title: Recover non-English queries with a multilingual encoder
steps.learn: BM25 cannot match a Spanish query to English abstracts because no tokens overlap. A multilingual encoder maps queries and passages from different languages into one space. multilingual-e5 expects 'query: ' and 'passage: ' prefixes; leaving them off is an easy way to lose quality.

decision.choice: multilingual-e5-small as the dense leg for non-English queries, with BM25 dropped from fusion for them
decision.why: It needs no translation call at query time and covers many languages with one model. Dropping BM25 for non-English queries avoids fusing a list that is mostly noise.

alternatives.name: Translate to English, then search
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps the tuned English pipeline and BM25; adds an LLM or MT call per query and must not use the model that made the translations.

alternatives.name: bge-m3
alternatives.tradeoff: Multilingual with dense and sparse outputs in one model; larger and slower to embed the corpus.

steps.delegate: Python. ml_dense.py: embed the corpus with intfloat/multilingual-e5-small using the 'passage: ' prefix and queries with 'query: ', normalized, exact cosine; save embeddings with the model name. Expose search(query, k). Tests: prefix is applied exactly once, an English query on this index returns sensible top results, embeddings reload identically.
verify: Report dev translation-family NDCG@10 per language before and after
Run the dev English originals through this encoder alone and compare with the bge-small leg

steps.title: Route queries so fixes never hurt the originals
steps.learn: At query time you do not know the shift family, so one pipeline must serve every query. Detect language, correct out-of-vocabulary tokens, then decide whether to add rewrites. Every component must be shown not to hurt the originals, and its cost recorded, since rewrites add LLM calls to every query.

decision.choice: lingua-py language detection to pick the path, spell-correction always on, multi-query only for English
decision.why: Language ID is cheap and decides between two very different retrievers. Spell-correction touches only unknown tokens, so it is safe to leave on. Multi-query is the costly step, so you decide from measured gains whether it earns its latency.

alternatives.name: Run all paths and fuse everything
alternatives.tradeoff: No routing errors, but the most latency and cost, and noisy lists can dilute good ones.

alternatives.name: Multilingual encoder for all queries
alternatives.tradeoff: One path and no detector, but may give up English quality from the tuned bge leg.

steps.delegate: Python. pipeline.py: lingua LanguageDetectorBuilder.from_languages with Language.ENGLISH, SPANISH, GERMAN, CHINESE; non-English goes to ml_dense, English goes to spell.correct then hybrid or multiquery (flag). Record per-stage time and LLM call count. Tests: routing of fixture queries per language, flag toggles multi-query, short or mixed-language query falls back to the multilingual path.
verify: Report language-detection accuracy on the dev translation family and the dev originals
Report dev NDCG@10 per family for each ablation: corrector off, multi-query off, router off

steps.title: Measure it: drop, recovery and cost on the frozen set
steps.learn: Run baseline and final pipeline once on the frozen originals and every frozen family. Report NDCG@10, the drop vs originals, recovery as the share of lost NDCG regained, the share of collapsed queries, p50 and p95 latency and LLM calls per query. Any change after seeing these numbers must be reported as such.
steps.delegate: Python. report.py: load config JSON, verify the sha256 of test qrels and shifted_test.jsonl before running, run harness.py for baseline and final, compute recovery = (final minus baseline on shifted) / (original minus baseline on shifted), print a Markdown table and per-query JSON with ranx compare (stat_test='fisher'). Flag --split. Time queries with time.perf_counter after a warm-up.
verify: The table has originals plus each family, baseline vs final, with NDCG@10, drop and recovery
Confirm both hashes matched the ones recorded in steps 1 and 2
Record CPU, RAM, OS, Python, library and model versions and the exact command

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example tuning on 10 queries hurting test originals, or a fix that hurt clean queries); what this does not prove (synthetic shifts, one small scientific corpus, LLM-generated variants).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives drop and recovery per family with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise with a concrete query id
Part 4 lists assumptions: synthetic shifts, meaning-check drop rate, LLMs used, single corpus

projects.title: Distilled reranker
projects.problem: LLM rerankers are great but cost 50 to 100x more
projects.proveIt: % of LLM quality kept vs cost and latency saved
projects.question: How much of an LLM listwise reranker's NDCG@10 can a small cross-encoder trained on its rankings keep, and how much latency and cost does it save?

steps.title: Frame the question, the teacher, and the frozen test set
steps.learn: Teacher: an LLM listwise reranker. Student: a small cross-encoder trained to copy its order. Score both with human qrels from TREC DL 2019 (43 judged queries, dev) and DL 2020 (54, test), not the teacher. Report quality kept as (student minus BM25) over (teacher minus BM25), plus raw NDCG@10, latency and cost.
verify: Load msmarco-passage/trec-dl-2019/judged and trec-dl-2020/judged with ir_datasets and confirm 43 and 54 queries
Write the quality-kept formula and the latency and cost units in a README before any training
Freeze DL 2020 as test: record its file hashes and do not score anything on it until the Measure step

steps.title: Fix one BM25 candidate list for teacher and student
steps.learn: Distillation only compares fairly if teacher and student rerank the exact same candidates. Retrieve top 100 per query once, save it as a TREC run file, and reuse it everywhere. The first stage caps recall: a passage BM25 misses cannot be fixed by any reranker.

decision.choice: Pyserini BM25 on the prebuilt msmarco-v1-passage index, top 100, saved as a run file
decision.why: The prebuilt index and reproduction commands mean no indexing work, and BM25 is the standard first stage the LLM reranker papers report on, so your teacher numbers are comparable to published ones.

alternatives.name: Learned sparse or dense first stage
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher recall and higher ceiling for both rerankers, but more setup and the gain mixes first-stage and reranker effects.

alternatives.name: Rerank only top 20
alternatives.tradeoff: Much cheaper teacher runs, but the student is then only tested on a shallow list and the cost comparison is less realistic.

steps.delegate: Python. retrieve.py: use pyserini LuceneSearcher.from_prebuilt_index('msmarco-v1-passage') with BM25 (k1=0.9, b=0.4) to retrieve top 100 for a topics file; write a TREC run file. Support train query samples from ir_datasets msmarco-passage/train and DL 2019/2020 topics. Tests: run file format (6 columns), exactly 100 hits per query, deterministic output on rerun.
verify: Reproduce BM25 NDCG@10 on DL 2019 with pyserini.eval.trec_eval and compare it to the Pyserini 2CR page
Count DL 2019 queries where no passage of grade 2 or more appears in the top 100
Diff two runs of the script and confirm the run files are byte-identical

steps.title: Generate teacher rankings with an LLM listwise reranker
steps.learn: A listwise LLM reads a window of passages and outputs a permutation. A sliding window (RankGPT used window 20, step 10 over top 100) lets it rank more than fits in context. Output is an order, not scores, which shapes the loss you can use. Outputs can be malformed: missing or repeated ids.

decision.choice: RankZephyr 7B run locally through rank_llm with the vLLM backend, cached per query
decision.why: Open weights make the teacher reproducible and the cost measurable as GPU time on your machine. rank_llm already implements sliding windows and BM25 candidates for DL, so you can check your teacher NDCG against the paper first.

alternatives.name: Proprietary API teacher (RankGPT style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Possibly stronger and no GPU needed, but cost is per token, models change under you and runs are hard to reproduce.

alternatives.name: Large cross-encoder teacher with scores
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives real-valued scores for MarginMSE distillation, but it is not the LLM whose cost you are trying to avoid.

steps.delegate: Python. teacher.py: wrap rank_llm (ZephyrReranker, castorini/rank_zephyr_7b_v1_full) to rerank the saved BM25 top 100 for a list of query ids. Cache results in SQLite keyed by (query_id, candidate hash, model, prompt version). Log per query: wall time, prompt and output tokens, malformed outputs. Repair missing ids by appending them in BM25 order. Tests: cache hit skips the model, repair logic on a fake bad permutation.
verify: Reproduce teacher NDCG@10 on DL 2019 and compare to the RankZephyr paper's table, noting any gap
Report the % of windows with malformed permutations and confirm each was repaired
Record GPU model and teacher seconds per query on 20 queries

steps.title: Build the distillation set from MS MARCO train queries
steps.learn: The student learns from teacher orderings on training queries only. DL test queries were sampled from the MS MARCO eval set, not train, so train queries do not overlap them, but check anyway. More queries help until teacher cost dominates; RankGPT distilled from permutations on 10K MS MARCO train queries.

decision.choice: Sample a few thousand MS MARCO train queries, teacher-rank their BM25 top lists, hold out 5% as validation
decision.why: Train queries are plentiful and from the same distribution as DL, and a held-out slice of teacher-labeled queries lets you tune and early-stop without touching DL 2020.

alternatives.name: Use MS MARCO human labels only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and no teacher cost, but that is ordinary fine-tuning, not distillation, and it has one positive per query.

alternatives.name: Generate synthetic queries for your own corpus
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches a target domain, but query quality becomes a new variable to control.

steps.delegate: Python. build_train.py: sample N query ids (seeded) from ir_datasets msmarco-passage/train, assert none appear in DL 2019 or 2020 query ids or texts, run retrieve.py then teacher.py, and write a JSONL of {query, docs, teacher_rank}. Split 95/5 by query id. Tests: seed reproducibility, no query in both splits, overlap assertion fires on a planted DL query.
verify: Confirm zero overlap between training query ids and DL 2019 and 2020 query ids
Record N, teacher GPU hours spent and the validation split size
Inspect 5 teacher rankings by hand and note one you think is wrong

steps.title: Choose a loss that learns from rank order
steps.learn: A listwise teacher gives a permutation, not scores. Convert it to graded labels (for example higher for better ranks) and train with a pairwise or listwise ranking loss that only cares about order. MarginMSE needs teacher score margins, which this teacher does not output.

decision.choice: sentence-transformers LambdaLoss on per-query lists with labels derived from teacher rank
decision.why: LambdaLoss takes (query, [docs]) with a label per doc and weights pairs by their effect on NDCG, which matches the metric you report. RankNetLoss is the plain pairwise version and makes a good ablation, mirroring RankGPT's rank_net option.

alternatives.name: RankNetLoss (pairwise)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler and treats every swapped pair equally; useful baseline but ignores that top positions matter more for NDCG@10.

alternatives.name: Pointwise BCE on teacher top k as positive
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest data format, but it throws away order inside the top k and depends on an arbitrary k.

alternatives.name: MarginMSELoss
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong when the teacher has scores; here you would need a scoring teacher instead of a listwise one.

steps.delegate: Python, sentence-transformers. losses.py: function to_labels(teacher_rank, scheme) with schemes 'reciprocal' and 'topk_graded'; build a datasets.Dataset with columns query, docs, labels. Configure LambdaLoss (NDCGLoss2PPScheme default) and RankNetLoss for comparison. Tests: label monotonic in rank, padding of variable list lengths, loss decreases on a tiny overfit batch.
verify: Overfit 20 queries and confirm the student reproduces teacher order on them (Kendall tau near 1)
Plot the label scheme as label vs teacher rank and justify it in one sentence
Confirm the dataset has no query whose labels are all equal

steps.title: Pick the student model and its starting checkpoint
steps.learn: Student size sets latency and the ceiling on quality. Starting from a cross-encoder already trained on MS MARCO human labels gives a strong baseline, and the honest question becomes whether teacher distillation adds anything over that baseline.

decision.choice: Fine-tune cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L12-v2; keep the untouched checkpoint as a baseline
decision.why: It is small enough for CPU serving and already a sensible reranker, so you measure distillation gain directly as student minus baseline under identical inference cost.

alternatives.name: Start from microsoft/MiniLM-L12-H384-uncased
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleaner attribution since all ranking skill comes from the teacher, but the student starts much weaker and needs more teacher labels.

alternatives.name: microsoft/deberta-v3-base (RankGPT's choice)
alternatives.tradeoff: Likely keeps more quality, but costs more per pair and is harder to serve on CPU.

alternatives.name: ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster still, with a lower quality ceiling; good second point on the cost curve.

steps.delegate: Python. train.py with CrossEncoderTrainer: load the chosen checkpoint, train on the distillation set with the chosen loss, evaluate every N steps on the validation slice (NDCG@10 against teacher-derived labels and Kendall tau vs teacher), keep the best checkpoint, log config and seed. Tests: one-step smoke run, checkpoint reload gives identical scores.
verify: Record baseline and student NDCG@10 on DL 2019 only (not 2020)
Report validation Kendall tau vs teacher for baseline and student
Confirm training config, seed and data hash are saved with the checkpoint

steps.title: Set rerank depth and max sequence length on DL 2019
steps.learn: Cross-encoder cost is roughly linear in the number of (query, passage) pairs and grows with token length. Reranking 100 versus 50 candidates and truncating long passages are the main latency knobs. Tune them on DL 2019 only, then lock them.

decision.choice: Sweep depth {20, 50, 100} and max length on DL 2019, pick the cheapest within a small NDCG margin
decision.why: The project's claim is quality per unit cost, so these knobs belong in the design, chosen on dev data so the test number stays clean.

alternatives.name: Always rerank 100 at full length
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and highest recall for the student, but you may pay latency for no measurable gain.

alternatives.name: Adaptive depth per query
alternatives.tradeoff: Can save more, but adds a routing model and its own failure modes.

steps.delegate: Python. sweep.py: for each depth and max_length (set on the CrossEncoder), rerank DL 2019 BM25 runs, compute NDCG@10 with ranx and median latency per query at a fixed batch size. Output a CSV and a plot of NDCG vs latency. Tests: depth=0 returns BM25 order, truncation actually changes token counts.
verify: Plot NDCG@10 vs median latency for every setting on DL 2019
Write down the locked depth and max length before touching DL 2020
Confirm passages above max length exist in the data (count them)

steps.title: Speed up student inference without losing ranking quality
steps.learn: Export and quantization change the arithmetic, so they can change rankings. sentence-transformers can load a CrossEncoder with an ONNX or OpenVINO backend and export a dynamically int8 quantized ONNX model. Treat each as a new model and re-check NDCG.

decision.choice: ONNX backend with dynamic int8 quantization for CPU, keep fp32 PyTorch as reference
decision.why: The cost argument is strongest if the student runs on CPU next to the search service. The library supports this export path directly, so it is little extra code.

alternatives.name: Plain PyTorch on GPU
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and no export risk, but needs a GPU, which weakens the cost-saving claim.

alternatives.name: OpenVINO backend
alternatives.tradeoff: Similar CPU gains on Intel hardware; less useful on ARM machines.

steps.delegate: Python. export.py: load the student with CrossEncoder(path, backend='onnx'), call export_dynamic_quantized_onnx_model with a config matching the CPU, save it. compare.py: score DL 2019 with fp32 and int8, report NDCG@10, per-query score correlation and latency. Tests: exported model loads and returns one score per pair; int8 and fp32 top-1 agree on a fixture.
verify: Report NDCG@10 for fp32 and int8 on DL 2019 and the difference
Record CPU model and quantization config used
Check that int8 changes the top 10 for fewer than a stated share of queries

steps.title: Serve the reranker with a timeout and BM25 fallback
steps.learn: In production the reranker is one stage with a latency budget. If it is slow or fails, returning the first-stage order is better than an error. Batching pairs per request matters more than micro-optimizing the model.

decision.choice: Per-request deadline; on timeout or error return BM25 order and log a fallback flag
decision.why: It keeps worst-case latency bounded and makes failures visible in metrics, which you need when comparing a cheap student against a slow LLM path.

alternatives.name: Route uncertain queries to the LLM teacher
alternatives.tradeoff: Could recover quality on hard queries, but adds the expensive path back and needs a confidence signal you must validate.

alternatives.name: No fallback, fail the request
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but one slow call breaks the page.

steps.delegate: Python, FastAPI. server.py: POST /rerank {query, candidates[]} scores all pairs in one batch with the ONNX student via asyncio.to_thread inside asyncio.wait_for with a configurable deadline; on timeout return input order with fallback=true. Count fallbacks in a metrics endpoint. Tests: forced slow model triggers fallback, normal path returns sorted ids, empty candidate list.
verify: Force a timeout and confirm the response is BM25 order with fallback=true
Run 200 DL 2019 queries and report the fallback rate at your chosen deadline
Confirm results from the server match offline scoring for 5 queries

steps.title: Measure it: quality kept vs latency and cost saved
steps.learn: Now unfreeze DL 2020. Compare BM25, baseline cross-encoder, student fp32, student int8 and the teacher on both DL sets with human qrels. Latency: warm up, fix batch size, synchronize the GPU before timing, report p50 and p99 per query. Cost: GPU or CPU seconds per 1,000 queries times a stated hourly price.
steps.delegate: Python. bench.py: for each system, rerank DL 2019 and 2020, compute NDCG@10 with ranx and run ranx compare (paired t-test) against the teacher and baseline. Time each query after warmup with time.perf_counter, call torch.cuda.synchronize for GPU systems, record p50/p99 and total seconds. Output one Markdown table plus per-query JSON. CLI --system --split.
verify: Report NDCG@10, quality kept %, p50, p99 and cost per 1,000 queries for all 5 systems on DL 2020
Recompute NDCG@10 for two systems with pyserini.eval.trec_eval -c -m ndcg_cut.10 and confirm they match ranx
Record machine, CPU, GPU, library versions and the exact command for every row

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: Write the 4-part write-up: the one question, numbers for every claim with machine and command, why surprising results happened (for example where the student beat the teacher or where int8 hurt), and what this does not prove (one domain, a small test set, models possibly trained on MS MARCO).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives NDCG, quality kept, latency and cost with machine and command for each system
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a concrete query
Part 4 lists assumptions, including test size (54 queries) and possible training-data overlap

projects.title: Calibrated LLM relevance judge
projects.problem: LLM judges have position and length bias
projects.proveIt: Agreement with human labels, bias measured and reduced
projects.question: Can an LLM relevance judge agree with TREC human labels while its position and length biases are measured and reduced?

steps.title: Frame the question, human labels and frozen test split
steps.learn: Ground truth is NIST human qrels on TREC DL passages, graded 0 (irrelevant) to 3 (perfectly relevant). Use DL 2019 as dev and DL 2020 as test. Success: agreement with humans (kappa, and system-ranking correlation) goes up while measured position and length bias goes down.
verify: Load both judged qrels with ir_datasets and print counts per grade for each year
Sample a stratified pool of query-passage pairs per grade from each year, save it, and record hashes
Freeze the DL 2020 pool: no prompt or calibration work may look at it until Measure

steps.title: Define agreement and bias metrics before judging
steps.learn: Label agreement and evaluation usefulness differ. Measure pair-level agreement with Cohen's kappa (binary at grade 2 or more, as TREC binary metrics use, and weighted on 0 to 3), and system-level agreement as Kendall tau between system rankings scored with human vs judge qrels.

decision.choice: Report binary kappa, quadratic-weighted kappa and Kendall tau of system rankings
decision.why: Kappa corrects for chance agreement, which matters because most judged DL pairs are irrelevant. System tau answers whether the judge picks the same winners, which is what judges are used for.

alternatives.name: Raw accuracy
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to read, but inflated by the large irrelevant class.

alternatives.name: Only system-level tau
alternatives.tradeoff: The practical question, but hides systematic label errors that cancel out across systems.

steps.delegate: Python. metrics.py: kappa(human, judge, binary_threshold=2, weights=None|'quadratic') via sklearn cohen_kappa_score; system_tau(runs, qrels_a, qrels_b, metric='ndcg@10') via ranx evaluate and scipy.stats.kendalltau; bootstrap CIs over queries. Tests: identical labels give kappa 1, a hand-computed 2x2 case, tau 1 for identical qrels.
verify: Unit tests pass, including the hand-computed kappa case
Write the metric definitions and the binary threshold in the README before any judging
Confirm the bootstrap resamples queries, not individual pairs

steps.title: Build a few runs whose ranking the judge must recover
steps.learn: System-level agreement needs systems of different quality. Build them yourself so you control what is retrieved, then have the judge label the passages they return that humans also judged. Pairs humans never judged cannot be scored against humans.

decision.choice: 4 to 6 runs: BM25, BM25 with RM3, and BM25 reranked by different MiniLM cross-encoders
decision.why: All are reproducible from Pyserini and sentence-transformers and span a clear quality range, so a good judge should order them as the human qrels do.

alternatives.name: Official TREC submitted runs
alternatives.tradeoff: More varied and realistic, but access and licensing take effort and you have no control over them.

alternatives.name: Only pair-level agreement
alternatives.tradeoff: Skips this work, but you lose the system-ranking question.

steps.delegate: Python. runs.py: produce TREC run files for DL 2019 and 2020 with pyserini BM25 (k1=0.9,b=0.4), BM25+RM3, and BM25 top 100 reranked by cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 and L12-v2. Report NDCG@10 per run with human qrels and the fraction of top-10 passages that are human-judged. Tests: run file format, deterministic reruns.
verify: Report NDCG@10 per run on DL 2019 with human qrels and confirm the runs differ
Report the % of each run's top 10 that has a human label
Match BM25 NDCG@10 against the Pyserini 2CR page

steps.title: Write the pointwise grading prompt and structured output
steps.learn: Thomas et al. (Bing) showed prompt wording changes label accuracy, even simple paraphrases. UMBRELA reproduces their approach with a 0 to 3 scale aligned to TREC grades. Grade one passage per call first so no position effect exists, and force a parseable integer output.

decision.choice: Start from the UMBRELA prompt, one passage per call, JSON output {grade: 0-3}, temperature 0
decision.why: It is an open, published baseline on these exact datasets, so your first numbers can be compared with UMBRELA's reports, and one passage per call isolates the model's judgment before you add batching.

alternatives.name: Batch many passages per call
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper per label, but introduces position effects you then must measure.

alternatives.name: Pairwise preference prompts
alternatives.tradeoff: Natural for comparisons, but scales quadratically and does not give graded qrels directly.

steps.delegate: Python. judge.py: grade(query, passage) returning an int, using a prompt template file and structured output (OpenAI JSON schema or vLLM structured outputs for an open model). Retries on invalid output, then record 'invalid' rather than guessing. Log model id, prompt hash, tokens. Tests: parser accepts only 0-3, invalid path, template renders with special characters.
verify: Run the judge on 200 DL 2019 pool pairs and report binary and weighted kappa
Report the invalid-output rate
Read 10 disagreements with humans and categorize the cause

links.label: Thomas et al., Bing LLM labels

steps.title: Cache judgments and make runs reproducible
steps.learn: Every later step reruns the judge on variants (swapped orders, padded passages). Without a cache, cost explodes and repeated calls can return different labels. Key cache entries on everything that can change the output.

decision.choice: SQLite cache keyed by (model, prompt hash, query id, passage text hash, variant), async calls with a concurrency cap
decision.why: Hashing the passage text, not just its id, means perturbed passages get their own entries, and a single file makes runs repeatable and shareable.

alternatives.name: Provider batch APIs
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper for large offline jobs, but slower turnaround while iterating on prompts.

alternatives.name: No cache, rely on temperature 0
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but temperature 0 may still vary between calls and you pay for every rerun.

steps.delegate: Python asyncio. cache.py with get/put over sqlite3; judge_many(pairs, variant) runs with an asyncio.Semaphore, exponential backoff on rate limits, and writes token counts. Tests: second run makes zero model calls, different variant misses cache, backoff retried on a fake 429.
verify: Rerun the 200-pair job and confirm zero new model calls
Report total tokens and cost for the job
Repeat 50 uncached calls twice and report how often the label changes

steps.title: Measure position bias with swapped and shuffled orders
steps.learn: Position bias appears when a prompt contains several passages. Zheng et al. measured it by swapping the order of two answers and checking consistency. Test two settings: pairwise preference on pairs humans graded differently, and multi-passage grading where the same passage moves between slots.

decision.choice: Judge every pair in both orders; measure consistency and first-slot win rate; grade batches under 3 shuffles
decision.why: Swapping is the direct test from the literature, and shuffles show how much a grade depends on slot rather than content, which is the bias you must report.

alternatives.name: Only random order
alternatives.tradeoff: Bias averages out at scale, but you cannot report how large it is.

alternatives.name: Skip multi-passage prompts
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids the bias entirely, at the cost of one call per passage.

steps.delegate: Python. position.py: for DL 2019 pairs with different human grades, ask the judge which passage is more relevant in order AB and BA; compute consistency, first-slot preference rate and agreement with the human order. For batched grading, grade 5-passage lists under 3 seeded shuffles and compute grade variance by slot. Tests: a fake judge that always picks A gives 0% consistency.
verify: Report consistency and first-slot preference rate on DL 2019 pairs
Report the mean grade by slot in batched grading with a CI
Confirm the fake always-first judge is flagged by your metric

steps.title: Measure length bias with controlled padding
steps.learn: Longer passages may get higher grades even at the same human grade. Measure it two ways: correlation of judge grade with passage length within each human grade, and a controlled test that pads a passage with off-topic text from another query and checks whether the grade rises.

decision.choice: Within-grade regression plus a padding perturbation test on the same pairs
decision.why: Observational correlation alone is confounded (longer passages may truly contain more answers); the perturbation adds length while holding relevant content fixed, so a grade change is attributable to length.

alternatives.name: Correlation only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but cannot separate length bias from real content differences.

alternatives.name: Paraphrase to longer text with an LLM
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to Zheng et al.'s verbosity attack, but the rewriter may change meaning.

steps.delegate: Python. length.py: for DL 2019 pool pairs, fit grade ~ human_grade + log(length) (statsmodels OLS) and report the length coefficient with CI. Padding test: append 1 and 2 off-topic passages from a different query, rejudge (cached by variant), report mean grade change for grade 0 and grade 3 pairs. Tests: padding never includes text from the same query.
verify: Report the length coefficient and its CI within human grade
Report mean grade change after padding for human grade 0 pairs
Spot-check 5 padded passages to confirm the padding is truly off-topic

steps.title: Reduce the measured biases
steps.learn: Fixes must target what you measured. For position, aggregate over orders (Wang et al.'s balanced position calibration) or avoid multi-passage prompts. For length, tell the judge length is not evidence and grade only the answer-bearing content, then re-run the same bias tests.

decision.choice: Both-order aggregation for pairwise and batched prompts, plus an explicit length instruction in the prompt
decision.why: Order aggregation removes slot effects by construction at a known cost multiplier, and the prompt change is cheap to test with the padding experiment you already built.

alternatives.name: Pointwise only, one passage per call
alternatives.tradeoff: No position effect at all, but more calls and still exposed to length bias.

alternatives.name: Ensemble of several judge models
alternatives.tradeoff: Can cancel model-specific biases, but multiplies cost and adds disagreement handling.

steps.delegate: Python. Add variants to judge.py: 'swap_avg' (judge both orders, average or tie on conflict) and 'length_instr' (prompt v2). Rerun position.py and length.py for each variant on DL 2019 and output a before/after table with kappa. Tests: swap_avg is order invariant on a fake judge, prompt v2 hash differs and is cached separately.
verify: Report position consistency and the length coefficient before and after on DL 2019
Confirm kappa on DL 2019 did not drop by more than its CI after mitigation
Record the extra cost multiplier for each mitigation

steps.title: Calibrate judge outputs to human grades on dev data
steps.learn: Calibration maps the judge's raw output to the human scale. If the model exposes token log probabilities, an expected grade over 0 to 3 gives a continuous score; fit thresholds or isotonic regression on DL 2019 only, then apply unchanged to DL 2020.

decision.choice: Expected grade from top logprobs, then isotonic regression to human grade fit on DL 2019
decision.why: A continuous score lets the mapping fix systematic over- or under-grading, and isotonic regression only assumes monotonicity, which suits ordinal grades.

alternatives.name: Raw argmax grade
alternatives.tradeoff: No fitting and no leakage risk, but systematic offsets stay.

alternatives.name: Threshold tuning on the argmax
alternatives.tradeoff: Works when logprobs are unavailable, but coarser.

alternatives.name: Average of several samples
alternatives.tradeoff: Works with any API, but multiplies cost.

steps.delegate: Python. calibrate.py: request logprobs with top_logprobs for the grade token, compute expected grade, fit sklearn IsotonicRegression(out_of_bounds='clip') on DL 2019 human grades, round to 0-3. Save the fitted model. Plot reliability for binary relevance with sklearn calibration_curve. Tests: fit refuses DL 2020 ids, monotonic output, missing logprobs falls back to argmax.
verify: Plot the reliability curve on DL 2019 before and after calibration
Assert in code that no DL 2020 pair was used to fit
Report DL 2019 kappa before and after calibration

steps.title: Measure it: agreement and bias on the frozen DL 2020 set
steps.learn: Now open DL 2020. Score each variant (baseline prompt, mitigated, mitigated plus calibrated) against human qrels only: binary and weighted kappa, system tau, position consistency, length coefficient. Bootstrap over queries. Note the judge never grades itself: humans are the reference.
