steps.delegate: Python. eval.py --split test: load frozen pool, run each variant from cache, compute all metrics with bootstrap CIs over queries, write a Markdown table and per-query JSON. Include the system ranking under human vs judge qrels. Record model id, date, prompt hash and command.
verify: Report all metrics with CIs for each variant on DL 2020 in one table
Show system rankings under human and judge qrels side by side
Record model id, date, cost and the exact command

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: Write the 4-part write-up: the one question, numbers for every claim with machine and command, why surprising results happened (for example a mitigation that cut bias but also cut kappa), and what this does not prove (one domain, short passages, one judge model version, NIST assessors are not end users).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives kappa, tau and bias numbers with CIs, model id and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with an example pair
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including passage length range and model version

projects.title: Unbiased learning-to-rank from clicks
projects.problem: Users click top results because they're on top, not because they're best
projects.proveIt: Ranking quality on simulated clicks with vs without bias correction
projects.question: If clicks favor the top slots, does correcting for position bias train a ranker that beats one trained on raw clicks, judged by true relevance labels?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the frozen test fold
steps.learn: Clicks are biased because users examine top results more. The prove-it: NDCG@10 on human relevance labels, for rankers trained on simulated clicks with vs without bias correction. Data: MSLR-WEB10K fold 1 (10,000 queries, 136 features per query-document pair, graded labels).
verify: Load mslr_web/10k_fold1 and record the train, validation and test query counts and the label distribution yourself
Freeze the test split now: write its query ids to a file and never read its labels until the measure step
Write the one-sentence question and the exact metric (NDCG@10 on test labels, not on clicks) at the top of your notes

steps.title: Train the weak production ranker that shows results
steps.learn: Simulated clicks need a ranking that users 'saw'. Joachims et al. trained this production ranker on 1 percent of the labeled training data, so it is decent but imperfect. Its mistakes are what position bias hides: relevant documents shown low get few clicks.

decision.choice: LightGBM lambdarank trained on a fixed 1 percent sample of training queries, saved and never retrained
decision.why: It mirrors the published setup, is fast, and leaves real room for improvement. Freezing it means every method sees the exact same displayed rankings, so differences come only from how clicks are used.

alternatives.name: Random display order
alternatives.tradeoff: Removes the link between rank and relevance, which makes bias trivial to fix and the experiment unrealistic.

alternatives.name: Ranker trained on all labels
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows near-ideal rankings, so clicks add little and debiasing has almost nothing to recover.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, lightgbm, numpy. Write logging_ranker.py: load MSLR-WEB10K fold 1 train, sample 1% of query ids with a fixed seed, train LGBMRanker(objective='lambdarank') with group sizes, save the model and the sampled ids. Function display(qid) returns the top-10 doc indices for any query. Tests: group sizes sum to row count, the same seed gives the same sample, display order is deterministic.
verify: Report the logging ranker's validation NDCG@10 and also train the same LGBMRanker on all train queries; the 1% ranker should be clearly lower
Confirm the 1% sample ids are saved and reused on a second run

steps.title: Simulate position-biased, noisy clicks
steps.learn: Under a position-based model a click needs examination and perceived relevance. Joachims et al. set examination at rank r to (1/r)^eta and added noise: irrelevant results still get clicked with small probability. eta controls bias severity; eta = 0 means no position bias.

decision.choice: Position-based model on the top 10: examination (1/r)^eta, binarized relevance, click noise on irrelevant docs
decision.why: It is the model the IPS estimator assumes, so it tests the method cleanly first. Exposing eta and the noise rate lets you vary severity later instead of hard-coding one world.

alternatives.name: Cascade click model
alternatives.tradeoff: Users scan down and stop after a click; more realistic for some search pages, but IPS under a position-based model is then misspecified.

alternatives.name: ULTRA's built-in click models
alternatives.tradeoff: Ready-made and documented, but you learn less about what each parameter does and inherit its data format.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. clicks.py: simulate(sessions, eta, eps_neg, eps_pos, seed) draws queries from a split, gets the logging ranker's top 10, binarizes labels at a threshold you pass in, and samples examination ~ Bernoulli((1/rank)^eta) and click given examination. Write clicks as (qid, doc, rank, clicked) rows to Parquet. Tests: eta=0 gives flat CTR by rank, eps_neg=0 gives no clicks on irrelevant docs, fixed seed reproduces output.
verify: Plot CTR by rank for eta=1 and eta=0 and confirm the shapes differ as expected
Measure the share of clicks on irrelevant documents and compare to what your noise rate predicts

steps.title: Build the naive click ranker and the full-label skyline
steps.learn: Two reference points bound the result. Naive: treat every click as relevant and every non-click as not, ignoring position. Skyline: train on the true labels with no noise. Debiasing should move from naive toward skyline; the gap tells you how much there was to recover.

decision.choice: One PyTorch scorer (MLP on the 136 features) with a listwise softmax loss, shared by every click-trained method
decision.why: If naive and debiased runs use the same model and loss, the only difference is the weighting of clicks, so the comparison is fair. A small MLP trains quickly on a laptop.

alternatives.name: Different model per method
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets each method use its best model, but you cannot tell if gains come from debiasing or the model.

alternatives.name: Linear scorer
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to inspect and closer to Propensity SVM-Rank, but may cap the skyline lower.

steps.delegate: Python, PyTorch. ranker.py: MLP(136, hidden=64) scoring docs; loss = softmax cross-entropy over the displayed list with per-click weights (default 1). train(clicks, weights_fn, seed). Also train_skyline(labels) on true labels of all train queries. Standardize features with train-split statistics only. Tests: weights of 1 match an unweighted loss, a list with no clicks contributes zero loss, a forward pass is deterministic with a seed.
verify: Report validation NDCG@10 for naive and skyline; the skyline should be higher
Confirm feature standardization statistics come from the train split only

steps.title: Estimate examination propensities with a swap experiment
steps.learn: IPS needs the probability each rank was examined. Joachims et al. swap the result at rank k with rank r in a small randomized slice; CTR after the swap is proportional to the examination probability of the new rank. Only relative propensities are needed.

decision.choice: Swap intervention on a small slice of simulated sessions, propensities relative to rank 1, smoothed across ranks
decision.why: It needs only cheap randomization, matches the paper, and in simulation you can compare the estimate to the true (1/r)^eta curve to see estimation error.

alternatives.name: Oracle propensities
alternatives.tradeoff: Use the true curve; gives the best case for IPS but hides the estimation error a real system has.

alternatives.name: Regression EM (Wang et al.)
alternatives.tradeoff: Estimates bias from ordinary clicks with no randomization, at the cost of a more complex fitting loop.

alternatives.name: Dual Learning Algorithm
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns propensity and ranker jointly with no preprocessing, but is harder to debug and verify.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. propensity.py: run_swap_sessions(n, k=1, seed) uses clicks.simulate with rank k swapped to a random rank r in 2..10; estimate p_r = CTR(at r after swap) / CTR(at k without swap), then normalize p_1=1. Return per-rank estimates with bootstrap confidence intervals. Tests: with eta=0 all estimates are near 1; more sessions shrink the interval.
verify: Plot estimated vs true propensity for ranks 1 to 10 at two session counts
Record how many swap sessions you needed before every rank's interval was acceptably narrow

steps.title: Train the inverse-propensity-weighted ranker
steps.learn: IPW divides each click's loss by the propensity of the rank it was clicked at, so a click at rank 8 counts more than one at rank 1. This removes position bias in expectation, but small propensities make high-variance weights; Joachims et al. compare with and without clipping.

decision.choice: Shared PyTorch ranker, click weight 1/p_rank from estimated propensities, clipped at a floor tuned on validation
decision.why: Reusing the naive model isolates the effect of the weights. Clipping trades a little bias for lower variance, which matters when clicks are few.

alternatives.name: No clipping
alternatives.tradeoff: Unbiased in expectation, but a few deep-rank clicks can dominate training and make results noisy across seeds.

alternatives.name: LightGBM with per-row weights
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast trees, but LightGBM multiplies each row's lambdarank gradient by its weight, which is not the same as the pairwise IPS estimator.

steps.delegate: Python, PyTorch. In ipw.py, weights_fn(rank) = 1 / max(p_hat[rank], floor). Train with ranker.train for floor in a small grid. Model selection must use an IPS-weighted click metric on validation clicks, not validation labels. Tests: floor=1 reproduces the naive ranker, weights are finite, and the IPS validation metric on simulated clicks with oracle propensities tracks true NDCG on a toy example.
verify: Compare validation NDCG@10 (labels, for your notes only) of naive vs IPW at eta=1
Check that model selection used only clicks, by confirming the selection script never loads validation labels

steps.title: Add LightGBM's position-aware lambdarank as a second method
steps.learn: LightGBM (4.1.0 and later) accepts a position array on the Dataset and fits score = f(x) + g(position), returning only f(x) for ranking. lambdarank_position_bias_regularization shrinks the learned position factors. This learns bias jointly instead of estimating it first.

decision.choice: LGBMRanker on click labels with position passed to the Dataset, regularization tuned on validation clicks
decision.why: It is a production-grade library feature, needs no separate propensity experiment, and gives a tree-based comparison point next to the IPW neural ranker.

alternatives.name: Position as an ordinary feature
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but the model can mix position into relevance and you must pick a constant position at inference.

alternatives.name: DLA via ULTRA
alternatives.tradeoff: A published joint method, but requires adopting ULTRA's data pipeline.

steps.delegate: Python, lightgbm>=4.1. lgb_position.py: build lgb.Dataset(X, label=clicked, group=sizes, position=rank-1) from the click log and train objective='lambdarank' for lambdarank_position_bias_regularization in a small grid. Predict with features only. Tests: training fails clearly if position length differs from rows, and the model with shuffled positions does not beat the one with real positions on validation clicks.
verify: Confirm your installed LightGBM version is 4.1.0 or later before trusting the position argument
Record validation click metric for each regularization value and the one you picked

steps.title: Stress the correction: bias severity, noise and wrong propensities
steps.learn: A correction that only works when its assumptions are exact is fragile. Vary eta, the click noise rate, and deliberately misspecify the propensities (wrong eta in the weights) to see where IPW stops helping. Joachims et al. report robustness to noise and misspecification; check it yourself.

decision.choice: A small grid: eta in a few values, two noise rates, propensities from the true eta, a wrong eta, and the swap estimate
decision.why: A grid covers the questions a reviewer will ask while staying cheap. Fixing seeds and click counts across cells makes each cell comparable.

alternatives.name: Only the default setting
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but one setting cannot show whether the gain survives realistic mismatch.

alternatives.name: Switch the simulator to a cascade model
alternatives.tradeoff: Tests a different user model, which is a bigger and slower change; do it after the grid.

steps.delegate: Python. sweep.py runs naive, IPW (estimated, oracle, misspecified) and LightGBM-position for each grid cell with 3 seeds, writing one CSV row per run with eta, noise, method, seed, n_clicks and validation metrics. Resume from the CSV if interrupted. Tests: rerunning a finished cell is skipped, and each row records the git commit.
verify: Check every grid cell has all methods and seeds in the CSV
Find the eta value where IPW and naive are closest and note it

steps.title: Measure it on the frozen test fold
steps.learn: Now open the test labels once. Report NDCG@10 for the logging ranker, naive, IPW (estimated and oracle propensities), LightGBM-position and the skyline, across seeds and click counts. Use per-query paired tests, and keep hyperparameters fixed from validation.
verify: Report mean and spread of test NDCG@10 over at least 3 seeds for every method
Run a paired test (for example Wilcoxon) on per-query NDCG@10 of IPW vs naive and report the p-value
Plot test NDCG@10 vs number of training clicks for naive and IPW
Record the machine, library versions and the exact command that produced each number

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example, where IPW lost to naive); and assumptions. Key limit: simulated clicks follow your model, and on real Baidu-ULTR data, better click prediction did not reliably mean better ranking.
verify: Part 1 states the one question and the metric in a sentence
Part 2 gives a number with machine and command for every claim, including the naive vs IPW test result
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result using the robustness grid
Part 4 lists assumptions (position-based model, simulated users, MSLR features) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Query-aware hybrid fusion
projects.problem: BM25 wins on exact names and IDs, dense wins on meaning; one fixed weight is wrong
projects.proveIt: NDCG by query type vs fixed-weight fusion
projects.question: Does choosing the BM25 vs dense fusion weight per query beat one fixed weight on NDCG@10 for each query type?

steps.title: Frame the question, datasets and frozen test queries
steps.learn: BM25 rewards exact token overlap (names, codes); dense embeddings reward meaning. Prove-it: NDCG@10 per query type, query-aware fusion vs the best fixed-weight fusion. Data: BEIR SciFact, NFCorpus and FiQA-2018, which ship train and test splits with relevance judgments.
verify: Download the three datasets with the BEIR loader and record corpus size and query count per split yourself
Freeze the test splits: tune every weight and model on train (and dev) queries only
Write the question and the metric (NDCG@10 from the official qrels) at the top of your notes

steps.title: Define query types with a frozen tagger
steps.learn: 'By query type' needs a fixed definition before any tuning, or you can redraw the groups until your method wins. Useful types here: contains an identifier or number (gene names, tickers, codes), short keyword query, and long natural-language question or claim.

decision.choice: Deterministic rules (regex for digits and mixed-case codes, token count, question words), frozen and versioned
decision.why: Rules are transparent, cheap and reproducible, and the types are defined independently of retrieval scores so they cannot be tuned toward a result.

alternatives.name: LLM classifier
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles subtle cases better, but adds cost and nondeterminism, and you must pin the model and prompt.

alternatives.name: Cluster query embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds natural groups, but the groups are hard to name and may not match 'names vs meaning'.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. query_types.py: tag(query:str) returns one of {identifier, keyword, natural}; precedence identifier > keyword > natural. Store the rule version string with every output. Tests: 15 fixture queries covering each type, including hyphenated codes and numbers inside sentences.
verify: Hand-label 50 train queries and report agreement with the tagger
Report how many test queries fall into each type; flag any type with too few queries to trust a per-type NDCG

steps.title: Build the BM25 retriever
steps.learn: BM25 scores depend on how text is tokenized. Stemming and stopword removal help topical queries, but a tokenizer that splits or lowercases codes can break the exact-match cases this project relies on. Retrieve the top 100 per query so fusion has candidates.

decision.choice: bm25s in Python with an English stemmer, top 100 per query, index saved to disk
decision.why: Pure Python, fast for corpora of this size, and easy to inspect tokenization. Keeping everything in one process simplifies the experiment.

alternatives.name: Pyserini (Lucene)
alternatives.tradeoff: A widely used reference implementation, but needs Java and its analyzer differs from yours.

alternatives.name: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch
alternatives.tradeoff: Production-like, but a server to run and more knobs to control for a research harness.

steps.delegate: Python, bm25s, PyStemmer. bm25_run.py: index each BEIR corpus (title + text), retrieve top 100 for all queries, write TREC-style runs {qid: {docid: score}}. Tests: an exact-title query returns that doc at rank 1, the index reloads with identical results, and a query with no matching tokens returns an empty list without crashing.
verify: Compute BM25 NDCG@10 on train queries for each dataset and record it
Tokenize 10 identifier-type queries and check that codes survive as you expect

steps.title: Build the dense retriever
steps.learn: Dense retrieval embeds queries and documents into one space. bge-small-en-v1.5 expects queries prefixed with an instruction ('Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ') and documents without it. These corpora are small enough for exact search.

decision.choice: BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 via sentence-transformers, normalized vectors, FAISS IndexFlatIP exact top 100
decision.why: A small model runs on a laptop, and exact search removes ANN recall loss as a confounder when you compare fusion methods.

alternatives.name: all-MiniLM-L6-v2
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller and faster, no query prefix, but usually weaker on retrieval, which shifts the best fusion weight.

alternatives.name: HNSW index
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed at large scale, but adds approximate-recall error that muddies the fusion comparison here.

steps.delegate: Python, sentence-transformers, faiss-cpu. dense_run.py: encode corpus (title + text) with normalize_embeddings=True, cache to .npy, encode queries with the bge query prefix, search IndexFlatIP top 100, write runs in the same format as BM25. Tests: cached embeddings reload identically, and an exact-duplicate query of a doc text ranks that doc first.
verify: Compute dense NDCG@10 on train queries per dataset and compare with BM25
Run once without the query prefix and record the difference

steps.title: Build the fixed-weight fusion baselines
steps.learn: Convex combination: alpha * norm(BM25) + (1 - alpha) * norm(dense). RRF sums 1/(k + rank); Cormack et al. fixed k = 60. Bruch et al. found convex combination beat RRF, RRF was sensitive to its parameters, and one alpha needs few training queries.

decision.choice: ranx fuse with min-max normalization and weighted sum, alpha tuned on train queries; RRF as a second baseline
decision.why: These are the baselines the prove-it names. ranx implements both plus optimize_fusion, so baselines are standard rather than hand-rolled.

alternatives.name: Z-score normalization
alternatives.tradeoff: Less sensitive to a single outlier score than min-max, but assumes a roughly bell-shaped score list.

alternatives.name: Hand-written fusion
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control over edge cases, but easy to get subtly wrong and harder for others to reproduce.

steps.delegate: Python, ranx. fusion.py: fixed_cc(bm25_run, dense_run, alpha, norm='min-max') and rrf(runs, k). Use optimize_fusion on train qrels for method='wsum' and 'rrf'. State in code how a doc missing from one list is scored and test it. Tests: alpha=1 equals BM25 ranking, alpha=0 equals dense ranking, a doc in only one list is handled as documented.
verify: Record the tuned fixed alpha and RRF k per dataset and pooled
Plot train NDCG@10 vs alpha from 0 to 1 per query type to see if the curves peak in different places

steps.title: Measure the headroom with a per-query oracle alpha
steps.learn: Before building a router, ask how much a perfect one could gain. For each train query, find the alpha that maximizes its NDCG@10. If the oracle barely beats the fixed alpha, query-aware fusion cannot help much; if it helps mainly one type, focus there.

decision.choice: Grid alpha in steps of 0.1 per train query, record best alpha and NDCG gain over fixed alpha
decision.why: A coarse grid is cheap and enough to show headroom and how best alpha differs across types.

alternatives.name: Skip the oracle
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves time, but you cannot tell a weak router from a problem with no headroom.

alternatives.name: Continuous optimization per query
alternatives.tradeoff: Slightly higher ceiling, but NDCG is piecewise constant in alpha, so a grid loses little.

steps.delegate: Python, ranx. oracle.py: for each train query compute NDCG@10 for alpha in 0.0..1.0 step 0.1; output CSV (qid, dataset, type, best_alpha, best_ndcg, fixed_ndcg). Break ties toward the fixed alpha. Tests: a query where both runs are identical has all alphas tied, and output row count equals train query count.
verify: Report mean oracle NDCG@10 vs fixed alpha on train queries, per type
Plot the distribution of best alpha per type

steps.title: Route by query type with one alpha per type
steps.learn: The simplest query-aware method: tune a separate alpha for each query type on train queries and look it up at query time. It directly tests the claim that identifier queries want more BM25 weight.

decision.choice: One alpha per type, tuned on pooled train queries of that type, with a fallback to the global alpha for rare types
decision.why: Few parameters, so little risk of overfitting small train sets, and the result is easy to explain.

alternatives.name: Per-type and per-dataset alpha
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures domain differences, but multiplies parameters and needs dataset identity at query time.

alternatives.name: Different fusion method per type
alternatives.tradeoff: Could pick RRF for some types, but adds a discrete choice that is easy to overfit.

steps.delegate: Python. route_type.py: fit_alphas(train_rows) returns {type: alpha} using ranx optimize_fusion per type, with a minimum query count below which the global alpha is used; fuse(qid) looks up the type via query_types.tag. Tests: an unseen type falls back to global, and alphas are within [0, 1].
verify: Report the alpha chosen for each type and compare to your oracle distributions
Run 5-fold cross-validation on train queries and report per-type NDCG@10 vs fixed alpha

steps.title: Predict alpha per query from retrieval signals
steps.learn: Type is coarse. Retrieval signals carry more: BM25 top score and its gap to rank 2, dense top cosine and gap, overlap of the two top 10 lists, query length, max term IDF, and digit presence. A small model maps these to an alpha.

decision.choice: Predict a class over the 11 grid alphas with regularized logistic regression on these features, trained on oracle labels
decision.why: Cheap at query time, uses scores you already computed, and regularization limits overfitting on a few thousand train queries.

alternatives.name: Gradient-boosted regressor on alpha
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures interactions, but overfits more easily on small train sets.

alternatives.name: Cross-encoder rerank of the union
alternatives.tradeoff: Often stronger than any fusion weight, but much slower per query and changes the question being asked.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn. router.py: features(qid) from the BM25 and dense runs and query text; train LogisticRegression on oracle best_alpha classes with class weights; predict_alpha(qid). Fit on train folds only, evaluate on held-out folds. Tests: features are finite for empty BM25 results, and prediction always returns an alpha in the grid.
verify: Report cross-validated per-type NDCG@10 for the feature router vs per-type alpha vs fixed alpha
List the 3 largest-magnitude coefficients and check they make sense

steps.title: Handle empty, tied and one-sided result lists
steps.learn: Fusion breaks at the edges: BM25 can return nothing for a query with no shared tokens, min-max over a list with one score divides by zero, and a doc retrieved by only one system needs a defined score from the other. Decide each case explicitly.

decision.choice: Explicit fallbacks: empty BM25 means dense only, constant lists normalize to 1, missing docs score 0
decision.why: Each rule is simple and testable, and making them explicit keeps a hidden default from changing results between libraries.

alternatives.name: Rely on library defaults
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but behavior can change with versions and is hard to explain.

alternatives.name: Retrieve deeper for missing scores
alternatives.tradeoff: Score every candidate in both systems; more accurate, more compute.

steps.delegate: Python. Add guards to fusion.py and router.py for empty lists, single-element lists and constant scores; log a counter per fallback. Tests: one unit test per fallback, plus an end-to-end run over all train queries asserting no NaN scores.
verify: Report how many train queries hit each fallback
Confirm no fused run contains NaN or infinite scores

steps.title: Measure it on the frozen test splits
steps.learn: Run every method once on test queries with parameters fixed from train: BM25, dense, best fixed alpha, RRF, per-type alpha, feature router and oracle. Report NDCG@10 per query type and overall, with paired tests, since small type groups give noisy means.
verify: Report a table of test NDCG@10 by method and query type, with the query count of each type
Run ranx compare with a paired test against the fixed-alpha baseline and report p-values per type
Measure added router latency per query separately from retrieval time
Record machine, library versions, model name and the exact command for each number

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example, a type where the router lost); and assumptions: three BEIR datasets, one embedding model, rule-based types, and what this does not prove about other domains.
verify: Part 1 states the one question and the per-type NDCG@10 comparison
Part 2 has a number with machine and command for every claim, including the oracle headroom
Part 3 explains at least one surprising per-type result with an example query
Part 4 lists assumptions and what this does not prove

projects.title: Title, school and company normalizer
projects.problem: "SWE II", "Software Engineer 2" and "SDE-2" are one thing
projects.proveIt: Merge precision and recall on a labeled sample
projects.question: Can a rules plus fuzzy matching normalizer merge variant job titles, schools and companies with high pairwise precision and recall on a labeled sample?

steps.title: Frame the merge question and freeze a labeled test sample
steps.learn: Normalizing means deciding which strings name the same entity. Score it as pairwise merge precision (merged pairs that truly match) and recall (true pairs you merged). Titles, companies: Kaggle LinkedIn Job Postings. Schools: collect raw strings outside Scorecard; use its UNITID only as the key.
verify: Load postings.csv and companies/companies.csv and count distinct raw titles and company names yourself
Hand-label about 300 strings per entity type into clusters, noting the rule you used for each borderline case
Freeze one third of the labeled clusters as a test set before writing any matching code

steps.title: Define what 'same entity' means for each type
steps.learn: Many errors are policy errors, not matching errors. Is 'Senior Software Engineer' the same as 'Software Engineer'? Is a subsidiary its parent? Is a university system one school or many campuses? Write the rules down before matching, or your labels and code will disagree.

decision.choice: Titles as (role, specialty, level); companies keyed by LinkedIn company_id; schools keyed by Scorecard UNITID
decision.why: Splitting level from role lets 'SWE II' and 'SDE-2' merge on both fields while 'Senior SWE' stays separate. Reusing IDs already in the source data gives a join key and avoids inventing one.

alternatives.name: One canonical string per cluster
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest to build and display, but role and level are fused, so you cannot filter by level or merge level spellings cleanly.

alternatives.name: Map titles to O*NET-SOC codes
alternatives.tradeoff: A public taxonomy with alternate titles, but occupations are too coarse to separate the levels and specialties a recruiter cares about.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with Pydantic. Write schema.py with CanonicalTitle(id, role, specialty|None, level|None), CanonicalCompany(id, name, source_id), CanonicalSchool(id, name, unitid) and Mention(raw, entity_type, canonical_id|None). Put the merge policy rules in a module docstring. Tests: model validation, level must be int or None, a Mention round-trips through JSON.
verify: Write 10 policy rules and apply them to 30 borderline training pairs; count pairs the rules leave undecided
Relabel any training clusters that break the policy (never touch the frozen test split)

steps.title: Clean strings and expand abbreviations
steps.learn: Before comparing, map surface noise to one form: lowercase, strip punctuation, expand abbreviations (sr, swe, sde, mgr), drop legal suffixes (inc, llc), and unify Roman numerals and digits. RapidFuzz does no preprocessing unless you pass a processor such as utils.default_process.

decision.choice: A versioned, hand-curated abbreviation and suffix table, seeded from frequent tokens in the training split
decision.why: Title and company abbreviations are a small vocabulary with a long tail, and a table is auditable and testable. Seeding it from token counts keeps it grounded in this data rather than guesses.

alternatives.name: No cleanup, embeddings only
alternatives.tradeoff: Nothing to maintain, but nothing guarantees level tokens like 'II' and 'III' stay apart, so levels can blur.

alternatives.name: LLM rewrites each string
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles rare abbreviations, but costs a call per distinct string, needs caching to be reproducible, and may invent expansions.

steps.delegate: Python. normalize.py with clean(raw: str, entity_type) returning a token list. Load abbreviations.csv and legal_suffixes.csv. Map Roman numerals I to V and trailing digits to a level token. Use rapidfuzz.utils.default_process for base cleanup. mine_tokens.py prints the 300 most frequent training tokens. Tests: 'SWE II', 'Software Engineer 2' and 'SDE-2' give the same tokens; 'Acme, Inc.' equals 'ACME'; 'IT' is not read as a numeral.
verify: Read 50 cleaned training strings and list any expansion that changed the meaning
Record distinct string counts before and after cleaning for each entity type

steps.title: Parse level and role as separate fields
steps.learn: Level appears as 'Senior', 'Sr', 'II', '2', 'L5', 'Staff' or 'Lead', and ladders differ by company. Decide whether 'L5' maps to a shared ladder or stays company-specific. Removing the level first leaves a cleaner role string to match.

decision.choice: Ordered regex rules for level tokens, with an LLM fallback only for titles the rules leave ambiguous
decision.why: Most level markers are a small closed set that rules catch reliably and testably. Sending only leftovers to an LLM with a strict schema keeps cost low and keeps the common path deterministic.

alternatives.name: LLM for every title
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code and better on odd phrasings, but cost grows with distinct titles and results must be cached to be reproducible.

alternatives.name: Ignore level
alternatives.tradeoff: Merges more and raises recall, but 'Engineer I' and 'Engineer III' merge, a precision error under your policy.

steps.delegate: Python. level.py: parse_level(tokens) returns (role_tokens, level: int|None, level_word: str|None). Rules for Roman numerals, trailing digits, senior/sr, junior/jr, staff, principal, lead. Ambiguous titles go to llm_level.py with a Pydantic schema and a JSONL cache. Tests: 'SDE-2' gives level 2, 'Sr Engineer' gives level_word senior, 'Python Developer' gives no level.
verify: Hand-check level output on 100 training titles and record the error count
Count distinct titles that reach the LLM fallback and estimate their cost at your provider's current price

steps.title: Generate candidate pairs without comparing everything
steps.learn: Comparing all pairs grows with the square of distinct strings. Blocking compares only pairs that share something cheap: a rare token, or being near neighbors in embedding space. Any true pair no block catches is lost recall that later steps cannot recover.

decision.choice: Union of two blocks: shared rare token (inverted index) and top-k embedding neighbors
decision.why: Token blocks catch matches that share words after cleaning; embedding neighbors catch synonyms with no shared token ('developer' vs 'engineer'). The union trades extra pairs for recall, and the scorer filters them.

alternatives.name: All pairs with rapidfuzz cdist
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact, simple and can use several workers; fine for a few thousand strings, but time and memory grow quadratically.

alternatives.name: Splink blocking rules
alternatives.tradeoff: Mature blocking and scoring for multi-column records, but Splink's docs say it is not designed for a single bag-of-words column, which is what a title is.

steps.delegate: Python. blocking.py: build an inverted index over cleaned tokens, skip tokens found in more than N strings, emit pairs sharing a remaining token. Add embedding neighbors with sentence-transformers all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and exact cosine top-k in NumPy. Return a deduplicated set of (i, j) with i < j. Tests: pairs unique and ordered, a known synonym pair appears, stopword-only strings yield no pairs.
verify: Measure blocking recall: the share of true training pairs present in the candidate set
Record candidate pair count against the all-pairs count for each entity type

steps.title: Score candidate pairs and pick a merge threshold
steps.learn: Similarity measures fail differently. token_set_ratio compares unique and common words, so word order and repeats stop mattering, but a short string can score high against a longer one containing its words. Combine a few signals and pick the threshold on training pairs only.

decision.choice: Logistic regression over token_set_ratio, token_sort_ratio, embedding cosine, level match and shared rare token
decision.why: A few hundred labeled training pairs can weight a handful of features, and the output probability can be thresholded for a precision target. Each feature stays inspectable when a merge goes wrong.

alternatives.name: One rapidfuzz score and a threshold
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest to build and explain, but one threshold rarely suits both short abbreviations and long titles.

alternatives.name: Fellegi-Sunter model in Splink
alternatives.tradeoff: Principled m and u probabilities and match weights, strongest when records have several columns (name plus city), less suited to one title string.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn, rapidfuzz. features.py computes the features per candidate pair (inputs are already cleaned). train.py fits LogisticRegression on training pairs and saves it. pick_threshold.py uses sklearn.metrics.precision_recall_curve to pick the lowest threshold that meets your training precision target. Tests: feature vector shape, identical strings get cosine 1.0, level mismatch feature set correctly.
verify: Plot training precision and recall against threshold and record the chosen threshold and why
Read the 20 highest-scoring wrong merges in training and name the feature that misled the model

steps.title: Turn pairwise merges into clusters without chaining
steps.learn: Pairwise decisions are not transitive. Connected components join A to C through B even when A and C clearly differ, so one weak edge can fuse two large clusters. Cannot-link rules (different level, different campus) stop the worst chains.

decision.choice: Union-find over accepted edges in descending score order, refusing unions that join cannot-link mentions
decision.why: Greedy union by score is simple and near linear in edges, and the cannot-link check enforces your policy where it matters most. Each cluster stays explainable as a list of accepted edges.

alternatives.name: Plain connected components
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but one false edge merges whole clusters and precision drops.

alternatives.name: Agglomerative clustering, average linkage
alternatives.tradeoff: Less prone to chaining because it compares whole clusters, but needs a distance matrix per block and another threshold to tune.

steps.delegate: Python. cluster.py: DisjointSet with path compression and union by size. Sort scored edges descending, skip edges below threshold, and before each union check cannot_link(root_a, root_b) using level and campus sets kept per root. Output mention_id to cluster_id. Tests: chain A, B, C blocked when A and C cannot link; rerun is idempotent; singletons kept.
verify: List the 10 largest training clusters and read each for chained errors
Compare training pairwise precision with and without cannot-link rules

steps.title: Resolve company and school aliases before fuzzy matching
steps.learn: Acronyms (MIT) and rebrands share few characters with the full name, so string similarity misses them. College Scorecard has an alias field per institution. Hard cases stay policy: subsidiaries vs parents, and campuses that share a system name.

decision.choice: Exact lookup in alias tables (Scorecard ALIAS, a curated company alias file), fuzzy scorer only for the rest
decision.why: An alias table resolves the acronyms and rebrands that string similarity cannot, and lookups are exact and cheap. Only strings with no alias hit go through the learned scorer.

alternatives.name: Wikidata labels and aliases
alternatives.tradeoff: Broad alias coverage queryable by SPARQL, but you must resolve which item an ambiguous name means, and coverage varies by entity.

alternatives.name: Fuzzy scorer only
alternatives.tradeoff: One code path, but acronyms and rebrands are missed, lowering recall on strings people actually type.

steps.delegate: Python. aliases.py loads Scorecard INSTNM, ALIAS and UNITID (inspect how ALIAS separates multiple aliases before splitting) plus company_aliases.csv you curate. resolve(raw, entity_type) returns a canonical id via exact cleaned-alias lookup, else None; the pipeline scores only the None cases. Tests: an acronym alias resolves, two campuses of one system stay distinct, unknown strings return None.
verify: Read 20 raw Scorecard ALIAS values and record how multiple aliases are separated
Measure the share of training school and company mentions resolved by lookup, and the precision of those lookups

steps.title: Measure merge precision and recall on the frozen test set
steps.learn: Score the whole pipeline once on the frozen test clusters. Pairwise metrics weight large clusters heavily (a cluster of n mentions has n(n-1)/2 pairs), so report each entity type separately and read the largest clusters' errors. Baselines show what each stage adds.
steps.delegate: Python. eval.py: from predicted and gold cluster ids for test mentions, compute pairwise precision, recall and F1 per entity type. Systems: exact match after lowercasing, cleaning only, cleaning plus one rapidfuzz threshold, full pipeline. Print a table and save JSON with git commit, machine and command. Tests: perfect clustering scores 1.0; all singletons give recall 0 and precision reported as undefined.
verify: Run the test evaluation once and record precision, recall, machine and command for every system
Report numbers per entity type, not only pooled
Confirm no rule or threshold changed after seeing test results; if one did, say so in the write-up

steps.title: Write it up in four parts
steps.learn: The write-up is the deliverable: does the normalizer merge variant titles, schools and companies precisely and completely, and which stage (cleaning, level parsing, aliases, clustering) earns its keep? Every number needs the machine and command that produced it, and the surprises need explanations, not just reports.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2 gives a number for every claim, each with the machine and command that produced it
Part 3 explains at least two surprising results with evidence (for example a specific failing example)
Part 4 lists assumptions and what the results do not prove (dataset, labeler, reference date)

projects.title: Temporal reasoning in search
projects.problem: "5+ years in fintech, currently at a startup" needs date math, not embeddings
projects.proveIt: Accuracy on 100 temporal queries
projects.question: Does parsing candidate timelines and doing explicit date math answer temporal queries more accurately than embedding search?

steps.title: Frame the temporal query question and freeze 100 test queries
steps.learn: '5+ years in fintech, currently at a startup' is a predicate over a timeline, not text similarity. Metric: accuracy on 100 temporal queries, a query counting as correct when its result set equals a hand-labeled gold set. Data: Kaggle Resume Dataset. Fix one reference date for 'current'.
verify: Download the resume CSV, read 30 resumes and record how date ranges and current roles are written
Hand-label timelines for about 150 resumes without pipeline code: 100 form the frozen test pool all systems search, 50 are for tuning
Write 100 test and 40 training queries (duration, current, recency, order), derive gold sets from hand timelines, and freeze the 100 test queries

steps.title: Model a candidate as a timeline of roles
steps.learn: Each role needs a start, an end (or open, meaning current), the precision of each date (year only or month), and attributes like industry and company stage. Keep 'unknown' distinct from 'false' so missing data never silently counts as a no.

decision.choice: Month-granularity dates with a precision flag; an open end means current as of a fixed reference date
decision.why: Resumes state months or years, so days add false precision. The precision flag lets a year-only date become a range (first to last month) when a query falls on a boundary.

alternatives.name: Day-level datetimes
alternatives.tradeoff: Uniform arithmetic, but invents day precision and makes 'from 2019' look exact.

alternatives.name: Store only total years per attribute
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to query, but loses order, so 'currently' and 'in the last 3 years' cannot be answered.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, Pydantic. timeline.py: YearMonth(year, month|None) with earliest() and latest(); Role(title, company|None, start, end|None, industries, stage, evidence); Timeline(candidate_id, roles, reference_date). Tests: year-only bounds, open end resolves to reference date, end before start fails validation.
verify: Encode 5 of your hand timelines in the schema and confirm nothing you labeled is lost
List the query types each field supports and any query in your set the schema cannot express

steps.title: Extract role date ranges from resume text
steps.learn: Date strings vary ('01/2015 to Current', 'Jan 2015 - Present', '2015'). Parse with explicit settings: in dateparser, PREFER_DAY_OF_MONTH and RELATIVE_BASE make partial and relative dates deterministic, and REQUIRE_PARTS rejects strings missing a part such as the month.

decision.choice: LLM extracts role spans and raw date strings to a schema; dateparser with fixed settings converts them in code
decision.why: The LLM is good at deciding which date belongs to which role in messy layouts, while code makes date conversion testable and reproducible. Splitting the two shows which stage caused an error.

alternatives.name: Regex for date ranges only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and deterministic, but layouts vary and attaching dates to the right role is the hard part.

alternatives.name: LLM returns final dates
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer parts, but conversions inside the model cannot be unit tested and errors are silent.

steps.delegate: Python. extract_roles.py: LLM call with a Pydantic schema returning roles with raw start/end strings and evidence spans; cache JSONL by resume ID. parse_dates.py: DateDataParser(settings={'PREFER_DAY_OF_MONTH': 'first', 'RELATIVE_BASE': ref}).get_date_data(s); set precision from its period/parts, since parse() fills a missing month. 'Current' and 'Present' map to an open end. Tests: 'Jan 2015', '01/2015', '2015' (year precision), 'Present', garbage returns None.
verify: Compare extracted dates with your hand timelines on 30 training resumes; record exact-month and same-year agreement
Count resumes with at least one unparsed role date and read 5 of them

steps.title: Compute durations by merging intervals
steps.learn: '5+ years in fintech' is the length of the union of fintech role intervals, not their sum: concurrent roles must not double count. Sort, merge overlaps, then sum. Allen's interval relations (before, meets, overlaps, during) name the cases your code must handle.

decision.choice: Merge sorted intervals per attribute and count months, with low and high bounds when dates are year-only
decision.why: Sorting and merging is exact and cheap, and month counts match the data's precision. Bounds let a predicate return true, false or unknown when a year-only date straddles the threshold.

alternatives.name: Sum role durations
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial, but double counts concurrent roles and overstates experience.

alternatives.name: relativedelta from first start to last end
alternatives.tradeoff: Readable year and month differences, but counts gaps between roles as experience.

steps.delegate: Python. intervals.py: merge(intervals) over (start_month_index, end_month_index); duration_months(roles, predicate) returns (low, high) using earliest and latest bounds for year-only dates. Tests: overlapping roles, adjacent roles, a gap, a year-only role straddling a threshold, an open end at the reference date.
verify: Hand-compute months in one industry for 5 timelines with overlaps and compare with the code
Find a training resume where summing and merging disagree and record both numbers

steps.title: Tag each role with industry and company stage
steps.learn: Date math is only as good as the attribute it filters on. 'Fintech' and 'startup' describe the employer at that time. Resume examples may omit or mask employer names, so the role text is often the only evidence: keep a quote and allow 'unknown'.

decision.choice: Per-role LLM tagging into a fixed industry list and a stage enum (startup, established, unknown) with evidence quotes
decision.why: A closed vocabulary matches what the query parser will emit, and quotes make each tag auditable. 'Unknown' keeps missing data from turning into false matches.

alternatives.name: Join an external company table
alternatives.tradeoff: Firmer facts (such as company_size in the LinkedIn postings companies.csv), but needs a named, linkable employer, and a snapshot says nothing about the past.

alternatives.name: Keyword rules ('payments', 'bank')
alternatives.tradeoff: Transparent and free, but noisy: a bank's software team and a payments startup look alike.

steps.delegate: Python. tag_roles.py: per extracted role, call an LLM with a Pydantic schema {industries: list[Industry], stage: Stage, evidence: str}; validate in code that evidence is a substring of the resume. Cache by resume ID and role index. Tests: invented evidence rejected, unknown stage allowed, unknown enum values rejected.
verify: Compare industry and stage tags with your hand labels on 50 training roles and record agreement per field
Count the share of roles tagged stage 'unknown' and write down how queries will treat it

steps.title: Parse temporal queries into a small predicate language
steps.learn: Query phrases map to a few predicate types: duration over an attribute ('5+ years in fintech'), current state ('currently at a startup'), recency ('in the last 2 years') and order ('moved from X to Y'). A small typed language keeps parsing separate from evaluation.

decision.choice: LLM with structured output into a typed predicate tree, one retry on validation failure
decision.why: Recruiter phrasing varies too much for templates, while a typed tree makes evaluation plain, testable code. Sharing enums with role tagging stops 'fintech' meaning two different things.

alternatives.name: Temporal taggers (HeidelTime, Duckling)
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic parsing of expressions like 'in two minutes', but they tag time expressions, not which attribute or comparison is meant.

alternatives.name: Regex templates
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and exact for fixed patterns; new phrasings fail silently as no-match.

steps.delegate: Python. query_ast.py: Pydantic models DurationAtLeast(attr, months), CurrentIs(attr, value), WithinLast(attr, months), And(children), Or(children). parse.py: LLM call with the schema, one retry, else raise ParseError. Tests: 15 fixture queries with expected trees, a nonsense query raises, '5+ years' gives 60 months.
verify: Hand-write trees for 40 training queries and measure exact-match parse accuracy
Check 5 queries using 'over', 'at least' and 'more than' and confirm each bound is inclusive or exclusive as intended

steps.title: Evaluate predicates with three-valued logic
steps.learn: Each predicate returns true, false or unknown (missing dates, unknown stage, year-only bounds), and And/Or follow Kleene's three-valued logic. Then choose a policy for unknowns. This is the step where 'date math, not embeddings' becomes code.

decision.choice: Strict results contain only true; a separate 'possible' list shows unknowns with the reason
decision.why: Accuracy is scored on exact sets, so strict results keep precision honest, while the 'possible' list keeps terse resumes visible instead of silently dropping them.

alternatives.name: Treat unknown as false
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but silently drops candidates whose resumes are just terse.

alternatives.name: Treat unknown as true
alternatives.tradeoff: Raises recall, but floods results with unverified matches.

steps.delegate: Python. evaluate.py: evaluate(tree, timeline) returns True, False or None with Kleene And/Or plus a reason string. search.py applies predicates as a pre-filter over all timelines, then orders survivors by embedding similarity on the non-temporal part of the query. Tests: Kleene truth table, an open-ended current role, WithinLast at the reference-date boundary, unknown stage.
verify: On 3 training queries, hand-check every returned and every excluded candidate
Count results landing in the 'possible' list per query type

steps.title: Handle messy timelines and reference-date drift
steps.learn: Real timelines break assumptions: end before start, dates after the reference date, roles with no dates, two open-ended roles, and 'current' that was true only when the resume was written. Each needs a rule and a test, and the reference date must be explicit everywhere.

decision.choice: Validate each timeline, repair only unambiguous cases (swapped start and end), mark the rest unknown
decision.why: Guessing repairs silently corrupts durations; marking unknown routes those candidates to the 'possible' list where a person can check them.

alternatives.name: Drop invalid timelines
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean data, but removes candidates and biases results toward neat resumes.

alternatives.name: LLM re-extraction on failure
alternatives.tradeoff: Can fix extraction mistakes, but costs calls and may still be wrong; worth it only if most errors come from extraction.

steps.delegate: Python. validate.py: check end >= start, no date after the reference date, flag multiple open-ended roles, exclude dateless roles from duration math and flag them. Return the repaired timeline plus an issue list. Tests for each issue type, and a test that the reference date comes from config, never the system clock.
verify: Count each issue type across training timelines and read 3 examples of the most common one
Rerun training queries with a different reference date and confirm results change only where they should

steps.title: Measure accuracy against an embeddings-only baseline
steps.learn: Run the frozen 100 queries once. Report exact-set accuracy, plus per (query, candidate) precision and recall so near misses show. Baselines: embeddings only, and an LLM judging each resume directly. Break results down by query type and by failing stage.
steps.delegate: Python. bench.py: load frozen queries and gold sets; run the pipeline, an embedding baseline (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cosine, k set to the gold set size, an oracle choice that favors the baseline), and an optional LLM-per-resume baseline. Output accuracy, precision and recall overall and per query type, with machine, model names and git commit. Tests: scorer on toy gold sets.
verify: Run the test set once and record each system's accuracy with machine and command
Attribute every failed test query to a stage (extraction, tagging, parsing, evaluation)
Confirm gold sets came from hand timelines and never from pipeline output

steps.title: Write it up in four parts
steps.learn: The write-up is the deliverable: does explicit timeline math beat embeddings on temporal queries, and where does it still fail (dates, tags, parsing)? Every number needs the machine and command that produced it, and the surprises need explanations, not just reports.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2 gives a number for every claim, each with the machine and command that produced it
Part 3 explains at least two surprising results with evidence (for example a specific failing example)
Part 4 lists assumptions and what the results do not prove (dataset, labeler, reference date)

projects.title: Multi-vector retrieval for long documents
projects.problem: One vector per long profile blurs details
projects.proveIt: ColBERT-style quality vs single vector, memory cost
projects.question: On long documents, how much retrieval quality does ColBERT-style multi-vector scoring add over one vector per document, and at what memory cost?

steps.title: Frame the question, the two metrics and the long-document set
steps.learn: Prove-it: ColBERT-style quality vs single vector, plus memory cost. Use MLDR English: long Wikipedia articles, each query generated by GPT-3.5 from one random paragraph, so the answer is a detail inside a long text. Report nDCG@10 and Recall@100, and bytes per document for each representation.
verify: Load the English dev, test and corpus configs and confirm the split sizes against the dataset card table
Read 10 test queries with their positive article and find the paragraph each one was drawn from
Freeze the 800 test queries now (save their ids); tune only on the 200 dev queries
Build a working corpus: every dev and test positive plus a fixed-seed random sample of distractors; save the doc id list

steps.title: Measure document lengths and pick one truncation policy
steps.learn: Every encoder has a maximum input length; tokens past it are silently dropped, which hides exactly the details this project is about. BGE-M3 accepts up to 8192 tokens. Tokenize the working corpus, see how many documents exceed each limit, and apply the same limit to every method so the comparison is fair.

decision.choice: One max_length for both single-vector and multi-vector modes, set from the measured length distribution
decision.why: If the dense baseline sees 512 tokens and the multi-vector model sees 8192, any quality gap mixes two effects. One shared limit isolates the effect of one vector vs many, which is the question.

alternatives.name: Truncate everything to 512 tokens
alternatives.tradeoff: Much cheaper to encode and store, but the question becomes about the first page of each article, not long documents.

alternatives.name: No limit, sliding windows
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers every token, but it changes the representation and belongs in the chunked baseline step instead.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. lengths.py: load the working corpus, tokenize with the BGE-M3 tokenizer (transformers AutoTokenizer), write a CSV of doc_id,n_tokens and print percentiles plus the share of docs above 512, 2048 and 8192 tokens. Save the chosen max_length in config.yaml used by all later scripts. Tests: tokenizer count matches len(input_ids) for 3 docs; config value is read, not hard-coded.
verify: Report the median and p95 token length and the share of docs over your chosen limit
Confirm every later script reads max_length from the same config file
Note how many test positives get truncated; these queries may have lost their answer paragraph

steps.title: Build the BM25 and single-vector dense baselines
steps.learn: The single-vector baseline compresses a whole article into one embedding, which is the blurring the problem describes. BM25 is the lexical reference: generated queries often reuse words from the source paragraph, so BM25 can be strong here. Both baselines must use the same corpus and truncation.

decision.choice: BGE-M3 dense_vecs as the single vector, BM25 via bm25s as the lexical baseline
decision.why: BGE-M3 returns a dense vector and ColBERT vectors from one model and one forward pass, so the comparison changes only the representation, not the model or its training data.

alternatives.name: A different dense model
alternatives.tradeoff: Could be stronger, but then gaps mix model quality with single vs multi-vector and the question gets muddy.

alternatives.name: BGE-M3 sparse lexical weights
alternatives.tradeoff: Learned term weights instead of BM25; worth adding later, but BM25 is the standard reference everyone can reproduce.

steps.delegate: Python. baselines.py: (1) bm25s.tokenize plus bm25s.BM25 index over the working corpus, retrieve top 100 per query; (2) FlagEmbedding BGEM3FlagModel('BAAI/bge-m3', use_fp16=True).encode(..., return_dense=True, max_length from config), store dense vectors as a float32 .npy, exact inner-product top 100 with numpy. Write TREC-style run files. Tests: a toy corpus where the right doc ranks first; run file has 100 rows per query.
verify: Compute nDCG@10 and Recall@100 on dev for both baselines with ranx
Record dense encode throughput (docs per second) and the .npy size on disk
Spot-check 5 dev queries where BM25 beats dense and note why

steps.title: Add a chunked single-vector baseline (one vector per passage)
steps.learn: The cheap fix for a blurred vector is more vectors per document at passage level: split the article, embed each chunk, score the document by its best chunk. This is the real competitor to token-level multi-vector, since it sits between one vector and one vector per token in memory.

decision.choice: Fixed-size token chunks with overlap, document score is the max chunk score
decision.why: Max over chunks matches the task: the query targets one paragraph, so the best matching chunk should decide the document. Fixed token windows are simple, reproducible and independent of article markup.

alternatives.name: Split on paragraphs or headings
alternatives.tradeoff: Follows meaning better, but chunk sizes vary widely and the corpus text may not keep clean boundaries.

alternatives.name: Mean of chunk vectors
alternatives.tradeoff: One vector per doc again, so memory stays low, but averaging brings back the blurring you are trying to remove.

steps.delegate: Python. chunked.py: split each doc into windows of N tokens with stride S (N and S from config), encode chunks with BGE-M3 dense, keep a chunk_to_doc int array, retrieve top 1000 chunks per query and aggregate to doc scores by max, output top 100 docs. Tests: aggregation keeps the max, not the sum; a doc appears once in the run; chunk count matches ceil formula.
verify: Try 2 or 3 chunk sizes on dev only and record nDCG@10 and vectors per doc for each
Report total chunk vectors and bytes for the chosen setting
Confirm no test query was used to choose the chunk size

steps.title: Encode token-level vectors and store them compactly
steps.learn: Late interaction keeps one vector per document token, so storage grows with document length; the ColBERTv2 paper notes this inflates space by an order of magnitude. A flat contiguous matrix plus per-doc offsets keeps memory layout simple and lets you memory-map the whole store.

decision.choice: BGE-M3 colbert_vecs saved as one float16 matrix plus an offsets array, opened with numpy.memmap
decision.why: Same model as the dense baseline, so only the representation changes. A flat array avoids Python object overhead per document and makes bytes per doc a simple, exact count.

alternatives.name: PyLate with a PLAID index
alternatives.tradeoff: Compressed, fast end-to-end search, but quantization hides raw memory cost; use it as a later comparison point.

alternatives.name: Per-document arrays in a pickle
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest to write, but slow to load, larger on disk and harder to measure exactly.

steps.delegate: Python. encode_mv.py: BGEM3FlagModel.encode(docs, return_colbert_vecs=True, max_length from config) in batches; append each doc's vectors to a float16 file, record offsets (int64, len n_docs+1) and doc ids. loader.py exposes get(doc_idx) returning a memmap slice. Tests: vectors for doc i round-trip exactly (within float16) after reload; offsets are monotonic; vector count equals the per-doc count returned by encode.
verify: Print the vector dimension and vectors per doc (median, p95) from your own arrays
Report total store size in bytes and bytes per doc vs the single dense vector
Reload 3 docs and confirm they match the in-memory encode output

steps.title: Score with MaxSim and choose how to find candidates
steps.learn: MaxSim: for each query token take its best similarity over all document tokens, then sum (BGE-M3's colbert_score also divides by query length). Scoring every doc exhaustively is exact but costly at this size, so candidates usually come from a cheaper first stage. Measure how much that cut costs.

decision.choice: Union of dense and BM25 top 100 run files as candidates, then exact MaxSim rerank with numpy matmul
decision.why: Two different first stages make it less likely the answer is missing from the candidate pool, and exact MaxSim on a few hundred docs is fast in numpy. The candidate cut is measurable by comparing against exhaustive scoring on dev.

alternatives.name: Exhaustive MaxSim over all docs
alternatives.tradeoff: No candidate loss, but cost grows with total corpus tokens; fine for a small dev check, slow for the full set.

alternatives.name: PLAID or MUVERA style end-to-end retrieval
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales to large corpora, but adds an approximate index whose errors you must also measure.

steps.delegate: Python. maxsim.py: maxsim(q[Lq,d], D[Ld,d]) = (q @ D.T).max(axis=1).sum() / Lq, batched over candidates in float32. rerank.py: build candidate union from the two run files, score, write top 100 run. exhaustive.py for dev only. Tests: maxsim equals BGEM3FlagModel.colbert_score on 5 pairs within 1e-3; a doc with an exact copy of the query scores highest; candidate union has no duplicates.
verify: On dev, report the share of queries whose positive is in the candidate pool
Compare nDCG@10 of candidate rerank vs exhaustive MaxSim on dev
Record p50 and p95 rerank latency per query

steps.title: Cut multi-vector memory with token pooling
steps.learn: Memory cost is the other half of the prove-it. Token pooling clusters similar token vectors in each document and keeps their means; its paper reports about 50% fewer vectors with little loss. Residual compression (ColBERTv2) and PQ shrink bytes per vector instead. Measure quality at each memory level.

decision.choice: Hierarchical token pooling at pool factors 2 and 3, applied at index time only
decision.why: It needs no model or query changes, is easy to verify, and directly trades vectors per doc for quality, which gives a clean memory vs nDCG curve.

alternatives.name: ColBERTv2 residual compression via PLAID
alternatives.tradeoff: Much smaller bytes per vector, but it is tied to a specific index engine and harder to reason about piece by piece.

alternatives.name: Binary or int8 quantization of each vector
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and large savings per vector, but quality loss depends on the model and needs its own sweep.

steps.delegate: Python. pool.py: for each doc, cluster its token vectors (scipy.cluster.hierarchy, Ward linkage) into ceil(n/pool_factor) groups, store group means (normalized) in a new store with the same layout as encode_mv.py. Rerun rerank.py against each store. Tests: vector count per doc equals ceil(n/factor); factor 1 returns the original vectors; output stays normalized.
verify: Report bytes per doc and dev nDCG@10 for pool factors 1, 2 and 3
Plot dev nDCG@10 vs total store size, including dense and chunked points
Confirm pooling ran on documents only, never on queries

steps.title: Harden the pipeline: masks, empty docs, reproducibility
steps.learn: Multi-vector code fails quietly: padding vectors counted as tokens, special tokens left in, a doc encoded twice, or runs that differ between reruns. Any of these shifts scores by small amounts that look like real effects. Pin seeds, versions and corpus order, and cache encodings by content hash.

decision.choice: Cache encodings keyed by hash of model name, max_length and doc text; one manifest per run
decision.why: Encoding long docs is the slowest part, so caching makes reruns cheap, and the manifest lets you prove two runs used identical inputs.

alternatives.name: Re-encode every run
alternatives.tradeoff: No cache bugs, but slow and GPU nondeterminism can change scores slightly between runs.

alternatives.name: Cache by doc id only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler key, but a changed max_length or model silently reuses stale vectors.

steps.delegate: Python. Add cache.py (sha256 key over model, max_length, text) and manifest.json (git commit, library versions, config, corpus id list hash). Tests: vector counts never include padding (compare with attention mask); an empty or whitespace doc is handled without crashing and logged; rerunning rerank twice gives byte-identical run files.
verify: Rerun the full dev pipeline and confirm identical run files
Change max_length and confirm the cache misses
List any docs that failed to encode and how they were handled

steps.title: Measure it: quality, memory and latency on the frozen test set
steps.learn: Run every method once on the 800 frozen test queries: BM25, dense, chunked dense, MaxSim rerank, pooled MaxSim. Report nDCG@10, Recall@100, bytes per doc and query latency. Slice results by document length to test the claim that long docs hurt one vector most. Use paired tests per query.
steps.delegate: Python. eval.py: load qrels and runs with ranx, compute ndcg@10 and recall@100, run ranx compare with the paired t-test, and print a Markdown table. bench.py: warm up, then time each method over all test queries, report p50 and p95; read store sizes from disk. Add a slice by test-positive length quartile. CLI flag --split. Tests: toy qrels with hand-computed nDCG; slice counts sum to all queries.
verify: Report the full table on test with p-values vs the dense baseline
Report nDCG@10 per length quartile for dense, chunked and MaxSim
Record machine, CPU or GPU, library versions and the exact commands

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example if chunked dense matched MaxSim at less memory), (4) what this does not prove: generated queries, a sampled corpus, one model, English only.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives quality, bytes per doc and latency for every method, with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a concrete query
Part 4 lists assumptions, including the sampled corpus and LLM-generated queries

projects.title: Visual document search (ColPali)
projects.problem: Search slides and scanned PDFs without OCR
projects.proveIt: Recall@5 vs an OCR + text pipeline
projects.question: Does retrieving page images with ColPali beat an OCR plus text search pipeline on Recall@5 for scanned documents and slides?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the two page corpora
steps.learn: Prove-it: Recall@5 of ColPali vs OCR plus text. Use two public corpora with page-level qrels: ViDoRe DocVQA (scanned industry documents, 500 pages) and ViDoRe V3 Physics (French lecture slides, 1674 pages, often several relevant pages per query). Report Recall@5 and Hit rate@5.
verify: Load corpus, queries and qrels for both sets and confirm the counts on each dataset card
Keep only the French queries in Physics so translations of one query cannot land in both splits
Split queries into dev and test with a fixed seed and freeze test ids before building anything
Count queries with more than 5 relevant pages; standard Recall@5 cannot reach 1 for them

steps.title: Load page images once and feed the same pixels to both pipelines
steps.learn: Both pipelines must see the same page: if OCR reads a higher resolution scan than the vision model, the comparison is about inputs, not methods. Inspect image sizes, orientation and colour mode. ColPali resizes pages to its own input size internally, so very dense pages may lose small text.

decision.choice: Use the page images shipped in the datasets, saved once as PNG with a page id manifest
decision.why: The qrels refer to these exact images, so using them avoids page-number mismatches, and both pipelines read identical files.

alternatives.name: Re-render source PDFs with PyMuPDF at fixed DPI
alternatives.tradeoff: Control over resolution, but page indices must be re-matched to qrels and not every source PDF may still be online.

alternatives.name: Use the dataset markdown text, skip images
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but it skips the OCR step the project is meant to compare against.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. pages.py: load both corpora with datasets.load_dataset, write each image to pages/<set>/<corpus_id>.png, and a manifest CSV with corpus_id, width, height, mode, sha256. Tests: manifest row count equals corpus size; every qrels corpus id has an image; re-running does not rewrite unchanged files.
verify: Report min, median and max page width and height per corpus
Open 10 random pages from each set and note scans with skew, noise or tiny text
Confirm every qrels corpus id maps to an image file

steps.title: Run OCR on every page and check its quality
steps.learn: The text pipeline is only as good as its OCR: missed words cannot be retrieved. Tesseract needs the right language pack (fra for the slides) and is sensitive to resolution and noise. ViDoRe also ships a Tesseract text version of DocVQA and an OCR markdown column for V3, useful as cross-checks.

decision.choice: Tesseract via pytesseract, lang eng for DocVQA and fra+eng for Physics, page-level plain text
decision.why: Tesseract is the standard open OCR baseline and runs on CPU. Page-level output matches the page-level qrels, so no aggregation step is needed.

alternatives.name: docTR (deep learning OCR)
alternatives.tradeoff: Often better on hard layouts, but heavier to run and needs a GPU for speed.

alternatives.name: The dataset's own OCR text
alternatives.tradeoff: No OCR work and a stronger pipeline for V3, but you no longer measure your own OCR; keep it as an upper reference run.

steps.delegate: Python. ocr.py: for each PNG in the manifest call pytesseract.image_to_string(img, lang=...) with a timeout, write ocr/<set>/<corpus_id>.txt, log failures and empty outputs, record seconds per page. Use multiprocessing for pages. Tests: a rendered test image with known text is read back; timeout and empty output are logged not raised; output count equals manifest count.
verify: Compare your DocVQA OCR text with the dataset's Tesseract text on 10 pages and note differences
Hand-read 5 slides and estimate how many key words OCR missed (formulas, figure labels)
Report the number of empty OCR pages and mean seconds per page

steps.title: Index OCR text with BM25 and a dense text embedder
steps.learn: The baseline is OCR then text retrieval, the kind of pipeline the ColPali paper compared against (it used BM25 and BGE-M3 on parsed text). Queries for Physics are French, so the dense model must be multilingual and BM25 needs French tokenization or stemming.

decision.choice: Two text runs per corpus: BM25 (bm25s) and BGE-M3 dense, one document per page
decision.why: Two strong, different text baselines keep ColPali from winning against a weak opponent. BGE-M3 is multilingual, and one doc per page matches the qrels directly.

alternatives.name: Chunk pages and take the best chunk
alternatives.tradeoff: Helps very long pages, but slides and scanned forms are short, so it adds code for little gain.

alternatives.name: RRF fusion of BM25 and dense
alternatives.tradeoff: Often the strongest text baseline; add it if the two text runs disagree a lot on dev.

steps.delegate: Python. text_runs.py: bm25s.tokenize (stopwords and a PyStemmer stemmer per language) plus bm25s.BM25 retrieve top 100; FlagEmbedding BGEM3FlagModel dense encode of page texts and queries, exact inner product top 100. Write TREC-style runs per corpus. Tests: an empty page text yields a valid but low score; run files have 100 rows per query; toy corpus ranks the matching page first.
verify: Report dev Recall@5 for BM25 and dense on both corpora
Also run both on the dataset OCR text (V3 markdown, DocVQA Tesseract) as a reference
Inspect 5 dev misses and decide if OCR or retrieval caused each

steps.title: Embed page images and queries with a ColPali model
steps.learn: ColPali feeds image patches through PaliGemma and projects each output to 128 dims: 1024 patch vectors plus a few prompt-token vectors per page. Queries become token vectors and pages are scored by late interaction. Its training set is English only by design, so the French slides test zero-shot language transfer.

decision.choice: vidore/colpali-v1.3 loaded with colpali-engine (ColPali, ColPaliProcessor), bfloat16 on GPU
decision.why: It is the ColPali model named in the project, so results map onto the paper. The engine provides process_images, process_queries and score_multi_vector, keeping custom code small.

alternatives.name: vidore/colqwen2-v1.0
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher score on ViDoRe per the repo table and Apache 2.0, but a different backbone; run it as an extra row, not a swap.

alternatives.name: vidore/colSmol-256M
alternatives.tradeoff: Small enough for weaker hardware, but lower ViDoRe score, so it answers a different question.

steps.delegate: Python. encode_pages.py: ColPali.from_pretrained('vidore/colpali-v1.3', torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16), ColPaliProcessor; batch process_images over the PNGs, save each page's embeddings (float16) plus counts; encode queries with process_queries. Optionally use sentence_transformers MultiVectorEncoder instead. Tests: embeddings shape is [n_vectors,128]; same image twice gives the same vectors; batch size does not change results beyond fp tolerance.
verify: Read the model card license and base model terms before downloading
Report vectors per page and pages per second on your hardware
Confirm query and page embeddings come from the same model revision (record it)

steps.title: Score pages with MaxSim and size the index
steps.learn: With a few thousand pages, exhaustive MaxSim over every page is affordable and exact, so there is no candidate stage to blame for misses. The paper reports about 257.5 KB per page for raw ColPali vectors; compute your own number and compare it with the OCR text index size.

decision.choice: Exhaustive scoring with processor.score_multi_vector over all pages, embeddings kept in memory
decision.why: Corpora here are small, so exact scoring is fast enough and removes approximation error from the comparison.

alternatives.name: fast-plaid index via colpali-engine
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for large corpora, but adds compression and pruning whose recall loss you would have to measure.

alternatives.name: Single-vector first stage then MaxSim rerank
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper at scale, but a weak first stage can drop the right page before MaxSim sees it.

steps.delegate: Python. search_colpali.py: load page embeddings, score query embeddings against all pages with processor.score_multi_vector in batches, write top 100 runs per corpus. sizes.py: bytes for ColPali embeddings, BM25 index and dense text vectors. Tests: a page scores itself highest for a query copied from its OCR text on 3 clean pages; run has 100 rows per query.
verify: Report dev Recall@5 and Hit rate@5 for ColPali on both corpora
Report KB per page for ColPali vs the text indexes
Record p50 and p95 query latency (encode plus scoring)

steps.title: Shrink the page index with token pooling
steps.learn: Many patches are near-identical (white margins), so pooling similar patch vectors saves memory. The ColPali paper reports that pool factor 3 cuts vectors by 66.7% while keeping 97.8% of performance on its benchmark. Check whether that holds on scans and on French slides.

decision.choice: HierarchicalTokenPooler from colpali-engine at pool factors 2 and 3, on page vectors only
decision.why: It is a drop-in at index time, needs no retraining and gives a direct memory vs Recall@5 tradeoff.

alternatives.name: No pooling (keep every page vector)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and exact, at full memory cost.

alternatives.name: Lower resolution or fewer patches
alternatives.tradeoff: Cuts memory and compute, but the paper found halving patches costs a lot of quality.
