steps.delegate: Python. pool_pages.py: HierarchicalTokenPooler().pool_embeddings(list_of_page_embeddings, pool_factor=f) for f in 2,3; save each store; rerun search_colpali.py on each. Tests: pooled vector count is about n/f per page; pool factor 1 path returns originals; queries are never pooled.
verify: Report dev Recall@5 and KB per page for pool factors 1, 2 and 3 on both corpora
Compare your relative drop with the paper's figure and note any corpus where it differs
Confirm the pooled store is used only through the same scoring code

steps.title: Explain wins and losses by content type
steps.learn: Recall@5 alone does not show why one pipeline wins. V3 qrels carry a content_type per relevant page (for example Text or Mixed), so slice results by it. ColPali similarity maps show which patches matched each query token; OCR text shows what words were available.

decision.choice: Slice dev results by content_type and inspect 10 disagreements with similarity maps
decision.why: A slice by content type tests the claim that images help most on visual pages, using labels the system did not produce.

alternatives.name: Only aggregate numbers
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but you cannot say whether OCR errors or visual content drove the gap.

alternatives.name: Label failure causes yourself on all queries
alternatives.tradeoff: More detail, but slow and your labels may be biased toward your favourite method.

steps.delegate: Python. analyze.py: join per-query Recall@5 for ColPali, BM25 and dense with qrels content_type; print a table per slice. maps.py: use colpali_engine.interpretability to save similarity maps for given query and page ids, and save the OCR text side by side. Tests: slice counts sum to the dev query count; map images are written for each requested pair.
verify: Report dev Recall@5 per content_type for each method on Physics
For 10 dev queries where methods disagree, record whether OCR missed the key text
Use only dev queries here; test stays untouched

steps.title: Measure it: Recall@5 vs OCR pipeline on the frozen test split
steps.learn: Run every method once on the frozen test queries for both corpora: BM25 on OCR, dense on OCR, both on the dataset's OCR text, ColPali, pooled ColPali. Report Recall@5 and Hit rate@5 with paired tests, plus indexing time per page, query latency and KB per page. Indexing time must include OCR.
steps.delegate: Python. eval.py: ranx evaluate with recall@5, hit_rate@5 and ndcg@5, ranx compare with the paired t-test, Markdown tables per corpus. bench.py: time OCR plus text encoding per page vs ColPali encoding per page, after a warm-up batch; time queries end to end. CLI flag --split. Tests: toy qrels with hand-computed recall; hit_rate is 1 when any relevant page is in top 5.
verify: Report the test table for both corpora with p-values vs the best text baseline
Report indexing seconds per page for OCR plus text and for ColPali on the same machine
Record GPU or CPU model, library versions, model revisions and exact commands

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example OCR winning on text-heavy scans), (4) what this does not prove: two small corpora, French-only slides, one OCR engine, models possibly trained on similar data.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives Recall@5, latency and KB per page for every method and corpus, with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a page example
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including corpus size and language

projects.title: Conversational search refinement
projects.problem: "More senior" or "not in NYC" must update the previous query
projects.proveIt: Multi-turn task success rate
projects.question: Can a typed query state updated by small edits each turn ('more senior', 'not in NYC') beat rewriting the query from scratch on multi-turn task success?

steps.title: Frame the refinement question, the corpus and a frozen task set
steps.learn: A refinement only makes sense relative to the previous query. Metric: task success, the % of conversations whose final results hold min(10, gold matches) rows, all satisfying the gold constraints. Corpus: LinkedIn Job Postings 2023-2024 on Kaggle (title, location, formatted_experience_level, remote_allowed, salary).
verify: Download job_postings.csv and record the row count and the distinct values of formatted_experience_level yourself
Write 100 conversations of 2 to 5 turns, each with a hand-written gold constraint set after every turn
Freeze 30 conversations as a held-out test file (hash it) before writing any system code
Make sure your task set covers: add, replace, negate ('not in NYC'), relative shift ('more senior'), relax and reset

steps.title: Normalize seniority and location into filterable fields
steps.learn: 'More senior' needs an ordered scale, and 'not in NYC' needs NYC to mean one canonical place. Map experience levels to an ordinal ladder and parse location strings into city and state. Keep unknown as its own value so filters do not silently drop rows that never stated a level.

decision.choice: Ordinal seniority ladder from formatted_experience_level, plus a canonical city/state table with an alias list
decision.why: The dataset already carries a structured experience level, so ordering it is cheap and auditable. An alias list (NYC, New York, New York City) is small for the cities your tasks mention and makes negation exact instead of fuzzy.

alternatives.name: Infer seniority from title keywords
alternatives.tradeoff: Works when the level column is empty, but 'Senior', 'Lead', 'Staff' and 'Principal' order differently across companies, so the ladder becomes guesswork.

alternatives.name: Embed titles and locations, no fields
alternatives.tradeoff: No normalization work, but you cannot express 'not in NYC' or 'one level up' as an exact filter.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with pandas. normalize.py: load job_postings.csv, map formatted_experience_level to an int ladder (unknown kept as None), parse location into city and state with an alias dict, write jobs.parquet. Tests: alias resolution (NYC, New York, New York City map to one key), unknown level stays None, round-trip of 20 fixture rows.
verify: Print the count of rows per ladder rung and per unknown; note which rungs are too thin to test
Hand-check 30 parsed locations, including remote and multi-city postings
Confirm every city your task set mentions resolves to exactly one canonical key

steps.title: Define the query state the conversation edits
steps.learn: The state is the single source of truth for 'what the user wants now': a list of typed constraints (field, op, value, hard or soft) plus free text for the keyword part. Every turn edits this object; retrieval only ever sees the state, never the raw chat.

decision.choice: Explicit typed state (Pydantic) with ops eq, neq, in, not_in, gte, lte, and a hard/soft flag
decision.why: Refinements like negation and relative shifts are operations on a previous value. A typed state makes each turn inspectable, diffable and testable, and it maps directly onto SQL filters.

alternatives.name: Rewrite to a standalone query each turn
alternatives.tradeoff: The QReCC-style approach; easy to plug into any search box, but the next turn must re-parse prose, and negations and shifts can be dropped in the rewrite.

alternatives.name: Send the full chat history to retrieval
alternatives.tradeoff: No state code, but long histories mix stale and current constraints and the retriever cannot tell which ones still hold.

steps.delegate: Python, Pydantic v2. state.py: Constraint(field: Literal[...], op: Literal['eq','neq','in','not_in','gte','lte'], value, hard: bool), QueryState(constraints: list[Constraint], text: str). Add validators: value types per field, no duplicate (field, op) pairs. Tests: invalid field rejected, neq on seniority allowed, JSON round trip, duplicate pair rejected.
verify: Express 10 of your gold turn states in the schema by hand; list any that do not fit
Confirm a contradictory state (eq NYC and neq NYC) is either rejected or flagged

steps.title: Turn each utterance into edit operations on the state
steps.learn: Given the previous state and the new utterance, the model emits edits: add, replace, remove, negate, shift (relative move on an ordinal field) or reset. Applying edits is plain code, so 'more senior' is computed from the current rung, not guessed by the model.

decision.choice: LLM emits a list of typed edit ops via structured output; deterministic code applies them
decision.why: The model handles phrasing, code handles arithmetic and set logic. A small edit list is easier to validate than a whole new state, and unchanged constraints cannot be accidentally lost.

alternatives.name: LLM regenerates the full state each turn
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler contract, but the model can silently drop or alter constraints the user never touched.

alternatives.name: Rule-based patterns ('not in X', 'more Y')
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and deterministic, but breaks on phrasing outside the patterns.

steps.delegate: Python. update.py: propose_edits(prev: QueryState, utterance: str) returns list[Edit] using an LLM with a JSON schema for Edit; apply_edits(prev, edits) is pure code (shift clamps at ladder ends). Retry once on validation failure, else return prev unchanged plus a flag. Use temperature 0 and cache by (state hash, utterance). Tests: shift at top rung clamps, negate after eq replaces it, reset clears, invalid LLM output path.
verify: On 20 training conversations, compare your applied state to the gold state per turn and count exact matches
Check 'more senior' from the top rung and 'less senior' from the bottom rung behave as you specified
Confirm untouched constraints survive 5 consecutive turns unchanged

steps.title: Resolve references, ellipsis and values to the vocabulary
steps.learn: 'What about Boston?' replaces the location; 'same but remote' adds a constraint; 'there' refers back. Values the model emits must land on canonical keys from the normalize step, or the filter matches nothing. Unresolvable values must surface, not vanish.

decision.choice: Post-process every value through the alias table, then a fuzzy fallback with a minimum score; below it, ask the user
decision.why: The alias table is exact for known cities, the fuzzy fallback catches typos, and the threshold keeps a wrong guess from quietly changing results.

alternatives.name: Pass the canonical vocabulary in the prompt
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer stray values, but the prompt grows with the vocabulary and the model can still invent values.

alternatives.name: Accept free values, match with LIKE
alternatives.tradeoff: No resolution code, but 'NY' also matches unrelated strings and negation becomes unsafe.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz. resolve.py: resolve(field, raw) returns canonical key or Unresolved(raw, candidates). Wire it into apply_edits. Tests: 'NYC', 'new york city', 'Bostn' resolve; 'Springfield' with several states returns Unresolved with candidates; resolved negation stays a negation.
verify: Feed 15 misspelled or abbreviated cities and record how many resolve correctly
Confirm an ambiguous city produces a clarifying question instead of a silent pick

steps.title: Compile the state into filters plus keyword ranking
steps.learn: Hard constraints become WHERE clauses applied before ranking; soft ones and the free text affect only the score. Pre-filtering guarantees the top 10 obey hard constraints, which is exactly what task success checks.

decision.choice: SQLite with an FTS5 table ranked by bm25(), hard constraints as SQL WHERE clauses
decision.why: The corpus fits on a laptop, FTS5 ships with SQLite and has a bm25() ranking function, and filters plus ranking in one query keep the system easy to debug.

alternatives.name: Vector search with metadata filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for vague text ('fun startup'), but adds an embedding model and index while the refinements here are mostly structured.

alternatives.name: Retrieve top N, then post-filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but tight filters can leave fewer than 10 results even when matches exist.

steps.delegate: Python sqlite3. index.py builds jobs table plus FTS5 virtual table over title and description. search.py: compile(state) returns parameterized SQL (never string-concatenate values), ORDER BY bm25 with soft constraints as score boosts, LIMIT 10. Tests: neq location excludes all NYC rows, gte seniority boundary, empty-text query still filters, SQL injection string is treated as a literal.
verify: For 10 states, check by a separate pandas filter that every returned row satisfies all hard constraints
Time 100 queries and record median latency and the machine

steps.title: Handle empty results, contradictions and resets
steps.learn: A refinement can over-constrain ('senior, remote, not NYC, under 50k' may match nothing). The system should say which constraint emptied the set, offer the smallest relaxation, and never relax a hard constraint without telling the user. 'Start over' must clear state.

decision.choice: On zero results, drop one constraint at a time (newest first), report which one restores results, and ask
decision.why: Explaining the blocking constraint keeps the user in control and is cheap: a handful of count queries on a small table.

alternatives.name: Silently relax until results appear
alternatives.tradeoff: Feels smooth, but returns rows that violate what the user asked for, which task success counts as failure.

alternatives.name: Just say 'no results'
alternatives.tradeoff: Honest, but the user has to guess which refinement broke it.

steps.delegate: Python. relax.py: on empty result, run COUNT queries with each constraint removed, return a suggestion naming the constraint and the count it would restore. Add explicit reset handling. Tests: over-constrained fixture suggests the right constraint, reset clears state, contradiction from update-ops yields a clarifying message.
verify: Write 5 over-constrained conversations and confirm the suggestion names the constraint you expected
Confirm no response ever contains a row that violates a hard constraint without saying so

steps.title: Build the baselines you will compare against
steps.learn: Task success only means something next to alternatives run on the same tasks: (a) last utterance only, (b) full history concatenated and parsed fresh, (c) LLM rewrite to a standalone query, then parsed fresh. Same parser, same index, same model for all.

decision.choice: Three baselines sharing the parser and the SQL engine, differing only in how context reaches the parser
decision.why: Holding everything else fixed isolates the effect of carrying state, which is the project's question.

alternatives.name: Compare against a hosted chat search product
alternatives.tradeoff: Realistic, but nothing is held fixed, so differences cannot be attributed.

alternatives.name: Only compare to last utterance
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy win that proves little; history and rewrite baselines are the serious competitors.

steps.delegate: Python. baselines.py with three runners implementing run(conversation) returning the final top 10 ids and the final parsed state. Each parses its context text from scratch with parse(text) = apply_edits(empty_state, propose_edits(empty_state, text)) and reuses search.py. Same model, temperature 0, same cache. Tests: each runner returns 10 or fewer ids; no runner passes a previous state into propose_edits.
verify: Run every baseline on 5 training conversations and read the outputs side by side
Confirm all runners log the same model name and prompt version

steps.title: Measure task success on the frozen conversations
steps.learn: Grade with an independent checker: a pandas filter built from the hand-written gold constraints, not from the system's parsed state. Report task success overall and per edit type (negate, shift, replace, relax), plus per-turn state exact match, for each method.
steps.delegate: Python. eval.py: load the frozen test file, verify its hash, run each method 3 times (LLM variance), grade final top 10 with gold_filter(df, gold_constraints) written independently of the system, output a CSV with method, run, success, per-edit-type breakdown and latency. Print mean and spread.
verify: Confirm the test-file hash matches the one recorded in the frame step
Report task success per method with spread over 3 runs and the number of conversations
Read 5 failed held-out conversations and label the failing turn and edit type
Record model name, prompt version, machine and the exact command

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (e.g. where rewriting lost a negation), (4) assumptions and limits (scripted conversations, one corpus, one model, your own gold labels).
verify: Part 1 states the question in one sentence
Part 2 gives task success per method with spread, machine and command for every number
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with an example conversation
Part 4 lists assumptions and what this does not prove

projects.title: HNSW from scratch
projects.problem: Understand the recall / speed / memory triangle by building it
projects.proveIt: Recall@10 vs queries/sec, compared to hnswlib and FAISS
projects.question: How do M, efConstruction and ef trade recall, speed and memory in HNSW, and how close does a from-scratch build get to hnswlib and FAISS?

steps.title: Frame the question, metric and dataset
steps.learn: The deliverable is a curve, not a number: Recall@10 (overlap of your top 10 with the exact top 10) against queries per second, one point per ef value. Dataset: sift-128-euclidean from ann-benchmarks (1M train, 10k test, Euclidean, exact top-100 neighbors included).
verify: You can state the one question and the metric pair (Recall@10, single-thread QPS) in one sentence each
You opened the HDF5 file and printed the shapes of train, test, neighbors and distances
You wrote down which three systems will appear on the final plot: yours, hnswlib, FAISS IndexHNSWFlat

steps.title: Build the exact search baseline and recall scorer
steps.learn: Brute force is both the ground truth and the speed floor every ANN index must beat. ann-benchmarks counts a returned neighbor as correct if its distance is within the true k-th distance plus a small epsilon, so ties do not punish you. Your scorer should do the same.

decision.choice: Iterate on a 100k-vector prefix of train with ground truth recomputed by exact search; run final numbers on the full 1M
decision.why: The shipped ground truth is for the full 1M set, so a subset needs its own. A 100k prefix makes a from-scratch build fast enough to rerun many times a day while debugging, and the 1M run then tests that conclusions hold at scale.

alternatives.name: Full 1M from day one
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses the shipped ground truth directly, but every build of a slow from-scratch index costs a long wait, so you debug far less often.

alternatives.name: fashion-mnist-784-euclidean (60k)
alternatives.tradeoff: Small enough to use whole with shipped ground truth, but 784 dims makes each distance costlier and the data is less typical of embedding search.

steps.delegate: Python 3, numpy, h5py, faiss-cpu. Write data.py: load(path, n=None) returns train[:n], test, ground-truth ids and distances; when n is set, recompute exact top-100 with faiss.IndexFlatL2 and take sqrt so distances match the shipped Euclidean ones. Write metrics.py: recall_at_k(found_dists, true_dists, k, eps=1e-3) with the distance-threshold rule; take sqrt of squared-L2 results first. Tests: recall 1.0 for identical, 0.0 for disjoint, ties at the k-th distance count.
verify: Exact search on the 100k subset gives Recall@10 of exactly 1.0 against your recomputed ground truth
Your recomputed top-10 for the full 1M matches the shipped neighbors for a sample of 100 queries
You recorded brute-force QPS on one thread as the floor to beat

steps.title: Choose the language and in-memory layout
steps.learn: HNSW search is pointer chasing: read a node's neighbor list, then fetch those vectors from scattered places. Speed depends on how compactly vectors and adjacency lists sit in memory. SIFT vectors are 128 float32 values, so 512 bytes each before any graph links.

decision.choice: Python with numpy: one contiguous float32 vector matrix plus fixed-width int32 neighbor arrays per layer
decision.why: This is a Starter build whose goal is understanding the triangle, not winning on speed. Contiguous arrays keep distance math vectorized and make memory easy to count exactly, and the gap to hnswlib (C++) becomes a finding you can explain.

alternatives.name: Rust or C++
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick it to compete on QPS with hnswlib; costs more code, and manual memory and concurrency care.

alternatives.name: Python lists of lists for adjacency
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest to write, but per-object overhead hides the true memory cost and slows traversal.

alternatives.name: Numba JIT over numpy arrays
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps Python syntax with much faster loops; adds a compile step and debugging is harder.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + numpy. Create class HNSWIndex(dim, max_elements, M, ef_construction, seed) holding vectors as one float32 array (max_elements x dim), a level per node (int8), layer-0 neighbors as int32 (max_elements x 2M) with a count array, and upper layers as dict level to (ids, int32 neighbor matrix). Add memory_bytes() that sums array nbytes. Tests: memory_bytes matches a hand calculation for small sizes; adding past max_elements raises.
verify: memory_bytes() for 100k SIFT vectors with M=16 matches your hand calculation within 1 percent
You can say how many bytes per node are vectors and how many are graph links

steps.title: Write the distance kernel and count distance calls
steps.learn: Almost all search time is distance computations. hnswlib's l2 space is squared L2, which preserves ranking and skips the square root. Counting distance calls per query gives a hardware-independent cost measure to put next to QPS.

decision.choice: Batch squared L2: compute distances from the query to all unvisited neighbors of a node in one numpy call
decision.why: In Python, one vectorized call over up to 2M neighbors costs far less interpreter overhead than a loop of single distances, and numpy can use SIMD inside the call.

alternatives.name: One distance at a time in a Python loop
alternatives.tradeoff: Mirrors the paper's pseudocode line by line, useful for a first correct version, but very slow.

alternatives.name: Norm expansion |x|^2 - 2x.q + |q|^2
alternatives.tradeoff: Turns batches into a matrix product with precomputed norms; faster for big batches but loses precision for near-equal distances.

steps.delegate: Add distances(q, ids) to HNSWIndex returning squared L2 from q to vectors[ids] as float32 via numpy, and increment a self.dist_count counter by len(ids). Tests: matches a naive per-row loop to 1e-4 relative error on random data; counter increments correctly; empty ids returns an empty array.
verify: Your kernel agrees with faiss.IndexFlatL2 distances on 1,000 random pairs
You measured kernel time for a batch of 32 neighbors with warmup and many repetitions, and wrote down the median

steps.title: Implement greedy beam search on one layer
steps.learn: SEARCH-LAYER (paper alg. 2) keeps a candidate set C (closest first) and a result list W of size ef (furthest first), and stops when the closest unexpanded candidate is further than the furthest result. ef is the beam width that buys recall with distance computations.

decision.choice: heapq min-heap for candidates, negated max-heap for results, visited tracked by a per-query stamp array
decision.why: Two heaps give the paper's two priority queues directly. A stamp array (store the query number per node) avoids allocating a set or clearing a bitmap on every query, which matters when you run 10k queries per ef value.

alternatives.name: Python set for visited
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fine for a first version; allocation and hashing cost grows with ef.

alternatives.name: Boolean array cleared per query
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast lookups, but clearing N entries each query costs O(N) unless you clear only touched ids.

steps.delegate: Implement search_layer(q, entry_ids, ef, level) in HNSWIndex following alg. 2 of arXiv 1603.09320, returning (dist, id) pairs sorted ascending. Use heapq and a stamp array. Tests: on a hand-built 2D graph, the result equals brute force when ef is at least the graph size; result length is min(ef, reachable nodes); no node is expanded twice.
verify: On a fully connected small graph, search_layer returns the exact nearest neighbors
You can point to the line that implements the early stop and explain why it is safe

steps.title: Insert nodes and assign random levels
steps.learn: Each node gets level floor(-ln(U) * mL). The paper suggests mL = 1/ln(M), which matches a skip list with p = 1/M. Insertion (alg. 1) descends greedily with ef=1 to the node's level, then runs SEARCH-LAYER with efConstruction on each lower layer to pick links.

decision.choice: Paper settings: mL = 1/ln(M), Mmax = M on upper layers, Mmax0 = 2M on layer 0
decision.why: The paper shows these autoselected values as reasonable choices in its parameter plots, and they are what you will compare against. Starting from them means any gap to hnswlib comes from your code, not from different knobs.

alternatives.name: mL = 0 (single layer)
alternatives.tradeoff: A flat navigable graph: simpler, and a useful ablation, but the paper reports losing the logarithmic scaling the hierarchy provides.

alternatives.name: Mmax0 = M
alternatives.tradeoff: Less memory on layer 0, but the paper's Mmax0 plot suggests slower search than near 2M.

steps.delegate: Implement add(vec) in HNSWIndex per alg. 1 of arXiv 1603.09320 with a seeded numpy RNG for levels, entry point update when a new top level appears, bidirectional links, and pruning when a list exceeds Mmax or Mmax0 (call a select_neighbors function, simple version for now). Tests: level histogram roughly geometric with ratio near 1/M; no list exceeds its cap; every link is to a valid id; same seed gives an identical graph.
verify: Level histogram for 100k inserts falls by roughly a factor of M per level
Same seed and data produce byte-identical neighbor arrays on two runs
No neighbor list exceeds Mmax or Mmax0 after building

steps.title: Select neighbors with the diversity heuristic
steps.learn: The simple rule links the M closest candidates. The heuristic (alg. 4) keeps a candidate only if it is closer to the new node than to any neighbor already kept, which spreads links in different directions. The paper reports it helps most at high recall and on clustered data.

decision.choice: Heuristic (alg. 4) with extendCandidates off, keeping the simple rule as a switch for an ablation
decision.why: SIFT is real data, not uniform noise, and high recall is where you will compare against the libraries. The paper sets extendCandidates false by default and describes it as useful only for extremely clustered data.

alternatives.name: Simple: M closest (alg. 3)
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but the paper shows search can get stuck at cluster boundaries and fail to reach high recall.

alternatives.name: Heuristic with extendCandidates on
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for extremely clustered data; adds distance computations at build time.

alternatives.name: keepPrunedConnections on
alternatives.tradeoff: Fills lists back up to a fixed size with discarded candidates; more links and memory per node.

steps.delegate: Implement select_neighbors_heuristic(q_id, candidates, M, extend=False, keep_pruned=False) per alg. 4 of arXiv 1603.09320, used both at insertion and when shrinking full lists. Add a flag on HNSWIndex to choose simple or heuristic. Tests: on two well-separated 2D clusters the heuristic links across clusters while the simple rule does not; output size never exceeds M.
verify: On the 100k subset at a fixed ef, Recall@10 with the heuristic is at least as high as with the simple rule
The two-cluster toy test shows at least one cross-cluster link only with the heuristic

steps.title: Expose k-NN search and the ef knob
steps.learn: K-NN-SEARCH (alg. 5) descends with ef=1 to layer 0, then searches layer 0 with ef and returns the best k. hnswlib documents that ef cannot be lower than k. ef only changes query time; M and efConstruction are fixed at build.

decision.choice: knn_query(q, k, ef) with ef as a per-call argument, swept over 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320, 640
decision.why: A per-call ef lets you trace the whole recall vs QPS curve from one built index, which is exactly the prove-it plot, and doubling steps space points evenly on a log axis.

alternatives.name: ef fixed at build time
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler API, but every curve point needs a rebuild.

alternatives.name: Target-recall auto-tuning
alternatives.tradeoff: Picks ef per workload for users; needs a held-out query set and hides the knob you are trying to understand.

steps.delegate: Implement knn_query(queries, k=10, ef=50) per alg. 5 returning (ids, dists) arrays shaped (nq, k); raise ValueError if ef < k or index is empty. Record mean distance computations per query. Tests: with ef equal to the dataset size on 2k points, results equal brute force; ef < k raises; returned distances are sorted ascending.
verify: Recall@10 rises monotonically (within noise) as ef grows on the 100k subset
You logged mean distance computations per query for each ef value

steps.title: Account for memory, save and load, handle edge cases
steps.learn: hnswlib documents graph memory as roughly M * 8 to 10 bytes per element, on top of the raw vectors. Measuring your own bytes per node for several M values gives the memory side of the triangle. A real index also needs save and load and must survive duplicates and tiny inputs.

decision.choice: Save the vector matrix as its own .npy (load with mmap_mode='r') and the graph arrays plus parameters with numpy.savez
decision.why: The arrays are already the index, so saving is just writing them out; memory-mapping vectors lets a large index open without reading it all first, and the file size is a second memory measurement.

alternatives.name: pickle the Python object
alternatives.tradeoff: One line, but slow for big arrays, tied to Python versions, and unsafe to load from untrusted files.

alternatives.name: Custom binary format
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for cross-language use, like hnswlib's save_index; costs a format spec and versioning.

steps.delegate: Add save(path) and load(path) to HNSWIndex: vectors via np.save to a .npy file loaded with np.load(mmap_mode='r'); graph arrays, M, ef_construction, mL, seed, entry point and max level via numpy.savez. Tests: save then load gives identical query results; loaded vectors are a numpy.memmap; inserting duplicate vectors does not crash or self-link; k larger than the index size raises a clear error; a one-element index returns that element.
verify: Loaded index returns identical ids to the in-memory index on 1,000 queries
You tabulated graph bytes per node for M = 8, 16, 32 and compared to the M * 8 to 10 bytes rule

steps.title: Measure it against hnswlib and FAISS
steps.learn: Fair comparison means same data, same M and efConstruction, same ef sweep, same thread count. hnswlib's init_index defaults are M=16, ef_construction=200; FAISS HNSW defaults efConstruction to 40, so set it explicitly. Time queries only, after warmup, and record build time and memory separately.

decision.choice: Single-threaded queries for all three systems, M=16 and efConstruction=200 everywhere, ef swept identically
decision.why: One thread isolates algorithm and implementation quality from parallelism. Matching build parameters removes the most common unfair gap, since FAISS and hnswlib ship different efConstruction defaults.

alternatives.name: Each library at its own defaults
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows out-of-the-box behavior, but differences then mix parameters with implementation.

alternatives.name: All cores, batch queries
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to production throughput, but thread scheduling noise and library threading differences blur the comparison.

steps.delegate: Write bench.py (Python, hnswlib, faiss-cpu, h5py, matplotlib). Build once each: hnswlib.Index('l2', 128), init_index(M=16, ef_construction=200); faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(128, 16), hnsw.efConstruction=200. Per ef set p.set_ef(ef) and index.hnsw.efSearch=ef, run warmup then 3 timed passes, one thread (knn_query num_threads=1, faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1)). CSV: system, ef, recall@10, median QPS, build s, memory bytes. Plot recall vs QPS, log y.
verify: The CSV has all three systems at every ef value, and the plot uses a log scale for QPS
You recorded CPU model, RAM, OS, library versions and the exact command used
Repeated runs agree within 10 percent on QPS; if not, you found and removed the noise source
A flame graph or profiler output shows where your implementation spends query time

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer the one question with the curve. Explain gaps with your own counters: distance computations per query separate algorithm quality from implementation speed, so you can say whether you lose on recall per distance call or only on time per call.
verify: Part 1: the write-up opens with the one question about the recall, speed and memory triangle
Part 2: every claim has a number with the machine, library versions and command that produced it
Part 3: it explains the surprising results, such as the QPS gap, using distance-call counts or profiles
Part 4: it lists assumptions and limits, such as one dataset, one thread, no deletes or filters

projects.title: Filtered ANN under tight filters
projects.problem: With a 1%-selective filter, graph search loses recall or scans everything
projects.proveIt: Recall and latency at 50%, 10%, 1% selectivity
projects.question: Which filtered vector search strategy keeps recall@10 high without scanning everything as filter selectivity drops from 50% to 1%?

steps.title: Frame the question, dataset and controlled selectivity
steps.learn: Metric: recall@10 and latency at 50%, 10% and 1% filter selectivity. Data: ANN_SIFT1M (128-d SIFT vectors, fvecs format) from the TEXMEX corpus. Attach a synthetic integer attribute uniform in [0,100) so 'attr < s' hits an exact selectivity you control.
verify: Download ANN_SIFT1M and confirm base, query and dimension counts yourself from the files
Generate attributes with a fixed seed and check the measured fraction for each filter is within 0.1% of target
Split queries into a tuning set and a held-out set now; record which ids are held out

steps.title: Compute exact filtered ground truth independently
steps.learn: The ground truth shipped with SIFT1M is for unfiltered search, so it is wrong for every filtered query. Compute exact top 10 among matching vectors only, with a brute-force method that shares no code with any index under test.

decision.choice: Exact search with faiss IndexFlatL2 over the matching subset per filter, cached to disk
decision.why: Exact flat search is correct by construction, fast enough at 1M x 128 dims, and independent of the graph code being graded.

alternatives.name: NumPy matrix products
alternatives.tradeoff: Even more transparent, but slower and needs care with memory for 1M rows at once.

alternatives.name: High-ef HNSW as 'ground truth'
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper, but grades the system with its own kind of approximation, so recall is overstated.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy, faiss-cpu. gt.py: read fvecs, for each selectivity build the mask, slice base vectors, run IndexFlatL2 search for k=10, map back to global ids, save gt_{s}.npy. Tests: on a 10k subset compare to a pure numpy brute force; a 100% filter reproduces the shipped unfiltered ground truth for the top 10.
verify: Confirm the 100% filter matches the shipped ground truth top 10 on all queries you test
Spot check 5 queries at 1%: every ground-truth id passes the filter

steps.title: Baseline 1: pre-filter, then scan the matching subset
steps.learn: With a 1% filter only 10k of 1M vectors match, so an exact scan of just those is cheap and has perfect recall. Its cost grows with the match count, which is why it loses at 50%. This is the bar any index must beat at tight filters.

decision.choice: Bitmap of matching ids, exact distance scan over only those rows
decision.why: Perfect recall and simple; it shows where graph search stops being worth it.

alternatives.name: Inverted list per attribute value
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast lookup of matching ids for equality filters, but range filters need extra structure.

alternatives.name: Skip this baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves a day, but you cannot claim a graph method helps at 1% without it.

steps.delegate: Python plus faiss-cpu: given a boolean mask, gather matching ids and run exact search on them (or faiss IndexFlatL2 search with SearchParameters sel set to an IDSelectorBitmap built with np.packbits(mask, bitorder='little')). Tests: recall 1.0 vs ground truth at all selectivities.
verify: Record recall@10 (expect 1.0) and per-query latency at 50%, 10% and 1% on tuning queries
Confirm the bitmap bit order by checking 10 known ids are selected

steps.title: Baseline 2: unfiltered HNSW, then post-filter
steps.learn: Search unfiltered for k' candidates, then drop non-matching ones. At 1% selectivity you expect only about k'/100 survivors, so k' must grow roughly with 1/selectivity, and recall collapses when it does not.

decision.choice: hnswlib index (M=16, ef_construction=200), oversample k' = k / selectivity times a safety factor, with ef >= k'
decision.why: It is the simplest strategy most systems start with, and it makes the 1% failure visible.

alternatives.name: Fixed k' (e.g. 100) for all filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but at 1% it often returns fewer than 10 results.

alternatives.name: Iteratively double k' until 10 survive
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovers recall, but latency becomes unpredictable at tight filters.

steps.delegate: Python hnswlib. Build one index on SIFT1M base with init_index(max_elements, M=16, ef_construction=200), save it. postfilter.py: for each query, set_ef(max(k', 10)), knn_query k', filter by mask, keep 10. Report recall and how often fewer than 10 survive. Tests: 100% filter equals plain search.
verify: Plot recall@10 vs k' at each selectivity on tuning queries
Count queries at 1% that return fewer than 10 results for each k'

steps.title: Filter inside graph traversal and see why it slows at 1%
steps.learn: hnswlib's knn_query(filter=...) and faiss HNSW with SearchParametersHNSW(sel=...) still walk non-matching nodes but only add matching ones to results. In hnswlib the search stops only once ef matching results are held, so at 1% it visits far more nodes, approaching a scan.

decision.choice: Measure both hnswlib filter and faiss IndexHNSWFlat with an IDSelectorBitmap, sweeping ef/efSearch
decision.why: Two implementations of the same idea separate algorithm behavior from library overhead (hnswlib's Python filter callback is limited by the GIL).

alternatives.name: Only hnswlib
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer moving parts, but the Python callback cost can be mistaken for an algorithm cost.

alternatives.name: A vector database (Qdrant, Weaviate)
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to production, but planners and full-scan fallbacks hide which strategy actually ran.

steps.delegate: Python. intraversal.py: hnswlib knn_query(q, k=10, num_threads=1, filter=lambda i: mask[i]); faiss IndexHNSWFlat(128, 16) with search(..., params=faiss.SearchParametersHNSW(efSearch=ef, sel=faiss.IDSelectorBitmap(...))). Count distance computations where possible (time as fallback). Tests: 100% filter matches unfiltered search; all results pass the mask.
verify: At each selectivity, record recall@10 and latency for ef in 16, 64, 256 on tuning queries
Compare 1% latency to the pre-filter scan and note which is faster

steps.title: Build ACORN and compare predicate-subgraph traversal
steps.learn: ACORN builds a denser HNSW (neighbor lists expanded by a factor gamma, compressed with M_beta) so the subgraph of matching nodes stays navigable, then traverses only matching neighbors. ACORN-1 skips the denser build and expands neighbors at search time.

decision.choice: The authors' C++ IndexACORNFlat (built on faiss) with ACORN-gamma and ACORN-1 variants
decision.why: Using the reference code tests the idea as published instead of your reimplementation of it.

alternatives.name: Weaviate's ACORN filter strategy
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to run, but it is Weaviate's own implementation inspired by the paper, with other planner logic around it.

alternatives.name: Qdrant filterable HNSW (payload index edges)
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds extra edges per indexed field; Qdrant's docs note combined strict filters can still leave disconnected components.

steps.delegate: C++17. Clone stanford-futuredata/ACORN, build with cmake as in its README. Write bench_acorn.cpp: load SIFT1M fvecs, build IndexACORNFlat(d=128, M, gamma, metadata, M_beta) (check the header signature) and ACORN-1 (gamma=1, M_beta=2M), build the per-query filter map in batches (it is nq x N bytes), output ids for the Python recall scorer. Record build time and index memory.
verify: Record build time and peak memory for ACORN-gamma vs plain HNSW
Record recall@10 vs latency at 50%, 10%, 1% using the same Python scorer and ground truth

steps.title: Add a selectivity-based planner with a flat-scan cutoff
steps.learn: Production engines estimate how many points match and switch strategy: Qdrant uses full-scan below a size threshold and Weaviate can switch to flat search when a filter is very restrictive. Your planner picks scan vs graph per query from the mask's count.

decision.choice: Exact count from the bitmap, cutoff tuned on tuning queries only
decision.why: The bitmap gives an exact count for free here, so the only open question is where the crossover lies on this machine.

alternatives.name: Estimate selectivity from histograms
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed when filters combine many fields and exact counts are expensive; estimates can be badly wrong for correlated fields.

alternatives.name: Always use one strategy
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but leaves either the 1% or the 50% case slow.

steps.delegate: Python. planner.py: choose(mask) returns 'scan' if mask.sum() < cutoff else 'graph'. Script sweeps the cutoff on tuning queries and picks the one minimizing mean latency subject to recall@10 >= your target. Tests: boundary behavior at exactly cutoff.
verify: Plot latency of scan and graph vs selectivity and mark the crossover
Confirm the cutoff was chosen without touching held-out queries

steps.title: Stress test with correlated and anti-correlated filters
steps.learn: Uniform random attributes are the easy case. If matching vectors sit far from the query (filter anti-correlated with the query), graph search must travel through many non-matching nodes. Weaviate's docs note ACORN helps most when the filter has low correlation with the query vector.

decision.choice: Derive a second attribute from k-means cluster id, and build filters that match the query's cluster or exclude it
decision.why: Cluster-based attributes give controlled positive and negative correlation at the same selectivity, so you can separate correlation from selectivity.

alternatives.name: Use real tags (YFCC-10M from big-ann-benchmarks)
alternatives.tradeoff: Realistic correlations, but 10M vectors and multi-tag filters make the run much heavier and harder to control.

alternatives.name: Only uniform filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but hides the case where graph methods break.

steps.delegate: Python, faiss-cpu. corr.py: k-means (faiss.Kmeans) with 100 clusters on base vectors, attribute = cluster id; for each query build filters of chosen selectivity that include or exclude its nearest centroid's cluster; regenerate exact ground truth with gt.py. Tests: measured selectivity within tolerance, positive filter contains the query's own cluster.
verify: Report recall@10 and latency per method for positive vs negative correlation at 1%
Confirm ground truth was recomputed for each new filter

steps.title: Measure recall and latency at 50%, 10% and 1%
steps.learn: One harness for every method: same held-out queries, same ground truth, single thread, warm caches, build time excluded from query latency. Report recall@10 with p50 and p99 per-query latency (or QPS) per selectivity, as curves over ef rather than single points.
steps.delegate: Python bench.py: methods = scan, postfilter, hnswlib filter, faiss sel, ACORN (ids loaded from its C++ output with timings), planner. For each selectivity and ef: run held-out queries one at a time after a warmup pass, record per-query latency with time.perf_counter_ns, recall@10 vs cached ground truth. Write a CSV and plot recall vs latency per selectivity. Pin thread count to 1 in every library.
verify: Every method uses the same held-out query ids and ground-truth files (check hashes)
Report p50 and p99 latency, not just the mean, for each method and selectivity
Repeat the full run twice and confirm the curves agree within your noise band
Record CPU model, RAM, OS, library versions and the exact command

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (e.g. where the scan beat the graph), (4) assumptions and limits (SIFT1M only, synthetic attributes, single thread, in-memory).
verify: Part 1 states the question in one sentence
Part 2 has recall and p50/p99 latency per method at 50%, 10%, 1% with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a mechanism (nodes visited, distance counts)
Part 4 lists assumptions and what this does not prove

projects.title: Quantization ladder
projects.problem: Vectors in RAM are expensive
projects.proveIt: Memory vs recall for float32, int8, PQ, binary and RaBitQ, each with reranking
projects.question: How much Recall@10 does each rung (float32, int8, PQ, binary, RaBitQ) lose per byte saved, and how much does reranking win back?

steps.title: Frame the question, metric and dataset
steps.learn: The deliverable is one chart: Recall@10 against bytes per vector in RAM, two points per rung (codes only, codes plus rerank). Dataset: sift-128-euclidean from ann-benchmarks (1M base vectors, 10k queries, 128 dims, exact top-100 neighbors shipped).

decision.choice: Split the 10k queries now: 1,000 for tuning, 9,000 frozen for final numbers, saved to disk with a fixed seed
decision.why: Every rung has knobs (PQ size, query bits, rerank depth). Tuning them on the same queries you report would flatter every method. Freezing the split before any code runs keeps the final chart honest.

alternatives.name: Tune and report on all 10k queries
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but knob choices leak into the reported recall and you cannot tell how much.

alternatives.name: Tune on queries sampled from the base set
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps all 10k test queries for reporting, but base vectors are in the index, so their neighbor structure differs from real queries.

verify: You opened the HDF5 file and printed the shapes of train, test, neighbors and distances
The tuning and frozen query id files exist, are disjoint, and have 1,000 and 9,000 ids
You wrote the five rungs and the two memory columns (codes only, codes plus rerank store) as the chart's axes

steps.title: Build the float32 baseline, recall scorer and byte counter
steps.learn: float32 brute force is the top rung: 4 * d bytes per vector (512 for SIFT) and recall 1.0 by definition. The byte counter must separate per-vector code size from fixed costs such as codebooks or trained ranges, which shrink to almost nothing per vector at 1M.

decision.choice: Bytes per vector = code size + trained state / N, computed from the index, not process RSS
decision.why: Faiss flat-code indexes store ntotal * code_size bytes, so the code size is exact and reproducible. RSS mixes in Python, the loaded dataset and allocator slack, which would swamp the difference between 16 and 24 bytes.

alternatives.name: Measure process RSS before and after add
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches hidden overhead, but noisy and allocator dependent; keep it as a cross-check, not the headline.

alternatives.name: Serialized index file size
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy and includes trained state, but adds format headers and says nothing about runtime buffers.

steps.delegate: Python 3, numpy, h5py, faiss-cpu. data.py: load sift-128-euclidean, return train, tune/frozen queries and ground truth. metrics.py: recall_at_k(found_ids, gt_ids, k=10). memory.py: bytes_per_vector(index, n) using index.sa_code_size() plus a per-method fixed-state size you pass in. Baseline: faiss.IndexFlatL2(128). Tests: flat index gives recall 1.0; recall of disjoint ids is 0; bytes_per_vector of IndexFlatL2 is 512.
verify: IndexFlatL2 gives Recall@10 of 1.0 on the tuning queries (any shortfall is explained by tied distances, checked against the shipped distances)
Your byte counter reports 512 bytes per vector for the float32 rung
You recorded single-thread brute-force query time as the speed reference

steps.title: Add the int8 rung with a scalar quantizer
steps.learn: Scalar quantization maps each dimension to 256 levels, so a vector costs d bytes (4x smaller). The range per dimension is learned from training data; values outside it get clipped, so the training sample must cover the data.

decision.choice: faiss IndexScalarQuantizer with QT_8bit (per-dimension min and max range, the default range statistic)
decision.why: SIFT dimensions do not share one range, so a range per dimension spends the 256 levels where each dimension actually varies. It is one line in faiss and a well-understood middle rung between float32 and the 1-bit methods.

alternatives.name: QT_8bit_uniform (one range for all dims)
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller trained state and simpler math, but wastes levels on dimensions with narrow ranges.

alternatives.name: QT_fp16
alternatives.tradeoff: 2x compression with tiny loss and no training; pick it if int8 recall disappoints, at twice the bytes.

alternatives.name: Hand-written numpy quantizer
alternatives.tradeoff: Teaches the math exactly, but slower search unless you also write a fast distance kernel.

steps.delegate: Add rung_sq8.py: build faiss.IndexScalarQuantizer(128, faiss.ScalarQuantizer.QT_8bit, faiss.METRIC_L2), train on a 100k random sample of train (fixed seed), add all 1M, search k=10. Return ids, distances, bytes per vector (code size 128 plus the trained range state divided by N). Tests: code size is 128 bytes; decoding with sa_decode then re-encoding gives the same codes; recall on tuning queries is above the 1-bit rungs once those exist.
verify: The index reports a code size of 128 bytes per vector
You recorded int8 Recall@10 on the tuning queries next to the float32 row
You checked the maximum absolute error between original and decoded vectors on 1,000 samples

steps.title: Add the PQ rung and sweep its code size
steps.learn: PQ splits a vector into M sub-vectors and replaces each with the id of its nearest of 2^nbits learned centroids, so with 8 bits a vector costs M bytes. Distances are computed in the compressed domain via per-query lookup tables, and d must be a multiple of M.

decision.choice: faiss IndexPQ(128, M, 8) swept over M = 8, 16, 32, 64, trained on a fixed 100k sample
decision.why: A sweep turns PQ into a curve on the memory axis instead of one point, and M = 16 (16 bytes) lands next to the binary rung, so the chart compares methods at equal bytes.

alternatives.name: OPQ rotation before PQ (factory OPQ16,PQ16)
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns a rotation that balances sub-vectors, usually better recall at the same bytes, but adds training time and a d x d matrix.

alternatives.name: PQ fast scan (4-bit codes, PQ32x4fs)
alternatives.tradeoff: Much faster SIMD scanning; pick it when query speed matters, at coarser 16-centroid sub-quantizers.

steps.delegate: Add rung_pq.py: for M in (8, 16, 32, 64) build faiss.IndexPQ(128, M, 8), train on the same 100k seeded sample, add 1M, search k=10. Record train time, add time, code size (index.sa_code_size()) and codebook bytes (M * 256 * (128 / M) * 4) divided by N. Tests: code size equals M; an assert rejects M that does not divide 128; results are identical across two runs with the same seed and thread count.
verify: Code sizes are exactly 8, 16, 32 and 64 bytes for the four M values
Recall@10 rises with M on the tuning queries; you noted where it flattens
Training logs show no faiss warning about too few training points per centroid

steps.title: Add the binary rung: sign bits and Hamming distance
steps.learn: Binary quantization keeps one bit per dimension (d / 8 bytes, 16 for SIFT) and ranks by Hamming distance, which CPUs compute with popcount. The sign of a raw coordinate only carries information if the data is spread around zero, so where you put the zero matters.

decision.choice: Subtract the training-set mean, take the sign, pack with numpy.packbits, search with faiss IndexBinaryFlat
decision.why: Centering puts the threshold in the middle of each dimension's distribution, so bits split the data instead of being nearly constant. IndexBinaryFlat gives an exhaustive popcount search, so the recall you measure is the code's, not an index's.

alternatives.name: Raw sign without centering
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero setup, but if coordinates are mostly non-negative most bits are identical and recall collapses; worth one run to see it.

alternatives.name: Random rotation, then center and sign
alternatives.tradeoff: Spreads information evenly across bits (the RaBitQ insight) at the cost of a d x d multiply per vector and query.

alternatives.name: numpy bitwise_count over XOR
alternatives.tradeoff: No faiss needed (numpy 2.0 or newer) and easy to read, but much slower for 1M x 9k queries.

steps.delegate: Add rung_binary.py: mean = train_sample.mean(0); codes = np.packbits((x - mean) > 0, axis=1) giving uint8 arrays of 16 bytes; index = faiss.IndexBinaryFlat(128); add codes; encode queries the same way; search k=10. Also run the uncentered variant. Tests: code shape is (N, 16); Hamming distance of a code to itself is 0; flipping one input sign changes distance by exactly 1.
verify: You printed the min of the raw data and the fraction of 1 bits per dimension, before and after centering
Centered and uncentered binary recall are both in your table, with the gap explained
Bytes per vector for this rung is 16 plus the stored mean divided by N

steps.title: Add the RaBitQ rung with a random rotation
steps.learn: RaBitQ also stores about one bit per dimension, but after a random rotation and with a few per-vector correction factors, so its distance estimate is unbiased with a provable error bound. Queries stay more precise: faiss quantizes them to qb bits (default 4), making the comparison asymmetric.

decision.choice: faiss IndexRaBitQ(128, METRIC_L2) wrapped in IndexPreTransform with a seeded RandomRotationMatrix; sweep qb over 1, 4, 8
decision.why: The faiss docs say RaBitQ needs random rotation preprocessing, and the faiss tests build it exactly this way. Its code is d/8 + 8 bytes (24 for SIFT), so it sits next to PQ16 and binary on the chart, which is the comparison the project is about.

alternatives.name: Multi-bit RaBitQ (factory RaBitQ4)
alternatives.tradeoff: More bits per dimension for higher recall without reranking, at d x nbits / 8 + 20 bytes per vector (84 for SIFT at 4 bits); add it as an extra rung if time allows.

alternatives.name: Implement RaBitQ from the paper in numpy
alternatives.tradeoff: Deepest understanding of the estimator, but you must also match faiss on a sample to trust your numbers.

steps.delegate: Add rung_rabitq.py: rrot = faiss.RandomRotationMatrix(128, 128); rrot.init(123); index = faiss.IndexPreTransform(rrot, faiss.IndexRaBitQ(128, faiss.METRIC_L2)); train on the 100k sample, add 1M. For qb in (1, 4, 8) search with faiss.RaBitQSearchParameters(qb=qb). Tests: code size of the inner index is 24 bytes; two builds with the same seed return identical ids; recall with qb=8 is not lower than with qb=1 on tuning queries.
verify: The inner IndexRaBitQ reports a 24-byte code for d = 128
You have RaBitQ recall at qb = 1, 4 and 8 on the tuning queries
At similar bytes, you compared RaBitQ against PQ16 and centered binary in one table

steps.title: Add one shared rerank stage for every rung
steps.learn: Reranking takes the top k * factor candidates from compressed codes and reorders them with exact float32 distances. It recovers neighbors that the codes ranked slightly too low, but it needs the full vectors somewhere, so the memory claim depends on where they live.

decision.choice: Own rerank function that reads the float32 vectors from a numpy.memmap on disk, sweeping factor over 1, 2, 5, 10, 20
decision.why: The point of quantizing is that full vectors are not in RAM. A memmap keeps them on disk and touches only the candidate rows, so RAM stays at code size and the cost shows up as rerank reads you can count.

alternatives.name: faiss IndexRefineFlat (factory suffix RFlat)
alternatives.tradeoff: One line and fast, with k_factor as the knob, but it keeps all float32 vectors in RAM, which erases the memory saving you are measuring.

alternatives.name: Rerank from int8 codes (faiss Refine(SQ8))
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps everything in RAM at 128 extra bytes per vector; pick it when disk reads are too slow, at lower final recall than float32.

steps.delegate: Add rerank.py: save train as a raw float32 .npy; rerank(query, cand_ids, vecs_memmap, k) loads np.load(path, mmap_mode='r'), gathers the candidate rows, computes exact squared L2, returns the top k. Wrap each rung: search k * factor, then rerank. Count rows read per query. Tests: with factor large enough to include all true neighbors, recall is 1.0; reranking float32 candidates changes nothing; output is sorted by distance.
verify: For each rung you have recall at each factor and the rows read per query
Reranked recall never drops below the codes-only recall at the same rung
The chart shows reranked points with RAM equal to code size and disk bytes noted separately

steps.title: Make the ladder one reproducible harness with edge cases
steps.learn: Five rungs times several knobs is a grid, and grids drift unless every run reads one config. Each rung also has its own shape rules: PQ needs M to divide d, binary needs d a multiple of 8, and every trained rung needs a seed and a sample size.

decision.choice: One YAML grid of (rung, knobs, rerank factor) and a runner that writes one CSV row per cell, with seeds and versions
decision.why: A single grid makes the chart regenerable from one command and makes the frozen-query run a one-flag change, so nothing is tuned by hand after the split.

alternatives.name: One script per rung
alternatives.tradeoff: Quicker to start, but settings drift between scripts and the final comparison stops being like for like.

alternatives.name: Faiss index_factory strings only
alternatives.tradeoff: Compact and standard, but your own binary and memmap rerank paths do not fit the factory, so you still need a wrapper.

steps.delegate: Write run_grid.py (Python, PyYAML, pandas): read grid.yaml, build each rung once, save trained state with faiss.write_index (or np.save for binary), run every rerank factor, append CSV rows: rung, knobs, factor, split, recall@10, bytes_per_vector, rows_read, ms_per_query, faiss version, seed. Validate shapes up front with clear errors. Tests: rerun of a cached cell reproduces recall exactly; invalid M raises before training; --split frozen refuses to run if knobs differ from the tuned file.
verify: Deleting the CSV and rerunning one command regenerates identical recall values
An invalid configuration (M = 12 for d = 128) fails with a clear message before any training
Your chosen knobs per rung are written to a file before the frozen split is ever run

steps.title: Measure it on the frozen queries
steps.learn: The chart's x axis is bytes, but speed matters to whoever reads it, so time each rung too, after warmup, on one thread. Cold memmap reads hit the disk while warm ones hit the page cache, so rerank timing must say which.

decision.choice: One thread, warmup then three timed passes, median ms per query; rerank timed cold and warm
decision.why: One thread isolates the code format from parallelism. The cold and warm split shows the real price of keeping full vectors on disk, which is the tradeoff reranking hides.

alternatives.name: All cores, batched queries
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to production throughput, but faiss threading and the binary path parallelize differently, blurring the comparison.

alternatives.name: Recall only, no timing
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleaner story about information loss, but a reader cannot judge whether rerank depth 20 is affordable.

steps.delegate: Add bench mode to run_grid.py: faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1), one warmup pass, three timed passes, median ms per query. Cold rerank: drop the page cache or use a fresh file copy before the pass, and document the method. Plot recall@10 vs bytes per vector (log x), codes-only and reranked markers per rung, with matplotlib. Tests: plot script fails if any rung lacks a frozen-split row.
verify: Every rung has codes-only and reranked rows on the frozen queries in the CSV
You recorded CPU model, RAM, disk type, OS, faiss and numpy versions and the exact command
Repeated timed passes agree within 10 percent, or you found the noise source

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer the question with the chart: which rung gives the best recall per byte without reranking, and which with it. Explain surprises with your own measurements, such as bit balance after centering or rows read per query.
verify: Part 1: the write-up opens with the one question about recall lost per byte saved
Part 2: every claim has a number from the frozen split with the machine, versions and command
Part 3: it explains surprising results, such as uncentered binary or PQ vs RaBitQ at equal bytes
Part 4: it lists assumptions and limits, such as one dataset, flat search only, no graph index

projects.title: Deletes and updates without decay
projects.problem: HNSW recall degrades as nodes are deleted and reinserted
projects.proveIt: Recall over 10 rounds of 10% churn
projects.question: Over 10 rounds of 10% delete-and-reinsert churn, how far does HNSW recall fall under each update policy, and what does keeping it flat cost?

steps.title: Frame the question, metric and churn protocol
steps.learn: The deliverable is recall per round: Recall@10 at a fixed ef for rounds 0 to 10, one line per policy. Each round deletes a random 10% of live points, then reinserts those same vectors, so the dataset (and the true neighbors) never change and any drop is the index decaying.

decision.choice: sift-128-euclidean, 100k-vector prefix, all 10k test queries; save all 10 deletion sets now, fixed seed
decision.why: Reinserting the same vectors is the protocol FreshDiskANN used on SIFT1M, and it keeps ground truth fixed. Freezing the churn schedule and queries before any tuning means every policy faces the identical update stream.

alternatives.name: Sliding window (delete old, insert new vectors)
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to a real feed, but ground truth changes every round and must be recomputed, and recall changes mix data shift with index decay.

alternatives.name: Full 1M from day one
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches published experiments, but a Python repair implementation would be too slow to iterate on; use it for a final confirmation run.

verify: Ten deletion-set files exist, each exactly 10% of the live set, generated from one recorded seed
You wrote the fixed ef and k = 10 that every round and policy will use
You listed the policies that will appear on the final plot before writing any of them

steps.title: Build the churn harness, ground truth and recall scorer
steps.learn: Every policy must sit behind the same interface (delete, insert, search, stats) so the churn loop cannot favor one. Ground truth comes from exact search over the 100k prefix, computed once, because the reinsert protocol keeps the set fixed.

decision.choice: A Python Strategy interface with external ids that the harness owns, and a loop that measures after every round
decision.why: Some update paths need fresh internal labels for reinserted points. If the harness owns external ids and each strategy maps them, recall is always scored on the same ids, never on whatever the index happens to call them.

alternatives.name: Use the index's own labels as ids
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but policies that relabel on reinsert would need special cases in the scorer, which is where silent bugs hide.

alternatives.name: Separate script per policy
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster to start, but loops drift apart (order of deletes, when you measure) and the comparison breaks.

steps.delegate: Python 3, numpy, h5py, faiss-cpu. data.py loads the 100k prefix and computes exact top-100 with faiss.IndexFlatL2. strategy.py defines Strategy with build(vecs, ids), delete(ids), insert(vecs, ids), search(q, k, ef) returning external ids, stats() returning a dict. churn.py runs build, measures, then 10 rounds of delete, reinsert, measure, writing CSV rows. Tests: an exact brute-force Strategy gets recall 1.0 every round; deletion sets never contain already-deleted ids.
verify: The brute-force strategy scores Recall@10 of exactly 1.0 in all 11 measurements
The CSV has one row per round with recall, update seconds and the stats fields
Your recomputed top-10 for the prefix matches an independent exact search on 100 queries

steps.title: Set the ceiling: rebuild from scratch every round
steps.learn: Rebuilding gives the recall a fresh graph has on this data, so it is the line every update policy should stay near. Its cost (full build time per round) is what in-place updates are trying to avoid; FreshDiskANN names periodic rebuilds as the expensive industry practice it replaces.

decision.choice: hnswlib with M=16, ef_construction=200, rebuilt with the same parameters after every round
decision.why: hnswlib is the reference HNSW implementation and the same library as two of the update policies, so the ceiling differs from them only in how updates were applied.

alternatives.name: No ceiling, compare to round 0 only
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves build time, but round 0 is one random graph; a per-round rebuild shows how much recall varies with no churn at all.

alternatives.name: Rebuild only at round 10
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper, and still gives an end point, but hides whether build randomness alone moves recall between rounds.

steps.delegate: Add RebuildStrategy: on each round, hnswlib.Index('l2', 128), init_index(max_elements=n, M=16, ef_construction=200, random_seed=round), add all live vectors with their external ids using add_items(..., num_threads=1) so builds are deterministic. Record build seconds in stats(). Tests: recall at round 0 equals a direct single-threaded hnswlib build with the same seed; after 10 rounds the live count is still 100k.
verify: You have rebuild recall for all 11 measurements and its spread across rounds
You recorded build seconds per round as the cost every other policy is compared to

steps.title: Policy A: tombstones with mark_deleted, reinsert in place
steps.learn: hnswlib's mark_deleted hides a point from results, but search still walks through it, so the graph keeps its routes. Re-adding a deleted label (with replacement disabled) unmarks it and runs the update path that repairs its neighbors, so the node keeps its slot.

decision.choice: init_index with allow_replace_deleted=False; delete via mark_deleted, reinsert via add_items with the same labels
decision.why: It is the default hnswlib path and keeps memory constant, since no new slots are used. It isolates one question: does repeatedly running the update repair on the same nodes erode the graph?

alternatives.name: Reinsert under new labels into new slots
alternatives.tradeoff: Fresh insertion for each point, but the graph grows 10% per round with dead nodes; needs resize_index and memory grows.

alternatives.name: Delete and never reinsert
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows pure tombstone behavior, but the dataset shrinks, so recall is no longer comparable to the fixed ground truth.

steps.delegate: Add TombstoneStrategy over hnswlib: init_index(max_elements=n, M=16, ef_construction=200, allow_replace_deleted=False); delete calls mark_deleted per id; insert calls add_items(vecs, ids). search sets set_ef(ef), uses knn_query(num_threads=1) and catches RuntimeError from too few results, recording it as a failure. Stats: element_count, update seconds, index_file_size(). Tests: a deleted id never appears in results; element_count stays at n after reinsert.
verify: Deleted ids never appear in search results in any round
element_count stays constant across all rounds
You have recall at fixed ef for rounds 0 to 10 next to the rebuild line

steps.title: Policy B: replace deleted slots with replace_deleted
steps.learn: With allow_replace_deleted=True, add_items(replace_deleted=True) puts a new point into some deleted slot and rewires that slot's neighborhood. The MN-RU paper shows this path can leave points with no incoming edges (unreachable) and that recall drifts down over many cycles on SIFT.

decision.choice: allow_replace_deleted=True, reinsert each point under a fresh internal label mapped to its external id
decision.why: hnswlib refuses to re-add a deleted label when replacement is enabled, so fresh labels are required. This is the memory-saving path production users reach for, and the one the MN-RU paper studied, so you can compare to a published result.

alternatives.name: Patch hnswlib with the MN-RU repair
alternatives.tradeoff: Tests the published fix directly, but you are then measuring someone else's algorithm, not building your own.

alternatives.name: Skip it, keep only Policy A
alternatives.tradeoff: Less work, but loses the slot-reuse behavior that the unreachable-points result is about.

steps.delegate: Add ReplaceStrategy over hnswlib: init_index(..., allow_replace_deleted=True); keep dicts ext_to_label and label_to_ext; delete calls mark_deleted on the current label; insert assigns new labels from a counter and calls add_items(vecs, new_labels, replace_deleted=True). search maps labels back to external ids. Tests: element_count never exceeds n; re-adding an old deleted label raises; results contain only live external ids.
verify: element_count never exceeds the initial n in any round
Every returned label maps to a live external id
Policy B recall per round is plotted beside Policy A and the rebuild ceiling

steps.title: Measure reachability, not just recall
steps.learn: Recall at one ef can hide decay: a point nobody links to is never found, and raising ef cannot help (the MN-RU paper reports exactly this). A direct probe counts live points the search cannot reach, which explains recall drops instead of just showing them.

decision.choice: Self-query probe for every policy (each live vector, k=1), plus exact BFS on your own graph
decision.why: hnswlib exposes its graph in Python only as raw bytes in its pickle state, so a black-box probe is the simplest check that works the same for every policy. Accepting distance-0 duplicates stops any exact duplicate vectors in the data from counting as unreachable.

alternatives.name: Decode hnswlib link lists from its pickle state
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact in-degree counts, but couples your harness to an internal memory layout that can change between versions.

alternatives.name: Track the ef needed for 0.95 recall per round
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows cost of decay in search work, but conflates unreachable points with merely longer paths; report it as a second column.

steps.delegate: Add probe.py: for a Strategy, run search on every live vector with k=1 at the fixed ef and count misses (returned id differs and returned distance > 0). For graph strategies that expose adjacency, also BFS from the entry point on layer 0 and count live nodes not visited. Add both counts to stats(). Tests: on a fresh build the BFS count is 0; artificially deleting all in-edges of one node makes BFS count 1.
verify: Unreachable counts for every policy and round are in the CSV
On a fresh hnswlib build the self-query miss rate is recorded as the noise floor
For your own graph, BFS and self-query counts agree on direction across rounds

steps.title: Build your own graph with a lazy delete list
steps.learn: To repair a graph you must own it. FreshDiskANN's lazy delete adds a point to a DeleteList without touching edges; search still routes through it but filters it from results. That matches hnswlib's behavior, so your graph should reproduce Policy A's numbers before you add repair.

decision.choice: Reuse your from-scratch HNSW (project 13) in numpy, with a deleted bitmask and fixed-width int32 neighbor arrays
decision.why: Fixed-width arrays make repairs local writes and make BFS cheap. Matching hnswlib with no repair first proves later gains come from the repair, not from a different graph.

alternatives.name: Fork hnswlib in C++ and add repair there
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast enough for 1M rounds, but the change lives in someone else's concurrency and memory layout.

alternatives.name: Single-layer graph (Vamana style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler to repair since there are no levels, and it is what FreshDiskANN repairs, but no longer HNSW.

steps.delegate: Extend the project 13 HNSWIndex (Python, numpy; numba optional): add deleted = np.zeros(n, bool); delete(ids) sets the mask; search expands deleted nodes as usual but excludes them from the result heap; insert of a deleted id clears the mask and relinks the node. Expose neighbors(level, node) for the probe. Tests: deleted ids never returned; with zero churn recall matches the pre-change version; round 0 recall is within a few points of hnswlib at the same M and ef.
verify: With no repair, your graph's recall curve has the same shape as hnswlib Policy A
Deleted nodes are still expanded during search (count expansions on a test query)

steps.title: Policy C: consolidate deletes by rewiring around them
steps.learn: FreshDiskANN's consolidation: for each live node with out-edges into deleted nodes, take its other neighbors plus the deleted nodes' out-neighbors as candidates, then re-prune to the degree bound. Its authors found plain edge dropping lets the graph get sparser each cycle; a relaxed prune (alpha > 1) keeps it denser.

decision.choice: Batch consolidation once per round before reinsert, re-pruning with alpha in {1.0, 1.2} on every HNSW level
decision.why: Batching does one pass over affected in-neighbors per round instead of per delete. Sweeping alpha tests the paper's claim that pruning aggressiveness drives decay, using your own degree counts as evidence.

alternatives.name: Eager repair on every delete
alternatives.tradeoff: Graph is always clean, but each delete scans its in-neighbors, which is costly without a reverse edge index.

alternatives.name: Drop edges to deleted nodes, no rewiring
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest, and worth one run as a control: FreshDiskANN reports this policy decays.

steps.delegate: Add consolidate(alpha) to your index: for each level, find live nodes whose neighbor lists contain deleted ids; candidates = live neighbors plus live out-neighbors of the deleted ones; apply robust_prune(node, candidates, alpha, M_level); then physically free deleted slots. Track mean out-degree per level. Tests: after consolidate no list contains a deleted id; degrees never exceed the bound; alpha=1.0 never yields more edges than alpha=1.2 on a fixed graph.
verify: No neighbor list contains a deleted id after consolidation
Mean out-degree per round is plotted for no repair, alpha 1.0 and alpha 1.2
You recorded consolidation seconds per round next to the rebuild seconds

steps.title: Handle orphans, a deleted entry point and empty results
steps.learn: Consolidation fixes edges into deleted nodes, but a live node can still lose all in-edges. The entry point itself may be deleted, and heavy deletion can leave fewer than k live results at a small ef. Each is a correctness bug, not a tuning issue.

decision.choice: After consolidating, BFS from the entry point, reinsert unvisited live nodes, move a deleted entry point
decision.why: BFS gives an exact orphan list on your own graph, and reinserting reuses code you already trust. Moving the entry point to a live top-level node keeps every search starting from a valid node.

alternatives.name: Backup index for unreachable points (MN-RU)
alternatives.tradeoff: Search both indexes and merge; no rewiring needed, but every query pays for two searches.

alternatives.name: Ignore orphans, rely on periodic rebuild
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but recall silently degrades between rebuilds, which is the bug this project is about.

steps.delegate: Add repair_orphans(): BFS on level 0 from the entry point, collect live unvisited nodes, unlink and reinsert them. If the entry point is deleted, pick a live node on the highest level. search returns fewer than k with a flag instead of raising when fewer live nodes are reachable. Tests: a graph with a hand-made orphan has 0 orphans after repair; deleting the entry point then searching still works; deleting 99% then k=10 returns the rest without error.
verify: Orphan count after repair is 0 in every round
A test deletes the entry point and search still returns correct results
Your policy-comparison table includes an orphan count per round for every policy

steps.title: Measure it: 10 rounds, every policy, same machine
steps.learn: The result is a set of lines over rounds: recall at fixed ef, unreachable count, update seconds and memory. Search speed changes too, since dead nodes still cost hops, so time queries per round with the same thread count, after warmup.

decision.choice: One run of all policies on the 100k prefix with three seeds, single-thread queries, reporting median and range per round
decision.why: Random deletion sets and random levels both add noise; three seeds show whether a 1-point recall drop is decay or chance. One thread keeps hnswlib and Python comparable on hops, if not on raw speed.

alternatives.name: One seed, 1M points
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to published scale, but a single run cannot separate decay from seed noise.

alternatives.name: Report only round 10 vs round 0
alternatives.tradeoff: Compact, but hides whether decay is linear, accelerating or flattening.

steps.delegate: Add bench.py (Python, matplotlib): run churn.py for every Strategy and seeds (1, 2, 3), queries single-thread after a warmup pass. Plot recall@10 vs round (median line, min to max band) per policy, plus panels for unreachable count, update seconds per round and element_count. Tests: script fails if any policy lacks a round; plots regenerate from the CSV alone.
verify: All policies have 11 measurements for each of three seeds in the CSV
