You recorded CPU model, RAM, OS, hnswlib and numpy versions and the exact command
Recall drift for each policy is stated with its seed range, not a single number

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer the question with the recall-per-round plot and the cost columns. Explain decay with your own evidence: unreachable counts and mean degree per round tell you why a policy drifted, not only that it did.
verify: Part 1: the write-up opens with the one question about recall under 10 rounds of 10% churn
Part 2: every claim has a number with seeds, the machine, library versions and command
Part 3: it explains surprising results using unreachable counts or degree changes
Part 4: it lists limits, such as reinserting the same vectors, a 100k prefix and one dataset

projects.title: Disk-based ANN (Vamana / DiskANN)
projects.problem: Index 100M+ vectors on one machine from SSD
projects.proveIt: SSD reads per query, p99 latency
projects.question: How few 4 KB SSD reads per query, and what p99 latency, can a from-scratch Vamana index with PQ in RAM reach on 100M vectors on one machine?

steps.title: Frame the question, metrics and dataset
steps.learn: DiskANN keeps compressed vectors in RAM and the graph plus full vectors on SSD, so a query costs SSD reads. Report per setting: 10-recall@10, mean 4 KB reads per query, p99 latency. Data: bigann-100M from big-ann-benchmarks (128-dim uint8 SIFT, 10K public queries, ground truth for the 100M subset).
verify: You split the 10K public queries with a fixed seed into 2K for tuning and 8K frozen for the final test, and saved both id lists before tuning
You wrote down the RAM budget, SSD model and the three metrics you will report
You downloaded bigann-10M for development and checked the header (count, dim) of the base file

steps.title: Load the binary files and build the recall scorer
steps.learn: The big-ann-benchmarks files are a small header (point count, dimension as uint32) then raw rows, so they can be memory-mapped. The 10M and 100M subsets are prefixes of the 1B base file with their own ground truth files. Your scorer is the only judge of recall, so it must not share code with the index.

decision.choice: Use the shipped subset ground truth, spot-checked by exact search on a sample of queries
decision.why: Exact top-k over 100M vectors for 10K queries is expensive to recompute. The shipped files are the benchmark's reference, and a spot check on a sample catches loader bugs such as an off-by-one header or wrong dtype.

alternatives.name: Recompute all ground truth yourself
alternatives.tradeoff: Removes trust in third-party files, but costs a long brute-force run with faiss or DiskANN's compute_groundtruth tool.

alternatives.name: Develop on bigann-1M with your own ground truth
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast iteration, but a 1M graph fits in RAM easily and hides the disk behavior you are studying.

steps.delegate: Python 3, numpy, faiss-cpu. Write bigann_io.py: read_u8bin(path, n=None) via np.memmap honoring the 8-byte header; read_gt(path) returning ids and distances. Write score.py: recall_at_k(found_ids, gt_ids, k) as intersection size over k, averaged over queries; it must import nothing from the index code. Tests: tiny synthetic files round-trip; recall is 1.0 for identical lists and 0.0 for disjoint; exact faiss IndexFlatL2 search on 20 sample queries over bigann-10M matches shipped ground truth.
verify: Exact search on 20 sampled queries over bigann-10M matches the shipped top-10 distances (ids may differ only where distances tie)
Your scorer gives 1.0 when fed the ground truth itself
You can state the size in GB of bigann-100M raw vectors (100M x 128 bytes)

steps.title: Build the Vamana graph in memory
steps.learn: Vamana starts from the medoid, runs GreedySearch for each point, then RobustPrune with alpha keeps a diverse set of at most R neighbors and adds back-edges. With alpha above 1 the pruning keeps longer edges, so search needs fewer hops. The paper builds in two passes: alpha 1 first, then the user alpha.

decision.choice: R=64, L=100, alpha=1.2, two passes, full-precision distances during build
decision.why: Each hop on disk is an SSD round trip, so fewer hops matter more here than in RAM. These are the defaults of the legacy DiskANN C++ code, which gives a fair comparison later. R also sets the record size on disk, so a moderate R keeps a node inside one sector.

alternatives.name: HNSW layers
alternatives.tradeoff: Well known and fast in RAM, but the DiskANN paper notes it implicitly uses alpha=1, giving more hops per query, which costs more SSD round trips.

alternatives.name: Larger R (128) and L (200)
alternatives.tradeoff: Better recall per hop, but bigger records, fewer nodes per 4 KB sector and a much longer build.

alternatives.name: PQ distances during build
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster and lighter build, but a lower quality graph that can cap recall.

steps.delegate: Rust (or C++17 with OpenMP). Implement greedy_search(start, query, L) returning candidates and the visited set, robust_prune(p, candidates, alpha, R), and build(vectors, R, L, alpha) with two passes in random order and parallel insertion under per-node locks. Distances on uint8 vectors as squared L2 in i32. Tests: on 10K random points max out-degree is R and all nodes are reachable from the medoid; with large L on bigann-1M (ground truth computed by faiss IndexFlatL2) 10-recall@10 is above 0.95.
verify: Every node's out-degree is at most R and a BFS from the medoid reaches all nodes
On bigann-10M in RAM, you plotted recall@10 vs search list size L with your scorer
You compared mean hops per query with alpha=1.0 and alpha=1.2 at the same recall

steps.title: Build 100M within the RAM budget with overlapping shards
steps.learn: A one-shot build needs all vectors and the whole graph in RAM. The DiskANN paper instead runs k-means, sends each point to its 2 nearest clusters, builds a Vamana graph per shard and merges by taking the union of edges. The overlap is what keeps the merged graph connected.

decision.choice: k-means into overlapping shards (each point in its 2 closest), per-shard Vamana, union-merge, then re-prune to R
decision.why: It lets a 100M build run on a machine whose RAM cannot hold the full graph, which is the point of the project. Legacy DiskANN does the same when its build memory budget is too small, and documents it as up to 1.5 times slower than one shot.

alternatives.name: One-shot build on a large-RAM machine
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler and slightly better graph, but needs a much larger machine than the one you serve from.

alternatives.name: Disjoint shards searched separately
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to build, but every query must search many shards, multiplying SSD reads.

steps.delegate: Rust or C++. Train k-means centroids on a 1M sample (faiss.Kmeans from a Python prep script is fine), assign each base point to its 2 nearest centroids, write per-shard id lists, build each shard with the step 3 code, then merge adjacency lists by global id and re-run robust_prune where degree exceeds R. Track peak RSS. Tests: every id appears in exactly 2 shards; merged degree is at most R; on bigann-10M the merged graph's recall at fixed L is within a few points of the one-shot graph.
verify: Peak RSS during the 100M build stayed under your stated budget (record the number)
On bigann-10M, merged vs one-shot recall@10 at the same L is recorded side by side
A BFS from the medoid in the merged 100M graph reaches every node

steps.title: Compress vectors with PQ to steer the search from RAM
steps.learn: At search time DiskANN keeps only short PQ codes in RAM and uses them to decide which nodes to read next. PQ distances are approximate, so the final ranking uses full vectors read from disk. The code size sets the RAM bill: 100M points times bytes per code.

decision.choice: 32-byte PQ codes (32 subspaces, 256 centroids each) trained on a 1M sample
decision.why: 32 bytes is the example size in the DiskANN paper and puts 100M codes at about 3.2 GB, which leaves room for a node cache. Since full vectors come back with each read for re-ranking, PQ only has to steer well, not rank exactly.

alternatives.name: 16-byte PQ
alternatives.tradeoff: Halves RAM, but coarser distances send the search to worse nodes, so it needs more reads for the same recall.

alternatives.name: Binary or RaBitQ codes
alternatives.tradeoff: Very fast bit distances and small codes; quality on uint8 SIFT must be measured and the code is less standard.

steps.delegate: Python prep with faiss: train faiss.ProductQuantizer(128, 32, 8) on a 1M float32 sample, encode all 100M in chunks to a codes file, save the codebooks. In Rust/C++ implement asymmetric distance: per query build a 32x256 lookup table, then sum table entries per code. Tests: ADC distance matches faiss's decoded-vector distance within float tolerance on 1,000 pairs; the codes file size equals n x 32 bytes.
verify: Codes file is exactly 100M x 32 bytes plus any header you defined
On 1,000 random pairs your ADC distance matches the faiss reference
Recall@10 of PQ-only ranking (no re-rank) on the tuning queries is recorded as a baseline

steps.title: Lay out fixed-size node records in 4 KB sectors
steps.learn: DiskANN stores each node as its full vector followed by its at most R neighbor ids, padded to a fixed size, so a node's disk offset is computed from its id with no offset table in RAM. Reading one 4 KB aligned sector costs about the same as reading 512 bytes, so the vector rides along with the neighbor list.

decision.choice: Fixed records (vector, degree, R ids), whole records per 4 KB sector, header with magic, version, checksums
decision.why: One read per hop returns both the neighbor list and the full vector for re-ranking. Never splitting a record across sectors keeps every hop to one read. A header with a checksum catches a truncated or mismatched index before it serves wrong answers.

alternatives.name: Separate vector and graph files
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller graph reads, but re-ranking then needs extra reads per candidate.

alternatives.name: Locality reordering (Starling-style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Puts graph neighbors in the same sector so one read serves several hops; adds a reordering pass and an id remap table.

steps.delegate: Rust or C++. Write index_writer that streams nodes in id order into records of size 128 + 4 + 4*R bytes, packs floor(4096 / record) records per sector, pads the rest, writes a header sector (magic, version, n, dim, R, records per sector, medoid id, CRC32 per 1 GB chunk), writes to a temp file, fsyncs and renames. Add offset_of(id). Tests: round-trip 10K nodes; offset_of matches written position; a flipped byte fails the checksum check at load.
verify: You computed records per sector for R=64 by hand and it matches the writer
The 100M index file size equals header plus ceil(n / per-sector) x 4096 bytes
Loading a copy with one corrupted byte is refused with a clear error

steps.title: Choose how sector reads reach the SSD
steps.learn: To count real SSD reads you must bypass the page cache: O_DIRECT needs buffers, offsets and sizes aligned to the device block size. A query issues a small batch of independent sector reads per hop, so the API must submit several at once and wait for all of them.

decision.choice: io_uring with O_DIRECT and aligned 4 KB buffers, one ring per search thread
decision.why: It submits a batch of reads in one call and reaps completions without a thread per read, which fits beam search exactly. Per-thread rings avoid locking. Legacy DiskANN uses Linux libaio for the same pattern, so the two are comparable.

alternatives.name: libaio (io_submit / io_getevents)
alternatives.tradeoff: What legacy DiskANN uses with O_DIRECT, so it is a proven fit; an older, narrower interface than io_uring.

alternatives.name: mmap the index file
alternatives.tradeoff: Least code, but the page cache hides real reads, faults are synchronous and you cannot control or count IO.

alternatives.name: pread from a thread pool
alternatives.tradeoff: Portable and simple, but each in-flight read costs a thread and context switches.

steps.delegate: Rust with the io-uring crate (or C with liburing). Implement SectorReader::open(path) using O_DIRECT, read_batch(&[sector_ids]) -> aligned buffers, and counters for sectors read and time spent waiting. Allocate 4096-aligned buffers. Tests: read_batch returns bytes equal to a buffered pread of the same sectors; misaligned requests are rejected; counters equal the number of sectors requested.
verify: fio random 4K direct reads at queue depth 1 and 8 on the same SSD are recorded as the device floor
Your reader's single-sector latency at queue depth 1 is within reach of the fio number
With page cache dropped, a second identical batch still shows real reads in iostat

steps.title: Implement beam search with implicit re-ranking
steps.learn: BeamSearch keeps a list of L candidates ranked by PQ distance and, each round, reads the sectors of the W closest unvisited candidates in one batch. Each read also returns the node's full vector, which is kept to re-rank the final top k exactly. W trades round trips against wasted reads.

decision.choice: Search list L swept per query budget, beam width W=4, re-rank top k with full vectors seen during the search
decision.why: The DiskANN docs say W=1 gives the highest throughput at a fixed IOPS rating and W of 4 to 8 gives the best latency. This project reports p99 latency, so start at 4 and sweep. Re-ranking uses vectors already read, so it costs no extra IO.

alternatives.name: W=1 (plain greedy search)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewest total reads and best throughput, but one SSD round trip per hop, so latency is higher.

alternatives.name: W=8 or more
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer round trips, but more wasted reads and SSD bandwidth per query, which hurts at high load.

alternatives.name: Separate re-rank fetch of top candidates
alternatives.tradeoff: Decouples layout from search, but adds a burst of random reads at the end of each query.

steps.delegate: Rust or C++. Implement beam_search(query, k, L, W) using the PQ table from step 5 to rank candidates, SectorReader::read_batch for W nodes per round, parse records, insert unseen neighbors, keep full vectors of visited nodes, return top k by exact distance plus stats (rounds, sectors read, IO time). Tests: with W=1 visit order equals greedy search using the same PQ distances; with large L on bigann-1M (faiss exact ground truth) recall@10 exceeds 0.95; stats sectors equal the reader's counter.
verify: On tuning queries, you have a table of recall@10, mean sectors read and mean rounds for W in 1, 2, 4, 8
Re-ranked recall is higher than PQ-only recall at the same L
Per-query sector counts from search stats match the IO reader's counters

steps.title: Cache the hot nodes near the entry point in RAM
steps.learn: Every query starts at the medoid, so the first few hops read the same nodes. The DiskANN paper caches all nodes within C hops (3 or 4) of the start, or nodes chosen from a known query distribution. The number of nodes grows quickly with C, so cap by bytes.

decision.choice: Static cache of nodes in BFS order from the medoid up to a fixed byte budget, loaded at startup
decision.why: It is read-only, needs no eviction logic and directly removes the first rounds of reads for every query. A fixed byte budget keeps the RAM bill explicit next to the PQ codes.

alternatives.name: Cache from tuning query traces
alternatives.tradeoff: Targets nodes real queries visit; must be built from the tuning split only, or it leaks the test set.

alternatives.name: Dynamic LRU over sectors
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to drift, but needs locking and eviction on the hot path and makes runs less repeatable.

steps.delegate: Rust or C++. Add NodeCache::build(index, medoid, budget_bytes) doing BFS over on-disk records until the budget is reached, stored in a hash map from id to record bytes. beam_search checks the cache before scheduling a read and counts hits. Tests: cache size never exceeds the budget; a query whose whole path is cached issues zero reads; results with and without cache are identical.
verify: Search results are identical with the cache on and off for 100 queries
You recorded mean sectors read per query for cache budgets of 0, 0.25 and 1 GB
Total RAM (PQ codes plus cache plus overhead) is measured from RSS, not estimated

steps.title: Measure reads per query and p99 against DiskANN
steps.learn: Latency depends on SSD load: more threads raise throughput but queue reads and push up p99. Fix the thread count and report the curve. Cold runs need the page cache dropped, and every run must use the frozen test queries scored by your separate scorer.

decision.choice: Baselines: legacy DiskANN search_disk_index with matched R, L and RAM budget, plus the fio device floor
decision.why: search_disk_index prints mean IOs, mean and 99.9th percentile latency and recall per L, the same quantities you report, so the comparison is direct. The fio floor shows how close each query is to pure device time.

alternatives.name: In-memory HNSW as the baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows the latency cost of going to disk, but needs RAM for all 100M vectors and does not test the disk design.

alternatives.name: Compare to published DiskANN numbers
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra work, but different hardware makes the comparison meaningless.

steps.delegate: Bash and Python. bench.sh: record kernel, CPU, SSD model, filesystem; sync and echo 3 > /proc/sys/vm/drop_caches before cold runs; run your search and DiskANN search_disk_index on the 8K frozen queries for each L at fixed threads (1 and core count); store your per-query latency in an HdrHistogram. Plot recall vs mean reads for both, recall vs p99.9 for both (search_disk_index prints mean and 99.9 latency, not p99), and your own p99 separately.
verify: Every reported number has the exact command, thread count and machine written next to it
Plots show your index and DiskANN on the same axes at matched recall@10
You report p99 at 1 thread and at full threads, and note which run saturated the SSD

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up answers the one question with numbers. Explain surprises using the counters you collected (rounds, sectors, cache hits, SSD queue depth) rather than guesses, and say what a single SSD and the bigann data cannot tell you.
verify: Part 1 states the one question exactly as framed in step 1
Part 2 gives every number (reads per query, p99, recall, RAM) with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result using a measured counter
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, such as one SSD model, uint8 SIFT data and no updates

projects.title: Object-storage-backed vector search
projects.problem: S3 is cheap but slow; cold queries must still be fast
projects.proveIt: Cold vs warm p99, cost per million queries
projects.question: With a vector index stored only in S3, how close can cold-query p99 get to warm p99, and what does a million queries cost?

steps.title: Frame the question, metrics and dataset
steps.learn: Object storage is cheap per GB but each request has high latency, so a cold query is dominated by round trips, not math. Report cold p99 and warm p99 at a fixed recall@10, plus cost per million queries. Data: deep-10M from big-ann-benchmarks (96-dim float32, 10K public queries, ground truth for the 10M subset).
verify: You split the 10K queries with a fixed seed into 2K tuning and 8K frozen test, and saved both id lists before tuning
You wrote down the target recall@10, the AWS Region, and the definitions of cold and warm you will use
You downloaded deep-10M and checked the base file header (count, dim)

steps.title: Build the scorer and an in-memory reference index
steps.learn: Before adding S3, know what recall and latency the same index design gets fully in memory. That number is the floor warm queries can approach. The scorer reads only the shipped ground truth and must not share code with the index.

decision.choice: faiss IndexIVFFlat in RAM, rebuilt after step 4 on the final split centroids so it shares clusters with the S3 index
decision.why: It isolates the cost of storage: same clusters, same nprobe, only the data location differs. Any recall gap between it and your S3 index is a bug, not a design effect.

alternatives.name: In-memory HNSW (faiss IndexHNSWFlat)
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster warm queries, but a different algorithm, so the gap mixes algorithm and storage effects.

alternatives.name: Exact brute force only
alternatives.tradeoff: Perfect recall reference, but no meaningful latency floor for an ANN design.

steps.delegate: Python 3, numpy, faiss-cpu. Write io.py reading .fbin base and query files via np.memmap with the 8-byte header and the ground truth file. Write score.py with recall_at_k(found, gt, k), importing nothing from index code. Write ref.py building faiss.IndexIVFFlat with nlist from a config, then sweeping nprobe on the tuning split. Tests: recall 1.0 on ground truth itself; exact search on 20 queries matches shipped ids.
verify: Exact search on 20 sampled queries matches the shipped top-10 ids
You have a table of recall@10 and in-RAM latency vs nprobe on the tuning split
You picked the smallest nprobe that meets the target recall and wrote it down

steps.title: Choose a cluster index, not a graph, for object storage
steps.learn: A graph search is a chain of dependent hops; on S3 each hop is a full request round trip. A cluster index needs one round trip to read the centroids and one parallel round of range reads for the chosen clusters. turbopuffer documents this reasoning for its SPFresh-based index.

decision.choice: IVF: centroids in one small object, each cluster's vectors stored contiguously for one range read
decision.why: Cold latency is roughly the number of sequential round trips times request latency, and AWS describes small-object latency in the 100 to 200 ms range. IVF needs about 2 sequential trips regardless of nprobe, because cluster reads run in parallel.

alternatives.name: DiskANN-style graph on S3
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer bytes per query, but each hop waits on a request, so cold latency grows with path length.

alternatives.name: Download the whole index on first query
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, and fine for small tenants, but cold latency grows with index size.

alternatives.name: SPANN-style balanced clusters with duplication
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher recall per cluster read by placing boundary vectors in several clusters; more storage and a more complex build.

verify: You wrote the expected sequential round trips per cold query for IVF and for a graph search of H hops, with H taken from a cited source
You can explain in two sentences why cluster reads can run in parallel but graph hops cannot

steps.title: Size the clusters for one range read each
steps.learn: Cluster size sets bytes per request. Too small and a query needs many requests (request cost); too large and each request transfers data you score and discard. Unbalanced k-means makes some clusters huge, and those become the slow tail. SPANN uses balanced clustering for this reason.

decision.choice: faiss k-means with nlist chosen so the average cluster is a few hundred KB, then split any cluster over 2x the average
decision.why: A few hundred KB per GET keeps transfer time small relative to request latency while keeping request count per query near nprobe. Splitting oversized clusters bounds the worst-case read, which drives p99.

alternatives.name: Plain k-means, no balancing
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but the largest clusters set the tail latency and cost.

alternatives.name: Store PQ codes in clusters, full vectors elsewhere
alternatives.tradeoff: Much smaller cluster reads, but exact re-ranking needs another round trip.

steps.delegate: Python, faiss. Train faiss.Kmeans on a 1M sample of deep-10M with nlist from config, assign all vectors, then repeatedly split any cluster larger than 2x mean with 2-means until none exceeds the cap, and write assignments, final centroids and cluster byte sizes. Tests: every vector is in exactly one cluster; no cluster exceeds the cap; a histogram of cluster sizes is saved.
verify: Max cluster size is at most 2x the mean, shown in a saved histogram
Recall@10 at your chosen nprobe on the tuning split still meets the target after splitting

steps.title: Pack clusters into segment objects with an offset table
steps.learn: S3 supports byte-range GETs, so many clusters can live in one object and each be fetched alone. Fewer, larger objects mean fewer PUTs at build time; the offset table must be small enough to load in the first round trip. Within a cluster, keep vectors contiguous so scoring is one vectorized pass.

decision.choice: Segment objects holding many clusters (ids then float32 vectors); offsets in a small manifest
decision.why: One range GET returns exactly one cluster, and the manifest plus centroids are fetched together in round trip 1. Struct-of-arrays inside a cluster lets numpy score all vectors in one matrix multiply.

alternatives.name: One object per cluster
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest addressing, but many more PUTs to build and LIST calls to manage.

alternatives.name: Lance or Parquet files
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard formats with tooling, but you must check how many requests a single cluster read becomes.

steps.delegate: Python. Write build_segments.py: group clusters into segments up to a size cap, write each segment as ids (int64) then vectors (float32) per cluster, and a manifest JSON with dim, nlist, segment keys, and per cluster (segment, offset, length, count, crc32). Centroids saved as a .npy next to it. Tests: reading each cluster from the local file by offset and length reproduces its vectors; crc32 matches.
verify: Every cluster read by (offset, length) from the local segment files matches the source vectors
Manifest plus centroids size is recorded in KB, since it is part of every cold query

steps.title: Publish immutable segments and commit with one manifest write
steps.learn: A reader must never see half a build. If segments are write-once and only the manifest names them, publishing is a single object write. S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUT and DELETE, and conditional writes with If-None-Match refuse to overwrite an existing key.

decision.choice: Upload segments under a new version prefix, then create manifest-vN with If-None-Match, then update a small pointer
decision.why: Segments are never modified, so caches keyed by segment key never go stale. The conditional create stops two builders from both claiming version N, and strong consistency means a reader that sees the pointer can read the manifest.

alternatives.name: Overwrite segments in place
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves storage, but readers mid-query can mix old and new bytes and caches need invalidation.

alternatives.name: Keep the pointer in a database (DynamoDB)
alternatives.tradeoff: Rich transactions, but adds a second service to every cold query and to operations.

steps.delegate: Python, boto3. Write publish.py: upload segment files to s3://bucket/index/v{N}/, then put_object the manifest with IfNoneMatch='*', then write the pointer object. Readers load pointer, then manifest, then segments. Use moto server (moto_server) for local tests: concurrent publish of the same N makes exactly one succeed; a reader started before publish keeps using the old version consistently.
verify: In a moto test, two concurrent publishers of the same version produce exactly one success
Killing publish after segment upload but before manifest leaves readers on the old version

steps.title: Fetch clusters in one parallel round of range GETs
steps.learn: Round trip 1 loads the manifest and centroids; round trip 2 issues nprobe range GETs at once and scores each cluster as it arrives. AWS recommends spreading requests across connections and using byte ranges; the connection pool must be at least nprobe wide or requests queue.

decision.choice: Python with boto3 get_object(Range=...) on a thread pool sized to nprobe, reusing one client and its connection pool
decision.why: boto3 is the reference SDK and a thread pool gives real parallel GETs because they wait on the network. Python keeps the focus on round trips, which dominate cold latency, rather than on compute.

alternatives.name: Rust with tokio and aws-sdk-s3
alternatives.tradeoff: Lower per-request overhead and better tails under load, at the cost of more code.

alternatives.name: Sequential GETs
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but cold latency becomes nprobe times request latency.

steps.delegate: Python, boto3, numpy. Write query.py: open(pointer) loads manifest and centroids; search(q, k, nprobe) picks nearest centroids, submits range GETs to a ThreadPoolExecutor, scores each returned cluster with numpy, merges top k. Set botocore max_pool_connections at least nprobe. Record per query: round trips, GET count, bytes fetched, time per phase. Tests against moto: results match the in-memory IVF reference exactly for 50 queries.
verify: Results for 50 tuning queries match the in-memory IVF reference ids exactly
Per-query logs show GET count equals nprobe plus the round trip 1 requests
Phase timings show round trip 2 takes about one request latency, not nprobe of them

steps.title: Cut the tail with timeouts, retries and hedged GETs
steps.learn: A query waits for its slowest of nprobe GETs, so per-request tails compound. AWS advises aggressive timeouts and retries for latency-sensitive reads, since a retry likely takes a different path. S3 also returns 503 Slow Down when a prefix exceeds its request rate, which needs backoff, not hedging.

decision.choice: Hedge: if a GET is not done by its measured p95, send a duplicate and take the first; back off on 503
decision.why: Hedging at p95 adds about 5 percent more GETs but removes most of the slow-request tail, which is the cold p99 you report. Separating 503 handling avoids amplifying load when S3 is throttling.

alternatives.name: SDK default retries only
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra requests, but a slow but successful request is never retried, so tails remain.

alternatives.name: Always send two copies
alternatives.tradeoff: Best tail, but doubles request cost per query.

steps.delegate: Python. Wrap range GETs in fetch_with_hedge(key, range, hedge_after_s, timeout_s): start one request, start a second if the first is not done after hedge_after_s, return the first success, cancel or ignore the other, count hedges. Handle SlowDown errors with jittered exponential backoff. Tests with a fake client that injects delays and 503s: hedge fires only after the threshold; 503 triggers backoff, not a hedge; counters are exact.
verify: Hedge rate on real S3 runs is measured and close to your configured percentile
Cold p99 with and without hedging is recorded on the same query set
Extra GETs from hedges are included in the cost counters

steps.title: Add memory and local NVMe caches for warm queries
steps.learn: Warm means the bytes are already local. Because segments are immutable, a cluster's cache key is (segment key, offset), which never goes stale. turbopuffer caches on NVMe after the first query and suggests a pre-flight query to warm a namespace before latency-sensitive traffic.

decision.choice: Centroids and manifest pinned in RAM; clusters in an LRU on local NVMe, read on miss from S3 and written behind
decision.why: Centroids are needed by every query and are small. Clusters are the bulk, and NVMe holds far more than RAM. Write-behind keeps the cache fill off the query's critical path.

alternatives.name: S3 Express One Zone as a middle tier
alternatives.tradeoff: AWS describes single-digit millisecond access, but data lives in one Availability Zone and has its own pricing.

alternatives.name: RAM-only cache
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest hits, but a small cache means more cold misses and higher cost per query.

steps.delegate: Python. Write cache.py: ClusterCache(dir, max_bytes) with get(key) and put(key, bytes) storing files on local NVMe, LRU eviction by total bytes, and a RAM layer for centroids. query.py checks the cache before S3 and writes misses behind via a background thread. Add warm(pointer, n_clusters) for a pre-flight. Tests: evicts when over budget; identical results with cache on and off; hit and miss counters exact.
verify: Results with cache on and off are identical on 100 queries
Hit rate and NVMe bytes used are logged per run
A warm run shows zero S3 GETs for cached clusters

steps.title: Measure cold vs warm p99 and cost per million queries
steps.learn: Cold must mean empty local caches in a fresh process with the OS page cache dropped. Run from an EC2 instance in the bucket's Region, since local laptops add network distance. Cost per million queries comes from counted GETs and bytes times current list prices, plus instance hours.

decision.choice: Baselines: in-memory IVF reference (warm floor) and download-whole-index on first query (naive cold)
decision.why: The floor shows how much warm latency storage still adds, and the naive baseline shows what the cluster layout buys on cold queries. All three use the same frozen queries and scorer.

alternatives.name: Benchmark against moto locally
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and repeatable for correctness, but its latency says nothing about S3.

alternatives.name: Closed-loop clients only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy, but slow responses throttle the load and hide the tail (coordinated omission).

steps.delegate: Python. bench.py: for cold, start a new process, clear the NVMe cache dir, drop the page cache, run each frozen query once in its own fresh state or sample; for warm, run after a warm-up pass. Use an open-loop schedule at a fixed rate, record latency in HdrHistogram, and log GETs, bytes, hedges per query. cost.py: cost per 1M queries = GETs x GET price per 1,000 x 1,000 + instance $/hour x hours, with prices and date entered by hand from the AWS pricing page.

projects.title: SIMD distance kernels
projects.problem: Distance math dominates search time
projects.proveIt: Speedup of AVX2/NEON and fp16 kernels vs naive code
projects.question: How much faster are hand-written AVX2 and NEON distance kernels, in fp32 and fp16, than naive scalar code, and where does memory bandwidth cap the gain?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the data
steps.learn: The deliverable is a speedup table: ns per distance and GB/s for each kernel (scalar, auto-vectorized, AVX2, NEON, fp16) at d=100, 128 and 960, both cache-resident and streaming from RAM. Data: ann-benchmarks glove-100-angular, sift-128-euclidean and gist-960-euclidean.
verify: Your README states the question, the two metrics (ns per distance, GB/s) and the speedup baseline before any kernel code exists
You opened each HDF5 file and printed the shapes of train, test and neighbors
You froze the first 1,000 test queries of each dataset as the recall check set and never change them
You recorded both machines: an x86-64 CPU whose lscpu flags include avx2, fma and f16c, and an ARM64 CPU

steps.title: Write the naive kernels and a correctness oracle
steps.learn: Three metrics: squared L2, inner product, and cosine, which is the inner product of unit vectors (normalize GloVe once at load). Float addition is not associative, so any kernel that sums in a different order differs in the last bits: correct means within a tolerance of a double reference.

decision.choice: A double-precision reference with a relative-error tolerance, plus recall@10 of brute-force kNN as the end-to-end check
decision.why: SIMD kernels reorder the sum, so bit-equality with the scalar loop is impossible. A double reference gives a fixed target for every kernel, and recall against the dataset's own exact neighbors shows whether the error matters for search.

alternatives.name: Bit-exact match against scalar fp32
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to write, but every reordered or fused kernel fails it, so you end up loosening it ad hoc.

alternatives.name: Compare only top-k ids
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to what users see, but small systematic errors can hide behind ties and only show up on other data.

steps.delegate: C11: kernels.h with float l2sq_scalar(const float*,const float*,size_t d) and ip_scalar; oracle in double. Tests (any C test framework): random vectors for every d from 1 to 1024, error within a tolerance you derive from d and FLT_EPSILON. Tool knn_bruteforce(kernel, base, queries, k) and recall@10 against the HDF5 neighbors on the frozen 1,000 queries.
verify: Oracle tests pass for d values that are not multiples of 8 or 16
Scalar brute-force recall@10 on sift-128 frozen queries is at least 0.99; you inspected any misses and explained them (ties or bugs)
You wrote down the tolerance and why you chose it

steps.title: Measure what the compiler gives you for free
steps.learn: GCC 12 and later turn on loop vectorization at -O2 (very-cheap cost model), but a float sum can only be split across lanes if it may reassociate additions (-fassociative-math, enabled by -ffast-math via -funsafe-math-optimizations). -fopt-info-vec-missed prints why a loop was not vectorized.

decision.choice: Two baselines from the same source: strict -O2 scalar, and -O3 -march=native -ffast-math auto-vectorized
decision.why: The prove-it compares against naive code, but a hand kernel that only beats strict -O2 overstates its value. The fast-math build shows how much of the gap the compiler closes alone, so the hand-written kernel must justify itself against it.

alternatives.name: -O0 baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives huge speedups that mean nothing, since nobody ships unoptimized code.

alternatives.name: Only the strict -O2 baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler table, but hides that compiler flags alone may deliver much of the win.

steps.delegate: CMake: build kernels_scalar.c twice, as scalar_strict (-O2) and scalar_fast (-O3 -march=native -ffast-math), both linked into the oracle tests. Add -fopt-info-vec-missed for the strict build and save its output. Script dumps the inner loop of each with objdump -d for review. Tests: both builds pass the oracle.
verify: The fast-math x86 build's inner loop uses ymm registers; the strict build's does not, or you explained why
You saved the -fopt-info-vec-missed note that explains the strict build's reduction loop
Both builds pass the oracle tests

steps.title: Write the AVX2 plus FMA kernel
steps.learn: An AVX2 register holds 8 floats and _mm256_fmadd_ps computes a*b+c per lane in one instruction. With one accumulator every FMA waits for the previous one (a loop-carried dependency), so use several independent accumulators and add them together once, with a horizontal sum at the end.

decision.choice: 4 independent 8-float accumulators (32 floats per iteration), unaligned loads, one horizontal sum at the end
decision.why: Independent accumulators let FMAs overlap instead of queueing on one register. Unaligned loads (_mm256_loadu_ps) keep the kernel usable on any caller's buffer; alignment is then a measured optimization, not a correctness rule.

alternatives.name: One accumulator
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest code; latency-bound on the FMA chain. Keep it as an ablation point.

alternatives.name: AVX-512 (16 floats per register)
alternatives.tradeoff: Twice the width, but only some x86 CPUs have it, so it needs its own dispatch tier and test machine.

steps.delegate: kernels_avx2.c compiled with -mavx2 -mfma: l2sq_avx2 and ip_avx2 using _mm256_loadu_ps, _mm256_sub_ps and _mm256_fmadd_ps, accumulator count as a compile-time constant (1, 2, 4) for ablation. Assert d is a multiple of 32 for now. Oracle tests at d=128 and 960; Google Benchmark of ns per call with both vectors in L1.
verify: Oracle tests pass at d=128 and d=960
You measured ns per call for 1, 2 and 4 accumulators at d=128 and recorded which wins
The AVX2 kernel beats the fast-math auto-vectorized build at d=960 with data in L1, or you explained why not

steps.title: Handle dimensions that are not a multiple of the width
steps.learn: GloVe has 100 dims, which is 3 groups of 32 plus 4. Options: a scalar tail loop, a masked load (_mm256_maskload_ps loads only lanes whose mask bit is set), or padding each stored vector with zeros, which leaves L2 and inner product unchanged. hnswlib keeps a SIMD path plus a residual path.

decision.choice: Zero-pad base and query vectors to a multiple of 16 floats at load time, rows contiguous and 64-byte aligned
decision.why: The kernel stays branch-free and identical for all three datasets. Padding costs 12 extra floats per vector at d=100 and nothing at 128 or 960, and contiguous rows suit the one-query-against-many scan used later.

alternatives.name: Scalar tail loop
alternatives.tradeoff: No memory overhead, but adds a branch and scalar work that is a large share of the time at small d.

alternatives.name: Masked loads for the tail
alternatives.tradeoff: No padding and one code path, but needs a mask per call and is x86-specific.

alternatives.name: Dimension-major (SoA) layout
alternatives.tradeoff: Several vectors per register, no horizontal sum; awkward for random access by id, as graph indexes need.

steps.delegate: Python (h5py, numpy) converter: write train and test as padded float32 .bin files with a small header (n, d, padded_d). C loader using aligned_alloc(64, ...). Remove the multiple-of-32 assert by handling the last 16 floats with 2 accumulators. Tests: padded kernel equals the unpadded oracle on glove-100; every row pointer is 64-byte aligned.
verify: Oracle tests pass at d=100 on padded data
You recorded the memory overhead of padding for each dataset
A test asserts every row pointer is 64-byte aligned

steps.title: Port the kernel to ARM NEON
steps.learn: NEON registers are 128 bits, 4 floats. vfmaq_f32 is the fused multiply-add and vaddvq_f32 sums the 4 lanes of a register on AArch64. Same plan as AVX2: several accumulators, padded input so there is no tail. Run it on a real ARM64 machine, not an emulator.

decision.choice: Hand-written NEON intrinsics with 4 accumulators of 4 floats
decision.why: Writing it by hand shows how the narrower width changes the speedup against scalar, which is the comparison the prove-it asks for on ARM. Same structure as the AVX2 kernel keeps the two directly comparable.

alternatives.name: Google Highway
alternatives.tradeoff: One portable source for many targets with runtime dispatch; adds a dependency and hides the per-ISA detail this project is about.

alternatives.name: NumKong (formerly SimSIMD) kernels
alternatives.tradeoff: Mature mixed-precision kernels; best used as an external ceiling to compare against, not as your implementation.

alternatives.name: SVE
alternatives.tradeoff: Vector-length agnostic code, but only on some ARM cores, so you need a specific test machine.

steps.delegate: kernels_neon.c using arm_neon.h: l2sq_neon and ip_neon with vld1q_f32, vsubq_f32, vfmaq_f32 and a final vaddvq_f32. Same oracle tests and Google Benchmark cases as the AVX2 kernel, built on the ARM64 machine.
verify: Oracle tests pass on the ARM64 machine at d=100, 128 and 960
You measured NEON ns per call against the fast-math auto-vectorized build on the same ARM64 machine

steps.title: Store vectors as fp16 and accumulate in fp32
steps.learn: fp16 halves the bytes per vector, so a scan limited by memory bandwidth can get faster. Its largest finite value is 65504, so squared distances must be summed in fp32. On x86, F16C's _mm256_cvtph_ps widens 8 halves to floats; on ARM, vcvt_f32_f16 widens 4.

decision.choice: fp16 storage for base vectors, widen to fp32 in registers, fp32 FMA accumulation; queries stay fp32
decision.why: Storage shrinks by half while arithmetic precision stays fp32, so any recall change comes only from rounding the stored values. That isolates the cost of the format from the cost of the math.

alternatives.name: Native fp16 arithmetic (vfmaq_f16)
alternatives.tradeoff: Twice the lanes on ARM cores with FP16 support, but accumulating in fp16 risks overflow and larger rounding error.

alternatives.name: bf16 storage
alternatives.tradeoff: Same exponent range as fp32 so no overflow worry, but fewer mantissa bits than fp16.

alternatives.name: int8 scalar quantization
alternatives.tradeoff: 4x smaller than fp32, but needs per-dimension scales chosen from data, and a calibration step.

steps.delegate: Converter writes fp16 copies with numpy astype(np.float16). Kernels: l2sq_f16_avx2 (compile with -mavx2 -mfma -mf16c, _mm256_cvtph_ps) and l2sq_f16_neon (vld1_f16, vcvt_f32_f16, vfmaq_f32). Tests compare to the double oracle run on the dequantized fp16 values. Report recall@10 on the frozen queries for fp32 vs fp16.
verify: recall@10 for fp16 and fp32 on sift-128 and glove-100 frozen queries is recorded side by side
You counted how many GloVe components change when rounded to fp16, and noted why SIFT integers round-trip exactly
The max relative distance error of fp16 vs the double oracle is recorded per dataset

steps.title: Pick the kernel at runtime, safely
steps.learn: Code built with -mavx2 can die with an illegal instruction on a CPU without AVX2. Compile each ISA's kernels in their own file with their own flags and choose once at startup. GCC's __builtin_cpu_supports accepts names like "avx2" and "fma" and levels like "x86-64-v3".

decision.choice: Per-ISA source files plus one function-pointer table filled at startup from __builtin_cpu_supports
decision.why: One binary runs on any x86-64 machine and still uses AVX2, FMA and F16C where present. Explicit selection also lets tests force each kernel, so every path is checked against the oracle on one machine.

alternatives.name: -march=native for the whole program
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and often fastest, but the binary may crash on older or different CPUs.

alternatives.name: GCC target_clones multiversioning
alternatives.tradeoff: The compiler builds and dispatches the variants; less code, less control, and compiler-specific.

alternatives.name: ifunc resolvers
alternatives.tradeoff: Dispatch resolved once by the dynamic linker, but tied to ELF platforms.

steps.delegate: dispatch.c: struct kernels { l2sq, ip, l2sq_f16 } filled by kernels_init() using __builtin_cpu_supports("x86-64-v3") on x86 and NEON on AArch64. Env var FORCE_KERNEL=scalar|avx2|neon overrides. Tests loop over every kernel the CPU supports and run the oracle. Build the dispatcher file without -march=native.
verify: A binary built without -march=native selects the AVX2 kernel on the x86 machine and prints its choice
FORCE_KERNEL=scalar gives the same recall@10 on the frozen queries as the dispatched kernel
Every benchmark output row includes the kernel name

steps.title: Scan one query against many vectors and find the memory wall
steps.learn: Each loaded float feeds about one subtract and one FMA, so scanning vectors from RAM is limited by memory bandwidth, not FMA units. Measure two regimes: a block that fits in L1 or L2 (where SIMD width pays) and the full base set (where bytes per vector, so fp16, matters more).

decision.choice: A query-vs-block API (one query, n contiguous vectors, n distances out) measured from 32 KB to above LLC size
decision.why: This is the access pattern of brute-force search and of scanning candidate lists. Sweeping working-set size shows exactly where each kernel stops being compute-bound and the speedup over scalar shrinks.

alternatives.name: One distance per call
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches graph-index access, but call overhead and random-access misses blur the kernel's own speed.

alternatives.name: Several queries per pass
alternatives.tradeoff: Reuses each loaded vector, raising arithmetic intensity, but only fits batch workloads.

alternatives.name: Multithreaded scan
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows whole-socket bandwidth, but mixes thread scaling into a per-kernel question.

steps.delegate: l2sq_block(const float* q, const void* base, size_t n, size_t d, float* out) for each kernel and dtype. Google Benchmark with Args over working-set sizes (powers of 2 from 32 KB to 2 GB) and SetBytesProcessed so it reports bytes per second. Add a plain sum-of-floats read loop over the same buffer as a read-bandwidth ceiling.
verify: A plot of GB/s against working-set size per kernel shows where it drops; you marked L1, L2 and L3 sizes from lscpu on it
fp16 vs fp32 speedup is recorded separately for cache-resident and RAM-resident sizes
Each kernel's RAM-resident GB/s is compared to your read-bandwidth ceiling

steps.title: Measure it
steps.learn: Pitfalls: the compiler deleting unused results (use benchmark::DoNotOptimize), frequency scaling and turbo, other processes, and claiming RAM numbers from data that is still in cache. Baselines from prove-it: naive scalar; also the fast-math build and a library ceiling.

decision.choice: Google Benchmark on one pinned core, 10 repetitions, median ns per distance and GB/s; perf stat for instructions
decision.why: The library handles iteration counts, repetitions and aggregates, and its docs list ways to reduce variance. Counting instructions per distance explains speedups instead of just reporting them.

alternatives.name: Hand-rolled timing loop
alternatives.tradeoff: No dependency, but easy to get wrong: dead code removal, too few iterations, no spread reported.

alternatives.name: Only end-to-end kNN QPS
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to what users feel, but hides which kernel change caused what.

steps.delegate: bench target with the matrix kernel x dtype x d x working set. Script: taskset -c 2 ./bench --benchmark_repetitions=10 --benchmark_report_aggregates_only=true --benchmark_format=csv. Run perf stat -e cycles,instructions on scalar_strict vs AVX2 brute-force kNN over the frozen 1,000 sift-128 queries and record instructions per distance and QPS.

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) a speedup table with numbers for every claim plus machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example small cache-resident speedups vs RAM-bound ones), (4) assumptions, such as which CPUs and dims were tested.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2 gives a number for every claim, each with the machine (CPU, compiler, flags) and the exact command
Part 3 explains each surprising result with a measurement, not a guess
Part 4 lists assumptions and what the results do not prove, such as other CPUs, dims or metrics

projects.title: Graph reordering for cache locality
projects.problem: Random memory hops on the graph cause cache misses
projects.proveIt: Cache misses and QPS before vs after reordering
projects.question: Does relabeling HNSW graph nodes with RCM or Gorder cut cache misses and raise single-thread QPS at unchanged recall, and by how much?

steps.title: Frame the question, metrics and dataset
steps.learn: Reordering changes only where nodes sit in memory, not the graph, so recall should stay put while speed and misses move. Metrics: QPS at matched Recall@10 over an ef sweep, plus cache and TLB misses per query. Data: ann-benchmarks sift-128-euclidean and glove-100-angular.
verify: Your README states the question, the metric pair and the orderings you will compare before any code
You froze a split of the 10,000 test queries: 1,000 for choosing ef values, 9,000 only for final numbers
You recorded L1, L2 and LLC sizes from lscpu and confirmed the 1M SIFT vectors (about 512 MB as fp32) exceed the LLC

links.label: Graph reordering for ANN (Coleman et al.)

steps.title: Build one HNSW graph and freeze it
steps.learn: Every ordering must be compared on the identical graph, so build once, save, and only permute copies of the saved index. FAISS IndexHNSWFlat stores the graph in hnsw.neighbors with per-node offsets, and IndexHNSW.permute_entries relabels both the graph and the flat vector storage.

decision.choice: Build with FAISS IndexHNSWFlat (fixed M and efConstruction), save with write_index, permute copies with permute_entries
decision.why: The library already implements a correct relabel of all levels, the entry point and the vectors, so your time goes into orderings and measurement. Search code stays fixed, so only memory layout varies.

alternatives.name: hnswlib
alternatives.tradeoff: Stores links, vector and label together per node (one memory region), which is the layout the paper studied, but has no permute API.

alternatives.name: Your own HNSW
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control over layout and counters, but a bug in your search can masquerade as a layout effect.

steps.delegate: Python (faiss-cpu, h5py, numpy): build.py loads sift-128 train, builds faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(128, 32) with hnsw.efConstruction=200, records build time, write_index to sift_hnsw.faiss. Repeat for glove-100 on unit-normalized vectors. Test: reload gives identical search results on 100 queries.
verify: Build time and index size on disk are recorded for both datasets
Reloading the saved index returns identical ids for 100 queries
recall@10 on the 1,000 tuning queries at a few ef values is recorded as the original-order baseline

steps.title: Export the base layer and inspect its shape
steps.learn: Every node lives in level 0, which FAISS sizes at 2*M neighbor slots; in hnsw.neighbors, node i's level-0 slots start at offsets[i], with -1 for empty slots. Orderings are computed from this graph. Coleman et al. note pruning gives such graphs uneven degrees, though not a power law.

decision.choice: Compute orderings from the level-0 graph only, as a directed CSR matrix
decision.why: Level 0 holds all nodes and most search hops, so it decides locality. Upper levels hold few nodes and are permuted consistently by permute_entries anyway.

alternatives.name: Union of all levels
alternatives.tradeoff: Slightly more complete, but adds edges from layers the search barely touches.

alternatives.name: Symmetrized graph
alternatives.tradeoff: What RCM effectively uses anyway; matters if you write your own BFS-style ordering.

steps.delegate: export.py: bind hnsw = index.hnsw, then faiss.vector_to_array on hnsw.neighbors and hnsw.offsets; slice each node's level-0 slots, drop -1, build scipy.sparse.csr_array (n x n). Save as .npz and as a tab-separated edge list. Tests: edge count equals non-negative level-0 slots; a few nodes' neighbor lists match the FAISS arrays.
verify: You plotted the out-degree and in-degree histograms of the level-0 graph
Edge count in the CSR equals the count of non-negative level-0 slots
You computed the mean |i - j| over edges (label distance) for the original order as a locality baseline

steps.title: Set up the original and random orders as controls
steps.learn: A reordering result means nothing without controls. The original order is insertion order (dataset file order). A random permutation destroys whatever accidental locality the file had and shows what scattered access costs. Both keep the same graph and the same distance count.

decision.choice: Two controls: original insertion order and one fixed-seed random permutation
decision.why: Original is what a user gets by default; random bounds the bad case. If RCM or Gorder barely beat original but strongly beat random, the file order already had locality, which changes the conclusion.

alternatives.name: Original order only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer runs, but you cannot tell whether the input order was already good.

alternatives.name: Several random seeds
alternatives.tradeoff: Tighter error bars on the bad case, more benchmark time.

steps.delegate: orders.py: write perm_original.npy (arange) and perm_random.npy (fixed seed) in FAISS's convention perm[new] = old. Test: each is a valid permutation of 0..n-1. Report mean |i - j| over edges for each.
verify: Both permutation files pass a check that they contain every id exactly once
Mean label distance over edges is recorded for original and random

links.label: Graph reordering for ANN (Coleman et al.)

steps.title: Compute a Reverse Cuthill-McKee order
steps.learn: RCM is a heuristic that relabels nodes so connected nodes get nearby labels (it reduces matrix bandwidth). scipy's reverse_cuthill_mckee takes a CSR or CSC matrix, works on A+A.T unless symmetric_mode=True, and returns the permutation array.

decision.choice: scipy.sparse.csgraph.reverse_cuthill_mckee on the level-0 CSR, default symmetric_mode=False
decision.why: Coleman et al. found RCM one of the two consistently helpful orderings for HNSW, and scipy's version is a one-call, well-tested implementation that runs on a 1M-node graph.

alternatives.name: BFS order from the entry point
alternatives.tradeoff: Very cheap and intuitive, but a plain BFS has no objective tying neighbors close.

alternatives.name: Degree or hub sorting
alternatives.tradeoff: Very cheap, but the paper found degree-based methods far less effective on near neighbor graphs.

steps.delegate: rcm.py: load the CSR, time reverse_cuthill_mckee, save perm_rcm.npy. scipy's perm lists old ids in their new order, which matches FAISS's new-to-old convention; assert this with a 5-node example. Report bandwidth (max |i - j| over edges) and mean |i - j| before and after.
verify: Reorder time for RCM is recorded next to the index build time
Mean label distance over edges for RCM is lower than for original and random
A tiny hand-checked example confirms the permutation direction

links.label: Graph reordering for ANN (Coleman et al.)

steps.title: Compute a Gorder order
steps.learn: Gorder (Wei et al., SIGMOD 2016) greedily places nodes so those within a window of w consecutive labels share many neighbors. The reference code's default is w=5. Its main() first relabels with an internal RCM, then runs Gorder, and writes only the relabeled edge list (neighbor lists sorted), not the permutation.

decision.choice: The reference Gorder code with w=5, patched to also write the final old-to-new mapping
decision.why: On SIFT100M, Coleman et al. report Gorder cut P99 latency by 30 percent vs 17 percent for RCM. The reference code is the tested implementation; patching it to dump the composed mapping (internal RCM then Gorder) avoids reverse-engineering labels from the edge file.

alternatives.name: Reimplement Gorder yourself
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control over the objective and window, but slow to get right and easy to diverge from the paper.

alternatives.name: Use the edge-list output directly
alternatives.tradeoff: No patch, but the sorted neighbor lists change slot order, so search behaviour could differ slightly.

steps.delegate: C++: build datourat/Gorder, patch main.cpp and Graph::Transform to write the composed old-to-new mapping to a file. Run ./Gorder edges.txt -w 5. Python: invert to new-to-old, save perm_gorder.npy. Test: applying the mapping to the original edge list reproduces the tool's output edge set exactly.
verify: Applying your mapping to the original edges reproduces Gorder's output edge set
Gorder reorder time is recorded next to build time and RCM time
Mean label distance over edges for Gorder is recorded

links.label: Graph reordering for ANN (Coleman et al.)

steps.title: Apply each permutation and map result ids back
steps.learn: After permute_entries, FAISS returns new labels, so results must be mapped back with old = perm[new] before scoring against ground truth. Because only labels change, the search visits the same nodes in the same order, so recall and distance count should match the original apart from rare distance ties.

decision.choice: Keep perm next to each permuted index and translate results before every recall computation
decision.why: The recall scorer stays untouched and ground truth stays in original ids, so a mistake in permutation direction shows up as recall collapse instead of silently wrong numbers.

alternatives.name: Wrap in IndexIDMap
alternatives.tradeoff: Returns original ids automatically, but adds a lookup layer to the measured search path.

alternatives.name: Permute the ground truth instead
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids per-query mapping, but now the evaluation data depends on the system under test.

steps.delegate: apply.py: for each perm (original, random, rcm, gorder): read_index, permute_entries(faiss.swig_ptr(perm.astype('int64'))), write_index. Search the 1,000 tuning queries at fixed efSearch, map ids back, compute recall@10. Test: recall equals the original-order recall at every ef.
verify: recall@10 is identical across all four orderings at each ef, or you explained every difference
A deliberately inverted permutation makes recall collapse, proving the check works

steps.title: Decide how to treat huge pages
steps.learn: Random hops miss not only in data caches but in the TLB; Coleman et al. report lower TLB miss rates after reordering. Transparent huge pages are controlled by /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled (always, madvise, never), and AnonHugePages in /proc/meminfo shows usage.

decision.choice: Run the full matrix twice: THP set to never and THP set to always, recorded per run
decision.why: Huge pages and reordering both cut TLB misses, so a gain measured under one setting can shrink or grow under the other. Measuring both prevents attributing a THP effect to the ordering.

alternatives.name: Leave the system default
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but results depend on a setting you did not record.

alternatives.name: madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) on the index memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Targeted, but FAISS allocates the arrays itself, so you would have to patch allocation.

steps.delegate: Script thp.sh that reads and sets /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled (needs root), logs the setting and AnonHugePages from /proc/meminfo before and after loading the index, and refuses to start a benchmark if the setting does not match the requested one.
verify: Each result row records the THP setting it ran under
AnonHugePages grows after loading the index with THP=always and stays near zero with THP=never

steps.title: Measure it
steps.learn: Follow the paper's setup: warm start (index loaded, one untimed pass), one pinned core, nothing else running, total time for many queries. perf stat --delay=-1 with --control lets you count only the search phase, not loading. Cachegrind's --cache-sim=yes gives a deterministic second opinion.

decision.choice: Single pinned thread, 9,000 held-out queries, 5 runs per point, perf stat counters for the search phase only
decision.why: One core removes shared-LLC interference between threads; counting only search time keeps load and build misses out. Prove-it asks for misses and QPS before vs after, at matched recall, which this produces.

alternatives.name: All cores, batched queries
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to production throughput, but threads share the LLC and blur per-ordering effects.

alternatives.name: Cachegrind only
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and line-level, but simulated caches and far slower, so use it as a cross-check.

steps.delegate: bench.py: faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1); per ordering x THP x ef: warmup pass, then 5 timed passes over the 9,000 held-out queries, one query per search call; CSV of ordering, THP, ef, recall@10, QPS, p99 latency. The script writes enable and disable to a perf control FIFO around the timed passes; run under taskset -c 2 perf stat --delay=-1 --control fifo:ctl -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses plus dTLB and LLC events from perf list. Plot recall vs QPS.
verify: The CSV has every ordering at every ef under both THP settings, with misses per query
Repeat runs agree within 5 percent on QPS, or you found and removed the noise source
You recorded CPU model, LLC size, kernel, FAISS version and exact commands
A Cachegrind run on 500 queries ranks orderings by D1 and LL misses the same way perf does, or you explained why not
