steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) QPS and misses per query for each ordering at matched recall, with machine and command, (3) why gains differ between SIFT and GloVe or between controls, (4) assumptions, such as one graph, one machine and single-thread search.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2 gives a number for every claim, each with the machine (CPU, compiler, flags) and the exact command
Part 3 explains each surprising result with a measurement, not a guess
Part 4 lists assumptions and what the results do not prove, such as larger datasets or other graph indexes

projects.title: Fresh streaming index
projects.problem: New items should be searchable in under 1 second without a full rebuild
projects.proveIt: Insert-to-visible latency, recall during heavy writes
projects.question: Can a large HNSW index plus a small fresh buffer make new vectors searchable in under 1 second while recall holds under heavy writes?

steps.title: Frame the question, metrics and dataset
steps.learn: Two numbers answer it: insert-to-visible latency (from when the insert is sent until a query can return it), as p50 and p99, and Recall@10 against exact search over the points alive at that moment, sampled during a write-heavy run. Data: sift-128-euclidean from ann-benchmarks (1M train, 10k test, Euclidean).
verify: You can state the one question and both metrics in one sentence each, including the 1 second target
You opened the HDF5 file and printed the shapes of train and test
You froze a query sample from test and a random seed in a committed file before writing any index code

steps.title: Write the runbook and live ground truth
steps.learn: A streaming benchmark is a script of operations: insert a batch, delete a batch, run a search checkpoint. The answer set changes after every write, so recall must be scored against exact search over exactly the live points at each checkpoint, never against the dataset's shipped static neighbors.

decision.choice: Your own seeded runbook on SIFT1M: bulk load half, then rounds of inserts, deletes and search checkpoints
decision.why: It runs on a laptop, every checkpoint gets exact ground truth you compute yourself, and you control the write mix. The seed makes every design replay the identical sequence, so differences come from the index, not the workload.

alternatives.name: big-ann-benchmarks streaming runbooks
alternatives.tradeoff: Comparable to published NeurIPS'23 entries, but they use 10M to 30M MS Turing points and their own harness, which is heavy for a first build.

alternatives.name: Clustered insertion order
alternatives.tradeoff: Inserting one k-means cluster at a time (as the NeurIPS'23 clustered runbooks do) tests data drift; harder, so add it as a second run once the uniform one works.

steps.delegate: Python 3, numpy, h5py, faiss-cpu. runbook.py: from a seed, emit a JSON list of ops (insert ids, delete ids, search) over SIFT1M train ids. gt.py: replay the ops, keep the live id set, and at each search op compute exact top-10 with faiss.IndexIDMap(faiss.IndexFlatL2(128)) over live vectors. Tests: live set equals set arithmetic of the ops; ground truth on a tiny random case equals numpy argsort.
verify: The live-set size at every checkpoint equals inserts minus deletes so far
On 3 checkpoints, your ground truth matches an independent numpy brute force over the live set, id for id apart from distance ties
The runbook file and seed are committed before any index code exists

steps.title: Choose the main index for the bulk of the data
steps.learn: The main index holds almost every point and is tuned for query speed. In hnswlib, add_items is thread-safe with other add_items calls but not with knn_query, and resize_index is safe with neither. Mutating the index you are serving from therefore needs a lock that blocks readers.

decision.choice: hnswlib HNSW as the main index, kept read-only while it serves and replaced by a newer copy after merges
decision.why: It is fast and well documented, and treating it as immutable sidesteps its insert versus query thread-safety limit, so queries never wait on writes. Freshness then becomes the job of a separate small structure.

alternatives.name: In-place add_items behind a lock
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest design with one structure, but every insert batch stalls queries, so p99 query latency climbs with the write rate.

alternatives.name: FAISS IVF-Flat
alternatives.tradeoff: Adding a vector is just assigning it to a list, but centroids trained on old data fit new data worse as the corpus drifts.

alternatives.name: DiskANN (FreshVamana)
alternatives.tradeoff: Built for streaming inserts and deletes, but a larger C++ build to set up and understand.

steps.delegate: Python, hnswlib, numpy. main.py wraps hnswlib.Index('l2', 128): build(vectors, ids, M, ef_construction), search(q, k, ef) returning (ids, dists), save(path), load(path, max_elements). Tests: returned labels are the ids you passed; on a 100k static subset Recall@10 at ef=100 is above a threshold you record; save then load returns identical results.
verify: You plotted static Recall@10 against ef for the main index alone on the initial bulk load
You recorded build time and process memory for that bulk load

steps.title: Add a fresh buffer that makes inserts visible at once
steps.learn: This is the LSM memtable idea applied to vectors: new writes land in a small structure that is searchable at once, while the large one is rebuilt in the background. FreshDiskANN does the same with an in-memory read-write TempIndex that later becomes read-only and is merged into the long-term index.

decision.choice: A preallocated append-only float32 array searched by brute force, with a size cap that triggers a merge
decision.why: Brute force is exact, so the buffer adds no recall loss, and an insert is a memory copy, so visibility depends only on how fast you publish it. The cap bounds the extra scan cost each query pays.

alternatives.name: Small hnswlib index as the buffer
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales to much larger buffers, but each insert does a graph search and the insert versus query thread-safety limit comes back.

alternatives.name: Insert straight into the main index
alternatives.tradeoff: No merge logic at all, but inserts and queries contend for one structure.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy, faiss-cpu. buffer.py: preallocated (capacity, 128) float32 array plus int64 ids and a count; append(vecs, ids) raises when full; search(q, k, upto=count) does exact L2 on rows [0, upto) with faiss.knn or a numpy matmul using the squared-norm trick. Tests: matches brute force exactly; a vector searched for itself comes back first at distance 0; full buffer raises.
verify: You measured buffer query time at several fill levels and compared it to one main-index query at your chosen ef
You picked the cap so a full buffer scan stays a small fraction of total query time, and wrote the number down

steps.title: Merge results from main index and buffers per query
steps.learn: A query fans out to every live segment (main, frozen buffers, active buffer) and merges by true distance. All segments return L2 distances on the same scale, so a k-way merge is correct. Deleted ids must be dropped before cutting to k, so each segment must return more than k.

decision.choice: Ask each segment for k plus a margin sized from its current deleted fraction, drop tombstones, heap-merge, cut to k
decision.why: Over-fetch keeps results full when deletes are common without paying a fixed large cost when they are rare. Filtering in the merge works the same for every segment type.

alternatives.name: hnswlib filter callback
alternatives.tradeoff: Filters inside the graph search, but the README notes Python filters are slow in multithreaded mode and recommends num_threads=1.

alternatives.name: Fixed over-fetch such as 2k
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but can return fewer than k results when deletes cluster near the query.

steps.delegate: Python. query.py: search(snapshot, q, k) gathers candidates from every segment in the snapshot, removes ids in the tombstone set, deduplicates ids present in two segments during a merge (keep the newest), heap-merges by distance, returns top k. Tests: duplicate id appears once; when every main top-k id is deleted the result is still full; output sorted by distance.
verify: Replaying the full runbook, no query ever returns a deleted id
At each checkpoint you compared combined Recall@10 with the main index static Recall@10 at the same ef, and explained any gap

steps.title: Handle deletes with tombstones and periodic rebuilds
steps.learn: Removing a node from a proximity graph breaks paths through it. FreshDiskANN shows recall falling over repeated delete and reinsert cycles on SIFT1M for HNSW, Vamana and NSG under simple policies, and uses lazy deletion: deleted points still guide search, are filtered from results, and are consolidated in batches.

decision.choice: A tombstone set checked at query time; tombstoned points are dropped when the main index is fully rebuilt
decision.why: A delete is a set insert and is visible immediately. Graph quality is restored by a rebuild instead of in-place repair, which is the hardest part to get right and is not this project's question.

alternatives.name: hnswlib mark_deleted
alternatives.tradeoff: Built in and omitted from results; with allow_replace_deleted new points can reuse the slots, but it mutates the serving index.

alternatives.name: Eager graph repair per delete
alternatives.tradeoff: Best steady-state graph (FreshVamana reconnects neighbors with alpha pruning), but complex and costly per delete.

steps.delegate: Python. tombstones.py: a set of deleted ids plus a version counter, copied into each published snapshot. Cover delete of a buffer-only id, delete of a main-index id, and delete then reinsert of the same id (the new vector must win). Tests for all three cases.
verify: You plotted Recall@10 and query latency against tombstone fraction, from zero up to your rebuild threshold
Delete then reinsert of one id returns the new vector, not the old one

steps.title: Publish snapshots so readers never wait on writers
steps.learn: A query needs a consistent view: one main index, a fixed prefix of each buffer, one tombstone version. If buffers are append-only and the writer publishes a new snapshot after writing rows, a reader holding a snapshot sees a stable view. Insert-to-visible latency is the gap between write and publish.

decision.choice: One writer builds a new immutable snapshot and swaps one shared reference; readers take it at query start
decision.why: Readers never hold a lock while the writer works, so writes do not stretch query tail latency. Old snapshots are freed once no query references them, which is the RCU pattern.

alternatives.name: Readers-writer lock
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to reason about, but writers can stall readers or starve, which shows up directly in p99.

alternatives.name: Rust with atomically swapped Arc snapshots
alternatives.tradeoff: True parallel readers without the Python GIL and stronger guarantees, at the cost of more code.

steps.delegate: Python, threading. store.py: Snapshot dataclass (main, frozen buffers, active buffer and its count, tombstones version). Writer: apply op, then build and publish a new Snapshot. Readers: snap = store.current, then search(snap, ...). Stress test: 4 reader threads plus the writer replaying the runbook for 10 minutes, asserting no exceptions and no result id that was not live in that snapshot.
verify: The 10 minute stress test finishes with zero exceptions and zero results outside the snapshot's live set
You measured p99 query latency with writes off and with writes on, using the same query sample

steps.title: Merge buffers into the main index in the background
steps.learn: Merging is compaction. When the active buffer fills, freeze it as read-only and start a new one, the same read-write to read-only handoff FreshDiskANN uses. A merge then folds frozen buffers into a new main index and swaps it in. The CPU it takes from queries is what hurts latency during heavy writes.

decision.choice: Extend a copy of the main index with frozen buffers in a separate process; fully rebuild past a tombstone threshold
decision.why: Extending is cheaper than rebuilding, the serving index stays read-only, and a separate process keeps merge work off the query threads. Full rebuilds bound the recall loss from accumulated tombstones.

alternatives.name: Full rebuild on every merge
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleanest graph every time, but merge cost grows with total size, so buffers sit longer and visibility depends on brute-force size.

alternatives.name: In-place add_items under a lock
alternatives.tradeoff: No second copy in memory, but queries block for the whole merge.

steps.delegate: Python, hnswlib, multiprocessing. merger.py: given saved main index path, frozen buffer arrays and tombstones, load_index with a larger max_elements, add_items the buffers, save to a new path; or rebuild from scratch when tombstones exceed the threshold. Parent loads the result, publishes a snapshot without those buffers, then frees them. Tests: no id lost or duplicated across a merge.
verify: During a merge, the writer logged write-to-publish gap stays under 1 second at p99
After a full rebuild, Recall@10 returns to the static level for that ef
You recorded peak memory during a merge (two main indexes exist briefly)

steps.title: Make acknowledged inserts survive a crash
steps.learn: Fast visibility is only useful if acknowledged writes are not lost. FreshDiskANN writes every update to a redo log, rebuilds the mutable in-memory index by replaying the log since the last snapshot, and reloads the read-only parts from disk. fsync is the cost; group commit spreads it over many writes.

decision.choice: Log inserts and deletes, fsync per small group, acknowledge after fsync; snapshot the main index, then truncate the log
decision.why: Group commit keeps the per-insert fsync cost inside the 1 second budget while making every acknowledged write durable. Snapshots bound recovery time.

alternatives.name: Acknowledge before fsync
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest latency, but a crash loses the most recent writes that callers believe succeeded.

alternatives.name: No log, rebuild from an upstream source
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest here, but only works if another system can replay every change in order.

steps.delegate: Python, os.fsync. wal.py: append(op) to a binary log with length and checksum per record; a commit thread fsyncs every few ms and releases waiting writers. recover(): load the last main snapshot, replay later records into buffers and tombstones, skip a torn final record. Tests: torn tail is ignored; replay is idempotent.
verify: You killed the process with SIGKILL during a write burst and every acknowledged id was searchable after restart
You recorded recovery time and the logged insert-to-publish p99 with fsync on and off

steps.title: Measure freshness and recall under heavy writes
steps.learn: Measure visibility from outside: a probe inserts a vector, then queries with that same vector until its id comes back. Drive writes open-loop at fixed rates; a closed-loop driver slows when the system does and hides the tail (coordinated omission). Baselines: periodic full rebuild, and locked in-place hnswlib inserts.

decision.choice: Open-loop writes at fixed rates, a timed freshness probe, recall at checkpoints, identical machine and threads for all
decision.why: Fixed rates show where each design stops meeting 1 second, and identical conditions make the three designs comparable. Recall over time with merge events marked shows when quality dips.

alternatives.name: Closed-loop max throughput
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives peak inserts per second, but understates latency because the load backs off when the system stalls.

alternatives.name: big-ann-benchmarks streaming harness
alternatives.tradeoff: Reports average recall across runbook checkpoints in a comparable setup, but you still add your own freshness probe.

steps.delegate: Python. bench.py: run each design (yours, rebuild-every-N-seconds, in-place hnswlib with a lock) on the same runbook; writer thread issues inserts on a fixed schedule and records intended send time; probe inserts a marker vector every 100 ms and polls until visible; log Recall@10 at checkpoints and merge start and end times. Output CSV and plots.
verify: You have p50, p99 and max insert-to-visible for every design at every write rate, timed from the intended send time
The recall-over-time plot marks merge and rebuild events for every design
You recorded CPU model, RAM, OS, library versions and the exact command
Repeated runs agree within 10 percent; if not, you found and removed the noise source

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer the one question with two plots: insert-to-visible latency against write rate, and recall over time. Explain dips with your own event log: merges, rebuilds and tombstone fraction at each moment.
verify: Part 1: it opens with the one question and the 1 second target
Part 2: every claim has a number with the machine, library versions and command that produced it
Part 3: it explains surprising results, such as recall dips or latency spikes, using merge and tombstone logs

projects.title: Matryoshka adaptive retrieval
projects.problem: Full-size embeddings are slow; truncated ones lose quality
projects.proveIt: Cost curve: search at 64 dims, rerank at 1024
projects.question: How much search cost does a 64-dim first pass save, and does reranking its shortlist at 1024 dims recover full-size retrieval quality?

steps.title: Frame the question, metric and dataset
steps.learn: The deliverable is a cost curve: NDCG@10 and Recall@100 from human relevance labels, against cost per query (multiply-adds, bytes touched, milliseconds). Data: BEIR FiQA-2018 (57,638 financial posts) with separate dev and test relevance labels. Tune on dev; test stays frozen until the end.
verify: You printed the corpus size, query count and the number of judged pairs in the dev and test splits
You committed the test query id list before running anything, and wrote that it will be run once
You can state the question and both baselines (1024 exact alone, 64 exact alone) in one sentence each

steps.title: Choose a Matryoshka-trained embedding model
steps.learn: Truncation only works if the model was trained so the first dimensions carry the most information (MRL). Retrieval models are often asymmetric: mxbai-embed-large-v1 wants 'Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ' on queries only; nomic-embed-text-v1.5 uses search_query: and search_document: prefixes.

decision.choice: mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-large-v1: 1024 dims, and its card states support for MRL and binary quantization
decision.why: Its full size is exactly the 1024 in the prove-it, and open weights let you embed the corpus locally and reproduce every number.

alternatives.name: nomic-embed-text-v1.5
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller MRL model with 768 full dims; its card applies layer_norm before slicing. Cheaper to encode, but there is no 1024 point.

alternatives.name: all-mpnet-base-v2 as a control
alternatives.tradeoff: 768 dims, not trained with MRL. Truncating it shows how much MRL training matters, but it cannot be the main system.

steps.delegate: Python, sentence-transformers. embed.py: load FiQA corpus (title plus text) and queries; encode corpus with model.encode(batch_size=64, normalize_embeddings=False), queries with the query prompt; save float32 .npy (N x 1024) and id lists. Tests: shapes; encoding the same text twice gives cosine above 0.9999; the prompt is applied to queries only.
verify: The saved corpus matrix has one 1024-dim row per document and ids line up with the corpus file
You recorded encoding time, batch size and hardware
You checked that 10 sample queries carry the query prompt and 10 sample corpus texts do not

steps.title: Derive every smaller size by slicing and renormalizing
steps.learn: A d-dim Matryoshka vector is the first d coordinates of the full one. After slicing, vectors are no longer unit length, so cosine similarity needs an L2 renormalization; raw dot products would let the leftover norm change the ranking. Slice 64, 128, 256 and 512 from the cached 1024 instead of re-encoding.

decision.choice: Slice the cached 1024-dim vectors and L2-normalize each size; check once against SentenceTransformer(truncate_dim=64)
decision.why: One encoding pass serves every size, so the comparison isolates dimension count. The one-time check against the library's own truncate_dim path catches an off-by-one or a missed normalization.

alternatives.name: Re-encode with truncate_dim per size
alternatives.tradeoff: The library's official path, but costs a full encoding pass per size for the same numbers.

alternatives.name: Skip renormalization
alternatives.tradeoff: One less operation, but scores mix in vector length and no longer equal cosine similarity.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. dims.py: make_dim(full, d) returns full[:, :d] divided by its row L2 norm, as contiguous float32; write 64, 128, 256, 512 and 1024 versions to .npy. Tests: rows have unit norm; d=1024 equals normalized full; for 100 texts the 64-dim vectors match SentenceTransformer(model, truncate_dim=64) outputs after normalization (cosine above 0.9999).
verify: Your sliced 64-dim vectors match the truncate_dim=64 library output on 100 sample texts
You recorded the bytes per vector at each size (float32: 4 bytes per dimension)

steps.title: Build exact baselines at every dimension
steps.learn: Before any shortlist, measure single-stage exact search at 64, 128, 256, 512 and 1024 on dev. This separates truncation loss from approximate search loss and gives the two ends of the curve. Grade with the human labels, never with the 1024 system's own ranking.

decision.choice: FAISS IndexFlatIP per size, scored with pytrec_eval (ndcg_cut.10, recall.100)
decision.why: Exact inner product on unit vectors is cosine with no approximation, and pytrec_eval wraps trec_eval, so metrics match the standard definitions used by BEIR results.

alternatives.name: BEIR's evaluation helpers
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer lines of code with the same datasets, but less control over what is computed per query.

alternatives.name: Overlap with the 1024 top-k as the metric
alternatives.tradeoff: Measures fidelity to the full model, not relevance; report it only as a secondary number.

steps.delegate: Python, faiss-cpu, pytrec_eval. baseline.py: for each size build faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), add vectors, search dev queries for top 100, convert to a run dict {qid: {docid: score}}, evaluate with pytrec_eval.RelevanceEvaluator(qrels, {'ndcg_cut.10', 'recall.100'}). Output a table. Tests: a run equal to the qrels scores NDCG@10 of 1.0.
verify: You have a dev table of NDCG@10 and Recall@100 for all five sizes
Running the same size twice gives identical results
You noted how much 64-dim alone loses versus 1024, which is the gap reranking must close

steps.title: Choose the 64-dim first-stage index
steps.learn: The first stage only has to get relevant documents into the shortlist; order inside it can be rough. At 64 dims a float32 vector is 256 bytes versus 4 KB at 1024, so a scan touches 16 times less memory. The MRL paper reports that HNSW shortlisting did not reduce accuracy in its image retrieval setting.

decision.choice: Exact flat scan at 64 dims (FAISS IndexFlatIP) as the main pipeline; HNSW at 64 dims as a scaling variant
decision.why: FiQA is small enough that an exact scan is cheap, which keeps approximate search error out of the main comparison. The HNSW variant shows how the design behaves at corpus sizes where a scan is too slow.

alternatives.name: HNSW at 64 dims (hnswlib)
alternatives.tradeoff: Sublinear and needed at millions of documents, but adds its own recall loss and build time to the shortlist.

alternatives.name: Binary-quantized vectors with rescoring
alternatives.tradeoff: sentence-transformers quantize_embeddings(precision='ubinary') packs 8 dims per byte, but loses more and must be rescored.

steps.delegate: Python, faiss-cpu, hnswlib. stage1.py: shortlist(q64, K) using faiss.IndexFlatIP(64); variant using hnswlib.Index('ip', 64) with M and ef parameters. Tests: flat shortlist equals numpy argsort of dot products; HNSW shortlist recall against flat is reported, not asserted.
verify: For each K in your grid you measured shortlist recall: the share of dev-relevant documents found by 1024 exact top-100 that appear in the 64-dim top-K
You measured stage 1 time per query for the flat scan and the HNSW variant

steps.title: Pick the shortlist size and rerank at 1024
steps.learn: Reranking K candidates at 1024 dims costs K times 1024 multiply-adds per query, whatever the corpus size. The quality ceiling is whether relevant documents made the shortlist. The MRL paper used K=200 and found gains stopped beyond a shortlist length that depended on the dataset.

decision.choice: Sweep K over 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 on dev; pick the smallest K within a preset NDCG@10 tolerance of 1024 exact
decision.why: K is the main cost knob of the second stage, and the right value for financial text is not known in advance. A tolerance fixed before the sweep stops you from picking whatever looks best.

alternatives.name: Fixed K=200 as in the MRL paper
alternatives.tradeoff: No tuning, but that value came from image retrieval and may be too large or too small here.

alternatives.name: Per-query K from the score gap
alternatives.tradeoff: Lower average cost on easy queries, but more logic and harder to reason about tail cost.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. rerank.py: rerank(q_full, shortlist_ids, full_vectors) gathers rows, computes dot products, returns ids sorted by score. pipeline.py: two_stage(q, K). Tests: K equal to corpus size reproduces the 1024 exact ranking exactly; output ids are a subset of the shortlist.
verify: Two-stage with K equal to the corpus size matches 1024 exact search document for document
You plotted dev NDCG@10 against K with the 1024 and 64 baselines as horizontal lines
Your chosen K and the tolerance rule are written down before any test run

steps.title: Keep 64 dims in RAM and full vectors on disk
steps.learn: The memory win of adaptive retrieval is that only the shortlist needs full vectors. Keep the 64-dim matrix in RAM and map the 1024-dim matrix from a file; a rerank touches K scattered rows. Whether those pages are already in the OS page cache changes latency a lot, so measure cold and warm.

decision.choice: numpy.memmap over a row-major float32 1024-dim file; gather shortlist rows in sorted id order
decision.why: The OS loads only the pages touched, so resident memory follows the shortlist, not the corpus. Sorting ids makes reads more sequential.

alternatives.name: Everything in RAM
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest rerank with no I/O, but gives up the memory saving that motivates the design.

alternatives.name: float16 full vectors
alternatives.tradeoff: Half the bytes read per candidate; you must confirm NDCG@10 does not change.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. store.py: write full vectors to full.f32 once; open with np.memmap(path, dtype='float32', mode='r', shape=(N, 1024)); gather(ids) sorts ids, reads rows, restores original order. Optional float16 variant. Tests: gathered rows equal the in-RAM matrix; order restored correctly.
verify: You measured process resident memory with memmap versus fully in RAM
You measured rerank latency on a cold cache (first queries after a reboot or cache drop) and warm
If you tried float16, dev NDCG@10 is within your tolerance of float32

steps.title: Compare a funnel cascade with one jump
steps.learn: The MRL paper's Funnel Retrieval halves the shortlist and doubles the dimensions at each rerank step, a cascade that reduces the need to pick one shortlist and one rerank size. Each step reads more bytes per candidate but scores fewer candidates.

decision.choice: Compare two-stage (64 then 1024) against a funnel (64, 128, 256, 512, 1024, halving K each step) on dev at equal NDCG@10
decision.why: It tests whether intermediate sizes buy anything on this data, an ablation the cost curve needs either way.

alternatives.name: Three stages: 64, 256, 1024
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer steps to tune than a full funnel; may capture most of its benefit.

alternatives.name: Cross-encoder after the 1024 rerank
alternatives.tradeoff: Can raise quality further, but adds a model call per candidate and much higher latency; a different question.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. funnel.py: funnel(q, dims=[64,128,256,512,1024], K0) where each step reranks the current list using the next size from the in-RAM sliced matrices (1024 from memmap) and keeps half. Count multiply-adds per query analytically. Tests: a one-step funnel equals two_stage.
verify: Both pipelines appear on the same dev plot of NDCG@10 against multiply-adds per query
You can state which one wins at your tolerance and by how much cost

steps.title: Lock the operating point on dev, then run test once
steps.learn: Dimensions, K and funnel shape are several knobs tuned on the same queries, which overfits. FiQA ships separate dev and test labels: choose everything on dev with the rule you wrote earlier, then run test exactly once for every configuration you will report.

decision.choice: Freeze the chosen config and the full list of reported configs in a committed file, then run test once
decision.why: The test numbers then measure generalization, not how well you searched the knob space.

alternatives.name: Cross-validate across train and dev queries
alternatives.tradeoff: More stable choice with more queries, but more compute and still no substitute for an untouched test split.

alternatives.name: Tune directly on test
alternatives.tradeoff: Looks better, but the reported numbers no longer mean anything.

steps.delegate: Python. final.py: read frozen config.json, assert its commit predates the run, evaluate every listed config on test with pytrec_eval, write results to test_results.csv without overwriting earlier files.
verify: config.json is committed before test_results.csv exists
Test results are reported for every listed config, including the ones that lost on dev

steps.title: Measure the cost curve against both baselines
steps.learn: Report cost three ways: multiply-adds per query (computed), bytes touched, and measured latency p50 and p99. Baselines: 1024 exact alone and 64 exact alone. Time search separately from query encoding, and report encoding time too, since it may dwarf the search time.

decision.choice: Single thread for FAISS and BLAS, warmup pass, median of 3 runs, one query at a time
decision.why: One thread and one query isolate per-query cost, which is what the shortlist design changes. Warmup removes one-time costs such as page faults on first touch.

alternatives.name: Batched queries on all cores
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to throughput serving, but batching and threading effects blur per-query cost.

alternatives.name: One end-to-end number including encoding
alternatives.tradeoff: Honest about user-visible latency, but hides the search savings this project measures.

steps.delegate: Python. bench.py: faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1) and OMP_NUM_THREADS=1; for 64 exact, 1024 exact, two-stage at chosen K, funnel, and the memmap variant: warmup, then 3 timed passes over test queries, recording per-query latency. CSV: config, NDCG@10, Recall@100, multiply-adds, bytes, p50, p99. Plot NDCG@10 against p50 latency.
verify: The CSV and plot include both baselines and every pipeline on the test split
You recorded CPU model, RAM, OS, library versions, model revision and the exact command
Repeated runs agree within 10 percent on p50; if not, you found and removed the noise source

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer the question with the cost curve: how much cheaper the chosen pipeline is than 1024 exact, and how much NDCG@10 it gives up, if any. Explain results with shortlist recall: a quality gap means relevant documents never reached the shortlist.
verify: Part 1: it opens with the one question about 64-dim search and 1024-dim reranking
Part 2: every claim has a number with the machine, versions and command that produced it
Part 3: it explains surprising results, such as a K beyond which quality stops improving, using shortlist recall
Part 4: it lists assumptions and limits, such as one corpus, one model, a small corpus, single-thread timing

projects.title: Multi-tenant vector index
projects.problem: Thousands of small customers: one index each, or one shared index with filters?
projects.proveIt: Memory, latency and recall for both designs
projects.question: For thousands of small tenants, does one index per tenant or one shared index with a tenant filter win on memory, latency and recall?

steps.title: Frame the question, metrics and tenant dataset
steps.learn: Prove-it asks for three numbers per design: memory, latency and recall. Tenants are a data property, so you need many tenants with skewed sizes: a few large, a long tail of tiny ones. Real vectors come from dbpedia-entities-openai-1M (1536-dim ada-002 embeddings of DBpedia title plus text).

decision.choice: Real vectors, synthetic tenants: 200k vectors split into 2,000 tenants with seeded Zipf-like sizes; queries frozen now
decision.why: No public dataset has thousands of natural tenants with embeddings. Real embeddings keep distances realistic, a seeded size draw is reproducible, and freezing each tenant's held-out queries before any tuning keeps the test honest.

alternatives.name: Uniform tenant sizes
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler to reason about, but hides the real problem: tiny tenants are where shared filtered indexes struggle and where per-tenant overhead dominates.

alternatives.name: Natural tenants (BEIR CQADupStack forums)
alternatives.tradeoff: Topically real tenants, but only a dozen of them, so it cannot show per-index overhead at thousands of tenants.

alternatives.name: Tenants from k-means clusters
alternatives.tradeoff: Models tenants whose data is topically clustered; worth running as a second condition, but alone it hides the random-membership case.

steps.delegate: Python 3, datasets (Hugging Face), numpy, pyarrow. Write data.py: load the first 210k rows of KShivendu/dbpedia-entities-openai-1M, L2-normalize, keep 200k as corpus and 10k as query pool. assign_tenants(n=2000, seed=0) draws Zipf-like sizes (minimum 5) and returns tenant_id per row; give each tenant queries from the pool proportional to size (at least 1). Save corpus, tenant ids and queries to .npy. Tests: sizes sum to 200k, seed is deterministic.
verify: You can state the one question and the three metrics (bytes per vector, p50/p99 latency, Recall@10) in one sentence each
You printed tenant size quantiles (min, median, p99, max) and the count of tenants under 100 vectors
The query file is saved with a checksum you recorded, and you will not change it later

steps.title: Compute exact per-tenant ground truth and a recall scorer
steps.learn: Recall must be graded by brute force inside each tenant, never by either design's own index. Exact top-10 within a tenant is cheap because tenants are small. Store it once so every design is scored against the same file.

decision.choice: numpy brute force (dot product on normalized vectors) over each tenant's rows, top 10 saved per query
decision.why: Tenants are small, so exact search per tenant is fast in plain numpy, has no index to misconfigure, and is independent of both designs under test.

alternatives.name: faiss IndexFlatIP per tenant
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster for big tenants via optimized BLAS kernels, but adds a library to the grader that you also use in a design under test.

alternatives.name: Global top-k then filter by tenant
alternatives.tradeoff: One big matrix product, but needs a large k to be sure every tenant gets 10 results, so it is easy to get subtly wrong.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. Write truth.py: for each query, take its tenant's row ids, score by dot product, return exact top-10 ids (tenant-local ids mapped back to global ids). Save to truth.npy. Write metrics.py: recall_at_k(found, truth, k=10) that also returns a leak flag if any found id belongs to another tenant. Tests: identical lists give 1.0, a cross-tenant id sets the leak flag, tenants with fewer than 10 rows are scored on their size.
verify: Exact search scored against truth.npy gives Recall@10 of exactly 1.0 for every query
A planted cross-tenant id is flagged by the scorer
Tenants smaller than 10 vectors are handled without crashing or dividing by zero

steps.title: Build design A: one index per tenant
steps.learn: Each index has fixed overhead (headers, entry points, preallocated capacity) on top of per-vector cost; hnswlib documents graph memory as roughly M * 8 to 10 bytes per element. With thousands of tenants the fixed part multiplies, and an HNSW graph on 20 vectors buys nothing over a scan.

decision.choice: hnswlib HNSW per tenant above a size threshold; below it, an exact scan (hnswlib.BFIndex or numpy)
decision.why: Tiny tenants are cheaper and exact with a scan, and skipping their graphs removes most of the per-index overhead. Large tenants keep HNSW speed. The threshold becomes a knob you measure, not a guess.

alternatives.name: HNSW for every tenant
alternatives.tradeoff: One code path, but pays graph overhead on thousands of tiny tenants for no recall or speed gain.

alternatives.name: Qdrant collection per tenant
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong isolation, but Qdrant's guide warns each collection carries overhead and Qdrant Cloud caps clusters at 1000 collections by default.

steps.delegate: Python, hnswlib, numpy. Write design_a.py: class PerTenantIndex(threshold, M=16, ef_construction=200). build(vectors, tenant_ids) creates hnswlib.Index('ip', dim) per tenant at or above threshold (max_elements set to its size) and stores a numpy block for smaller ones. query(tenant, q, k, ef) routes to the right structure and caps k at the tenant size. Tests: only that tenant's ids return; threshold=0 works on a 5-vector tenant; threshold=inf gives exact results; unknown tenant raises KeyError.
verify: Recall@10 against truth.npy is 1.0 for all tenants below the threshold
You recorded process RSS after build for threshold = 0 (all HNSW) and for your chosen threshold
No query returns an id from another tenant across the whole query set

steps.title: Decide what stays in memory for per-tenant indexes
steps.learn: Most tenants are idle most of the time. Keeping every index resident costs memory for tenants nobody is querying; loading on demand costs a cold-start delay on the first query. This is the same tradeoff as a database buffer pool, with whole indexes as pages.

decision.choice: All indexes saved to disk; an LRU cache keeps a bounded number of tenant indexes loaded
decision.why: Gives design A a memory knob that the shared design does not have, so the comparison is fair at a fixed memory budget, and it exposes cold-load latency as a measured cost instead of a hidden one.

alternatives.name: Keep everything resident
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest latency and simplest; memory grows with every tenant, so it is the worst case for design A's memory number.

alternatives.name: Memory-map index files
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets the OS page data in and out, but needs an index format designed for mmap, which hnswlib's save_index and load_index do not document.

steps.delegate: Python, hnswlib, collections.OrderedDict. Extend PerTenantIndex: save_all(dir) with save_index per tenant; TenantCache(capacity) loads with load_index on miss, evicts least recently used, and re-applies set_ef after load (hnswlib does not save ef). Count hits, misses and load time. Tests: capacity 1 alternating two tenants gives all misses; results after reload equal results before save; ef after reload equals the configured value.
verify: Cold-load latency for a large and a small tenant is recorded separately
With capacity set to 10 percent of tenants and a Zipf query mix, you recorded the hit rate and RSS
Results after save and reload match the in-memory results on 1,000 queries

steps.title: Build design B: one shared index with a tenant filter
steps.learn: In a shared index the tenant filter decides recall. Post-filtering (search, then drop other tenants) returns too few results for small tenants. Filtering during traversal keeps only allowed results, but when a tenant is a tiny fraction of the graph the search must walk many disallowed nodes.

decision.choice: One hnswlib index over all 200k vectors, tenant filter applied during search via knn_query(filter=...)
decision.why: It is the in-graph filtering approach most shared designs rely on, it reuses the same library as design A so the comparison isolates the design rather than the implementation, and its weakness on tiny tenants is exactly what prove-it should expose.

alternatives.name: Post-filter with over-fetch
alternatives.tradeoff: Works with any index, but you must guess an over-fetch factor, and tiny tenants still come back short or need huge k.

alternatives.name: faiss IndexHNSWFlat with IDSelectorBatch
alternatives.tradeoff: Same idea via SearchParametersHNSW(sel=...), with optimized C++ selectors; pick it to check that results are not a hnswlib quirk.

steps.delegate: Python, hnswlib, numpy. Write design_b.py: SharedIndex builds one hnswlib.Index('ip', dim, M=16, ef_construction=200) with global ids as labels and a tenant_of array. query(tenant, q, k, ef) calls knn_query(q, min(k, tenant size), num_threads=1, filter=lambda i: tenant_of[i] == tenant) and catches RuntimeError as a short result. Also implement post_filter(tenant, q, k, fetch). Tests: zero cross-tenant ids; a 5-vector tenant does not crash; post_filter can return fewer than k.
verify: You plotted Recall@10 by tenant-size bucket for in-graph filtering and post-filtering at the same ef
You recorded p50 latency for the smallest and largest tenant buckets and noted which is slower
No result contains another tenant's id

steps.title: Add a planner that scans tiny tenants in the shared design
steps.learn: Qdrant's docs describe the fix used in production: when a filter matches few points, its planner skips HNSW and does a full scan of the matching points (full_scan_threshold). A tenant's id list is known in advance, so a scan over just those rows is exact and cheap.

decision.choice: Keep a per-tenant id list; tenants under a measured size threshold get an exact scan, others use filtered HNSW
decision.why: It removes the worst case of design B (tiny tenants in a big graph) with a few lines of code, and it mirrors what real vector databases do, so design B is tested at its realistic best rather than at its naive worst.

alternatives.name: Always filtered HNSW
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but tiny tenants pay the most for the least data, which is the wrong cost shape for a long-tail customer base.

alternatives.name: Per-tenant subgraphs (Qdrant payload_m with m=0)
alternatives.tradeoff: Qdrant can build HNSW links per tenant value and disable the global graph; fast tenant search, but searches without a tenant filter become much slower.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. Extend SharedIndex: tenant_rows maps tenant to a contiguous copy of its vectors and global ids. query routes to exact scan when size < threshold, else filtered HNSW. Add sweep_threshold(values) that reports recall, p50 and p99 per size bucket. Tests: threshold above max tenant size equals exact search; threshold 0 equals pure filtered HNSW; routing decision is logged per query.
verify: You chose the threshold from a sweep and recorded the latency curve that justified it
Recall@10 for tenants below the threshold is exactly 1.0
You counted the extra memory the per-tenant vector copies add and included it in design B's total

steps.title: Run the same test against Qdrant's multitenancy setup
steps.learn: Qdrant recommends partition by payload for many small tenants: a keyword index on the tenant field with is_tenant=true (co-locates a tenant's vectors), and optionally payload_m=16 with m=0 to index each tenant separately. This is a production reference point for your two in-process designs.

decision.choice: Qdrant in Docker: one collection, is_tenant keyword index, compared with and without payload_m=16, m=0
decision.why: It checks whether your prototype conclusions hold in a real engine, and the two configurations correspond to your designs: global graph plus filter versus per-tenant graphs inside one collection.

alternatives.name: Weaviate native multi-tenancy
alternatives.tradeoff: Stores each tenant on its own shard, a production version of design A; pick it to test the per-tenant side instead.

alternatives.name: Pinecone namespaces
alternatives.tradeoff: Managed one-namespace-per-tenant; easy to run, but you cannot see or measure memory, which is one of the three required numbers.

steps.delegate: Python, qdrant-client, Docker qdrant/qdrant. Script qdrant_run.py: create collection (size 1536, Cosine), create_payload_index on tenant with KeywordIndexParams(is_tenant=True) before upload, upload 200k points with tenant payload, query each test query with a must match filter on tenant. Second collection with hnsw_config payload_m=16, m=0. Record container memory from docker stats after indexing completes. Tests: zero cross-tenant results.
verify: You confirmed indexing finished (collection status green) before measuring anything
Recall@10 per size bucket is scored against truth.npy, not against Qdrant's own exact search
Container memory for both configurations is recorded with the Qdrant version

steps.title: Enforce tenant isolation and handle tenant changes
steps.learn: In multi-tenant search a leak is a security bug, not a relevance bug. Both designs also need tenant onboarding, deletes and growth: hnswlib has mark_deleted and resize_index; resize_index is not thread safe with add_items or knn_query, and knn_query is not thread safe with add_items, so guard writes with a lock.

decision.choice: Tenant id comes only from the authenticated request inside one query function; callers can never pass raw filters
decision.why: A single choke point makes isolation testable: one function to fuzz, one place to audit. It also keeps both designs behind the same interface, so the benchmark compares designs and not API shapes.

alternatives.name: Caller-supplied filter expressions
alternatives.tradeoff: More flexible queries, but every caller can forget or widen the tenant clause, so isolation depends on all of them.

alternatives.name: Separate process per large tenant
alternatives.tradeoff: Hard isolation and noisy-neighbor protection, at the cost of memory and operational overhead per process.

steps.delegate: Python. Write service.py with search(tenant_id, query, k) over either design. Add add_tenant, delete_doc (mark_deleted in hnswlib) and grow (resize_index) guarded by a writer lock that also blocks queries on that index. Tests: property test with random tenants asserts zero cross-tenant ids; deleted docs never return; concurrent search and insert under the lock do not crash; unknown tenant returns an empty result or error by design.
verify: A randomized run of at least 100k queries across both designs returns zero cross-tenant ids
Deleting a document removes it from that tenant's results immediately in both designs
Adding a new tenant does not require rebuilding design A, and you recorded what it costs in design B

steps.title: Measure memory, latency and recall for both designs
steps.learn: Averages hide the answer: design B's cost lands on tiny tenants, design A's on memory and cold loads. Report every metric per tenant-size bucket and with the real query mix. Measure RSS in a fresh process per design so one design's allocations do not pollute the other.

decision.choice: Per-bucket results (tiny, small, medium, large tenants) plus a traffic-weighted total, one fresh process per design
decision.why: Customers experience their own bucket, not the global mean. Fresh processes make RSS comparable, and a traffic-weighted total still gives the single headline number prove-it asks for.

alternatives.name: One global average
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple headline, but hides that one design can be fine on average and bad for the long tail.

alternatives.name: Multi-threaded throughput
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to production load, but hnswlib warns filtered search in Python is slow when multithreaded, which would skew design B.

steps.delegate: Python, psutil, numpy, matplotlib. bench.py runs each design (A all-resident, A with LRU, B pure filter, B with planner, Qdrant both configs) in a fresh subprocess: build, record RSS and build time, warm up, then run the frozen queries single-threaded with the fixed ef sweep. Output CSV: design, ef, bucket, recall@10, p50, p99, RSS bytes, bytes per vector. Plot recall vs p99 per bucket.
verify: The CSV has every design at every ef value and bucket, with p99 and not only p50
You recorded CPU, RAM, OS, library and Qdrant versions and the exact command
Two repeated runs agree within 10 percent on p50; if not, you found the noise source
Recall for every row is graded against truth.npy

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer the question per tenant-size bucket, then give a rule: for what size distribution and memory budget does each design win? The planner and the LRU cache are ablations; show what each adds on its own.
verify: Part 1: the write-up opens with the one question about per-tenant versus shared indexes
Part 2: every memory, latency and recall claim has a number with the machine, versions and command
Part 3: it explains surprises, such as where filtered HNSW slowed down, using the size-bucket data
Part 4: it lists assumptions and limits: synthetic tenant split, one dataset, single thread, no real traffic

projects.title: Zero-downtime embedding migration
projects.problem: Switching embedding models means re-embedding millions of docs live
projects.proveIt: Query quality and uptime during the backfill
projects.question: Can a live search index switch embedding models with no failed queries, no lost writes and no quality dip, and what does the backfill cost?

steps.title: Frame the question, metrics and dataset
steps.learn: Prove-it asks for query quality and uptime during the backfill. Quality: nDCG@10 on a frozen labeled query set. Uptime: share of live queries answered successfully within a latency budget, plus zero lost writes. Dataset: BEIR FiQA-2018 (57K docs, 648 test queries with relevance labels).

decision.choice: FiQA-2018, old model all-MiniLM-L6-v2, new model bge-small-en-v1.5; test queries frozen now
decision.why: FiQA is large enough that a CPU backfill takes long enough to watch, and it has labels for quality. Both models output 384 dimensions, which makes a mixed-model mistake silent: the index accepts the wrong vectors, so the guard you build later matters.

alternatives.name: BEIR SciFact (5K docs)
alternatives.tradeoff: Very fast to embed, but the backfill is over too quickly to observe query behavior during it.

alternatives.name: BEIR NQ (2.68M docs)
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to millions of docs in prove-it, but a CPU re-embed takes far longer; pick it with a GPU.

steps.delegate: Python, beir, sentence-transformers. Write data.py: util.download_and_unzip the fiqa zip, GenericDataLoader(path).load(split='test'). Pick 5 percent of docs not cited in test qrels as future arrivals (held out of the initial load). Save corpus ids, arrival ids, test query ids and qrels with a checksum. Tests: no arrival doc appears in test qrels; split is deterministic with a seed.
verify: You can state the one question and the three measures (nDCG@10, query success rate within budget, lost writes) in one sentence each
Corpus, query and qrels counts match the BEIR table for FiQA-2018
The frozen test set has a recorded checksum and will not be edited

steps.title: Set the go/no-go quality bar offline
steps.learn: A new model is not automatically better on your data. Score both models with exact search on the frozen set first. bge-small-en-v1.5 lists a query instruction ('Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: ') for retrieval; MiniLM uses none. Getting this wrong changes the result.

decision.choice: Exact search per model, nDCG@10 and Recall@100; the bar to switch is written down before seeing results
decision.why: Exact search removes ANN error so the comparison is about the models. Fixing the bar first stops you from moving the goalposts, and Qdrant's migration guide recommends exactly this check before moving traffic.

alternatives.name: Compare on the live ANN index
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches production, but mixes model quality with index tuning; do it later as a second check.

alternatives.name: Trust public leaderboards
alternatives.tradeoff: Free, but a model that wins on generic benchmarks can still lose on your domain.

steps.delegate: Python, beir, sentence-transformers, ranx. offline_eval.py: embed corpus and test queries with each model (normalize; prefix bge queries with its instruction, not docs), exact cosine top-100 with numpy, score nDCG@10 and Recall@100 with ranx or BEIR EvaluateRetrieval.evaluate. Also run bge without the prefix as an ablation. Tests: ids are strings on both sides; a perfect run scores 1.0.
verify: You wrote the switch bar (for example, minimum nDCG@10 gain) before running the comparison
Both models' nDCG@10 and Recall@100 are recorded, plus bge with and without the query instruction
You saved per-query scores so you can see which queries got worse

steps.title: Stand up the live search service behind an alias
steps.learn: The service must never name a physical index directly. Qdrant aliases are extra names for a collection, and alias changes are atomic, so a later cutover is one request with no window where queries hit nothing. The query encoder must always match the collection behind the alias.

decision.choice: Qdrant collection fiqa_v1 behind alias prod; collection-to-model mapping stored in one config the service reads
decision.why: Atomic alias switches give zero-downtime cutover and instant rollback for free, and coupling model name to collection in one place prevents querying one vector space with another model's vectors.

alternatives.name: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch alias
alternatives.tradeoff: Same alias pattern; pick it if lexical search already lives there, at the cost of heavier operations for a pure vector workload.

alternatives.name: Collection name in app config only
alternatives.tradeoff: No database feature needed, but cutover needs a deploy or reload, and instances can briefly disagree.

steps.delegate: Python, FastAPI, qdrant-client, sentence-transformers, Docker qdrant/qdrant. Create fiqa_v1 (size 384, Cosine), upload the initial corpus with MiniLM vectors and doc text in payload, create alias prod. Service: GET /search?q= resolves alias to collection, looks up its model, embeds, queries; POST /docs and DELETE /docs/{id}. Tests: search returns results via the alias; the model lookup fails loudly for an unknown collection.
verify: Search through the alias returns the same top 10 as querying fiqa_v1 directly
nDCG@10 from the live service on the frozen set is close to the offline exact score for MiniLM
You recorded steady-state p50 and p99 latency before any migration work

steps.title: Build the load generator for queries and writes
steps.learn: Uptime is only meaningful under load. A closed-loop client that waits for each reply sends less when the server stalls, hiding the stall (coordinated omission). An open-loop generator sends at a fixed rate and measures from the intended send time.

decision.choice: Open-loop asyncio generator: fixed-rate queries plus a write stream of arrivals, edits and deletes
decision.why: It reports stalls honestly, and the write stream is what makes migration hard: without concurrent writes, a backfill is just a batch job.

alternatives.name: wrk2 or k6
alternatives.tradeoff: Mature constant-rate tools; pick them for raw HTTP load, but custom write logic and per-request correctness checks are harder to add.

alternatives.name: Closed-loop Python client
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest to write, but understates tail latency exactly when the system is struggling.

steps.delegate: Python, asyncio, httpx. loadgen.py: send queries at a fixed rate from the non-test query pool, time each from its scheduled start, and log status and latency. In parallel, insert held-out arrival docs and edit or delete random docs never cited in the test qrels, logging every acknowledged write with a sequence number. Use one seed so every run sends the same writes. Tests: at a rate the server cannot meet, latency grows instead of the send rate dropping.
verify: A 10 minute steady-state run shows 100 percent success within your latency budget
The write log has a sequence number and expected final state for every doc it touched
You recorded the query rate and write rate you will use for all migration runs

steps.title: Turn on dual writes to the new collection
steps.learn: From now on every write must reach both the old and new collections, or the new one falls behind forever. The old collection stays the source of truth: if a new-side write fails, the old one still succeeded, so you need a repair path, not a rollback.

decision.choice: Blue-green: new collection fiqa_v2 (bge vectors); writes go to v1 first, then v2, with failed v2 writes queued for retry
decision.why: Works with any collection layout (insert-only backfill needs Qdrant 1.16+), keeps v1 untouched for rollback, and the retry queue makes v2 failures visible and repairable instead of silent.

alternatives.name: Named vectors in one collection
alternatives.tradeoff: Qdrant 1.18+ can add a second named vector to the same points: no duplicated payloads, but old and new share one collection's fate.

alternatives.name: Freeze writes during migration
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and safe, but it is downtime for writers, which prove-it rules out.

steps.delegate: Python, qdrant-client. Extend the service: create fiqa_v2 (size 384, Cosine). On POST /docs embed with both models and upsert to v1 then v2; on DELETE delete from both. If the v2 call fails, append to a durable retry file and return success. A worker drains it. Tests: injected v2 failure still returns success and lands in the retry file; the worker drains it; v1 is unaffected.
verify: After 5 minutes of load with dual writes on, every write in the log since enabling is present in v2
An injected v2 outage leaves zero failed client writes and an empty retry queue after recovery
p99 write latency with dual writes is recorded next to the single-write baseline

steps.title: Backfill existing docs without clobbering fresh writes
steps.learn: The backfill reads from v1, re-embeds, writes to v2. Races: it may read a doc, then a live edit writes newer text to v2, then the backfill overwrites it with stale text. A delete can also be resurrected. Qdrant's guide uses an insert-only upsert mode so the backfill never overwrites existing points.

decision.choice: Scroll v1 in batches, re-embed, insert-only into v2, skip ids in a tombstone set, checkpoint the scroll offset
decision.why: Insert-only makes live writes always win; tombstones stop deleted docs coming back; a checkpoint lets a killed backfill resume instead of restarting. Batching keeps the embedding model busy without starving query traffic.

alternatives.name: Overwrite every point
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest code, but silently reverts edits made during the backfill window.

alternatives.name: Per-doc version compare
alternatives.tradeoff: Store a version in the payload and write only if newer; more general (handles partial updates), more code and reads.

steps.delegate: Python, qdrant-client, sentence-transformers. backfill.py: client.scroll(v1, limit=batch, offset, with_payload=True, with_vectors=False), embed payload text with bge, upsert to v2 with update_mode INSERT_ONLY, skip tombstoned ids, then after the upsert re-check tombstones and delete any that landed, persist offset after each batch, sleep to cap docs per second. Tests: edit during backfill survives; delete during backfill stays deleted; resume after kill.
verify: count on v1 and v2 match at the end once deletes are accounted for
Every doc edited during the backfill has its newest text in v2, checked against the write log
Killing and restarting the backfill finishes without duplicates or gaps
Query p99 during the backfill stays within your latency budget at your chosen rate cap

steps.title: Shadow-read and verify v2 before cutover
steps.learn: Offline numbers came from exact search on a static corpus; v2 is an ANN index built under live writes. Before cutover, measure v2 itself: the frozen set's nDCG@10 through v2, and a sample of live queries sent to both collections to compare overlap and latency.

decision.choice: Shadow a small share of live queries to v2 asynchronously; never return v2 results to users before cutover
decision.why: Exercises v2 with real load and query shapes at low risk: a slow or failing v2 cannot affect users because its answers are discarded after logging.

alternatives.name: Offline eval only
alternatives.tradeoff: No added load, but misses problems only live traffic shows, such as v2 latency under concurrent writes.

alternatives.name: Canary a share of users to v2
alternatives.tradeoff: Real user impact data, but some users see the new model before you have checked it.

steps.delegate: Python. In the service, for a configurable fraction of queries, fire a background v2 query (embedded with bge plus its query instruction) and log top-10 ids and latency. eval_live.py: run the frozen test queries through v2 and score nDCG@10 with ranx. Tests: v2 errors or timeouts never change the user response or its latency.
verify: nDCG@10 of the frozen set through v2 meets the bar you wrote in the offline step
Shadow v2 p99 latency is within budget at the shadow rate
An injected v2 timeout leaves user-facing p99 unchanged

steps.title: Cut over atomically and keep a rollback path
steps.learn: Cutover changes two things that must move together: the collection and the query model. Qdrant can delete and recreate an alias in one update_collection_aliases call, which makes the switch atomic. Keeping dual writes on after cutover keeps v1 current, so rollback is the same call in reverse.

decision.choice: One atomic alias swap, query model chosen by the collection behind the alias, dual writes kept on a while
decision.why: No query can see v2 with the old encoder or v1 with the new one, and rollback stays a single request with no lost writes as long as v1 keeps receiving them.

alternatives.name: Gradual traffic shift
alternatives.tradeoff: Limits blast radius, but both models serve at once, so you need per-request routing and quality is mixed during the shift.

alternatives.name: Turn off dual writes at cutover
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper immediately, but rollback then loses every write since cutover.

steps.delegate: Python, qdrant-client. cutover.py: update_collection_aliases with DeleteAlias(prod) and CreateAlias(v2, prod) in one call; rollback.py does the reverse. Service caches alias resolution for at most a short TTL and re-resolves on change. Add a guard: if the resolved collection's model differs from the encoder in use, refuse the query. Tests: under load, swap and swap back; zero failed queries; guard trips on a forced mismatch.
verify: Under full load, cutover and rollback each produce zero failed queries in the loadgen log
After cutover, the frozen set's nDCG@10 through the alias matches the v2 shadow number
A forced model mismatch is refused by the guard instead of returning results

steps.title: Run failure drills during the migration
steps.learn: A migration plan is only proven by breaking it mid-flight: kill the backfill, restart Qdrant, drop v2 writes, restart the service while the retry queue has entries. The write log from the load generator is the oracle: after recovery, both collections must match it.

decision.choice: Scripted fault drills checked against the load generator's write log, not against the service's own counters
decision.why: The service's counters share its bugs; an independent log of acknowledged writes catches lost or resurrected docs that the service would report as fine.

alternatives.name: Manual ad hoc kills
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick to try, but not repeatable, so a fix cannot be shown to work.

alternatives.name: Full Jepsen-style harness
alternatives.tradeoff: Network partitions and clock faults with formal checking; far more rigor than a single-node Qdrant setup needs.

steps.delegate: Python, Docker. drills.py runs each scenario under load: kill -9 backfill and restart; docker restart qdrant; block v2 writes for 60 s; restart the service with a non-empty retry file. After each, reconcile.py compares every doc in the write log to v1 and v2 (present, absent, newest text). Tests: reconcile flags a planted stale doc.
verify: Every drill ends with zero mismatches between the write log and both collections
You recorded failed-query count and duration for each drill
The retry file is flushed to disk before a write is acknowledged, and a restart drill proves it

steps.title: Measure quality and uptime across the whole migration
steps.learn: The result is a timeline, not one number: success rate, p50 and p99 latency, and frozen-set nDCG@10 sampled every minute from start to after cutover, with backfill progress overlaid. The baseline is a stop-the-world rebuild that takes writes offline and swaps at the end.

decision.choice: Two full runs on the same machine and rates: zero-downtime plan versus stop-the-world rebuild
decision.why: The baseline shows what the extra machinery buys. Identical machine, rates and data make differences attributable to the plan rather than the environment.

alternatives.name: Only the zero-downtime run
alternatives.tradeoff: Less work, but without a baseline you cannot say what the dual writes and shadowing cost or saved.

alternatives.name: Simulated timings
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to iterate, but misses real contention between backfill embedding and query serving on one machine.

steps.delegate: Python, matplotlib. timeline.py merges loadgen logs, backfill progress and a probe that runs the frozen test queries through the alias every minute. Plot over time: success rate within budget, p50 and p99, nDCG@10, percent backfilled, with cutover marked. Output a summary table: total failed queries, lost writes, backfill docs per second, extra write latency.
verify: The timeline covers before, during and after the backfill, with cutover marked
Both runs report failed queries, lost writes, p99 and nDCG@10 in one table
You recorded CPU, RAM, OS, Qdrant and library versions and every command

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer whether the switch was invisible to users and what it cost: extra write latency, time to backfill, peak resource use. Explain each spike on the timeline from the logs.
verify: Part 1: the write-up opens with the one question about switching models live
Part 2: every claim (failed queries, lost writes, nDCG@10, p99, backfill rate) has a number with machine and command
Part 3: it explains surprising results, such as latency spikes during backfill, from the logs
Part 4: it lists assumptions and limits: one node, 57K docs not millions, same-dimension models, synthetic traffic

projects.title: malloc from scratch in C
projects.problem: How allocators trade speed against wasted memory
projects.proveIt: Throughput and fragmentation vs glibc malloc
projects.question: How much speed and how much wasted memory does each allocator design choice cost, measured against glibc malloc?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the workloads
steps.learn: Two numbers decide every choice: throughput (malloc/free ops per second) and space utilization. Use CS:APP's verified definition: peak live payload bytes divided by peak heap size (1.0 is perfect). Workloads: mimalloc-bench programs (cfrac, espresso, larson) plus your own trace replays.
verify: Write the question and both metric formulas in your README before any code
Clone mimalloc-bench and the CS:APP malloclab handout; confirm the handout ships only short1/short2 traces
Record the glibc version (ldd --version), CPU model and kernel you will benchmark on

steps.title: Choose how to get memory from the OS
steps.learn: sbrk moves the program break (brk(2) itself says avoid it and use malloc). mmap with MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS returns zeroed, page-aligned memory anywhere in the address space, and munmap can release any region independently. Your allocator carves small blocks out of big OS regions.

decision.choice: mmap large regions (for example 1 MiB arenas) and carve blocks from them; never call sbrk
decision.why: Under LD_PRELOAD other code may also touch the break; mmap regions are independent, can be returned to the OS one at a time, and work the same in a test harness and a preloaded library.

alternatives.name: sbrk-grown contiguous heap
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, matches CS:APP mem_sbrk and lets you coalesce across the whole heap, but you can only shrink from the top and it clashes with anything else using brk.

alternatives.name: One huge mmap reserved up front
alternatives.tradeoff: Contiguous like sbrk without brk conflicts; pages are committed on first touch, but you must pick a maximum heap size in advance.

steps.delegate: In C11, write region.c with void *region_alloc(size_t bytes) and void region_free(void *p, size_t bytes) using mmap(MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS) and munmap, rounding up to sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE). Return NULL and set errno to ENOMEM on failure. Add a unit test that allocates 100 regions, writes every byte, frees them, and checks /proc/self/maps shrinks back.
verify: Run the unit test and show /proc/self/maps before and after: region count returns to baseline
strace -e trace=mmap,munmap,brk: no brk calls come from your allocator (ignore ld.so's startup brk(NULL))

steps.title: Design the block header and alignment
steps.learn: glibc aligns to the larger of 2*sizeof(size_t) and alignof(long double), 16 bytes on x86-64, matching max_align_t: malloc must suit any fundamental type. With sizes rounded to 16, the low 4 bits of the size word are free for flags (allocated, previous-allocated), the boundary-tag trick glibc also uses.

decision.choice: One 8-byte header (size | flags), 16-byte aligned payloads, footer only on free blocks
decision.why: Keeps per-block overhead to one word for allocated blocks, which directly improves utilization on small-object workloads, while a footer on free blocks still lets free() find and merge the previous neighbor.

alternatives.name: Header plus footer on every block
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler coalescing code (the CS:APP textbook start), but costs an extra word per allocated block, which hurts utilization for small sizes.

alternatives.name: Headerless pages with per-page size class
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero per-object overhead (segregated-fit designs), but free() must look up the page metadata and you need size classes first.

steps.delegate: In C, write block.h with inline helpers: hdr_pack(size, flags), blk_size, blk_alloc, prev_alloc, payload_of(block), block_of(payload), next_block, prev_block (valid only when prev is free). Use static_assert for 16-byte alignment. Unit tests: random sizes 1 to 4096 round up correctly, every payload pointer satisfies ((uintptr_t)p % 16) == 0, flags survive size changes.
verify: Hand-draw one allocated and one free block with byte offsets and check it against your code
Unit test shows 0 misaligned payloads across 1,000,000 random sizes

steps.title: Pick the free-list structure and fit policy
steps.learn: An implicit list walks every block; an explicit doubly linked list stores next/prev pointers inside free payloads, so search touches only free blocks. The fit policy (first, next, best) decides which free block serves a request, trading search time against leftover holes.

decision.choice: Explicit free list, first fit, LIFO insertion as the baseline
decision.why: It is the simplest design that is not linear in heap size, and it gives a clean baseline to measure later changes (best fit, size classes) against on the same workloads.

alternatives.name: Implicit list, first fit
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewest lines of code, but every malloc scans allocated blocks too, so throughput collapses as the heap grows.

alternatives.name: Best fit over the whole list
alternatives.tradeoff: Often leaves smaller leftover holes, but scans the full list per request unless you add an ordered structure.

alternatives.name: Address-ordered free list
alternatives.tradeoff: Can reduce fragmentation, but insertion becomes a search, slowing free().

steps.delegate: In C, implement mm_malloc/mm_free on top of region.c and block.h with an explicit doubly linked free list and a fit policy selectable at compile time (-DFIT=FIRST|BEST). Add mm_check() that walks every region and asserts: every free-list entry is marked free, every free block is on the list, no blocks overlap. Call it after every op in debug builds.
verify: Run a 1,000,000-op random trace with mm_check on every op: 0 failures
Compare first vs best fit utilization on the same trace and record both numbers

steps.title: Split oversized blocks and coalesce on free
steps.learn: Splitting returns the unused tail of a large free block to the list (cuts internal waste); coalescing merges a freed block with free neighbors so later large requests fit (cuts external fragmentation). Never split below the minimum free-block size (header, two list pointers, footer).

decision.choice: Split when the remainder is at least the minimum free block; coalesce immediately on free
decision.why: Immediate coalescing keeps the heap invariant simple (no two adjacent free blocks), which makes mm_check strong and the fragmentation numbers easy to explain.

alternatives.name: Deferred coalescing
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster for workloads that free and reallocate the same size (glibc fastbins do this), but footprint can grow and the invariant is weaker.

alternatives.name: Never split
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest path, but every request may waste most of a large block, so utilization drops sharply.

steps.delegate: In C, add split(block, asize) and coalesce(block) covering all 4 neighbor cases (prev/next alloc or free). Maintain the prev-allocated bit in the next block's header. Implement mm_realloc that grows in place when the next block is free. Tests: a scripted sequence hitting each coalesce case, and realloc preserving contents up to min(old,new) size.
verify: mm_check asserts no two adjacent free blocks, passing on 1,000,000 random ops
Show a test where realloc grows in place (same pointer returned) and contents match

steps.title: Add segregated size classes for small objects
steps.learn: Production allocators bucket requests into size classes so a small malloc is a pop from a per-class list instead of a search. Rounding up to a class adds internal fragmentation; class spacing sets that waste.

decision.choice: Segregated free lists: one list per size class for small sizes, the explicit list for the rest
decision.why: Turns the common small-object path into O(1) pops, which is where glibc will beat a single-list allocator on benchmarks like cfrac and espresso; you can then measure exactly what the class spacing costs in utilization.

alternatives.name: Slab pages per size class
alternatives.tradeoff: Very fast and headerless, but memory is stuck in a class's pages until the whole page is empty.

alternatives.name: Buddy allocator (power-of-two)
alternatives.tradeoff: Coalescing is cheap, but rounding to powers of two can waste close to half a block.

steps.delegate: In C, add size classes (configurable table, e.g. 16-byte steps to 128, then geometric) with one free list each; requests above the largest class use the explicit list. Expose a debug counter of bytes lost to rounding. Tests: every class boundary size maps to the expected class, mm_check still passes, and a histogram dump of class usage for a trace.
verify: Report utilization and ops/s before and after size classes on the same workload
Measure bytes lost to rounding as a percent of requested bytes

steps.title: Route large requests to mmap and return memory
steps.learn: glibc serves requests at or above M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KiB initially, adjusted dynamically) with their own mmap, so they can be returned independently; the cost is page-rounding waste and a syscall per allocation. Decide when your empty arenas go back to the OS.

decision.choice: Direct mmap for requests above a fixed threshold; munmap an arena when it becomes fully free
decision.why: Large blocks otherwise pin whole arenas and inflate peak RSS, which is the fragmentation number you report. A fixed threshold is easier to reason about than a dynamic one.

alternatives.name: Dynamic threshold like glibc
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to programs that repeatedly free large blocks, but makes results depend on history and harder to explain.

alternatives.name: Keep everything in arenas
alternatives.tradeoff: No syscalls on the large path, but freed large blocks never return to the OS.

steps.delegate: In C, mark directly mapped blocks with an IS_MMAPPED flag in the header, munmap them in free, and handle realloc across the threshold. Add an arena-empty check that munmaps the arena. Tests: allocate and free 1,000 blocks of 1 MiB and check RSS returns near baseline via getrusage and /proc/self/status VmRSS.
verify: strace shows one mmap and one munmap per large allocation
VmRSS after freeing all large blocks is within one arena of the starting value

steps.title: Make it thread-safe
steps.learn: malloc(3) is MT-Safe; glibc protects arenas with mutexes and creates extra arenas when it detects contention. A single lock is correct but serializes threads; thread caches avoid the lock on the hot path but hold memory per thread.

decision.choice: One global pthread mutex first, then small per-thread caches per size class
decision.why: The lock makes the allocator correct for real programs under LD_PRELOAD immediately; adding thread caches second lets you measure the speedup on larson and the extra footprint they cost.

alternatives.name: Multiple arenas, thread hashed to arena
alternatives.tradeoff: Like glibc: fewer collisions, but cross-thread frees must find and lock the owning arena.

alternatives.name: Lock-free free lists
alternatives.tradeoff: No lock convoys, but you must handle ABA and safe memory reclamation, which is much harder to get right.

steps.delegate: In C with pthreads, wrap the global allocator in a pthread_mutex_t and register pthread_atfork handlers that take it before fork and release it in parent and child. Add __thread caches (tls_model("initial-exec"), as glibc requires for TLS in a malloc replacement) of up to N blocks per class. Flush a cache on thread exit; pthread_setspecific itself calls malloc, so guard reentry. Tests: 8 threads with cross-thread frees under ThreadSanitizer, and fork from a multithreaded process.
verify: 8-thread stress run of 10,000,000 ops: 0 TSan reports, mm_check passes after join
Record larson ops/s with the lock only and with thread caches

steps.title: Interpose with LD_PRELOAD and test on real programs
