steps.learn: glibc supports replacing malloc via LD_PRELOAD interposition. Provide malloc, free, calloc and realloc; a general replacement should also provide aligned_alloc, posix_memalign, memalign, malloc_usable_size and others. free must preserve errno, and malloc must not call glibc code that allocates (fopen, dlopen, stdio).

decision.choice: Build a shared library (libmymalloc.so) exporting the full glibc replacement set
decision.why: mimalloc-bench runs allocators through LD_PRELOAD, so this is how you get an apples-to-apples comparison with glibc on unmodified programs.

alternatives.name: Trace-driven harness only (mdriver style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and easy to debug, but misses real programs' calloc, realloc and alignment calls.

alternatives.name: Static linking into each benchmark
alternatives.tradeoff: No interposition surprises, but needs rebuilding every program and hides missing symbols.

steps.delegate: In C, build libmymalloc.so (-fPIC -shared -O2) exporting malloc, free, calloc (with overflow check), realloc, aligned_alloc, posix_memalign, memalign, valloc, pvalloc, malloc_usable_size, free_sized and free_aligned_sized. Set errno=ENOMEM on failure; save and restore errno in free. Tests: LD_PRELOAD it into ls, python3 -c, and a git clone; a C test for calloc overflow returning NULL and posix_memalign(4096) alignment.
verify: LD_PRELOAD=./libmymalloc.so python3 -c 'print(sum(range(10**6)))' runs correctly
Confirm interposition with a debug counter or ltrace, not just exit code 0
calloc(SIZE_MAX, 2) returns NULL with errno ENOMEM

steps.title: Measure throughput and fragmentation against glibc
steps.learn: Run the same binaries with and without LD_PRELOAD. Throughput: wall time, except larson, which runs a fixed time and reports its own rate. Fragmentation: peak RSS (ru_maxrss, KiB on Linux; mimalloc-bench logs /usr/bin/time %M) vs peak live bytes from your own counter. Pitfalls: frequency scaling, noise, one run.
steps.delegate: Write bench.sh that runs each mimalloc-bench workload (cfrac, espresso, larson, plus your trace replayer) 10 times for glibc and for libmymalloc.so via LD_PRELOAD, pinned with taskset to as many cores as the workload's threads, logging wall time (larson: its reported rate) and max RSS to CSV. Add a Python script that prints median and spread per workload and a table of ratios vs glibc.
verify: Report median and min/max of 10 runs per workload for both allocators
Record exact command, CPU, kernel, glibc version and compiler flags with the CSV
Use perf record on your slowest workload and name the hottest function

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) throughput and utilization numbers for every claim, with machine and command; (3) why surprising results happened (e.g. where glibc's fast paths win); (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2: every number has a machine, glibc version and command next to it
Part 3 explains at least one result using a profile or counter, not a guess
Part 4 lists limits: workloads covered, single machine, no security hardening

projects.title: Allocator fragmentation study
projects.problem: Allocators look fast in microbenchmarks but bloat on real workloads
projects.proveIt: Memory over time on recorded traces vs jemalloc and mimalloc
projects.question: On recorded traces of real programs, how much more memory than the live heap do glibc, jemalloc and mimalloc hold over time, and why?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the workloads
steps.learn: Fragmentation here is memory held minus memory live. Track resident memory divided by live bytes over the whole run: the peak and the time-weighted average tell different stories. Live bytes come from the trace, never from an allocator. Workloads: real programs whose allocations you record yourself.
verify: Write the question and the RSS / live-bytes formula in your README before writing code
Freeze the workload list now: Redis (built MALLOC=libc) under redis-benchmark, plus cfrac, espresso and gs from mimalloc-bench
Mark one workload as held out: no knob tuning may look at it until the final run
Record CPU, kernel, glibc version (ldd --version) and THP mode from /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled

steps.title: Choose how to record allocation traces
steps.learn: A trace is the ordered stream of malloc, calloc, realloc, free (and memalign variants) with size, returned pointer and thread. Every entry point must be captured or replay leaks or double-frees. Recording itself allocates, so the recorder needs a reentrancy guard and its own buffers.

decision.choice: An LD_PRELOAD shim that forwards to the real allocator via dlsym(RTLD_NEXT) and logs fixed-size binary records
decision.why: Captures every call in unmodified binaries (Redis, cfrac, gs), adds only a buffered write per call, and the binary format keeps multi-gigabyte traces cheap to store and parse.

alternatives.name: heaptrack
alternatives.tradeoff: Records all allocations with stack traces and is battle tested, but its format is built for profiling analysis, so you must convert it and you pay for stack unwinding.

alternatives.name: bpftrace uprobes on libc malloc/free
alternatives.tradeoff: No code in the target process, but probes cost more per call, can drop events under load, and only see the libc symbols you attach to.

steps.delegate: In C11 write libtrace.so: interpose malloc, calloc, realloc, free, posix_memalign, aligned_alloc, memalign; resolve real functions with dlsym(RTLD_NEXT); use a thread-local reentrancy flag and a static bootstrap buffer for calloc during dlsym. Each record: op, thread id, size, old ptr, new ptr, sequence number; per-thread buffers flushed to one file with a global atomic sequence. Test: a program with known calls produces exactly the expected records.
verify: Run the shim on a test program with 10 known calls and diff the decoded trace against the expected list
Record each workload and confirm every free/realloc pointer was previously returned (zero orphans)
Compare wall time with and without the shim on cfrac and note the recording overhead

steps.title: Build a replayer that touches the memory it allocates
steps.learn: Replay maps each recorded pointer to a slot id, then issues the same calls in order. Untouched pages may never become resident, so a replayer that only calls malloc understates RSS; write to every allocated byte (or at least one byte per page) like the real program would.

decision.choice: Single-threaded replay in global sequence order, writing a pattern into every allocated block
decision.why: Deterministic and identical across allocators, so differences in the RSS curve come from the allocator, not from scheduling. Writing the block makes pages resident as the original program did.

alternatives.name: Per-thread replay with original threads
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps thread caches, arenas and cross-thread frees realistic, but needs ordering between threads and runs differ run to run (added in a later step).

alternatives.name: Replay without touching memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Much faster, but RSS then measures address space reservations, not real memory use.

steps.delegate: In C, write replay.c that reads the binary trace, keeps a slot table (hash map from recorded pointer to slot index, resolved offline into a compact trace), and issues malloc/calloc/realloc/free/posix_memalign with the same sizes. memset each new block. Track live bytes from the trace sizes. Tests: a hand-made trace of 1000 ops ends with live bytes 0 and no ASan errors when built with -fsanitize=address.
verify: Replay every recorded trace under ASan with zero errors
Live bytes at the end of replay match live bytes computed offline from the trace file
Show RSS is lower when memset is disabled, proving the touch matters

steps.title: Sample resident memory against logical time
steps.learn: Use trace position (op count), not wall time, as the x-axis so allocators of different speed are compared at the same program state. Count anonymous resident memory only, which excludes binaries and shared libraries. Live bytes come from the trace, so no allocator grades itself.

decision.choice: Read the Anonymous line of /proc/self/smaps_rollup every N ops and log (op, live bytes, anon kB)
decision.why: Allocator-neutral, and the statm man page says the fast counters (VmRSS, RssAnon) are inaccurate by design while smaps_rollup is accurate, only slower. Sampling by op count keeps the cost bounded.

alternatives.name: RssAnon from /proc/self/status
alternatives.tradeoff: Much cheaper to read, but documented as inaccurate due to a kernel scalability optimization, so small differences are noise.

alternatives.name: Peak only (VmHWM or ru_maxrss)
alternatives.tradeoff: One number per run and trivial to collect, but hides memory that is never returned after a phase ends.

steps.delegate: Add a sampler to replay.c: every N ops (flag, default 10000) read /proc/self/smaps_rollup, parse Anonymous and AnonHugePages, and append a CSV row: op, live_bytes, anon_kb, anon_huge_kb. Write a Python script that plots anon memory and live bytes vs op and computes peak ratio and time-weighted mean ratio. Test the parser on a saved smaps_rollup file.
verify: Plot one trace: the live-bytes line never exceeds anon memory converted to bytes
Halve N and confirm the peak ratio changes by less than your stated tolerance
Report the anon memory of an empty replay as the baseline you subtract

steps.title: Pin allocator versions and how they are loaded
steps.learn: glibc malloc uses arenas and bins; jemalloc uses arenas, size classes and thread caches; mimalloc uses per-thread heaps with free lists sharded per page. Each can be swapped into the same binary with LD_PRELOAD, so the replayer stays byte-identical.

decision.choice: One replayer binary; jemalloc and mimalloc built from pinned release tags and injected with LD_PRELOAD
decision.why: The only variable is the allocator. Pinned tags make results reproducible, and building jemalloc yourself keeps stats on (they are on unless --disable-stats).

alternatives.name: Distro packages
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest, but versions and build options vary by distro and are often old.

alternatives.name: Link each allocator statically
alternatives.tradeoff: No dynamic symbol interposition questions, but three binaries can differ in layout and inlining.

steps.delegate: Write build-allocators.sh that clones jemalloc and mimalloc at pinned tags, builds release shared libraries into ./alloc/, and prints versions. Write run.sh ALLOC TRACE that runs replay with LD_PRELOAD set for je/mi and unset for glibc. Test: a tiny program prints which allocator served it (jemalloc mallctl "version", mimalloc mi_version).
verify: For each allocator, prove it is active: jemalloc mallctl version string, mimalloc mi_version, glibc malloc_info output
Record the git tag and configure flags for jemalloc and mimalloc in results/meta.txt

steps.title: Attribute held-but-not-live memory to causes
steps.learn: Memory held minus live splits into: rounding up to size classes (internal), free space inside partly used pages or runs (external), freed pages kept dirty for reuse, and metadata. jemalloc exposes allocated, active, metadata and resident after refreshing epoch; glibc exports state via malloc_info.

decision.choice: At each sample, also dump allocator-native stats and map them onto the four causes
decision.why: The anon-memory curve says how much; only native stats say why, which is what the write-up must explain.

alternatives.name: RSS curves only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and fair, but you cannot tell size-class waste from retained dirty pages.

alternatives.name: Compute internal waste offline from size classes
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs no allocator APIs, but you must reimplement each size-class table exactly and it ignores page-level waste.

steps.delegate: Extend replay.c with an optional hook (compiled per allocator): jemalloc, write epoch then read stats.allocated, stats.active, stats.metadata, stats.resident, stats.retained via mallctl; mimalloc, use a second build with -DMI_STAT=1 (release builds keep no stats) and mi_stats_print_out to a file, for attribution runs only; glibc, call malloc_info(0, f). Write a parser producing one CSV per run. Test: after freeing everything, jemalloc stats.allocated drops near zero.
verify: For one jemalloc run, show allocated <= active <= resident at every sample
Name the largest of the four causes for each allocator on the Redis trace

steps.title: Decide which memory-return knobs to test
steps.learn: Allocators keep freed pages for speed and return them on a policy. jemalloc purges dirty pages after opt.dirty_decay_ms; mimalloc purges after MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY; glibc trims via M_TRIM_THRESHOLD and malloc_trim, and MALLOC_ARENA_MAX caps arenas. The THP guide warns huge pages can raise memory footprint.

decision.choice: Run defaults first, then one tuned config per allocator, tuned only on the non-held-out traces
decision.why: Defaults are what users get; one documented tuned point shows how much is policy rather than design, without overfitting.

alternatives.name: Defaults only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleanest comparison, but blames designs for what a one-line setting fixes.

alternatives.name: Grid search over all knobs
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds the best point per trace, but overfits and multiplies run time.

steps.delegate: Extend run.sh with CONFIG: default or tuned. Tuned: MALLOC_CONF=dirty_decay_ms=0,muzzy_decay_ms=0 for jemalloc; MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY=0 for mimalloc; MALLOC_ARENA_MAX and a malloc_trim(0) call at phase ends for glibc. Run THP enabled=never and madvise as separate labeled runs. Log env and THP mode in each CSV header.
verify: Show each tuned setting took effect (jemalloc opt.dirty_decay_ms readback, env dump for others)
Report peak and time-weighted ratios for default vs tuned on tuning traces only
State the throughput cost of each tuned config in ops per second

steps.title: Add per-thread replay for thread caches and arenas
steps.learn: Single-thread replay hides per-thread caches and arenas, and frees of memory allocated by another thread (larson calls this bleeding). Replay each recorded thread on its own thread, waiting only when an op depends on another thread's allocation.

decision.choice: One replay thread per recorded thread; a free waits until the matching malloc's sequence number has executed
decision.why: Keeps cross-thread frees and per-thread caching real while staying close to the recorded order, which matters for Redis and other threaded programs.

alternatives.name: Global sequence barrier for every op
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact order, but serializes threads so caching behavior looks single-threaded.

alternatives.name: Stay single-threaded
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic, but underestimates memory held in per-thread caches and arenas.

steps.delegate: Add --threads mode to replay: split the trace per recorded thread id, run each on a pthread, and before free/realloc spin-wait (with sched_yield) until the allocating op's sequence number is marked done in an atomic bitmap. Keep the sampler on a separate thread. Test: a two-thread synthetic trace with cross-thread frees ends with zero live bytes under TSan.
verify: Run the cross-thread test under ThreadSanitizer with zero reports
Compare single vs per-thread peak ratio for one threaded trace and report the difference

steps.title: Validate replay against the live program
steps.learn: Replay is only evidence if it reproduces what the real program does with each allocator. Redis documents its fragmentation ratio as RSS divided by memory in use; compare its curve with your replay of the same session.
verify: Run redis-server (MALLOC=libc) with each allocator preloaded under the same redis-benchmark script, logging smaps_rollup Anonymous each second
Plot live-run vs replay RSS for each allocator and state the largest gap as a percentage
If the allocator ranking differs between live and replay, record it as a limitation

steps.title: Measure memory over time on every trace
steps.learn: Baselines: glibc, jemalloc and mimalloc at defaults, then tuned. Pitfalls: THP mode changes resident memory, CPU frequency changes throughput, sampling cost slows the run, and one run hides variance. Run the held-out trace last, once, with frozen configs.
steps.delegate: Write bench.sh that for each trace x allocator x config (default, tuned) runs replay 5 times, pinned with taskset, saving CSVs under results/<machine>/. A Python report prints per cell: median peak ratio, time-weighted ratio, final ratio, ops/s with min/max, and draws anon-memory-over-op plots with live bytes overlaid.
verify: Each cell shows median and min/max of 5 runs for peak and time-weighted ratio
Every CSV records machine, kernel, THP mode, allocator tag and the exact command
Held-out trace results come from configs frozen before it was run

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) peak and time-weighted ratios for every claim, with machine and command; (3) why surprising curves happened, from the cause breakdown; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2: every number cites machine, allocator version, THP mode and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise using native stats, not a guess
Part 4 lists limits: few workloads, replay fidelity gap, one machine, one kernel

projects.title: Verified lock-free MPMC queue
projects.problem: Lock-free bugs appear once in a billion runs
projects.proveIt: Bugs found with loom or ThreadSanitizer, throughput vs a mutex queue
projects.question: Can a bounded lock-free MPMC queue be checked by loom, Miri and ThreadSanitizer, and still beat a mutex-protected queue on throughput?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the setup
steps.learn: Two results: (1) correctness evidence, meaning which seeded bugs each tool catches and that the final queue passes all of them; (2) throughput in ops per second vs Mutex<VecDeque> across producer/consumer counts. Setup: Rust stable plus nightly (for TSan and Miri), Linux x86_64.
verify: Write the question and both metrics in your README before any code
Freeze the benchmark matrix now: thread pairs, capacity, item type, run count
Freeze a list of 5+ bug mutations you will seed later (for example one weakened ordering)
Record CPU model, core count, kernel and rustc versions (stable and nightly)

steps.title: Choose the queue design and its API
steps.learn: Unbounded linked queues (Michael-Scott) free nodes other threads may still read, so they need a reclamation scheme. A bounded ring of preallocated slots never frees memory while running, which removes that whole problem and makes full/empty explicit.

decision.choice: Bounded ring of slots with per-slot stamps (Vyukov's design, as in crossbeam ArrayQueue); try_push and try_pop
decision.why: No reclamation, one CAS per operation in the common case, and an existing implementation (crossbeam) to compare against for both correctness tests and speed.

alternatives.name: Michael-Scott linked queue
alternatives.tradeoff: Unbounded, but needs epoch-based or hazard-pointer reclamation, which is a second project to verify.

alternatives.name: Blocking push/pop with parking
alternatives.tradeoff: Friendlier API, but mixes a lock-free core with parking logic that loom must also model.

steps.delegate: In Rust, create crate mpmc with pub struct Queue<T> { new(cap), try_push(&self, T) -> Result<(), T>, try_pop(&self) -> Option<T>, capacity() }. Add a stub implementation backed by Mutex<VecDeque<T>> so tests can be written first. Tests: FIFO with one thread, Err(value) returned when full, None when empty, capacity 1 works.
verify: Single-threaded tests pass against the mutex stub
Read crossbeam's array_queue.rs and write in your own words what a stamp's lap and index mean

steps.title: Design slot stamps and the head/tail CAS
steps.learn: Head and tail are counters that keep growing; a slot's stamp says whose turn it is. In crossbeam a stamp packs an index plus a lap, so a wrapped-around counter is distinguishable from the last lap. A producer may write a slot only if its stamp equals tail, a consumer only if it equals head + 1.

decision.choice: Stamps hold index plus lap; producers CAS tail forward, then write the value, then publish the new stamp
decision.why: The lap makes a slot from a previous round look different, which is how this design avoids ABA without tagged pointers.

alternatives.name: Per-slot full/empty flag
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but a slow thread can see a reused slot from a later lap and act on stale state (ABA).

alternatives.name: Single lock-free counter of items
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy full/empty checks, but becomes another contended atomic every operation.

steps.delegate: Implement Queue<T> with buffer: Box<[Slot<T>]>, Slot { stamp: AtomicUsize, value: UnsafeCell<MaybeUninit<T>> }, head and tail AtomicUsize, one_lap = (cap+1).next_power_of_two(). Use compare_exchange_weak in loops. Route atomics and UnsafeCell through a crate::sync module so loom can swap them in. Keep the single-thread tests green; add a test pushing and popping 10 laps around capacity 3.
verify: Write the stamp state table (empty, being written, full, being read) for one slot and check the code against it
10-lap single-thread test passes for capacities 1, 2, 3 and 8

steps.title: Choose the memory orderings
steps.learn: The value is plain memory written by one thread and read by another; the stamp store must be Release and the stamp load that sees it must be Acquire so the value's write happens-before the read. Which orderings the head/tail CAS needs is the question loom and Miri will test.

decision.choice: Acquire/Release on stamps, the weakest CAS orderings you can justify, each choice written as a comment
decision.why: Every ordering has a stated reason that the checkers then try to break, which teaches more than defaulting to SeqCst.

alternatives.name: SeqCst everywhere
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to reason about, but can cost speed on some CPUs and hides which edges matter.

alternatives.name: Copy crossbeam's orderings (it also uses SeqCst fences)
alternatives.tradeoff: Known good, but ThreadSanitizer does not support atomic fences, so TSan results become less trustworthy.

steps.delegate: Annotate every atomic operation in Queue with a comment naming the happens-before edge it creates or why Relaxed is safe. Do not use atomic::fence. Add a stress test: 4 producers each push 1e6 tagged values, 4 consumers pop; assert every value appears exactly once and per-producer order is preserved.
verify: Every atomic op has a one-line justification comment
Stress test passes 20 runs in a row in --release on your machine

steps.title: Separate head and tail onto their own cache lines
steps.learn: Producers hammer tail and consumers hammer head; if both share a cache line, every update by one side invalidates it for the other. crossbeam's CachePadded aligns a value to 128 bytes on x86-64 and aarch64 (a guess, not the real line size).

decision.choice: Wrap head and tail in CachePadded; leave slots unpadded
decision.why: Head and tail are the hottest shared words; padding them is cheap. Padding every slot multiplies memory and hurts locality for small T.

alternatives.name: No padding
alternatives.tradeoff: Smallest struct, but expect a throughput drop under contention that you should measure.

alternatives.name: Pad every slot
alternatives.tradeoff: Removes slot-level false sharing between neighbors, at a large memory cost per slot.

steps.delegate: Add crossbeam-utils and wrap head and tail in CachePadded<AtomicUsize>. Add a feature flag no_pad that removes the padding so the benchmark can compare both. Test: a size_of/align_of assertion that head and tail are on different 128-byte lines.
verify: Alignment test shows head and tail addresses differ by at least 128 bytes
Keep both builds for the measure step; do not quote a speedup yet

steps.title: Make the unsafe parts sound: Send, Sync and Drop
steps.learn: Queue<T> moves T across threads, so Sync should require T: Send. Slots hold MaybeUninit<T>; on Drop the queue must drop exactly the items still inside, which needs head and tail read with exclusive access (&mut self).

decision.choice: unsafe impl Send and Sync for Queue<T> where T: Send; Drop pops remaining items via &mut self
decision.why: Matches what the queue actually does with T, and dropping under &mut needs no atomics reasoning.

alternatives.name: Require T: Copy
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids Drop logic entirely, but excludes Box, String and most real payloads.

alternatives.name: Leak remaining items on Drop
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but leaks memory and resources held by T.

steps.delegate: Add the unsafe impls with SAFETY comments, and impl Drop that walks from head to tail dropping initialized slots. Tests: a counter type that increments a static on drop; push 5, pop 2, drop the queue, assert 5 drops total. Run the unit tests under Miri (cargo +nightly miri test).
verify: Drop-count test passes
cargo miri test on the single-threaded tests reports no undefined behavior

steps.title: Model-check the queue with loom
steps.learn: loom reruns a test under every interleaving allowed by the C11 model, up to a preemption bound (LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS). It only sees loom types, so atomics and UnsafeCell must be swapped under cfg(loom). It cannot model every relaxed reordering, and threads are capped, so keep models tiny.

decision.choice: Exhaustive loom models with capacity 1 or 2 and 2 or 3 threads
decision.why: Small capacities force wraparound and full/empty races quickly, and tiny models finish exhaustively.

alternatives.name: shuttle (randomized scheduling)
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales to more threads and larger tests, but is not exhaustive, so a pass is weaker evidence.

alternatives.name: Plain stress loops
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra tooling, but bugs that need rare interleavings may never show up.

steps.delegate: Add [target.'cfg(loom)'.dependencies] loom and tests/loom_queue.rs with loom::model tests: 2 producers 1 consumer cap 1; 1 producer 2 consumers cap 2; push-pop-push wraparound cap 1. Use loom::cell::UnsafeCell with_mut/with in the sync module. Each test asserts every value is popped exactly once. Command: RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom" cargo test --test loom_queue --release.
verify: All loom tests pass and you record each test's run time
Rerun with LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS=2 and 3 and note run times
Confirm by grep that no std::sync::atomic import remains outside the sync module

steps.title: Run ThreadSanitizer and Miri on the real-thread tests
steps.learn: TSan instruments real threads on real hardware and reports data races on non-atomic memory; it needs nightly with -Zsanitizer=thread and -Zbuild-std, and does not support atomic fences. Miri interprets the program, detects data races and emulates some weak-memory effects; -Zmiri-many-seeds varies scheduling.

decision.choice: Run both: TSan on the full-size stress test, Miri on a shrunken version with many seeds
decision.why: They catch different things: TSan runs real hardware at scale, Miri explores weak-memory outcomes and checks unsafe code. Miri is slow, so the test must be small.

alternatives.name: TSan only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast feedback at full size, but misses UB and weak-memory outcomes x86 never shows.

alternatives.name: Miri only
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest UB checking, but too slow for long stress runs.

steps.delegate: Add a cfg(miri) branch to the stress test that shrinks it to 2+2 threads and 200 items. Add scripts/tsan.sh: RUSTFLAGS=-Zsanitizer=thread cargo +nightly test -Zbuild-std --target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --release --test stress. Add scripts/miri.sh: MIRIFLAGS=-Zmiri-many-seeds cargo +nightly miri test --test stress.
verify: TSan run on the stress test reports zero warnings
Miri with many seeds passes; record seed range and wall time
Run TSan on crossbeam ArrayQueue's stress test too and note any reports (it uses fences)

steps.title: Seed bugs and record which tool catches each
steps.learn: A checker that never fails proves little. Apply each mutation frozen in step 1 one at a time and run every tool. The oracle is independent of the queue: each value popped exactly once and per-producer FIFO, checked by the test, not by queue code.

decision.choice: A mutation matrix: bugs by tool (loom, Miri, TSan, stress loop), each cell found or not plus time
decision.why: This is the project's correctness metric, and it shows each tool's blind spots on your own code.

alternatives.name: Rely on passing tests
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but you never learn whether the tests could fail.

alternatives.name: Hunt real bugs in other queues
alternatives.tradeoff: More realistic, but you cannot know the true bug count to score against.

steps.delegate: Write scripts/mutants.sh that applies each patch in mutants/*.patch (for example: stamp store Release to Relaxed, stamp load Acquire to Relaxed, drop the lap from the stamp, skip the stamp check before read), runs loom, Miri, TSan and stress with a timeout, records pass/fail and time to CSV, and reverts the patch.
verify: Matrix covers every frozen mutation and all four tools
For every mutation a tool missed, explain why using that tool's documented limits (or state that none were missed)
The unmutated queue passes every column

steps.title: Measure throughput against a mutex queue
steps.learn: Baselines: Mutex<VecDeque<T>> and crossbeam ArrayQueue, same capacity and item type. Pitfalls: more threads than cores makes spinning on full/empty pathological, debug builds, CPU frequency scaling, timing thread spawn, and quoting one run.
steps.delegate: Write benches/throughput.rs (plain harness, --release): for P:C in the frozen matrix, spawn threads, start them together with a Barrier, each producer pushes N items (retry with std::hint::spin_loop when full), consumers pop until N*P received. Time from barrier to last pop. Queues: ours, ours with no_pad, Mutex<VecDeque>, ArrayQueue. 10 runs each; print median, min, max ops/s to CSV.
verify: Every cell reports median and min/max of 10 runs for all four queues
No configuration uses more threads than physical cores, or it is marked oversubscribed
CSV header records CPU, core count, rustc version and the exact command
Use perf stat on one cell to compare cache misses between padded and no_pad

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) numbers for every claim (mutation matrix, ops/s) with machine and command; (3) why surprising results happened, such as the mutex winning at low thread counts or a tool missing a bug; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2: the mutation matrix and throughput table each cite machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise with a counter, a profile or a tool's documented limit
Part 4 says loom and Miri are bounded checks, not proofs, and x86 hides weak-memory bugs

projects.title: Concurrent hash map that resizes online
projects.problem: Growing a table while threads read and write it
projects.proveIt: Throughput and p99 during a resize
projects.question: Can a concurrent hash map keep throughput up and p99 latency flat while it doubles its table under live reads and writes?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the workload
steps.learn: Two numbers decide this project: ops per second and p99 per-op latency during a growth phase (table resizing repeatedly) compared with a control run on a pre-sized table. Workload: the conc-map-bench mixes (Read Heavy 98/1/1/0, Rapid Grow 5/80/5/10 read/insert/remove/update) with random u64 keys.
verify: README states the question, both metrics and the growth-vs-presized comparison before any code is written
Clone conc-map-bench and confirm the Read Heavy and Rapid Grow percentages in its README
Record CPU model, core count, OS, kernel and rustc version you will benchmark on

steps.title: Choose the table layout
steps.learn: Java's ConcurrentHashMap is a power-of-two array of bins, each an atomic pointer to a short node list; at its 0.75 resize threshold most bins hold zero or one node. DashMap instead shards the key space over RwLock-protected hashbrown maps, so each shard resizes under its own write lock.

decision.choice: Power-of-two array of AtomicPtr bins, each a singly linked node list (ConcurrentHashMap style)
decision.why: Bins can be moved one at a time to a new table, which is exactly what online resizing needs, and a read is one atomic load plus a short list walk with no lock.

alternatives.name: Sharded RwLock<HashMap> (DashMap style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fast, but a shard's resize holds its write lock, so every op on that shard waits; this is your baseline, not your design.

alternatives.name: Open addressing with linear probing
alternatives.tradeoff: Better cache locality per lookup, but moving entries while other threads probe needs per-slot state machines and tombstones; much harder to get right.

steps.delegate: In Rust (edition 2021), create crate cmap with struct Table { bins: Box<[Atomic<Node>]>, mask: usize } using crossbeam-epoch Atomic, and Node { hash: u64, key: u64, value: AtomicU64, next: Atomic<Node> }. Write fn bin_index(hash, mask). Hash with a seeded hasher (ahash or std RandomState). Unit tests: table length is a power of two, every index is in range, and a single-threaded get/insert round trip over 100k keys.
verify: Hand-draw a 8-bin table with 5 keys and check your bin_index results against it
Single-threaded test passes: 100k inserted keys all found, 100k absent keys not found

steps.title: Make reads lock-free and writes per-bin
steps.learn: In ConcurrentHashMap, inserting into an empty bin is a single CAS; other updates lock the bin (the first node acts as the lock) and recheck that node is still first. Readers take no lock: an Acquire load of the bin pairs with the writer's Release publish, so a reader that sees a node also sees its fields.

decision.choice: CAS for the empty-bin insert, a small per-bin lock for other updates, lock-free Acquire reads
decision.why: Most puts land in empty bins, so the common write path is one CAS, while per-bin locks keep delete and update logic simple and contention between distinct keys rare.

alternatives.name: Fully lock-free bins (CAS on every list link)
alternatives.tradeoff: No writer ever blocks, but deletes need mark bits and helping logic, and the resize interacts with every CAS; much more code to verify.

alternatives.name: Striped locks (lock array indexed by hash)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fixed memory for locks, but unrelated keys share a stripe and the stripe count must be chosen up front.

steps.delegate: In the cmap crate add get(&self, k, &Guard) and insert/remove(&self, k, v). Empty bin: compare_exchange the new node in with Release on success. Non-empty bin: take a per-bin spin lock (AtomicBool with Acquire/Release) then recheck the head. get uses Acquire loads only. Tests: 8 threads insert disjoint key ranges then all keys are readable; 8 threads remove/insert the same 64 keys for 1s with no panic.
verify: Write down, for each atomic in get and insert, the Ordering you chose and which store it pairs with
The 8-thread disjoint-insert test finds every key on 20 consecutive runs

steps.title: Count entries and decide when to resize
steps.learn: One shared AtomicUsize for the size makes every insert fight over one cache line. ConcurrentHashMap keeps a LongAdder-style set of counter cells and, under contention, only checks the threshold when adding to a bin that already has two or more nodes, so most puts never read the total.

decision.choice: Per-thread or striped counters padded to cache lines; check the 0.75 threshold only on a cheap trigger
decision.why: During a Rapid Grow run every insert updates the count, so a single counter would serialize writers exactly when resizing matters most.

alternatives.name: Single AtomicUsize counter
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact and simplest, but every insert writes the same cache line; expect throughput to stop scaling with threads.

alternatives.name: Resize on bin length only
alternatives.tradeoff: No global count at all, but a few long bins can trigger growth early or late under skewed keys.

steps.delegate: Add a Counter with N CachePadded<AtomicIsize> stripes (crossbeam-utils CachePadded), add(delta) picks a stripe by thread id, sum() adds all stripes. Insert calls should_resize() only when the bin already held 2 or more nodes, comparing sum() to 0.75 * capacity. Tests: after 16 threads each insert 100k distinct keys, sum() equals 1.6M; a microbench of add() at 1, 4, 16 threads for stripes=1 vs stripes=64.
verify: Plot add() throughput at 1, 4, 16 threads for 1 stripe vs 64 stripes and note where they diverge
After the parallel insert test, sum() matches the exact number of distinct keys

steps.title: Choose how the table grows
steps.learn: Doubling a power-of-two table sends each node either to the same index or to index plus old length. ConcurrentHashMap lets the initiating thread allocate the new array, then any writer that hits the resize claims a block of bins (a stride, at least 16) via a shared transfer index and moves them.

decision.choice: Incremental cooperative migration: writers that see a resize claim strides of bins and move them before their own op
decision.why: The cost of moving a large table is spread over many ops and threads, so no single insert pays for the whole copy, which is what keeps p99 flat during growth.

alternatives.name: Blocking resize (all writers wait, may help)
alternatives.tradeoff: papaya documents this as better for throughput with many writers but prone to insert latency spikes on large tables; keep it as an ablation mode.

alternatives.name: One background thread copies
alternatives.tradeoff: Writers never do copy work, but the copy can fall behind a fast insert stream and the map stays in two-table mode longer.

steps.delegate: Add struct Resize { next: Atomic<Table>, transfer_index: AtomicUsize } and fn help_transfer(&self, guard). Threads claim [start,end) strides with fetch_sub on transfer_index, lock each old bin, split its list into lo/hi lists for the new table, then mark the old bin moved. The last finisher installs next as the current table. Add a ResizeMode::{Incremental, Blocking} switch. Test: 8 threads insert 1M keys from capacity 16; all keys present after.
verify: Instrument and log the number of resizes for 1M inserts from capacity 16; check it equals the doublings you predicted
All 1M keys are present after the 8-thread growth test, in both ResizeMode settings

steps.title: Keep reads and writes correct mid-resize
steps.learn: After a bin is moved, ConcurrentHashMap leaves a forwarding node holding the new table; reads that hit it retry in the new table and writers help transfer then retry. papaya notes the cost: ops during a resize may search both tables, trading median latency for tail latency.

decision.choice: Moved bins hold a forwarding marker; get follows it to the new table, writers help migrate then retry there
decision.why: Every key is always findable in exactly one live place, so readers never block and writers never write to a bin that is being or has been moved.

alternatives.name: Readers check both tables every time
alternatives.tradeoff: No marker needed, but each lookup during a resize pays two probes even for bins not yet touched.

alternatives.name: Seqlock around the whole table swap
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple reasoning, but readers retry whenever any resize step happens, which shows up as read latency spikes.

steps.delegate: Add a Forward variant to the bin head (tagged pointer or Node with a sentinel hash). get: on Forward, load next table and retry. insert/remove: on Forward, call help_transfer then retry. Mark a bin Forward only after its lo/hi lists are published to the new table with Release. Test: 4 readers loop get() over a fixed key set that is present throughout while 4 writers grow the map; any miss is a failure.
verify: The concurrent read-during-growth test reports zero misses for keys present the whole time over 50 runs
Write down why a reader cannot see an empty new bin for a key that the old bin still had

steps.title: Free the old table and removed nodes safely
steps.learn: A reader may still be walking an old bin when the resize finishes or a node is removed, so you cannot free it immediately. crossbeam-epoch handles this: pin() before loading Atomics, and defer_destroy retired objects; they are freed only after all participants pinned at the time have unpinned.

decision.choice: Epoch-based reclamation with crossbeam-epoch: retire old tables and removed nodes via defer_destroy
decision.why: Reads stay a pin plus loads with no per-node bookkeeping, and the old table is one large object that is retired once, after the last stride moves.

alternatives.name: Hazard pointers (haphazard crate)
alternatives.tradeoff: Bounded garbage even if a reader stalls, but every node visited on a list walk needs protect-and-validate, adding cost to the read path.

alternatives.name: Reference counting (Arc per node)
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to reason about, but every read writes a shared counter, which hurts read-heavy scaling.

steps.delegate: Use crossbeam_epoch::pin() at the start of every public op; after installing the new table call guard.defer_destroy(old_table_shared); on remove, defer_destroy the unlinked node. Add a counting global allocator (GlobalAlloc wrapper) in tests. Test: grow to 1M then remove all keys, drop the map, call flush on a pinned guard a few times, and assert live allocated bytes return near baseline.
verify: Live bytes after insert-all, remove-all and drop return to within a small fixed slack of the starting value
Run the growth test under Miri on a tiny size (for example 200 keys) with no undefined-behavior report

steps.title: Model-check the tricky interleavings
steps.learn: loom runs a test many times, permuting thread interleavings under the C11 memory model; it only scales to tiny models (2 or 3 threads, a few ops). ThreadSanitizer finds races in real runs but the Rust docs state it does not support atomic fences, which epoch reclamation relies on.

decision.choice: loom for a 2-bin, 2-thread insert-during-resize model, plus long randomized stress runs checked against a reference
decision.why: The bugs here are interleavings of migration and update that random stress rarely hits; loom explores them exhaustively at small size, and stress covers scale.

alternatives.name: ThreadSanitizer only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap to add to stress runs, but may give false reports around fences and misses orderings the hardware did not happen to show.

alternatives.name: Stress testing only
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds crashes at scale, but a run passing says little about rare interleavings.

steps.delegate: Gate atomics behind cfg(loom) under RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom --cfg crossbeam_loom" with crossbeam-epoch's loom feature. Write loom tests: (a) T1 inserts key k while T2 triggers a resize from 2 bins, then k is found; (b) T1 removes k while T2 migrates its bin, then k is absent. Separately, a stress test runs 16 threads of random ops for 60s, logs per-thread op results, and checks final contents against a Mutex<HashMap> replay of the same per-key op sequence.
verify: Both loom tests pass; then deliberately weaken one Release to Relaxed and confirm loom catches it
60s stress run ends with final map contents equal to the reference for every key

steps.title: Measure throughput and p99 during growth
steps.learn: Compare your map (incremental and blocking modes) with RwLock<HashMap>, DashMap and papaya. Record per-op latency in an HdrHistogram per thread; a closed loop measures service time only, so also run an open-loop paced variant timed from each op's intended start, and subtract timer overhead.

decision.choice: Rapid Grow from capacity 16 vs the same run pre-sized, 1 to all cores, report ops/s, p50, p99, p99.9
decision.why: The growth-vs-presized gap isolates what resizing costs, and works for baselines whose internal resize events you cannot see.

alternatives.name: Use conc-map-bench as is
alternatives.tradeoff: Comparable to published results and quick, but you must add your own latency recording around resizes.

alternatives.name: Criterion microbenchmarks
alternatives.tradeoff: Good statistics for single-op cost, but it does not model many threads growing one shared map.

steps.delegate: Write a Rust bench binary: args map={mine-inc,mine-block,rwlock,dashmap,papaya-inc,papaya-block}, threads, mix, presize. Each thread runs the op mix with Instant timing into an hdrhistogram::Histogram, merged at the end; print ops/s, p50, p99, p99.9 as CSV. Also an open-loop mode with a fixed target rate timing each op from its intended start. Pin the build to --release, warm up 2s, run 5 repetitions.
verify: Record the exact command, machine and rustc version next to every CSV row
Measured Instant::now overhead is reported and is small relative to the p50 you report
Repetition spread (min to max) is shown for ops/s and p99 of every configuration

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up answers whether incremental growth keeps p99 flat and what it costs in throughput. Four parts: the question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprises happened (for example lock waits in blocking mode); assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2: every throughput and p99 claim has a number, the machine, and the command that produced it
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a measurement (flame graph, counter, or ablation)
Part 4 lists assumptions (uniform u64 keys, one machine, op mixes) and what the results do not show

projects.title: Memory reclamation showdown
projects.problem: Freeing memory another thread may still read: epochs vs hazard pointers vs RCU
projects.proveIt: Memory growth when one reader stalls, throughput of each
projects.question: When one reader stalls, how much unreclaimed memory and lost throughput do epochs, hazard pointers and QSBR-style RCU each cost?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the workload
steps.learn: Hart's comparison of QSBR, EBR and hazard pointers (SMR) found memory use unbounded for QSBR and EBR and bounded for hazard pointers, with QSBR cheapest when updates are few. Your metrics: ops/s per scheme, and live retired-but-unfreed bytes over time while one reader is stalled.
verify: README states the question, the two metrics and the read/update mixes (for example 90/10 and 50/50) before any code
Read Hart's Table 7.1 and write down its predicted ranking for your two mixes, to compare with results later
Record CPU model, core count, OS, kernel and rustc version

steps.title: Pick the data structure all schemes protect
steps.learn: Hart used Michael's lock-free sorted list (an improvement on Harris's) inside a fixed-bucket hash table. A deleted node's next pointer is first marked (a tag bit), then unlinked. Harris's original list must reference logically deleted nodes, which Hart notes makes it unusable with any of these three schemes.

decision.choice: Fixed-bucket hash set of Michael lock-free sorted lists, keys u64, mark bit in the low bit of next
decision.why: Lookups traverse several nodes, exposing per-node read cost (where hazard pointers pay most), and deletes produce a steady stream of garbage to reclaim.

alternatives.name: Treiber stack
alternatives.tradeoff: Tiny and easy to get right, but every op hits one head pointer, so you measure contention more than reclamation cost.

alternatives.name: Michael-Scott queue
alternatives.tradeoff: The hazard pointer paper walks through it in detail, but there are no long traversals, so read-side cost differences shrink.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write crate reclaim-bench with struct ListSet<R: Reclaimer> implementing insert, remove, contains on a sorted list with mark bit in the next pointer low bit (use usize tagging with AtomicUsize or crossbeam Shared tags). Wrap 32 or more of these in HashSet<R>. First implement it with a Leak reclaimer (never frees). Tests: single-thread set semantics vs BTreeSet over 1M random ops; 8-thread disjoint-key inserts all present.
verify: Single-thread differential test vs BTreeSet passes on 1M random ops
Draw a remove of a middle node: mark step, unlink CAS, and where retire must be called

steps.title: Define one interface for three schemes
steps.learn: All three schemes defer freeing until no reader can still hold the pointer; they differ in how readers announce themselves: EBR readers enter and leave critical sections, hazard pointer readers publish each pointer they hold, QSBR readers periodically report quiescent states.

decision.choice: A Reclaimer trait with enter/leave, protect(slot, &AtomicPtr), retire(ptr), quiescent(); unused hooks are no-ops
decision.why: One list implementation runs under every scheme, so throughput differences come from reclamation, not from four slightly different lists.

alternatives.name: Separate list code per scheme
alternatives.tradeoff: Each can be tuned (no protect calls under EBR), but bugs and optimizations differ per copy and confound results.

alternatives.name: Only use crates (crossbeam-epoch, haphazard)
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but no QSBR crate on the same footing and APIs that force different list code anyway.

steps.delegate: Define trait Reclaimer { type Guard; fn enter(&self) with Guard; fn protect(&self, g: &mut Guard, slot: usize, src: &AtomicUsize) returning usize; fn retire(&self, g: &Guard, ptr: *mut Node); fn quiescent(&self); }. Port ListSet to call protect on each node it dereferences during traversal and retire after a successful unlink. Implement Leak against it. Tests from the previous step still pass with Leak.
verify: Every dereference of a shared node in ListSet is preceded by a protect call; count them in a code review
Leak-reclaimer tests pass unchanged after the refactor

steps.title: Implement epoch-based reclamation
steps.learn: Fraser's EBR: a global epoch, and each thread records the epoch it saw when entering. Hart: with global epoch e, threads in critical sections are in e or e+1, never e-1 (mod 3), so garbage retired two epochs back is safe to free. crossbeam-epoch is a production version to compare against.

decision.choice: Own minimal EBR (3 limbo lists per thread, advance when all active threads saw the epoch); crossbeam-epoch as reference
decision.why: Writing it shows exactly why a pinned stalled reader blocks epoch advance; the crate checks that your version's cost is in a sane range.

alternatives.name: crossbeam-epoch only
alternatives.tradeoff: Production quality and less code, but its batching and global queue make the stalled-reader growth curve harder to explain.

alternatives.name: Interval-based or hybrid schemes
alternatives.tradeoff: Bound garbage under stalls, but they are research designs beyond this project's three-way comparison.

steps.delegate: Implement Ebr: Reclaimer with global AtomicUsize epoch, per-thread CachePadded record {active: AtomicBool, epoch: AtomicUsize} in a registry, per-thread limbo [Vec<*mut Node>; 3]. enter stores active and epoch then issues fence(SeqCst); try_advance succeeds only if every active record shows the current epoch. Also a CrossbeamEbr adapter. Tests: 8-thread mixed workload for 10s shows retired minus dropped nodes (counted in Node Drop) stays bounded when no thread stalls.
verify: Explain in one paragraph why the fence after setting active is needed, citing a concrete bad interleaving
Without stalls, retired minus dropped nodes (a counter bumped in Node Drop) stays flat over a 10s run for both Ebr and CrossbeamEbr

steps.title: Implement hazard pointers
steps.learn: Michael's method: store the pointer in a hazard slot, then re-read the source to validate it is still reachable, and retry if not. Retired nodes go to a per-thread list; once it reaches a threshold R (R = H + Omega(H), H the total hazard pointers) the thread frees every node not found in any slot.

decision.choice: Fixed K slots per thread (enough for prev, cur, next), scan when retired list reaches 2x total slots
decision.why: Garbage per thread stays bounded no matter how long a reader stalls, which is the property under test; R proportional to H keeps scan cost amortized.

alternatives.name: haphazard crate
alternatives.tradeoff: Folly-derived and tested, but its domain and reclaim policy differ from the paper; use it as a reference point rather than the subject.

alternatives.name: Scan on every retire
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest garbage, but a full scan of all slots per remove makes update-heavy throughput collapse.

steps.delegate: Implement Hp: Reclaimer with a registry of per-thread CachePadded [AtomicUsize; K] slots. protect: loop { p = src.load(Acquire); slot.store(p); fence(SeqCst); if src.load(Acquire) == p break }. retire pushes to a thread-local Vec; when len reaches threshold, snapshot all slots into a sorted Vec and free unmatched nodes. Tests: stress 16 threads for 30s under AddressSanitizer with no use-after-free; retired-list length never exceeds threshold plus K.
verify: Count protect calls per contains() at your list lengths and compare to EBR's one enter per op
ASan stress run of 30s reports no use-after-free; drop the re-read, add a yield between load and slot store, and confirm ASan or loom reports it

steps.title: Implement QSBR-style RCU
steps.learn: In QSBR, readers do nothing on entry or exit; each thread periodically announces a quiescent state (holding no references). liburcu's qsbr flavor works this way. A grace period ends once every thread has passed one, then memory retired before it can be freed.

decision.choice: Deferred freeing (call_rcu style): free after a later grace period; quiescent() once per op loop
decision.why: Writers keep running during a stall, so the cost shows up as memory growth, matching the other two schemes and the prove-it metric.

alternatives.name: synchronize_rcu (writer waits for a grace period)
alternatives.tradeoff: No backlog, but during a stall writers block, so you measure zero throughput instead of memory growth.

alternatives.name: liburcu qsbr via FFI
alternatives.tradeoff: Real production implementation, but C FFI and a different allocator path complicate the same-harness comparison.

steps.delegate: Implement Qsbr: Reclaimer with global AtomicU64 counter and per-thread CachePadded AtomicU64 last_seen; quiescent() stores the global value with Release; retire tags nodes with the current global counter and increments it; free nodes whose tag is below the minimum last_seen across registered threads. Threads must register/unregister. Test: run without a stalled thread and assert retired minus dropped nodes stays bounded; a thread that never calls quiescent() makes it grow.
verify: A test with one thread that never calls quiescent() shows retired minus dropped nodes (Node Drop counter) growing linearly with removes
Write down which call sites in the benchmark loop are quiescent points and why no node reference survives them

steps.title: Measure memory independently of the schemes
steps.learn: Do not trust each scheme's own garbage counter to grade it. Wrap the global allocator so every alloc and dealloc updates live-bytes counters, and sample them on a timer. RSS from /proc/self/status (VmRSS) is a second view, but it may not fall after frees because allocators can keep pages.

decision.choice: Counting GlobalAlloc wrapper (striped counters) sampled every 10 ms, VmRSS logged alongside
decision.why: The allocator sees every free regardless of scheme, so the memory curve is graded by code none of the schemes control.

alternatives.name: Each scheme reports its retired list length
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but it grades the scheme with its own bookkeeping and misses per-node size differences.

alternatives.name: VmRSS only
alternatives.tradeoff: No code needed, but allocator caching hides frees, so a scheme can look worse or better than it is.

steps.delegate: Write a CountingAlloc implementing GlobalAlloc that forwards to System and adds/subtracts size on per-thread-striped AtomicIsize counters. A sampler thread logs (t_ms, live_bytes, vmrss_kb) every 10 ms to CSV, parsing VmRSS from /proc/self/status. Test: allocate and free 100 MB in a loop; live_bytes returns to baseline each time.
verify: Allocate-and-free test shows live_bytes return to baseline within a small slack each cycle
Leak reclaimer run shows live_bytes rising linearly with removes, confirming the counter sees list nodes

steps.title: Design the stalled-reader experiment
steps.learn: Hart illustrates why QSBR and EBR are blocking: one thread that does not pass a quiescent state or leave its critical section keeps everyone else's garbage alive. Hazard pointers only pin the few nodes in the stalled thread's slots.

decision.choice: One reader enters a critical section, protects a node, then sleeps for a fixed window while writers keep removing
decision.why: Deterministic and repeatable: the stall starts and ends at known times, so memory curves line up across schemes and runs.

alternatives.name: Oversubscribe threads beyond cores
alternatives.tradeoff: Realistic preemption stalls (Hart's CPU contention case), but stall timing is random so curves are noisy.

alternatives.name: Reader in a long traversal
alternatives.tradeoff: Natural stall, but its length varies with list size and scheme, mixing two effects.

steps.delegate: Add a --stall-ms flag to the bench: thread 0 calls enter(), protects the list head node, sleeps stall_ms, then leaves (and for Qsbr skips quiescent() during the sleep). All other threads run the update-heavy mix. Emit stall start/end timestamps into the sampler CSV. Test: with Leak and Hp, peak live bytes during the stall differ as predicted.
verify: Plot live_bytes vs time with stall start and end marked for Ebr, CrossbeamEbr, Hp, Qsbr
After the stall ends, check each scheme's live_bytes returns near its pre-stall level and record how long it took

steps.title: Prove no use-after-free before measuring
steps.learn: A reclamation bug is a use-after-free that may not crash. AddressSanitizer catches it when freed memory is touched; loom explores interleavings of small models under the C11 memory model. The Rust docs note ThreadSanitizer does not support atomic fences, which EBR and HP use.

decision.choice: AddressSanitizer stress runs for every scheme plus loom models of protect-validate and epoch advance
decision.why: ASan turns silent use-after-free into a report at scale; loom checks the fence-dependent handshake that random runs rarely break.

alternatives.name: ThreadSanitizer
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for data races in general, but fence-based protocols can produce false reports.

alternatives.name: Miri
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise undefined-behavior checking, but very slow, so only tiny workloads fit.

steps.delegate: Add CI jobs: (1) RUSTFLAGS=-Zsanitizer=address cargo +nightly test with -Zbuild-std on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu, running a 60s 16-thread stress test per scheme; (2) loom tests under cfg(loom): two threads, one removes and retires node n while the other protects/enters and reads n, asserting n is not freed while read. Include a deliberately broken variant (no validation re-read) that must fail.
verify: ASan stress passes for Ebr, Hp, Qsbr; the broken variant is reported
loom test for the protect-validate handshake passes; dropping the fence makes it fail

steps.title: Measure throughput and memory for each scheme
steps.learn: Baselines: Leak (upper bound on throughput, no frees) and a Mutex-protected set. Run each scheme at 1 to all cores, two mixes, with and without a stall. Pin the allocator choice across runs, warm up, repeat, and report spread, not one number.

decision.choice: Fixed key range pre-filled to half, 10s runs, 5 repetitions, ops/s plus peak and post-stall live bytes
decision.why: A fixed key range keeps list lengths steady so per-node read costs are comparable, and pre-filling avoids measuring an empty-list warm-up.

alternatives.name: Vary list length too
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows Hart's traversal-length effect on hazard pointers directly, at the cost of more runs; add it if time allows.

alternatives.name: Criterion microbenchmarks per op
alternatives.tradeoff: Tight confidence intervals, but no multi-thread contention or stall behavior.

steps.delegate: Write scripts/run.sh that loops scheme in {leak,mutex,ebr,crossbeam,hp,qsbr} (add haphazard only if you wrote an adapter), threads in {1,2,4,8,all}, mix in {90/10,50/50}, stall in {0,2000ms}, 5 reps, writing CSV rows (scheme,threads,mix,stall,rep,ops_per_s,peak_live_bytes,post_stall_live_bytes). Build with --release, fixed seed. Add a plot script for ops/s vs threads and live bytes vs time.
verify: Every CSV row carries the machine, rustc version and command line
Leak is the fastest or within noise of the fastest configuration; if not, investigate before trusting results
perf stat (or similar) counters recorded for at least one HP vs EBR pair to explain a throughput gap

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up answers which scheme you would pick for a read-mostly versus an update-heavy structure that may see stalls. Four parts: the question; numbers with machine and command; why surprises happened; assumptions and what this does not prove (one structure, one machine, synthetic stalls).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2: every throughput and memory claim has a number, the machine and the command
Part 3 explains at least one result that differs from Hart's Table 7.1 prediction, or says none did
Part 4 lists assumptions and what the results do not show

projects.title: Work-stealing thread pool
projects.problem: Uneven tasks leave some cores idle
projects.proveIt: Speedup on irregular workloads vs Rayon or Tokio
projects.question: On irregular, recursively split workloads, how close does a hand-built work-stealing pool get to Rayon and Tokio, and why?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the workloads
steps.learn: Irregular work means tasks whose cost you cannot predict up front, so static splitting leaves cores idle. Metric: wall time at P threads, speedup T1/TP, and the ratio to Rayon and Tokio at the same P. Workloads: a seeded unbalanced random tree walk, Mandelbrot rows (cost varies per row), and parallel quicksort.
steps.delegate: In Rust, create a workloads crate with three pure functions, each taking a seed and size: tree_walk (random branching, seeded), mandelbrot_rows (returns per-row iteration counts), quicksort input generator (seeded u64s). Each returns a checksum. Add a sequential reference implementation for each and tests that pin the checksums for fixed seeds.
verify: README states the question and the speedup formula before any pool code exists
Seeds, sizes and expected checksums are committed and frozen; tests pass on the sequential versions
Record CPU model, physical and logical core counts, OS and rustc --version

steps.title: Build a single shared queue pool as the baseline
steps.learn: The simplest pool is N threads popping from one Mutex-protected queue with a Condvar for sleeping. Every push and pop contends on one lock, which is exactly the cost work stealing removes. Building it first gives you a number to beat and a harness to reuse.

decision.choice: One Mutex<VecDeque<Job>> plus Condvar, N worker threads, boxed FnOnce jobs
decision.why: It isolates the effect of per-worker queues: same job type, same harness, only the queue structure changes later. It is small enough to be obviously correct.

alternatives.name: Static partition per thread
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero synchronization and great for uniform work, but on irregular workloads the thread with the expensive chunk finishes last while others idle.

alternatives.name: Skip the baseline, compare only to Rayon
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but you cannot tell whether your gains come from stealing or from other choices.

steps.delegate: In Rust (std only), write CentralPool::new(n) with spawn(F) where F: FnOnce() + Send + 'static, and a scope-style wait_all(). Use Mutex<VecDeque<Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send>>> and Condvar; shut down cleanly on Drop. Tests: 100k tiny jobs incrementing an AtomicUsize reach exactly 100k; pool drops without hanging; a panicking job does not deadlock wait_all.
verify: All three workloads produce the frozen checksums on CentralPool at 1, 2 and max threads
Record CentralPool wall time per workload at max threads as the first baseline row

steps.title: Give each worker its own deque plus a global injector
steps.learn: Each worker pushes and pops its own deque at one end; thieves take from the other end, so the owner rarely contends. Popping the newest task keeps data cache-warm; stealing the oldest tends to grab a big unsplit subtree. A shared FIFO injector takes tasks submitted from outside the pool.

decision.choice: crossbeam-deque: Worker::new_lifo per thread, Stealer handles shared, one Injector
decision.why: It is a tested Chase-Lev style deque, so you can get the scheduler right before writing your own deque. Its docs show the exact find-task loop: local pop, then injector batch steal, then peer steals, retrying on Steal::Retry.

alternatives.name: Mutex<VecDeque> per worker
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy and correct, removes the single global lock, but every pop still takes a lock; a good intermediate data point.

alternatives.name: Fixed-size ring per worker (Tokio style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Tokio caps each local queue at 256 and moves half to the global queue on overflow; no growth logic, but needs an overflow path.

steps.delegate: In Rust with crossbeam-deque, write StealPool::new(n): each worker owns a Worker<Job> (new_lifo), all Stealers live in an Arc<[Stealer<Job>]>, plus an Injector<Job>. Implement find_task as in the crossbeam-deque docs. spawn() from a worker thread pushes locally (use a thread_local index), otherwise into the injector. Tests: same as CentralPool, plus a test that 1M jobs spawned from inside jobs all run.
verify: Checksums match on all three workloads at 1, 2 and max threads
Count steals per worker with a counter: on tree_walk at max threads, steals are nonzero on every worker

links.label: Chase and Lev, Dynamic Circular Work-Stealing Deque

steps.title: Write your own Chase-Lev deque with explicit orderings
steps.learn: Chase-Lev stores tasks in a circular array that grows when full. The hard part is the race on the last element between the owner's pop and a thief's steal, settled by a CAS on top. Le et al. prove an ARM version and give a C11 port. Growing frees the old array while thieves may read it, a reclamation problem.

decision.choice: Port Le et al.'s C11 version to Rust atomics; leak old buffers (or defer frees) at first
decision.why: Using the published orderings means you test your port, not your guesses. Leaking old arrays is bounded (each grow doubles) and removes the use-after-free risk until you add epochs; crossbeam-deque itself depends on crossbeam-epoch for this.

alternatives.name: Keep crossbeam-deque
alternatives.tradeoff: Correct and fast with no unsafe code of yours, but you skip the part of the project that teaches memory ordering.

alternatives.name: SeqCst on every atomic
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to reason about, but adds barriers you may not need, including on x86 where SeqCst stores become xchg; good as a first correct version to compare.

alternatives.name: Fixed-capacity ring, no growth
alternatives.tradeoff: No reclamation problem at all, but you need an overflow path such as the global injector.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write deque.rs with Worker<T>::{push, pop} and Stealer<T>::steal returning Empty/Success/Retry, following the C11 algorithm in Le et al. (PPoPP 2013). Use AtomicIsize for top/bottom, AtomicPtr for the buffer, and std::sync::atomic::fence where the paper has fences. Mark every unsafe block with the invariant it relies on. Tests: single-thread push/pop order, and a 4-thief stress test where every pushed item is received exactly once.
verify: Stress test with 1 owner and 4 thieves over 10M items: each item seen exactly once, run 20 times
Each atomic ordering in your code cites the line of the paper's figure it came from

links.label: Le et al., Correct and Efficient Work-Stealing for Weak Memory Models

steps.title: Add join() that helps while it waits
steps.learn: Rayon's join runs closure A on the current thread and advertises B for others to steal. After A, it runs B itself if nobody took it; if B was stolen, it looks for other work while waiting for the thief. A worker that simply blocks while waiting wastes a core, and nested joins can block every worker.

decision.choice: join(a, b): push B, run A, then pop B back or run other tasks until B's latch is set
decision.why: The recursive workloads (tree walk, quicksort) are naturally fork-join. Helping while waiting keeps every core busy and avoids the all-workers-blocked case.

alternatives.name: Block on a latch while B runs
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but the waiting worker is idle and nested joins can stall the pool entirely.

alternatives.name: spawn plus scope only
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches tokio::spawn style; fine for flat loops, but recursion allocates more and the parent cannot pick B back up cheaply.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add StealPool::join(a, b) returning (RA, RB), where a and b are FnOnce closures that are Send. Store B as a job with a result slot and an AtomicBool latch; after running A, try to pop B locally, else loop find_task and run jobs until the latch is set. Propagate panics from either side. Tests: recursive fib(30) via join equals sequential; parallel quicksort sorts 10M seeded u64s; join called from outside the pool works.
verify: Quicksort and tree_walk via join produce the frozen checksums at every thread count
With 1 thread, join-based tree_walk time is within a few percent of the sequential version (measure, record the gap)

steps.title: Choose the victim order and how much to steal
steps.learn: When idle, a worker must pick whom to rob and how much to take. Tokio picks a random sibling as a starting point, steals half of its queue, and limits how many workers search at once to cut contention. Stealing one task is cheaper per attempt; stealing many amortizes the trip for fine-grained tasks.

decision.choice: Random starting victim, try each peer once per round; steal one task from peers, batch from the injector
decision.why: Fork-join recursion leaves big subtrees at the steal end, so one steal is often enough work. Random start spreads thieves so they do not all hit worker 0.

alternatives.name: Steal half (steal_batch)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer steal trips for many tiny tasks such as Mandelbrot rows, but can take more than the thief needs and cause steal-backs.

alternatives.name: Fixed round-robin victim order
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and easy to debug, but thieves pile onto the same victims.

alternatives.name: Cap concurrent searchers (Tokio)
alternatives.tradeoff: Reduces contention when many workers go idle together, at the cost of slower wake-up of new workers.

steps.delegate: In Rust, make the steal policy a enum StealPolicy { One, Batch } plus a victim order { Random, RoundRobin } selectable by env var. Use a small xorshift RNG per worker (no shared RNG). Add counters for steal attempts, successes and Retry results per worker, printed at shutdown. Test: all policies give identical checksums.
verify: Table of wall time and steal success rate for each policy on all three workloads at max threads
Name the best policy per workload and keep the others as an ablation row

steps.title: Make idle workers sleep without losing wakeups
steps.learn: Idle workers that spin forever burn CPU that busy workers could use. Workers that sleep too early add wake-up latency. The bug to avoid is a lost wakeup: work is posted just after a worker checked and just before it slept. Rayon tracks idle rounds, a sleepy state and a jobs event counter for this.

decision.choice: Spin with crossbeam Backoff for a few rounds, then publish sleeping, recheck queues, then park
decision.why: Short spins catch work that arrives within microseconds (common in fork-join). Rechecking after announcing sleep, with push paths unparking a sleeper, closes the lost-wakeup window.

alternatives.name: Always spin
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest wake latency, but steals CPU from busy threads (and SMT siblings) and skews your measurements.

alternatives.name: Condvar under a mutex for every idle wait
alternatives.tradeoff: Hard to get wrong, but every push must touch the mutex, which brings back central contention.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add a Sleep module: AtomicUsize sleepers count plus a per-worker Thread handle. Idle loop: Backoff::snooze until is_completed, then increment sleepers, recheck all queues, then thread::park. spawn/push calls unpark on one sleeper if sleepers > 0. Tests: a pool with no work uses near zero CPU after 1s (read /proc/self/stat or getrusage); a job spawned after all workers sleep still runs within 10 ms.
verify: Idle pool CPU time over 5 s is near zero (record the getrusage numbers)
Late-spawn test passes 1000 times in a loop with no hang

steps.title: Lay out per-worker state to avoid false sharing
steps.learn: Per-worker counters and deque indices that sit on the same cache line as another worker's data force that line to bounce between cores on every write, even though no data is shared logically. Padding each worker's hot fields onto their own line removes the bounce.

decision.choice: Wrap each worker's hot state (deque top/bottom, counters) in crossbeam_utils::CachePadded
decision.why: Steal counters and deque indices are written constantly; padding is a one-line change whose effect you can measure directly with the counters you already have.

alternatives.name: No padding
alternatives.tradeoff: Less memory, simpler structs; acceptable if measurements show no difference on your machine.

alternatives.name: Manual #[repr(align(128))]
alternatives.tradeoff: Same effect without the dependency, but you must pick the alignment per platform yourself.

steps.delegate: In Rust, wrap per-worker stats and the deque's top and bottom atomics in CachePadded behind a cargo feature flag padded (default on). Add a microbenchmark where 8 workers each increment only their own counter 100M times, with and without the feature. Test that both builds pass the checksum suite.
verify: Microbenchmark wall time with and without padding, same machine, 5 runs each
Workload times with and without padding recorded; note if the difference is within run-to-run noise

steps.title: Model-check the deque and sleep protocol with loom
steps.learn: Stress tests only see interleavings your machine happens to produce. loom runs a test under many possible thread interleavings and memory-ordering outcomes, which is how you catch a wrong Relaxed or a lost wakeup. It only scales to tiny tests, so keep them to 2 or 3 threads and a few items.

decision.choice: loom for the deque (owner plus one thief, last-element race) and the sleep/wake handshake
decision.why: These two pieces are where weak-memory bugs live and they are small enough for loom. Stress tests and checksums cover the rest.

alternatives.name: ThreadSanitizer only
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches data races in real runs with less setup, but only on interleavings that occur and not all relaxed-ordering bugs.

alternatives.name: Stress tests only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and realistic, but a rare interleaving can pass a million runs and fail in production.

steps.delegate: In Rust, gate atomics behind a cfg(loom) shim (use loom::sync::atomic under loom, std otherwise). Write loom::model tests: owner push 2, pop 1 while a thief steals 1, assert each item is taken exactly once; worker announces sleep while another thread pushes, assert the job runs. Document how to run with RUSTFLAGS="--cfg loom" and LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS.
verify: loom tests pass; then weaken one ordering on purpose and confirm loom reports a failure
Record how long the loom suite takes and the preemption bound used

steps.title: Measure speedup against Rayon and Tokio fairly
steps.learn: Same workloads, same seeds, same sequential cutoff, same thread count for every pool. Set Rayon threads with ThreadPoolBuilder::num_threads and Tokio with Builder::worker_threads. Tokio's docs warn that long compute in a future without yielding is a problem; note that context. Warm up, repeat, report spread.

decision.choice: hyperfine with warmup and 10+ runs per (pool, workload, threads), plus perf stat for context switches and migrations
decision.why: Whole-process timing includes pool startup, which is identical in style across pools, and hyperfine reports mean and spread. perf stat counters explain differences the clock alone cannot.

alternatives.name: criterion in-process benchmarks
alternatives.tradeoff: Better statistics for short operations, but pools live across iterations, so startup and sleep behavior differ from real runs.

alternatives.name: Single timed run per config
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but frequency scaling and noise make small differences meaningless.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a bench binary taking --pool {central,steal,own,rayon,tokio} --workload {tree,mandel,qsort} --threads N, printing checksum and wall time. For tokio, implement tree and qsort with tokio::spawn recursion on a new_multi_thread runtime. Add a bash script running hyperfine --warmup 3 --runs 10 --export-markdown over threads 1,2,4,...,max and perf stat -r 5 -e context-switches,cpu-migrations.
verify: Speedup T1/TP table for every pool and workload at each thread count, with spread
Checksums identical for all pools in every run (no fast wrong answers)
Machine, governor or power mode, rustc version and exact commands recorded next to the table

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question, (2) the speedup tables with machine and commands, (3) why surprises happened, for example where Rayon wins and which counter shows it, (4) assumptions: one machine, three synthetic workloads, Tokio used outside its I/O sweet spot, no NUMA testing.
verify: Write-up opens with the one question, word for word from step 1
Every number has the machine, thread count and exact command that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with evidence (a counter, profile or ablation)
A section lists assumptions and what this does not prove

projects.title: Honest latency load generator
projects.problem: Most benchmarks hide tail latency (coordinated omission)
projects.proveIt: p99.9 from a naive tool vs your corrected one
projects.question: When a server stalls, how far does a closed-loop load tool understate p99.9 latency, and does an open-loop corrected tool get it right?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the ground truth
steps.learn: Coordinated omission: a tool that waits for each response before sending the next stops sending during a stall, so it never records the requests that would have queued. Metric: p99, p99.9 and max from each tool. Ground truth comes from a server with a known stall schedule, computed by hand, not by any tool.
