steps.delegate: In Rust, write expected.rs: given request rate R, stall length S, stall period P, base service time B, compute the expected latency distribution for an open-loop client (requests intended during a stall wait until it ends, then drain at C/B per second over C connections) and print p50, p99, p99.9, max. Unit test the stall-free case returns B for all percentiles.
verify: README states the question and the expected p99.9 for your chosen R, S, P before any measurement
The expected-value calculation is checked by hand for one setting and matches the program
Record CPU, cores, OS, kernel and whether client and server share a machine

links.label: Gil Tene, How NOT to Measure Latency

steps.title: Build a test server with deterministic stalls
steps.learn: To grade a load tool you need a server whose true behavior you already know. A server that answers in a fixed short time but freezes all handling for S seconds every P seconds gives a tail that is easy to predict and easy to hide.

decision.choice: axum server; a background task toggles a global stall gate; every handler awaits the gate before replying
decision.why: Stalls are exact and repeatable, independent of the client, and the stall log gives you timestamps to cross-check measured latencies against.

alternatives.name: Pause the server process with SIGSTOP/SIGCONT
alternatives.tradeoff: Very realistic freeze (like a GC or VM pause), but timing is driven by an external script and less precise.

alternatives.name: Real server with real load
alternatives.tradeoff: More realistic, but you lose the ground truth, so you cannot tell which tool is right.

steps.delegate: In Rust with axum and tokio, write stall-server --stall-ms S --period-ms P --port N. GET / returns 200 with a small body after awaiting a tokio::sync::watch gate. A task flips the gate on schedule and logs each stall start/end with timestamps. Tests: with S=0, 1000 sequential requests all succeed; with S=200, a request sent at stall start returns after at least 190 ms.
verify: curl a request during a stall and confirm it returns roughly when the logged stall ends
Stall log shows the expected count of stalls over a 60 s run

steps.title: Build the naive closed-loop mode on purpose
steps.learn: A closed-loop client keeps C connections busy: send, wait, record send-to-response time, send again. During a stall each connection records one long sample and then nothing, so the tail is a handful of samples among many fast ones. This is the model of wrk and most simple benchmarks.

decision.choice: Your own closed-loop mode with C connections, timing from actual send to response
decision.why: Having naive and corrected modes in one binary, with the same HTTP stack and histogram, means any difference comes from the measurement model alone.

alternatives.name: Use only wrk as the naive tool
alternatives.tradeoff: No code needed and it is the real-world baseline, but its HTTP stack differs from yours, which muddies the comparison.

alternatives.name: Skip naive mode
alternatives.tradeoff: Less work, but you lose the cleanest demonstration of the effect.

steps.delegate: In Rust with tokio and hyper (client::conn::http1::handshake), write loadgen --mode closed --connections C --duration D URL. Each connection task loops: record Instant, send request, await response, record elapsed into a per-task hdrhistogram Histogram, merge at the end with add. Print p50/p99/p99.9/max and total requests. Test against stall-server with S=0.
verify: Against a stall-free server, closed-mode p50 is close to the server's base latency
Against the stall server, total requests sent drops during stalls (log per-second counts)

steps.title: Send on a fixed schedule and time from intended send
steps.learn: An open-loop client sends request i at start + i/R no matter how the server is doing, and records latency from that intended time, not from when it actually sent. This is wrk2's model. A request that should have gone out during a stall is charged the wait it would really have seen.

decision.choice: Constant-rate schedule; latency = response time minus intended send time
decision.why: Constant rate makes the ground-truth math simple and matches wrk2, so you can cross-check your numbers against a known corrected tool.

alternatives.name: Poisson arrivals
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to many real open systems, but expected percentiles are harder to derive by hand; a good second mode later.

alternatives.name: Post-hoc correction of closed-loop data
alternatives.tradeoff: HdrHistogram's record_correct backfills synthetic samples using an expected interval; cheap, but an estimate, not a measurement.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add --mode open --rate R to loadgen. Compute intended_i = start + i * (1/R) as an Instant; the request carries intended_i; on response record (now - intended_i) into the corrected histogram and (now - actual_send) into an uncorrected one. Test with a fake transport that serves one request at a time and sleeps: if every response takes 3x the interval, corrected latency grows over time while uncorrected stays flat.
verify: Against the stall-free server, corrected and uncorrected p99 are close
Against the stall server, corrected p99.9 is much larger than uncorrected; record both

links.label: Open Versus Closed: A Cautionary Tale

steps.title: Pick a timer behavior that keeps intended times
steps.learn: If the sending loop falls behind, the timer decides what happens to missed ticks. Tokio's Interval defaults to MissedTickBehavior::Burst (fire as fast as possible until caught up). Skip drops missed ticks, which silently lowers the offered rate during exactly the moments you need to measure.

decision.choice: Compute intended times from the index; if late, send immediately but still time from the intended time
decision.why: Intended times never drift and never get dropped, so every planned request is accounted for. It does not depend on timer defaults that could change.

alternatives.name: tokio::time::interval with Burst
alternatives.tradeoff: Same catch-up behavior with less code; fine if you also keep the intended Instant per tick.

alternatives.name: MissedTickBehavior::Skip or Delay
alternatives.tradeoff: Smooth sending after a hiccup, but it drops or shifts planned requests, reintroducing coordinated omission in the client.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement the sender loop: for i in 0.., let t = start + period * i; tokio::time::sleep_until(t) if t is in the future; spawn the request with t attached. Count late sends (now - t > 1 ms) in a counter. Test with a simulated 500 ms freeze of the sender: the number of requests sent over the run still equals R * duration within 1%.
verify: Total requests sent equals R x duration within 1% even with the stall server running
Per-second send counts show a burst right after each stall, not a gap

steps.title: Decide how requests map onto connections
steps.learn: HTTP/1.1 allows one request in flight per connection unless you pipeline. In a stall, every connection is busy, so newly scheduled requests must wait for a free one. That wait is real latency and must count from intended time; a tool that waits for a connection before starting the clock hides it.

decision.choice: Fixed pool of keep-alive connections; requests queue for a free connection with the clock already running
decision.why: Keeps the client from opening sockets in a storm during stalls, while the queue wait is still charged to the request, so no planned request escapes measurement.

alternatives.name: New connection per request
alternatives.tradeoff: No queueing in the client, but TCP setup inflates every sample and a stall can exhaust ports or file descriptors.

alternatives.name: Unbounded connection growth
alternatives.tradeoff: Measures pure server latency, but under long stalls the client may open thousands of sockets and change server behavior.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add a connection pool: C tasks each own a hyper http1 SendRequest and pull jobs from a tokio mpsc channel; each job carries its intended Instant. Record queue wait (dequeue time minus intended) in its own histogram. Add flags --connections and a --delay-ms option to stall-server. Test: with C=1 and a 100 ms server delay at R=50/s, corrected latency grows over the run as expected.
verify: Queue-wait histogram is near zero on the stall-free server and large during stalls
Corrected p99.9 changes little when doubling --connections on the stall server (record both)

steps.title: Record latencies in HdrHistogram
steps.learn: To report p99.9 you need the tail recorded accurately, not averaged away. HdrHistogram records values with a fixed number of significant digits across a wide range in fixed memory, and histograms from many tasks merge with add. value_at_quantile gives percentiles.

decision.choice: hdrhistogram crate, new_with_bounds(1 us, 60 s, 3 sig figs), per-task histograms merged at the end
decision.why: Fixed memory regardless of run length, precise enough at high percentiles, mergeable without locks on the hot path, and the same structure wrk2 uses.

alternatives.name: Store every sample in a Vec
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact percentiles, but memory grows with rate x duration, and sorting at the end is slow for long runs.

alternatives.name: Mean and fixed coarse buckets
alternatives.tradeoff: Tiny and simple, but the tail collapses into one bucket and you cannot report p99.9 honestly.

steps.delegate: In Rust with hdrhistogram, keep three histograms per task: corrected, uncorrected, queue-wait, all in microseconds with new_with_bounds(1, 60_000_000, 3). Merge with add. Print a percentile table (50, 90, 99, 99.9, 99.99, max) and write the corrected histogram with V2Serializer to a file. Test: recording known values 1..=1000 gives p50 near 500.
verify: Percentile table printed for all three histograms on one run
Saved histogram reloads and prints the same p99.9

steps.title: Detect when the load generator is the bottleneck
steps.learn: If the client cannot keep up (CPU saturated, scheduler delays, too few runtime threads), it sends late and the corrected latency includes client delay that the server never caused. You must measure send lag (actual send minus intended) and refuse to trust runs where it is large without a server stall.

decision.choice: Send-lag histogram plus a run validity rule: on the stall-free server, send-lag p99 must stay under 1 ms
decision.why: It gives you a direct test that the tool measures the server, not itself, and tells you the maximum rate your client can honestly drive on this machine.

alternatives.name: Run client on a separate machine
alternatives.tradeoff: Removes CPU sharing with the server, but adds network jitter that you must then measure separately.

alternatives.name: Trust the client
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra code, but at high rates you may publish the client's own stalls as server latency.

steps.delegate: In Rust, record actual_send - intended into a send-lag histogram. At the end, print its p99 and max and mark the run INVALID if p99 exceeds a --max-lag threshold. Add a --sweep mode that runs 10 s at increasing rates against the stall-free server and reports the highest rate that stays valid.
verify: Record the highest valid rate for your machine from the sweep
All measurement runs in the next step use a rate below that limit

steps.title: Compare naive, corrected and reference tools
steps.learn: Run every tool against the same stall schedule; run wrk2 and your open mode at one rate, and give wrk and your closed mode connections whose stall-free throughput is near that rate. wrk2 calibrates for 10 s, so run for minutes. --u_latency prints its uncorrected view.

decision.choice: Matrix: wrk2 -R and your open mode at one valid rate, wrk and closed mode at matching throughput, stall on/off, 3 runs
decision.why: wrk is the naive reference, wrk2 the corrected reference, and your two modes share one stack, so you can separate the measurement model from tool differences, all graded against expected.rs.

alternatives.name: Only your own two modes
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleaner comparison, but no external check that your corrected numbers agree with an established tool.

alternatives.name: Many rates and stall lengths
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows how the gap scales, but multiplies run time; do it after the main matrix.

steps.delegate: Write a bash script that starts stall-server, then for each tool runs a 120 s test at the chosen rate (wrk -t2 -c C -d120s; wrk2 -t2 -c C -d120s -R rate --latency --u_latency; loadgen closed and open), saves raw output, and repeats 3 times. A Python script parses p99, p99.9 and max into one CSV next to expected.rs output.
verify: Table of p99.9 per tool vs the expected value, stall on and off, with spread across 3 runs
Your open mode and wrk2 agree with each other and with expected p99.9 within a stated tolerance
Machine, tool versions, rate, connections and commands recorded beside the table

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question, (2) the p99.9 table per tool vs ground truth with machine and commands, (3) why the naive numbers were so low (count how many samples each tool recorded during stalls), (4) assumptions: constant-rate load, synthetic stalls, one machine, HTTP/1.1 only.
verify: Write-up opens with the one question, word for word from step 1
Every number has the machine, thread count and exact command that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with evidence (a counter, profile or ablation)
A section lists assumptions and what this does not prove

projects.title: Cache-friendly lookup showdown
projects.problem: Big-O ignores cache misses
projects.proveIt: Lookup ns for B-tree, hash, sorted array and Eytzinger layout at 32 KiB to 1 GiB
projects.question: How do B-tree, hash, sorted array and Eytzinger lookups compare in nanoseconds as the data grows from 32 KiB to 1 GiB, and why?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the key sets
steps.learn: Big-O says binary search and B-tree search are both O(log n) and hashing is O(1), yet real cost is dominated by which cache level each probe hits. The metric is nanoseconds per lookup at key-array sizes from 32 KiB to 1 GiB. Keys: real 64-bit keys from the SOSD benchmark (fb and wiki datasets).
verify: README states the question, the metric (ns per lookup) and the exact size grid, written before any code
Record CPU model and L1d/L2/L3 sizes from lscpu, total RAM, kernel and compiler version
Download two SOSD uint64 files with scripts/download.sh and confirm the checksum lines print ok

links.label: SOSD: A Benchmark for Learned Indexes

steps.title: Sample key sets per size and freeze the query sets
steps.learn: Each SOSD file starts with a uint64 count followed by the sorted keys. For each target size (keys = bytes / 8) take an evenly spaced sample so the key distribution is preserved. Query sets are generated once with a fixed seed and saved, so every structure answers exactly the same lookups.

decision.choice: Real SOSD keys, deduplicated, with saved query files: 90% present keys, 10% absent
decision.why: Real keys have skew and gaps that uniform random keys lack, which matters for hash quality and B-tree node fill. Saving queries to disk freezes the test set before any tuning and makes runs comparable across structures and days.

alternatives.name: Uniform random uint64 keys
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to generate at any size and easy to reason about, but hides the effect of real distributions on hashing and layout.

alternatives.name: Present keys only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler correctness checks, but misses the miss path, where hash tables probe until an empty slot and searches go to a leaf.

steps.delegate: In C++17, write keys.h/.cc: load_sosd(path) reading a uint64 count then that many uint64 keys; sample_keys(keys, n) taking an evenly spaced subsample and removing duplicates; make_queries(keys, m, seed, present_frac) writing a binary query file. Test: sampled arrays are strictly increasing, query files are byte-identical across two runs with the same seed.
verify: For each size, print key count, bytes and number of duplicates removed
Hash the saved query files and record the hashes in the README; they must not change later

steps.title: Build the sorted array baseline, branchy and branchless
steps.learn: Binary search on a sorted array touches about log2(n) cache lines, and only the last few probes share a line. A branchless version replaces the comparison branch with a conditional move, removing mispredictions, but loses the speculative fetch a predicted branch gives for free on large arrays.

decision.choice: Keep both std::lower_bound and a branchless lower_bound as two contestants
decision.why: The showdown is about why curves bend. Two versions of the same layout separate branch effects from memory layout effects, which is the comparison readers will ask about.

alternatives.name: std::lower_bound only
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code and the obvious baseline, but you cannot tell whether later wins come from layout or from removing branches.

alternatives.name: Interpolation search
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer probes on smooth key distributions, but its cost depends heavily on the dataset and adds a third variable.

steps.delegate: In C++17, implement size_t lb_std(const uint64_t*, size_t n, uint64_t x) using std::lower_bound and size_t lb_branchless(...) using the halving loop with base += (base[half-1] < x) * half. Unit test against std::lower_bound on 10,000 random queries for every size up to 1M keys, including absent keys and keys beyond both ends.
verify: Unit tests pass for both variants, including below-min and above-max queries
Inspect the branchless loop with objdump or Compiler Explorer and confirm it compiled to a cmov, not a jump

steps.title: Lay out the Eytzinger array and add prefetching
steps.learn: The Eytzinger layout stores the implicit search tree in breadth-first order: children of index k are 2k and 2k+1. Hot top levels pack together in cache, and because a node's descendants are contiguous, one prefetch can fetch several levels ahead. With 64-bit keys, a 64-byte line holds 8 keys.

decision.choice: 1-indexed, 64-byte aligned Eytzinger array with a branchless descent and one prefetch several levels ahead
decision.why: Aligning the array makes each group of descendants start on a cache line, so one prefetch per iteration overlaps memory requests and hides latency on arrays far bigger than L3.

alternatives.name: Eytzinger without prefetch
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler and shows the pure layout effect, but on large arrays each level is a dependent cache miss.

alternatives.name: Van Emde Boas layout
alternatives.tradeoff: Cache-oblivious recursive blocking, but indexing is more complex; Khuong and Morin compare it against Eytzinger in detail.

steps.delegate: In C++17, write eytzinger.h: build(sorted, n) filling a 64-byte-aligned array (std::aligned_alloc) by in-order traversal from index 1; search(x) using k = 2*k + (t[k] < x), __builtin_prefetch on the descendant block, then k >>= __builtin_ffs(~k) to recover the answer; map back to the sorted index. Test equality with lb_std on all sizes and on absent keys.
verify: Unit tests give identical lower_bound results to lb_std for every query file
Time the saved queries at one large size with and without the prefetch line using a simple steady_clock loop; record both

links.label: Khuong and Morin: Array Layouts for Comparison-Based Searching

steps.title: Choose the B-tree contestant
steps.learn: A B-tree node holds many keys, so each level costs about one cache miss instead of one per binary step. A static, pointer-free B-tree whose nodes are exactly one cache line reduces the number of line fetches per query compared with binary search, and keys inside a node can be compared with SIMD.

decision.choice: A static implicit B-tree (S-tree) with cache-line-sized nodes, plus absl::btree_set as the pointer-based reference
decision.why: The read-only showdown lets you use the static layout that best shows the cache effect, while absl::btree_set shows what a general-purpose, insertable B-tree costs. Readers get both the ceiling and the practical option.

alternatives.name: absl::btree_set only
alternatives.tradeoff: No custom code and supports inserts, but node size and pointer chasing are fixed by the library, so you measure one design point.

alternatives.name: std::set
alternatives.tradeoff: A red-black tree with one key per node; illustrates the worst case for pointer chasing but is not a B-tree.

steps.delegate: In C++17, write stree.h implementing a static B-tree over sorted uint64 keys: nodes of 8 keys (one 64-byte line), children of node k at k*9+i+1, 64-byte aligned storage, in-node search with a scalar loop and an optional AVX2 path behind a compile flag. Also wrap absl::btree_set<uint64_t>::lower_bound. Test both against lb_std on all query files.
verify: Unit tests match lb_std for the S-tree with and without the SIMD path
Report memory used by the S-tree and by absl::btree_set at 1 GiB of keys (RSS before and after build)

steps.title: Choose the hash table contestant
steps.learn: A hash lookup is ideally one or two cache misses regardless of n, but node-based tables add a pointer dereference per element. Swiss tables keep a dense one-byte-per-slot metadata array and use SSE to compare 16 slots at once. Hash tables answer equality only, not lower_bound.

decision.choice: absl::flat_hash_set<uint64_t> as the main hash contestant, std::unordered_set as a node-based reference
decision.why: An open-addressing table stores keys inline, which is the cache-friendly hash design; the node-based table shows what pointer chasing costs at the same O(1).

alternatives.name: Hand-written linear probing
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control of load factor and hash function, but you must handle tombstones and resizing and risk benchmarking your bugs.

alternatives.name: std::unordered_set only
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard and familiar, but its separate allocation per element makes hashing look worse than a flat design.

steps.delegate: In C++17, wrap absl::flat_hash_set<uint64_t> and std::unordered_set<uint64_t> behind the same bool contains(uint64_t) interface used by the other contestants (which return found = (lb result equals x)). Reserve capacity before inserting. Test: contains() agrees with binary search on every query file, including absent keys.
verify: Unit tests agree with binary search membership on all query files
Record load factor and memory (RSS delta) of both tables at the 1 GiB key size

steps.title: Decide on page size for the large arrays
steps.learn: At hundreds of MiB, random probes miss not only in cache but in the TLB, adding page-walk cost to every probe. Transparent huge pages can back an aligned region with 2 MiB pages when the system setting is always, or madvise and the region is advised with MADV_HUGEPAGE.

decision.choice: Run every contestant twice: default 4 KiB pages and THP via madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE), reported separately
decision.why: TLB misses explain a large part of the far-right curve, and they affect structures differently. Reporting both stops a page-size effect being credited to a layout.

alternatives.name: Default pages only
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches what most programs get, but conflates TLB and cache effects at large sizes.

alternatives.name: hugetlbfs reserved pages
alternatives.tradeoff: Guaranteed huge pages, but needs root to reserve memory up front; heavier setup for the same question.

steps.delegate: In C++17, write alloc.h with void* big_alloc(size_t bytes, bool huge): mmap anonymous memory, align to 2 MiB, and call madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE) when huge is true. Use it for the sorted, Eytzinger and S-tree arrays. Add a check that reads AnonHugePages for the process from /proc/self/smaps_rollup after touching the memory.
verify: Record /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled on the test machine
With huge=true at 1 GiB, AnonHugePages in smaps_rollup is nonzero; with huge=false note its value too

steps.title: Decide what one lookup time means
steps.learn: Independent lookups let the CPU overlap many misses, measuring throughput; making each query depend on the previous result serializes them, measuring latency. Structures that win on one can lose on the other, so the harness must say which it reports.

decision.choice: Report both: independent-query throughput (ns per lookup) and dependent-chain latency
decision.why: Prefetching layouts gain most when misses overlap, while a real point-lookup service often sees one query at a time. Both views keep the comparison honest.

alternatives.name: Throughput only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest loop and highest numbers, but flatters layouts that rely on memory-level parallelism.

alternatives.name: Latency only
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches single-request cost, but hides how much batching or overlap could recover.

steps.delegate: In C++17 with Google Benchmark, write bench.cc: for each contestant and size, BM_throughput loops over the saved queries and calls benchmark::DoNotOptimize on each result; BM_latency mixes the previous result into the next query index so lookups form a dependent chain. Use state.SetItemsProcessed so output is per lookup. Register sizes from 32 KiB to 1 GiB in powers of two.
verify: Disassemble one benchmark loop and confirm the lookup call is not hoisted or removed
At the smallest size the dependent-chain number is at least as large as the throughput number for every contestant

steps.title: Measure it: the full size sweep
steps.learn: Pitfalls: frequency scaling and turbo, other processes, first-touch page faults inside the timed region, and too few repetitions. Build data structures outside the timed loop, pin to one core, and repeat each point. Baselines are std::lower_bound and std::unordered_set.
verify: Run with --benchmark_repetitions=5 and --benchmark_out=results.json; record the full command and commit hash
Pin with taskset and record the CPU governor; report median and spread for every point
Plot ns per lookup vs size (log x) for all contestants, both page sizes and both modes
Rerun one size a day later on the same machine and confirm the median moves less than your stated noise band

links.label: Drepper: What Every Programmer Should Know About Memory

steps.title: Explain the curves with hardware counters
steps.learn: Each knee in a curve should line up with a capacity boundary: L1, L2, L3, then TLB reach. Hardware counters turn a guess into evidence: cache misses and TLB misses per lookup should jump where ns per lookup jumps.

decision.choice: perf stat on a single-contestant, single-size run, counters divided by lookups
decision.why: One contestant and one size per run keeps counters attributable; dividing by lookups makes them comparable across sizes.

alternatives.name: Google Benchmark --benchmark_perf_counters
alternatives.tradeoff: Counters land beside timings in the same JSON, but needs a libpfm-enabled build and counter names are platform specific.

alternatives.name: Timing only
alternatives.tradeoff: No tooling setup, but knees stay unexplained and you cannot separate cache from TLB effects.

verify: For three sizes (in L2, in L3, far beyond L3) record cache-misses and dTLB-load-misses per lookup, if your CPU exposes them
Show at least one curve knee that coincides with an lscpu cache size within one step of your size grid

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) a number for every claim with machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (with counter evidence), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove, such as read-only static data and one CPU.
verify: Part 1 states the question exactly as in the README
Part 2: every ns figure has the machine, compiler flags, page mode and exact benchmark command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise using counter data from the previous step
Part 4 lists limits: static keys, uint64 only, one machine, equality-only hash lookups

projects.title: Crash-safe key-value store
projects.problem: Writes must survive a crash at any instant
projects.proveIt: Zero data loss across 1,000 random kill -9 runs
projects.question: Can a simple log-based key-value store lose zero acknowledged writes no matter when the process is killed?

steps.title: Frame the question, the guarantee and the test
steps.learn: Define the guarantee: once put() returns success, the write survives a crash. Prove it: 1,000 random SIGKILL runs with zero lost acknowledged writes. No dataset is needed: generate keys and values from a seeded RNG so every failing run can be replayed exactly.
verify: Write the durability contract in one sentence in your README before coding
Write down what counts as loss: an acknowledged key missing or holding an older or garbage value
Record the OS, kernel version and filesystem type (e.g. ext4) you will test on

steps.title: Decide when a write is acknowledged
steps.learn: write(2) returning does not mean data is on disk; only fsync(2) (or O_SYNC/O_DSYNC) does, and fsync blocks until the device reports completion, including flushing a disk cache. fdatasync skips metadata not needed to read the data back, but file size changes still count.

decision.choice: Acknowledge only after the log record is fsynced; batch concurrent puts into one fsync (group commit)
decision.why: The prove-it target is zero loss of acknowledged writes, so ack must wait for durability. Group commit recovers most of the throughput that per-write fsync throws away.

alternatives.name: fsync on a timer (e.g. every 100 ms)
alternatives.tradeoff: Much higher throughput, but a crash loses the last window of acked writes, so it fails this project's guarantee.

alternatives.name: Open the log with O_DSYNC
alternatives.tradeoff: Each write(2) becomes durable on return without separate calls; you can still batch by issuing one big write per batch, but cannot separate writing from syncing.

steps.delegate: In Rust or C, define the API: open(dir), put(key, value), get(key), delete(key), close(). put returns only after the record is durable. Implement a group-commit writer: callers enqueue records, one thread writes the batch with a single write and calls fdatasync, then wakes all waiters. Tests: 16 threads x 10,000 puts, assert number of fsyncs is far below number of puts.
verify: Count fdatasync calls with strace -c -f during a 16-thread run, record puts per fdatasync, and cross-check with an in-process counter
Measure puts/s with group commit vs one fsync per put

steps.title: Frame log records with length and checksum
steps.learn: Recovery must tell a complete record from a torn or garbage tail. LevelDB frames each log record with a CRC32C of type and data, a length, and a type, inside 32 KB blocks. A checksum over the whole record lets the reader stop at the first record that does not verify.

decision.choice: Record = crc32c(4) | length(4) | type(1) | key_len | key | value, all little-endian
decision.why: Self-describing records let recovery detect a partial final write by a short read or checksum mismatch without any extra index, and the type byte encodes put vs delete (tombstone).

alternatives.name: LevelDB-style 32 KB blocks with fragments
alternatives.tradeoff: Corruption is skipped by jumping to the next block boundary, but writing fragments adds complexity.

alternatives.name: No checksum, length only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but a torn tail with a plausible length is replayed as garbage data.

steps.delegate: Write record.rs (or record.c) with encode(record) returning bytes and decode(buf) returning Ok(record, consumed), Incomplete or Corrupt, using the crc32c crate (Rust) or a tested CRC32C table (C). The CRC covers every byte after it, length included; reject lengths above a max record size. Property tests: round-trip for random records; every strict prefix returns Incomplete; no single flipped bit ever returns Ok (a length flip may give Incomplete).
verify: Property test passes on 100,000 random records including empty values and 1 MiB values
Show a flipped bit in the value bytes is detected, not just in the header

steps.title: Create files durably, including the directory
steps.learn: fsync(2) on a file does not guarantee its directory entry reached disk; an explicit fsync on a descriptor for the directory is needed. So a new log file can vanish after power loss even if its data was fsynced. Apply this every time you create, rename or delete a file.

decision.choice: After creating or renaming any file: fsync the file, then open the directory O_RDONLY and fsync it
decision.why: This is the step most hand-written stores get wrong, and ALICE found crash vulnerabilities in widely used systems from subtle update-protocol assumptions. It costs one extra fsync per file event, which is rare.

alternatives.name: Preallocate a fixed set of log files once
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer directory changes at runtime, but you still need the directory fsync at setup and must handle reuse.

alternatives.name: Rely on the filesystem's journaling order
alternatives.tradeoff: May work on one filesystem, but persistence properties differ across Linux filesystems.

steps.delegate: Add a fs_util module: create_durable(dir, name), rename_durable(dir, from, to), fsync_dir(dir). Each returns errors, never ignores them. Tests: wrap syscalls behind a trait or function pointer so a test records the exact syscall order and asserts fsync(file) happens before rename and fsync(dir) after it.
verify: strace -f -e trace=%file,fsync,fdatasync shows a directory fsync after every create and rename (rename may appear as renameat2)
Test asserting syscall order passes

steps.title: Decide what to do when fsync fails
steps.learn: After a write-back error the kernel may have dropped the dirty pages and marked them clean, so retrying fsync can report success while data is lost. PostgreSQL's default is to PANIC on a failed data flush and recover from the WAL.

decision.choice: Any write or fsync error is fatal: fail the batch, abort, and after restart append only to a fresh log file
decision.why: An unacknowledged failure is allowed by the contract; a retried fsync that falsely succeeds would silently break it. Crashing reuses the recovery path you already test 1,000 times.

alternatives.name: Retry fsync
alternatives.tradeoff: Looks robust, but may report success for data the kernel already discarded.

alternatives.name: Mark store read-only
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps serving reads, but writers stall and you need a second recovery path.

steps.delegate: In the group-commit writer, on any write or fsync error: return an error to every waiter in the batch, log the errno, and abort the process. Test with a fault-injection wrapper that fails the Nth fsync with EIO and asserts no waiter in that batch receives success.
verify: Injected EIO test: 0 waiters in the failed batch get success
After restart, every key acked before the failure is present

steps.title: Recover by replaying the log and truncating torn tails
steps.learn: On open, read the log from the start, apply each valid record to the index, and stop at the first Incomplete or Corrupt record. A bad record at the tail is an expected torn write; truncate it so new appends never follow garbage. A bad record followed by valid ones means real corruption.

decision.choice: Replay logs in order; truncate an invalid final batch; refuse to open if corruption precedes a later complete batch
decision.why: Truncating the tail is safe because a torn record was never acknowledged. Refusing on mid-log corruption avoids silently dropping acknowledged writes, which is exactly the loss you are proving does not happen.

alternatives.name: Skip corrupt records and continue
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more data available, but can silently lose or reorder acknowledged writes.

alternatives.name: Checkpoint the index periodically
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster recovery on big logs, but adds a second file whose own crash safety must be proven.

steps.delegate: Implement recover(dir): list log files by sequence number, decode records, rebuild the index, ftruncate the last file to the end of the last valid record and fsync it. Tests: append N records, cut the file at every byte offset in the last record, reopen, assert exactly N-1 records and no error; corrupt a middle record and assert open fails.
verify: Cut-at-every-offset test passes for at least 3 record sizes
Recovery time for a 1 GB log is measured and recorded

steps.title: Choose the in-memory index
steps.learn: Bitcask keeps a keydir: a hash table from every key to the file, offset and size of its latest record, so a read is one lookup plus one disk read. The cost is that all keys must fit in RAM and recovery must rebuild the table.

decision.choice: Bitcask-style hash map: key to (file id, offset, length)
decision.why: The project is about durability, not range scans; a hash index keeps the read path trivial so the crash tests stress the log, not the index.

alternatives.name: Sorted map (BTreeMap)
alternatives.tradeoff: Enables range scans and ordered compaction output, at the cost of O(log n) lookups.

alternatives.name: Values in memory too
alternatives.tradeoff: No disk read on get, but RAM bounds the dataset and recovery rereads everything.

steps.delegate: Implement the keydir as a HashMap<Vec<u8>, Loc>. put updates it only after the record is durable; delete inserts a tombstone record and removes the key. get reads with pread at the stored offset and re-verifies the record CRC. Tests: model-based test comparing against a plain in-memory HashMap over 1,000,000 random ops.
verify: Model-based test: 0 mismatches over 1,000,000 random ops
get detects and errors on a value corrupted on disk after write

steps.title: Compact with write, fsync, atomic rename
steps.learn: The log grows with overwritten values and tombstones. Compaction writes only live records to a new file. rename(2) atomically replaces the target for other processes; on journaling filesystems like ext4 a crash leaves the old or new name, and it is durable only after you fsync the directory.

decision.choice: Compact closed files to tmp, fsync it, rename to final name, fsync dir, then delete inputs
decision.why: Every crash point leaves a recoverable state: before rename the tmp file is ignored and deleted on open; after rename both old and new may exist and replay order must make that harmless.

alternatives.name: Rewrite the log in place
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra disk space, but a crash mid-rewrite destroys data.

alternatives.name: Manifest file naming live files
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales to many files, but the manifest itself needs the same atomic update protocol.

steps.delegate: Implement compact(): pick closed log files, write live records to NNN.compact.tmp (keep tombstones while any older file may hold the key), fsync, rename_durable to a sequence number that replays after its inputs and before the active log, update the keydir, delete inputs and fsync the dir. On open, delete any *.tmp. Tests: inject an abort at each step (5 points) and assert recovery yields the same key/value set as before compaction.
verify: Abort-at-each-step test passes for all crash points
Disk usage after compacting a log with 90% overwrites is measured and recorded

steps.title: Build the kill -9 crash-test harness
steps.learn: SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so the process stops at an arbitrary point and user-space buffers are lost. But data already handed to write(2) stays in the kernel page cache, so kill -9 does not test lost unsynced data or missing fsyncs: a store with no fsync could pass.

decision.choice: Parent spawns writer, records acks over a pipe, SIGKILLs at a random time, reopens and checks every ack
decision.why: Acks are the contract, so the checker needs the exact set of acknowledged writes from outside the killed process. Seeding delay and workload makes any failing run reproducible.

alternatives.name: Power-loss simulation with LazyFS
alternatives.tradeoff: Drops unsynced data (clear-cache) and tears writes, which kill -9 cannot; needs FUSE and is slower per run.

alternatives.name: VM hard reset
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real power loss, but each run takes much longer and is hard to automate 1,000 times.

steps.delegate: Write crashtest (Rust or Python): for run in 1..1000 with seed s: start writer (puts with values derived from key+seq, prints key,seq to a pipe after each ack), sleep a seeded random time (also sometimes during compaction), kill -9, reopen, verify every acked key has its latest acked seq or a later unacked one and no value fails its derivation. Write failing seeds to a file.
verify: 1,000 runs, 0 lost acked writes, with seed list saved
Prove the checker works: disable fsync and use LazyFS clear-cache, or break framing, and see it fail
Confirm some kills landed mid-compaction (log counts)

steps.title: Measure durability cost and recovery time
steps.learn: Measure put throughput and p50/p99 latency for: no fsync (unsafe baseline), fsync per put, group commit at 1, 4, 16 threads; plus recovery time vs log size. Pitfalls: page cache hiding reads, drive write caches, measuring only averages, and a closed-loop client that hides queueing.
steps.delegate: Write bench (Rust or C) with an open-loop generator at a fixed request rate, recording per-op latency into an HDR histogram, for each durability mode and thread count. Output CSV with mode, threads, ops/s, p50, p99, p99.9. Add a recovery benchmark that times open() for logs of 100 MB, 1 GB and 4 GB after dropping caches.
verify: Table of ops/s and p99 for each mode, with device model and filesystem recorded
Record the exact commands and whether the drive has a volatile write cache
Recovery time vs log size plotted or tabulated

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) numbers for every claim (runs, loss count, throughput, p99) with machine and command; (3) why surprising results happened; (4) assumptions and limits: kill -9 is not power loss, drives with volatile caches can lie, one filesystem only.
verify: Part 1 states the one question
Part 2: every number cites the machine, filesystem and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise with evidence (strace, profile, test)
Part 4 says plainly what kill -9 runs do not prove about power loss

projects.title: LSM-tree with pluggable compaction
projects.problem: Leveled vs tiered compaction trade write, read and space amplification
projects.proveIt: All three amplification numbers per strategy
projects.question: How do leveled, tiered and hybrid compaction trade write, read and space amplification on the same workload in one LSM-tree?

steps.title: Frame the question, the three metrics and the workload
steps.learn: Write-amp: bytes written to storage per byte of user data written. Read-amp: work per logical read; here SST blocks read per point get, counted with no block cache. Space-amp: on-disk size divided by live logical data size. Workloads: YCSB core workload traces, generated once.
verify: README defines all three formulas (numerator, denominator, when sampled) before any code
Generate YCSB traces with the basic binding (bin/ycsb.sh load basic, then run basic) for workloads A and B, and save them
Record trace hashes, recordcount and operationcount; these files are frozen from now on

links.label: Callaghan: read, write and space amplification

steps.title: Build the write path: WAL plus memtable
steps.learn: Every put is appended to a write-ahead log, then applied to a sorted in-memory memtable. When the memtable reaches its size limit it becomes immutable and is flushed to a new sorted file, and its log can be deleted. WAL bytes count toward write-amp, so record them separately.

decision.choice: BTreeMap memtable behind a trait, WAL with CRC-framed records and fsync per batch of writes
decision.why: A single-threaded BTreeMap is correct and simple, and the experiment is about compaction, not memtable concurrency. Batching fsync keeps the run fast while every acknowledged batch is still durable.

alternatives.name: Concurrent skiplist (crossbeam-skiplist)
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches the RocksDB default memtable and allows concurrent writers, but adds complexity the amplification question does not need.

alternatives.name: No fsync on WAL
alternatives.tradeoff: Much faster runs, but durability is gone and crash tests later become meaningless.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write wal.rs (append(key, value or tombstone) with length plus crc32 framing via crc32fast, sync() calling File::sync_data, replay(path) stopping at the first bad CRC) and memtable.rs (trait Memtable with put, delete, get, iter, approx_bytes; BTreeMap impl). Tests: replay after truncating the file mid-record returns all complete records; tombstones shadow earlier puts.
verify: Truncation test passes: a torn last record is dropped, earlier ones survive
Count WAL bytes written separately from SST bytes in a counter you will use for write-amp

steps.title: Design the SST file format
steps.learn: An SST is an immutable sorted run on disk: data blocks of sorted entries, an index of each block's last key, a filter, and a footer pointing to them. A point lookup reads the index, picks one block and reads it, so block reads per get is a natural read-amp unit.

decision.choice: Fixed-target 4 KiB data blocks, a block index, a per-file filter, a footer with offsets and a checksum per block
decision.why: 4 KiB blocks match the default block size of RocksDB's block-based table and a common page size, so one block read is a clear unit for read-amp.

alternatives.name: One key per index entry (no blocks)
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact seeks, but the index grows with every key and must stay in memory.

alternatives.name: Larger blocks, for example 64 KiB
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller index and better compression, but each point read pulls more bytes, raising read-amp in bytes.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write sst.rs: SstWriter::add(key, value_or_tombstone) in sorted order, finish() writing data blocks, index block, filter block and footer; SstReader::open, get(key) returning value plus blocks_read, and iter_from(key). Count every byte written and read through one IoStats struct. Tests: round-trip 100k random entries, reject unsorted input, detect a flipped byte via checksum.
verify: Round-trip test passes and a corrupted block returns a checksum error, not wrong data
A get on an existing key reports exactly one data block read (index and filter held in memory)

steps.title: Add per-file Bloom filters
steps.learn: Without filters a get for a missing or old key checks every sorted run. A Bloom filter per SST lets the read skip files that cannot contain the key. RocksDB's docs give about 10 bits per key for roughly a 1% false positive rate, with diminishing returns beyond.

decision.choice: One Bloom filter per SST at 10 bits per key, kept in memory, same setting for every strategy
decision.why: Tiered layouts have more sorted runs, so filters change their read-amp the most. Holding the setting fixed makes the comparison about compaction, not filter tuning.

alternatives.name: No filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows the raw read-amp gap between strategies, but no real LSM runs this way; report it as an ablation if you like.

alternatives.name: Ribbon or other space-efficient filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Less memory for the same false positive rate, but more CPU to build and more code than this question needs.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write bloom.rs: build(keys, bits_per_key) choosing k hash probes from bits per key, may_contain(key), and serialize/deserialize into the SST filter block. Use a 64-bit hash (for example xxhash-rust) with double hashing. Tests: zero false negatives on 1M inserted keys; measured false positive rate on 1M absent keys printed for 10 bits per key.
verify: Zero false negatives in the test
Your measured false positive rate at 10 bits per key is close to 1%; record the exact value

steps.title: Build the read path across sorted runs
steps.learn: A get checks the memtable, then sorted runs from newest to oldest, stopping at the first hit; a tombstone is a hit that means deleted. A range scan merges all runs with a heap, newest version winning. Read-amp grows with the number of runs a get must probe.

decision.choice: Newest-first point lookup with filter checks, k-way heap merge for scans, read-amp counted per call
decision.why: This is the read path every strategy shares, so differences in read-amp come only from how many runs and levels each strategy leaves behind.

alternatives.name: Scan all runs and pick the newest version
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler logic, but reads every run on every get, inflating read-amp for all strategies equally.

alternatives.name: Per-level fence-pointer search only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine for leveled levels with one run each, but does not handle tiered levels holding several overlapping runs.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write db.rs: get(key) returning Option<Value> and ReadStats { runs_checked, filter_skips, blocks_read }; scan(start, end) via a BinaryHeap merge that keeps the newest sequence number per key and drops tombstones. Tests against a BTreeMap oracle with 200k random puts, deletes and overwrites, with flushes forced at random points.
verify: Oracle test passes for gets and scans across forced flushes
Print ReadStats for a get on a deleted key and confirm it stops at the tombstone

steps.title: Define the pluggable compaction interface
steps.learn: A compaction strategy decides when to merge and which sorted runs go in; the merge itself (read runs, drop shadowed versions and droppable tombstones, write new SSTs) is shared. Separating picking from executing is what makes strategies swappable and comparable.

decision.choice: A trait whose pick(&LsmShape) returns an optional CompactionTask (inputs, output level); one shared executor
decision.why: Strategies become pure functions of the tree shape, easy to unit test without disk, and every strategy is charged by the same executor, so byte counts are comparable.

alternatives.name: Each strategy does its own I/O
alternatives.tradeoff: More freedom (for example partial file splits), but byte accounting can diverge between strategies.

alternatives.name: Hard-coded leveled with tuning knobs
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but cannot express tiered layouts with several runs per level.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write compaction.rs: struct LsmShape (levels, each a list of runs with sizes and key ranges), trait CompactionStrategy { fn pick(&self, shape: &LsmShape) returning Option<CompactionTask> }, and execute(task) doing the merge via the read-path heap. Drop tombstones only when the output is the last level. Tests: execute keeps newest versions; picking on a hand-built shape is deterministic.
verify: A test shows a tombstone is kept when compacting into a non-last level and dropped at the last level
Executor counts read and written bytes into the same IoStats as flush and WAL

links.label: Luo and Carey: LSM-based Storage Techniques: A Survey

steps.title: Implement leveled compaction
steps.learn: Leveled keeps one sorted run per level (except L0), each level a fixed multiple larger than the last. When a level exceeds its target, a file is merged with the overlapping files of the next level, so data is rewritten many times: low read and space amp, higher write amp.

decision.choice: Size ratio 10, L0 trigger of 4 files, pick the level with the highest size/target score
decision.why: These match LevelDB's 10x levels and four-file L0 trigger and RocksDB's score-based picking, so your numbers can be compared to known designs.

alternatives.name: Larger size ratio
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer levels so fewer runs per read, but each merge into a level rewrites more overlapping data.

alternatives.name: Dynamic level targets
alternatives.tradeoff: RocksDB's level_compaction_dynamic_level_bytes sizes levels from the last level, giving a space-amp bound, at the cost of more logic.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement LeveledStrategy for CompactionStrategy: targets base * ratio^n, L0 trigger by file count, score = size / target, pick one file from the top-scoring level plus all overlapping files in the next level (all L0 files for L0). Unit tests on hand-built shapes: the right level and file set are chosen.
verify: After loading YCSB records, every level beyond L0 holds a single non-overlapping run
Level sizes are within one file of their targets after compaction quiesces

steps.title: Implement tiered compaction
steps.learn: Tiered waits until a level holds several sorted runs of similar size, then merges them into one run in the next level, without rewriting that level's existing runs. Each write is rewritten less often, but reads probe more runs and obsolete versions linger longer.

decision.choice: Merge when a level has T = 10 runs, with a cap on runs at the last level
decision.why: Using the same factor as leveled keeps the comparison fair; capping last-level runs avoids holding up to T full copies of the data, which Callaghan flags as excessive space-amp.

alternatives.name: Size-ratio merging without levels
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to RocksDB universal compaction, but harder to reason about with the level model.

alternatives.name: No cap at the last level
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest write-amp, but space-amp can grow toward several copies of the data.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement TieredStrategy for CompactionStrategy: each level holds up to T runs; when a level reaches T, merge all its runs into one new run appended to the next level; at the last level merge when K runs exist (K configurable, default 2). Unit tests on hand-built shapes, plus an oracle test under random writes.
verify: Oracle test from the read-path step passes with this strategy
Log runs per level over time and confirm no level exceeds T runs after compaction quiesces

steps.title: Implement a tiered plus leveled hybrid
steps.learn: A hybrid uses tiered merging for small levels, where most writes land, and leveled for the larger levels, where most data lives. Callaghan describes it as having less write-amp than leveled and less space-amp than tiered. The switch level is the knob.

decision.choice: Tiered for levels above a switch level, leveled from the switch level down; switch level configurable
decision.why: It is the natural third point between the two extremes and reuses both pickers, so the code is small and the comparison is direct.

alternatives.name: Leveled-N (several runs per level, leveled into the next)
alternatives.tradeoff: Another middle point (Callaghan links it to Fluid LSM from the Dostoevsky paper), but definitions vary and it is harder to implement faithfully.

alternatives.name: Only two strategies
alternatives.tradeoff: Less work, but leaves out the design most production systems effectively use.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement HybridStrategy holding a TieredStrategy and a LeveledStrategy and a switch_level: delegate pick() for levels above switch_level to tiered and the rest to leveled, merging tiered output into a leveled level as a leveled compaction. Unit tests for both sides of the switch and the oracle test.
verify: Oracle test passes with the hybrid
Levels below the switch hold one run each; levels above may hold several

steps.title: Make compaction crash safe with a manifest
steps.learn: A compaction writes new files then deletes old ones; a crash in between must not lose or duplicate data. A manifest log records each version edit (files added and removed), so recovery rebuilds the tree from the manifest plus WAL replay. fsync(2) notes the directory needs its own fsync for new entries.

decision.choice: Append-only manifest of version edits, fsync output files, then the manifest record, delete old files last
decision.why: This mirrors LevelDB's MANIFEST design; the manifest record is the commit point, so any crash leaves either the old or the new set of files live.

alternatives.name: Rewrite a full snapshot file and rename
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler recovery logic, but rewrites the whole file list on every compaction.

alternatives.name: Infer state by listing the directory
alternatives.tradeoff: No manifest code, but cannot tell finished outputs from half-written ones after a crash.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write manifest.rs: append VersionEdit { added, removed, next_file_no } with CRC framing, recover() rebuilding LsmShape, and fsync the directory after creating files. Add a crash test that kills the process at random points during compaction (via a fault-injection flag) and checks recovery against the oracle.
verify: Run the crash test at least 100 times: recovered contents always match the oracle
After recovery, no orphan SST files are counted in space-amp

steps.title: Measure it: all three amplifications per strategy
steps.learn: Run the same frozen trace through each strategy. Pitfalls: measuring before compaction settles, counting page-cache writes as device writes, and ignoring SSD internal write-amp, which your counters cannot see. RocksDB with leveled vs universal compaction is an external baseline.
verify: Per strategy and workload, report write-amp (WAL, flush, compaction shown separately), read-amp (blocks per get) and space-amp after quiescing
Cross-check your byte counter with write_bytes in /proc/self/io; explain any gap
Baseline: db_bench --compaction_style=0 and =1 with --statistics; record COMPACT_WRITE_BYTES and FLUSH_WRITE_BYTES
Record machine, filesystem, disk model, commit hash and the exact command for every run

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) a number for every claim with machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened, (4) assumptions and what this does not prove, such as single-threaded compaction and no SSD-level write-amp.
verify: Part 1 states the question exactly as in the README
Part 2 has a table: strategy by workload with all three amplification numbers, each with its command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with per-level byte counts
Part 4 lists assumptions: YCSB traces only, one machine, no block cache, logical not device bytes

links.label: Luo and Carey: LSM-based Storage Techniques: A Survey

projects.title: B+tree with a buffer pool
projects.problem: Which pages to keep in RAM (clock, LRU-K, 2Q)
projects.proveIt: Hit rate and throughput per eviction policy
projects.question: For a disk-backed B+tree, which eviction policy (CLOCK, LRU-K, 2Q) keeps the right pages in RAM, measured by hit rate and throughput?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the workload
steps.learn: A buffer pool is a cache of fixed-size pages between RAM and disk. With a B+tree on top, the root and inner pages are hot and leaves are mostly cold. You will compare policies by hit rate (hits / page requests) and ops/s at several pool sizes, on one recorded, skewed trace.

decision.choice: Synthetic YCSB-style workloads (point reads, inserts, short scans) over a generated key set, replayed as a trace
decision.why: No public dataset is needed to study page replacement; what matters is the access pattern. YCSB's documented workload mixes give named, reproducible patterns, and a recorded trace lets every policy see the identical request stream.

alternatives.name: Real DB page-access traces
alternatives.tradeoff: More realistic, but hard to find with a clear license and you cannot vary skew or scan mix to explain why a policy wins.

alternatives.name: Run YCSB against an existing database
alternatives.tradeoff: Tests a whole engine, not your policies; buffer pool effects get mixed with logging, locking and the OS cache.

verify: Write the question, the two metrics and the pool sizes (as a percent of index pages) you will test in one paragraph
Name the 3 or 4 workload mixes you will run and what each is meant to stress (skew, scans, inserts)
Pick the machine and storage device now and record CPU, RAM, disk model and OS version

steps.title: Build fixed-size pages and a disk manager
steps.learn: Everything above the disk manager speaks page ids; it maps page_id to a file offset (page_id * page size) and reads or writes whole pages. CMU's BusTub uses 4 KB pages. The OS page cache will silently absorb your misses unless you bypass it or count misses yourself.

decision.choice: 4 KiB pages in one file, pread/pwrite at page_id * 4096, optional OS cache bypass (O_DIRECT or F_NOCACHE)
decision.why: Fixed 4 KiB pages keep frame math trivial and match the reference course. Positional reads need no shared file cursor, so threads can share one fd. Bypassing the OS cache makes a buffer pool miss cost a real device read, so throughput differences between policies show up.

alternatives.name: mmap the file and let the OS manage it
alternatives.tradeoff: Least code, but the CMU notes list the costs: no control over eviction or flush order, stalls on page faults, SIGBUS on I/O errors. It also removes the thing you want to study.

alternatives.name: Larger pages (8 or 16 KiB)
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher fanout and fewer levels, but fewer frames for the same RAM and more bytes read per miss. Worth a later ablation.

alternatives.name: Buffered I/O only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler and no alignment rules, but misses become OS cache hits and throughput gaps between policies shrink or vanish.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a DiskManager with read_page(page_id, &mut [u8; 4096]), write_page(page_id, &[u8; 4096]), allocate_page() and sync(). Use pread/pwrite (std::os::unix::fs::FileExt). Add a bypass flag: open with O_DIRECT on Linux (4096-aligned buffers), or call fcntl(fd, F_NOCACHE, 1) on macOS. Count reads and writes. Tests: round-trip 10k random pages, reopen file and reread, allocate past end of file, concurrent reads from 8 threads.
verify: Write 1,000 pages with known patterns, restart the process, and confirm every page reads back byte-identical
With cache bypass on, confirm a cold random page read takes device-level time (time 10k reads) and compare to bypass off
Confirm the read and write counters match the number of calls in a scripted test

steps.title: Build the buffer pool: frames, page table, pins, dirty bits
steps.learn: Frames are a fixed array of page-sized buffers. The page table (in-memory hash map) maps page_id to frame. Each frame has a pin count (pinned frames can never be evicted) and a dirty flag (must be written back before reuse). If every frame is pinned, a fetch must fail, not block forever.

decision.choice: A Replacer trait (record_access, set_evictable, evict, remove) behind the pool, plus RAII page guards that unpin on drop
decision.why: This is the interface CMU's BusTub uses, so you can swap CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q without touching the pool, and every policy sees the same calls. Guards make forgotten unpins (the most common bug, which slowly starves the pool) impossible in normal code paths.

alternatives.name: Hard-code one policy into the pool
alternatives.tradeoff: Less indirection, but each new policy means editing pool logic, and comparisons get confounded by incidental code differences.

alternatives.name: Manual pin/unpin calls
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to a C design and explicit, but leaks are easy; you would need a pin-leak check in every test.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement BufferPool<R: Replacer> over the DiskManager: new(num_frames), fetch_read(page_id), fetch_write(page_id), new_page(), flush_page, flush_all. Use a HashMap page table, a free list, per-frame pin count and dirty flag, and a single pool Mutex for now. Return guards that unpin on Drop and mark dirty on write. Count hits and misses. Tests: pinned pages never evicted, dirty page written before frame reuse, error when all frames pinned, hit/miss counts on a scripted sequence.
verify: Run a test that pins every frame and confirm the next fetch returns an error instead of evicting or hanging
Modify a page, force its eviction, refetch it, and confirm the change survived (dirty write-back works)
Hand-trace a 10-request sequence on a 3-frame pool and confirm the hit and miss counters match your trace

steps.title: Implement LRU and CLOCK as baselines
steps.learn: LRU evicts the least recently used page. CLOCK approximates it with one reference bit per frame and a sweeping hand that clears set bits and evicts the first clear one. Both suffer sequential flooding: one large scan pushes out the hot pages. That weakness is what LRU-K and 2Q target.

decision.choice: Exact LRU (hash map plus list) and CLOCK (reference bit plus persistent hand), both skipping pinned frames
decision.why: LRU is the reference point every paper compares against, and CLOCK is the cheap approximation many systems use. Having both shows whether CLOCK's approximation costs hit rate on your workloads before you add smarter policies.

alternatives.name: Only CLOCK as the baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but you cannot separate the cost of approximating LRU from the cost of LRU's own blind spots.

alternatives.name: Random eviction as an extra floor
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to add and a useful sanity floor; on its own it says little about real policies.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement LruReplacer and ClockReplacer for the Replacer trait. CLOCK: Vec of (ref_bit, evictable), hand index kept between evictions, set ref bit on access, skip non-evictable frames, return None if nothing evictable. Tests: textbook CLOCK example sequence, all-pinned returns None, a scan of N+1 distinct pages over N frames evicts the hot page under both policies (flooding).
verify: Reproduce a small CLOCK example by hand and confirm the evicted frames match the code
Show sequential flooding: hot page plus one scan larger than the pool, and confirm the hot page is evicted under LRU and CLOCK
Measure ns per evict call for each policy at 10k frames with a microbenchmark

steps.title: Implement LRU-K with backward k-distance
steps.learn: LRU-K (O'Neil, O'Neil and Weikum) evicts the frame whose K-th most recent access is oldest, its backward K-distance. Frames with fewer than K accesses get infinite distance; ties go to the earliest access. A page touched once by a scan therefore leaves before a page touched repeatedly.

decision.choice: K = 2, history kept per frame, eviction by scanning or a priority queue keyed by the K-th timestamp
decision.why: The 2Q paper reports that O'Neil et al. found LRU-2 got most of the benefit. K = 2 already separates once-touched scan pages from re-referenced ones, and it is what CMU's project uses as a target.

alternatives.name: K = 3 or more
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs more history before a page earns protection, so it reacts more slowly to a shifting hot set; worth one ablation run.

alternatives.name: K = 1 (plain LRU)
alternatives.tradeoff: No history overhead, but no scan resistance; this is your baseline already.

alternatives.name: Approximate LRU-2 with young and old lists
alternatives.tradeoff: The CMU notes describe this cheap two-list approximation; constant-time, but it is closer to 2Q than to true LRU-K.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement LruKReplacer(k, num_frames): per frame a VecDeque of the last k logical timestamps, an evictable flag; evict picks max backward k-distance, infinite for fewer than k accesses, ties broken by earliest recorded access; remove clears history. Start with O(n) scan, then add a BTreeSet index. Tests: the CMU-style scenario with inf ties, set_evictable changes size, scan pages evicted before twice-touched pages.
verify: On a sequence where a hot page is read twice and then a scan runs, confirm LRU-2 keeps the hot page while LRU evicts it
Confirm ties among infinite-distance frames evict the one with the earliest access
Compare ns per access for the O(n) and indexed versions at 1k and 100k frames

steps.title: Implement 2Q with A1in, A1out and Am
steps.learn: 2Q (Johnson and Shasha) admits new pages to a FIFO A1in. Pages pushed out of A1in leave only their id in a ghost queue A1out. A page re-referenced while its id is in A1out enters Am, an LRU queue. The paper reports LRU-2-like hit rates with constant work per access.

decision.choice: Full 2Q with the paper's suggested sizes: Kin about 25% of frames, Kout holding ids for about 50% of frames
decision.why: These are the values the paper says work well, so you test 2Q as published before tuning. Constant-time updates also make the throughput comparison against LRU-K fair: any hit-rate tie becomes a CPU-cost question.

alternatives.name: Simplified 2Q (from the same paper)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer moving parts, but the paper notes it needs tuning and adapts less well; use it as an ablation.

alternatives.name: Tune Kin per workload
alternatives.tradeoff: The paper also ran Kin at 20% and 30%; tuning can win a few points but risks fitting your own trace.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement TwoQReplacer(num_frames, kin_frac=0.25, kout_frac=0.5): A1in FIFO of frames, A1out bounded FIFO of page ids (ghosts, no data), Am LRU of frames. On a miss whose page id is in A1out, admit to Am; else to A1in. Evict from A1in if over Kin, else from the Am tail; skip pinned frames. Tests: correlated re-reference stays in A1in, ghost hit promotes to Am, scan pages never reach Am.
verify: Confirm a page read twice within A1in is not promoted, and one re-read after leaving A1in (ghost hit) goes to Am
With A1in already above Kin, confirm a long one-pass scan evicts only A1in pages and every Am page stays resident
Confirm per-access cost stays flat as frame count grows 1k to 100k

steps.title: Lay out B+tree nodes in pages and implement search
steps.learn: Each node is one page. Inner pages hold m sorted keys and m+1 child page ids (first key slot unused); leaves hold sorted keys, values and a next-leaf page id. Every node except the root stays at least half full. Search pins one page per level, binary-searches it, unpins, and descends.

decision.choice: Fixed-size u64 keys and u64 values (record ids), header with type, size and max_size, binary search inside a node
decision.why: Fixed-size entries make node capacity a constant you can compute from 4 KiB, so fanout and tree height are predictable, which you need to reason about which pages a policy should keep.

alternatives.name: Slotted pages with variable-length keys
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for string keys; adds slot directories and prefix compression, and makes fanout depend on data.

alternatives.name: Store full tuples in leaves
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves a second lookup, but fewer entries per leaf, more leaves, and a different hot-set shape.

steps.delegate: In Rust, define InternalPage and LeafPage views over a [u8; 4096] (zero-copy, little-endian, no padding surprises): header {page_type, size, max_size}, leaf next_page_id. Implement BPlusTree::get(key) that fetches pages only through the BufferPool and holds at most one pin per level while descending. Tests: max_size computed from page size, binary search edge cases, get on an empty tree and a hand-built 2-level tree.
verify: Compute leaf and inner capacity by hand from 4096 bytes and confirm max_size in code matches
Confirm a point lookup on a 3-level tree touches exactly 3 pages (check the pool's request counter)
Confirm no pins remain after 10k lookups (pool pin total returns to zero)

steps.title: Insert with splits and range scans over leaf links
steps.learn: When a leaf overflows, split it in two, copy the middle key up to the parent, and link the new leaf into the sibling chain. When an inner node overflows, split it and push the middle key up; a root split grows the tree by one level. Range scans find the first leaf, then follow next-leaf links.

decision.choice: Insert with splits; deletes as tombstones in the leaf with no merging
decision.why: The study is about caching, and the workloads are reads, inserts and scans. Merge and redistribute logic is the hardest part of a B+tree and does not change which pages are hot. CMU's own leaderboard notes suggest tombstones for deletes.

alternatives.name: Full delete with merge and redistribution
alternatives.tradeoff: A complete structure that shrinks, but much more code and test surface for little effect on this experiment.

alternatives.name: Bulk load sorted keys bottom-up
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and makes full leaves for the initial load; you still need splits for later inserts. Good as an extra for setup.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement BPlusTree::insert(key, value) with leaf split (copy up), inner split (push up), and new root on root split; delete as a tombstone flag; scan(start, end) returning an iterator that holds one leaf pin at a time and follows next_page_id. Tests: 1M random inserts then compare every key with a BTreeMap, scans match BTreeMap ranges, tree invariants (sorted, half full, equal leaf depth) checked after every 10k inserts.
verify: Run 1M random inserts and confirm every get and every range scan matches a BTreeMap oracle
Run the invariant checker: all leaves at the same depth, every non-root node at least half full
Confirm a 1,000-key range scan reads only the expected number of leaf pages

steps.title: Add only the concurrency the experiment needs
steps.learn: Policy cost shows up under threads: LRU-K updates history on every access, 2Q and CLOCK do constant work. Latch crabbing lets B+tree operations release a parent latch once the child is safe; leaf scans need no-wait sibling latching to avoid deadlock. You may not need it to answer the question.

decision.choice: One pool latch plus a tree reader-writer lock; hit rate single-threaded, throughput at 1, 2, 4, 8 threads
decision.why: Hit rate does not depend on threads if the trace is fixed, so single-threaded replay keeps it exact. A coarse lock is enough to see whether a policy's bookkeeping becomes the bottleneck as threads grow, without weeks of crabbing bugs.

alternatives.name: Latch crabbing (optimistic version)
alternatives.tradeoff: Real parallelism on the tree and closer to production, but deadlock and pin-leak risk; needs ThreadSanitizer and long stress tests.

alternatives.name: Shard the pool by hashing page id
alternatives.tradeoff: Cuts pool latch contention, but each shard runs its own policy on a slice of frames, which changes hit rates.

steps.delegate: In Rust, wrap the pool state in a Mutex and the tree in a RwLock (reads shared, inserts exclusive). Add a multithreaded driver that splits a trace across N threads. Tests: 8-thread mixed workload for 60 s with an oracle check at the end, pin total returns to zero, run under loom for the replacer or with ThreadSanitizer via cargo +nightly.
verify: Run the 8-thread stress test for 10 minutes with no panic, deadlock or oracle mismatch
Confirm single-threaded replay of the same trace gives the identical hit count twice in a row
Profile the 8-thread run and note what share of time is spent holding the pool latch

steps.title: Build a skewed workload generator and trace replayer
steps.learn: Skew decides everything: with Zipfian keys a small hot set gets most requests. YCSB's Zipfian generator follows Gray et al. (SIGMOD 1994) with constant 0.99, and a scrambled variant scatters hot keys across the key space so they do not sit in the same leaves. Mixing in scans tests flooding.

decision.choice: Zipfian (scrambled and clustered) plus uniform and scan-heavy mixes, written to a trace file of key-level operations
decision.why: Scrambled vs clustered hot keys change how many leaf pages are hot, which is the exact thing eviction must find. Replaying one trace file per mix removes random-number noise from policy comparisons.

alternatives.name: Uniform keys only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to reason about, but leaf hits then track pool size over leaf count for every policy, so policies differ only in keeping inner pages; you learn little.

alternatives.name: Port YCSB's generators exactly
alternatives.tradeoff: Best comparability with published YCSB numbers, at the cost of porting Java code instead of writing a small generator.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a workload generator: Zipfian per Gray et al. (theta configurable, default 0.99), a scrambled variant (hash the rank), uniform, and a mixer for read/insert/scan ratios with scan length. Output a binary trace (op, key, len). Add a replayer that drives the tree from a trace. Tests: empirical rank-frequency of 10M samples follows the target slope, same seed gives the same trace hash.
verify: Plot rank vs frequency on log-log axes for 10M draws and confirm it is a straight line near the chosen theta
Confirm the share of requests going to the top 1% of keys for each mix and write it down
Confirm the same seed produces a byte-identical trace file

steps.title: Measure hit rate and throughput per policy
steps.learn: Run the matrix: policy (LRU, CLOCK, LRU-2, 2Q) by pool size by workload. Hit rate comes from counters on a single-threaded replay and is exact. Throughput needs warm-up, cache bypass, repeated runs and a recorded command. An offline clairvoyant policy, computed from the trace, gives a ceiling.

decision.choice: Report hit rate after warm-up and median ops/s over 5 runs, with cache bypass on, plus p99 per-op latency
decision.why: Hit rate isolates the policy's choice; ops/s shows whether bookkeeping cost eats the gain. Medians over repeated runs and a fixed warm-up remove the first-run cold cache and noisy-neighbor effects that otherwise decide the ranking.

alternatives.name: Hit rate only
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and cheap, but hides that LRU-K's per-access work can lose on throughput when hit rates are close.

alternatives.name: Leave the OS page cache on
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to some real systems (PostgreSQL uses it), but OS cache hits mask pool misses; report it only as a separate configuration.

steps.delegate: Write a benchmark harness (Rust binary plus a Python plotting script) that runs every policy x pool size (1%, 5%, 10%, 25% of index pages) x workload, discards a warm-up prefix, records hits, misses, disk reads and writes, ops/s and p99 latency to CSV with git commit, machine and command line. Plot hit rate vs pool size per workload and ops/s vs threads.
verify: Confirm LRU and LRU-2 hit rate never falls as pool size grows (a drop is a bug); small dips for CLOCK or 2Q are possible, investigate large ones
Confirm run-to-run spread of ops/s is under 5% for the 5 repeats, or report the spread
Record the exact command, commit, CPU, RAM, disk model and OS in the CSV header
Run perf (or a sampling profiler) once per policy and note where time goes

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command; (3) why the surprising results happened, for example why 2Q matched LRU-2 or why CLOCK lost under scans; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: The write-up states the one question in its first paragraph
Every claim has a number with the machine, commit and command that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with evidence (a counter, a trace slice or a profile)
An assumptions section says what this does not prove (synthetic traces, one device, coarse locking, no deletes)

projects.title: MVCC with snapshot isolation
projects.problem: Concurrent transactions can produce anomalies like write skew
projects.proveIt: Anomaly reproduced, then prevented with serializable checks
projects.question: Can a from-scratch MVCC store show write skew under snapshot isolation, then prevent it with serializable checks, and what do those checks cost?
