steps.title: Frame the question, the anomaly tests and the metrics
steps.learn: Snapshot isolation (SI) reads from a start-time snapshot and blocks lost updates, but allows write skew (Berenson et al. call it A5B): two transactions read overlapping data and write disjoint rows. Success: the anomaly reproduces under SI, never commits under your serializable mode, at a measured abort cost.
verify: README states the question, the invariant (at least one doctor on call) and the metrics: anomalies committed, abort rate, throughput
Anomaly test scripts (doctors on call, Hermitage G2-item and G2) are written and committed before any engine code
Record CPU model, core count, OS and compiler version you will measure on

links.label: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels

steps.title: Choose how versions are stored and chained
steps.learn: Each write creates a new version tagged with its creator's commit timestamp; readers pick the newest version visible to their snapshot. Wu et al. compare append-only chains (oldest-to-newest or newest-to-oldest), time-travel tables and delta storage. Newest-first means most reads stop at the chain head.

decision.choice: In-memory ordered map from key to an append-only, newest-to-oldest version chain
decision.why: This project is about isolation, not storage. Newest-first keeps the common read short, and with one primary map there are no secondary indexes to repoint when the head changes, which is the main cost Wu et al. note for this ordering.

alternatives.name: Oldest-to-newest chain
alternatives.tradeoff: Index never needs updating on writes, but reads walk old versions to reach the latest, so performance depends on pruning old versions quickly.

alternatives.name: Delta storage (undo records)
alternatives.tradeoff: Main table holds the latest value and old values live in a separate delta area; saves space for wide rows, but old reads must rebuild versions by applying deltas.

alternatives.name: Single version plus locks (no MVCC)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest store, but readers block writers, and there is no snapshot to reproduce SI behavior with.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a Store with a BTreeMap<Key, Vec<Version>> (newest first) where Version {value: Option<Bytes>, begin_ts: u64, creator: TxnId}. A None value marks a delete. Expose read_at(key, snapshot_ts) and range_at(lo, hi, snapshot_ts). Unit tests: three versions at ts 10, 20, 30 and reads at 5, 15, 25, 35 return none, v10, v20, v30; a delete hides the key only for snapshots after it.
verify: Unit tests for visibility at each snapshot pass, including the delete case
Draw one key's chain after three updates and check it matches a debug dump of the store

links.label: Wu et al., empirical evaluation of in-memory MVCC

steps.title: Assign start and commit timestamps and define visibility
steps.learn: A transaction's snapshot is its start timestamp; it sees a version only if that version committed at or before the snapshot, plus its own uncommitted writes. Commit must be atomic from readers' point of view: no reader may see half of a transaction's writes.

decision.choice: One global counter: under a commit lock, commit_ts = clock + 1, stored to the clock only after installing versions
decision.why: A single node needs no clock synchronization, and a monotonic counter makes visibility a plain integer comparison, which keeps the anomaly tests deterministic.

alternatives.name: Postgres-style transaction ids plus snapshot lists
alternatives.tradeoff: Snapshot records which transaction ids were in progress, so commit order and id order can differ; more flexible, more bookkeeping to get right.

alternatives.name: Hybrid logical clocks
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed when timestamps come from several nodes; on one node it adds complexity with no benefit.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add a TxnManager with an AtomicU64 clock. begin() returns Txn {id, start_ts, write_set: HashMap<Key, Option<Bytes>>}. Reads check the txn's own write_set first, then read_at(start_ts). commit() takes a commit lock, assigns commit_ts, installs versions, then publishes the new clock value. Tests: a reader that began before a commit never sees any of its writes; a reader that began after sees all of them (atomic visibility).
verify: A test with a 2-key write and a concurrent reader never observes only one of the two keys
Read-your-own-writes test passes: an uncommitted write is visible to its own transaction only

links.label: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels

steps.title: Detect write-write conflicts so lost updates cannot happen
steps.learn: SI forbids two concurrent transactions from both committing writes to the same key. Berenson et al. describe first-committer-wins: at commit, abort if any key you wrote was committed by someone after your start. PostgreSQL instead makes a later writer wait for the first updater, then fail if it commits.

decision.choice: First-committer-wins validation at commit time against each written key's newest version
decision.why: It needs no lock manager or waiting, keeps every interleaving scriptable step by step in tests, and the check is a single timestamp comparison per written key.

alternatives.name: First-updater-wins with row write locks
alternatives.tradeoff: Conflicts are found at write time so doomed work stops early (the PostgreSQL behavior), but you need lock waits and deadlock handling.

alternatives.name: No write-write check
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows lost update (P4) on purpose for a demo, but the result is weaker than SI and the later tests stop meaning anything.

steps.delegate: In Rust, extend commit(): for each key in write_set, if the newest committed version has begin_ts > txn.start_ts, return Err(Conflict) and install nothing. Add a scripted test for lost update: two transactions read counter=0, both write counter+1, exactly one commits and the final value is 1. Add a test that disjoint-key writers both commit.
verify: Lost-update test: exactly one of two conflicting transactions commits, final counter is 1
Disjoint-key writers both commit, so the check is not over-aborting

links.label: A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels

steps.title: Reproduce write skew with a scripted interleaving
steps.learn: In the doctors example from Ports and Grittner, each transaction counts on-call doctors, sees two, and takes a different doctor off call. Under SI both commit because they write different rows, leaving zero on call. Hermitage shows PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ (its SI level) allows this G2-item case.

decision.choice: A deterministic step scheduler that runs the frozen scripts in an exact interleaving
decision.why: Write skew only appears in specific orders. Scripting the order makes the anomaly reproduce on every run, so a later pass means the check worked, not that the threads happened to serialize.

alternatives.name: Real threads with random sleeps
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to production timing, but the anomaly appears only sometimes, so a pass proves little.

alternatives.name: Run the scripts against PostgreSQL only
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows the behavior on a real engine, but tests nothing you built; use it as a cross-check instead.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a Scheduler that takes a list of (txn_name, Op) steps, where Op is Begin, Read(key), Scan(lo, hi), Write(key, val), Commit, and executes them in order against the store, recording each result. Encode the doctors scenario and the Hermitage G2-item script. Assert under Isolation::Snapshot that both commit and the invariant is broken; print the step trace on failure.
verify: Under SI, the doctors script ends with zero doctors on call on 100 of 100 runs
Optional cross-check: the same script on PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ also commits both transactions

steps.title: Add serializable checks by tracking rw-antidependencies
steps.learn: Fekete et al. showed every cycle in an SI history has two adjacent rw-antidependency edges (T1 reads what T2 later overwrites, T2 likewise to T3). SSI (Cahill et al.) records SIREAD marks on reads, flags these edges, and aborts when a transaction has both an incoming and an outgoing one.

decision.choice: SSI: SIREAD marks per key read, in/out conflict flags per transaction, abort on a dangerous structure
decision.why: It keeps SI's non-blocking reads and only adds bookkeeping, and it lets single rw-conflicts commit, which S2PL would block and classic OCC would abort. The cost is some false-positive aborts, which you will measure.

alternatives.name: Commit-time read-set validation (OCC)
alternatives.tradeoff: Abort if anything you read changed since your snapshot; simple and serializable, but aborts on any single rw-conflict, so more aborts than SSI.

alternatives.name: Strict two-phase locking
alternatives.tradeoff: Readers take shared locks that block writers; no false-positive aborts from dependency tracking, but reads block and deadlocks need detection.

alternatives.name: Precise cycle testing (PSSI)
alternatives.tradeoff: Builds the full dependency graph to remove false positives, but must also track wr and ww edges and uses more memory.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add Isolation::Serializable. On read, record a SIREAD mark (key, txn). On write, and on reading a key that has a newer committed version, set reader.out_conflict and writer.in_conflict. At commit, abort with Err(SerializationFailure) if the txn has both flags. Keep marks of committed txns until no overlapping txn is active. Tests: doctors and G2-item scripts commit exactly one transaction; a single rw-conflict with no second edge commits both.
verify: Doctors and G2-item scripts: exactly one transaction commits, invariant holds on 100 of 100 runs
A history with only one rw-antidependency commits both transactions (no needless abort)
Marks from a committed reader are still present while a concurrent writer is active

links.label: Fekete et al., Making SI Serializable

steps.title: Cover range scans so predicate write skew is caught
steps.learn: Hermitage's G2 test is write skew on a predicate read: each transaction scans for matching rows, then inserts a new row the other's scan would have matched. Per-key marks miss it because the inserted key did not exist when read. PostgreSQL keeps predicate locks on what a scan touched and may coarsen them.

decision.choice: Record a SIREAD mark on each scanned key range [lo, hi], and check inserts and updates against stored ranges
decision.why: The store is an ordered map, so a scan is a key range and an insert conflicts exactly when its key falls inside one. This catches phantoms without locking the whole table.

alternatives.name: One mark per table for any scan
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial and safe, but every write to that table conflicts with every scanner, so aborts rise sharply.

alternatives.name: Next-key marks only on existing keys
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer stored ranges, but you must handle the gaps at both ends correctly or inserts slip through.

steps.delegate: In Rust, store range marks in an interval structure keyed by (lo, hi, txn). On every write or insert, look up overlapping ranges of concurrent txns and set the rw flags. Tests: Hermitage G2 script (two scans plus two inserts) commits exactly one under Serializable and both under Snapshot; inserting outside every scanned range raises no conflict.
verify: Hermitage G2 script: both commit under Snapshot, exactly one under Serializable
Insert outside every scanned range causes no abort

steps.title: Handle aborts with retries and reclaim old versions
steps.learn: Serialization failures are expected, so the client must retry the whole transaction (PostgreSQL's docs say the same for SQLSTATE 40001). Old versions and SIREAD marks can be dropped once no active transaction's snapshot could need them; the low watermark is the oldest active start timestamp.

decision.choice: Client-side retry loop with a retry cap, plus a GC pass that prunes below the oldest active start_ts
decision.why: Retries turn aborts into a measurable cost instead of lost work, and watermark GC is simple to reason about in a single-node store with one active-transaction registry.

alternatives.name: Background vacuum thread scanning all chains
alternatives.tradeoff: Works with any storage layout, but scans keys that never changed; Wu et al. note it scales poorly with few GC threads.

alternatives.name: Cooperative cleaning during reads
alternatives.tradeoff: Readers prune what they walk past, but Wu et al. note it only fits oldest-to-newest chains and rarely read keys are never cleaned.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add run_with_retry(f, max_retries) that re-runs a closure on Conflict or SerializationFailure and counts attempts. Add gc(): compute min start_ts of active txns, drop versions shadowed by a newer version that is also below it, and drop SIREAD marks of committed txns that overlap no active txn. Tests: a long-running reader keeps its versions alive; after it ends, gc shrinks chains to one version.
verify: Long reader test: its snapshot still reads old values while gc runs concurrently
After all txns finish, gc leaves one version per live key and zero SIREAD marks

links.label: Wu et al., in-memory MVCC (GC section)

steps.title: Check random histories with an independent checker
steps.learn: Your own tests share your assumptions. Elle infers anomalies from client-observed histories alone; its README says it finds every non-predicate anomaly in Adya's definitions. A list-append workload lets it recover version order, so it can tell SI from serializable without trusting your engine.

decision.choice: Generate random list-append transactions, log histories as JSON, check them with elle-cli
decision.why: The grade comes from a separate tool that knows nothing about your SSI code, so a bug in your conflict logic cannot also hide itself in the checker.

alternatives.name: Your own dependency-graph cycle checker
alternatives.tradeoff: No JVM needed, but it shares your understanding of the rules, so it can miss the same mistakes.

alternatives.name: Elle rw-register workload
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler values, but Elle can infer less about version order from registers than from appends.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a workload generator: N client threads, M keys, transactions of 1 to 4 ops mixing read(key) and append(key, unique_int), run under each isolation level with run_with_retry. Write each attempt as invoke/ok/fail records in the elle-cli JSON history format. Script: run elle-cli with the list-append model, expecting serializable, for 20 seeds per level.
verify: elle-cli reports valid for every Serializable run across 20 seeds
Under Snapshot with high contention, elle-cli reports at least one G2-item for some seed (the checker can see the anomaly)
Confirm aborted transactions are logged as fail, not ok

steps.title: Measure the cost of serializability
steps.learn: The prove-it needs the anomaly gone; the write-up also needs its price. Compare SI, your SSI and a serial baseline (one global lock) on the same workload while varying key count (contention). Count committed transactions, not attempts, and report abort rate as aborts per committed transaction.

decision.choice: Fixed-duration runs per (isolation, threads, keys) with fixed seeds, 5 repeats, median and spread
decision.why: Abort rate depends on contention, so a sweep over key count shows where SSI's false positives appear, and repeats expose noise before you explain a difference.

alternatives.name: Fixed transaction count
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to compare totals, but slow retrying configs run longer and can hide throughput collapse.

alternatives.name: Open-loop load at a set arrival rate
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives honest latency percentiles without coordinated omission, but takes more harness work than this question needs.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a bench binary: flags --isolation {snapshot,serializable,serial} --threads --keys --secs --seed. Workload: the doctors transaction plus random list-append transactions. Output CSV: committed, aborted by reason, retries, throughput, p50 and p99 commit latency. Build with --release and print git commit, CPU and thread count in the header.
verify: Table of throughput and abort rate for all three modes at 3 or more key counts, 5 repeats each
Doctors invariant violations counted per mode: nonzero for Snapshot, zero for Serializable and Serial
The exact command line and machine details are saved with the CSV

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened, for example false-positive aborts on histories Elle says were serializable, (4) assumptions and limits: single node, in-memory, no durability, your workload only.
verify: Part 1 states the question and the doctors invariant
Part 2 has anomaly counts, abort rates and throughput, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result using your traces or Elle output
Part 4 lists assumptions and what this does not prove (no crashes, no distribution)

projects.title: Vectorized columnar query engine
projects.problem: Row-at-a-time execution wastes the CPU
projects.proveIt: TPC-H Q1 runtime vs DuckDB
projects.question: How close can a small vectorized columnar engine get to DuckDB on TPC-H Q1, and which design choices close the gap?

steps.title: Frame the question, generate TPC-H data and freeze the answer
steps.learn: Q1 scans lineitem, keeps rows with l_shipdate <= 1998-09-02 (about 98.6% at SF1), and computes sums, averages and a count over 4 (returnflag, linestatus) groups. Metric: Q1 wall time vs DuckDB on the same machine and threads, with results equal to DuckDB's expected answer.
verify: Generate SF1 and SF10 with CALL dbgen(sf = N), export lineitem to Parquet, save DuckDB's SF10 Q1 result, record DuckDB version
Save the SF1 Q1 answer from tpch_answers() to a file now, before writing engine code
README states the metric, scale factors (SF1 and SF10), thread counts and the machine

steps.title: Load lineitem into typed in-memory columns
steps.learn: Q1 touches 7 of lineitem's 16 columns. Storing each column as its own contiguous array means a scan reads only those bytes. DuckDB's Parquet export stores the decimals as INT64 scaled by 100 and dates as INT32 days, which map directly to plain integer arrays.

decision.choice: Read the Parquet file once with the Rust parquet/arrow crates into owned Vec<i64>, Vec<i32> and Vec<u8> columns
decision.why: Loading is not what we measure. Owning plain aligned arrays gives full control of layout for the kernels, and dictionary-encoding the two flag columns to u8 makes grouping cheap.

alternatives.name: Run kernels directly on Arrow arrays
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids a copy and Arrow's columnar format is designed for this, but ties your kernels to Arrow's buffer and null-bitmap APIs.

alternatives.name: Own binary column files with mmap
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast startup and no dependencies at query time, but you write and validate a file format first.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write load_lineitem(path) returning Lineitem {quantity, extendedprice, discount, tax: Vec<i64>, shipdate: Vec<i32>, returnflag, linestatus: Vec<u8>} using the parquet crate's Arrow reader, projecting only those 7 columns. Map flag strings to u8 codes with a stored dictionary. Tests: row count equals DuckDB's count(*), and the sums of each numeric column match DuckDB's sums exactly.
verify: Row count and per-column sums match DuckDB on SF1
Loader time is printed separately and never included in query timings

steps.title: Choose exact arithmetic for the aggregates
steps.learn: Kersten et al. list Q1's bottleneck as fixed-point arithmetic. With scale-2 inputs, extendedprice*(1-discount) has scale 4 and the charge expression has scale 6 (DuckDB returns DECIMAL(38,6)). Those scale-6 sums can exceed the 64-bit range at large scale factors.

decision.choice: Scaled i64 for per-row values, i128 accumulators for sums, averages computed at the end
decision.why: Exact integer math lets you compare against DuckDB's answer digit for digit, and i128 removes overflow risk at any scale factor you will run at a modest per-add cost.

alternatives.name: f64 everywhere
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and SIMD-friendly, but sums will not match the reference exactly, so correctness checks need tolerances.

alternatives.name: General decimal library type
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles any precision, but per-value object overhead defeats the point of tight vectorized loops.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write fixed-point helpers: disc_price(price, disc) = price * (100 - disc) at scale 4, charge(price, disc, tax) = disc_price * (100 + tax) at scale 6, both as i64, accumulated into i128. Unit tests: hand-computed rows, a property test that results equal a big-integer reference on random inputs in TPC-H value ranges.
verify: Property test passes on 1,000,000 random rows
Compute the worst-case scale-6 sum for SF1 and SF10 by hand and note whether i64 would overflow

links.label: Kersten et al., compiled vs vectorized

steps.title: Build a tuple-at-a-time baseline first
steps.learn: The project claims row-at-a-time execution wastes the CPU, so measure it. A Volcano iterator calls next() per tuple through virtual dispatch; X100's paper traced MySQL on Q1 and found most time in interpretation overhead rather than arithmetic. Your baseline gives the first point on the chart.

decision.choice: Volcano-style operators (Scan, Filter, Project, HashAggregate) behind a trait object, one row per next() call
decision.why: It is the textbook model most row stores follow, and using the same columns and fixed-point helpers isolates the effect of the execution model alone.

alternatives.name: Skip the baseline, compare only to DuckDB
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but you cannot show what vectorization itself bought you.

alternatives.name: Hand-written single loop as baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest scalar code, but that is a compiled-style plan, not row-at-a-time interpretation.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write trait RowOp with next(&mut self) returning Option<Row> with Scan, Filter(boxed predicate closure over &Row), Project(expressions as boxed closures) and HashAggregate(HashMap<(u8,u8), Acc>). Build Q1 from them. Test: output equals the frozen SF1 answer after formatting.
verify: Baseline output matches the frozen SF1 Q1 answer
Record baseline single-thread SF1 time (median of 5 runs)

steps.title: Pick the vectorized execution model and vector size
steps.learn: Vectorized engines pass small batches of column values between operators, so per-call overhead is paid per batch. X100 used 1024 by default and found 128 to 8K worked well for Q1 as long as vectors stayed in cache; DuckDB's default is 2048. Kersten et al. found compiled code beat vectorized on Q1.

decision.choice: Pull-based operators that return batches of 2048 values per column
decision.why: Matches DuckDB's default so the comparison is about your kernels, keeps Q1's working vectors cache-resident, and stays an interpreter so each primitive can be profiled on its own.

alternatives.name: Data-centric compiled loop (HyPer style)
alternatives.tradeoff: One fused loop keeps values in registers and won on Q1 in Kersten et al., but needs code generation and gives less per-operator profiling.

alternatives.name: Full column-at-a-time materialization (MonetDB/MIL)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple bulk primitives, but intermediate results the size of the table spill out of cache.

steps.delegate: In Rust, define struct Batch { cols: Vec<Column>, sel: Option<Vec<u32>>, len: usize } and trait VecOp with next(&mut self) returning Option<Batch>. Make vector size a const generic or runtime flag. Write VecScan over the loaded columns. Test: scanning with sizes 1, 7, 2048 and 1,000,000 yields every row exactly once.
verify: Scan test passes for all four batch sizes, including a final partial batch
Time VecScan alone at batch sizes 1, 64, 2048 and 65536 and record ns per row for each

links.label: Kersten et al., compiled vs vectorized

steps.title: Implement the filter with a selection vector
steps.learn: In X100, Select writes the positions of matching tuples into a selection vector, and later primitives compute only at those positions, without copying the other columns. For a filter that keeps almost every row, as Q1's does, how you build that vector and whether you branch matter.

decision.choice: Branchless selection-vector build (write index, advance by predicate result) and propagate it to later operators
decision.why: No column is copied, and the branchless form avoids mispredictions if selectivity changes; with 98% passing, you can also test skipping the vector entirely when all rows pass.

alternatives.name: Compact all needed columns after filtering
alternatives.tradeoff: Later loops become dense, but you copy every surviving value of every column.

alternatives.name: Compute all rows and mask at aggregation
alternatives.tradeoff: Dense SIMD-friendly loops for a 98% filter, but wasted work if the filter is selective.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write select_le_i32(col: &[i32], bound: i32, out: &mut Vec<u32>) branchless, and a branchy variant for comparison. VecFilter sets Batch.sel. Tests: on random data with selectivity 1%, 50%, 99%, both variants return identical index lists; count of selected rows over SF1 equals DuckDB's count with the same predicate.
verify: Selected row count over SF1 matches DuckDB's count(*) with the Q1 predicate
Microbenchmark both variants at 1%, 50%, 99% selectivity and record branch-misses with perf stat

steps.title: Write typed primitives for the Q1 expressions
steps.learn: A vectorized primitive is a tight loop over arrays of one type, such as multiplying two i64 vectors under a selection vector. Such loops are easy for the compiler to auto-vectorize, but Kersten et al. warn auto-vectorization is not fire-and-forget, so check the generated code.

decision.choice: Monomorphized Rust primitives per (operation, type), with a dense path when sel is None
decision.why: Generic code compiled per type has no per-value dispatch, and keeping a dense variant lets the compiler emit SIMD for the common all-rows-selected case.

alternatives.name: Hand-written SIMD intrinsics
alternatives.tradeoff: Guaranteed vector instructions, but tied to one instruction set and much more code to test.

alternatives.name: Expression tree evaluated per value
alternatives.tradeoff: Flexible, but per-value dispatch is the overhead vectorization exists to remove.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write primitives: sub_const_i64, mul_i64, mul_add helpers producing disc_price and charge vectors, each with sel and dense variants. Build in --release with target-cpu documented. Tests: every primitive equals the scalar fixed-point helpers on random batches with and without sel. Include a cargo bench comparing dense vs sel variants.
verify: Primitive tests match the scalar helpers bit for bit
Inspect the dense loop's assembly (cargo asm or objdump) and note whether SIMD instructions appear

steps.title: Aggregate the four groups
steps.learn: Q1 has only 4 groups, so the aggregate state fits in a few cache lines. X100's Q1 trace uses direct aggregation: it maps the two small flag codes to a group index and updates arrays of sums, instead of hashing. A general engine still needs hashing for high-cardinality keys.

decision.choice: Direct aggregation: group index = flag_code * linestatus_count + status_code, accumulators in small arrays
decision.why: With dictionary codes of known small domain it is exact and avoids hashing; the general hash table remains as the fallback when the domain is large.

alternatives.name: General hash aggregation
alternatives.tradeoff: Works for any key, which you need for other queries, but adds hashing and probing per row on Q1.

alternatives.name: Sort then aggregate
alternatives.tradeoff: No hash table, but sorting 6M rows costs far more than the aggregation itself.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write VecDirectAgg computing group ids into a u8 vector, then per-aggregate loops adding into [i128; G] arrays, plus counts. Also write VecHashAgg with a HashMap for comparison. Finalize sums and averages, sort by flags. Test: full vectorized Q1 equals the frozen SF1 answer, and VecHashAgg gives the same result.
verify: Vectorized Q1 output equals the frozen SF1 answer exactly for sums and counts
Record single-thread SF1 time for direct vs hash aggregation

steps.title: Parallelize with morsels and thread-local aggregates
steps.learn: Morsel-driven parallelism (Leis et al.) splits input into small chunks that worker threads grab dynamically, which balances load. For Q1, each thread aggregates into its own private state and the few partial results are merged at the end.

decision.choice: Atomic morsel counter over row ranges, per-thread accumulator arrays padded to cache lines, merge at end
decision.why: Q1 has no joins and tiny state, so per-thread state plus a final merge removes all sharing during the scan; padding avoids false sharing between neighbors.

alternatives.name: Static equal split per thread
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but a slow core or noisy neighbor delays the whole query.

alternatives.name: Rayon parallel iterators
alternatives.tradeoff: Work stealing for free, but less control over morsel size and state layout.

steps.delegate: In Rust, use std::thread::scope with an AtomicUsize morsel cursor (morsel size configurable, default 100,000 rows as a starting point). Each worker runs the vectorized pipeline over its morsel into a #[repr(align(64))] accumulator. Merge and finalize on the main thread. Tests: results equal the frozen answer for 1, 2, 4 and max threads, and for morsel sizes 1,000 and 1,000,000.
verify: Results identical across all thread counts and morsel sizes tested
Plot speedup vs threads for SF10 and note where it flattens

steps.title: Measure Q1 against DuckDB fairly
steps.learn: Compare like for like: both engines with data already in memory, same thread count (DuckDB: SET threads), warm runs, median of several repeats, result materialized but not printed. Use perf stat for cycles, instructions and misses per tuple, as Kersten et al. normalize counters, and flame graphs to find hot primitives.

decision.choice: One harness timing DuckDB (in-memory table from dbgen) and your engine at SF1 and SF10, threads 1 and all cores
decision.why: Same process conditions, data residency and thread counts make the ratio meaningful, and two scale factors show whether the gap is fixed overhead or per-row cost.

alternatives.name: DuckDB querying the Parquet file directly
alternatives.tradeoff: Includes Parquet decoding in DuckDB's time but not yours, which biases the result toward your engine.

alternatives.name: Single cold run each
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches a first query, but disk cache and allocation noise dominate a sub-second query.

steps.delegate: Write bench.py using the duckdb Python package: CALL dbgen(sf), SET threads, run PRAGMA tpch(1) 2 warmup plus 10 timed runs; invoke your Rust binary with matching sf and threads, which also does 2 warmup plus 10 runs internally after loading. Output CSV with engine, sf, threads, median, min, max. Check both results equal before recording times. Add a perf stat wrapper for the single-thread runs.
verify: CSV with medians for row baseline, vectorized, and DuckDB at SF1 and SF10, 1 thread and all threads
perf stat cycles and instructions per tuple for your engine and DuckDB at 1 thread
Machine, CPU governor or power mode, DuckDB version and exact commands are recorded

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question, (2) numbers for every claim (baseline, vectorized, DuckDB) with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened, using perf counters, for example a batch size that did not help, (4) assumptions and limits: one query, in-memory data, no joins, no nulls.
verify: Part 1 states the question and that results matched the reference answer
Part 2 has every timing with machine, thread count, scale factor and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise with counter or profile evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions and what one query on in-memory data does not prove

links.label: Kersten et al., compiled vs vectorized

projects.title: Learned index vs B-tree
projects.problem: Can a model of the key distribution beat a tree?
projects.proveIt: Lookup ns and memory on real key sets, including worst cases
projects.question: On real sorted 64-bit key sets, does a learned index find keys faster and in less memory than a B-tree, and where does it lose?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen key sets
steps.learn: An index over a sorted array maps a key to its position; a learned index approximates the key CDF with a model and then searches a small window. You will compare ns per lookup and index bytes (not counting the data array) on real key sets, and look hardest at the cases where the model fits badly.

decision.choice: SOSD real datasets (books, fb, osm_cellids, wiki_ts) with a lookup file generated once from a fixed seed
decision.why: SOSD is the standard benchmark for this question, ships download scripts with checksums, and its datasets have known hard cases (fb has about 100 huge outlier keys; osm is hard to model). Freezing the lookup set before tuning keeps you from tuning to it.

alternatives.name: Synthetic uniform or normal keys
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to generate at any size, but smooth CDFs flatter learned models; SOSD's authors use real data because synthetic sets hide the structure and noise of real keys.

alternatives.name: Your own production keys
alternatives.tradeoff: Most relevant to you, but nobody can reproduce the result and you may not have a hard case to show where the model loses.

verify: Run SOSD's download script and confirm every file prints 'checksum ok'
Write the question, the two metrics and the index size range you will sweep in one paragraph
Generate the lookup files, absent-key lookups and poisoned books now with fixed seeds, save their sha256, and never regenerate them

links.label: The Case for Learned Index Structures

steps.title: Load the keys and build a binary search oracle
steps.learn: SOSD files are a little-endian uint64 count followed by the keys. Every index here must return a position window that contains the lower bound of the lookup key; std::lower_bound over the whole array is both your correctness oracle and the first baseline every index must beat.

decision.choice: C++17, keys in one contiguous std::vector<uint64_t>, std::lower_bound as oracle and baseline
decision.why: The learned and tree libraries you will compare (PGM-index, RadixSpline, RMI output, tlx) are C++ or emit C++, so one language keeps call overhead equal. A plain sorted vector is the dense array the SOSD setup assumes.

alternatives.name: Rust with slice::partition_point
alternatives.tradeoff: Safer, but the reference learned indexes are C++; FFI or ports add overhead and risk that muddies ns-level comparisons.

alternatives.name: Branchless binary search as the baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Often faster than std::lower_bound and a stronger baseline; add it as a second baseline once the simple one works.

steps.delegate: In C++17, write load_sosd(path) that reads a uint64 count then that many uint64 keys (little-endian) into std::vector<uint64_t>, and an Index interface: build(const vector<uint64_t>&), SearchBound search(uint64_t key) returning [lo, hi), size_bytes(). Implement BinarySearchIndex with std::lower_bound. Tests: bound contains lower_bound for 1M random present keys, for absent keys, for keys below min and above max, and for duplicate keys.
verify: Confirm loaded key counts and min/max match what the SOSD file header and a quick numpy check report
Confirm the oracle test passes on all four datasets, including absent and out-of-range keys

steps.title: Build the B-tree baseline and its size knob
steps.learn: A B-tree is fast in memory because each node holds many keys, so a lookup touches few cache lines compared with a binary tree. To trade size for speed fairly, SOSD inserts only every k-th key into the tree and finishes with a last-mile search in the array. Learn why a too-large tree can get slower.

decision.choice: tlx::btree_map from every k-th key to its array position, then last-mile std::lower_bound; sweep k
decision.why: This mirrors SOSD's method for trees, so your B-tree points sit on the same size versus ns axes as the learned indexes. tlx's B+tree is a C++ template header, so it drops into the same harness.

alternatives.name: absl::btree_map
alternatives.tradeoff: Well-engineered and memory-lean (leaf nodes skip child pointers), but pulls in Abseil; a fine second B-tree to confirm your baseline is not weak.

alternatives.name: Hand-written static B+tree with cache-line nodes
alternatives.tradeoff: Likely the fastest read-only tree and teaches layout, but more code and a bug here makes every comparison wrong.

steps.delegate: In C++17, add BTreeIndex implementing the Index interface: insert every k-th key with its position into tlx::btree_map<uint64_t,size_t>, search returns the window between the predecessor sample and the next sample, then std::lower_bound in that window. size_bytes counts node memory via a counting allocator. Tests: same oracle tests as BinarySearchIndex for k in {1, 16, 256}.
verify: Confirm the oracle tests pass for every k you sweep
Plot size_bytes against k and confirm size falls roughly in proportion to 1/k
Confirm at k=1 every search window has width 1, so the tree alone gives the exact position; leave timing to the measure step

steps.title: Write a two-stage linear RMI yourself
steps.learn: A recursive model index (RMI) uses a root model to pick one of B second-stage models, and that model predicts the position. With linear models, each lookup is a few multiplies plus one or two cache misses. Writing a small one shows exactly where error comes from: keys that a leaf's line cannot fit.

decision.choice: Root linear model plus B linear leaf models fit by least squares, B swept by powers of 2
decision.why: Linear-linear is the simplest RMI that still shows the core tradeoff (more leaves, smaller error, more memory) and is easy to verify by hand. Storing leaf parameters in flat arrays keeps lookups to predictable memory reads.

alternatives.name: Use the RMI reference compiler (Rust, emits C++)
alternatives.tradeoff: Tuned and closer to SOSD's numbers, but hides the fitting; use it in a later step as the strong RMI.

alternatives.name: Neural network root model
alternatives.tradeoff: What the original paper explored, but inference cost per lookup is far higher than a few multiplies for in-memory arrays.

steps.delegate: In C++17, add RmiIndex<B>: fit a root linear regression from key to position scaled to [0,B), assign each key to a leaf, fit a linear model per leaf, store slopes and intercepts in two flat double arrays. Clamp predictions to [0,n). Tests: oracle tests on all datasets; a unit test where keys are exactly linear and every prediction is exact; a test with an empty leaf.
verify: Confirm oracle tests pass with the error window from the next step stubbed as the full array
Print the mean and max absolute prediction error per dataset for B in {2^10, 2^14, 2^18}
Confirm max error is clearly larger on osm than on books, as SOSD reports osm is hard to model

links.label: The Case for Learned Index Structures

steps.title: Bound each model's error and choose the last-mile search
steps.learn: A learned index is only correct if it returns a window guaranteed to contain the key. Record each leaf's max error at build time; the window is prediction plus or minus that error. Then the last-mile search over that window dominates lookup cost when errors are large, so its shape matters.

decision.choice: Store per-leaf max error; binary search inside [pred - err, pred + err]
decision.why: Per-leaf bounds keep windows small where the data is easy and only widen them where it is hard, and binary search over a bounded window has predictable cost even when a leaf fits badly.

alternatives.name: One global max error
alternatives.tradeoff: Half the metadata, but one bad leaf (for example near fb's outliers) widens every lookup.

alternatives.name: Linear or exponential search from the prediction
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster when errors are tiny because it touches adjacent cache lines, but cost grows with error, which hurts exactly the worst cases you want to study.

steps.delegate: In C++17, extend RmiIndex to compute per-leaf max |predicted - actual| over build keys and return SearchBound [max(0,pred-err), min(n,pred+err+1)). Handle absent keys so the bound still contains lower_bound (test keys between and outside training keys). Add a compile-time switch for binary vs exponential last-mile search. Tests: oracle tests on all four datasets for both search modes.
verify: Confirm zero oracle failures across all lookup files and both search modes
Report the average log2 of window size per dataset; SOSD treats this as the information-loss view of a learned index

steps.title: Add PGM-index and RadixSpline as tuned learned baselines
steps.learn: PGM-index fits piecewise linear segments with a user-chosen epsilon (max error) and indexes the segments recursively. RadixSpline builds a spline in one pass and indexes spline points with a radix table on key prefixes; it has two knobs, radix bits and max error. Both give a guaranteed window by construction.

decision.choice: Wrap pgm::PGMIndex and rs::RadixSpline behind your Index interface and sweep their error knobs
decision.why: Your RMI shows the idea; author-tuned libraries show what the idea achieves. Sweeping epsilon and max error produces many size and speed points, which is how SOSD draws Pareto curves.

alternatives.name: Only your own RMI
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but if your RMI is untuned you will conclude learned indexes lose when only your implementation does.

alternatives.name: ALEX (updatable learned index)
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles inserts, which matters for real databases, but this project is read-only lookups; mixing in updates changes the question.

steps.delegate: In C++17, add PgmIndex<EPS> wrapping pgm::PGMIndex<uint64_t,EPS> (search returns range.lo, range.hi) and RsIndex: rs::Builder<uint64_t>(min,max,radix_bits,max_error), AddKey for every key, Finalize() to get an rs::RadixSpline, then GetSearchBound. Instantiate EPS in {16,32,64,128,256} and (radix_bits, max_error) over a small grid. size_bytes from each library's size method or by counting allocations. Tests: oracle tests for every configuration.
verify: Confirm every configuration passes the oracle tests on all four datasets
Confirm the PGM-index size shrinks as epsilon grows, and record size and build time per configuration

steps.title: Measure index memory the same way for every structure
steps.learn: The claim is about memory, so measure it consistently: bytes the index allocates beyond the shared key array. Analytic sizes (parameters times 8 bytes) miss allocator overhead and node slack; process RSS mixes in everything else. A counting allocator or allocation hook gives one rule for all structures.

decision.choice: Count bytes allocated during build via a counting allocator or global operator new hook, minus freed bytes
decision.why: It captures B-tree node slack and library internals without trusting each library's own size method, and it is the same rule for every index.

alternatives.name: Each library's reported size
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy, but definitions differ (some count only the model, some include buffers), so comparisons can be unfair.

alternatives.name: Process RSS before and after build
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures everything, but includes page rounding and allocator caching, so small indexes look identical.

steps.delegate: In C++17, add a global operator new/delete override that tracks live bytes in an atomic counter, enabled only in a measure_size binary. For each index config, record live bytes after build minus live bytes before. Tests: allocate a known vector and confirm the counter matches; confirm each index's reported size_bytes is within a stated tolerance of the counted value, or log the gap.
verify: Confirm the counter reports the expected bytes for a 1M-element vector<uint64_t> test
For each index, record counted bytes next to its self-reported size and explain any large gap

steps.title: Build the worst cases on purpose
steps.learn: Average speed on friendly data is not the claim. Learned indexes lose when the CDF is hard to fit: outliers (fb), locally erratic keys (osm, a Hilbert-curve projection), and adversarially inserted keys that poison a regression. B-trees have bounded worst-case cost, so these cases decide the answer.

decision.choice: Report fb and osm separately, add a poisoned variant of books, and include absent-key lookups
decision.why: These come from published failure modes (SOSD's fb and osm analysis, data poisoning of learned indexes), so you test known weaknesses rather than invented ones. Absent keys exercise the bound adjustment from the error step.

alternatives.name: Only report averages over all datasets
alternatives.tradeoff: Shorter, but hides exactly the cases where a learned index is slower than binary search.

alternatives.name: Per-lookup max latency only
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows rare stalls but is noisy at ns scale; prefer window size per lookup plus a high percentile of measured time.

steps.delegate: In C++17 or Python, write make_poisoned(input, fraction, seed) that inserts extra keys concentrated in a few narrow key ranges into a copy of books (keep it sorted, write SOSD format), and make_absent_lookups(keys, n, seed) that draws keys between present keys. Save outputs with their seeds. Tests: outputs are sorted, counts are correct, absent keys are truly absent.
verify: Confirm poisoned files are sorted and the count equals original plus injected keys
For each index, report the max and 99th percentile window size on fb, osm and poisoned books

links.label: Testing the Robustness of Learned Index Structures

steps.title: Measure it: harness, baselines and pitfalls
steps.learn: At a few hundred ns per lookup, measurement choices change rankings. SOSD found a warm cache tight loop flatters every index versus a flushed cache, and that a memory fence between lookups slowed RMI and RadixSpline the most because lookups stop overlapping. Report both settings and the baselines.

decision.choice: One harness timing 10M frozen lookups per config, warm and with a fence, summing payloads, pinned to one core
decision.why: Summing a payload per lookup stops the compiler from deleting work; the fence variant shows the cost when lookups cannot overlap, which is closer to a database doing other work between lookups.

alternatives.name: Google Benchmark per configuration
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives repetitions and DoNotOptimize helpers, but its per-iteration model fits one lookup awkwardly; useful to cross-check one config.

alternatives.name: Run SOSD's own harness
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest path to comparable numbers, but you do not learn how the pitfalls arise and cannot easily add your RMI.

steps.delegate: In C++17, write bench(index, keys, lookups, mode) where mode is warm or fenced (std::atomic_thread_fence(seq_cst) between lookups). Each lookup searches, finds the key in the window, adds a payload value to a sum that is printed. Report ns per lookup as median of 5 runs, plus build time and counted bytes. Output CSV. Run baselines: binary search, B-tree sweep, your RMI, PGM, RadixSpline.
verify: Record CPU model, cache sizes, compiler version and flags, and the exact command
Confirm run-to-run spread on one config is small (report it) before comparing indexes
Collect cache-misses with perf stat for one config per index and check that faster indexes miss less

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Your write-up answers one question with a size versus ns plot per dataset. Explain any surprise with evidence (cache misses, window sizes, fit error). State scope: read-only, in-memory, 64-bit integer keys, one machine.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a sentence
Part 2 gives ns per lookup and bytes for every index with machine, compiler flags and command
Part 3 explains each surprise (for example osm or fb) with window size or cache-miss data
Part 4 lists assumptions and what it does not prove (inserts, strings, disk-resident data)

projects.title: Database storage on S3
projects.problem: Object storage is cheap and durable but slow and billed per request
projects.proveIt: Write latency and $ per million writes with batching and caching
projects.question: How much does batching and caching cut durable write latency and dollars per million writes for a key-value store whose only storage is S3?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the workload
steps.learn: S3 is durable and cheap per GB but each request has latency and a per-request price, billed per 1,000 PUT and GET requests. Your metrics: durable write latency (p50, p99) and dollars per million writes = request counts times the current regional price. Fix the workload and record prices before building.

decision.choice: Synthetic YCSB-style key-value workloads (write-only and 50/50 read-update) replayed from a seeded trace
decision.why: No public dataset is needed: the question is about request patterns, not content. YCSB's named workload mixes are reproducible, and a recorded trace gives every configuration the identical request stream.

alternatives.name: Run YCSB against an existing S3-backed store
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows a real system, but you measure its choices, not yours, and cannot count requests per design decision.

alternatives.name: A real application's write log
alternatives.tradeoff: More realistic key and value sizes, but rarely shareable and you cannot vary write rate to find the batching crossover.

verify: Write the question, both metrics and the write rates you will test in one paragraph
Record the region and today's S3 Standard per-1,000 PUT and GET prices from the pricing page with the date
Save the trace files with seed, key count and value size before any tuning

steps.title: Choose the object store client and a test double
steps.learn: Everything above this layer should speak put, get, range get and conditional put. A fake store lets you test logic and inject delays without paying for requests; the real client must be the same interface so measurements reflect the code you tested.

decision.choice: Rust with the object_store crate: InMemory plus ThrottledStore for tests, AmazonS3 for real runs
decision.why: object_store exposes conditional puts (PutMode) and range reads behind one trait, and its InMemory and ThrottledStore implementations give deterministic tests with injected sleeps. SlateDB builds on the same trait.

alternatives.name: aws-sdk-s3 directly
alternatives.tradeoff: Full S3 API surface, but you write your own test double and every test needs a mock or a bucket.

alternatives.name: Python with boto3
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster to prototype, but per-request client overhead and the GIL can blur the latency you are trying to measure.

steps.delegate: In Rust with tokio and object_store, define struct Store { inner: Arc<dyn ObjectStore>, counters: RequestCounters } that wraps put_opts, get_opts and get_ranges and counts PUT and GET requests and bytes. Provide constructors for InMemory, ThrottledStore over InMemory with configurable put and get wait, and AmazonS3Builder from env. Tests: counters match a scripted sequence; ThrottledStore adds the configured delay.
verify: Confirm the counters match a scripted sequence of 10 puts and 7 gets exactly
Time one PUT and one GET of a small object against a real bucket from an instance in the same region and record them

steps.title: Define when a write is durable
steps.learn: With no local disk, a write is durable only once the object holding it is stored in S3. S3 gives strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs, so after a PUT returns success any reader sees the object. Decide what your put() promises, because latency numbers mean nothing without it.

decision.choice: put() acks only after the WAL object containing the write is successfully PUT to S3
decision.why: It makes durable write latency a clean measurement (time from put() call to ack) and matches SlateDB's await_durable semantics, so your numbers are comparable to a real engine.

alternatives.name: Ack from memory, persist later
alternatives.tradeoff: Very low latency and fewer PUTs, but a crash loses acknowledged writes; fine for caches, wrong for a database.

alternatives.name: Local disk WAL, ship to S3 later
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast durable acks from local fsync, but durability then depends on that disk, which is what S3-only designs try to remove.

verify: Write the durability promise in one sentence and the exact moment latency stops being measured
With the test double, show that killing the writer before the PUT completes loses only unacked writes

steps.title: Batch writes into WAL objects with group commit
steps.learn: One PUT per write makes cost scale with write count. Group commit buffers writes and PUTs one WAL object per batch, so PUTs per million writes is roughly one million divided by average batch size, at the price of waiting for the batch. SlateDB exposes this tradeoff as flush_interval.

decision.choice: Flush a WAL object when either a time interval or a byte threshold is reached, whichever comes first
decision.why: The interval caps the latency a lone write waits; the byte cap bounds object size and memory under load. Both knobs map directly onto the latency versus dollars curve you need to plot.

alternatives.name: One PUT per write
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest latency at low load and simplest, but the most PUTs, so the highest cost per million writes.

alternatives.name: Fixed-size batches only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewest PUTs, but at low write rates a write can wait unboundedly for the batch to fill.

steps.delegate: In Rust with tokio, write a WalWriter: put(key, value) returns a future that resolves when durable. A background task collects writes into a buffer, flushes on interval or byte threshold, encodes the batch (length-prefixed records plus a checksum), PUTs it as wal/{seq:020}, then resolves all waiters. Tests with ThrottledStore: batch sizes respond to both triggers; every acked write appears in exactly one WAL object; waiters resolve only after the PUT.
verify: With the test double, confirm PUT count equals the number of flushed batches and every write is in exactly one object
Plot simulated ack latency against flush interval at two write rates and check the lone-write case waits about one interval

steps.title: Enforce a single writer with conditional puts
steps.learn: If an old writer pauses and a new one starts, both may write WAL object N. S3 conditional writes fix this: with If-None-Match the first PUT to a key wins and later ones get 412 Precondition Failed (a concurrent one may get 409 Conflict: retry it). Numbered WAL keys plus create-only puts give fencing without a lock.

decision.choice: Write each WAL object with PutMode::Create; on 412 the writer treats itself as fenced and stops
decision.why: It uses a guarantee S3 documents (first write to a key wins), needs no extra service, and the same create-only pattern is how Delta Lake publishes log versions with put-if-absent.

alternatives.name: External lock or lease (for example a DynamoDB item)
alternatives.tradeoff: Works on stores without conditional writes, but adds a second system, its latency and its failure modes.

alternatives.name: No fencing, trust deployment
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but a zombie writer can silently overwrite acknowledged data.

steps.delegate: In Rust with object_store, change WalWriter to use put_opts with PutMode::Create. On AlreadyExists, mark the writer fenced, fail pending and future writes. On startup, list wal/ to find the highest sequence and continue from there. Tests with InMemory: two writers race for the same sequence and exactly one wins; the loser fails its waiters and never acks.
verify: Run the two-writer race test 1,000 times and confirm exactly one winner each time and no acked write lost
Against the real bucket, confirm a second create-only PUT to an existing WAL key returns a precondition failure

steps.title: Flush memtables to SSTs and track them in a manifest
steps.learn: Reading from WAL objects means scanning many small objects. An LSM keeps recent writes in a sorted memtable, flushes it as a sorted table (SST) object, and records the live SSTs in a manifest. The manifest is the single source of truth, so updating it must be atomic and conditional.

decision.choice: SSTs with sorted blocks, a block index and a bloom filter; manifest updated by If-Match put (PutMode::Update)
decision.why: A block index lets a read fetch one block with a range GET instead of the whole SST; a bloom filter skips SSTs that cannot hold the key, saving GETs. A conditional manifest update stops two processes from losing each other's changes.

alternatives.name: Store everything in WAL objects only
alternatives.tradeoff: No flush code, but reads must scan and replay many objects, so read GETs grow without bound.

alternatives.name: B-tree pages as objects
alternatives.tradeoff: Good point reads, but each update rewrites pages, which on S3 means many PUTs per write.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add a Memtable (BTreeMap), flush to sst/{id} with 4 KiB data blocks, a block index (first key and offset per block) and a bloom filter, then update manifest with put_opts PutMode::Update using the version from the last get. On version conflict, reread and retry. Record in the manifest the last WAL sequence covered by SSTs. Tests: get returns latest value across memtable and SSTs; concurrent manifest updates never lose an SST entry.
verify: Count GETs for one get of a flushed key: report index and filter fetches separately from data-block range GETs (at most one per candidate SST)
Confirm the concurrent manifest update test keeps every SST entry over 1,000 runs

steps.title: Cache blocks so reads stop paying S3 latency
steps.learn: Each uncached read costs a GET and its latency. SlateDB reports that working sets fitting in local memory or disk caches answer in under a millisecond, while reads scattered over a large keyspace see object-storage latency. Your cache decides which regime your reads live in and how many GETs you pay for.

decision.choice: In-memory LRU block cache keyed by (sst id, block offset), plus caching manifest and SST index blocks permanently
decision.why: Index and filter blocks are small and touched by every read, so pinning them removes most GETs; LRU on data blocks is simple and good enough to measure the hit rate versus GET cost curve.

alternatives.name: No cache
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and shows the raw S3 cost per read, which you should keep as a baseline, but every read pays a GET.

alternatives.name: Local disk cache of whole SSTs
alternatives.tradeoff: Holds far more data than RAM, but warming downloads whole objects and adds disk eviction policy to tune.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add BlockCache with a byte capacity and LRU eviction (e.g. the lru crate or a hand-rolled list plus HashMap), used by SST reads before issuing get_ranges. Pin index and filter blocks on SST open. Expose hit and miss counters. Tests: capacity is never exceeded; a repeated read issues zero GETs; eviction order matches LRU on a scripted sequence.
verify: On the read-update trace with the test double, plot GETs per 1,000 reads against cache size
Confirm a cache-hit read issues zero object store requests using the request counters

steps.title: Handle slow requests, errors and crash recovery
steps.learn: S3 can answer 503 Slow Down when request rates spike, and AWS recommends aggressive timeouts and retries for latency-sensitive apps. A timed-out PUT has an unknown outcome, so a retry with create-only may get 412 for your own earlier success. On restart, replay WAL objects newer than the manifest's covered sequence.

decision.choice: Bounded retries with backoff and a per-request timeout; on 412 after a retry, read the object and compare a batch id
decision.why: Retries cut tail latency and absorb throttling; checking the stored batch id resolves the ambiguous timed-out PUT without double-applying or falsely fencing yourself.

alternatives.name: Rely on the client library's default retries
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but object_store retries timeouts only for safe or read-only requests, so a PUT timeout still surfaces and must be handled.

alternatives.name: Fail the write on any error
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and safe, but turns short throttling bursts into user-visible errors.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add a FaultyStore wrapper over InMemory that, from a seeded RNG, delays, fails with 503-like errors, or completes a PUT but returns a timeout. Make WalWriter retry with backoff and resolve 412 by reading the object's batch id. Add recover(): read manifest, replay wal objects after covered sequence into the memtable. Tests: seeded fault runs never lose or duplicate an acked write; crash at random points then recover returns every acked write.
verify: Run 1,000 seeded fault and crash schedules and confirm zero lost or duplicated acked writes
Confirm a failing seed reproduces the same failure when rerun

steps.title: Compact SSTs and delete dead objects, and count their cost
steps.learn: Without compaction, reads check more and more SSTs and old WAL objects pile up in storage. Compaction GETs inputs and PUTs merged outputs, so it adds requests that belong in your dollars per million writes. Garbage collection deletes objects no longer in the manifest, but only after no reader can still need them.

decision.choice: Merge L0 SSTs into one sorted run when their count passes a threshold; delete unreferenced objects after a grace period
decision.why: A count trigger is simple and bounds read amplification; the grace period protects readers holding an older manifest. Both create request counts you can attribute separately in the cost model.

alternatives.name: No compaction
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest in requests, but read GETs and latency grow with every flush.

alternatives.name: Leveled compaction
alternatives.tradeoff: Better read and space amplification at scale, but rewrites data more often, adding PUTs that raise cost per write.

steps.delegate: In Rust, add a compactor that, when L0 SST count exceeds N, streams them via get_ranges, merges keeping newest versions, writes one new SST, updates the manifest conditionally, then marks inputs for deletion after a grace period. Count compaction and GC requests in separate counters. Tests: reads return the same values before and after compaction; no object referenced by the current manifest is ever deleted.
verify: Confirm read results are identical before and after compaction over the full trace
Report compaction PUTs and GETs per million writes separately from foreground requests

steps.title: Measure it: latency and dollars per million writes
steps.learn: Run from an instance in the bucket's region, since S3 recommends co-locating compute and storage. Drive writes open-loop at a fixed rate so slow PUTs do not hide queueing (coordinated omission). Cost comes from request counts times the recorded prices, plus compaction requests.

decision.choice: Open-loop load at 3 write rates; sweep flush interval and cache size; baselines: one PUT per write and no cache
decision.why: The baselines are the unbatched, uncached store the project claims to beat. Open-loop timing measures latency from the intended send time, so p99 reflects queueing.

alternatives.name: Closed-loop (send next after ack)
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to write, but hides queueing delay and understates tail latency.

alternatives.name: Add S3 Express One Zone as a run
alternatives.tradeoff: AWS describes it as single-digit millisecond with lower request costs; a good extra point, but it is one Availability Zone, which changes durability assumptions.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write bench: replays the frozen trace open-loop at a target rate, records per-write latency from scheduled send time to ack in an HDR histogram, and dumps p50, p99, p99.9, PUTs, GETs, compaction requests, and computed dollars per million writes from a prices.toml. Run each config 3 times. Output CSV with config, instance type, region, and commit hash.
verify: Record instance type, region, bucket storage class, prices with date, and the exact command
Cross-check client PUT counts with S3 CloudWatch request metrics for one run (they are opt-in and may cost extra)
Confirm baseline PUTs per million writes is about one million and batched runs fall as batch size grows

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Your write-up answers one question with a latency versus dollars per million writes plot, one point per configuration. Explain surprises with request counts and cache hit rates. Name what the result depends on: region, prices on a date, value size, write rate.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a sentence
Part 2 gives p50, p99 and dollars per million writes for every configuration with instance, region, prices date and command
Part 3 explains each surprise using request counts, batch sizes or cache hit rates
Part 4 lists assumptions and what it does not prove (multi-writer, other object stores, larger values)

projects.title: SSD-aware log layout
projects.problem: Random writes wear out SSDs and slow down over time
projects.proveIt: Write amplification and sustained throughput measured with fio
projects.question: How much does a segment log with cleaning cut write amplification and hold sustained throughput versus in-place random 4 KiB writes on one SSD?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the test drive
steps.learn: Two numbers decide every choice. Host write amplification: bytes your layout writes to the device divided by bytes the user asked to write. Sustained throughput: user writes per second once the drive reaches steady state, measured with fio. No public dataset fits; the workload is synthetic random 4 KiB overwrites.
verify: README states the question, both metric formulas and the two workloads (uniform, 90/10 hot/cold) before any code
Freeze workload seeds, logical capacity and run lengths in a committed config file before tuning anything
Name a spare NVMe drive or partition you can erase; confirm with lsblk that it is not your system disk

steps.title: Reproduce the slowdown on the raw drive
steps.learn: SNIA's WSAT test purges the drive, then runs continuous random 4 KiB writes and plots IOPS over time and drive fills: a fresh-out-of-box peak, a transition, then a lower steady state. That curve is the problem your layout must flatten, and its steady state is your in-place baseline.

decision.choice: Purge with nvme format (or blkdiscard, noted), then fio rw=randwrite bs=4k direct=1 over several drive fills
decision.why: Starting from a purged state makes runs comparable, direct=1 keeps the page cache out, and running past multiple fills shows the steady state instead of the misleading early plateau.

alternatives.name: Run on a used filesystem as-is
alternatives.tradeoff: Realistic, but the starting state is unknown, so two runs on different days are not comparable.

alternatives.name: Short benchmark (minutes)
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but it mostly measures the fresh-out-of-box plateau and hides the drop you are trying to fix.

steps.delegate: Write a bash script wsat.sh DEV that refuses to run if DEV is mounted, runs blkdiscard DEV, then fio --name=wsat --filename=DEV --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --direct=1 --ioengine=io_uring --iodepth=32 --time_based --runtime=$RUNTIME --write_bw_log=wsat --log_avg_msec=1000 --output-format=json. Add a Python script that plots IOPS versus total bytes written divided by device capacity.
verify: Your plot shows IOPS against drive fills; mark where the early plateau ends
Record steady-state IOPS as the mean over the last fill, with min and max
Script exits with an error when pointed at a mounted device

steps.title: Choose the segment size and the block mapping
steps.learn: A log layout never overwrites in place: each logical 4 KiB block is appended to the open segment and an in-memory map records where its newest copy lives. Old copies become dead space that a cleaner reclaims. Segment size sets how large and sequential every device write and every discard is.

decision.choice: Fixed-size segments aligned to the discard granularity (lsblk -D), plus a flat array map to physical slots
decision.why: Large aligned segments turn random user writes into sequential device writes and let a whole segment be discarded at once; a flat array is the simplest correct map for a fixed logical capacity.

alternatives.name: In-place update (the baseline)
alternatives.tradeoff: No cleaning and no map, but every user write is a random device write, which is what degrades on the drive.

alternatives.name: Threaded logging into holes (F2FS)
alternatives.tradeoff: F2FS writes into dead slots of dirty segments when free segments run low; avoids cleaning stalls but issues more scattered writes.

alternatives.name: Hash or B-tree map
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for sparse or huge key spaces; extra memory and lookups you do not need for a dense block range.

steps.delegate: In Rust, create a crate loglayout with struct Layout { map: Vec<u32>, seg_size, nsegs } and fn write(lblock: u32, data: &[u8;4096]). Keep per-segment live counts and a reverse table (physical slot to logical block). Unit tests: overwriting a block marks the old slot dead, live counts always sum to the number of mapped blocks, map and reverse table stay inverse after 1,000,000 random writes.
verify: Record lsblk -D output for your drive and the segment size you chose
Invariant test passes: sum of live counts equals mapped blocks after 1,000,000 random writes

steps.title: Build the write path with direct, aligned I/O
steps.learn: O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache but may require aligned buffers, offsets and lengths; since Linux 6.1 statx with STATX_DIOALIGN reports the rules, and blockdev --getss gives the logical block size. O_DIRECT alone does not guarantee durability; you still need fdatasync or O_DSYNC.

decision.choice: Buffer user writes into a large aligned write unit, write it with O_DIRECT, then one fdatasync per unit (group commit)
decision.why: Large aligned writes are what the drive handles best, and amortizing one sync over many user writes keeps durability without paying a flush per 4 KiB.

alternatives.name: Buffered I/O through the page cache
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but the kernel decides when and how big the writes are, so you no longer control the device pattern you are measuring.

alternatives.name: O_DIRECT|O_DSYNC on every 4 KiB write
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest durability story, but each user write waits for the device, which caps throughput.

steps.delegate: Extend loglayout with a Writer that opens the device with O_DIRECT, allocates buffers aligned to the statx DIOALIGN values (fallback: blockdev --getss and 4096), packs 4 KiB blocks into a write unit and calls pwrite then fdatasync. Tests on a loop device: data read back after reopen matches, misaligned buffers are rejected before any syscall.
verify: strace -e trace=pwrite64,fdatasync shows one fdatasync per write unit, not per block
Read-back test after process restart returns identical bytes for 10,000 random blocks

steps.title: Pick which segments the cleaner reclaims
steps.learn: Cleaning a segment with live fraction u rewrites its live blocks to free 1 minus u of space, so host writes per new byte grow as u grows. LFS found greedy (lowest u first) did badly with hot/cold locality and proposed cost-benefit: pick the highest (1 minus u) times age divided by (1 plus u).

decision.choice: Implement greedy and cost-benefit behind one trait; default to cost-benefit, keep greedy for comparison
decision.why: Your hot/cold workload is exactly where LFS saw greedy fail, and having both lets the write-up show the difference with your own numbers instead of quoting the paper.

alternatives.name: Greedy only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fine for uniform random writes; under skew, cold segments linger just above the cleaning point for a long time and tie up free space.

alternatives.name: Oldest-first (FIFO) cleaning
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial bookkeeping, but ignores how much live data it must copy, so it can rewrite nearly full segments.

steps.delegate: In loglayout add trait VictimPolicy { fn pick(&self, segs: &[SegInfo]) returning a usize segment index } with Greedy and CostBenefit (age = now minus newest write time in the segment). Cleaner runs when free segments drop below a threshold, relocates live blocks, updates the map. Count user_bytes and device_bytes. Tests: cleaning never loses a live block; on a 90/10 workload CostBenefit and Greedy both terminate and report write amplification.
verify: Run both policies on uniform and 90/10 workloads at the same utilization and tabulate host write amplification
Checksum every live block before and after 100 cleaning rounds: zero mismatches

steps.title: Separate hot and cold data into different logs
steps.learn: If short-lived and long-lived blocks share a segment, the cleaner keeps copying the long-lived ones. F2FS keeps several logs open (six by default: hot, warm and cold for node and data blocks) so data of similar lifetime fills the same segments, pushing segments toward nearly empty or nearly full.

decision.choice: Two write heads: one for fresh user writes, one for blocks relocated by the cleaner (survivors are likely cold)
decision.why: It needs no hints from the workload, and blocks that survived a cleaning are evidence of a longer lifetime, so they stop mixing with hot overwrites.

alternatives.name: Single log with LFS age sort
alternatives.tradeoff: The cleaner sorts live blocks by age before rewriting; less state, but user writes still mix hot and cold.

alternatives.name: Per-block write-frequency classes
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to true temperature, but needs counters per block and tuning thresholds you might overfit to your synthetic workload.

steps.delegate: Add a WriteHead abstraction so Layout keeps N open segments; route user writes to head 0 and cleaner relocations to head 1. Make N=1 a config switch. Tests: with N=2, relocated blocks never land in head 0's segments; write amplification is reported per run.
verify: Compare host write amplification for N=1 and N=2 on the 90/10 workload at two utilizations
Plot the histogram of segment live fraction at the end of each run and check whether N=2 is more bimodal

steps.title: Tell the drive which segments are free
steps.learn: A discard (TRIM) tells the SSD a range no longer holds data, so its own garbage collection need not copy it. The F2FS paper found ext4 issued many small discards with visible overhead; F2FS discards whole segments at checkpoints. On a raw device use the BLKDISCARD ioctl; inside a file use fallocate punch hole.

decision.choice: After a segment is cleaned and its relocations are durable, issue one discard covering the whole segment
decision.why: Segment-sized discards match the drive's discard granularity and avoid many tiny commands, and waiting until relocations are durable means a crash can never discard the only copy.

alternatives.name: No discard
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but the drive keeps treating dead segments as live data and copies them during its own garbage collection.

alternatives.name: Periodic fstrim on a filesystem
alternatives.tradeoff: Batches discards for a mounted filesystem; only applies if your layout sits in a file, and freed space waits until the next run.

steps.delegate: Add fn discard_segment(seg) that issues BLKDISCARD for the segment range on a block device, or fallocate(FALLOC_FL_PUNCH_HOLE|FALLOC_FL_KEEP_SIZE) when the target is a file. Call it only after the fdatasync that made relocations durable. Make it a config switch. Test on a loop device: reads of a discarded file range return zeros.
verify: /proc/diskstats sectors discarded (field 14) rises by one segment's worth per cleaned segment; field 12 counts requests, which may be split
Code review: no discard path runs before the relocation fdatasync returns

steps.title: Make the map recoverable after a crash
steps.learn: The map lives in memory, so a crash loses it unless the log can rebuild it. LFS writes a segment summary that names the owner of each block, a checkpoint region with a consistent state, and on restart rolls forward through segments written after the checkpoint.

decision.choice: Per-write-unit summary (logical ids, sequence number), periodic map checkpoint, recovery by roll-forward
decision.why: Summaries add a small, sequential cost to every write unit, checkpoints bound recovery time, and the sequence number decides which copy of a block is newest.

alternatives.name: Full scan of every segment on start
alternatives.tradeoff: No checkpoints to write, but recovery time grows with device size.

alternatives.name: Separate write-ahead log for map updates
alternatives.tradeoff: Familiar database pattern, but every update is written twice, which adds the very write amplification you are measuring.

steps.delegate: Add a summary header to each write unit (magic, seq, CRC32C, list of logical ids) and a checkpoint writer that stores the map in two alternating slots with a CRC. Implement recover(). Test: a fault-injection harness kills the writer at random points 1,000 times; after recover() every block acknowledged as durable reads back its last value.
verify: Fault-injection run: 1,000 kills, zero lost acknowledged writes
Measure recovery time with and without a recent checkpoint and note it

steps.title: Emit the layout's I/O as a trace and replay it with fio
steps.learn: fio can replay a text iolog (version 2: write, trim, datasync lines with byte offsets) via read_iolog. With replay_no_stall=1 it ignores timestamps and issues the I/O as fast as possible in order, so fio measures the device throughput of exactly the pattern your layout produces. Trims need a block device.

decision.choice: Layout runs as a simulator that writes a fio v2 iolog; fio replays it with direct=1 on the purged block device
decision.why: The proof must be measured with fio, and replay keeps the device pattern identical across runs while separating layout logic cost from device behavior.

alternatives.name: Time the layout running live on the device
alternatives.tradeoff: Includes your code's CPU cost, which is real, but the numbers are no longer fio's and are harder to compare to the baseline.

alternatives.name: Capture with blktrace and replay
alternatives.tradeoff: fio also replays blkparse binary traces; useful for an existing program, but more tooling than emitting the log yourself.

steps.delegate: Add a --emit-iolog PATH mode to loglayout that writes 'fio version 2 iolog', add/open lines for the device, then write, trim and datasync lines in issue order. Add a job file replay.fio with read_iolog, replay_no_stall=1, direct=1, ioengine=io_uring, write_bw_log. Test: a 1,000-write workload produces an iolog whose total write bytes equal the simulator's device_bytes counter.
verify: Bytes written reported by fio equal the simulator's device_bytes for the same trace
