Delta of /proc/diskstats field 7 (512-byte sectors) during replay matches fio's bytes within 1%

steps.title: Measure write amplification and sustained throughput
steps.learn: Compare in-place random writes (step 2) with layout replays (each policy, 1 or 2 heads, discard on or off) at several utilizations. SNIA PTS calls a run steady when range is within 20% and best-fit slope within 10% of the window mean. Host WA comes from your counters; device WA only if the drive reports media writes.
verify: Each config is purged, preconditioned and run to steady state; report mean throughput over the steady window
Record nvme smart-log Data Units Written (1 unit = 1000 x 512 bytes, rounded up) before and after; it agrees with diskstats
If nvme endurance-log or nvme ocp smart-add-log reports media writes, compute device WA; otherwise say it is unavailable
Record drive model and firmware (nvme list), kernel (uname -r), fio --version and every command line

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question; (2) every claim with a number, the drive, kernel and exact fio command; (3) why surprising results happened, for example a policy losing on skew or discard not helping; (4) assumptions: one drive, synthetic workloads, host WA versus device WA, what it does not prove about other SSDs.
verify: Part 1 states the one question from step 1 verbatim
Part 2 has a table of host WA and steady throughput per config, each with drive model and fio command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result using your segment live-fraction histograms
Part 4 lists assumptions, including whether device WA was measurable on your drive

projects.title: io_uring server vs epoll
projects.problem: System-call overhead caps throughput at high request rates
projects.proveIt: Requests/sec and p99 for both designs
projects.question: At which request rates does an io_uring server beat an epoll server on requests/sec and p99 latency, and where does each spend its CPU?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the load setup
steps.learn: Two numbers per design: the highest request rate sustained, and p99 latency at fixed offered rates below that. Same handler, same machine, only the I/O layer differs. No dataset: load is generated with wrk2, which holds a constant request rate so latency is not hidden by coordinated omission.
verify: README states the question, the two metrics and the fixed list of offered rates before any code
Record kernel version (uname -r): multishot accept needs 5.19, multishot recv 6.0, DEFER_TASKRUN 6.1
If /proc/sys/kernel/io_uring_disabled exists (kernel 6.6+), check it prints 0; on older kernels the file is absent and io_uring is enabled

steps.title: Fix the protocol and share the handler
steps.learn: To compare I/O layers, everything above them must be identical: request parsing, response bytes, keep-alive behavior. A tiny HTTP/1.1 keep-alive server returning a fixed small body lets wrk2 drive both servers unchanged.

decision.choice: Minimal HTTP/1.1 keep-alive handler in a shared C file used by both servers
decision.why: wrk2 speaks HTTP, so no custom load generator is needed, and sharing one parser means any difference comes from epoll versus io_uring.

alternatives.name: Echo protocol over raw TCP
alternatives.tradeoff: Even less parsing, but you must build or find a load generator that measures latency without coordinated omission.

alternatives.name: A full HTTP library
alternatives.tradeoff: Realistic, but its own buffering and allocation can dominate the profile and hide the I/O layer difference.

steps.delegate: In C11, write http.c/http.h with size_t parse_request(const char *buf, size_t len, int *done) that finds the end of one GET request, and a const response buffer (200 OK, Content-Length, keep-alive). Unit tests: split requests across two buffers, two requests in one buffer, malformed input returns an error.
verify: curl -v against each server shows identical response headers and body bytes
Unit tests cover a request split across two reads and two requests in one read

steps.title: Choose the threading and accept model
steps.learn: Both servers should scale across cores the same way. With SO_REUSEPORT each thread binds its own listening socket to the same port and the kernel spreads incoming connections across them, avoiding a single accept thread or many threads contending on one socket.

decision.choice: One thread per core, each with its own SO_REUSEPORT listener and its own epoll instance or io_uring ring
decision.why: No shared event state between threads in either design, which matches io_uring's advice not to share rings, so the comparison is per-core loop against per-core loop.

alternatives.name: One listener shared with EPOLLEXCLUSIVE
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids the thundering herd on a shared socket, but only the epoll side has this exact mechanism, which skews the comparison.

alternatives.name: Single acceptor thread handing out connections
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple to reason about, but the acceptor can become the bottleneck and adds a cross-thread handoff.

steps.delegate: Write common.c with int make_listener(int port) that sets SO_REUSEPORT and SO_REUSEADDR, binds and listens, and a run_threads(n, fn) that pins thread i to CPU i with pthread_setaffinity_np. Test: start 4 threads, open 1,000 connections, and log per-thread accept counts.
verify: Per-thread accept counts for 1,000 connections are all nonzero; record the spread
Startup log shows a distinct listening fd per worker thread, all bound to the same port

steps.title: Build the epoll server
steps.learn: epoll is readiness based: it tells you a socket can be read, then you call read yourself, so each request costs at least an epoll_wait share plus read and write calls. Edge-triggered mode needs nonblocking sockets and reading until EAGAIN, or the loop can hang with data still buffered.

decision.choice: Edge-triggered epoll, nonblocking sockets, read and write until EAGAIN; keep a level-triggered build flag
decision.why: ET reports a socket only when new data arrives, so a drained socket is not reported again; keeping an LT build lets you show whether the mode matters at your rates instead of assuming it does.

alternatives.name: Level-triggered only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler and safer (no EAGAIN loop needed), but may return the same ready socket repeatedly.

alternatives.name: Blocking thread per connection
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest code, but thousands of threads add context switches and memory, so it is not a fair epoll baseline.

steps.delegate: Write epoll_server.c using common.c and http.c: accept4 with SOCK_NONBLOCK, EPOLLIN|EPOLLET (or level-triggered with -DLT), read until EAGAIN, parse all complete requests, write responses, register EPOLLOUT only when a write returns EAGAIN. Tests: pipelined requests in one read all get answered; slow client reading 1 byte at a time still gets full responses.
verify: Both ET and LT builds pass the pipelined and slow-client tests
strace -c -f for a 10,000-request run: record calls per request for epoll_wait, read and write

steps.title: Build the io_uring event loop
steps.learn: io_uring is completion based: you queue requests (SQEs) and reap results (CQEs) from rings shared with the kernel. io_uring_submit_and_wait submits and waits in one syscall. Multishot accept posts a CQE per new connection until IORING_CQE_F_MORE is missing, then you must re-arm.

decision.choice: liburing, one ring per thread created with IORING_SETUP_SINGLE_ISSUER and IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN, multishot accept
decision.why: Each ring has one submitter in this design, and DEFER_TASKRUN (which requires SINGLE_ISSUER) runs completion work only when you wait, giving you control of batching, as Axboe's networking guide recommends.

alternatives.name: Default ring setup flags
alternatives.tradeoff: Works on older kernels, but task work can interrupt the thread at any syscall, which hurts batching.

alternatives.name: IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL
alternatives.tradeoff: A kernel thread polls the submission queue so you may need no syscalls, but it uses an extra CPU while busy, which complicates a per-core comparison.

steps.delegate: Write uring_server.c with liburing: io_uring_queue_init_params with SINGLE_ISSUER|DEFER_TASKRUN (fall back to default via a flag), io_uring_prep_multishot_accept, encode op type and fd in user_data, loop on io_uring_submit_and_wait then io_uring_for_each_cqe. Re-arm accept when IORING_CQE_F_MORE is absent. Tests: 1,000 connections all accepted; forcing a cancel re-arms accept.
verify: strace -c -f for a 10,000-request run: record io_uring_enter calls per request
Log shows accept re-armed whenever a CQE arrives without IORING_CQE_F_MORE

steps.title: Choose how receives get their buffers
steps.learn: In a completion model the receive is queued before data arrives, so a buffer per connection wastes memory at scale. Provided buffer rings (5.19+) let the kernel pick a buffer when data arrives and report its id in the CQE. Multishot recv (6.0+) posts a CQE per arrival; an empty ring fails it with -ENOBUFS.

decision.choice: Buffer ring (io_uring_register_buf_ring) plus io_uring_prep_recv_multishot, returning buffers after parsing
decision.why: Memory scales with in-flight data, not connection count, and one recv submission per connection removes re-arm work from the hot path.

alternatives.name: Fixed buffer per connection, one-shot recv
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest to debug, but memory grows with connections and every receive needs a new SQE.

alternatives.name: Poll then read (readiness style on io_uring)
alternatives.tradeoff: Mirrors epoll closely, so the comparison isolates batching, but gives up the completion model's main benefit.

steps.delegate: Extend uring_server.c: set up a buffer ring with io_uring_register_buf_ring, add buffers with io_uring_buf_ring_add and io_uring_buf_ring_advance, submit io_uring_prep_recv_multishot with IOSQE_BUFFER_SELECT. Get the buffer id by shifting the CQE flags right by IORING_CQE_BUFFER_SHIFT. On -ENOBUFS replenish and re-arm. Tests: shrink the ring to 4 buffers and confirm no request is lost under 100 connections.
verify: With a 4-buffer ring and 100 connections, every request gets a response and the -ENOBUFS count is logged
Record peak RSS for 10,000 idle connections against the one-buffer-per-connection build

steps.title: Handle sends, short writes and connection close
steps.learn: A send can complete with fewer bytes than asked (a short send) in both designs; you must send the rest. A receive returning 0 means the peer closed. With io_uring, CQEs can still arrive for a connection you decided to close, so track outstanding ops per connection before freeing it.

decision.choice: One-shot send per response batch, resend the rest on a short send, close only with no ops in flight
decision.why: It is the simplest correct path for small fixed responses, and in-flight counting keeps a late CQE from touching freed connection state.

alternatives.name: Zero-copy send (io_uring_prep_send_zc)
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids copying the payload, but posts a second notification CQE before the buffer can be reused; test whether it helps at your response size.

alternatives.name: Linked SQEs (recv then send)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer round trips in user space, but a short send is not an error without MSG_WAITALL, so links can hide partial writes.

steps.delegate: Add a per-connection struct with pending_ops, out buffer and offset to uring_server.c. On send CQE with res < remaining, prep another send for the rest. On recv res == 0 or error, cancel outstanding ops and close when pending_ops hits 0. Tests: a client that stops reading forces short sends; abrupt client resets leave no leaked fds (check /proc/self/fd count).
verify: Slow-reader test completes with full responses in both servers
After 10,000 abrupt client resets, open fd count returns to its starting value

steps.title: Probe kernel features and fail loudly
steps.learn: io_uring can be disabled by sysctl (io_uring_setup then fails with -EPERM), and older kernels lack opcodes. io_uring_get_probe and io_uring_opcode_supported tell you what the running kernel supports. A silent fallback would mean benchmarking a different design than you think.

decision.choice: Probe at startup, print the features in use, and exit with an error if a required one is missing
decision.why: Benchmark results are only meaningful if you know exactly which code path ran, and a printed feature line goes straight into the write-up.

alternatives.name: Silent fallback to epoll or one-shot ops
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for production availability, but you can end up comparing epoll against epoll without noticing.

alternatives.name: Require the newest kernel only
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but the server will not start on many machines and you lose the chance to compare feature levels.

steps.delegate: Add probe.c: call io_uring_get_probe, check io_uring_opcode_supported for accept, recv, send and any others used, and try ring creation with the chosen setup flags. Print one line listing kernel, flags and multishot support. Tests: mock a missing opcode and confirm the server exits non-zero with a clear message.
verify: Startup line lists kernel version, ring flags and multishot support
With kernel.io_uring_disabled=2 on a test VM, the server exits with a clear EPERM message

steps.title: Measure requests/sec and p99 for both designs
steps.learn: Sweep fixed offered rates with wrk2 -R and --latency; the max sustained rate is where achieved rate falls below offered or p99 climbs sharply. Load generator and server compete for CPU, so use two machines or pin them to separate cores. Count syscalls with bpftrace and see where CPU goes with flame graphs.
verify: For each design (epoll ET, epoll LT, io_uring basic, io_uring full), table achieved rate and p99 at every offered rate
Server and wrk2 run on separate machines or separate cores via taskset; record which
Record syscalls per request from bpftrace tracepoint:raw_syscalls:sys_enter counts for each design
Save a perf flame graph per design at one common rate, plus CPU model, kernel and exact wrk2 commands

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question; (2) every claim with a number, the machine, kernel and exact wrk2 command; (3) why surprising results happened, for example a small gap if the flame graph shows TCP stack time dominating; (4) assumptions: tiny responses, one kernel, loopback or LAN, what it does not prove for real apps.
verify: Part 1 states the one question from step 1 verbatim
Part 2 has the rate sweep table with machine, kernel and wrk2 command for every number
Part 3 explains at least one surprise using syscall counts or a flame graph
Part 4 lists assumptions and what the results do not prove

projects.title: Raft with deterministic simulation testing
projects.problem: Consensus bugs hide in rare timing and failure orderings
projects.proveIt: Bugs found by randomized fault seeds, each reproducible from its seed
projects.question: Can a seeded deterministic simulator find Raft bugs hidden in rare fault orderings, and replay each one exactly from its seed?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the frozen bug list
steps.learn: Success means: randomized fault seeds find bugs, and every failing seed replays to the identical trace. There is no dataset; the setup is a 3 or 5 node Raft KV cluster inside one process. To prove the harness works, plant known bugs and fix that list before tuning any fault rates.
verify: README states the question, the two metrics (failing seeds per planted bug, replay identical yes/no) and the seed budget per bug
Planted-bug list (at least 4, e.g. skip the current-term commit rule) is committed before any fault tuning
Record Go version, CPU model and OS you will run the sweep on

steps.title: Model each Raft node as a pure state machine
steps.learn: etcd-io/raft models Raft as a state machine: input is a message or a timer tick, output is messages to send, entries to persist and state changes; network and disk are left to the caller. That split is what makes a simulator possible: the simulator owns every input, so a run is a function of the seed.

decision.choice: Sans-I/O node: Step(msg) and Tick() return a Ready{Messages, ToPersist, Committed} batch; no goroutines inside
decision.why: The simulator, not the node, decides when messages arrive and when ticks happen, so the same code runs in simulation and behind a real transport, and no scheduler nondeterminism leaks in.

alternatives.name: Simulated async runtime (turmoil or MadSim, Rust)
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps natural async code and swaps the runtime under it, but you depend on the framework catching every source of nondeterminism.

alternatives.name: Real goroutines and sockets with fault injection
alternatives.tradeoff: Tests the real stack, but schedules are not reproducible, so a failing run cannot be replayed from a seed.

steps.delegate: In Go, write package raft with type Node, func NewNode(id int, peers []int, rng *rand.Rand) *Node, methods Tick(), Step(m Message), Propose(cmd []byte) bool, and Ready() Ready {Messages []Message; HardState; Entries []Entry; Committed []Entry}. No goroutines, channels, time.Now or global rand inside the package. Unit tests: a lone node with peers=[self] elects itself after enough Ticks; Ready is empty when nothing changed.
verify: grep the raft package: zero uses of go statements, time.Now, time.Sleep, or top-level rand functions
Unit tests pass and you can explain which output fields must be persisted before messages are sent

steps.title: Build the single-threaded discrete-event simulator
steps.learn: FoundationDB simulates a whole cluster in one single-threaded process, with simulated time running faster than real time. Determinism traps in Go: map iteration order is unspecified, top-level math/rand calls ignore your seed, and wall-clock time differs per run. One seeded RNG must drive every random choice.

decision.choice: Event queue keyed by (virtual time, insertion seq), one rand.New(rand.NewPCG(seed, 0)), sorted map iteration
decision.why: The (time, seq) key breaks ties without depending on map or heap order, and a single RNG means the seed alone determines the run, which is the property the prove-it requires.

alternatives.name: Lockstep rounds (every node ticks, then deliver all)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler to write, but message delays collapse into whole rounds, so fine-grained timing races are under-explored.

alternatives.name: One RNG per node and per link, derived from the seed
alternatives.tradeoff: Adding a node does not shift other streams, which helps when comparing runs, but costs more plumbing.

steps.delegate: In Go, write package sim: type Sim{now int64; q eventHeap; seq uint64; rng *rand.Rand}, Schedule(at int64, ev Event), Run(until int64), and a trace writer that appends one line per processed event. Iterate node maps via sorted keys only. Test: run the same seed twice and compare SHA-256 of both traces (must match); two different seeds must produce different hashes.
verify: Same seed twice gives identical trace SHA-256; record both hashes
Run 1000 seeds twice each in a loop: zero hash mismatches
Change GOMAXPROCS between runs: hashes still match

steps.title: Implement leader election with randomized timeouts
steps.learn: Raft randomizes election timeouts (the paper suggests e.g. 150 to 300ms) so split votes are rare, and requires broadcast time to be well below the timeout. currentTerm and votedFor are persistent state. Election Safety: at most one leader per term, not at most one leader at a time; a stale leader can coexist briefly.

decision.choice: Timeouts drawn from the sim RNG over a tick range (e.g. 10 to 20 ticks, heartbeat 1 tick), no Pre-Vote at first
decision.why: Keeping the paper's ratio of heartbeat to timeout preserves its behavior, and drawing from the sim RNG keeps elections replayable. Leaving Pre-Vote out first keeps the core small and lets the simulator show the disruption it fixes.

alternatives.name: Fixed, equal timeouts
alternatives.tradeoff: No RNG needed, but in the paper's tests elections without randomness took over 10 seconds because of repeated split votes.

alternatives.name: Add Pre-Vote (thesis section 9.6)
alternatives.tradeoff: Stops a rejoining partitioned node from bumping the term and deposing a healthy leader, at the cost of an extra round per election.

steps.delegate: In Go, add RequestVote handling per Raft Figure 2: candidate increments currentTerm, votes for self, grants a vote only if votedFor is empty or the candidate, and the candidate's log is at least as up to date (last term, then last index). Step down on any higher term. Tests: 5 nodes with no faults elect exactly one leader; partitioning the leader yields a new leader in a higher term.
verify: Simulator invariant after every event: no two nodes are leader in the same term; 1000 fault-free seeds pass
On a no-fault run, plot election count versus timeout range width and confirm narrow ranges cause more elections

steps.title: Replicate the log and apply the current-term commit rule
steps.learn: AppendEntries carries prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm so logs satisfy Log Matching. Figure 8 shows an entry stored on a majority can still be overwritten, so a leader only commits entries from its own term by counting replicas; earlier entries commit indirectly. A no-op at term start lets a new leader learn the commit point.

decision.choice: Implement Figure 2 literally, including the current-term-only commit rule and a no-op entry on election
decision.why: The point of the project is to catch subtle safety bugs, so the reference must be the exact published rules; the no-op is also what read handling relies on later.

alternatives.name: Commit any entry once a majority stores it
alternatives.tradeoff: Looks correct and passes most runs, but is the Figure 8 bug; keep it as a planted bug for the measure step.

alternatives.name: Commit only when all replicas store it
alternatives.tradeoff: Safe but stalls on any single slow or crashed node, which removes the availability Raft exists to give.

steps.delegate: In Go, implement AppendEntries send/receive with nextIndex/matchIndex, conflict truncation, and commitIndex advance only for entries whose term equals currentTerm. Append a no-op on becoming leader. Tests: a follower with a conflicting suffix is truncated and repaired; the Figure 8 sequence scripted in the simulator never commits the overwritten entry.
verify: Invariant after every event: if two logs have an entry with the same index and term, all earlier entries match
Invariant: no two nodes apply different commands at the same index; 1000 seeds with scripted leader partitions pass
Scripted Figure 8 scenario passes; with the planted majority-commit bug enabled it fails

steps.title: Simulate the disk and crash-restart
steps.learn: Raft requires currentTerm, votedFor and log to be on stable storage before responding to RPCs. A crash in your simulator must lose anything not yet synced, otherwise persistence bugs (like voting twice in one term after a restart) are invisible. TigerBeetle's VOPR stubs out clock, network and disk for this reason.

decision.choice: Simulated disk with explicit Write and Sync; crash drops unsynced writes, restart rebuilds from synced state
decision.why: It reproduces the exact failure that matters (acknowledged but not durable) deterministically and fast, with no real files involved.

alternatives.name: Treat all writes as durable
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but the forgot-my-vote class of bug can never be found.

alternatives.name: Real files with fsync
alternatives.tradeoff: Exercises the real I/O path, but is slow and its timing is not controlled by the seed, so replays drift.

alternatives.name: Also corrupt or tear writes
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to real disks (VOPR corrupts reads and writes), but needs checksums and recovery logic first.

steps.delegate: In Go, write package simdisk: Disk{synced, pending map[string][]byte} with Write(key, val), Sync(), Crash() (drops pending), Read(key). Node persists HardState and new entries, then calls Sync before its messages are released by the simulator. Add Crash(node) and Restart(node) events. Tests: crash between Write and Sync loses the write; a restarted node never grants two votes in one term.
verify: Planted bug 'send vote before Sync' is caught by the one-vote-per-term invariant within your seed budget
Trace shows at least one crash between Write and Sync in a typical seed
Restarted nodes rejoin and catch up in a fault-free tail

steps.title: Drive every fault from the seed
steps.learn: VOPR uses the seed to tune fault parameters: dropping, reordering, partitioning. FoundationDB's 'swizzle-clogging' (stop a random subset's links one by one, then restore them in random order) is described as especially good at finding deep bugs. Bugs hide in fault mixes you would not write by hand.

decision.choice: Each seed first draws its own fault profile (drop, delay, duplicate, partition, crash rates), then draws events from it
decision.why: Varying the intensity per seed explores both gentle and brutal runs, and the profile is part of the replayed state, so a failing seed still reproduces exactly.

alternatives.name: One fixed fault rate for all seeds
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to reason about, but either too gentle to reach rare states or so harsh that nothing makes progress.

alternatives.name: Hand-written scenario tests only
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise for known cases (VOPR keeps some), but only finds bugs you already imagined.

steps.delegate: In Go, add sim.FaultProfile drawn from the RNG: dropProb, dupProb, maxDelay, partitionEvery, crashEvery, plus a swizzle-clog event. The network delivers each message with a drawn delay, may drop or duplicate it, and blocks it across an active partition. Log every fault to the trace. Test: profile and trace are identical across two runs of one seed; a seed with dropProb=0 and no partitions delivers every message.
verify: Histogram over 1000 seeds shows a spread of fault intensities, not one rate
Count seeds with zero committed entries; if most stall, the profile is too harsh: record the fraction
Two runs of a faulty seed still give identical trace hashes

steps.title: Add the KV client, deduplication and the history log
steps.learn: Raft section 8: clients tag commands with unique serial numbers so a retried command is not applied twice, and linearizable reads need the leader to commit a no-op in its term and confirm with a majority it is still leader. Every client call and return is recorded in virtual time for the checker.

decision.choice: Reads go through the log as ordinary commands; writes carry (clientID, seq) for dedupe
decision.why: Logging reads is the simplest correct read path, so a checker failure points at core Raft rather than a read optimization.

alternatives.name: ReadIndex: confirm leadership with a heartbeat round
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids a log write per read (the paper's approach), but adds another path that must be tested separately.

alternatives.name: Lease-based reads
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but the paper notes it relies on bounded clock skew, so the simulator must also skew clocks.

steps.delegate: In Go, write a KV state machine (Put, Get, Append) with a per-client last-seq table, and simulated clients that pick keys from a small set, retry on timeout with the same seq, and record {client, op, key, value, call, return, outcome} where outcome is ok or unknown (timed out). Tests: a duplicated Put is applied once; history is identical across two runs of one seed.
verify: Planted bug 'no dedupe table' is visible as a double Append in a seed with duplicated messages
History file for one seed is byte-identical across two runs

steps.title: Check invariants online and linearizability offline
steps.learn: Cheap invariants run after every event (one leader per term, log matching, same command per applied index); the client history is then checked against a sequential KV model. Porcupine checks linearizability from a Go Model and can partition a history per key; with a timeout it may return Unknown, which is not a pass.

decision.choice: Online invariants plus Porcupine with a per-key Partition function and a timeout; timed-out ops stay open-ended
decision.why: Invariants catch internal violations at the exact event, and Porcupine judges what clients saw, independently of Raft's own logic, so the system never grades itself.

alternatives.name: Compare final state machines only
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to write, but misses stale reads and lost acknowledged writes that later get overwritten.

alternatives.name: Knossos (Clojure)
alternatives.tradeoff: Jepsen's original checker; Porcupine reports being 1,000x to 10,000x faster on Jepsen's test data.

steps.delegate: In Go, implement porcupine.Model for a KV map with Partition splitting by key, Init and Step. Convert history to []porcupine.Operation; give unknown-outcome ops a Return after the last event so they may linearize late. Call CheckOperationsVerbose (with a timeout) and treat Unknown separately. On Illegal pass its LinearizationInfo to porcupine.VisualizePath. Tests: a hand-made stale-read history is Illegal; a sequential history is Ok.
verify: Hand-built stale-read history is reported Illegal and the HTML shows where
Report Unknown counts separately from Ok across a 1000-seed run
Planted 'reads served by any leader without confirming' bug is caught by Porcupine, not by invariants

steps.title: Measure it: seed sweeps against planted bugs
steps.learn: The prove-it is about bugs found per seed and exact replay. Baselines: the same seed budget with faults off, and with one fixed fault rate. Pitfalls: counting a hang as a pass (add a liveness check after faults heal), and reporting a single sweep when results depend on the seed range.

decision.choice: For each planted bug and the clean build: N seeds under three regimes (no faults, fixed rate, per-seed profile)
decision.why: Comparing regimes on the same seed budget shows whether randomized profiles actually find more, and the clean build bounds false alarms.

alternatives.name: Run until first failure only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper, but gives one noisy sample per bug; a fixed budget lets you report detection rate.

alternatives.name: Coverage-guided seed search
alternatives.tradeoff: Can reach rare states faster, but adds feedback machinery and makes runs harder to compare.

steps.delegate: In Go, write cmd/sweep: flags -bug, -regime, -seeds, -start; runs seeds in parallel processes (each sim stays single-threaded), records per seed: pass/fail, which checker fired, events processed, virtual and wall time. Add -replay SEED that reruns one seed and diffs its trace hash. Output CSV.
verify: Table: detection rate per planted bug under each regime with the same seed count
Every failing seed replays with an identical trace hash: report count replayed and mismatches
Clean build: zero failures over the full budget, or each failure triaged as a real bug
Record machine, Go version and the exact sweep command lines

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (e.g. which fault mix exposed a bug), (4) assumptions and limits: simulation tests your model of the network and disk, not the real ones.
verify: States the one question in a sentence
Every number names the machine and the sweep command that produced it
Explains at least one surprising result with a replayed trace excerpt
Lists what this does not prove (real I/O, real clocks, unmodeled faults)

projects.title: Jepsen-style tester for an open-source database
projects.problem: Databases claim guarantees they don't always keep under partitions
projects.proveIt: A documented consistency anomaly, or evidence there is none
projects.question: Does etcd keep its documented strict-serializable key-value guarantees under partitions, pauses and crashes, checked by my own black-box tester?

steps.title: Frame the claim, the outcome and the frozen test plan
steps.learn: etcd documents linearizable KV ops by default, with possibly stale reads only under the serializable option; Jepsen (2020) found they appear strict serializable. Success: a documented anomaly with a minimal history, or many clean runs plus proof the tester catches a known anomaly. No dataset; workloads are generated.
verify: README quotes the exact guarantee being tested, with the etcd docs link and version
Workloads, fault mixes, run length and run count are committed before the first real run
Record host CPU, kernel, Docker version and the pinned etcd release

steps.title: Stand up a disposable 5-node cluster
steps.learn: Jepsen runs a control node that sets up DB nodes, runs logically single-threaded client processes, and lets a nemesis inject faults. Its README notes separate VMs let you test clock skew. Five nodes allow minority/majority splits that tolerate two failures. Each run must start from wiped data.

decision.choice: Five etcd containers (official image), each with an iptables sidecar sharing its network namespace; data wiped per run
decision.why: Containers start in seconds and are cheap to destroy, which matters for many runs. The etcd image is distroless (no iptables), so a NET_ADMIN sidecar in each node's network namespace applies the partitions.

alternatives.name: Five VMs (or Jepsen's AWS setup)
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets you test clock skew and real network stacks, but setup is slower and costs money per run.

alternatives.name: Write the test in Clojure with the Jepsen library
alternatives.tradeoff: Mature generators, nemeses and checkers out of the box, but you learn less by building and must learn Clojure.

steps.delegate: Write docker-compose.yml for 5 etcd nodes (pinned image tag, static IPs, one sidecar per node with iptables, cap_add NET_ADMIN and network_mode service:<node>, initial-cluster flags, data in a tmpfs or per-run volume) and a Go package harness with Up(), Down(), WipeData(), Leader() using clientv3 Status. Test: Up then a Put/Get round trip on every member; Down leaves no containers or volumes.
verify: etcdctl endpoint status on all 5 members shows one leader and equal raft term
Ten Up/Down cycles leave zero stray containers or volumes
Leader() agrees with etcdctl output

steps.title: Record every operation as invoke and ok, fail or info
steps.learn: Jepsen completes each invocation as ok (happened), fail (definitely did not happen) or info (unknown, e.g. a timeout). Treating a timeout as fail can produce false alarms: the write may have committed and a later read sees it. Only mark fail when the error proves the op had no effect.

decision.choice: Go clientv3, one client per logical process, per-op context timeout; timeouts and connection errors become info
decision.why: Info is the only safe default under partitions, and a fixed per-process client keeps each process sequential, which the checkers assume.

alternatives.name: Mark all errors as fail
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler histories, but a write that committed after the timeout makes valid behavior look like an anomaly.

alternatives.name: Drop timed-out operations from the history
alternatives.tradeoff: Hides the write that a later read observes, again producing false anomalies.

steps.delegate: In Go, write package history: Op{Process, Type (invoke|ok|fail|info), F (read|write|cas), Key, Value, Time (monotonic ns)} appended to a JSON Lines file, plus a Client wrapper around clientv3 that records invoke before the call and the completion after. After an info, the process is retired and a fresh process ID takes over. Tests: a context timeout yields info; a failed CAS compare yields fail.
verify: Kill the leader mid-run: history shows info ops and no process issues an op after its own info
Every invoke has exactly one completion or ends the history open

steps.title: Design the register workload
steps.learn: Jepsen's etcd test used randomized reads, writes and compare-and-set over single keys, checked with a CAS-register model. Unique write values make every read point to the one write it saw. Many independent keys keep each per-key history small enough to check.

decision.choice: Per-key CAS register: read, write unique values, CAS via Txn comparing the value; about 100 keys rotated over time
decision.why: Single-key linearizability is exactly what etcd claims by default, and small per-key histories keep the checker from timing out.

alternatives.name: Multi-key transactions checked by Elle
alternatives.tradeoff: Tests the transactional claim too, but needs a different history encoding and checker (done in a later step).

alternatives.name: Set workload (append to a set, read it)
alternatives.tradeoff: Jepsen used it to count stale reads; simpler to check, but weaker than full linearizability.

steps.delegate: In Go, write a generator seeded by a run seed: for each process pick a key from the active window, then read, write (value = processID*1e9+counter) or CAS(old,new) as Txn().If(clientv3.Compare(clientv3.Value(key), "=", old)).Then(OpPut).Else(OpGet). Rate-limit per process. Tests: values are unique across the run; same seed produces the same op sequence offline.
verify: Count writes and confirm no value repeats in a 10-minute history
Ops per key stay under the size your checker finishes in its timeout (measure it)

steps.title: Build the nemesis: partitions, pauses and crashes
steps.learn: Jepsen's etcd analysis used single-node isolation, majority/minority splits, non-transitive partitions with overlapping majorities, crashes, and pauses, some targeting the leader. docker pause uses the freezer cgroup, so the process cannot observe the suspension, unlike SIGSTOP.

decision.choice: iptables DROP rules inside containers for partitions, docker pause for pauses, docker kill then start for crashes
decision.why: iptables can express any per-pair cut, including non-transitive bridges that docker network disconnect cannot, and pause/kill map directly to real process faults.

alternatives.name: docker network disconnect
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs no extra capability, but cuts a node off the whole network, so per-pair cuts like bridges are awkward.

alternatives.name: tc netem delay and loss
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds latency, loss and reordering instead of clean cuts; good as an extra fault, not a partition substitute.

steps.delegate: In Go, write package nemesis with Partition(groups [][]string), Bridge(), IsolateLeader(), Heal(), Pause(node), Resume(node), Kill(node), Restart(node). Partitions run iptables -A INPUT -s <peer> -j DROP via docker exec into each node's iptables sidecar. Every start and stop is logged into the history as a nemesis op with a timestamp. A seeded schedule alternates fault and heal windows. Tests: after Partition, minority nodes cannot reach the majority; after Heal, all can.
verify: During a majority/minority split, writes to the minority time out and the majority elects a leader
After Heal, iptables -S in every node's sidecar shows no leftover DROP rules
History contains a nemesis start and stop for every fault

steps.title: Check single-key histories for linearizability
steps.learn: Linearizability: each op appears to take effect at one instant between its invocation and response. Porcupine checks a history against an executable Go model, can partition by key, and returns Unknown on timeout. An info op must be allowed to take effect at any later time or never.

decision.choice: Porcupine with a CAS-register model, Partition by key, CheckOperationsTimeout; info ops get an open-ended return time
decision.why: It is native Go like the harness, and Porcupine reports being far faster than Knossos on Jepsen's test data, which matters for long histories.

alternatives.name: Knossos via elle-cli
alternatives.tradeoff: Same family as Jepsen's own analysis, but runs on the JVM and is slower on large histories.

alternatives.name: Write your own checker
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for learning, but your checker could share your bugs; use it only alongside a proven one.

steps.delegate: In Go, convert JSONL history to []porcupine.Operation: ok ops use real return times; info writes and CAS get Return after the last op; fail ops are dropped; info reads are dropped. Model: Init 0/nil, Step for read, write, cas; Partition by key. Run CheckOperationsVerbose per run and on Illegal pass its LinearizationInfo to porcupine.VisualizePath. Tests: a crafted stale read is Illegal; a crafted concurrent history is Ok.
verify: Crafted stale-read history is Illegal and the visualization marks it
Per run, report Ok, Illegal and Unknown counts per key; Unknown is not counted as a pass

steps.title: Prove the tester can catch a real anomaly
steps.learn: A tester that never fails proves nothing until it has caught something real. etcd documents that the serializable read option may return stale data, and Jepsen observed exactly that. etcd's robustness suite also lists past bugs with reproduction targets, e.g. a single-node cluster losing a write on crash.

decision.choice: Rerun the workload with clientv3.WithSerializable() reads under partitions; the checker must flag stale reads
decision.why: It uses the real target and a documented behavior, so detection is expected rather than hoped for, and it calibrates how long runs must be.

alternatives.name: Reproduce a listed etcd robustness bug on its old version
alternatives.tradeoff: A true bug rather than a documented option, but needs the right version and fault (e.g. crash during load), which takes setup.

alternatives.name: Plant a bug in a toy KV store
alternatives.tradeoff: Fully controlled, but proves less about the harness against a real system.

steps.delegate: Add a -serializable-reads flag to the workload that passes clientv3.WithSerializable() to Get. Script: 20 runs with leader-isolation faults, flag on, then 20 with flag off; collect checker verdicts into a CSV with run seed and duration.
verify: With serializable reads under partitions, the checker reports Illegal in some runs; record how many of 20
Open one Illegal visualization and explain the stale read in your own words
Record the minimum run length at which the anomaly appeared

steps.title: Check multi-key transactions with Elle
steps.learn: Elle infers an Adya-style dependency graph between client-observed transactions and looks for cycles, choosing objects and operations so reads reveal version history. elle-cli runs Elle on JSON or EDN histories from any language, needs Java 21, and supports rw-register and list-append models.

decision.choice: rw-register txns (2 to 4 reads and unique writes) in one etcd Txn, checked by elle-cli for strict-serializable
decision.why: etcd claims multi-key Txn atomicity and strict serializability; rw-register maps directly onto Get and Put inside one Txn.

alternatives.name: list-append model
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets Elle infer more of the version order from each read, but appends need read-modify-write encoding in etcd.

alternatives.name: Skip multi-key checks
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but leaves the transactional half of the claim untested.

steps.delegate: In Go, add a txn workload: each op is a list of [r k nil] or [w k v] micro-ops executed as one clientv3 Txn().Then(...ops); fill read results from the response. Emit an elle-cli-compatible JSON history (type, f=txn, value, process, index). Script running java -jar elle-cli --model rw-register with consistency-models strict-serializable. Tests: a crafted G1c cycle history is reported invalid.
verify: Crafted anomaly history is false and a clean single-process history is true in elle-cli
Record valid, invalid and unknown counts for the txn workload across all fault mixes

steps.title: Measure it: run the fault campaign
steps.learn: Results only count for faults that actually hit: log when each fault started relative to the leader. Report availability (ok fraction) and latency per fault window, not only verdicts. Pitfalls: runs too short to span a failover, checker timeouts counted as passes, and a closed-loop client hiding stalls.

decision.choice: Fixed matrix: each fault mix (isolate leader, split, bridge, pause, kill, mixed) for N seeded runs per workload
decision.why: A fixed, pre-registered matrix makes 'no anomaly found' a measurable statement (fault mix, run count, op count) instead of an impression.

alternatives.name: One long soak run
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap to set up, but one history is one sample and grows too large to check.

alternatives.name: Adaptive search for failing schedules
alternatives.tradeoff: May find bugs faster, but runs are not comparable and coverage is hard to state.

steps.delegate: Write cmd/campaign in Go: for each (workload, fault mix, seed) bring up a fresh cluster, run T minutes, tear down, run checkers, append a CSV row: verdicts, ops by type, info count, ok rate during faults, p50/p99 latency, leader changes, faults that hit the leader. Save each history and nemesis log under runs/<id>/.
verify: Matrix table with run count, op count and verdict counts per cell; no cell empty
Every Unknown verdict is listed and rerun or reported as unchecked
Record machine, etcd version and the exact campaign command

steps.title: Triage and minimize any anomaly
steps.learn: An anomaly is only a finding once you rule out tester bugs (clock, history encoding, info handling) and can reproduce it. Shrink it: fewer keys, shorter run, one fault type. Compare against etcd's documented guarantees and its robustness track record before claiming novelty.
verify: For each Illegal or invalid verdict: a reproduction rate over at least 10 reruns of its settings
Each anomaly is matched to a documented exception (e.g. serializable reads), a known issue, or marked new with evidence
If none found: state fault mixes, total ops and runs that came back clean

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine, etcd version and command, (3) why surprising results happened (e.g. why a fault mix produced more info ops), (4) assumptions and limits: no clock skew in containers, finite runs, only the APIs you exercised.
verify: States the one question and the exact guarantee tested
Every number names the machine, etcd version and command
Explains at least one surprising result with a history excerpt
Lists what clean runs do not prove (untested faults, APIs, versions)

projects.title: Fused GPU kernel in Triton
projects.problem: Separate kernels waste memory bandwidth
projects.proveIt: Speedup and % of peak bandwidth vs PyTorch
projects.question: How much faster than PyTorch is one fused Triton kernel for residual add + LayerNorm, and what % of peak DRAM bandwidth does it reach?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the frozen shapes
steps.learn: Residual add followed by LayerNorm is memory bound: each element is touched a few times and needs little math. Unfused, PyTorch writes the sum to DRAM and reads it back. Success = speedup over PyTorch eager and torch.compile, plus achieved GB/s as a % of peak, on shapes you fix now.
verify: README states the question, both metrics and the formula GB/s = bytes moved / time before any kernel code
Shapes frozen in a file: rows 4096, hidden sizes such as 768, 1024, 2048, 4096, 8192, plus one odd size like 781, in fp16 and bf16
GPU model, driver, CUDA, PyTorch and Triton versions recorded (nvidia-smi, torch.__version__, triton.__version__)

steps.title: Measure the bandwidth ceiling you will compare against
steps.learn: For a memory-bound kernel the roofline ceiling is DRAM bandwidth. The theoretical number is memory clock x bus width x 2 (double data rate) / 8; triton.testing.get_dram_gbps computes exactly that. A large device-to-device copy shows what is actually reachable on your card.

decision.choice: Report % of measured copy bandwidth as the headline, and % of theoretical alongside it
decision.why: A plain copy is the best any memory-bound kernel can do on this card, so it is an honest 100%. Showing theoretical too keeps the reader from thinking the gap to the datasheet is your kernel's fault.

alternatives.name: Datasheet or theoretical peak only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to cite, but no real kernel reaches it, so every result looks worse and the gap is unexplained.

alternatives.name: Nsight Compute speed-of-light % only
alternatives.tradeoff: Per-kernel and precise, but a profiler view; you still need a wall-clock number for the speedup claim.

steps.delegate: Write bench_copy.py in Python with PyTorch and Triton: allocate fp16 tensors from 64 MiB to 2 GiB, time y.copy_(x) with triton.testing.do_bench (return_mode='median'), compute GB/s as 2*numel*element_size/time, print it next to triton.testing.get_dram_gbps(). Save results to ceiling.csv. Include a test that the GB/s formula matches a hand-computed example.
verify: Copy GB/s plateaus as size grows; record the plateau value and the size where it starts
Plateau is below the theoretical figure; note the ratio in the README

steps.title: Profile the unfused PyTorch baseline and count its bytes
steps.learn: Write the byte model per row-major M x N input of element size s. Unfused: h = x + r reads 2MNs, writes MNs; layer_norm(h) reads MNs, writes MNs. Fused, you read x and r once and write y and h (h feeds the next residual). Fusion removes only the reread of h (5MNs to 4MNs), not all traffic.

decision.choice: Fuse add + LayerNorm and still write h, matching how a pre-norm transformer block uses it
decision.why: It is the realistic contract: the next block needs h. The byte model then predicts a modest win from bytes alone, so any extra speedup must come from fewer launches or better access patterns, which keeps the write-up honest.

alternatives.name: Do not write h (inference-only shortcut)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer bytes and a bigger headline speedup, but only valid when nothing downstream needs the sum.

alternatives.name: Fuse softmax instead (Triton tutorial op)
alternatives.tradeoff: Well trodden with a published byte analysis, but you would mostly be retyping the tutorial.

steps.delegate: Write baseline.py: def ref_add_ln(x, r, w, b, eps) returning (y, h) via h = x + r and torch.nn.functional.layer_norm. Run it under torch.profiler with ProfilerActivity.CUDA for one frozen shape and print the CUDA kernel names and count. Also run torch.compile(ref_add_ln) and print its kernels. Write bytes_model(M, N, s, fused) and unit tests for both cases.
verify: Profiler table shows how many CUDA kernels eager launches versus torch.compile for the same call; record both counts
bytes_model output for 4096 x 4096 fp16 matches your hand calculation

steps.title: Map rows to Triton programs and choose the block shape
steps.learn: A Triton program works on blocks; tl.program_id picks the row. Block sizes must be powers of two, so use triton.next_power_of_2(N) and mask loads and stores with cols < N (tl.load takes mask and other). The layer norm tutorial instead loops over the row in BLOCK_SIZE chunks and reloads X per pass.

decision.choice: One program per row, whole row loaded once into registers, BLOCK_SIZE = next_power_of_2(N)
decision.why: Each element of x and r is read from DRAM exactly once, which is the point of fusion, and every frozen hidden size fits in one block. Reductions for mean and variance then run on data already on chip.

alternatives.name: Chunked loop over the row (tutorial style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles any N with bounded registers, but rereads x per pass and relies on caches to hide it.

alternatives.name: Several rows per program for small N
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for tiny rows where one row underfills a program; adds a 2D block and more masking.

steps.delegate: Write fused_add_ln.py with a @triton.jit kernel taking pointers to x, r, w, b, y, h, the row stride, N, eps and BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr. Load x and r with mask cols < N and other=0, compute h = x + r, store h, compute mean and variance over the masked row, normalize, scale by w, add b, store y. Grid = (M,). Add a pytest comparing against baseline.py for N=781.
verify: Kernel matches the reference on the odd size 781 (masking works) and on 4096
Profiler shows one Triton kernel per call in place of the eager kernel sequence

steps.title: Pick the accumulation precision and variance formula
steps.learn: Inputs are fp16 or bf16 but sums of thousands of elements lose precision in those types. The Triton tutorial casts loads to float32 before reducing. With the whole row in registers, variance can be computed as mean of (x - mean)^2 in a second pass over registers, with no extra DRAM traffic.

decision.choice: Upcast to fp32, two-pass mean then centered variance on registers, cast outputs back to input dtype
decision.why: The centered two-pass formula avoids the cancellation of E[x^2] - E[x]^2, and because the row is already on chip the second pass costs only arithmetic, which is cheap in a memory-bound kernel.

alternatives.name: Single pass E[x^2] - E[x]^2
alternatives.tradeoff: One reduction fewer, but can cancel badly when the mean is large relative to the spread.

alternatives.name: Welford online update
alternatives.tradeoff: Numerically stable in one pass and needed when streaming chunks; more code than you need when the row fits.

steps.delegate: Extend fused_add_ln.py: cast loaded x and r to tl.float32, keep h in fp32 for the statistics, store h and y in the input dtype. Write test_numerics.py: compare against a float32 PyTorch reference with torch.testing.assert_close, and add a case with a large offset (inputs around 1000 with small spread) where a naive E[x^2] - E[x]^2 version should fail.
verify: assert_close passes for fp16 and bf16 against the fp32 reference on every frozen shape
The large-offset test fails for a deliberately naive variant and passes for yours

steps.title: Tune num_warps with the autotuner keyed on N
steps.learn: num_warps sets how many warps (32 threads each) cooperate on one program; wide rows need more. triton.autotune benchmarks a list of triton.Config objects and re-runs the search when any argument named in key changes. TRITON_PRINT_AUTOTUNING=1 prints the winner.

decision.choice: triton.autotune over num_warps in {1, 2, 4, 8, 16} with key=['N']
decision.why: The best warp count depends on row width, and N is the only shape argument that changes it here. Tuning once per N is cheap and removes a hand-picked heuristic from the results.

alternatives.name: Fixed heuristic from the tutorial
alternatives.tradeoff: The layer norm tutorial uses min(max(BLOCK_SIZE // 256, 1), 8): zero tuning time, but may leave speed on the table.

alternatives.name: Offline sweep baked into a table
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic launches with no first-call tuning, but must be redone per GPU.

steps.delegate: Wrap the kernel in @triton.autotune(configs=[triton.Config({}, num_warps=w) for w in (1,2,4,8,16)], key=['N']). Write tune_report.py that runs each frozen N once with TRITON_PRINT_AUTOTUNING=1 and records the chosen num_warps to tuned.csv. Keep a flag to bypass autotune and use the tutorial heuristic for comparison.
verify: tuned.csv lists a chosen num_warps for every frozen N
For at least two sizes, compare tuned versus heuristic time and record both

steps.title: Wrap the kernel with input checks and a PyTorch fallback
steps.learn: The kernel assumes each row is contiguous (stride 1 along N), a supported dtype, and N small enough that the row fits in one block. Inputs outside that contract must not reach the kernel. Tensor.contiguous returns the tensor itself if already contiguous, otherwise a copy.

decision.choice: Python wrapper: reshape to 2D, force last-dim stride 1 via .contiguous(), PyTorch fallback for unsupported inputs
decision.why: Silent wrong answers on strided or oversized inputs are the worst failure for a kernel. A fallback keeps the function always correct and makes the fast path an explicit, testable contract.

alternatives.name: Raise an error on unsupported inputs
alternatives.tradeoff: The tutorial raises when N is too large: simplest, but callers must handle it.

alternatives.name: Pass both strides and support any layout
alternatives.tradeoff: More general, but strided loads can break coalescing and need their own benchmark.

steps.delegate: Write add_layernorm(x, r, w, b, eps=1e-5) returning (y, h) in Python: check device is CUDA, dtypes in {fp16, bf16, fp32} and equal, shapes broadcast-free, reshape to (M, N), call .contiguous() when stride(-1) != 1, and above a max N or on CPU call baseline.ref_add_ln. Log which path ran. Tests: transposed input, CPU input, N above the limit, mismatched dtypes, all equal to the reference.
verify: Each unsupported case returns results equal to the reference and logs the fallback path
A non-contiguous input still matches the reference on the fast path after .contiguous()

steps.title: Run the full correctness suite before any timing
steps.learn: Speed numbers mean nothing for a wrong kernel. torch.testing.assert_close picks default rtol and atol from the dtype (for example fp16 rtol 1e-3, atol 1e-5). The reference must be PyTorch, never your own kernel, so the check is independent of your code.

decision.choice: Compare against PyTorch computed in fp32, then cast, with explicit tolerances per dtype
decision.why: Your kernel accumulates in fp32, so an fp32 reference is the right target; comparing to an fp16 reference would blame you for PyTorch's own rounding. Explicit tolerances make the pass criterion visible in the write-up.

alternatives.name: Compare to eager PyTorch in the same dtype
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches what users run today, but differences may be the reference's rounding, not your bug.

alternatives.name: Compare to float64 reference
alternatives.tradeoff: Strictest ground truth, but slower and tolerances need more thought for bf16.

steps.delegate: Write test_suite.py with pytest parametrized over every frozen shape, fp16 and bf16, and random seeds 0 to 4. Inputs: randn, randn*100, rows of constant value (variance 0), and inputs with a few large outliers. Check y and h with torch.testing.assert_close and explicit rtol/atol, and check no NaN or Inf appear.
verify: All parametrized cases pass; record the count of cases
Constant rows give finite outputs equal to b (variance 0 handled by eps)

steps.title: Measure speedup and % of peak bandwidth against baselines
steps.learn: triton.testing.do_bench clears the L2 cache before each timed run and reports milliseconds; ask for median or quantiles. GPU clocks vary, so lock them or record them. Nsight Compute fixes GPU clocks by default while profiling (see --clock-control) and its SpeedOfLight section reports memory throughput as % of peak.

decision.choice: do_bench median with quantiles [0.2, 0.5, 0.8], baselines eager and torch.compile, ncu SpeedOfLight as cross-check
decision.why: Clearing L2 keeps small shapes from looking faster than DRAM allows, quantiles show noise, and two baselines separate the value of fusing by hand from what the compiler already does.

alternatives.name: torch.cuda.Event loop by hand
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control, but you must handle warmup and cache flushing yourself.

alternatives.name: do_bench_cudagraph
alternatives.tradeoff: Removes CPU launch overhead from timing; useful for tiny shapes, but hides overhead users do pay.

steps.delegate: Write bench.py: for every frozen shape and dtype, time triton add_layernorm, eager ref_add_ln and torch.compile(ref_add_ln) (compile and warm up first) with triton.testing.do_bench(quantiles=[0.2,0.5,0.8]). Compute GB/s from bytes_model and % of the measured copy plateau and of get_dram_gbps. Write results.csv and a plot. Print nvidia-smi clocks before and after.
verify: results.csv has every shape x dtype x provider with p20/p50/p80, GB/s and % of both peaks
Run ncu --section SpeedOfLight on one shape and compare its memory % with your computed %
Rerun the benchmark once; medians agree within your stated noise band

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the question; numbers for every claim with GPU, versions and the exact bench command; why surprising results happened (for example small N where launch overhead dominates, or torch.compile matching you); assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question exactly as in step 1
Part 2: every speedup and % of peak cites results.csv, the GPU model and the command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise using the byte model or the profiler
Part 4 lists limits: forward only, one GPU, frozen shapes, no backward pass

projects.title: Distributed cache with hot-key handling
projects.problem: Consistent hashing balances keys, but one viral key overloads a node
projects.proveIt: p99 under a skewed (Zipfian) workload, with and without the fix
projects.question: Under a skewed Zipfian workload, how much does hot-key replication cut p99 latency of a consistent-hashed cache cluster?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the workloads
steps.learn: Consistent hashing spreads keys, not requests: under skew one key's traffic lands on one node. Metric: client-observed p99 (and p99.9) at a fixed offered load, with and without the fix. Workloads: YCSB-style Zipfian (constant 0.99) and a real Twitter cache trace sample.
verify: README states the question, the offered load(s) and the p99 metric before any code
Download one sample from the Twitter cache-trace repo, record its file name and checksum, and freeze it
Freeze generator seeds, key count and run length in a config file

steps.title: Build the single-node cache server and its wire protocol
steps.learn: Each node is an in-memory key-value store with GET, SET and DELETE plus a stats call reporting request count. Keep it simple and measurable: the experiment is about load distribution across nodes, not single-node peak throughput.

decision.choice: Rust + Tokio TCP server, length-prefixed binary GET/SET/DEL/STATS, sharded HashMap with a size cap
decision.why: Tokio handles many client connections on few threads, a binary frame keeps parsing out of the latency picture, and sharding the map avoids one global lock skewing p99 for reasons unrelated to hot keys.

alternatives.name: Memcached text protocol
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets you reuse existing tools and clients, but parsing text adds work and edge cases to every request.

alternatives.name: Run real memcached or Redis nodes
alternatives.tradeoff: Production-grade servers, but you cannot add per-node hot-key detection inside them.

steps.delegate: In Rust with tokio, write cache-node: listen on a port, frames are u32 length + u8 opcode + payload. Ops GET(key), SET(key, value, ttl_ms), DEL(key), STATS (returns request count and bytes). Storage: 16 shards of Mutex<HashMap> with a max-entries cap and simple eviction. Integration tests: set/get round trip, TTL expiry, delete, 100 concurrent clients.
verify: Integration tests pass, including 100 concurrent clients
STATS request count equals the number of requests a test client sent

steps.title: Place keys with a consistent-hash ring and virtual nodes
steps.learn: Karger et al. map each cache to many points on a circle and each item to the closest point (implementations take the next point clockwise), so adding a node moves only the keys it now owns. More points per node evens out the key share. Jump consistent hash needs no storage but requires buckets numbered sequentially.

decision.choice: Hash ring with 100 to 200 virtual nodes per server, sorted vector and binary search
decision.why: Nodes can join and leave by name, the ring is tiny, and the key-movement property is easy to verify, which is what the hot-key experiment builds on.

alternatives.name: Jump consistent hash
alternatives.tradeoff: No memory and very even split, but buckets must be numbered 0..n-1, so removing a middle node is awkward.

alternatives.name: Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing
alternatives.tradeoff: No ring to maintain, but each lookup hashes the key against every node.

steps.delegate: Write a Rust crate ring with Ring::new(nodes, vnodes), add(node), remove(node), owner(key) returning a NodeId, and successors(key, r) returning r distinct nodes clockwise. Use a 64-bit hash (for example xxhash). Tests: deterministic owner, distinct successors, and adding a 5th node to 4 moves roughly a fifth of 1M keys.
verify: With 4 nodes and 1M uniform keys, report each node's key share for 1, 50 and 200 vnodes
Adding a node moves only keys now owned by the new node (count them)

steps.title: Route requests from a client library with timeouts
steps.learn: Facebook's memcache client on each web server does request routing over consistent hashing, as a library or as the mcrouter proxy. Ours holds a connection pool per node and a timeout per request; without the timeout one slow node stalls callers and hides in averages.

decision.choice: Client-side routing library with a per-node connection pool and per-request timeout
decision.why: Routing in the client keeps latency to one network hop, so p99 reflects the cache nodes, and it is where the hot-key logic will later choose among replicas.

alternatives.name: Routing proxy in front of nodes (like mcrouter)
alternatives.tradeoff: Clients stay simple and config is central, but a remote proxy adds a hop to every request and to p99.

alternatives.name: Server-side redirect
alternatives.tradeoff: No client ring needed, but misrouted requests cost a round trip.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write cache-client: Client::new(ring, pool_size, timeout) with async get/set/del that pick ring.owner(key), reuse pooled connections, and return a Timeout error after the deadline. Track per-node request counts on the client. Tests with a mock node that sleeps: timeout fires, other nodes unaffected.
verify: Mock slow node triggers timeouts while requests to other nodes keep normal latency
Client per-node counts equal the nodes' STATS counts after a run

steps.title: Build an open-loop load generator that shows the hot node
steps.learn: A closed-loop client waits for each reply before sending, so slow periods get fewer samples (coordinated omission). wrk2 instead sends at a constant rate and measures latency from when each request should have been sent. YCSB's Zipfian constant is 0.99; its scrambled variant spreads hot items across the key space.

decision.choice: Open-loop generator at a fixed rate, latency from intended send time, HdrHistogram per run
decision.why: The claim is about p99 under overload of one node; a closed loop would back off exactly when that node is slow and understate the tail you are trying to fix.

alternatives.name: Closed-loop clients (N in flight)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, measures throughput well, but suffers coordinated omission at the tail.

alternatives.name: Existing tools such as YCSB
alternatives.tradeoff: Proven generators, but they will not speak your binary protocol without a binding.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write loadgen: args rate, duration, read_ratio, keys, dist (zipf with s=0.99 scrambled by hashing, uniform, or trace file replay). Schedule sends on a fixed timetable, record latency = completion minus scheduled time in an hdrhistogram::Histogram, and print p50/p99/p99.9 plus per-node request share from the client. Add a --closed-loop mode (N in flight) for comparison. Test: generated Zipf frequencies match the expected ratio for the top ranks.
verify: Uniform run: per-node request shares are close to the key shares from the ring step
Zipf 0.99 run: one node's request share and p99 stand out; record both
Stall a node for 1 s mid-run: open-loop p99 jumps while a closed-loop variant barely moves

steps.title: Detect hot keys in bounded memory
steps.learn: Space-Saving keeps m counters; an unmonitored item replaces the minimum counter and inherits its count, so estimates only overestimate and the minimum is at most N/m. Count-Min never underestimates and stays within eps times the total with probability 1 - delta, but needs a heap to list the top keys.

decision.choice: Space-Saving top-k per node over fixed time windows, reported in STATS
decision.why: It directly yields the top-k list with bounded error and small memory, and windows let a key that cools down stop being treated as hot.

alternatives.name: Count-Min Sketch plus a min-heap
alternatives.tradeoff: Good point estimates for any key, but more structures to keep in sync for a top-k list.

alternatives.name: Exact HashMap of counts
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and exact, but memory grows with distinct keys, which a real trace makes large.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a SpaceSaving struct with new(m), offer(key), top(k) returning (key, count, error) tuples, and reset(). Each node offers every GET key and exposes top(k) for the current window (for example 1 s) via STATS. Tests: on a Zipf stream, the true top 10 keys (computed exactly in the test) all appear in top(20); every count is >= the true count.
verify: On a frozen Zipf stream, recall of the exact top 10 within top(20) is 10/10
Every reported count is at or above the exact count computed independently in the test

steps.title: Spread hot-key reads across replicas
steps.learn: Facebook replicates some key categories within a pool when request rate exceeds one server, letting a request go to any replica, at the cost of sending invalidations to all replicas. Bounded-load consistent hashing caps keys per node, but one key still maps to one node.

decision.choice: For keys in the hot list, copy to the next R ring successors; clients read from a random replica
decision.why: Replicating only the hot set multiplies capacity for exactly the keys that overload a node, while the rest of the key space keeps one copy and normal hit rates.

alternatives.name: Client-side near cache with short TTL
alternatives.tradeoff: Absorbs hot reads with no server change, but every client may serve stale data until TTL expires.

alternatives.name: Consistent hashing with bounded loads
alternatives.tradeoff: Evens out keys per node, but cannot split one key's traffic.

steps.delegate: Extend cache-client: poll each node's top(k) every window and keep a hot set (keys above a request-rate threshold). For hot keys, get() picks a random node from ring.successors(key, R); on miss at a replica, fetch from the owner and fill the replica. Make R and the threshold configurable, with R=1 meaning the fix is off. Tests: hot key reads spread across R nodes; non-hot keys still go to the owner.
verify: With the fix on, the hot key's reads split roughly evenly across its R replicas (per-node STATS)
Non-hot keys still route only to their owner

steps.title: Keep replicated hot keys consistent on writes
steps.learn: Once a key has several copies, a write must update or invalidate all of them or readers see old values. Facebook delivers invalidations to all replicas and uses leases (a token per miss) to stop stale sets and thundering herds. Decide what staleness the cache promises.

decision.choice: Writes go to the owner, which deletes the key on all replicas; replicas refill on miss
decision.why: Delete-based invalidation is simple and idempotent, and refills come from the owner so a replica never invents a value. The cost is a burst of misses after each write to a hot key, which you will see in the numbers.

alternatives.name: Write-through to every replica
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer misses after writes, but writes slow down with R and concurrent writers can race.

alternatives.name: Leases on miss (Facebook style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Prevents stale sets and herds, but adds a token protocol to every miss.

steps.delegate: Add to cache-node: record which replicas it served fills to for each key; on SET or DEL of such a key, send DEL to those replicas before acking. Replica copies get a short TTL. Add a version number per value so a replica fill with an older version is rejected. Tests: after SET, no replica returns the old value, even after the key leaves the hot set; a concurrent stale fill is rejected by version.
verify: Run a 95/5 read/write Zipf workload and count stale reads seen by a checker client; record the count
After a write to a hot key, observe and record the miss burst in replica STATS

steps.title: Handle a failed node without moving the hot key onto a neighbor
steps.learn: Facebook notes that rehashing a failed server's keys onto the remaining servers risks cascading failures, because one key can be 20% of a server's requests. They send failed requests to a small Gutter pool with short-lived entries instead.

decision.choice: On timeout, mark the node down and send its traffic to a small fallback pool with short TTLs
decision.why: It isolates the failed node's load, including any hot key, from healthy nodes that are already loaded, which matters most in a skewed workload.

alternatives.name: Rehash to the ring successor
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra machines, but the successor may receive a hot key and overload in turn.

alternatives.name: Treat failures as misses and go to the backend
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but the backing store absorbs all of the failed node's traffic.

steps.delegate: Extend cache-client: after K consecutive timeouts mark a node down for a cool-off period, route its keys to a fallback pool (another ring of 1 or 2 nodes) whose SETs use a short TTL, and probe the node to bring it back. Add a --fallback=successor mode that rehashes to the ring successor, for comparison. Tests: kill a node mid-run; requests keep succeeding; when it returns, traffic goes back.
verify: Kill the node owning the hottest key mid-run: record error rate and p99 for healthy nodes vs a rehash-to-successor variant
Node restarts and receives traffic again within the configured cool-off

steps.title: Measure p99 with and without the fix
steps.learn: Compare like with like: same nodes, rate, seeds and trace slice, only R changes. Sweep offered load, since the fix matters most when the hot node nears saturation. Run the load generator on a separate machine, or pin it to separate cores, so it is not competing with nodes.

decision.choice: Load sweep on Zipf 0.99, uniform and the Twitter sample, fix off (R=1) vs on (R=3), 3 runs each
decision.why: Uniform is a control where the fix should change nothing; Zipf is the target; the real trace checks the effect is not an artifact of a synthetic distribution. Repeats expose run-to-run noise.

alternatives.name: Single offered load
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but may sit below saturation where the fix shows nothing, or far above where everything fails.

alternatives.name: Throughput at a p99 SLO
alternatives.tradeoff: A single number per config, but hides the shape of the latency curve.

steps.delegate: Write bench.sh that starts 4 nodes, then for each workload, R in {1, 3} and rates in a sweep runs loadgen 3 times for a fixed duration with frozen seeds, saving HdrHistogram output and per-node STATS to results/. Write plot.py for p99 vs offered load per workload and per-node request share. Record git commit, CPU, core pinning and command line in results/meta.txt.
verify: Uniform: p99 with R=1 and R=3 overlap within run-to-run noise
Zipf and trace: p99 vs load for both settings, with the hot node's request share before and after
meta.txt names machine, cores, commit and exact commands

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example no gain under uniform load, or miss bursts after writes); assumptions and what this does not prove (one machine, synthetic network, chosen R and threshold).
verify: Part 1 states the one question from step 1
Part 2: every p99 claim cites a results file, machine and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise with per-node STATS
Part 4 lists limits: cluster size, network, trace sample, write ratio

projects.title: GPU vector search
projects.problem: When does a GPU beat CPU HNSW, counting transfer costs?
projects.proveIt: QPS and recall vs CPU HNSW at different batch sizes
projects.question: At what query batch size does GPU vector search beat CPU HNSW in QPS at equal recall, once host-to-device transfers are counted?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the dataset
steps.learn: The answer is a crossover batch size: plot QPS against recall@10 for CPU HNSW and GPU indexes at batch sizes from 1 to a few thousand, with query upload and result download inside the timer. Dataset: ann-benchmarks SIFT1M (128-d, 1M base, 10k queries, top-100 ground truth, Euclidean).
verify: README states the question, recall@10 and QPS as metrics, and that transfers are timed, before any code exists
Split the 10,000 queries with a fixed seed into 2,000 tuning and 8,000 held-out queries and save the index lists to disk
Record GPU model, driver, CUDA version, CPU model and core count you will benchmark on

steps.title: Load vectors and score recall against fixed ground truth
steps.learn: The HDF5 file holds train, test and neighbors arrays. Recall@10 is the overlap between returned ids and the first 10 true neighbors, divided by 10. Scoring against the shipped ground truth keeps every index graded by the same external answer key.

decision.choice: Use the ground-truth neighbors shipped in the HDF5 file as the only answer key
decision.why: It was computed independently of every system under test, so neither the CPU nor GPU index grades its own output.

alternatives.name: Recompute exact neighbors with a GPU flat index
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets you use other datasets, but now one of the systems under test also produces the key; use it only as a cross-check.

alternatives.name: Score against a CPU brute-force pass
alternatives.tradeoff: Independent of the GPU path, but slow at 1M x 10k in Python and adds float rounding ties you must handle.

steps.delegate: In Python with h5py and numpy, write data.py: load sift-128-euclidean.hdf5, return train/test as C-contiguous float32 and neighbors as int64, plus load_split() reading the saved tuning/held-out index files. Write recall_at_k(found_ids, gt, k=10). Tests: recall of gt[:, :10] against itself is 1.0, shuffled ids within a row still score 1.0, and a row of all -1 ids scores 0.
verify: Print shapes: train (1000000, 128), test (10000, 128), neighbors (10000, 100)
Brute-force 20 tuning queries with numpy and confirm your top-10 matches the shipped neighbors

steps.title: Build the CPU HNSW baseline
steps.learn: HNSW search walks a layered graph greedily; ef is the size of the candidate list at query time and must be at least k. hnswlib's knn_query takes a whole batch and spreads it over num_threads, so CPU throughput also grows with batch size until all cores are busy.

decision.choice: hnswlib with M=16, ef_construction=200 (its documented defaults), all cores for batched queries
decision.why: hnswlib is a widely used header-only C++ HNSW library with a batched, multithreaded Python API, which makes it a strong and fair CPU baseline.

alternatives.name: Faiss IndexHNSWFlat
alternatives.tradeoff: Same family and keeps one library for CPU and GPU, but a different implementation; pick it if you want identical I/O code paths.

alternatives.name: Larger M such as 32 or 48
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher reachable recall on harder data, at more memory and slower build; worth a second run if M=16 caps recall.
