steps.delegate: In Python write cpu_hnsw.py using hnswlib: build Index(space='l2', dim=128), init_index(max_elements=1_000_000, M=16, ef_construction=200), add_items with num_threads=-1, save_index to disk so later runs reload it. Expose search(queries, k, ef, num_threads). Test on a 10k-vector random subset: recall@10 against numpy brute force is above 0.95 at ef=100.
verify: Record build time and index file size for the full 1M index
On the tuning split, recall@10 rises as ef goes 10, 20, 40, 80, 160 and you log every point

steps.title: Add exact GPU brute force as the simplest GPU point
steps.learn: Exact L2 search for a batch is one large matrix multiply plus a top-k selection, which GPUs are built for; its recall is 1.0 by construction. Faiss notes GPU indexes do best with batched queries and that large k slows them.

decision.choice: faiss GpuIndexFlatL2 with a StandardGpuResources object, whole base resident on the GPU
decision.why: SIFT1M at float32 is about 512 MB, so it fits in GPU memory, and exact search sets a recall 1.0 point no approximate index can beat on accuracy.

alternatives.name: cuVS brute_force
alternatives.tradeoff: Same idea in the cuVS library you will use for CAGRA; pick it to keep one GPU stack.

alternatives.name: Hand-written CUDA or Triton kernel
alternatives.tradeoff: Teaches more about the GEMM and top-k, but you would be benchmarking your kernel, not the CPU vs GPU question.

steps.delegate: In Python write gpu_flat.py with faiss (faiss-gpu from conda): res = faiss.StandardGpuResources(); index = faiss.GpuIndexFlatL2(res, 128); index.add(train). Expose search(queries_host_numpy, k) returning ids. Test: on 100 held-out queries recall@10 is 1.0 against the shipped ground truth.
verify: Recall@10 on the 2,000 tuning queries is 1.0, or every miss is a distance tie with the 10th true neighbor
Check with nvidia-smi that GPU memory use after add is in line with the 512 MB base plus Faiss temporary space

steps.title: Choose the GPU graph index and its knobs
steps.learn: CAGRA builds a fixed-degree graph suited to GPUs. Its search has a single-CTA mode (one thread block per query, aimed at larger batches) and a multi-CTA mode (several blocks per query, aimed at small batches). In cuVS, itopk_size is the main recall versus speed knob.

decision.choice: cuVS CAGRA with default graph_degree=64, intermediate_graph_degree=128, algo='auto', itopk_size swept
decision.why: It is a graph index like HNSW, so the comparison is graph vs graph on different hardware, and its two search modes target both ends of the batch-size range you are sweeping.

alternatives.name: GPU IVF-Flat or IVF-PQ (Faiss or cuVS)
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, very fast at big batches, but nprobe tuning and PQ compression change recall in ways unrelated to CPU vs GPU.

alternatives.name: Faiss GpuIndexCagra
alternatives.tradeoff: Same algorithm through the Faiss API (faiss-gpu-cuvs build); pick it if you prefer one library for all GPU indexes.

steps.delegate: In Python write gpu_cagra.py with cuvs and cupy: cagra.build(cagra.IndexParams(metric='sqeuclidean'), cupy_train), cagra.save to disk. Expose search(queries_device, k, itopk_size, algo) via cagra.search(cagra.SearchParams(itopk_size=..., algo=...), index, queries, k). Test: recall@10 on 500 tuning queries increases from itopk_size 32 to 128.
verify: Log build time and compare it with the hnswlib build time from the CPU step
On the tuning split, record recall@10 for itopk_size 32, 64, 128, 256 with algo auto, single_cta and multi_cta

steps.title: Put host-to-device transfers inside the timer
steps.learn: PCIe transfer is much slower than GPU memory bandwidth. Pageable host buffers force the driver to stage through a temporary pinned buffer, so pinned memory transfers faster, and each copy has fixed overhead, so one large copy beats many small ones. GPU calls are asynchronous: sync before stopping a timer.

decision.choice: Timed path per batch: pinned host queries, copy up, search, copy ids back, synchronize; index upload reported separately
decision.why: The question says counting transfer costs. In a real service queries arrive in host memory and results leave it, while the index stays resident, so its upload is a one-time cost.

alternatives.name: Queries already on the GPU
alternatives.tradeoff: Honest only if an embedding model on the same GPU produces them; report it as a second line, not the headline.

alternatives.name: Pageable numpy buffers
alternatives.tradeoff: What naive code does; slower copies. Measure it once to show how much pinning buys.

steps.delegate: In Python write transfer.py with cupy: allocate pinned host buffers with cupy.cuda.alloc_pinned_memory wrapped as numpy arrays, a function run_batch(index_fn, host_queries) that copies to device, calls the search, copies ids back to a pinned buffer, and synchronizes the stream. Time with cupy CUDA events around the whole path. Test: returned ids equal those from calling search on device arrays directly.
verify: Measure H2D bandwidth for a 4096 x 128 float32 batch with pinned and with pageable buffers and log both
For batch size 1, record what fraction of total time is transfer versus search

steps.title: Overlap copies with search using streams
steps.learn: Copies and kernels can run at the same time only with pinned host memory, non-default streams and a GPU that supports concurrent copy and execution. With two streams, batch i+1 uploads while batch i searches, hiding part of the transfer cost at large batch sizes.

decision.choice: Double buffering: two cupy streams, each with its own cuVS Resources and pinned staging buffers
decision.why: It is the standard way to hide PCIe time without changing the index, and it separates transfer cost that is inherent from cost that is just serialization.

alternatives.name: Single stream, synchronous
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and the honest worst case; keep it as the reference line.

alternatives.name: CUDA graphs or a persistent kernel
alternatives.tradeoff: Cut launch overhead for tiny batches, but add complexity and tie you to library internals.

steps.delegate: Extend transfer.py: run_stream(index_fn, all_queries, batch_size) using two cupy.cuda.Stream objects and cuvs.common.Resources(stream=s.ptr) per stream, alternating pinned buffers; upload with ndarray.set(host, stream=s) and download with ndarray.get(stream=s, out=pinned, blocking=False). Return total wall time for all batches. Test: ids from the pipelined run equal ids from the synchronous run for every query.
verify: Capture one run in Nsight Systems and confirm copies on one stream overlap search kernels on the other
Compare total time for 8,000 held-out queries at batch 1024, synchronous vs pipelined

steps.title: Tune each index to the same recall target
steps.learn: QPS means nothing without recall: a looser index is always faster. Pick target recalls such as 0.90 and 0.95, and for each index choose the cheapest ef or itopk_size that reaches the target on the tuning split. Only then run the held-out split, once.

decision.choice: Fix two recall targets, tune on the 2,000 tuning queries, report held-out QPS and recall
decision.why: It compares hardware at matched accuracy and keeps the 8,000 held-out queries untouched by tuning, so reported recall is not optimistic.

alternatives.name: Full Pareto curves only
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows everything, but a crossover batch size is harder to read off; keep the curves as a figure anyway.

alternatives.name: Fixed default parameters
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but each library's defaults sit at different recall, so the comparison is unfair.

steps.delegate: Write tune.py: for each index and each target recall, sweep its knob (hnswlib ef in [10..800], CAGRA itopk_size in [16..512]) on the tuning split at batch 1024, choose the smallest value meeting the target, write chosen params to params.json. Test: a fake index whose recall is a known function of the knob returns the expected choice.
verify: params.json lists one setting per index per target and was written before any held-out run
Held-out recall for each chosen setting is within 0.01 of its tuning recall, or you note the gap

steps.title: Measure QPS and recall across batch sizes
steps.learn: Sweep batch sizes 1, 8, 64, 512, 4096 over the held-out queries. Baselines from the prove-it: CPU HNSW at all cores. Pitfalls: first calls include CUDA context creation and lazy initialization, so warm up; GPU clocks and CPU turbo drift, so repeat runs and report the median; QPS hides per-batch latency.

decision.choice: One harness script, warmup then 5 repeats per point, median QPS plus per-batch p50 and p99 latency
decision.why: Small batches are about latency and big ones about throughput; reporting both shows when the GPU win requires waiting to fill a batch.

alternatives.name: ann-benchmarks harness
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard and comparable to published plots, but adapting it to time host-to-device copies per batch size is extra work.

alternatives.name: Single timed run per point
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but noise from clocks and caches can flip a close crossover.

steps.delegate: Write bench.py: for each index (hnswlib, GPU flat, CAGRA sync, CAGRA pipelined) and batch size, warm up with 2 batches, run all 8,000 held-out queries 5 times, record QPS, recall@10, per-batch p50/p99 latency to results.csv with git commit, GPU, CPU and command line. Plot QPS vs batch size per recall target with matplotlib.
verify: results.csv has every index x batch size x recall target cell with 5 repeats
Rerun one cell and confirm median QPS is within 5 percent of the first run, or record the spread
Read the crossover batch size off the plot for each recall target and write it down

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question; (2) numbers for every claim (crossover batch, QPS, recall, transfer share) with GPU, CPU and command; (3) why surprises happened, e.g. transfer dominating at batch 1; (4) assumptions: one dataset, index resident on GPU, one GPU model.
verify: Part 1 states the single question in one sentence
Every number in part 2 cites a row of results.csv, the machine and the exact command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result using a measurement (e.g. transfer share)
Part 4 lists assumptions and what is not proven (other dims, filters, multi-GPU, updates)

projects.title: KV-cache memory manager for LLM serving
projects.problem: Uneven request lengths fragment GPU memory (the PagedAttention problem)
projects.proveIt: Concurrent requests served and memory wasted vs naive allocation
projects.question: With a fixed GPU memory budget for the KV cache, how many more concurrent requests does block-based paging serve than contiguous per-request allocation?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the trace
steps.learn: Two numbers: concurrent requests running per decode step, and the share of the KV budget not holding real tokens, both under the same budget. Trace: ShareGPT first human turn and first reply, tokenized, with Poisson arrivals, the setup the PagedAttention paper used.
verify: README states the question, both metrics, the KV budget in bytes and the model shape before any code exists
Sample requests with a fixed seed, split them into a tuning trace and a held-out trace, and save both to disk now
Write down the paper's motivating figure: prior systems used only 20.4% to 38.2% of KV memory for actual token states

steps.title: Turn ShareGPT into a request trace
steps.learn: Output length is unknown when a request arrives, which is the whole problem. vLLM's ShareGPT loader takes the first two turns of each conversation, tokenizes them, and by default drops pairs with prompt or output under 4 tokens, prompts over 1024 tokens, or a total over 2048.

decision.choice: ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json, OPT tokenizer, vLLM's default length filters, Poisson arrivals
decision.why: Real prompt and reply lengths with high variance are what cause fragmentation; matching vLLM's filters keeps your trace comparable to theirs and within OPT's 2048 context.

alternatives.name: Alpaca instructions
alternatives.tradeoff: Much shorter prompts and outputs with lower variance; good as a second trace to show where paging matters less.

alternatives.name: Synthetic lengths from a fixed distribution
alternatives.tradeoff: Fully controllable, but you choose the variance that drives the result, so it proves less.

steps.delegate: In Python write trace.py: load the ShareGPT JSON, keep entries with at least 2 conversations, tokenize turn 0 and turn 1 with transformers AutoTokenizer('facebook/opt-125m'), apply filters (min 4, prompt <= 1024, total <= 2048), sample N with a seed, assign Poisson arrival times at rate R, write trace.jsonl with id, arrival, prompt_len, output_len. Tests: no record violates a filter; same seed gives an identical file.
verify: Plot histograms of prompt_len and output_len and record mean, median and max of each
Confirm every record satisfies the filters by a separate check, not by the filter code

steps.title: Compute bytes per token and fix the budget
steps.learn: Each token stores a key and a value vector in every layer. For OPT-13B (40 layers, hidden size 5120, FP16) that is 2 x 5120 x 40 x 2 bytes, about 800 KB per token, so one 2048-token request can need about 1.6 GB.

decision.choice: Model the OPT-13B shape at FP16 and a fixed KV budget (for example 12 GiB), expressed in tokens
decision.why: Using the paper's model makes your waste numbers comparable to its figure, and a token-denominated budget lets the simulator run on any machine.

alternatives.name: A grouped-query attention model
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer KV heads means fewer bytes per token and more requests fit; use it to show the budget effect, but numbers no longer match the paper.

alternatives.name: Budget from your own GPU's free memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Realistic for your box, but results depend on your GPU and weights size, which are not the question.

steps.delegate: Write kvshape.py: bytes_per_token(num_layers, num_kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes) and tokens_in_budget(budget_bytes, ...). Read OPT-13B values from its Hugging Face config.json. Tests: OPT-13B gives 819,200 bytes per token; budget math round-trips.
verify: Hand-compute bytes per token for OPT-13B and match the function output
Record the budget in bytes and in tokens in the README

steps.title: Build the contiguous allocation baseline
steps.learn: Contiguous systems reserve one chunk per request sized for its possible output. The paper names three wastes: slots reserved for future tokens, internal fragmentation from over-provisioning, and external fragmentation from the allocator. Its Orca baselines use a buddy allocator with Max, Pow2 and Oracle reservations.

decision.choice: Buddy allocator over the token budget, three reservation policies: Max (2048), Pow2 (up to 2x output), Oracle (exact)
decision.why: It matches the baselines in the paper, and Oracle is an upper bound no real contiguous system can reach, so beating it is a strong result.

alternatives.name: First-fit free list
alternatives.tradeoff: No power-of-two rounding, so less internal waste, but external fragmentation grows and allocation is a list scan.

alternatives.name: One torch.empty per request
alternatives.tradeoff: Real GPU memory via PyTorch's caching allocator, but its internal reuse hides which waste category you are paying.

steps.delegate: In Python write naive.py: a BuddyAllocator over a power-of-two token arena (alloc(n) returns offset or None, free(offset)), and NaiveManager(policy) that on admission reserves prompt_len + reserved_output tokens per policy. Expose accounting: used, reserved_future, internal_frag, external_frag. Tests: buddy split/merge returns the arena to one free block after freeing all; accounting categories sum to the budget.
verify: Allocate and free 1,000 random sizes and confirm the arena coalesces back to one block
For a 3-request toy trace, hand-compute each waste category and match the accounting

steps.title: Choose the block size and the physical pool
steps.learn: PagedAttention splits the KV cache into equal fixed-size blocks, so there is no external fragmentation and waste per request is limited to its last partial block. The paper found 16 tokens large enough to use the GPU well yet small enough to limit internal fragmentation, and made 16 vLLM's default.

decision.choice: Preallocate the whole budget as N blocks of 16 tokens, managed by a free list of block ids
decision.why: One upfront allocation means no allocator calls during decoding, and 16 tokens keeps per-request waste to at most 15 token slots.

alternatives.name: Block size 1
alternatives.tradeoff: No internal fragmentation, but a block-table entry per token and poor parallelism when reading KV; the paper notes small blocks underuse the GPU.

alternatives.name: Block size 128
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer table entries, but short requests waste most of a block; the paper saw large blocks hurt on the short Alpaca trace.

steps.delegate: In Python write blockpool.py: BlockPool(num_blocks) with allocate() returning a block id or None, free(id), num_free(). Optionally back it with one torch tensor of shape [num_blocks, 2, layers, block_size, kv_heads, head_dim] on the GPU. Tests: allocate all then one more returns None; double free raises; num_free is exact after random alloc/free sequences.
verify: With the GPU tensor option, check torch.cuda.memory_allocated() rises by the predicted pool size
Random alloc/free fuzz test (10,000 ops) never hands out the same block twice

steps.title: Map logical blocks to physical blocks per request
steps.learn: Like OS paging, each request keeps a block table from logical block index to physical block id. A new physical block is taken only when the last one is full, so memory grows with tokens actually generated, not with the possible maximum.

decision.choice: Per-request list of int block ids, grown on demand; flatten to a padded int32 tensor for the attention step
decision.why: It is the simplest structure that gives on-demand growth and lets the attention code find token t at block t // B, offset t % B.

alternatives.name: Contiguous chunk with realloc and copy
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps kernels unchanged, but each growth copies the whole cache and peaks at old plus new size.

alternatives.name: CUDA virtual memory mapping (vAttention)
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps the cache contiguous in virtual memory so stock kernels work, but relies on CUDA virtual memory APIs and workarounds for their limitations.

steps.delegate: In Python write paged.py: PagedManager(pool, block_size) with add_request(id, prompt_len), append_token(id) that allocates a block when the last is full (returns False if the pool is empty), free_request(id), and block_table(id). Accounting: used tokens vs allocated slots. Tests: after k appends the table length is ceil(len / B); free returns every block; waste per request never exceeds B - 1.
verify: For a request of length 37 with B=16, check the table has 3 blocks and waste is 11 slots
Assert across a full trace replay that per-request waste is always below the block size

steps.title: Prove attention over blocks equals contiguous attention
steps.learn: Attention must read keys and values through the block table instead of one contiguous tensor. The result has to equal contiguous attention up to floating point tolerance, or the memory savings are meaningless. The paper reports its paged kernel was 20 to 26% slower than a highly tuned contiguous one.

decision.choice: Reference implementation: gather K/V by block table in PyTorch, then call scaled_dot_product_attention
decision.why: This project is about memory management, so a simple correct reference is enough; it pins down the layout before any fast kernel is attempted.

alternatives.name: Triton kernel reading blocks directly
alternatives.tradeoff: Avoids the gather copy and teaches the real kernel, but is a project of its own to make fast and correct.

alternatives.name: Existing paged kernels (vLLM, FlashInfer)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and tested, but you must match their exact cache layout and you learn less about the mapping.

steps.delegate: In Python with PyTorch write paged_attn.py: write_kv(pool, block_table, pos, k, v) and paged_attention(q, pool, block_table, seq_len) that gathers K/V and calls torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention. Tests: for random lengths 1 to 300 and shuffled physical block ids, output matches SDPA on contiguous K/V under torch.testing.assert_close (float32).
verify: Test passes for at least 50 random lengths including lengths that are exact multiples of the block size
With facebook/opt-125m, store a prompt's per-layer K/V into blocks, read them back through the table, and confirm exact equality

steps.title: Schedule requests and preempt when blocks run out
steps.learn: vLLM serves requests first come first served and, when blocks run out, preempts the most recently arrived ones, evicting all of a sequence's blocks or none. Evicted state is either swapped to CPU memory or recomputed later from prompt plus generated tokens.

decision.choice: Iteration-level FCFS loop; on block shortage preempt newest requests and recompute them on resume
decision.why: Recomputation needs no CPU block pool. The paper found swapping costly at small block sizes because of many small PCIe copies, recomputation overhead never above 20% of swapping's latency, and the two comparable at block sizes 16 to 64.

alternatives.name: Swap blocks to pinned CPU memory
alternatives.tradeoff: No repeated compute, but many small PCIe copies per block; better with large blocks.

alternatives.name: Reserve max blocks at admission, never preempt
alternatives.tradeoff: No preemption logic, but it reintroduces reservation waste and lowers concurrency.

steps.delegate: Write sim.py: discrete step simulator. Each step: admit waiting requests in arrival order while the pool can hold their prompt blocks, append one token to every running request, preempt newest running requests when append fails (free all their blocks, requeue with prompt_len + generated), finish requests at output_len. Same loop drives NaiveManager. Log per step: running count, waste breakdown, preemptions. Tests: every request finishes; tokens generated equal output_len.
verify: On a tiny trace with a 64-token budget, hand-trace which request is preempted and match the log
Confirm no request ever finishes with fewer or more tokens than its output_len

steps.title: Share prompt blocks with copy-on-write
steps.learn: When several samples come from one prompt, their block tables can point to the same physical prompt blocks. A per-block reference count tracks sharers; a write to a shared block first copies it (copy-on-write), so only the last partial block is ever copied.

decision.choice: Reference-counted blocks; fork(request, n) shares all blocks; copy-on-write on first append into a shared block
decision.why: It shows the second benefit of paging, sharing, with little code, and the accounting change (count a shared block once) is easy to verify.

alternatives.name: No sharing
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest; each sample copies the prompt KV. Fine if your trace has no parallel sampling.

alternatives.name: Radix-tree prefix cache across requests (SGLang)
alternatives.tradeoff: Reuses common prefixes between different requests too, but needs a tree, eviction policy and matching on tokens.

steps.delegate: Extend paged.py with refcounts: fork(src_id, new_id) copies the block table and increments refcounts; append_token on a block with refcount > 1 allocates a new block, records a copy, decrements the old count. free decrements and returns blocks at zero. Tests: fork then free both returns all blocks; copies happen only on the last partial block.
verify: Fork a 40-token prompt into 4 samples with B=16 and confirm 3 physical prompt blocks, not 12
Count copy-on-write copies in a run and check it equals forks that wrote into a partial shared block

steps.title: Measure concurrency and waste against the baselines
steps.learn: Replay the held-out trace through paged and the three contiguous baselines at the same budget and arrival rate. The simulator is deterministic, so the pitfalls are accounting ones: count waste over time, not just at the end, and count a shared block once.

decision.choice: Report mean and peak running requests, time-averaged waste split by category, preemptions and recomputed tokens
decision.why: These answer the prove-it directly; time-averaging matters because waste peaks when many requests are mid-generation.

alternatives.name: Measure on a real serving engine
alternatives.tradeoff: Real latency numbers, but you would be measuring the whole engine, not your manager.

alternatives.name: Final memory snapshot only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but misses peak waste and is dominated by whichever requests happen to be running at the end.

steps.delegate: Write bench.py: run sim.py on the held-out trace for paged (B = 1, 16, 128) and naive (Max, Pow2, Oracle), at 3 arrival rates. Write results.csv with config, mean/peak running, waste by category, preemptions, recomputed tokens, git commit and command line. Plot running requests and waste over time with matplotlib.
verify: results.csv has every manager x block size x arrival rate cell
Compute paged vs Oracle mean concurrency ratio and paged waste share from the CSV and write both down
Rerun one cell with the same seed and get byte-identical output

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question; (2) numbers for every claim (concurrency ratio, waste share by category, preemptions) with machine and command; (3) why surprises happened, e.g. Pow2 near Oracle or block 128 losing; (4) assumptions: simulated steps, one model shape, no latency model.
verify: Part 1 states the single question in one sentence
Every number in part 2 cites a row of results.csv, the machine and the exact command
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a measurement
Part 4 lists assumptions and what is not proven (latency, kernel speed, real GPU contention)

projects.title: Prefix-cache-aware LLM request router
projects.problem: Sending requests with shared prompts to the same server saves compute
projects.proveIt: Cache hit rate, time to first token vs round-robin
projects.question: Does routing LLM requests by shared prompt prefix raise KV cache hit rate and cut time to first token versus round-robin, without overloading one server?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the trace
steps.learn: Each server keeps its own prefix cache, so a request only skips prefill for blocks already cached on the server it lands on. Metrics: fleet hit rate (prefix_cache_hits over prefix_cache_queries) and TTFT p50/p99 vs round-robin. Data: Mooncake FAST'25 traces, where equal hash_ids mean shared 512-token blocks.
steps.delegate: In Python, write trace_stats.py that loads Mooncake conversation_trace.jsonl and toolagent_trace.jsonl and prints: request count, input/output length percentiles, how many requests share their first k hash_ids for k=1,2,4,8, and the best possible block hit rate with one infinite cache. Split each trace by timestamp into a tuning window and a later held-out window and write both to disk. Tests on a 5-line fixture.
verify: The question, both metrics and the round-robin baseline are written down before any router code exists
Held-out windows are written to disk with a checksum and are not used again until the final measurement
Note the infinite-cache hit rate per trace: no router can beat it

steps.title: Turn hash_ids into real prompts you can replay
steps.learn: The traces carry no text, only lengths, arrival times and block hashes. To create real cache reuse, every occurrence of a hash_id must expand to the identical token sequence, and the replay must follow the trace timestamps so load is realistic rather than a closed loop.

decision.choice: vllm bench serve with --dataset-name timed_trace, chunk hash size 512, timestamps in ms
decision.why: It already reads timestamp, input_length, output_length and hash_ids, replays on trace timing, and reports TTFT percentiles, so the same client drives every routing policy and only the router changes.

alternatives.name: Write your own replayer
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control over token generation and logging, but you must prove identical hash_ids produce identical tokens and that send times follow the trace.

alternatives.name: prefix_repetition synthetic dataset
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple knobs (prefix length, number of prefixes), but sharing is uniform and unrealistic, so results say little about real traffic.

steps.delegate: Write replay.sh that runs vllm bench serve against a --base-url, with --dataset-name timed_trace --dataset-path <window.jsonl> --timed-trace-chunk-hash-size 512 --timed-trace-sec-multiplier 0.001 --percentile-metrics ttft,tpot,e2el --metric-percentiles 50,90,99 --save-result --save-detailed. Pre-filter requests whose input plus output exceeds the model context and log the dropped count. Pass the policy name via --metadata.
verify: Run once against a single server and confirm requests sharing hash_ids actually get prefix hits (prefix_cache_hits grows)
Record how many trace requests were dropped for exceeding context, per window

steps.title: Run identical workers with prefix caching on
steps.learn: vLLM hashes each full KV block together with its parent block hash, caches only full blocks, and evicts freed blocks in LRU order. Cache capacity per worker is set by GPU memory left after weights, so a smaller cache makes routing matter more. Prefix caching only speeds prefill, not decode.

decision.choice: N separate vLLM servers of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, --enable-prefix-caching, same flags
decision.why: A small model with a 32K context fits long trace prompts, leaves room to run several workers, and keeps every worker identical so differences come from routing only.

alternatives.name: SGLang workers
alternatives.tradeoff: Radix-tree prefix cache and a ready cache-aware router to compare with, but then engine and router change together.

alternatives.name: Engine-internal data parallel
alternatives.tradeoff: One command for many replicas, but the engine's own load balancing hides the routing decision you want to study.

steps.delegate: Write launch_workers.sh that starts N vllm serve processes for Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on ports 8001.. with --enable-prefix-caching, a fixed --gpu-memory-utilization, fixed --max-model-len and a pinned GPU per worker (CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES). Add a health wait loop on /health and a script that scrapes /metrics and sums vllm:prefix_cache_hits and vllm:prefix_cache_queries across workers.
verify: All workers report the same model, block size and max model length in their startup logs
Two identical long prompts sent to one worker: the second shows higher prefix_cache_hits and lower TTFT

steps.title: Build a streaming proxy with round-robin and least-load
steps.learn: The router sits on the critical path of TTFT, so it must stream tokens through without buffering and add little latency. It also needs a live count of in-flight requests per worker, which every smarter policy uses as its load signal.

decision.choice: Async Python proxy (FastAPI plus httpx streaming) with pluggable policy: round_robin, least_inflight
decision.why: Easy to change policies daily; the router does light work per request compared with prefill, and you will measure its overhead directly instead of assuming it.

alternatives.name: Rust (tokio plus axum)
alternatives.tradeoff: Lower and steadier overhead under high concurrency, but slower to iterate on policy logic.

alternatives.name: Envoy or nginx upstream
alternatives.tradeoff: Production-grade proxying, but custom prefix-aware choices need an external picker service, as llm-d does.

steps.delegate: In Python with FastAPI and httpx.AsyncClient, write router.py exposing /v1/completions and /v1/chat/completions that forwards to one of N workers and streams the SSE body back chunk by chunk. Policy interface: choose(request_tokens, workers) returning a worker. Track in-flight counts, decremented in a finally block. Tests: streaming passes chunks through unmodified, in-flight returns to 0 after client disconnect.
verify: Router overhead: TTFT through the router minus direct TTFT on a 1-worker setup, at p50 and p99
Replay the tuning window with round_robin and record fleet hit rate and TTFT p50/p99 as baseline row 1

steps.title: Simulate routing policies on the trace before using GPUs
steps.learn: Hit rate depends on which worker each request lands on and on per-worker eviction, which you can simulate from hash_ids alone. A simulator lets you compare many policies and knobs in seconds and gives an expected hit rate to check the real system against.

decision.choice: Per-worker LRU block cache with a fixed capacity in blocks, matching prefix only
decision.why: It mirrors the cached-full-blocks-and-LRU behavior in vLLM's design doc closely enough to rank policies, and capacity can be set from each worker's logged KV cache size.

alternatives.name: Infinite caches
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to build and gives an upper bound, but hides eviction, which is exactly where bad routing hurts.

alternatives.name: Skip simulation, test on GPUs
alternatives.tradeoff: No model mismatch, but each policy run takes the full trace duration and costs GPU time.

steps.delegate: In Python, write sim.py: N workers, each an OrderedDict LRU of block hashes with capacity C blocks; for each request, hits = longest prefix of hash_ids present on the chosen worker; then insert all its blocks. Policies are the same classes the router uses. Output hit rate per policy and per worker load share. Tests: a hand-built 6-request trace with known hits for round_robin and for a sticky policy.
verify: Simulated round_robin hit rate is within a few points of the measured baseline; explain any gap
Plot simulated hit rate vs cache capacity for round_robin and for one worker with N times capacity

steps.title: Route by longest matched prefix in a router-side tree
steps.learn: The router cannot see worker caches directly, so it keeps an approximate radix tree of prefixes it has sent to each worker and picks the worker with the longest match. It must tokenize with the worker's exact tokenizer (or hash chat text consistently) so router prefixes line up with worker blocks.

decision.choice: Approximate per-worker prefix tree updated on each routed request, keyed by token blocks
decision.why: No worker changes or extra protocol: SGLang's router uses the same idea, keeping an approximate tree from requests it has routed rather than syncing worker state.

alternatives.name: Exact state from KV cache events
alternatives.tradeoff: vLLM can publish KV cache events and Dynamo's router consumes them, giving true cache state, but adds an event pipeline and failure modes.

alternatives.name: Consistent hashing on the first k blocks
alternatives.tradeoff: Stateless and cheap, but blind to load and to longer shared prefixes, and one hot prefix pins to one worker.

steps.delegate: In Python, add PrefixTreePolicy: tokenize the prompt with the worker model's Hugging Face tokenizer, split into fixed blocks, hash each block chained with its parent hash, and keep a trie of block hashes per worker. choose() returns the worker with the longest matched chain, ties broken by fewest in-flight. Insert after routing. Tests: shared prefix goes to the same worker; disjoint prompts spread; tokenizer mismatch test fails loudly.
verify: In the simulator, tree routing beats round_robin hit rate on the tuning window; record both
On GPUs, router-predicted matched tokens per request correlate with the worker's prefix_cache_hits delta

steps.title: Guard against hot prefixes overloading one worker
steps.learn: Pure affinity sends every request with a popular prefix (a shared system prompt) to one worker, whose queue then inflates TTFT and wipes out the prefill savings. A good policy uses cache match only when it is long enough and falls back to load when workers are imbalanced.

decision.choice: Use match only if matched/input ratio passes a threshold and load imbalance is under abs and rel limits
decision.why: This is the shape of SGLang's cache_aware policy (defaults: cache-threshold 0.3, balance-abs-threshold 64, balance-rel-threshold 1.5), so you start from tested knobs and tune on your trace.

alternatives.name: Weighted score: match minus alpha times load
alternatives.tradeoff: One smooth knob, but alpha depends on prompt length and hardware and needs retuning per workload.

alternatives.name: Power of two choices among top matches
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap randomness spreads hot prefixes, but may skip the single worker holding a long prefix.

steps.delegate: In Python, extend PrefixTreePolicy with cache_threshold, balance_abs, balance_rel: if max(inflight) - min(inflight) > balance_abs and max > balance_rel * min, route to least in-flight; else route to the longest match if match ratio >= cache_threshold, otherwise to least in-flight. Expose knobs via CLI. Tests for each branch with fake loads. Sweep knobs in sim.py on the tuning window only.
verify: Count trace requests sharing only their first hash_id; show that a 1-block match does not decide routing
Max worker share of requests stays within your chosen bound in the replay
Knobs are chosen on the tuning window and frozen before the held-out run

steps.title: Keep the router tree honest under eviction and failures
steps.learn: The router's tree drifts from reality: workers evict blocks, restart with empty caches, or fail. A stale tree routes to a worker that no longer holds the prefix, or to a dead one. The tree also needs a size cap, or router memory grows with traffic.

decision.choice: Cap tree size with LRU eviction, clear a worker's subtree on restart, retry failed requests elsewhere
decision.why: These fix the common drift sources without needing worker events, and each is testable by killing a worker during a replay.

alternatives.name: Subscribe to KV cache events
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate removals, but you must handle lost or reordered events and a dead event channel.

alternatives.name: Time-based expiry only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but expiry time is a guess that ignores actual cache pressure on each worker.

steps.delegate: In Python, add a max_tree_blocks cap with LRU removal across all workers, a health checker polling /health every few seconds that drops the worker's subtree and removes it from the pool on failure and re-adds it empty, and one retry to another worker for connection errors before the first streamed byte. Tests: tree size never exceeds cap; killed worker gets no new requests; retry happens only before streaming starts.
verify: Kill one worker mid-replay: no client requests fail beyond those in flight on it, and the rest of the run completes
Router resident memory stays flat over a full window with the cap on

steps.title: Measure hit rate and TTFT on the held-out window
steps.learn: Every run must start from cold caches, use the same held-out window, worker count and flags, and differ only in policy. Hit rate comes from worker counters, not from the router's own predictions, so the router does not grade itself. Sweep load with the time multiplier to find where policies diverge.
steps.delegate: Write bench_all.sh: for policy in random, round_robin, least_inflight, prefix_tree, prefix_tree_balanced, restart workers, wait for health, scrape counters, run replay.sh on the held-out window, scrape counters again, and append policy, hit rate delta, TTFT p50/p90/p99, throughput and failures to results.csv. Repeat each 3 times and at 2 or 3 load levels.
verify: results.csv has 3 runs per policy and load level with spread reported, not just the best run
Hit rate is computed from vllm:prefix_cache_hits and queries deltas, not router logs
GPU model, driver, vLLM version, model, N workers and the exact commands are recorded

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up has four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why the surprising results happened (for example where hit rate rose but p99 TTFT did not); and assumptions plus what this does not prove (one trace source, one model size, synthetic tokens).
verify: Part 1 states the single question and the round-robin baseline
Part 2 gives hit rate and TTFT p50/p99 per policy with machine, versions and commands
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result using simulator or counter data
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including synthetic prompt tokens and the context-length filter

projects.title: Search pipeline under a 50 ms p99 budget
projects.problem: Retrieve + filter + rerank must stay fast under load
projects.proveIt: p99 at rising queries/sec, with batching and caching
projects.question: How many queries/sec can a retrieve, filter and rerank pipeline serve while p99 stays under 50 ms, and how much do batching and caching raise that?

steps.title: Frame the budget, the corpus and the quality floor
steps.learn: The metric is the highest offered queries/sec at which end-to-end p99 stays under 50 ms, with quality (RR@10 on MS MARCO dev) held above a floor so speedups cannot quietly drop relevance. Use MS MARCO passages (8.8M) and the 6,980-query dev/small set.
steps.delegate: In Python with ir_datasets, write prepare.py: load msmarco-passage docs, dev/small queries and qrels; build a seeded corpus subset (all judged passages plus random fill to a target size, or the full collection); add a synthetic per-passage attribute (seeded category id) for filtering; split queries into a tuning set and a frozen held-out set. Save as parquet with checksums. Tests: subset contains every judged passage.
verify: Question, 50 ms p99 target and RR@10 floor are written before any pipeline code
Held-out query split and corpus subset are saved with checksums and untouched until the final measurement
Record CPU model, cores, RAM, GPU if any, OS and Python versions

steps.title: Embed passages and build the ANN index
steps.learn: Retrieval must return a good candidate set in a few ms. HNSW trades recall for speed through ef at query time, while M and ef_construction set graph quality and memory. bge-small-en-v1.5 gives 384-dim vectors and suggests an instruction prefix on short queries for passage retrieval.

decision.choice: bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings in an hnswlib HNSW index (cosine), ef tuned for recall@100
decision.why: Small vectors keep memory and distance cost low, and hnswlib exposes M, ef_construction and set_ef directly plus a per-query label filter, which the next step needs.

alternatives.name: FAISS IVF-PQ
alternatives.tradeoff: Much less memory for big corpora, but lower recall per ms at small k and more knobs (nlist, nprobe, code size).

alternatives.name: Exact brute force
alternatives.tradeoff: Perfect recall and simple, but cost grows with corpus size and blows the budget at millions of passages on CPU.

steps.delegate: In Python with sentence-transformers and hnswlib, write index.py: embed passages with BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 (normalized), queries with the instruction prefix from the model card; build hnswlib.Index(space='cosine', dim=384) with chosen M and ef_construction; save index. Script recall_at_k.py compares set_ef sweeps against exact top-100 on 500 tuning queries. Tests: save and load return identical results (set ef again after load).
verify: Recall@100 vs exact search and per-query latency are recorded for at least 4 ef values
Chosen ef reaches your recall target on tuning queries only

steps.title: Apply the metadata filter inside or after the search
steps.learn: Post-filtering fetches top-k then drops non-matching hits, so selective filters return too few results. Filtering during the graph walk keeps k results but explores more nodes as selectivity drops, raising latency. Test 1%, 10% and 50% selectivity.

decision.choice: In-search filter via hnswlib knn_query(filter=...), with exact brute force below a selectivity cutoff
decision.why: In-search filtering keeps result counts right, and for very selective filters scanning the few matching vectors exactly is cheaper than walking a graph that mostly skips nodes.

alternatives.name: Post-filter with overfetch
alternatives.tradeoff: No index changes, but needs overfetch growing with 1/selectivity and still under-returns on rare categories.

alternatives.name: FAISS IDSelector in SearchParameters
alternatives.tradeoff: Same idea inside FAISS; Python-defined selectors are slow, so use built-in selector types.

steps.delegate: In Python, write filtered_search(q, category, k): estimate selectivity from category counts; above a cutoff call index.knn_query(q, k, filter=callable) with num_threads=1 (the README notes filtered search is slow in multithreaded Python mode); below it, brute-force over that category's vectors with numpy. Tests: every result matches the filter; k results returned when at least k exist; both paths agree on a small corpus.
verify: Latency p50/p99 and result count per query for 1%, 10% and 50% selectivity, both paths
The cutoff is chosen from these curves on tuning queries, not guessed

steps.title: Rerank the top candidates with a cross-encoder
steps.learn: A cross-encoder reads query and passage together, so it is far more accurate than the bi-encoder but costs one model forward per pair. Rerank latency grows roughly with candidate count, so the number of candidates is the main lever between quality and the 50 ms budget.

decision.choice: cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 on the top N, N chosen from an RR@10 vs latency curve
decision.why: It is trained on MS MARCO, small enough for tight budgets, and its model card lists smaller and larger siblings to swap in if the budget needs it.

alternatives.name: ms-marco-MiniLM-L2-v2 or TinyBERT-L2
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster per pair, so more candidates fit, at lower reported quality on MS MARCO dev.

alternatives.name: No reranker, dense only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easily inside the budget, but loses the quality jump the rerank stage gives.

steps.delegate: In Python with sentence_transformers.CrossEncoder, write rerank(query, passages) returning sorted ids and scores, batched internally. Script rerank_curve.py: for N in 10, 20, 50, 100 on tuning queries, report RR@10 (computed with qrels, not the model's scores) and rerank time p50/p99 at batch size N. Tests: deterministic ordering for fixed inputs; empty candidate list returns empty.
verify: RR@10 vs N and rerank latency vs N table from tuning queries
Chosen N meets the RR@10 floor with rerank p99 well under 50 ms at one query in flight

steps.title: Serve the pipeline with per-stage timing and a deadline
steps.learn: End-to-end latency is queueing plus embed, search, filter and rerank. Without per-stage timers you cannot tell which stage owns the tail. A request deadline, set at arrival, lets later stages know how much budget is left.

decision.choice: One async HTTP service; CPU-bound model and index calls in a bounded worker pool
decision.why: Keeps the event loop free to accept requests while compute runs elsewhere, and a bounded pool makes queueing explicit and measurable instead of hidden in the OS scheduler.

alternatives.name: Separate embed, search and rerank services
alternatives.tradeoff: Independent scaling, but every network hop adds latency and tail variance inside a 50 ms budget.

alternatives.name: Synchronous multi-process server
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and no async pitfalls, but per-process model copies cost memory and cross-request batching is harder.

steps.delegate: In Python with FastAPI and uvicorn, write server.py with POST /search {query, category, k}. Stamp arrival time; run embed, filtered_search and rerank in a fixed-size ThreadPoolExecutor; return results plus per-stage ms and queue wait. Export stage histograms via prometheus_client. Tests: response fields present; stage times sum to within 1 ms of total; deadline value passed to each stage.
verify: At 1 request in flight, per-stage p50 and p99 are recorded and the biggest stage is named
Results from the server match the offline pipeline for 100 tuning queries

steps.title: Build an open-loop load generator before tuning
steps.learn: A closed-loop client waits for each reply before sending more, so when the server stalls it sends less and the tail disappears from the numbers (coordinated omission). Open-loop load sends on a fixed schedule and times each request from when it should have been sent.

decision.choice: Constant arrival rate load with intended-start timing, recorded in HdrHistogram
decision.why: This is how wrk2 and k6's constant-arrival-rate executor model load; it keeps offered load independent of server speed so the p99 curve is honest.

alternatives.name: wrk2 with a Lua script
alternatives.tradeoff: Proven and precise at high rates, but query bodies and per-request quality checks need Lua scripting.

alternatives.name: k6 constant-arrival-rate
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy scripting and reporting, but needs enough preAllocatedVUs and maxVUs to actually reach the offered rate; check achieved vs offered.

steps.delegate: Write loadgen.py (Python asyncio plus aiohttp, or a k6 script) that sends tuning queries at a fixed rate R for D seconds after a warmup, measures latency from scheduled send time, records into HdrHistogram, and reports offered vs achieved rate, p50/p99/p99.9 and errors. Sweep R. Tests: with a fake server sleeping 10 ms then stalling 1 s once, the report shows the stall in p99.
verify: The fake-stall test shows a tail that a closed-loop client misses; keep both outputs
Baseline curve: p99 vs offered rate with no batching or caching, and the rate where p99 crosses 50 ms

steps.title: Batch embed and rerank work across concurrent queries
steps.learn: Model forwards are cheaper per item in batches, but waiting to fill a batch adds latency. A dynamic batcher sends when the batch is full or a short max wait expires, so at low load it barely waits and at high load it gains throughput.

decision.choice: In-process dynamic batcher per model with max batch size and max wait in microseconds
decision.why: Same shape as Triton's dynamic batcher (max_queue_delay_microseconds), but in-process so there is no network hop inside the 50 ms budget.

alternatives.name: Triton Inference Server
alternatives.tradeoff: Mature batching and scheduling, but adds a service hop, deployment and model export work.

alternatives.name: No batching, more threads
alternatives.tradeoff: No added wait, but per-pair overhead stays and CPU contention can widen the tail at high load.

steps.delegate: In Python asyncio, write Batcher(fn, max_batch, max_wait_us): callers await submit(item); a loop collects items until max_batch or max_wait, runs fn on the batch in the executor, and resolves each future. Use it for query embedding and for rerank pairs (pairs from several queries in one forward). Tests: results map back to the right caller; single request waits at most max_wait; exception fails only that batch.
verify: p99 vs offered rate with batching on, overlaid on the baseline curve
Report the max_wait and max_batch chosen on tuning queries and the batch-size histogram at the knee

steps.title: Cache results and embeddings with honest repeat rates
steps.learn: A result cache skips the whole pipeline for repeated queries, but its benefit depends entirely on the repeat rate, which MS MARCO dev queries (mostly unique) do not have. So the repeat distribution is an assumption you must state and vary, and cache keys must include the filter.

decision.choice: Bounded LRU result cache keyed by normalized query text plus filter, plus a query embedding cache
decision.why: Simple, bounded memory, and normalization (case, whitespace) raises hits without changing meaning; a separate embedding cache still helps when the filter differs.

alternatives.name: Semantic cache on embedding similarity
alternatives.tradeoff: More hits on paraphrases, but can return results for a different question and needs a threshold you must validate.

alternatives.name: No cache, spend effort on compute
alternatives.tradeoff: No staleness or skew assumptions, but leaves easy throughput on the table for head queries.

steps.delegate: In Python, add cachetools LRUCache for results (key: normalized query, category, k) and for embeddings (key: normalized query), with size limits from config and hit/miss counters. Extend loadgen.py to draw queries from a Zipf distribution with exponent s over the tuning set, seeded. Tests: cache hit returns identical results; different category misses; cache respects size bound.
verify: p99 vs offered rate for unique queries and for 2 Zipf exponents, with hit rate per run
Results with cache on match cache off for 200 queries

steps.title: Shed or shrink work when the deadline is at risk
steps.learn: Past the knee, queues grow and every request misses the budget. Using the deadline, the server can rerank fewer candidates, skip rerank, or reject early, so most requests still meet 50 ms. Each choice costs quality, which must be measured, not assumed.

decision.choice: Deadline-aware rerank depth: shrink N, then skip rerank, then reject when queue wait exceeds a limit
decision.why: Rerank is the largest controllable cost, and degrading it keeps answering with dense results instead of failing; rejection is the last resort and is counted.

alternatives.name: Reject only (admission control)
alternatives.tradeoff: Accepted requests keep full quality, but more users get errors at peak.

alternatives.name: Do nothing, scale out
alternatives.tradeoff: No quality loss, but needs more machines and does not protect against bursts.

steps.delegate: In Python, before rerank compute remaining = deadline - now; pick N from a table of measured rerank p99 per N that fits remaining; if none fits return dense results flagged degraded; if queue wait exceeds a limit return 503 fast. Log degraded and rejected counts. Tests: with a fake slow reranker, N shrinks; flags set; 503 path does no model work.
verify: Past the baseline knee, p99 stays under 50 ms with degrade on; report degraded and rejected fractions
RR@10 of degraded responses measured against qrels on tuning queries

steps.title: Measure the p99 curve on held-out queries
steps.learn: The final comparison uses held-out queries, a fixed machine, warm-up excluded, runs long enough for stable p99, and only one change per configuration. Report the max rate under 50 ms p99 and RR@10 per configuration so the speed gain and quality cost appear together.
steps.delegate: Write bench_all.sh: for config in baseline, +batching, +cache (each Zipf s), +batching+cache, +degrade, start server with pinned threads, warm up, run loadgen.py over a rate sweep on held-out queries, 3 repeats, append rate, p50/p99/p99.9, achieved rate, errors, degraded and RR@10 to results.csv. Capture one flame graph at the knee with py-spy.
verify: results.csv has 3 repeats per config and rate with spread, from held-out queries only
Max rate under 50 ms p99 and RR@10 reported for each config
Load generator runs on a separate core set or machine, and that setup plus exact commands are recorded

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up has four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why the surprising results happened (for example which stage owned the tail at the knee); and assumptions plus what this does not prove (synthetic filter attribute, assumed query repeat rate, one corpus size).
verify: Part 1 states the question, the 50 ms p99 target and the RR@10 floor
Part 2 has the p99 vs rate curves and max rate per config with machine and commands
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with stage timings or a flame graph
Part 4 lists assumptions: synthetic categories, Zipf repeats, corpus subset, single machine

projects.title: Crash-safe, live-updating search index
projects.problem: Updating text and vector indexes atomically without serving half-written results
projects.proveIt: Zero inconsistent results across crash tests, update-to-visible latency
projects.question: Can a text plus vector index take live updates and crashes while never serving a half-applied update, and how fast do updates become visible?

steps.title: Frame the question, the guarantees and the corpus
steps.learn: A hybrid index has two structures (BM25 postings and a vector graph) that must change together. The two metrics: inconsistent results across crash tests (target zero) and update-to-visible latency (ack to first query that sees it). Corpus: BEIR SciFact, embedded with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dims).
verify: README states the question, both metrics and what counts as an inconsistent result, written before any code
Download SciFact, embed every doc once, save vectors to a file and record its sha256
Generate and save the update workload (inserts, edits, deletes) with a fixed seed; record its sha256

steps.title: Define versions and an independent consistency oracle
steps.learn: Every write carries (doc_id, version) and the server assigns a log sequence number (LSN). A consistent answer is one computed on the exact state after some committed LSN: every returned doc shows the same version on its text side and its vector side, and no acked write is missing after a crash.

decision.choice: Client oracle logs every attempted write; unacked ones may or may not apply; check each response once acks drain
decision.why: A metric must not be graded by the system's own logic. The oracle shares no code with the index: it only knows what the client was told was durable, so bugs in the WAL, publish or recovery path cannot hide from it.

alternatives.name: Server self-check (assertions inside the index)
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and catches some bugs early, but the same bug can corrupt both the data and the check.

alternatives.name: Compare against a rebuild from scratch
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong end-state check after a crash, but says nothing about torn reads seen during live updates.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a crate oracle with: struct Oracle { log: Vec<(u64 lsn, Op)> }; fn state_at(lsn) returning HashMap<DocId, Version>; fn check(resp: &QueryResponse) returning Vec<Violation>, where a response carries snapshot_lsn and per-hit (doc_id, text_version, vector_version). Violation kinds: version mismatch, deleted doc returned, doc newer than snapshot. Unit tests with hand-built logs for each kind.
verify: Feed the oracle three hand-made bad responses (mismatch, deleted doc, future version) and confirm it flags each one
Confirm the oracle crate has no dependency on the index crate in Cargo.toml

steps.title: Build the write-ahead log with checksums and group commit
steps.learn: The WAL is the source of truth: a write is acked only after its record is fsynced. Each record is length + CRC32 + payload (lsn, op, doc_id, version, text, vector), so recovery can detect a torn tail. Group commit lets many writers share one fsync.

decision.choice: Single append-only WAL, one writer thread, group commit: batch pending writes, one fdatasync, then ack all
decision.why: Durability before ack is what makes 'no acked write lost' testable. Batching amortizes the fsync cost, which dominates write latency, and gives one total order of LSNs that both indexes apply.

alternatives.name: fsync per write
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest to reason about, but every write pays a full flush, which caps write throughput.

alternatives.name: Ack before fsync (periodic flush)
alternatives.tradeoff: Much lower write latency, but a power loss can drop acked writes, so you must weaken the guarantee you claim.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement wal.rs: Wal::open(dir), append(batch: &[Op]) returning Result<Vec<Lsn>> that writes framed records (u32 len, u32 crc32 via crc32fast, payload via bincode) then calls sync_data before returning; Wal::replay(from_lsn) returning an iterator that stops cleanly at the first short or bad-CRC record and truncates there. Tests: truncate the file at every byte offset of the last record and confirm replay returns exactly the earlier records.
verify: Run the truncate-at-every-offset test; replay never returns a partial or corrupt record
Measure write latency with and without group commit (batch sizes 1, 8, 64) and record the p50 and p99

steps.title: Apply the log to a BM25 text index with LSN-tagged commits
steps.learn: Tantivy is segment-based: a segment is its atomic unit of indexing and search, and commit publishes and persists pending adds and deletes. An update is delete_term(doc_id) then add, which is idempotent, so replaying a WAL range twice is safe. Each commit can carry a payload: here the highest LSN applied.

decision.choice: Tantivy with ReloadPolicy::Manual; PreparedCommit::set_payload stores the applied LSN
decision.why: Manual reload means the text reader never advances on its own, so the publisher decides when a new text view becomes visible together with the vector view. The payload tells recovery where the text index stopped.

alternatives.name: ReloadPolicy::OnCommitWithDelay
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but the reader advances on a background thread independent of the vector side, which is exactly the torn view to avoid.

alternatives.name: Own inverted index
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control over files and fsync order, but a large build that is not the point of this project.

steps.delegate: In Rust with tantivy, write text.rs: schema with doc_id (STRING, indexed), version (u64, stored), body (TEXT). apply(ops) does delete_term(doc_id) then add_document for upserts. commit_at(lsn) uses prepare_commit, set_payload(lsn), commit. Reader created with ReloadPolicy::Manual. Tests: applying the same ops twice gives identical num_docs and versions; payload after reopen equals the last committed LSN.
verify: Reopen the index after a commit and confirm the commit payload equals the LSN you committed
Apply a 1,000-op batch twice and confirm doc count and stored versions are unchanged the second time

steps.title: Build the vector side: mutable buffer plus sealed HNSW segments
steps.learn: HNSW graphs are cheap to search and expensive to modify; deletes are usually tombstones. So recent vectors live in a small buffer searched exactly, and when it fills it is sealed into an HNSW segment. Each segment has a tombstone set; queries filter tombstoned ids.

decision.choice: Brute-force buffer plus immutable hnsw_rs segments, each with a tombstone set applied via search_filter
decision.why: Immutable segments mirror the text side, so a snapshot is just a list of segments plus tombstone versions. Fresh writes become searchable without rebuilding a graph, which keeps update-to-visible latency low.

alternatives.name: One mutable HNSW with in-place deletes
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer moving parts, but concurrent readers see a graph mid-update, which needs locks and complicates snapshots.

alternatives.name: Exact search only
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivially correct and fine at SciFact scale, but hides the real cost of sealing and merging graphs.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write vec.rs with hnsw_rs: Buffer (Vec of (doc_id, version, [f32;384]), exact cosine top-k) and Segment { hnsw, ids, tombstones: Arc<RoaringBitmap> } where a delete clones the set into a new Arc (never mutate a published one). seal(buffer) builds a segment with parallel_insert. search(q, k) merges top-k across buffer and segments, filtering tombstones. Tests: recall@10 vs exact search over the same live docs above a recorded threshold; old snapshot unaffected by new deletes.
verify: Recall@10 against exact search over the live set, recorded for 3 random query samples
Delete 100 docs and confirm none of them is ever returned

steps.title: Publish text and vector views together as one snapshot
steps.learn: Readers must see the pair (text searcher, vector snapshot) at the same LSN or not at all. Build the new pair off to the side, then swap one pointer. Readers load the pointer once per query, and old snapshots stay alive until the last reader drops its Arc.

decision.choice: Snapshot { lsn, tantivy Searcher, vector segment list } behind arc_swap::ArcSwap; one publisher thread
decision.why: A single atomic pointer swap is the smallest publish step possible, so there is no moment where text and vector disagree. A tantivy Searcher stays on its generation, so holding it in the snapshot freezes the text view.

alternatives.name: RwLock around both indexes
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to get right, but writers block readers during publish and tail latency spikes.

alternatives.name: Per-index versions checked at query time
alternatives.tradeoff: No shared structure, but each query must retry until versions match, and may starve under heavy updates.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write publish.rs: after applying ops up to LSN L to both sides, call text.commit_at(L), reader.reload(), take reader.searcher(), clone the Arc'd vector segment list, and store Arc<Snapshot{lsn:L,..}> in an ArcSwap. Query path: let s = snap.load_full(); run BM25 and vector search on s; return snapshot_lsn and per-hit text and vector versions. Test with loom-free stress: 8 reader threads and 1 writer, oracle reports zero violations.
verify: Run 8 reader threads against a live writer for 10 minutes; the oracle reports zero violations
Build the naive variant (text auto-reload, vector updated in place) and confirm the oracle does flag violations

steps.title: Checkpoint the vector side with an atomic manifest
steps.learn: Sealed segments and tombstones go to files; a manifest lists them plus the checkpoint LSN. Write the manifest to a temp file, fsync it, rename over the old one, then fsync the directory. rename replaces atomically, but the directory entry is only durable after the directory fsync.

decision.choice: Write-temp, fsync file, rename, fsync directory; segment files are immutable and named by id
decision.why: Recovery then sees either the old manifest or the new one, never a half-written one, and every file it names was fsynced first. Immutable files mean a crash can only leave orphans, which are safe to delete.

alternatives.name: Overwrite the manifest in place
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer syscalls, but a crash mid-write leaves a corrupt manifest, so you need a checksum and a fallback copy.

alternatives.name: Store everything in SQLite
alternatives.tradeoff: SQLite provides atomic commit for you, but adds a dependency and moves vector blobs into a database file.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write manifest.rs: save(dir, &Manifest{lsn, segments}) writes manifest.tmp, sync_all, rename to MANIFEST, then opens dir and calls sync_all on it. load(dir) reads MANIFEST and deletes files not listed. Order: segment files are fsynced before the manifest that names them. Test: kill the process at each step boundary (inject a panic hook) and confirm load returns old or new, never an error.
verify: Inject a crash at each of the 4 step boundaries; load always returns the old or new manifest
Confirm via strace -f -e trace=fsync,fdatasync,rename,renameat,renameat2 that the directory fsync happens after the rename

links.label: All File Systems Are Not Created Equal

steps.title: Recover by replaying the log into both sides before serving
steps.learn: After a crash the text index stopped at its commit payload LSN and the vector side at its manifest LSN, and they may differ. Because every op is an idempotent upsert or delete, replay the WAL from the smaller one through the last valid record into both, publish one snapshot, and only then accept queries.

decision.choice: Redo-only recovery from min(text LSN, vector LSN) with idempotent ops; serve only after both reach the WAL end
decision.why: No undo is needed because nothing is visible or acked until it is in the WAL. Idempotent replay removes the need to make the two indexes commit atomically with each other on disk.

alternatives.name: Rebuild both indexes from the WAL
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest correct recovery, but restart time grows with history unless you also compact the WAL.

alternatives.name: Two-phase commit across both stores
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps disk states aligned, but needs prepare records and undo, which is far more code for the same guarantee.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write recover.rs: read text payload LSN and manifest LSN, replay wal from min+1 through text.apply and vec.apply, commit both at the final LSN, publish snapshot, then open the query port. Also truncate WAL segments older than min(checkpoints). Tests: craft states where text is ahead, vector is ahead, and both are behind; each recovers to the same doc set as the oracle.
verify: For the three crafted states, recovered doc set and versions equal the oracle state at the last valid LSN
Record restart time vs WAL length since last checkpoint at three lengths

steps.title: Crash it repeatedly, including lost unsynced writes
steps.learn: kill -9 only tests process crashes: the page cache survives. Power loss also drops data that was written but not fsynced. LazyFS is a FUSE file system that keeps its own page cache and can clear unsynced data or tear writes on command, so it simulates power loss.

decision.choice: Two harnesses: a kill -9 loop on ext4, and LazyFS clear-cache and torn-write faults; oracle checks after each restart
decision.why: Process crashes find ordering bugs between threads; LazyFS finds missing fsyncs (file or directory) that kill -9 can never reveal because the kernel still has the data.

alternatives.name: kill -9 only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy and fast, but misses every missing-fsync bug.

alternatives.name: VM or real power pulls
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic, but slow and hard to repeat, so you get few runs and no exact replay.

steps.delegate: Write a Python harness crash.py: start server, run writer and reader clients that log acks and responses, kill -9 at a random time (seeded), restart, run oracle checks (no acked write lost, zero violations in all responses before and after). Second mode mounts the data dir on LazyFS: kill -9 the server, then send lazyfs::clear-cache to its FIFO (wait on the completed FIFO), then restart. Record the seed of every failing run.
verify: At least 500 kill -9 cycles and 100 LazyFS clear-cache cycles complete with zero violations and zero lost acked writes
Remove the directory fsync on purpose and confirm the LazyFS harness catches it

steps.title: Measure update-to-visible latency and its cost
steps.learn: Update-to-visible latency = time from write ack to the first query snapshot that contains it. It is set by group commit wait, apply time and publish interval. Compare against the naive baseline. Use an open-loop load generator so slow responses do not silently reduce load.

decision.choice: Client logs each ack time and each query receive time; latency is ack to the first response showing the write
decision.why: Writer and query clients run on one machine with one monotonic clock, so no skew, and visibility is judged from real query results checked by the oracle, not from the server's publish log. Sweeping the publish interval shows the latency vs throughput tradeoff.

alternatives.name: Client polls until it sees its write
alternatives.tradeoff: Measures what users see, but polling rate adds error and load.

alternatives.name: Report averages only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but hides the tail where publish and merge pauses live.

steps.delegate: Add a bench binary: open-loop writer at a fixed rate (seeded schedule), 4 query threads, publish intervals 10 ms, 100 ms, 1 s. Record per-LSN ack and publish timestamps into an hdrhistogram, plus write throughput and query p99. Output a CSV row per config with machine info (lscpu, kernel, filesystem, disk model).
verify: CSV has p50, p99 and max visible latency for each publish interval, plus write and query throughput
Each config run 3 times; spread between runs reported next to the numbers
Machine, filesystem, kernel and exact command recorded with the results

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up answers the one question with evidence. Explain surprising results (for example why the visible latency tail tracks merge or seal events) and be explicit about what the crash tests do not cover.
verify: Part 1 states the one question and both metrics
Part 2 gives crash cycle counts, violations, and latency numbers with machine and command for each
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with evidence (trace, strace or timing)
Part 4 lists assumptions (ext4, single node, LazyFS fault model) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Catch-compliance checker
projects.problem: Anglers must know species, size limits and seasons on the spot
projects.concepts: Fine-tuned ViT/CLIP for species, length from a reference marker, RAG over local fishing rules
projects.tryIt: Photograph fish at a pier or fish market next to a ruler; compare measured vs estimated length
projects.question: Can a phone photo of a fish next to a printed marker give the species, its regulated length and a rule check that matches a ruler and the official rules?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and a frozen test set
steps.learn: Three sub-answers must all be right: species, length, and the rule that applies. Score each separately: species top-1 accuracy, length error against a ruler (cm and percent), and how often the verdict (keep, too small, too big, closed) matches a human reading the official rules.

decision.choice: One jurisdiction, 15 to 25 regulated species, iNaturalist photos split by observer; test frozen now
decision.why: A small regional list matches how anglers fish and keeps labeling cheap. iNaturalist Open Data has photo licenses, quality grade and observer ids, so you can keep each observer's photos on one side of the split and avoid near-duplicate leakage.

alternatives.name: FishNet (ICCV 2023)
alternatives.tradeoff: Very broad taxonomy with box labels, but few images per species, so it suits pretraining or family-level checks more than a regional species list.

alternatives.name: Only your own pier photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use, but you will have too few per species to train and the test set grows slowly.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, pandas. Read the iNaturalist Open Data observations, photos and taxa tables; filter quality_grade == 'research' and taxon_id in species.yaml; keep only CC0/CC-BY/CC-BY-NC photos and save attribution. Split by observer_id into train/val/test (70/15/15) with a fixed seed, write split CSVs and a hash of test.csv. Tests: no observer_id appears in two splits; every row has a license.
verify: Write the one question and the 3 metrics with a target for each before training anything
Confirm no observer_id is shared between train and test and record the test.csv hash
Count test photos per species and note any species with fewer than 20

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app identifies fish, not people. Pier and market photos will include faces and exact locations. Rules are legal obligations: the app must say the official source decides. Handling a live fish to photograph it also has a welfare cost.

decision.choice: On-device face blocking or blurring, coarse location, official-source link and handling tips on results
decision.why: Running face detection on the phone means faces never reach your server. Coarse location still selects the rule region. Linking the regulator's page and a quick-release tip keeps the app honest about its role.

alternatives.name: Server-side blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach the server first.

alternatives.name: Fully on-device app with no upload
alternatives.tradeoff: Best privacy, but harder to collect your own test photos and to update models.

steps.delegate: Add MediaPipe Face Detector on device: block upload or blur face boxes. Strip EXIF; round coordinates to region level before storing. Add a fixed footer: 'Helper only. Check the official regulations.' with the source link. Tests: a photo with a face never reaches the upload endpoint; stored rows hold no precise coordinates.
verify: Upload 10 photos with people in frame and confirm no stored image shows a face
Confirm every result screen shows the official source link and the helper-only notice

steps.title: Turn the official rules into a cited, versioned rule table
steps.learn: Rules vary by species, region and season, and each size limit names a measurement method. Florida FWC, for example, uses total length for some species and fork length for others, and red drum has the same slot statewide but bag and vessel limits that differ by region. The app can only be as correct as this table.

decision.choice: LLM extracts rule rows (species, region, measure type, limits, season, source, date); a human checks each
decision.why: Structured rows let code make the size check deterministically, and the source URL plus fetch date lets the app show where each answer came from and when it may be stale. Human review is cheap at 15 to 25 species and catches extraction errors.

alternatives.name: Hand-typed table only
alternatives.tradeoff: Most reliable for a tiny list, but tedious to refresh when rules change each season.

alternatives.name: Free-text RAG answers at query time
alternatives.tradeoff: No table to maintain, but the model may misread a slot limit or region and you cannot test it row by row.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, httpx, BeautifulSoup, pydantic. Fetch each official species page listed in sources.yaml, save the raw HTML with a timestamp, ask an LLM for JSON matching a pydantic Rule model (species, region, measure_type in {total, fork, lower_jaw_fork}, min_in, max_in, bag, season, source_url, fetched_at). Write rules.json for human review. Tests: schema validation rejects missing measure_type; a fixture page yields the expected slot.
verify: Compare every extracted row to the official page by hand and log each correction
Confirm every row has a measure type, a source URL and a fetch date

links.label: FWC red drum rules (regional bag limits)

steps.title: Measure a zero-shot species baseline on your list
steps.learn: A biology-trained CLIP model can rank your regulated species by text label with no training. This baseline tells you whether fine-tuning is worth it. Its training data may include iNaturalist photos, so treat its test score as possibly optimistic.

decision.choice: pybioclip CustomLabelsClassifier with scientific names of your regulated species
decision.why: It restricts predictions to the species your rules cover and needs no labels, so you get a number on day one. Using scientific names avoids ambiguous local common names.

alternatives.name: General open_clip model
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to swap in, but trained on general web images, so fine-grained fish species may be weaker.

alternatives.name: Skip the baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves a day, but you cannot tell how much fine-tuning actually added.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, pybioclip, pandas. Load test.csv, run CustomLabelsClassifier over the species list (scientific names), save top-3 predictions and scores per image to baseline.csv. Compute top-1 and top-3 accuracy and a per-species confusion table. Tests: label list matches species.yaml exactly; output has one row per test image.
verify: Record top-1 and top-3 accuracy on the frozen test split with the model name and command
List the 3 most confused species pairs and look at 5 examples of each
