steps.title: Fine-tune a ViT on your species and add an unsure answer
steps.learn: Fine-tuning a pretrained ViT on a few hundred photos per species usually sharpens fine-grained distinctions. A wrong species means a wrong rule, so the model must be allowed to say unsure. Tune that threshold on val, never on test.

decision.choice: Fine-tune a pretrained timm ViT with augmentation; abstain below a val-tuned top-1 probability
decision.why: timm offers many pretrained ViTs with one API, so you can trade size for phone latency. Abstaining sends hard cases to the user, which is safer than a confident wrong rule.

alternatives.name: Linear probe on frozen BioCLIP features
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and stable with little data, but may cap accuracy below full fine-tuning.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune CLIP end to end
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps text alignment for new species, but is more sensitive to learning rate and easy to overfit.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, PyTorch, timm. Fine-tune a pretrained ViT on train.csv with random resized crop and flips; early-stop on val accuracy. Save the checkpoint and val logits. Pick the abstain threshold that keeps val precision at or above your target. Report test top-1, coverage and accuracy on covered images. Tests: train and test file sets do not overlap; the threshold is read from val only.
verify: Compare test top-1 to the zero-shot baseline on the same frozen split
Record coverage (share not abstained) and accuracy on covered images
Confirm the threshold value was chosen before test predictions were opened

steps.title: Get real-world scale from a printed ArUco marker
steps.learn: A marker of known side length gives four corner points, so you can compute a homography that maps the photo to a top-down metric plane. This removes most perspective error, but only for points in the marker's plane: the fish must lie flat beside it.

decision.choice: OpenCV ArucoDetector with a DICT_4X4_50 marker printed at a known size; homography from its 4 corners
decision.why: Markers are cheap, detected automatically and give an orientation as well as scale. Correcting perspective matters because people rarely shoot exactly top-down at a pier.

alternatives.name: Detect the ruler itself
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra item to carry, but reading tick marks is hard in glare and the ruler must stay as ground truth for testing.

alternatives.name: Phone depth or AR measurement
alternatives.tradeoff: No marker needed, but support varies by device and errors are harder to audit.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, opencv-python (4.7 or newer). Implement marker_plane(image, side_mm) returning a 3x3 homography to millimetre coordinates using ArucoDetector and getPerspectiveTransform; return None when no marker is found. Script to print a marker sheet with the side length written on it. Tests: a synthetic image of a warped marker recovers side length within 1 percent; no marker returns None.
verify: Photograph a ruler beside the marker at 3 angles and measure 20 cm on it; record the error at each angle
Confirm photos without a marker are rejected with a clear message

steps.title: Segment the fish and measure the regulated length
steps.learn: Length rules name specific points: total length runs from the snout with mouth closed to the farthest tail tip with the tail squeezed; fork length ends at the center of the tail fork. A mask gives the outline; the measurement must follow the rule's definition, in the metric plane from the marker.

decision.choice: SAM 2 mask from one tap, warped to the metric plane; long-axis length; user confirms snout and tail
decision.why: A promptable segmenter needs no fish-specific training. Warping first means the length is in millimetres. Letting the user nudge the endpoints handles open mouths, fanned tails and fork length, which a mask alone cannot locate.

alternatives.name: Train a fish keypoint model
alternatives.tradeoff: Fully automatic snout and fork points, but needs labeled keypoints you do not have.

alternatives.name: User taps both ends only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and often accurate, but no outline to sanity check and more taps per fish.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, sam2 (SAM2ImagePredictor), opencv-python, numpy. Given image, tap point and homography: get the mask, warp mask contour to mm, find the long axis with minAreaRect, propose snout and tail endpoints, accept user overrides, return length_mm and measure_type. Tests: a synthetic ellipse of known length measures within 2 percent; overrides replace proposed points.
verify: Measure 10 objects of known length (not fish) lying beside the marker and record mean absolute error in mm
Check the reported length uses the measure type stored for that species in rules.json

steps.title: Answer rule questions with retrieval and a deterministic size check
steps.learn: Two jobs: the verdict (is this fish within limits now, here) and follow-up questions (gear, bag, closed areas). The verdict should come from code over rules.json, not from a model. RAG over the saved official pages answers the questions, with citations.

decision.choice: Code checks length against the rule row with a margin; RAG over saved rule pages (SQLite FTS5, bm25)
decision.why: Deterministic checks are testable and cannot invent a limit. A margin flags fish near a limit as 'too close to call, measure with a ruler'. FTS5 is built into SQLite and ranks with bm25, which suits exact species and region words.

alternatives.name: Dense embeddings for retrieval
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for paraphrased questions, but more moving parts and weaker on exact names and numbers.

alternatives.name: LLM decides the verdict
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles odd rules in prose, but a fluent wrong answer here can mean a fine.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, sqlite3 with FTS5, an LLM API. check(species, region, date, length_mm, margin_mm) returns keep, too_small, too_big, closed or too_close_to_call, with the rule row and source URL. ask(question) retrieves top chunks via bm25 and answers only from them with citations. Tests: table-driven cases for slot edges and margin; ask() refuses when retrieval returns nothing.
verify: Write 20 verdict cases by hand from the official pages and confirm check() matches all of them
Ask 10 rule questions and confirm every answer cites a saved page that actually says it

steps.title: Handle no marker, unsure species and stale rules
steps.learn: Most real failures are inputs: marker missing or not beside the fish, tail curled, wrong species guess, rules older than the season. Each must lead to a clear fallback, never a silent verdict.

decision.choice: Every verdict carries confidence flags; any flag downgrades it to 'check the official source and a ruler'
decision.why: The app is a helper, not the authority. Showing why it is unsure (no marker, species unsure, rules fetched long ago) teaches users when to trust it and keeps a wrong keep verdict rare.

alternatives.name: Always give a verdict
alternatives.tradeoff: Feels smoother, but hides the cases most likely to be wrong.

alternatives.name: Block the app when any flag fires
alternatives.tradeoff: Safest, but users stop opening it.

steps.delegate: Extend the pipeline with a Verdict object holding flags: no_marker, oblique_marker, species_unsure, near_limit, rules_stale (fetch date older than a configured number of days), region_unknown. Render the official source link on every result. Tests: each flag is triggered by a fixture and changes the displayed verdict.
verify: Feed 10 deliberately bad photos (no marker, curled tail, blurry) and confirm none gets a plain keep verdict
Set the clock past the stale window and confirm a stale-rules warning appears

steps.title: Test it outside at a pier or fish market with a ruler
steps.learn: The try-it: photograph fish next to a ruler and the marker, then compare estimated vs measured length. Read the ruler yourself before looking at the app's number, so the app cannot influence the ground truth. Ask the vendor or angler before photographing.
verify: Collect at least 30 fish; report length mean absolute error (mm and percent) and the worst 3 cases with causes
Report species accuracy on these fish and the share answered 'unsure'
Report verdict agreement with your own reading of the official rules, and how many were near a limit

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example a species pair the model confuses or angles where length drifts), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives species accuracy, length error and verdict agreement, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with example photos
Part 4 lists assumptions (one jurisdiction, rules fetch date, fish count) and that the app is not a legal authority

projects.title: Bird life list from song and photo
projects.problem: Hard to identify birds you hear but can't see
projects.concepts: Audio embeddings, nearest-neighbor search, a map of sightings
projects.tryIt: Record 30 mornings of birdsong in your yard or a park
projects.question: Can audio embeddings with nearest-neighbor search, plus photo checks, build an accurate yard bird life list from 30 mornings of recordings?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the test data
steps.learn: The product is a life list: species you have confirmed. Score it at two levels: per 3-second clip (is the species right) and per list (precision and recall of species against hand-verified detections). Public clips are a warm-up; your own hand-labeled mornings are the real test.

decision.choice: xeno-canto clips for a dev set, split by recordist; 3 of your 30 mornings hand-labeled and frozen as the test set
decision.why: The BirdNET FAQ says the team regularly downloads xeno-canto recordings to improve its models, so xeno-canto scores can be optimistic. Your own yard audio, labeled before tuning, measures what matters.

alternatives.name: BirdCLEF competition data
alternatives.tradeoff: Labeled soundscapes for a fixed region, but not your species mix or microphone.

alternatives.name: No hand labels, trust model output
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but then the system grades itself and errors stay invisible.

verify: Write the one question and the clip-level and list-level metrics with targets
Pick which 3 mornings form the test set and record that choice before any tuning
Get a xeno-canto API key and confirm a v3 query for one species returns recordings

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: A yard microphone also records neighbors talking. Identify birds, never people. BirdNET has non-event classes including Human vocal, Human non-vocal and Human whistle that can flag speech windows. Exact locations can expose your home and sensitive species.

decision.choice: Drop and never store windows flagged as human sounds; keep only bird clips; coarse location only
decision.why: Discarding speech windows at ingest means conversations never sit on disk. Coarse cells keep the map useful without pinpointing a house or a nest.

alternatives.name: Keep everything, filter at display
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier debugging, but you are storing other people's speech.

alternatives.name: Record only with a high-pass filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Cuts some low voices, but speech still overlaps bird frequencies.

steps.delegate: Add an ingest pass: run BirdNET analyze per window, delete windows with a human class above a low threshold before embedding, and delete raw files after windows are kept. Strip location to H3 cells. Tests: a fixture with speech yields no stored windows for that span; raw recordings are gone after ingest.
verify: Before recording any morning, run the human-sound filter on 2 minutes of your own speech and confirm no window of it is kept on disk
Tell neighbors the recorder is there, and confirm the app never records indoors

steps.title: Restrict candidates to species likely at your place and week
steps.learn: Most identification errors are plausible-sounding species that never occur near you. BirdNET's species range model estimates which species are likely for a latitude, longitude and week, trained on eBird checklist data; its docs warn coverage is weaker in regions with few eBird checklists.

decision.choice: Generate a weekly candidate list with BirdNET's species range model for your coordinates; filter results to it
decision.why: A location filter removes impossible species before they reach your life list. Regenerating weekly follows migration. Keeping the list as a file makes it easy to inspect and edit.

alternatives.name: No location filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Never hides a true vagrant, but lets in many impossible species.

alternatives.name: Hand-written list from a local field guide
alternatives.tradeoff: Trustworthy for a few dozen species, but misses seasonal visitors and takes time to keep current.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, birdnet_analyzer. Script weekly_list.py: for a lat, lon and week number, call the species module and write species_<week>.txt in scientific_common format; diff against last week. Tests: output lines match the model labels file format; changing the week changes the list for a migratory test species.
verify: Generate lists for 2 weeks months apart and check that known seasonal species appear and drop out
Note whether your region is one the docs say is well covered by eBird data

steps.title: Record mornings and cut them into overlapping 3-second windows
steps.learn: BirdNET 2.4 works on 3-second segments at 48 kHz (it resamples input); the 3.0 developer preview uses 32 kHz and drops the fixed 3 s window, so pin one version. Overlap between windows reduces calls split across a boundary at the cost of more compute. File names must carry start time so detections map to clock time.

decision.choice: Fixed dawn schedule, lossless audio, ISO timestamped files; windows with overlap, set once and kept fixed
decision.why: A fixed schedule makes mornings comparable. Lossless files avoid compression artifacts in high frequencies. Changing overlap after you start would change detection counts, so pick it once.

alternatives.name: Phone recorder app
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and easy, but battery, placement and auto gain vary day to day.

alternatives.name: Dedicated recorder such as AudioMoth
alternatives.tradeoff: Scheduled and weatherproofable, but costs money and needs setup.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, soundfile, numpy. ingest.py: validate new recordings (sample rate, channels, length), rename to <site>_<ISO start>.flac, write a manifest row per file. windows.py yields (file, start_s, end_s) for 3-second windows with a configurable overlap. Tests: window count for a 60 s file matches the formula; timestamps survive renaming.
verify: Record one test morning and confirm every file has a correct start time in the manifest
Listen to 5 random windows and confirm they line up with the audio at those times

steps.title: Turn each window into an embedding
steps.learn: A bird sound model's embedding is a fixed-size vector per 3-second window (1024 values for BirdNET 2.4, 1280 for 3.0) where similar sounds land close together. That lets you search for 'more like this clip' and add species or call types without retraining the network.

decision.choice: BirdNET embeddings via birdnet_analyzer.embeddings, with the model version stored next to every vector
decision.why: One package gives species scores, the range model and embeddings, so components agree. Storing the version prevents mixing vectors from different models, which live in different spaces.

alternatives.name: Perch embeddings via perch-hoplite
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong bird embeddings with an agile modeling workflow, but a second toolchain to install and maintain.

alternatives.name: Raw mel spectrogram features
alternatives.tradeoff: No model dependency, but similarity is dominated by noise and loudness, not species.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, birdnet_analyzer. Run the embeddings command over each morning, parse output into a table (file, start_s, end_s, model_version, vector). Store vectors as float32 in a .npy plus a SQLite metadata table. Tests: vector length matches the model version; re-running on the same file gives identical vectors.
verify: Embed one morning and record the vector length, model version and run time on your machine
Pick a clear call and confirm its nearest neighbors in the same morning sound like the same species

steps.title: Build a labeled reference library and nearest-neighbor search
steps.learn: Nearest-neighbor identification labels a new window by the labels of its closest reference clips. The library is xeno-canto clips for your candidate species plus clips you confirm from your own yard. At a few thousand to tens of thousands of vectors, exact search is fast and has no recall loss.

decision.choice: Exact cosine search in numpy; library of xeno-canto clips (recordist-split) plus your confirmed clips
decision.why: Exact search is simple, deterministic and gives a ground truth for any later ANN index. Adding your own confirmed clips adapts the library to your microphone and background noise.

alternatives.name: usearch or Faiss HNSW index
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed at millions of vectors, but adds recall loss and tuning you do not need yet.

alternatives.name: BirdNET's own embeddings database and search CLI
alternatives.tradeoff: Built in, but stores vectors in its own format, which makes custom voting and metadata harder.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, httpx, numpy. fetch_xc.py: query xeno-canto API v3 (key from env) for each candidate species, download recordings with license and recordist, and embed them. knn.py: search(vec, k) returning (clip_id, species, score). Tests: a library vector returns itself first; dev and reference sets share no recordist.
verify: Report top-1 neighbor accuracy on the xeno-canto dev split
Confirm every library clip has a license and recordist stored for attribution

steps.title: Vote among neighbors, abstain when unsure, compare to BirdNET
steps.learn: Most dawn windows hold no clear call, several species, or noise. A window gets a species only if enough of its k neighbors agree and the top similarity clears a floor. BirdNET's own classifier output (with your candidate list) is the baseline to beat.

decision.choice: Similarity-weighted k-NN vote with a minimum score and agreement; thresholds tuned on the dev split only
decision.why: Abstaining keeps false species off the life list, which is the error users notice. Tuning on dev and reporting on the frozen mornings keeps the test honest. The baseline shows whether k-NN adds anything.

alternatives.name: BirdNET species scores with min_conf only
alternatives.tradeoff: No library needed, but fixed to the model's label set and harder to adapt to your yard.

alternatives.name: Linear classifier on embeddings (agile modeling)
alternatives.tradeoff: Often better with enough labels, but needs labeled negatives and retraining when species are added.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, numpy, scikit-learn. identify(vec) returns species or None using k, min_score and min_agreement from config. tune.py grid-searches these on the dev split for a target precision. baseline.py runs birdnet_analyzer analyze with the candidate list. Tests: identical neighbors return that species; scores below the floor return None.
verify: On the dev split, report precision and recall of k-NN and the BirdNET baseline at the same coverage
Confirm the chosen thresholds were fixed before the 3 test mornings were scored

steps.title: Add photo identification restricted to candidate species
steps.learn: Photos confirm birds you can see, and help resolve sound-alikes. A biology-trained CLIP model can classify against a custom label list, so you can pass the same weekly candidate list. CUB-200-2011's own page warns its images overlap ImageNet, so pretrained scores on it can be inflated.

decision.choice: pybioclip CustomLabelsClassifier over this week's candidate scientific names; abstain below a val-tuned score
decision.why: No training data needed, and the candidate list keeps photo and audio answers in the same species space. Abstaining leaves blurry feeder shots for you to label.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune on NABirds
alternatives.tradeoff: Stronger for North American species, but needs training and is limited to that region's 400 species.

alternatives.name: BioCLIP tree-of-life classifier
alternatives.tradeoff: No candidate list needed, but it can return species that do not occur near you.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, pybioclip, Pillow. photo_id(path, week) loads species_<week>.txt, runs CustomLabelsClassifier with scientific names, returns top-3 with scores or 'unsure'. Tests: label list equals the weekly file; an image of a non-bird returns 'unsure' at the chosen threshold.
verify: Run on 30 of your own bird photos you can identify and report top-1 accuracy and the unsure share
Record the threshold and how it was chosen

steps.title: Confirm detections into a life list and map sightings
steps.learn: A single window is weak evidence; a life list entry should need repeated detections or your confirmation of the best clip. Each sighting keeps its evidence (clip or photo, scores, model version) so you can audit or revoke it later. The map shows where and when, at a coarse grid.

decision.choice: List a species after N detections or one human-confirmed clip; map sightings as H3 cells in Leaflet
decision.why: Requiring repeats or review keeps one-off errors off the list. H3 cells give a consistent coarse grid that hides exact spots. Keeping evidence makes every entry checkable.

alternatives.name: Add on first detection
alternatives.tradeoff: Grows the list fast, but each false positive becomes a permanent entry.

alternatives.name: Exact point markers
alternatives.tradeoff: More precise maps, but reveal your home and any sensitive nest sites.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, SQLite, h3, a small FastAPI app, Leaflet frontend. Tables: detections, sightings, life_list (species, first_seen, evidence_id, status). Endpoint to play the top clip and confirm or reject. Map shows H3 cells with species counts. Tests: rejected evidence removes a pending entry; stored rows contain cell ids, not raw coordinates.
verify: Confirm or reject 20 pending species and check the list updates and keeps the evidence link
Open the map and confirm no marker shows an exact coordinate

steps.title: Test it outside: 30 mornings of birdsong
steps.learn: The try-it: record 30 mornings in your yard or a park. Score the 3 frozen mornings against your own labels (made by listening and spectrograms, not from the app's output). Track how the life list grows and what the review queue costs you per day.
verify: On the 3 frozen mornings, report clip precision and recall for k-NN and the BirdNET baseline
Report final life list size, how many entries you rejected, and minutes of review per morning
Plot species added per day and note when the list stopped growing

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example dev scores much higher than yard scores, or one species dominating errors), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives clip and list metrics for k-NN and baseline, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with example clips
Part 4 lists assumptions (one site, one microphone, 30 mornings, season) and what it does not prove

projects.title: Invasive plant spotter
projects.problem: Volunteers need to find invasive species before they spread
projects.concepts: CLIP zero-shot then fine-tuning, geotagged map for cleanup groups
projects.tryIt: Walk a local trail and map every flagged plant
projects.question: Can a CLIP-style model, zero-shot first and then fine-tuned, flag local invasive plants on a trail precisely enough to give cleanup groups a map they trust?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the frozen test sets
steps.learn: Volunteers care about two numbers: of the plants the app flags, how many are really the invasive species (precision, wasted trips), and of the invasive plants on the trail, how many it flags (recall, missed spread). The try-it walk measures both in the field; offline sets measure them before you go.

decision.choice: DeepWeeds, whole collection dates held out (proxy for site visits) frozen now; local test frozen once species are set
decision.why: DeepWeeds (8 weed species plus a Negative class, CC BY 4.0, from 8 Queensland sites) has real background clutter, and holding out sites tests generalization to a new place. A local set of your own target species tells you what matters on your trail.

alternatives.name: DeepWeeds random split only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy, but photos from the same site and day land on both sides, so accuracy looks better than it will on your trail.

alternatives.name: Only your own trail photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic, but you need an expert to label them and you have none until after the walk.

verify: Write the one question and the two field metrics: share of flags confirmed, share of known plants on a surveyed segment that were flagged
Hold out whole collection dates (filename prefix YYYYMMDD) as the DeepWeeds test, save the file list with a hash, never open them while tuning
Write the local test rule now (split by observer); freeze those observation ids right after choosing species in step 3, before any model runs

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Identify plants, never people. Trail photos catch other hikers and faces, and a GPS track reveals where a volunteer lives. Some invasive plants injure people: NY DEC warns giant hogweed sap plus sunlight can cause severe burns. The app is a helper, not an authority on identification or removal rules.

decision.choice: On-device face check before upload, store only plant points (no tracks), and in-app do-not-touch and confirm-first rules
decision.why: Detecting faces on the phone (for example MediaPipe Face Detector, full-range model for rear-camera photos) means faces never reach your server. Storing only flag points, not the walk, keeps volunteers' routes private while the map still works.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler app, but raw faces reach your server even briefly.

alternatives.name: Store full GPS tracks for coverage maps
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows which trail segments were surveyed, but records volunteers' movements; only do it opt-in and trimmed away from start and end points.

steps.delegate: Add a capture gate using MediaPipe Face Detector (BlazeFace full-range): if a face is found, block the photo with a message or blur the box before upload. Server strips all EXIF on ingest and stores only the flag point and accuracy. Show a do-not-touch notice for species flagged as hazardous in targets.yaml. Tests: a photo with a face never reaches the upload handler; stored images have no EXIF.
verify: Try 10 photos with people in them and confirm none is stored with a visible face
Confirm the database has no table or column holding a volunteer's track or home location
Confirm every flag screen says to confirm with the official list or an expert before any removal

steps.title: Choose the target species and their native lookalikes
steps.learn: The model can only flag what is in its label set, and the costly error is calling a native lookalike invasive. Official lists say which species matter in your region; lookalike tables (for example giant hogweed versus cow parsnip on the NY DEC page) tell you which negatives must be explicit classes.

decision.choice: 5 to 15 species from your official regional invasive list, each paired with native lookalikes as classes
decision.why: A short list keeps per-species labeled data deep enough to measure precision per species. Explicit lookalike classes give the model somewhere to put a native plant instead of forcing it onto the nearest invasive label.

alternatives.name: Every introduced species iNaturalist lists nearby
alternatives.tradeoff: Broad coverage, but many classes have few photos, and 'introduced' is not the same as 'targeted for removal'.

alternatives.name: One species only
alternatives.tradeoff: Highest accuracy and simplest map, but cleanup groups usually work on several species per site.

alternatives.name: Invasive vs not invasive, two classes
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but the 'invasive' class mixes very different plants, and volunteers need the species to choose a removal method.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, httpx. Write targets.yaml (scientific name, common name, iNaturalist taxon_id, role: target or lookalike, source of listing). Script counts research-grade observations per taxon within your place_id via GET /v1/observations with taxon_id, place_id, quality_grade=research, photos=true, per_page=0. Cache responses on disk and sleep between calls. Test: every taxon_id resolves and every target has at least one lookalike.
verify: Every target species cites the official list it came from
Every target has at least one native lookalike class, or a written reason it has none
Drop or merge classes with too few local research-grade photos, and record the cutoff you used

steps.title: Build the training set from licensed iNaturalist photos
steps.learn: Research-grade iNaturalist observations have community-agreed IDs, but each photo keeps its own license and photographers keep copyright unless it is CC0. Many photos per observer and per place make leakage easy: if one person's photos sit in train and test, you measure memorized style, not species.

decision.choice: iNaturalist API v1, research grade, filtered by photo_license, split by observer, test set untouched
decision.why: The API lets you filter by taxon, place, quality_grade and photo_license, so you only keep photos whose license you can follow, and you store the attribution the open data README describes.

alternatives.name: iNaturalist Open Data on AWS
alternatives.tradeoff: Monthly CSV snapshots plus photos in S3 suit bulk pulls without API paging, but you join several tables yourself and some rows point to deleted photos.

alternatives.name: Use DeepWeeds only
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean labels and one license, but its 8 species are Queensland grassland weeds, likely not the ones on your trail.

steps.delegate: Python, httpx, pandas. Pull research-grade observations for targets.yaml taxa in your place with photo_license in cc0, cc-by, cc-by-nc. Keep only photos whose own license_code is in that set. Save observation id, observer login, license, photo URL (medium size), lat, lng, observed date. Exclude the frozen test ids. Split train and validation by observer. Tests: no observer in two splits; no frozen test id in train; every row has license and attribution text.
verify: Run the split check and confirm zero observers shared across train, validation and test
Spot-check 30 photos: is the target plant actually the subject, not a hand or a sign?
Record photos per class and note any class under your minimum

steps.title: Measure a zero-shot baseline with a biology-tuned CLIP
steps.learn: Zero-shot scores an image against text prompts with no training. BioCLIP is a CLIP ViT-B/16 trained on TreeOfLife-10M with taxonomic names, and its model card reports better zero-shot species accuracy than general CLIP. This baseline tells you how much fine-tuning must add.

decision.choice: BioCLIP via open_clip (hf-hub:imageomics/bioclip), scientific plus common name prompts, vs OpenCLIP ViT-B-32
decision.why: Plants are exactly the domain BioCLIP targets, it loads with the same open_clip API as general CLIP, and it is MIT licensed. Running general CLIP alongside shows whether the biology training matters on your species.

alternatives.name: Pl@ntNet identification API
alternatives.tradeoff: A mature plant ID service with many species, but you send every photo to a third party and cannot fine-tune it on your trail.

alternatives.name: General OpenCLIP only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer moving parts, but common-name prompts for similar plants are where general models are weakest.

steps.delegate: Python, open_clip, torch. Load hf-hub:imageomics/bioclip and ViT-B-32 laion2b_s34b_b79k. Build normalized text embeddings per class from 3 to 5 templates using scientific and common names. Evaluate on the frozen DeepWeeds test sites and local validation set: per-class precision, recall, confusion matrix. Cache image embeddings to disk. Tests: unit-norm vectors, deterministic class order.
verify: Record per-species precision and recall for both models on the frozen DeepWeeds test sites
Check how often DeepWeeds Negative images are assigned to a weed class
Note the 3 most confused pairs and whether they are invasive versus lookalike

steps.title: Fine-tune without losing robustness to new places
steps.learn: Fine-tuning raises accuracy on data like the training set but can hurt on new conditions (new site, season, light). WiSE-FT reports that averaging zero-shot and fine-tuned weights keeps most of the gain while improving robustness under distribution shift, which a new trail is.

decision.choice: Linear probe on frozen BioCLIP embeddings first; full fine-tune with WiSE-FT weight averaging only if the probe plateaus
decision.why: A logistic regression on cached embeddings trains in seconds and is easy to compare. If it is not enough, WiSE-FT is the cheap way to fine-tune while keeping the zero-shot model's robustness on held-out sites.

alternatives.name: Plain full fine-tune
alternatives.tradeoff: Often highest in-distribution accuracy, but the WiSE-FT paper shows it can lose robustness under shift, the case for a new trail.

alternatives.name: k-nearest neighbors on embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: No training and new examples help instantly (the BioCLIP card mentions KNN few-shot use), but it is slower per query and sensitive to class imbalance.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn, open_clip, torch. Train LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced') on cached train embeddings; tune C on validation only. Optional: full fine-tune with the head initialized from the zero-shot text embeddings, then WiSE-FT: theta = (1 - alpha) * zero_shot + alpha * fine_tuned for several alpha, chosen on validation. Report on frozen tests once at the end. Tests: test ids never seen in training; alpha=0 reproduces zero-shot scores.
verify: Compare zero-shot, probe and (if built) WiSE-FT on the frozen local test set; for DeepWeeds, train a separate probe on its non-test dates
Confirm C and alpha were chosen on validation, never on the frozen tests
Check whether lookalike confusion dropped compared to zero-shot

steps.title: Flag only when confident, and ask for a better photo otherwise
steps.learn: A classifier always returns some top species, even for a fern it never saw. Raw scores are not calibrated probabilities, so thresholds must come from validation data. Each species gets its own operating point because their error costs and score ranges differ.

decision.choice: Per-species threshold set on the validation precision-recall curve, plus an 'unsure, photograph leaf or flower' outcome
decision.why: A false flag sends a crew on a wasted trip and erodes trust, so pick thresholds for high precision. The unsure outcome turns borderline cases into a second, better photo instead of a wrong map point.

alternatives.name: One global threshold
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but species with low score ranges are never flagged while easy ones are over-flagged.

alternatives.name: Calibrate with CalibratedClassifierCV first
alternatives.tradeoff: Makes scores closer to probabilities so thresholds read as risk, but needs held-out data per class you may not have.

alternatives.name: Always flag top-1
alternatives.tradeoff: Highest recall, but floods the map with lookalikes and unknown plants.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn. For each target species compute precision_recall_curve on validation scores and store the lowest threshold meeting your target precision in thresholds.json. Implement decide(scores) returning flag(species), unsure, or not_target, also requiring a margin between top-1 and top-2. Tests: a not-target class never yields a flag; thresholds load and apply per species.
verify: Report precision and recall per target species at the chosen thresholds on the frozen local test set, once, after thresholds are fixed
Run 30 photos of plants outside the label set and count how many get flagged

steps.title: Capture a flag with its location and accuracy, even offline
steps.learn: A flag is only useful if a crew can find the plant again. Browser geolocation reports an accuracy radius in meters with each fix, and trails often have no signal, so the app must queue captures and upload later. EXIF GPS can be absent, so do not rely on it alone.

decision.choice: Web app records the Geolocation API fix and its accuracy at capture, queues locally, uploads when online
decision.why: The accuracy value lets the map draw a search circle and lets you reject fixes too poor to find a plant. Local queuing keeps a walk usable in dead zones without needing the model on the phone.

alternatives.name: Read GPS from photo EXIF
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra permission flow, but the tag can be missing and gives no accuracy value.

alternatives.name: Run the classifier on the phone
alternatives.tradeoff: Instant flags with no signal, but you must export and quantize the model and keep app and server versions in sync.

steps.delegate: TypeScript web app (PWA). On capture call navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition with enableHighAccuracy, store lat, lon, accuracy, timestamp and photo in IndexedDB; a sync worker uploads to a FastAPI endpoint with retries and idempotency keys. Tests: offline capture survives a reload; duplicate uploads create one row; fixes above an accuracy limit are marked low-confidence.
verify: Capture 10 points at known landmarks and record the distance between stored and true positions
Turn on airplane mode, capture 5 flags, reconnect, and confirm exactly 5 rows arrive

steps.title: Merge nearby flags into patches and publish the cleanup map
steps.learn: Invasive plants grow in patches, and several volunteers photograph the same patch, so raw points overstate the problem. Group flags of the same species within a distance tied to GPS accuracy. GeoJSON (RFC 7946) orders coordinates longitude then latitude, a classic bug.

decision.choice: PostGIS points, merge same-species flags with ST_DWithin into patches, export GeoJSON, map with Leaflet
decision.why: ST_DWithin on geography takes a distance in meters, so the merge radius maps directly to GPS accuracy. GeoJSON is what cleanup groups and GIS tools import, and Leaflet with markercluster keeps a dense map readable.

alternatives.name: H3 hexagon cells
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast grouping and easy counts per cell, but patches on cell borders split in two.

alternatives.name: SQLite plus haversine in Python
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine for one trail and no server setup, but slow and awkward once several groups share the map.

steps.delegate: SQL and Python. Table flags(id, species, geog geography(Point), accuracy_m, status, model_version, created_at). Job assigns patch_id by merging same-species flags where ST_DWithin(a.geog, b.geog, radius). Endpoint /patches.geojson returns FeatureCollection with lon, lat order and species, count, status. Leaflet page with Leaflet.markercluster. Tests: two flags inside radius merge, outside do not; GeoJSON coordinate order.
verify: Load the GeoJSON in a second tool (for example geojson.io or QGIS) and confirm points land on the trail, not mirrored
Count patches vs raw flags for one walk and note the reduction

steps.title: Route flags to human confirmation and report confirmed finds
steps.learn: The model's flag is a lead, not a record. A patch becomes 'confirmed' only when a person with plant ID skill checks it, and only confirmed patches go to official reporting systems such as EDDMapS. Confirmed labels can improve training, but must never leak into the frozen test sets.

decision.choice: Status flow flagged, confirmed or rejected, removed; a named reviewer confirms; export confirmed finds
decision.why: Cleanup groups and agencies act on verified reports, so a reviewer step protects their time. Rejections are the most useful new training data because they are the model's real mistakes on your trail.

alternatives.name: Community consensus inside the app
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales without experts, but a few keen volunteers can agree on a wrong ID.

alternatives.name: Post every flag straight to iNaturalist
alternatives.tradeoff: Gets community IDs for free, but floods a shared platform with unverified model output.

steps.delegate: Extend FastAPI: reviewer role, PATCH /patches/{id} with status and note, audit log table. Export confirmed patches as CSV with species, lat, lon, date, photo link for manual entry into EDDMapS. Retraining script adds rejected and confirmed examples to train only, asserting none are in the frozen test ids. Tests: only reviewers change status; audit log records each change.
verify: Confirm a non-reviewer account cannot mark a patch confirmed
Run the retraining data check and confirm zero overlap with the frozen test ids

steps.title: Test it outside: walk a trail and map every flagged plant
steps.learn: The field test answers what offline sets cannot: real light, partial views, seasons and lookalikes on your trail. Measure precision from reviewer confirmations, and recall on a short segment that a knowledgeable person surveys independently, so the app is not grading itself.
verify: Walk the trail and record km walked, photos taken, flags, unsure outcomes and patches
Get each flag confirmed or rejected by a reviewer and report precision per species
On one segment surveyed independently by a knowledgeable person, report how many known patches the app flagged
Return to 10 flagged patches using only the map and record how many you found and how far off the points were

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with the machine and command (offline tables and field counts); why surprising results happened (for example which lookalike pair failed and why); assumptions and limits, such as one season, one trail, one reviewer.
verify: Part 1 states the one question exactly as framed in step 1
Part 2 gives zero-shot, probe and field numbers, each with the machine and command or date and trail
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with evidence, such as example images
Part 4 lists assumptions and what this does not prove (other seasons, regions, species)

projects.title: Trail condition reporter
projects.problem: Hikers don't know about mud, snow or fallen trees until they arrive
projects.concepts: Image classification, vector search for similar past reports
projects.tryIt: Collect photos on trails over a few weekends; ask hikers to add theirs
projects.question: Can photo classification plus search over similar past reports tell hikers about mud, snow or fallen trees accurately and recently enough to trust?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the frozen test set
steps.learn: A hiker wants to know: if the app says mud, snow or a blocked trail, is it true now? So measure per-condition precision and recall on photos, and in the field, whether the next hiker on that segment agreed with the shown status. Public trail-condition labels are scarce, so you assemble a seed set.

decision.choice: Wikimedia Commons trail categories (mud, snow, fallen trees, clear), relabeled by hand, test split frozen now
decision.why: Commons images are real trail photos with reusable licenses and an API to list category members. Category membership is noisy, so you relabel each image yourself before freezing. Weekend-1 photos will form a second test set, frozen before any tuning.

alternatives.name: Only your own trail photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches your trails best, but you have no labeled data until after the privacy step and a few weekends.

alternatives.name: Road-surface condition datasets
alternatives.tradeoff: Larger and labeled, but roads look unlike forest trails, so accuracy there says little about mud on singletrack.

verify: Write the question and metrics: per-condition precision and recall, and field agreement rate with the next hiker
Relabel every seed image, then freeze a test split by saving file names and a hash before any model is run
Record each image's license and author for attribution

links.label: Commons: paths blocked by fallen trees

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Report conditions, never people. Hiker photos include faces and other hikers, and precise points near trailheads or homes can reveal where someone lives. Conditions can be dangerous: the app is a helper, and hikers must check the land manager's official closures and, in snow, the official avalanche forecast.

decision.choice: On-device face check, EXIF stripped, location snapped to the trail, no accounts, official-status link
decision.why: Faces detected on the phone (for example MediaPipe Face Detector, full-range) never reach the server. Snapping to the nearest trail segment keeps the useful part of location while dropping where exactly the person stood or parked.

alternatives.name: Server-side blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces pass through your server.

alternatives.name: Require accounts for every report
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to block spam and trace bad reports, but stores identities and puts off one-time hikers.

steps.delegate: Add a capture gate using MediaPipe Face Detector (BlazeFace full-range): block or blur faces before upload. Server: strip EXIF, snap the point to the nearest trail segment and store segment id plus distance along it, never the raw fix. Every status card links the land manager's official page. Tests: face photos never reach the upload handler; no raw coordinates in stored rows.
verify: Upload 10 photos with people and confirm none is stored with a visible face
Inspect the database and confirm only segment ids and snapped positions are stored
Confirm every status card links an official closure or forecast source and says not to detour for a photo

steps.title: Define conditions as multi-label with a labeling guide
steps.learn: Conditions co-occur: a photo can show snow and a fallen tree. Hikers also care about passability, not just presence, so severity matters. A one-page guide with example photos per label keeps your labels and volunteers' labels consistent.

decision.choice: Multi-label: mud, snow or ice, fallen tree or blockage, standing or flowing water, clear; plus passable or not passable
decision.why: Multi-label fits co-occurring hazards, and a separate passability field gives the one answer most hikers want. Keeping the label list short makes per-label precision measurable with modest data.

alternatives.name: Single label per photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler models and metrics, but forces a choice when two hazards appear and hides the second one.

alternatives.name: Free-text reports only
alternatives.tradeoff: Rich detail, but not searchable or comparable without parsing, and photos go unused.

steps.delegate: Write labels.yaml (label id, display name, definition, 3 example image ids from the seed set) and a tiny labeling web page (FastAPI plus HTML) that shows one image and checkboxes for labels and passability, saving to SQLite. Tests: label ids match labels.yaml; an image can hold several labels.
verify: Label 50 seed images twice, a day apart, and report your own agreement per label
Add a guide example for each case where you disagreed with yourself

steps.title: Score conditions zero-shot with CLIP
steps.learn: CLIP compares an image with text prompts like 'a muddy hiking trail'. For multi-label, score each label independently against a matching 'clear trail' prompt or a per-label threshold, instead of a softmax that forces one winner.

decision.choice: OpenCLIP ViT-B-32 (laion2b_s34b_b79k), several prompts per label averaged, per-label thresholds set on validation
decision.why: No training data is needed to get a baseline, it runs on a laptop or small server, and per-label thresholds fit multi-label output. It also gives the embeddings that similar-report search reuses.

alternatives.name: Vision-language model asked to describe the trail
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles odd cases and explains itself, but is slower and costlier per report and its text still needs mapping to labels.

alternatives.name: Larger CLIP (ViT-L)
alternatives.tradeoff: Often better zero-shot, but more memory and latency; worth it only if B-32 is clearly the bottleneck.

steps.delegate: Python, open_clip, torch. Build per-label text embeddings from 3 to 5 templates. score(image) returns cosine per label. Choose per-label thresholds on validation (not test) with precision_recall_curve. Evaluate on the frozen test: per-label precision, recall. Cache image embeddings. Tests: unit norms, a photo can pass several labels.
verify: Report per-label precision and recall on the frozen seed test set
List the 10 worst errors and note what fooled the model (wet leaves, shadows, dirt road)

steps.title: Train a small classifier on embeddings from your own trails
steps.learn: Once you have labeled photos from your trails, a linear classifier on frozen CLIP embeddings often beats prompts, and trains in seconds. One-vs-rest logistic regression gives one independent yes or no per label, matching the multi-label design.

decision.choice: One-vs-rest logistic regression on cached CLIP embeddings, trained on seed train now; retrained on weekends 2+ later
decision.why: It is cheap to retrain each weekend as reports arrive, easy to inspect, and keeps the CLIP embedding shared with search, so there is one model to version.

alternatives.name: Full fine-tune of the image encoder
alternatives.tradeoff: Can learn trail-specific textures, but needs more data and GPU time, and WiSE-FT shows plain fine-tuning can lose robustness under shift.

alternatives.name: Stay zero-shot
alternatives.tradeoff: No labeling work, but cannot learn your local look of mud or snow.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn. Train OneVsRestClassifier(LogisticRegression(class_weight='balanced')) on train embeddings; tune C and per-label thresholds on validation. Save model with a version string tied to the CLIP checkpoint. Evaluate once on both frozen test sets. Tests: no test file in train; model loads and returns one probability per label.
verify: Compare zero-shot and probe per label on the frozen seed test set in one table; repeat on weekend-1 photos during the field test
Confirm C and thresholds came from validation only

steps.title: Store reports with segment, time, labels and embedding
steps.learn: A report is a photo at a place and time with labels and a vector. Keeping geometry, time and vectors in one database lets one query ask 'similar photos within 500 m in the last two weeks' without stitching two systems together.

decision.choice: Postgres with PostGIS (geography) and pgvector in the same table, plus the model version on every row
decision.why: At hobby scale one Postgres holds everything, keeps filters and vectors transactional, and pgvector supports cosine distance and HNSW indexes when you need them. Model version lets you re-embed later without mixing incompatible vectors.

alternatives.name: SQLite plus FAISS files
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero server setup, but you keep the index and rows in sync yourself and filters happen outside the index.

alternatives.name: Managed vector database
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles scaling and filtered search, but adds a service and cost for a dataset that fits in one Postgres.

steps.delegate: SQL migrations: reports(id, segment_id, geog geography(Point), taken_at, uploaded_at, labels jsonb, passable bool, embedding vector(512), model_version, phash bigint). FastAPI POST /reports computes the embedding and labels server-side. Tests: insert and read back; vector dimension matches the model; model_version is required.
verify: Insert 100 seed reports and confirm a cosine nearest-neighbor query returns sensible neighbors for 5 spot-checks
Confirm every row carries model_version and taken_at

steps.title: Find similar past reports near this spot
steps.learn: Similar past reports answer 'this spot floods every spring' or 'others saw this tree too'. pgvector applies WHERE filters after an approximate index scan, and with the default hnsw.ef_search of 40 a selective filter can return few rows; its iterative index scans scan further when needed.

decision.choice: Pre-filter by ST_DWithin and a time window, then exact cosine ranking over that small candidate set
decision.why: Per-trail candidate sets are small, so an exact scan after the spatial filter is fast and returns every match. You avoid the post-filter starvation case entirely until the data grows.

alternatives.name: HNSW with iterative_scan enabled
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales to many reports, but results become approximate and need recall checks against exact search.

alternatives.name: Global ANN, then filter in Python
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest code, but a narrow spatial filter can leave zero results from the top-k.

steps.delegate: SQL plus FastAPI GET /reports/{id}/similar?radius_m=&days=: WHERE ST_DWithin(geog, :pt, :radius) AND taken_at > now() - make_interval(days => :days) ORDER BY embedding <=> :vec LIMIT 10. Also a same-season-last-year variant. Tests: results all within radius and window; ordering by cosine; a report never returns itself.
verify: For 10 reports, compare the top 10 from the filtered exact query with a brute-force Python check and confirm they match
Judge the top 5 by eye for 10 queries and record how many show the same condition

steps.title: Collapse duplicate photos so one hiker does not count twice
steps.learn: Hikers send bursts of near-identical photos, and the same photo can be resent. If duplicates count as independent reports, one person can make a segment look confirmed. Perceptual hashes catch exact and near-exact copies cheaply; embeddings catch the same scene from a new angle.

decision.choice: imagehash phash with a Hamming threshold for copies, plus same-segment, short-window embedding checks
decision.why: phash is cheap to compute and compare by Hamming distance, and the time-plus-place window limits embedding checks to a handful of reports. Both thresholds are tuned on your own burst photos.

alternatives.name: Exact file hash only
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial, but misses any resized or re-encoded copy.

alternatives.name: Embedding similarity only
alternatives.tradeoff: One mechanism, but two different hikers photographing the same mud can look identical and be wrongly merged.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, Pillow. On ingest compute phash, compare against reports on the same segment in a recent window; mark duplicates with duplicate_of. Count only distinct reports in status. Tests: a resized and recompressed copy is flagged; two distinct photos of different spots are not.
verify: Take 5 bursts of 3 photos and confirm each burst counts once
Confirm two hikers' separate photos of one spot both count

steps.title: Turn reports into a current status that ages out
steps.learn: Conditions change: snow melts, crews clear trees, mud dries. A status must say how old and how supported it is. Combine recent distinct reports per segment, weight newer ones more, and let each condition expire on its own schedule, tuned from how long reports stay true in your data.

decision.choice: Per segment and condition: recency-weighted vote of distinct reports, per-condition expiry, age shown
decision.why: Showing 'mud, 3 reports, newest 2 days ago' is honest about uncertainty, and expiry stops a spring blowdown showing in autumn. A newer clear report outweighs older hazard reports.

alternatives.name: Show only the latest report
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but one mislabeled photo flips the status.

alternatives.name: Forecast conditions from weather data
alternatives.tradeoff: Could warn before anyone reports, but needs weather feeds and labeled history you do not yet have.

steps.delegate: Python. status(segment, now) returns per condition: active bool, score, newest_age, distinct_reports, using exponential decay with per-condition half-life from config and model probabilities as weights. Tests with synthetic report sequences: a newer clear report clears a hazard; reports older than expiry are ignored; duplicates do not raise the score.
verify: Replay a scripted sequence of timestamped seed reports and check the status at 5 timestamps against the expected answer
Confirm every displayed status shows report age and count

steps.title: Test it outside: a few weekends of trail photos plus hikers' reports
steps.learn: The field test checks the full loop: photos in, status out, and whether the next person on the trail agrees. Agreement must come from a hiker's own observation, not from the model's labels, so the system is not grading itself.
verify: Over several weekends, record reports collected, distinct reports after dedup, segments covered and share of reports with faces blocked
For each status shown, ask the next hiker on that segment to tick what they saw, and report the agreement rate per condition
Freeze weekend-1 photos as a test set before training on later weekends, and report probe scores on it

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with the machine and command or the dates and trails; why surprising results happened (for example wet leaves read as mud); assumptions and limits, such as few trails, one season, volunteer hikers who may differ from typical ones.
verify: Part 1 states the question exactly as framed in step 1
Part 2 gives per-label offline numbers and field agreement, each with machine and command or dates
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with example photos
Part 4 lists assumptions and what this does not prove (other seasons, regions, hazards)

projects.title: Litter hotspot ranker
projects.problem: Cleanup groups don't know which spots are worst
projects.concepts: Object detection and counting, ranking by litter per square meter
projects.tryIt: Photograph the same 10 spots weekly and rank them
projects.question: Which of 10 local spots has the most litter per square meter, and does a photo count rank them the same way a hand count does, week after week?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: The system is detect, count, divide by surveyed area, rank. Success (from the try-it): photograph the same 10 spots weekly and rank them, scored against an independent hand count. Offline data: TACO, 1,500 photos of litter in context with 4,784 annotations in 60 categories (28 supercategories), COCO format.

decision.choice: TACO with your own seeded 70/15/15 image split, frozen today, plus field hand counts as ground truth
decision.why: TACO lets you measure detection and count error before going outside. Its split_dataset.py draws random splits without a fixed seed, so write a seeded split and freeze the test list now. A person, not the model, produces the hand counts that grade the ranking.

alternatives.name: Field photos only, hand-labeled
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to your spots, but slow to label and you cannot tune anything before the first survey.

alternatives.name: Add TACO's unofficial annotations
alternatives.tradeoff: More labeled images for training, but they are unreviewed, so labels are noisier; never mix them into the test split.

verify: README states the question and both metrics (Kendall tau vs hand-count ranking, per-photo count MAE), written before any code
Run the split script twice and confirm the saved test image list has the same hash
Print annotation counts per class in the test split and note the share of cigarettes

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Count litter only, never people. Ground photos still catch passers-by, faces, plates and house fronts, and litter itself can carry personal data (receipts, letters, pill labels). Cleanup has its own hazards: sharps, broken glass, traffic, private land. The app helps; local authority rules on hazardous waste win.

decision.choice: On-device face check blocks the shot; keep only the measured ground crop; never read text on litter; safety rules in app
decision.why: If a face never leaves the phone it is never stored. Keeping only the rectified crop of the surveyed area (built in a later step) drops most of the scene. Not running OCR on litter avoids collecting personal data the project has no use for.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw images with faces reach your server, even if only briefly.

alternatives.name: Keep full original photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets you re-run future models on the whole scene, but you store bystanders and addresses; if chosen, blur faces and set a deletion date.

steps.delegate: Capture step with MediaPipe Face Detector on device: if any face is detected, block the capture and ask the user to reframe at the ground. Strip EXIF before upload and store a spot_id instead of GPS. Add an in-app checklist: gloves, never touch needles or sharps (report them to the local authority), stay off roads and private land. Tests: an image containing a face never reaches the upload call; uploaded files carry no EXIF GPS tags.
verify: Try 10 shots with a person in frame and confirm none upload
Inspect an uploaded file with exiftool and confirm there are no GPS or device tags
Confirm the app tells users to report sharps and to check local rules for hazardous waste

steps.title: Fix a repeatable photo protocol with a reference marker
steps.learn: Litter per square meter is only as good as the area estimate and its repeatability. Week to week the photographer, height, angle and light change. Decide what ground is surveyed and how it is measured, so a change in count reflects litter, not framing.

decision.choice: A printed ArUco marker of known side at a fixed stake per spot; survey a fixed ground rectangle around it
decision.why: OpenCV detects ArUco markers and returns their ID and four corners, so one marker both identifies the spot and gives scale. Defining the rectangle in ground units keeps the surveyed area identical each week even when the phone position changes.

alternatives.name: Physical quadrat frame
alternatives.tradeoff: Robust, no math, and defines exactly what the hand counter counts, but bulky to carry to 10 spots and placement drifts.

alternatives.name: Fixed photo point, no marker
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest, but area is unknown and changes with height and tilt, so per square meter becomes a guess.

alternatives.name: Phone AR plane measurement
alternatives.tradeoff: No props, but ties you to specific devices and APIs and is harder to verify independently.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, opencv-python 4.7 or newer (ArUco is in the objdetect module). make_markers.py: Dictionary.generateImageMarker for IDs 0 to 9 from DICT_4X4_50, rendered at a stated printed side length. detect_spot(img) returns (marker_id, 4 corners) using cv2.aruco.ArucoDetector, or None. Tests: a synthetic image with a pasted marker returns the right id and corners within 1 px; an image without a marker returns None.
verify: Print the markers, measure each printed side with a ruler and record it (printers rescale)
Photograph one marker from 5 heights and angles and confirm it is detected in every shot

steps.title: Rectify the ground plane and compute the surveyed area
steps.learn: Four marker corners with known real positions define a homography from image to ground, assuming flat ground. Warping to a top-down view at a fixed pixels-per-cm scale makes area exact in the warped image and lets you crop the same rectangle every week. Error grows away from the marker and on slopes or bumps.

decision.choice: getPerspectiveTransform from the 4 marker corners, warpPerspective to a fixed scale, crop the fixed rectangle or reject
decision.why: Four point pairs determine a homography exactly, so one marker is enough. Rejecting shots where the rectangle leaves the frame keeps the area constant, which the per square meter comparison depends on.

alternatives.name: Markers at each rectangle corner, findHomography
alternatives.tradeoff: More accurate over a large area and tolerates one hidden marker, but more props to place and keep in position.

alternatives.name: Scale raw image by marker size only
alternatives.tradeoff: No warp, but ignores perspective, so far objects and far ground are mis-sized on tilted shots.

steps.delegate: rectify(img, corners, marker_cm, rect_cm, px_per_cm) returns (top_down_crop, area_m2) or a rejection reason, using cv2.getPerspectiveTransform and cv2.warpPerspective. Tests: a synthetic grid warped by a known homography is recovered with under 2% area error; a rectangle extending outside the frame is rejected.
verify: Lay a tape measure 1 m from the marker, rectify, and confirm the measured length is within 5%
For one spot, photograph from 3 positions and confirm the rectified crops overlay within a few cm and area_m2 is identical

steps.title: Choose and train the litter detector
steps.learn: Counting litter is detection plus a confidence threshold. A detector fine-tuned on TACO learns what litter looks like in context; an open-vocabulary detector finds objects from text prompts with no training. Measure both on validation data, then pick.

decision.choice: Fine-tune Ultralytics YOLO11 on TACO merged by its 10-class map (map_10.csv); OWLv2 zero-shot as the baseline
decision.why: Many of TACO's 60 classes have few examples; the repo's 10-class map merges them into classes cleanup groups care about. A small YOLO runs quickly per photo. The OWLv2 baseline shows whether training was worth it. Note Ultralytics is AGPL-3.0, which matters for a closed app.

alternatives.name: OWLv2 zero-shot only
alternatives.tradeoff: No training and a new litter type is a text prompt away, but slower per image; check its count error on TACO before trusting it.

alternatives.name: Single class-agnostic 'litter' class
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest for density, but loses the breakdown (cigarettes vs bottles) groups use to plan cleanups.

alternatives.name: Mask R-CNN, as in the TACO paper
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives instance masks, but heavier, and masks are not needed to count.

steps.delegate: Python, ultralytics, transformers. Convert TACO COCO json to YOLO format with map_10.csv, using the frozen split. Train yolo11n and yolo11s with a fixed seed. Baseline: Owlv2ForObjectDetection with google/owlv2-base-patch16-ensemble and one prompt per class. eval_counts.py reports mAP50 and per-image count MAE on val only. Tests: the converter preserves box count per image; class ids match the map.
verify: Record mAP50 and count MAE on val for YOLO11n, YOLO11s and OWLv2, with machine and command
Confirm no training or tuning script reads the frozen test list (grep the logs for its path)

steps.title: Handle small items with tiled inference
steps.learn: Cigarettes are TACO's most common annotation and are tiny in a full photo, more so after downscaling to the model's input size. Slicing the crop into overlapping tiles, detecting per tile and merging boxes recovers small objects, but overlap can double count if merging is wrong.

decision.choice: SAHI sliced prediction over the rectified crop, compared against full-image inference on val
decision.why: SAHI wraps Ultralytics models (model_type='ultralytics') and merges tile predictions, so you can test tiling without writing a merger. Tiling only the rectified crop spends compute on the surveyed ground, not the whole scene.

alternatives.name: Larger input size (imgsz)
alternatives.tradeoff: One pass and no merge step, but memory and latency grow with image area.

alternatives.name: Also train on tiles (slicing-aided fine-tuning)
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches train and test object scale, as in the SAHI paper, but adds data plumbing.

steps.delegate: Python, sahi. Use AutoDetectionModel.from_pretrained(model_type='ultralytics', ...) and get_sliced_prediction; grid over slice size and overlap ratio on val; report count MAE per class and latency. Tests: an image with one object straddling a tile boundary yields exactly one detection after merging.
verify: Report cigarette count MAE on val with and without tiling
Record latency per rectified crop for each tiling setting on your machine

steps.title: Pick the count threshold and reject bad photos
steps.learn: Counts depend on the confidence threshold: too low counts leaves and stones, too high misses items. Tune for count error, not mAP, because the ranking uses counts. Bad photos (blur, glare, missed marker) must be rejected at capture, not silently counted low.

decision.choice: Threshold that minimizes count MAE on val; capture-time gate on marker found, blur (variance of Laplacian) and exposure
decision.why: Tuning the quantity you rank keeps the metric honest. A gate at capture time lets the volunteer reshoot on the spot; a missing week cannot be recovered later.

alternatives.name: Library default confidence
alternatives.tradeoff: No tuning, but it was not chosen for counting this kind of scene.

alternatives.name: Accept all photos, flag later
alternatives.tradeoff: Never blocks volunteers, but rejected weeks leave gaps that make rankings uneven.

steps.delegate: tune_threshold.py sweeps confidence on val and reports count MAE and bias (mean signed error) per class. quality_gate(img) returns ok or a reason: no marker, Laplacian variance below a floor tuned on your own sharp and blurred photos, too dark or too bright. Tests: a blurred copy of a sharp image fails; threshold choice is deterministic for a fixed val set.
verify: Report the chosen threshold with val MAE and bias, then evaluate once on the frozen TACO test split
Take 10 deliberately bad photos and confirm the gate rejects each with the right reason

steps.title: Turn counts into litter per square meter and a ranking
steps.learn: Density is count divided by area_m2. With a handful of items per spot, chance alone moves spots up and down. Report an interval per spot, treat overlapping spots as tied, and decide whether you measure standing stock (what is there) or accumulation (how fast it returns).

decision.choice: Mean litter per square meter over weeks with bootstrap intervals; overlapping spots share a rank band
decision.why: Averaging over weeks smooths one-off events, and a bootstrap over weeks needs no distribution assumption. Kendall tau (scipy.stats.kendalltau) compares app and hand-count rankings and handles ties.

alternatives.name: Accumulation rate
alternatives.tradeoff: Clear the rectangle after each survey and count what returns; better for scheduling cleanups, but needs a cleanup at every spot every week.

alternatives.name: Latest week only
alternatives.tradeoff: Most current, but the noisiest ranking.

alternatives.name: Poisson interval on the total count
alternatives.tradeoff: Closed form, but assumes independent items; a dumped bag of litter breaks that.

steps.delegate: rank.py: density per spot-week, mean and bootstrap 90% interval per spot with a fixed seed, rank bands, Kendall tau against hand_counts.csv. Tests: identical inputs give identical bands; a spot with one extreme week gets a wider interval than a steady spot with the same mean.
verify: Feed synthetic data with a known true order and confirm tau is higher with 8 weeks than with 2
Confirm no script writes hand_counts.csv; rank.py only reads it, and it will be filled by a person in the field test

steps.title: Store surveys and handle gaps and model changes
steps.learn: Each survey ties spot, date, area, model version, threshold and counts. Weeks go missing, photos get rejected, cleanups happen between visits, and you will retrain the detector. Every ranking must say what data and which model produced it.

decision.choice: SQLite with spots, surveys and detections; model_id and threshold stored per survey; recount all weeks on model change
decision.why: One file, no server, easy for a volunteer group to back up. Re-running the stored ground crops with a new model keeps all weeks comparable instead of mixing models in one ranking.

alternatives.name: Shared spreadsheet
alternatives.tradeoff: Volunteers already use them, but there are no constraints and model versions get lost.

alternatives.name: Postgres
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles many concurrent writers and spatial queries later, but it is a server to run for 10 spots.

steps.delegate: Python sqlite3. Schema: spots(id, name, marker_id, rect_cm), surveys(id, spot_id, week, area_m2, model_id, threshold, status, cleanup_since_last), detections(survey_id, cls, conf, x, y, w, h). recount.py re-runs stored crops under a new model_id. Tests: unique (spot_id, week); the ranking query excludes rejected surveys and reports weeks per spot.
verify: Delete one spot's survey and confirm the report shows fewer weeks for it, not a zero count
Recount with a second model on a copy and confirm no ranking mixes model_ids

steps.title: Test it outside: 10 spots, weekly
steps.learn: The try-it is the real test: photograph the same 10 spots weekly and rank them. At each visit a second volunteer hand counts the marked rectangle before seeing the app's number, so ground truth is independent of the system.
verify: Survey all 10 spots weekly for at least 4 weeks and report rejected photos per week
Report per-photo count MAE and bias against hand counts, by class
Report Kendall tau between app and hand-count rankings per week and overall
List spots whose rank changed and whether their intervals overlapped

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened, (4) assumptions and what this does not prove. For example, why tiling helped cigarettes but not bottles, or why one spot's rank swung.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives count MAE, Kendall tau, area error and latency, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (flat ground, 10 spots, weeks surveyed) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Tide-pool and insect "dex"
projects.problem: Make nature walks a collecting game
projects.concepts: Zero-shot classification, rarity score from how few similar finds exist
projects.tryIt: Run it on a beach or garden walk with friends
projects.question: Can a zero-shot tree-of-life model name tide-pool animals and insects at the right rank, and score rarity by how few similar finds exist?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: Two ML calls in a game: zero-shot taxon naming (image vs taxon-name embeddings) and rarity (how few similar finds exist). Offline data: iNat21 validation, 10 images per species, COCO-style JSON with kingdom to species fields. Live: the try-it walk on a beach or in a garden with friends.

decision.choice: Freeze now: iNat21 val images of Insects, Mollusks, Arachnids and Animalia, split per species into tune and test halves
decision.why: Labels come from iNaturalist research data, not your model, so grading is independent. Caveat: BioCLIP 2 trained on TreeOfLife-200M, which includes iNaturalist records via GBIF, so test images may have been seen; treat scores as optimistic.

alternatives.name: Your own walk photos only
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use, but few and they need expert or community labels; keep some as a second test set later.

alternatives.name: iNat21 train images
alternatives.tradeoff: Far more images, but TreeOfLife-10M (original BioCLIP) was compiled from the iNat21 training split, so leakage is certain.

verify: README states the question and metrics: top-1 at species, genus and family; share of finds awarded per rank; live acceptance rate
Save tune and test image id lists with a seed and record their hashes
Note the iNat21 terms: non-commercial research and education use, no redistribution of images

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Collect animals, plants and places, never people. In tide pools the tide and waves are the main danger, so check official tide predictions first. Leave animals in place and put rocks back; collecting rules vary, so check the official source. An ID is never advice on whether something is safe to touch or eat.

decision.choice: On-device face block; coarse stored location; hide location for taxa iNaturalist flags as sensitive; safety screen
decision.why: Faces never leave the phone. iNaturalist sets taxon geoprivacy (conservation_status.geoprivacy obscured or private) for taxa threatened by location disclosure and blurs them to a 0.2 degree cell; mirror that so the game never maps a rare find.

alternatives.name: Exact pins for every find
alternatives.tradeoff: More fun for locating finds, but exposes sensitive species and players' routines.

alternatives.name: No location at all
alternatives.tradeoff: Safest, but loses place-based duplicate checks and local rarity.

steps.delegate: Client: MediaPipe Face Detector on device blocks shots with faces; strip EXIF. Server: round coordinates to about 1 km; if the taxon's iNaturalist conservation_status.geoprivacy is obscured or private, store only a region name. Pre-walk screen: link to official tide predictions, leave animals in place, do not handle stinging insects. Tests: face images never upload; sensitive-taxon rows hold no coordinates.
verify: Try 10 shots with a person in frame and confirm none upload
Pick a taxon whose API record has geoprivacy obscured, log a test find, and confirm no coordinates are stored
Confirm the pre-walk screen links to an official tide prediction source

steps.title: Build the local candidate list from iNaturalist
steps.learn: Zero-shot needs candidate labels. The full tree of life has hundreds of thousands of taxa, most impossible on your beach. Restricting to species observed nearby removes many look-alike errors, but makes a genuine stray impossible to name at species level.

decision.choice: iNaturalist /v1/observations/species_counts by lat, lng, radius, quality_grade=research and iconic_taxa, cached per area
decision.why: Each page returns species with their observation counts in the circle, which also seeds rarity later. Research grade means a community-agreed ID. Fetch once per walk area and cache it; never call the API per capture.

alternatives.name: Full TreeOfLife label set
alternatives.tradeoff: Can name anything, but many more confusable candidates for every photo.

alternatives.name: Hand-written common names with CustomLabelsClassifier
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to theme sets, but you maintain the list, and common names are ambiguous across regions.

steps.delegate: Python, requests. fetch_checklist(lat, lng, radius_km, iconic_taxa) pages through /v1/observations/species_counts and saves taxon id, name, rank, ancestry, count and conservation_status to checklist.json.
