Send a descriptive User-Agent and pause between pages. Tests: a second call reads from cache; only rank=species rows go into the species filter.
verify: Pull checklists for one beach and one garden; record species per iconic taxon
Record how many checklist rows are at species rank versus coarser ranks, and how many have conservation_status geoprivacy set

steps.title: Run BioCLIP restricted to the local list
steps.learn: BioCLIP embeds images and taxon names in one space; pybioclip's TreeOfLifeClassifier ships precomputed name embeddings. apply_filter keeps only chosen labels and the softmax then runs over that subset, so every photo is forced into some local species.

decision.choice: pybioclip TreeOfLifeClassifier (BioCLIP 2 by default) with create_taxa_filter on local species names
decision.why: No training, names come with full taxonomy, and filtering reuses shipped embeddings. create_taxa_filter raises ValueError on unknown names, so intersect the checklist with get_label_data() first and log what was dropped.

alternatives.name: Original BioCLIP (ViT-B/16)
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller and faster than BioCLIP 2's ViT-L/14; pick it if your test shows the accuracy loss is acceptable on your hardware.

alternatives.name: Generic CLIP with species prompts
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy via open_clip, but not trained on taxonomic names, so species-level naming is a weaker bet.

alternatives.name: Fine-tuned classifier on local species
alternatives.tradeoff: Can be the most accurate for a fixed list, but needs labeled images per species and retraining as the list changes.

steps.delegate: Python, pybioclip, Pillow. load_classifier(names, model_str) intersects names with get_label_data()['species'], then create_taxa_filter(Rank.SPECIES, names) and apply_filter. eval.py filters to the iNat21 tune and test species and runs predict(paths, Rank.SPECIES, k=5) on the tune half for BioCLIP 2 and BIOCLIP_V1_MODEL_STR; the app filters to the local checklist. Tests: unknown names dropped, not raised; predictions are in the filter.
verify: Report top-1 and top-5 species accuracy on the tune half for both models, with machine and command
Record milliseconds per image for both models on your machine

steps.title: Award at the deepest rank the model is sure about
steps.learn: Many insects cannot be told apart to species from a phone photo, but genus or family is often clear. pybioclip gets higher ranks by summing species probabilities, so a genus score is never below its best species. Award the deepest rank that clears its threshold, else 'unsorted'.

decision.choice: Per-rank thresholds tuned on the tune half for a target precision; fall back species, genus, family, then unsorted
decision.why: Wrong species names are the failure players notice; a correct genus entry is still a find. Tuning per rank for a stated precision makes 'how sure' explicit and testable, and off-topic photos (sand, rock, kelp) teach the floor.

alternatives.name: Always species top-1
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum detail, but many confident-looking wrong names.

alternatives.name: One threshold for all ranks
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but genus scores are sums, so one number means different confidence at each rank.

alternatives.name: Player picks from the top 3
alternatives.tradeoff: Teaches and yields labels, but players may pick the most exciting name.

steps.delegate: award(image) calls predict at Rank.SPECIES, GENUS and FAMILY and returns the deepest rank whose top score passes its threshold. tune_thresholds.py grid-searches per-rank thresholds on the tune half plus off-topic photos labeled none, maximizing coverage subject to precision at or above a target. Tests: genus score is at least the top species score in that genus; uniformly low scores return unsorted.
verify: Report precision and coverage per rank on the tune half, then evaluate once on the frozen test half
Add 50 of your own off-topic photos labeled none and report how many still get an award

steps.title: Store finds with embeddings and catch repeat photos
steps.learn: On a group walk, five friends photograph the same crab. Rarity must count individuals, not photos. Re-sent photos: perceptual hash. Same animal from a new angle: same taxon, high embedding similarity, close in time and place. Two real crabs of one species side by side is the hard case.

decision.choice: SQLite rows with embedding, pHash, taxon, time, place; duplicate = same taxon, nearby, recent, high cosine
decision.why: A walk yields hundreds of finds, so exact cosine over a NumPy array is instant and needs no vector database. Requiring nearby and recent stops the same species on another day or another beach being merged into one individual.

alternatives.name: Embedding similarity only
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches new angles, but merges distinct look-alike individuals and blocks honest finds.

alternatives.name: pgvector in Postgres
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles concurrent writers and indexes, but adds a server for a handful of friends.

alternatives.name: Count every photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial, but rarity then measures how often something gets photographed.

steps.delegate: Python, pybioclip, imagehash, sqlite3, numpy. Embed with the classifier's create_image_features (normalized); pHash with imagehash.phash. Table finds(id, user, taxon, rank, emb, phash, lat, lon, ts, model_id). is_duplicate(find) checks pHash distance, then same taxon within N meters and M minutes and cosine above a tuned value. Tests: a resized copy is a duplicate; the same species on another beach is not; different model_ids are never compared.
verify: Photograph 5 animals twice from different angles and confirm all 5 second shots are flagged
Photograph two individuals of one species in different pools and confirm neither is flagged

steps.title: Score rarity from how few similar finds exist
steps.learn: Rarity estimates how uncommon something is from little data. Two signals: your group's finds (very few after day one) and local iNaturalist counts (many, but biased toward conspicuous, photogenic species). Combine them so day one does not make everything legendary.

decision.choice: Smoothed frequency: group finds plus iNaturalist counts as a prior, at the awarded rank; tiers frozen at award
decision.why: The checklist counts from the earlier step act as a prior that group finds gradually override. Scoring at the awarded rank keeps genus finds comparable to species finds. Freezing the tier at award means a later recount never takes a prize away.

alternatives.name: Embedding neighborhood density
alternatives.tradeoff: Rewards unusual-looking individuals of common species, but very noisy with few finds.

alternatives.name: iNaturalist counts only
alternatives.tradeoff: Stable from day one, but ignores what your group sees and inherits observer bias.

alternatives.name: Group counts only
alternatives.tradeoff: Purely your game, but everything is 'rare' on day one.

steps.delegate: rarity.py: freq(taxon) = (group_count + a * prior_share) / (group_total + a), score = -log(freq); tiers from quantiles over the checklist; store the tier on the find. Tests: with no group finds, a common checklist species is not top tier; adding 20 finds of a taxon lowers the next find's score.
verify: Replay the tune half as a simulated week and plot tier counts per day
Show 5 top-tier and 5 bottom-tier finds to someone who knows the area and record agreement

steps.title: Work without signal and survive retries
steps.learn: Beaches and gardens often have weak signal. Captures must queue on the phone, upload later and be classified exactly once. Retries on a flaky connection must not double-award, and everyone must use the same model so rarity is comparable.

decision.choice: Queue on device, classify on the server at sync, an idempotency key per capture, model_id stored with every find
decision.why: BioCLIP 2 uses a ViT-L/14 image encoder, heavy for phones; a server keeps one model version for all players. Showing 'pending' until sync is acceptable for a walk-then-review game.

alternatives.name: On-device original BioCLIP
alternatives.tradeoff: Instant offline results, but conversion and quantization work, and version drift across devices.

alternatives.name: Require a connection
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but fails exactly where tide pools are.

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI: POST /finds with Idempotency-Key header, image, coarse lat/lon and timestamp; GET /dex/{user}. Client persists a local queue and retries with backoff. Server stores results with model_id. Tests with pytest and httpx: the same key twice yields one find; queued captures sync in order after reconnect.
verify: Capture 20 finds in airplane mode, reconnect, and confirm exactly 20 finds with no duplicates
Kill the server mid-upload, retry, and confirm exactly one stored find

steps.title: Test it outside: a beach or garden walk with friends
steps.learn: The try-it: run it on a beach or garden walk with friends. Give every find a one-tap 'wrong name' button. Afterwards, get independent labels for a sample (a local expert, or iNaturalist community IDs if players choose to post), never the app's own output.
verify: Report finds per player and the share awarded at species, genus, family and unsorted
Report award precision on 50 independently labeled finds
Audit 50 finds for missed duplicates and report the count
Confirm no sensitive-taxon find stored coordinates

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened, (4) assumptions and what this does not prove. For example, why insects backed off to family more than snails, or why a common species scored rare.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives accuracy per rank, coverage, duplicate and latency numbers, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (possible test overlap with training data, one area, few walkers) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Backyard camera-trap sorter
projects.problem: Trail cameras capture thousands of empty frames
projects.concepts: Edge AI on a Raspberry Pi, a distilled small model to drop empty frames
projects.tryIt: Leave a Pi camera out for a week; measure frames kept vs missed animals
projects.question: Can a small distilled model on a Raspberry Pi drop most empty camera-trap frames while missing almost no animals?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the held-out cameras
steps.learn: Trail cameras fire on wind, shadows and sun, so most frames are empty. The try-it gives two numbers: frames kept (lower is better) and animals missed (near zero is the goal). Missing an animal costs more than keeping an empty frame, so recall on animal frames is the headline metric.

decision.choice: Caltech Camera Traps (LILA BC) location split: tune on half the val locations, freeze the other half as test
decision.why: LILA reports about 70% of its images are labeled empty, which matches the real problem, and it has 140 camera locations. Splitting by location (not by image) tests what you need: a model that works on a camera it never saw, like your yard.

alternatives.name: Random image split
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier, but frames from the same camera leak into test, so scores look far better than on a new yard.

alternatives.name: Snapshot Serengeti
alternatives.tradeoff: Much larger and also on LILA, but African savanna species, so less like a backyard; good as a second test set.

alternatives.name: Only your own yard photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic, but you have no labels yet and must wait days before you can measure anything.

verify: Download the CCT splits file and list which location ids are train and which are val before training anything
Freeze a test set: pick held-out locations, write their ids to a file, and do not look at their scores until the final run
Count empty vs non-empty human labels in your test locations and record the empty fraction

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: This camera is for animals, not people. A backyard camera can still catch neighbors, children or delivery workers, and pointing it past your property line is a privacy problem. Wildlife should not be lured or disturbed to get better photos.

decision.choice: Delete person-or-vehicle frames on the Pi, keep only an anonymous count; aim only at your own yard
decision.why: The student's person class lets the device discard those frames before anything is stored or uploaded, so faces are never kept. A daily count of discarded person frames still tells you how often it happens without saving who it was.

alternatives.name: Blur people and keep the frame
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps the animal context, but blurring can fail and the raw frame exists until it runs.

alternatives.name: No person handling
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but you would store images of people who never agreed to it.

steps.delegate: Extend sorter.py: if p_person is above a low threshold, delete the frame in memory before any disk write and increment a per-day counter; never route person frames to audit/. Strip EXIF location from saved images. Tests: a frame scored as person is never written; the counter increments; saved JPEGs carry no GPS tags.
verify: Walk past the camera 5 times and confirm no image of you is saved and the counter shows 5 events or more
Check the camera view covers only your own property and no neighbor windows
Confirm no bait or food is used to attract animals

steps.title: Get teacher labels from MegaDetector
steps.learn: MegaDetector is a large detector for animals, people and vehicles in camera-trap images. It does not name species, it just finds them, which is exactly the empty vs not-empty signal you need. Its per-class confidences become the soft targets a small student learns from.

decision.choice: Use the precomputed MegaDetector results that LILA publishes for CCT, on training locations only
decision.why: LILA has already run MegaDetector on every camera-trap dataset it hosts and says these results are meant for classifier training. You skip hours of GPU time. LILA also warns most of these datasets were in MegaDetector's training data, so never use them to judge MegaDetector itself.

alternatives.name: Train on human labels only
alternatives.tradeoff: No teacher needed, but hard 0/1 labels carry no 'how sure' signal for dark or partly hidden animals.

alternatives.name: Run MegaDetector yourself (MDv5a or MDv1000-redwood)
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for your own yard photos later; on a laptop CPU it is slow, so batch it with run_detector_batch and checkpoints.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Script build_targets.py: load the CCT metadata JSON and the LILA MegaDetector results JSON for CCT; for each training-location image compute max detection confidence per category (animal, person, vehicle); write a Parquet table image_id, location, p_animal, p_person, p_vehicle, human_label. Tests: every image appears once, no val or test location appears, confidences lie in [0,1].
verify: Plot p_animal for images humans labeled empty vs animal and note where the two overlap
Hand-inspect 20 images where teacher and human disagree and note the cause (tiny animal, night, foliage)

steps.title: Choose a small student model that fits on a Pi
steps.learn: The student only answers 'empty, animal or person' for the whole frame, a classification task, so it can be far smaller than a detector. Classification hides where the animal is, which is fine because you keep the full frame for review anyway.

decision.choice: torchvision mobilenet_v3_small, ImageNet weights, 3-class head (empty, animal, person-or-vehicle)
decision.why: MobileNetV3 was tuned for mobile phone CPUs, and the small variant fits the Pi's compute and memory. A person class is needed so frames with people can be deleted on the device, not just kept as 'not empty'.

alternatives.name: Run MegaDetector on the Pi
alternatives.tradeoff: Best accuracy, but a large detector on a Pi CPU is slow; frames would queue up during a busy burst.

alternatives.name: Tiny YOLO detector (Ultralytics nano)
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives boxes and counts, but needs box labels and more compute per frame than a classifier.

alternatives.name: Larger student (EfficientNet, ResNet-50)
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher accuracy, but slower on the Pi; try it only if the small student misses too many animals.

steps.delegate: PyTorch + torchvision. Module model.py: build_student() returns mobilenet_v3_small with pretrained weights and a 3-way classifier head; transform() resizes to a fixed input size with the same normalization as the weights. Tests: forward pass on a batch gives shape (N,3); the model loads on CPU only; parameter count is printed and recorded.
verify: Record the parameter count and model file size
Time 100 forward passes on your laptop CPU as a baseline for the Pi later

steps.title: Train the student with a distillation loss
steps.learn: Distillation trains the student to match the teacher's soft outputs, which carry more information than 0/1 labels (a frame at 0.4 animal is 'maybe'). Mixing in the human label keeps the student from copying the teacher's mistakes.

decision.choice: Loss = weighted sum of soft-target loss vs teacher and cross-entropy vs human label; tune the weight on val locations
decision.why: Soft targets help the student on ambiguous frames (dark, partly hidden animals) that matter most for misses, while the human term anchors it where MegaDetector is wrong. Tuning on val, never test, keeps the frozen cameras honest.

alternatives.name: Teacher-only targets
alternatives.tradeoff: Works with unlabeled images (your yard), but inherits teacher errors with nothing to correct them.

alternatives.name: Human labels only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but loses the confidence signal and treats every empty-labeled sequence frame as certain.

steps.delegate: PyTorch train.py: from the Parquet table build a 3-class teacher target (empty = 1 minus max(p_animal, p_person, p_vehicle), then normalize); human label: empty, car to person-or-vehicle, other species to animal (CCT has no person label). Loss = alpha * soft cross-entropy(teacher_target, softmax(student_logits)) + (1-alpha) * CE(student, human_label). Class-balanced sampling, early stopping on val loss. Tests: loss finite on a tiny batch; alpha=0 equals plain cross-entropy.
verify: Compare alpha=0 vs your best alpha on val locations: animal recall and empty-frame drop rate
List the 20 val animal frames with the lowest student score and describe what they show

links.label: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network (arXiv)

steps.title: Set the keep threshold for a target animal recall
steps.learn: The model outputs a score; the threshold turns it into keep or drop. Because a missed animal costs more than an extra empty frame, pick the threshold from the precision-recall curve to hit a recall target, then read off how many frames you still drop.

decision.choice: Keep a frame if p_animal is above a threshold chosen on val locations to meet a fixed animal-recall target
decision.why: It ties the knob directly to the try-it metric (missed animals) and makes the tradeoff explicit: every point of recall you demand costs some extra kept frames. Choosing on val and reporting on frozen test avoids tuning to the answer.

alternatives.name: Argmax of the 3 classes
alternatives.tradeoff: No tuning, but the implied operating point is arbitrary and may miss more animals than you accept.

alternatives.name: Keep whole bursts if any frame passes
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer misses on fast animals, but keeps more empty frames; good as a second rule on top.

steps.delegate: Python script pick_threshold.py: load val predictions, use sklearn.metrics.precision_recall_curve on the animal class, choose the highest threshold reaching the target recall, write threshold.json. Also report frames dropped at that threshold. Tests: chosen threshold meets the target on val; script refuses to read test-location predictions.
verify: Plot frames kept vs animals missed on val for 5 thresholds
Record val recall and drop rate at the chosen threshold; score the frozen test locations only once, on the final int8 model

steps.title: Export to ONNX and quantize to int8 for the Pi
steps.learn: Int8 quantization shrinks the model and usually speeds up CPU inference, but it is not lossless. ONNX Runtime documents static quantization (with calibration data) as the recommended method for CNNs, so recheck recall after quantizing because the threshold may shift.

decision.choice: torch.onnx export, then onnxruntime quantize_static with a few hundred training-location frames as calibration data
decision.why: ONNX Runtime ships Python wheels for 64-bit ARM Linux (a 64-bit Pi OS), and static quantization is what its docs recommend for CNNs like MobileNet. Calibrating on training locations keeps test cameras unseen.

alternatives.name: Keep float32
alternatives.tradeoff: No accuracy risk, but larger and slower; fine if the Pi already keeps up with your frame rate.

alternatives.name: LiteRT (TensorFlow Lite) int8
alternatives.tradeoff: Also built for edge devices, but means a separate conversion path from PyTorch to check.

alternatives.name: quantize_dynamic
alternatives.tradeoff: No calibration set needed, but ONNX Runtime suggests it for RNNs and transformers, not CNNs.

steps.delegate: Python: export.py exports the student to ONNX with a fixed input size; quantize.py implements a CalibrationDataReader over 300 training-location frames and calls onnxruntime.quantization.quantize_static (QDQ format). bench.py times 200 runs with onnxruntime InferenceSession. Tests: float vs int8 top class agree on most of a val sample; script prints model sizes.
verify: On val locations, compare float vs int8 animal recall at the chosen threshold; re-pick the threshold if it drops
On the Pi, record median and p95 inference time per frame for float and int8, with Pi model and OS version

steps.title: Choose how the Pi decides when to take a frame
steps.learn: Something must decide when to capture. Options are a heat-sensing PIR motion sensor or comparing frames from a small low-resolution camera stream. Either trigger creates the empty frames the model then filters, and its sensitivity sets how many frames the model must process.

decision.choice: Picamera2: frame differencing on a small lores stream, full-resolution capture when motion passes a threshold
decision.why: Frame differencing needs no extra hardware and the lores stream keeps CPU use low. A loose motion threshold is fine because the classifier removes the empty frames; a tight one would miss animals before the model ever sees them.

alternatives.name: PIR motion sensor on GPIO
alternatives.tradeoff: Senses warm moving bodies and needs little CPU, but may miss small, distant or cool animals and needs wiring.

alternatives.name: Fixed-interval timelapse
alternatives.tradeoff: Never misses due to a trigger, but produces far more frames and drains storage and power.

steps.delegate: Python on Raspberry Pi OS: capture.py using picamera2 with create_video_configuration(main=full size, lores=small YUV); compute mean absolute difference between consecutive lores frames; on exceeding a threshold capture a short burst from main with capture_array, timestamp it, and push to a queue. Tests: with a recorded clip as input, the trigger fires on the motion segments and not on static ones.
verify: Point the camera at a still scene for 10 minutes and count false triggers
Wave an object through the frame 10 times at distance and count how many triggers fired

steps.title: Wire keep or drop, with an audit sample of dropped frames
steps.learn: You cannot count missed animals if you delete every dropped frame. Keeping a small random sample of drops, plus a score log for every frame, lets a human later measure misses without trusting the model's own judgment.

decision.choice: Keep frames above threshold; save a random fraction of dropped non-person frames to an audit folder; log every score
decision.why: The audit sample gives an unbiased estimate of missed animals for the try-it week while still saving most storage. Logging scores lets you replay a different threshold later without re-running the model.

alternatives.name: Keep everything during the test week
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact miss count, but you are no longer testing the storage savings the project claims.

alternatives.name: Keep only what the model keeps
alternatives.tradeoff: Least storage, but misses become invisible and the metric is graded by the model itself.

steps.delegate: Python service sorter.py: consume the capture queue, run the int8 ONNX model, route to kept/ or audit/ (random sample of drops) or delete; append image id, timestamp, scores and decision to a CSV. Run under systemd with Restart=on-failure; stop capturing when free disk is below a limit and log it. Tests: routing is correct for fixed scores; disk-full path stops cleanly; CSV row per frame.
verify: Run 1 hour on a recorded clip or an empty room and confirm every frame has exactly one CSV row and one outcome
Kill the process with kill -9 (SIGKILL) and confirm systemd restarts it and logging resumes

steps.title: Test it outside: one week in the backyard
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation: leave the Pi out for a week and measure frames kept vs missed animals. Your yard differs from CCT (lighting, plants, species), so expect the drop rate and recall to shift; that gap is a result, not a failure.
verify: Report total triggers, frames kept, and drop rate for the week
Hand-label the audit sample and estimate missed animals per 100 animal frames, with the sample size
Report uptime, restarts and any disk-full stops from the logs
List species or situations behind each missed animal (night, small, far)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example why night frames were missed), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives test-location and backyard recall, drop rate and Pi latency, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with example frames
Part 4 lists assumptions (one yard, one week, one season) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Night sky identifier
projects.problem: Which star, planet or satellite is that?
projects.concepts: Geometric hashing of star patterns (a search problem), satellite orbit data
projects.tryIt: Photograph the sky on clear nights; check against star charts
projects.question: Can geometric hashing of star patterns plus orbit data correctly name the stars, planets and satellites in a phone or camera photo of the night sky?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the reference photos
steps.learn: Identifying stars is a search problem: match the pattern of bright dots against a catalog without knowing where the camera pointed. Success, from the try-it: the share of photos solved, and the share of labeled objects that agree with a star chart for the same time and place.

decision.choice: Start with the two sample images in the tetra3 repo, then your own tripod photos; freeze a held-out set of your photos
decision.why: The tetra3 samples come with known camera details, so you can test the solver before going outside. Your own photos are the real target; freezing a set before tuning and getting reference solutions from nova.astrometry.net (an independent solver) keeps grading separate from your code.

alternatives.name: Only your own photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic, but you cannot tell a camera problem from a code problem early on.

alternatives.name: Grade against your own solver output
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy, but the system would be grading itself; always use an independent reference.

verify: Write the one question and 2 metrics: solve rate, and label agreement with a chart
Freeze a held-out photo list; strip GPS EXIF and upload as not public to nova.astrometry.net for reference solutions before tuning
Record each photo's time, rough location, lens and exposure

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: This app identifies sky objects, not people. Night photos can still include neighbors' windows or people, and photo metadata can reveal where the user lives. Stargazing in the dark brings its own risks: trespassing to find a dark spot, roads, and pointing a camera or eyes at the Sun.

decision.choice: Crop or mask the land and horizon before any upload; strip GPS from saved files and store only coarse location
decision.why: The solver needs only the sky region, and planet and satellite predictions need only an approximate location, so exact coordinates and ground scenes never need to leave the device.

alternatives.name: Upload full photos with EXIF
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but leaks home location and any people or windows in the frame.

alternatives.name: Process entirely offline
alternatives.tradeoff: Most private, but large index files and orbit updates must be stored on the device.

steps.delegate: Add privacy.py: read time from EXIF, then strip all GPS tags (exiftool or piexif) before saving or uploading; round user location to a coarse grid; optional mask of the bottom of the frame. Tests: output files contain no GPS tags; stored location is rounded; planet predictions with coarse vs exact location differ by less than your tolerance.
verify: Run exiftool on saved outputs and confirm no GPS fields remain
Compare satellite track error with coarse vs exact location and record the difference
Confirm the app warns never to aim at the Sun and to observe only from places you may legally be

steps.title: Find star centroids in the image
steps.learn: Before matching, turn pixels into a list of star positions. The sky background varies (light pollution, moonlight, gradients), so subtract a local background, then find compact blobs and take their brightness-weighted centers. Hot pixels and streaks are not stars.

decision.choice: sep (Source Extractor as a library): sep.Background, then sep.extract, keeping the brightest compact sources
decision.why: sep runs Source Extractor's core background and detection algorithms on in-memory arrays, which handle uneven city skies better than a single global threshold.

alternatives.name: tetra3 get_centroids_from_image
alternatives.tradeoff: Built into the solver with many filters (area, axis ratio), fewer dependencies; less flexible background modeling.

alternatives.name: Global threshold plus connected components
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to write, but fails on gradients from streetlights or the Moon.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, numpy, sep, Pillow/rawpy. detect.py: load image to grayscale float32, compute sep.Background, subtract, sep.extract with a sigma threshold, drop elongated or tiny sources, return (x, y, flux) sorted by flux. Tests: on a synthetic image with 20 Gaussian stars plus noise, it finds all 20 within 1 pixel; a hot single pixel is rejected.
verify: On a tetra3 sample image, overlay detections and count obvious misses and false hits
Record how many sources you get on one of your own photos and from a light-polluted vs dark sky

steps.title: Choose the plate solver: hash star patterns
steps.learn: Geometric hashing turns a small group of stars into a code that does not change with position, rotation or scale. tetra3 uses four stars, takes the distances between every pair, divides by the longest, and hashes those ratios; Astrometry.net hashes 4 or 5 star asterisms. Matches are then checked.

decision.choice: tetra3 for the main path, with a local Astrometry.net solve-field as a fallback and reference
decision.why: tetra3 is a lost-in-space solver in Python, whose default database covers 10 to 30 degree fields, which suits phone and small-lens photos. Astrometry.net handles almost any scale and gives an independent answer to compare against.

alternatives.name: Astrometry.net only
alternatives.tradeoff: Very robust and needs no FOV guess, but heavier to install and index files must match your scale.

alternatives.name: Your own hash from scratch
alternatives.tradeoff: Best for learning, but you must solve tolerance, false matches and verification yourself; do it after the baseline works.

steps.delegate: Python: solve.py wraps tetra3.Tetra3: solve_from_centroids(centroids, size, fov_estimate) with return_matches=True, converting step 3's (x, y) to (y, x) rows sorted brightest first and size to (height, width); also a wrapper that shells out to solve-field with --scale-units degwidth and scale bounds, parsing the .wcs output. Tests: both solve a tetra3 sample image; their center RA/Dec agree within a tolerance you set.
verify: Solve both tetra3 sample images and record RA, Dec, FOV, Matches and T_solve
Compare tetra3's center against solve-field's for the same image and record the separation

steps.title: Build a star pattern index for your camera's field of view
steps.learn: The index only works if its patterns are the right size on the sky for your lens. tetra3's generate_database takes max_fov (set it to your FOV), a catalog and a faintest magnitude; small-FOV databases can take hours, wide ones minutes.

decision.choice: Hipparcos (hip_main), the tetra3 default, max_fov from your lens, star_max_magnitude near your camera's limit
decision.why: tetra3's docs call hip_main the recommended catalog, sufficient down to about 3 degree fields, and it stores HIP numbers you can map to star names. Matching the faint limit to your photos avoids indexing stars the camera cannot record.

alternatives.name: Yale Bright Star Catalog (BSC5)
alternatives.tradeoff: Tiny and enough for fields over 10 degrees, but few stars for narrow lenses.

alternatives.name: Tycho (tyc_main)
alternatives.tradeoff: Complete to about magnitude 10 and works for any tetra3 database, but much larger and slower to build.

steps.delegate: Python: build_db.py computes FOV from focal length and sensor width (or from the reference solve), then calls tetra3.Tetra3().generate_database(max_fov=..., star_catalog='hip_main', star_max_magnitude=..., save_as=...). Log build time and file size. Tests: the saved database loads; database_properties reports the chosen max_fov and catalog.
verify: Record FOV, faint limit, build time and file size
Solve 5 of your non-held-out photos and record how many solve and their RMSE

steps.title: Accept a solution only when the evidence is strong
steps.learn: A hash hit is a hypothesis, not an answer: with many stars, chance matches happen. Both solvers verify by predicting where other stars should be and testing the match. tetra3 returns Prob (chance the solution is a false positive), Matches and RMSE.

decision.choice: Accept only if Prob is below a strict cutoff and Matches is above a minimum; otherwise report 'not solved' and say why
decision.why: A wrong solution labels every star wrongly, which is worse than no answer. Explicit reasons (too few stars, too much blur) tell the user what to change on the next shot.

alternatives.name: Trust any returned solution
alternatives.tradeoff: More photos labeled, but silent wrong labels destroy trust.

alternatives.name: Fall back to solve-field on failure
alternatives.tradeoff: Rescues more photos, but slower; good as a second attempt, still with its own acceptance rule.

steps.delegate: Python: accept.py takes a tetra3 result and returns (status, reason) using configurable max_prob and min_matches; reasons include too_few_stars, no_match, low_confidence. Add a retry that varies the distortion search if the first solve fails. Tests: fixed result dicts map to expected statuses; a None result yields no_match.
verify: On non-held-out photos, count accepted, rejected and wrong (vs the nova reference) at 3 cutoffs
Find one rejected photo and confirm the reason matches what you see

steps.title: Label the matched stars with names
steps.learn: The solver gives HIP catalog numbers for matched stars and their pixel positions. People want names, so join HIP numbers to the IAU Catalog of Star Names, which lists names with HIP ids; most faint stars have no proper name and keep a catalog id.

decision.choice: Join matched_catID (HIP) to the IAU-CSN file; label named stars only, show HIP for the rest on tap
decision.why: IAU-CSN is the official name list and includes HIP numbers, so the join is exact rather than fuzzy. Labeling only named stars keeps the image readable.

alternatives.name: Names from a planetarium app's data files
alternatives.tradeoff: Includes constellation lines, but you must check its license and format.

alternatives.name: Bayer designations for all bright stars
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers more stars, but needs another table and is less familiar to beginners.

steps.delegate: Python: names.py parses IAU-CSN.txt (fixed-width with comment lines) into a dict HIP to name; label.py draws names at matched_centroids on the image with Pillow. Tests: parsing returns entries with integer HIP ids; Polaris is present; a missing HIP returns None without error.
verify: Label one solved photo and check 5 named stars by eye against Stellarium for the same time and place
Record how many matched stars got a proper name vs only a HIP id

steps.title: Predict planets and match them to unexplained dots
steps.learn: Planets move against the stars, so no star catalog contains them. Compute where each planet is for the photo's time and place from an ephemeris, project that RA/Dec into the image with the solved pointing, and look for a bright source there that matched no star.

decision.choice: Skyfield with the JPL DE421 ephemeris; time from the photo's metadata, location from the user
decision.why: Skyfield's docs show DE421 covers 1900 to 2050 in a 17 MB file and ephemeris files never need updating. Matching only against unmatched bright sources avoids naming a star as a planet.

alternatives.name: DE440s
alternatives.tradeoff: Newer and covers 1849 to 2150, at about twice the file size; no practical gain for current photos.

alternatives.name: Look up positions in an online service
alternatives.tradeoff: No ephemeris file, but needs a network at the telescope and adds a dependency.

steps.delegate: Python: planets.py uses skyfield.api load('de421.bsp'), wgs84.latlon for the observer, computes apparent RA/Dec of Mercury to Saturn at the photo time, keeps those above the horizon, converts to pixels with the solved WCS (astropy.wcs) and matches to unmatched sources within a radius. Tests: a planet below the horizon is skipped; projection of a matched star's RA/Dec returns its pixel within the RMSE.
verify: On a photo containing a known bright planet, confirm it is labeled and record pixel error
Shift the photo time by 1 day and confirm the planet label moves or disappears

steps.title: Match satellite streaks to orbit predictions
steps.learn: In a long exposure a satellite leaves a streak. Its predicted path comes from published orbital elements, which Skyfield's docs warn go out of date within weeks and are accurate to about a kilometer at epoch. Only sunlit satellites are visible, and a wrong camera clock shifts the predicted track.

decision.choice: CelesTrak 'visual' group, refreshed every few days, propagated with Skyfield; streaks found by Hough lines
decision.why: CelesTrak's visual group is the 100 or so brightest satellites, so candidates are few and false matches rare. Skyfield's is_sunlit filters out satellites in Earth's shadow, and comparing the predicted track to the streak's angle and position is a cheap test.

alternatives.name: CelesTrak 'active' group
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers far more satellites, but many more candidates per streak and more chance of a wrong match.

alternatives.name: Ignore satellites
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but streaks then get mislabeled or break the star match.

steps.delegate: Python: sats.py loads elements with skyfield load.tle_file (reload when older than N days, as in the Skyfield docs), computes sunlit satellites above the horizon during the exposure, projects start and end points into the image; streaks.py finds line segments (OpenCV HoughLinesP on the background-subtracted image). Match by angle and offset. Tests: synthetic streak along a known track matches; a shadowed satellite is skipped.
verify: Photograph a predicted ISS pass (from Heavens-Above) and confirm the streak gets the right label
Offset the photo time by 30 seconds and record how far the predicted track moves in pixels

steps.title: Test it outside: clear nights vs star charts
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation: photograph the sky on several clear nights and check labels against star charts. Vary lens, exposure and sky darkness so you learn where it breaks, and grade with Stellarium and nova.astrometry.net, not with your own solver.
verify: Report solve rate on the frozen held-out photos and on all new photos, with the number of nights
Report label agreement with Stellarium for stars, planets and satellites separately
Record median solve time per photo with the machine and command
List every wrong label and its cause (clouds, wrong time, blur)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example why wide-angle photos failed), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives solve rate, label agreement and solve time, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with example photos
Part 4 lists assumptions (one camera, one site, a few nights) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Neighborhood smoke and air map
projects.problem: Official air sensors are kilometers apart
projects.concepts: Cheap sensors, streaming data pipeline, interpolation on a map
projects.tryIt: Place 3 to 5 sensors with friends across town
projects.question: Can 3 to 5 cheap PM2.5 sensors, corrected and interpolated, map neighborhood smoke better than reading the nearest official monitor?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: Official PM2.5 monitors are kilometers apart, so a block can differ from the reading you see. Success: at a held-out point, your corrected and interpolated estimate has lower error against a reference than the nearest official monitor does. Develop offline on EPA AQS hourly PM2.5 (88101) before any hardware arrives.

decision.choice: Offline: AQS hourly 88101 for a metro with many monitors, hold out whole monitors and a smoke week; live: 3 to 5 sensors
decision.why: AQS holds validated regulatory data, so a held-out monitor is an honest stand-in for 'a point between sensors'. Freezing the held-out monitors and dates now stops you tuning interpolation on the answer.

alternatives.name: AirNow API only
alternatives.tradeoff: Near real time and easy, but AirNow says its data is preliminary and not fully validated, so it is a weaker ground truth for grading.

alternatives.name: Sensor.Community archive
alternatives.tradeoff: Thousands of real cheap sensors with daily CSVs, great for pipeline and QC tests, but those sensors are uncorrected, so they cannot grade accuracy.

verify: Write the question, the metric (error at held-out points vs nearest monitor) and the held-out monitor IDs and dates in the README
Download one AQS hourly_88101 year file and count monitors in your chosen metro
Commit the held-out list before writing any interpolation code

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The sensors measure air, never people: no cameras, no microphones. But a sensor's coordinates reveal a friend's home, and a health-relevant map can be wrong. The app is a helper; for health decisions people must check official sources.

decision.choice: Publish only snapped coordinates, keep exact ones private, host consent, banner pointing to AirNow
decision.why: Snapping keeps the map useful at neighborhood scale while not pinpointing a house, and consent plus an official-source banner sets honest expectations before any real data is collected.

alternatives.name: Private map for the group only
alternatives.tradeoff: Removes location exposure, but loses the neighborhood benefit.

alternatives.name: Exact coordinates, public
alternatives.tradeoff: Best interpolation display, but discloses where friends live.

steps.delegate: Add snap_location(lat, lon, cell_m) used for public_lat/public_lon and a test that no API response contains exact coordinates. Add host consent records (device_id, host, consent_date, can_withdraw) and a delete_device_data(device_id) function. Add a persistent banner linking to AirNow on every page.
verify: grep every API response for exact coordinates (must be none)
Each host has signed consent and knows how to withdraw
Banner linking to the official source is visible on mobile

steps.title: Choose the PM sensor and the humidity sensor
steps.learn: Cheap PM sensors count laser-scattered light, not mass, and humidity makes particles swell, which is why the EPA PurpleAir correction adds an RH term. PurpleAir pairs two PMS5003 sensors (channels A and B) so a failing one shows up as disagreement.

decision.choice: Two Plantower PMS5003 per site plus a BME280 for temperature and humidity
decision.why: Using the same sensor family as PurpleAir lets you start from the EPA correction and its A/B cleaning rule, and the second sensor gives a built-in health check. Sensor.Community also accepts PMS5003 data, so its archive gives free test data in the same shape.

alternatives.name: Sensirion SPS30
alternatives.tradeoff: Sensirion advertises contamination resistance and a long lifetime, but the EPA US-wide correction was not fit on it, so you must build your own colocation correction.

alternatives.name: Buy PurpleAir units
alternatives.tradeoff: Least hardware work and mature cloud, but your data path depends on their API and keys, and you learn less about the pipeline.

alternatives.name: Nova SDS011
alternatives.tradeoff: Common in Sensor.Community builds and cheap, but larger and one sensor per site gives no internal agreement check.

steps.delegate: Write a bill of materials and wiring doc for an ESP32 with two PMS5003 on separate UARTs and a BME280 on I2C. Then a Python parser module for the PMS5003 serial frame (start bytes, length, checksum) returning a dataclass with the PM fields. Tests: a valid captured frame parses, a frame with a flipped checksum byte is rejected, and a truncated frame is rejected.
verify: Find in the AMT paper which PurpleAir column (cf_1 or cf_atm) the correction uses and note it
Parser rejects corrupted frames in tests; record the PM fields your firmware will send

steps.title: Make each device timestamp, average and buffer
steps.learn: A map compares sites at the same moment, so every reading needs a trustworthy UTC timestamp and a device ID. Wi-Fi at friends' houses will drop, so the device must keep readings and send them later rather than lose a smoke spike.

decision.choice: ESP32 syncs UTC by SNTP, averages raw readings into fixed intervals, and keeps a ring buffer for offline periods
decision.why: Device-side averaging cuts message volume and noise, SNTP gives comparable timestamps across houses, and a buffer means outages show up as late data, not missing data.

alternatives.name: Raspberry Pi per site
alternatives.tradeoff: Full Linux, easy Python and local disk, but more power, cost and SD-card failure risk at a friend's house.

alternatives.name: Stream every raw reading, let the server stamp time
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest firmware, but server time is wrong for buffered data and raw rate wastes bandwidth.

steps.delegate: ESP-IDF or Arduino-ESP32 firmware: sync time via SNTP at boot and periodically; read both PMS5003 and the BME280; emit one record per interval {device_id, ts_utc, pm25_a, pm25_b, rh, temp_c, n_samples, fw_version}; store unsent records in a ring buffer in flash. Host-side unit tests for the averaging and ring-buffer logic (overflow drops oldest, order preserved).
verify: Unplug Wi-Fi for 30 minutes and confirm buffered records arrive afterwards with original timestamps
Compare device ts_utc with your laptop clock and record the offset

steps.title: Choose how readings travel to the server
steps.learn: MQTT is a small publish/subscribe protocol for devices: devices publish to a topic on a broker, the ingester subscribes. QoS 1 means at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible and the ingester must be idempotent.

decision.choice: MQTT over TLS to a Mosquitto broker, QoS 1, topic air/<device_id>, idempotent ingest keyed by (device_id, ts_utc)
decision.why: Publish/subscribe decouples devices from storage, so you can restart the ingester without losing buffered data, and at-least-once plus a unique key gives exactly-once storage without complex protocols.

alternatives.name: HTTPS POST to your API
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest to debug with curl, but you write retry and backoff yourself and a down server rejects data.

alternatives.name: Push to Sensor.Community
alternatives.tradeoff: Free public map and archive, but your data becomes public at sensor coordinates and you still need your own copy for corrections.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 ingester with paho-mqtt: fixed client_id, clean_session=False and a QoS 1 subscription to air/+ so the broker queues messages while it is down; validate JSON against a schema; INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on (device_id, ts_utc). Mosquitto config with per-device usernames and ACLs limiting each device to its own topic. Tests: duplicate stored once, malformed message goes to a dead-letter table, device cannot publish to another device's topic.
verify: Publish the same record twice and confirm one row
Kill the ingester for 10 minutes, restart, and count rows lost (target zero)

steps.title: Store raw readings and derived values separately
steps.learn: You will change the correction and QC rules several times. If you only store corrected values you cannot recompute history. Keep raw readings immutable and write corrected, flagged values in a separate table tagged with the rule version that produced them.

decision.choice: SQLite in WAL mode: raw_readings (immutable), clean_readings (with correction_version, qc_flags)
decision.why: 5 sensors at minute resolution is a tiny dataset, SQLite is one file to back up, and WAL lets the map read while the ingester writes. Versioned derived rows make reprocessing safe.

alternatives.name: TimescaleDB (Postgres)
alternatives.tradeoff: Time bucketing and retention built in and many writers, but a server to run for a few thousand rows a day.

alternatives.name: InfluxDB
alternatives.tradeoff: Purpose built for time series, but a second query language and less natural joins with device metadata.

steps.delegate: Python module storage.py with SQLite WAL mode: tables devices(device_id, lat, lon, public_lat, public_lon, installed_at), raw_readings, clean_readings(correction_version, qc_flags). Function reprocess(version) rebuilds clean_readings from raw. Tests: reprocess is deterministic, raw rows are never updated, hourly and 24 h averages match a hand calculation.
verify: Run reprocess twice and diff outputs (must be identical)
Check hourly averages for one device against a spreadsheet calculation

steps.title: Colocate and correct the sensors
steps.learn: The EPA study found raw PurpleAir data overestimated FRM/FEM PM2.5 by about 40 percent in most of the US, and fit PM2.5 = 0.524 x PA_cf1 minus 0.0862 x RH + 5.75 on 24 h data. Sensors of one model also differ from each other, so colocate yours side by side first.

decision.choice: Start with the EPA US-wide correction plus its extension for extreme smoke, then check it by colocating with a reference
decision.why: The EPA equation is published and fit on many US sites, so it is a strong default. Your own colocation tells you whether it holds for your DIY PMS5003 build and local aerosol, without fitting on the held-out data.

alternatives.name: Fit your own regression from colocation
alternatives.tradeoff: Can match local conditions better, but a short colocation can overfit to that season and that smoke type.

alternatives.name: Raw readings, no correction
alternatives.tradeoff: No work, but the EPA study shows systematic overestimation, so the map would exaggerate.

steps.delegate: Python with pandas and scikit-learn: corrections.py with epa_us_wide(pa_cf1, rh) and fit_local(df) (linear model on 24 h averages with an RH term). Evaluate with time-blocked cross-validation (whole days held out). Store each correction with a version string. Tests: epa_us_wide matches a hand-computed value; fit_local on synthetic data recovers known coefficients.
verify: Run all sensors side by side for 2 or more days and record pairwise mean differences
Report RMSE vs reference for raw, EPA corrected and local fit on blocked days

steps.title: Flag bad data before it reaches the map
steps.learn: Cheap sensors fail quietly: one channel drifts, a fan dies, a reading sticks, humidity reads impossible values (the EPA paper reports RH readings of 255 percent). The EPA cleaning rule keeps 24 h data only when channels A and B differ by under 5 ug/m3 or 61 percent.

decision.choice: Rule-based flags (A/B disagreement, stuck values, bad RH, stale device); flagged points kept off the map
decision.why: Each rule is explainable to a friend hosting a sensor and testable, and the A/B rule comes from a published study. Hiding flagged points stops one broken sensor painting a fake plume.

alternatives.name: Statistical outlier detection across sites
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches subtle drift, but with 3 to 5 sites a real local smoke plume looks exactly like an outlier.

alternatives.name: No QC, show everything
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but one failed sensor dominates an interpolated map built from so few points.

steps.delegate: Python qc.py: functions ab_disagree(a, b) implementing the EPA 5 ug/m3 or 61 percent rule, stuck(series, n), rh_invalid(rh), stale(last_ts, now). Write flags into clean_readings.qc_flags. Tests from fixtures: a channel stuck for n intervals is flagged; a real smoke spike seen by both channels is not flagged; RH of 255 is flagged.
verify: Replay one Sensor.Community PMS5003 day file through QC and count flags per rule
Unplug one PMS5003 on a test device and confirm it is flagged within one interval

steps.title: Interpolate between sensors and say how sure you are
steps.learn: Inverse distance weighting (IDW) estimates a point as a distance-weighted average of nearby sensors; kriging fits a variogram to model how values correlate with distance. With 3 to 5 sensors a fitted variogram has almost no data, so simple methods and honest uncertainty matter more.

decision.choice: IDW, power and max radius tuned by leave-one-out CV on AQS training monitors; fade beyond the radius
decision.why: IDW has two knobs and no model to fit, so it degrades predictably with few points. Leave-one-out CV on training monitors tunes it without touching the frozen held-out set.

alternatives.name: Ordinary kriging (PyKrige)
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives a variance surface and can beat IDW with dense data, but a variogram fit from a handful of points is unreliable.

alternatives.name: Nearest sensor (Voronoi cells)
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to explain, but creates hard edges between houses and ignores the second-nearest sensor.

steps.delegate: Python interp.py with numpy: idw(points, values, grid, power, max_radius_m) on projected coordinates (metres); nearest(); a loo_cv(method, points, values) function. Optional kriging via pykrige OrdinaryKriging. Script evaluates all methods on AQS training monitors, then once on the frozen held-out monitors. Tests: IDW at a sensor location returns that value; equal values give a flat surface.
verify: Report leave-one-out error for nearest, IDW and kriging on training monitors
Run once on the frozen held-out monitors and compare with nearest-monitor error

steps.title: Build the map with staleness and official links
steps.learn: The map must make data age and uncertainty visible: a 2 hour old reading during a smoke event is misleading. Color by the official AQI categories so readers can compare with AirNow, and link to the official map for decisions.

decision.choice: Leaflet page: sensor dots with age, faded IDW layer, AQI category colors, link to AirNow Fire and Smoke Map
decision.why: Leaflet plus GeoJSON is small and hostable as a static page fed by one JSON endpoint, and borrowing official categories avoids inventing your own health scale.

alternatives.name: Grafana dashboard
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast time-series panels and alerts, but weak at interpolated map layers.

alternatives.name: Only a table of sensor values
alternatives.tradeoff: No interpolation errors to explain, but loses the 'where is the smoke' view that motivated the project.

steps.delegate: FastAPI endpoint /latest returning GeoJSON (sensor points at public coordinates, value, age_minutes, qc_flags) and /grid returning the IDW grid. Static Leaflet page rendering both, greying points older than a threshold. Tests: flagged sensors are excluded from /grid; stale points carry age_minutes; coordinates in the response are the public ones.
verify: Stop one device and confirm its dot greys out after the threshold
Check two values against AirNow AQI category colors by hand

steps.title: Test it outside: 3 to 5 sensors with friends across town
steps.learn: The live test measures what the offline check cannot: real uptime, real Wi-Fi, siting effects (a sensor near a grill or a dryer vent), and whether the map tracks a real smoke day. Place one sensor near an official monitor if you can so it acts as a live check.
verify: Record uptime per device and data lost per week
Leave one sensor out of the map and compare its corrected reading with the IDW estimate
Compare the sensor nearest an official monitor with that monitor hourly via the AirNow API
Log every siting issue (vents, grills, direct sun)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question; (2) numbers for every claim (errors for raw, corrected, IDW, nearest monitor, held-out results, uptime) with the machine and command; (3) why surprising results happened (siting, humidity, smoke type); (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Write-up states the one question at the top
Every number has the command and machine or device that produced it
A section explains at least one surprising result
A section lists assumptions and what 3 to 5 sensors cannot prove

projects.title: Street-tree health survey
projects.problem: Cities can't inspect every tree for disease
projects.concepts: Leaf-image classifier, geotagged dashboard
projects.tryIt: Survey one street's trees and share results with your city arborist
projects.question: Can leaf photos, a triage classifier and a geotagged map flag the street trees on one block that an arborist agrees need a closer look?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the data
steps.learn: This is triage, not diagnosis: the tool ranks trees for an arborist's attention. Success: on your street, the arborist agrees with your 'needs a look' flags (track recall and precision). Offline, use PlantDoc (field photos, CC BY 4.0, ships train and test folders) and keep its test folder frozen.

decision.choice: Train on PlantDoc train; frozen held-out: PlantDoc test plus the labeled Plant Pathology 2020 train images (apple)
decision.why: PlantDoc was built because lab-style images do not reflect field photos, which is closer to a phone on a sidewalk. A second dataset from a different source tests whether the model generalizes beyond one photo style.

alternatives.name: PlantVillage only
alternatives.tradeoff: Over 50,000 curated images, but the PlantDoc authors note its images were taken in laboratory settings, so accuracy will look better than on the street.

alternatives.name: Label your own street photos only
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic, but too few images to train and you would grade your own labels.

verify: Write the question and the metric (recall and precision of 'needs a look' vs arborist) in the README
Record PlantDoc train and test image counts and freeze the test folder hash
Confirm license terms for each dataset you use

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app identifies trees and leaves, never people. Leaf close-ups rarely include people, but street photos can catch faces, homes and plates. The model is a helper: only a qualified arborist decides on treatment or removal. Stay on the sidewalk, never in traffic, and do not climb.

decision.choice: On-device face check rejects photos with faces; strip EXIF; store only leaf photos and tree location
decision.why: Rejecting on the phone means no face ever reaches the server, and stripping EXIF removes device and time details you do not need. Storing tree location, not the surveyor's track, protects volunteers.

alternatives.name: Blur faces server side
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more photos, but the raw photo with a face is uploaded first.

alternatives.name: No photo storage, only verdicts
alternatives.tradeoff: Most private, but the arborist cannot check the evidence behind a flag.

steps.delegate: In the capture form, run MediaPipe Face Detector (web) on each photo before upload and block photos with any detection. Strip all EXIF client side after reading location. Add a disclaimer screen: helper only, contact the city arborist, stay on the sidewalk. Tests: a sample photo with a face is blocked; uploaded files contain no EXIF.
verify: Upload a test photo with a face and confirm it is blocked on the phone
Inspect an uploaded file and confirm EXIF is empty
Disclaimer names the city arborist as the decision maker

steps.title: Define triage labels a model and an arborist share
steps.learn: PlantDoc labels are crop species plus disease (for example apple scab, tomato blight), while street trees are mostly other species. Mapping every class to 'healthy leaf' or 'symptomatic leaf' turns a narrow diagnosis task into a transferable one. Keep an 'unsure' outcome for later.

decision.choice: Binary leaf label (healthy vs symptomatic) mapped from source classes; tree-level output: ok, needs a look, unsure
decision.why: Symptoms like spots, rust and blight look alike across species, so a binary label borrows strength from crop data. The arborist can grade 'needs a look' directly, which disease names on unfamiliar species would not allow.

alternatives.name: Keep fine-grained disease classes
alternatives.tradeoff: More informative, but classes do not exist for most street species and errors look like confident misdiagnoses.

alternatives.name: Whole-tree photo health score
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches the NYC census health field, but one canopy photo mixes trees, sky and buildings and is hard to label.

steps.delegate: Python script build_labels.py: read PlantDoc and Plant Pathology folder or CSV structures, map each source class to healthy or symptomatic via an explicit YAML mapping, and write manifest CSVs (path, source, source_class, label, split). Tests: every source class appears in the YAML; no test-split image appears in train; class counts printed per split.
verify: Review the YAML mapping by hand and note any ambiguous classes
Check class balance per split and record it

steps.title: Design a photo protocol that matches the training data
steps.learn: Models fail most on inputs unlike training. Decide what one 'observation' is: several close-up leaf photos per tree from reachable branches, plus the tree's position. A consistent protocol makes errors attributable to the model, not to random framing.

decision.choice: Per tree: 3 to 5 leaf close-ups, filling most of the frame, from different branches, plus one GPS fix
decision.why: Close-ups resemble PlantDoc crops and avoid capturing people, houses or plates. Several leaves per tree let you aggregate, since one damaged leaf does not make a sick tree.

alternatives.name: One photo per tree
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest survey, but one leaf is a noisy sample and a single misprediction flags the tree.

alternatives.name: Free-form photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy for volunteers, but backgrounds and scale vary wildly and some photos will include people.

steps.delegate: A simple mobile web form (HTML plus JS, camera input) that guides the user through N leaf photos for one tree, shows a checklist overlay, and attaches the device geolocation and accuracy. Tests: form refuses submission with fewer than 3 photos; geolocation accuracy is saved with the record.
verify: Do a dry run on 3 trees in your own yard or an empty park, leaf close-ups only, and time it per tree
Compare 5 of your leaf photos side by side with PlantDoc images and note differences

steps.title: Fine-tune a small pretrained image model
steps.learn: Fine-tuning a pretrained backbone needs far fewer labels than training from scratch. Always measure a zero-shot CLIP baseline first so you know what fine-tuning adds. Report accuracy on both frozen held-out sets separately: the gap between them is your domain shift.

decision.choice: timm mobilenetv3_large_100 pretrained, fine-tuned on the binary labels with augmentation
decision.why: A small model can run on a phone or a cheap server, timm loads it with one create_model call, and binary triage does not need a large model. Compare against CLIP zero-shot to justify it.

alternatives.name: CLIP zero-shot (no training)
alternatives.tradeoff: No labels needed and quick to try, but 'diseased leaf' prompts are vague and accuracy may be low.

alternatives.name: Larger ViT fine-tune
alternatives.tradeoff: Often more accurate, but slower and more memory; worth it only if the small model clearly underfits.

alternatives.name: Vision-language model per photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Can describe symptoms in words, but slower, costlier and harder to calibrate.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, PyTorch, timm, torchvision transforms. train.py: create_model('mobilenetv3_large_100', pretrained=True, num_classes=2), augmentations (random resized crop, flips, color jitter), early stopping on a validation split carved from train only. eval.py reports accuracy, recall and precision for 'symptomatic' on each held-out set. Also a CLIP zero-shot baseline script. Tests: eval never reads train images; seed fixes results.
verify: Report CLIP zero-shot vs fine-tuned recall on PlantDoc test
Report the same model on Plant Pathology 2020 and note the gap

steps.title: Calibrate scores and aggregate leaves into a tree verdict
steps.learn: Guo et al. showed modern neural nets are often overconfident and that temperature scaling is a simple fix. Calibrated leaf probabilities let you combine several leaves into a tree verdict and choose a threshold that favors recall, since a missed sick tree costs more than an extra look.

decision.choice: Temperature scaling on a validation split, then tree score = share of leaves above a threshold, with an 'unsure' band
decision.why: Temperature scaling is one parameter fit on validation data, so it cannot leak test data. A share-of-leaves rule is easy to explain to an arborist and tolerant of one bad photo.

alternatives.name: Max leaf score
alternatives.tradeoff: Highest recall, but any single noisy photo flags the tree.

alternatives.name: Platt or isotonic calibration (scikit-learn)
alternatives.tradeoff: More flexible, but isotonic needs more validation data than you will have per domain.

steps.delegate: Python calibrate.py: fit a temperature on validation logits, save it with the model version. aggregate.py: tree_verdict(leaf_probs, leaf_threshold, share_threshold, unsure_band) returns ok, needs_a_look or unsure. Tests: temperature 1 leaves probabilities unchanged; all-healthy leaves give ok; an empty list gives unsure.
verify: Plot a reliability diagram before and after temperature scaling on validation data
Choose thresholds on validation only and record recall and precision

links.label: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks

steps.title: Geotag each tree and match it to the city inventory
steps.learn: Phone GPS can be off by more than the spacing between street trees, so a fix alone may land on the wrong tree. City inventories such as the NYC 2015 Street Tree Census give tree_id, species, latitude and longitude per tree, which lets you match and confirm with species.

decision.choice: Nearest-tree join within a max distance in a metric CRS, confirmed by the user picking the tree on a map when ambiguous
decision.why: The join is automatic for isolated trees, and asking the user only when two candidates are close avoids silent mismatches. Matching to tree_id lets the arborist look up the record they already use.

alternatives.name: Raw GPS only, no inventory
alternatives.tradeoff: Works where no inventory exists, but the arborist cannot tie results to their tree records.

alternatives.name: Always pick on the map manually
alternatives.tradeoff: Most accurate, but slower per tree and tedious for a whole street.

steps.delegate: Python with geopandas: load the city inventory, reproject both layers to a local metric CRS, use geopandas.sjoin_nearest with max_distance and distance_col; flag observations where the second-nearest tree is within a margin. Read EXIF GPS with Pillow getexif().get_ifd(ExifTags.IFD.GPSInfo) as a fallback when the form's geolocation is missing. Tests: synthetic points match correctly; ties are flagged.
verify: Jitter 10 inventory tree locations by your phone's reported GPS error and count how many auto matches pick the right tree_id
Record median GPS accuracy reported by your phone on the street

steps.title: Store observations and build the geotagged dashboard
steps.learn: Each observation needs its tree, photos, model version, calibrated scores and verdict, so you can recompute when the model changes. The dashboard is a map of trees colored by verdict, with the leaf photos one click away for the arborist.

decision.choice: SQLite tables trees, observations, leaf_predictions(model_version) plus a Leaflet map fed by GeoJSON
decision.why: One street is tiny data, SQLite is one file to share, and storing model_version per prediction allows reprocessing. Leaflet with GeoJSON is a small static page the arborist can open on a phone.

alternatives.name: PostGIS
alternatives.tradeoff: Real spatial queries and multi-user writes, but a server to run for a few dozen trees.

alternatives.name: Spreadsheet plus a hosted map tool
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero code, but no model versioning and photos get separated from verdicts.

steps.delegate: FastAPI app with SQLite: POST /observations (photos, location, tree_id), GET /trees.geojson with verdict and last_observed. Leaflet page with markers colored by verdict and a popup showing leaf thumbnails. reprocess(model_version) recomputes verdicts. Tests: GeoJSON validates; reprocess changes only rows for the new version.
verify: Open the dashboard on a phone and check every tree has a marker and photos
Reprocess with a dummy model version and confirm old predictions are kept

steps.title: Handle bad photos, missing GPS and model upgrades
steps.learn: In the field, photos are blurry, too dark or not leaves; GPS is missing; and you will retrain the model. Each failure should produce 'unsure' or a clear request to retake, never a confident verdict.

decision.choice: Reject-and-retake for unusable photos, 'unsure' for low confidence, verdicts tied to a model version
decision.why: An arborist trusts a tool that admits uncertainty. Retake prompts happen while you are still under the tree, which is cheaper than another trip.

alternatives.name: Accept everything and let the model decide
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but blurry photos produce confident wrong verdicts.

alternatives.name: Human review of every photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Highest quality, but does not scale beyond one street.

steps.delegate: Add quality checks before inference: minimum resolution, a sharpness score threshold, and a 'leaf present' check using a CLIP prompt comparison. Return retake reasons to the form. Tests: a synthetic blurred image is rejected; a photo with no leaf (sky) returns retake; missing GPS routes to the manual map pick.
verify: Feed 10 deliberately bad photos and record how many are caught
Swap model versions and confirm the dashboard shows which version made each verdict

steps.title: Test it outside: survey one street with the city arborist
steps.learn: Survey every tree on one street with the protocol, then ask your city arborist for their own verdict per tree before they see the dashboard, so the tool is not grading itself. Share the dashboard afterwards and record any verdicts they change.
verify: Record trees surveyed, minutes per tree and photos rejected
Get arborist verdicts per tree and compute recall and precision of 'needs a look'
Count GPS mismatches found during the survey
List the trees where you and the arborist disagreed and why

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the question; (2) numbers for every claim (held-out results per dataset, zero-shot vs fine-tuned, field recall and precision vs arborist) with the machine and command; (3) why surprising results happened (domain shift, species); (4) assumptions and what one street does not prove.
verify: Write-up states the one question at the top
Every number has the command and machine that produced it
A section explains at least one surprising result
A section lists assumptions and limits, including that this is triage, not diagnosis

projects.title: Parking sign decoder
projects.problem: Stacked parking signs are confusing: can I park here now, for 2 hours?
projects.concepts: Vision-language model to read signs, temporal reasoning over days and times
projects.tryIt: Photograph 50 sign stacks downtown; check answers against reality
projects.question: Can a vision-language model read a stack of parking signs and correctly answer 'can I park here now, for N hours?' without ever giving a false yes?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: The system has two halves: reading (photo to sign text and rules) and reasoning (rules plus a time and duration to yes/no/until). The costly error is a false yes, which gets a ticket or a tow, so it is tracked separately from overall accuracy and from 'unsure' answers.

decision.choice: Dev set: NYC sign_description strings plus about 20 of your own stacks; test set: 50 new stacks, frozen and unseen
decision.why: NYC Open Data publishes every regulation sign with its text (for example '2 HMP SATURDAY 8AM-7PM <->'), so the parser can be developed on real wording for free. The 50-stack try-it is photographed later and never used for prompt or rule tuning.

alternatives.name: Test on the NYC strings only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and large, but skips the hard part: glare, angles, stacked layouts and arrows in real photos.

alternatives.name: Tune and test on the same 50 stacks
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but the reported accuracy will be optimistic because prompts were fitted to those exact signs.

verify: Write the question and 4 metrics: accuracy, false-yes rate, unsure rate, latency per photo
Download 500 rows of the NYC sign dataset and list the 10 most frequent sign_description patterns
Write down the rule that the 50 test stacks are never shown to the prompt or parser before the final run

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting any photos
steps.learn: Sign photos are about places, not people, but street shots catch faces, plates and house numbers. Parking rules are legal rules: the app is a helper, and the posted sign plus the city's official rules remain the source of truth the driver must check.

decision.choice: Crop to the sign on-device, keep no faces or plates, show a 'helper, check the sign' notice
decision.why: Only the sign pixels are needed to answer, so dropping the rest removes the privacy risk at the source. A visible notice and the transcribed sign text let the driver confirm the answer with their own eyes.

alternatives.name: Blur faces and plates, keep full frame
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps street context for debugging, but blurring can miss people, and you now store more than the task needs.

alternatives.name: Upload raw photos to a server
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest pipeline, but sends bystanders' images off the phone with no benefit to the answer.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, Pillow. Write sanitize(photo) -> (sign_crop, meta): crop to a user-drawn or detected sign box, drop all EXIF except capture time, return the crop. Add a CLI that refuses to save a frame unless it went through sanitize. Tests: output has no GPS EXIF, output size equals the crop box, original file is never written to the data folder.
verify: Run sanitize on 5 street photos and confirm with an EXIF viewer that GPS tags are gone
Check that no full-frame image exists in the data folder after a capture session
Confirm the capture CLI refuses to save any frame that did not pass through sanitize

steps.title: Design the rule schema the whole system speaks
steps.learn: Every sign reduces to a restriction type (no stopping, no standing, no parking, time limit, metered, permit or commercial only), the days and times it applies, an optional time limit, exceptions, and an arrow direction. Fixing this schema first lets the reader, parser and time engine be built and tested separately.

decision.choice: A typed schema (Pydantic models) with one Rule per sign line and a Stack of Rules in top-to-bottom order
decision.why: A schema gives the VLM a target, gives the parser a type to fill, and lets you validate output before any reasoning. Pydantic can emit a JSON Schema (model_json_schema) to put in the prompt.

alternatives.name: Free text answer from the VLM
alternatives.tradeoff: No schema work, but you cannot test the time logic or tell reading errors from reasoning errors.

alternatives.name: One flat list of intervals with no types
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple to evaluate, but loses the difference between a time limit and a ban, which changes the answer.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, Pydantic v2. Define Rule (kind enum, days set of weekdays, start and end as minutes since midnight, limit_minutes optional, except_days, arrow in {left,right,both,none}, raw_text) and Stack (rules list, source photo id). Export the JSON Schema to rules.schema.json. Tests: invalid kind rejected, an overnight range like 11PM-7AM is representable, round-trip JSON equality.
verify: Hand-encode 10 NYC sign_description strings into the schema and check none needs a field you lack
Confirm an overnight rule and an 'except Sunday' rule both validate

steps.title: Read each sign in the stack with a vision-language model
steps.learn: A VLM can read text and layout together: which plate is above which, colors, arrows and symbols that plain OCR flattens. It can still misread small digits or invent a plausible line, so ask it to transcribe verbatim, sign by sign, before anything is interpreted.

decision.choice: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, prompted to return verbatim lines per sign plus arrow direction as JSON
