decision.why: It is open weights, runs locally through transformers or Ollama, and its model card highlights structured outputs for documents. Verbatim transcription keeps the model's job to reading, which you can check against the photo.

alternatives.name: OCR engine (Tesseract or PaddleOCR) plus layout rules
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper and predictable, but stacked signs, red-on-white bans and arrows need layout logic you would hand-write.

alternatives.name: Hosted frontier VLM API
alternatives.tradeoff: Often reads hard photos better, but costs per call, needs network, and sends photos off-device.

alternatives.name: Smaller Qwen2.5-VL 3B on-device
alternatives.tradeoff: Lower latency and fully offline, but expect more misread digits; measure on the dev set first.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, transformers (Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration, AutoProcessor), qwen_vl_utils. Write read_stack(image_path) -> list of {sign_index, lines, arrow}. Prompt asks for verbatim text only, top to bottom, JSON only. Retry once on invalid JSON. Tests: JSON parses, sign_index is contiguous from 0, a fixture image of a single sign returns at least one line.
verify: On your 20 dev stacks, count lines transcribed exactly vs the photo by your own reading
Log every time the model output text that is not on the sign

steps.title: Parse sign text into rules with a deterministic grammar
steps.learn: Sign wording is a small language: day ranges (MON-FRI), time ranges (8AM-7PM, MIDNIGHT), limits (2 HOUR), and city abbreviations such as HMP in NYC data. Normalizing these into the schema in code makes reading errors visible as parse failures instead of silent wrong answers.

decision.choice: Rule-based parser with a normalization table, tested on NYC sign_description strings; unparsed lines become 'unknown'
decision.why: The NYC dataset gives thousands of real strings to test against, and a deterministic parser behaves the same every time. Unknown lines force an 'unsure' answer later rather than a guess.

alternatives.name: Let the VLM emit Rule JSON directly
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer components, but the model mixes reading and interpreting, so one error source hides the other.

alternatives.name: Fuzzy-match each line to a catalog of known sign texts
alternatives.tradeoff: Robust to small OCR errors, but only works where a full sign catalog exists for your city.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, no ML. Write parse_line(text) -> Rule | Unknown with a normalization dict (day names, abbreviations, MIDNIGHT/NOON, arrow tokens like <-> and -->). Tests: 30 hand-labeled NYC sign_description strings from the dataset as fixtures, overnight ranges, multi-range days, unknown wording returns Unknown not an exception.
verify: Run the parser on 1,000 NYC strings and report the share parsed vs Unknown
Spot-check 20 parsed rules by hand and record any wrong field

steps.title: Answer 'park now for N hours' with interval arithmetic
steps.learn: The question is an interval [now, now+N] checked against each rule's weekly windows. Ranges can cross midnight and stays can cross days, and local time must come from a real time zone, since daylight saving shifts the clock. Time limits apply only while their window is active.

decision.choice: Expand rules to minute-of-week windows in the local zone (zoneinfo) and intersect them with the requested stay
decision.why: Interval math is exact, testable and explainable: you can show which rule and which minute caused a 'no'. zoneinfo handles daylight saving from the system time zone database.

alternatives.name: Ask the LLM to reason about the time
alternatives.tradeoff: No code to write, but answers vary run to run and cannot be unit-tested for edge cases.

alternatives.name: Check only the current minute
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but misses a ban that starts 30 minutes into a 2 hour stay, the classic ticket.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, zoneinfo. Write evaluate(stack, start: datetime aware, minutes) -> Answer {verdict yes/no/until, until_time, governing_rule}. Tests: stay crossing midnight, ban starting mid-stay, 2 hour limit with a 3 hour request, a Saturday-only rule on Sunday, a stay spanning a DST change.
verify: Write 15 hand-solved cases on paper first, then confirm the engine matches all 15
Show that a 2 hour request 30 minutes before an 8AM ban returns 'until 8AM', not yes

steps.title: Combine stacked signs and arrows into one answer
steps.learn: A stack mixes bans, limits and meters, each with an arrow saying which side of the post it covers. The car's side of the post decides which signs count. Then every applicable rule is a hard constraint: one violated ban makes the answer no.

decision.choice: Ask the user which side of the post the car is on, then apply all relevant rules and return the most restrictive result
decision.why: The arrow side is easy for a person and hard to infer from one photo. Taking the most restrictive outcome errs toward 'no', which matches the goal of zero false yeses.

alternatives.name: Infer car position from the photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer taps, but the camera angle rarely shows where the car is relative to the post.

alternatives.name: Top sign wins
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches a common intuition but is not a rule you can rely on, and silently ignores lower bans.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Write answer(stack, side, start, minutes): filter rules by arrow and side, run evaluate per rule, combine as min of allowed time, attach the governing sign index. Tests: a left-arrow ban ignored for a car on the right, a both-ways limit applied, two overlapping limits yield the shorter.
verify: On 10 dev stacks, compare your own reading of each sign with the combined answer for 2 times each
Confirm the answer screen names the sign that decided it

steps.title: Handle holidays and city suspension calendars
steps.learn: Some rules switch off on certain days and others do not. NYC, for example, suspends alternate side parking on listed legal and religious holidays and for weather, while its page notes meters can stay in effect. A generic holiday library cannot know which rule types a city suspends.

decision.choice: Load the city's published suspension calendar as data, scoped to the rule types it names; default to 'rule applies'
decision.why: Only the city says which rules pause on which days, and defaulting to 'applies' keeps a missed suspension from becoming a false yes.

alternatives.name: holidays Python package
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for public holiday dates by country and subdivision, but it does not say which parking rules are suspended.

alternatives.name: Ignore suspensions
alternatives.tradeoff: Never wrong in the risky direction, but gives needless 'no' answers on suspension days.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Write suspensions.yaml (date, rule kinds suspended, source URL) and is_suspended(rule, date). Hook it into evaluate. Tests: a street-cleaning rule suspended on a listed date, a meter rule on the same date still applies, an unlisted date suspends nothing.
verify: Enter 5 dates from your city's current calendar and confirm the matching rule kind is skipped on each
Confirm a meter rule still applies on one of those dates if the city says meters stay on

links.label: NYC alternate side parking and suspensions

steps.title: Say 'unsure' when reading or parsing is shaky
steps.learn: Glare, snow, stickers and bent plates cause misreads, and a confident wrong 'yes' is the worst outcome. Signals you already have: Unknown lines from the parser, invalid JSON retries, and disagreement between two reads of the same photo.

decision.choice: Read two crops; answer only if both parse identically with no Unknown lines, else say 'unsure'
decision.why: Agreement checks are cheap and catch random misreads, and showing the transcription lets the driver check quickly. It trades some coverage for fewer false yeses.

alternatives.name: Use model token probabilities as confidence
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine-grained, but needs model internals and calibration data you do not yet have.

alternatives.name: Always answer
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum coverage, but every misread digit becomes a possible ticket.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Write decide(photo) that calls read_stack on the full crop and a slightly tighter crop, parses both, and returns 'unsure' on any Unknown or mismatch. Log the reason. Tests: mismatch returns unsure, Unknown returns unsure, identical parses return the engine's verdict.
verify: On the dev set, record the unsure rate and how many false yeses it removed
Photograph 3 signs with deliberate glare and confirm each returns unsure or a correct answer

steps.title: Test it outside on 50 downtown sign stacks
steps.learn: This is the try-it: real stacks, real light. Ground truth comes from your own careful reading of each sign plus the city's records where they exist, never from the app's parser, so the app is not grading itself.

decision.choice: Ask 3 fixed 2-hour questions per stack (now, weekday morning, Saturday evening); grade by hand
decision.why: Several times per stack test the time engine as well as reading, and fixing them in advance stops you picking easy cases after the fact.

alternatives.name: One question per stack
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but most answers then depend on the current hour and miss weekday and overnight logic.

alternatives.name: Let a friend grade
alternatives.tradeoff: More independent labels, but slower; worth it for any stack where you are unsure.

verify: Report accuracy, false-yes count, unsure rate and median latency over 150 questions
List every false yes with the photo, the transcription and the cause
Cross-check at least 10 stacks against the city sign records for that block

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up has four parts: the one question, numbers for every claim with the machine and command, why surprising results happened (for example which sign types caused misreads), and what this does not prove (one city, one season, your reading as ground truth).
verify: Part 1 states the one question
Part 2 gives accuracy, false-yes and unsure numbers with model, hardware and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising failures with photos
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including that the app is a helper only

projects.title: Duplicate-aware pothole reporter
projects.problem: Cities get the same pothole reported 20 times
projects.concepts: Near-duplicate image search plus a geo filter
projects.tryIt: Report potholes on your commute and measure duplicate merges
projects.question: Can a GPS radius plus image similarity merge repeat reports of the same pothole while keeping nearby distinct potholes separate?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: The task is clustering reports: each new report either joins an existing pothole or starts a new one. Two errors matter: a missed merge (city gets a duplicate) and a wrong merge (a real pothole gets hidden). Track both as pairwise precision and recall of 'same pothole' decisions.

decision.choice: Your own commute reports, each hand-tagged with a pothole id; first week tunes, second week is the frozen test
decision.why: No public dataset has repeat photos of the same pothole with ids, so you build one. Splitting by week and tagging ids by hand before tuning keeps the test honest. RDD2022 and NYC 311 pothole requests support the gate and the geo analysis.

alternatives.name: Synthetic duplicates (crops and flips of one photo)
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to make, but real repeats differ in angle, light and phone, which is the hard part.

alternatives.name: Use 311 records as duplicate labels
alternatives.tradeoff: Real scale, but 311 rows have no photos, and the city's grouping is not ground truth for your merger.

verify: Write the question and metrics: merge precision, merge recall, wrong-merge count
Pull 1,000 NYC 311 'Pothole' requests and count how many fall within a small radius of another
Write the tagging rule: you assign pothole ids on the spot, before any model runs

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting any reports
steps.learn: Road photos catch pedestrians, drivers and plates, and a stream of GPS-tagged reports reveals the reporter's commute. The system needs the pothole and its location, not the people or the route. And nobody should photograph potholes while driving.

decision.choice: Blur faces on-device, never store them, drop reporter ids; report only when stopped or on foot
decision.why: Blurring before upload means faces never leave the phone. Dropping reporter ids from stored reports breaks the commute trail while keeping what dedup needs: location, time and image.

alternatives.name: Crop tightly to the pothole
alternatives.tradeoff: Removes most people automatically, but loses road context that helps match the same pothole later.

alternatives.name: Blur on the server
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces travel and sit on your server for a while.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 prototype, MediaPipe Face Detector with the full-range BlazeFace model, OpenCV Gaussian blur, Pillow. Write sanitize(img) -> img with faces and license plates blurred and EXIF stripped except GPS and time. Strip any reporter id before storage. Tests: a fixture face is blurred, a fixture plate is blurred, no EXIF fields but GPS and time remain, stored record has no reporter field.
verify: Run sanitize on 10 street photos with people and check every face is blurred
Inspect a stored report and confirm there is no reporter id
Write the no-photos-while-driving rule into the app's capture screen

steps.title: Capture location and time reliably
steps.learn: Location comes from the photo's EXIF GPS block or the phone's location API, with an accuracy estimate. Phone GPS is noisy, worse near tall buildings, so the same pothole can be logged meters apart. Store the accuracy so the merge radius can depend on it.

decision.choice: Read GPS from EXIF (Pillow get_ifd on the GPS IFD) with device location as fallback; reject reports with no location
decision.why: EXIF ties location to the moment the shutter fired, and device location covers apps that strip EXIF. A report with no location cannot be deduplicated or routed to a city, so asking for a retry is better than guessing.

alternatives.name: Let the user drop a pin
alternatives.tradeoff: Works without GPS, but adds friction and user pins can be far off.

alternatives.name: Snap to the nearest road segment
alternatives.tradeoff: Reduces noise along a street, but needs a road map and can snap to the wrong lane or street.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, Pillow. Write read_location(path) -> (lat, lon, accuracy_m or None, timestamp) using Image.getexif().get_ifd for GPS, converting degrees/minutes/seconds and N/S/E/W refs to signed decimals. Tests: southern and western hemisphere fixtures give negative values, a photo without GPS returns None.
verify: Photograph one pothole 5 times from different spots and record the spread of the 5 GPS fixes
Confirm a western-hemisphere photo gives a negative longitude

steps.title: Reject photos that do not show a pothole
steps.learn: Before dedup, filter junk: a photo of a manhole cover or a crack is not a pothole report. RDD2022 has road images labeled with damage types (D40 is pothole) in Pascal VOC format, so you can measure a gate without labeling your own.

decision.choice: CLIP zero-shot gate (pothole vs other road prompts), threshold tuned on RDD2022 pothole and non-pothole crops
decision.why: No training needed, it runs on a laptop, and RDD2022 gives labeled positives and negatives to set the threshold. If accuracy is too low, the same labels train a detector.

alternatives.name: Detector trained on RDD2022 D40
alternatives.tradeoff: Also localizes the pothole for cropping, but needs a training run and a GPU.

alternatives.name: No gate, rely on users
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero work, but junk photos pollute clusters and waste city crews' time.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, open_clip, Pillow. Load RDD2022 train XML, crop D40 boxes as positives and other boxes as negatives. Write is_pothole(img, threshold) using prompt ensembles. Script that sweeps threshold and prints precision and recall. Tests: XML parsing of one fixture, gate returns bool, threshold sweep is monotonic in recall.
verify: Report gate precision and recall on 300 held-out RDD2022 crops
Run the gate on 20 of your own week-1 photos and count wrong rejections

steps.title: Find nearby open potholes with a geo index
steps.learn: Image search over the whole city is wasteful and risky: two potholes can look alike across town. Filter first by distance, then compare images only among nearby candidates. That is pre-filtering: the geo filter shrinks the set before any vector math.

decision.choice: H3 cells (latlng_to_cell, grid_disk) for candidates, then exact distance under a GPS-aware radius
decision.why: H3 makes 'cells around this point' a set lookup in any key-value store, and the exact distance check removes cell-edge effects. Scaling the radius with reported accuracy handles noisy fixes.

alternatives.name: PostGIS ST_DWithin
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact and robust at scale, but adds a database to a project that may fit in memory.

alternatives.name: Plain radius scan over all reports
alternatives.tradeoff: Correct and fine for one commute, but cost grows with every report citywide.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, h3 (v4 API). Write GeoIndex with add(report_id, lat, lon) and nearby(lat, lon, radius_m) using latlng_to_cell, grid_disk and great_circle_distance(unit='m'). Tests: a point just across a cell edge is found, points beyond radius are excluded, results match a brute-force scan on 1,000 random points.
verify: Measure recall of nearby() vs brute force on your week-1 data (should be equal)
Pick a radius from the GPS spread you measured and write it down with the reason

steps.title: Score image similarity between nearby reports
steps.learn: Perceptual hashes catch exact or lightly edited resends but break when the angle changes. Self-supervised embeddings such as DINOv2 capture the shape and texture of the scene, so two photos of one pothole from different spots stay close.

decision.choice: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 global embedding with cosine similarity, plus an imagehash pHash check for exact resends
decision.why: The geo filter leaves only a handful of candidates, so even a full embedding comparison is cheap. pHash catches the same photo uploaded twice for almost no cost.

alternatives.name: CLIP image embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: Already loaded for the gate, but trained to match captions, which may blur fine texture differences.

alternatives.name: pHash alone
alternatives.tradeoff: Tiny and fast, but different angles of the same pothole hash far apart.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, torch, DINOv2 via torch.hub (dinov2_vits14), imagehash. Write embed(img) -> normalized vector and phash(img). Write similarity(a, b) returning cosine and hamming distance. Tests: identical image gives cosine near 1 and hamming 0, vectors are unit norm, a flipped image still has high cosine.
verify: On week-1 pairs within the radius, plot cosine for same-pothole vs different-pothole pairs
Count how many same-pothole pairs pHash alone would catch

steps.title: Confirm borderline matches with local feature matching
steps.learn: Two potholes on one street can share asphalt, curb and lane paint, so embeddings may call them the same. Local keypoint matching plus a geometric fit (RANSAC) asks a sharper question: do many specific points line up under one consistent transform?

decision.choice: LightGlue with SuperPoint features, accept if RANSAC inliers exceed a tuned count; run only on borderline cosine scores
decision.why: LightGlue ships pretrained weights for SuperPoint and other features and adapts its compute to how hard a pair is. Running it only in the uncertain band keeps the extra cost small.

alternatives.name: OpenCV ORB plus ratio test and RANSAC
alternatives.tradeoff: No deep model and very fast, but fewer reliable matches on low-texture asphalt.

alternatives.name: Skip geometry, use embedding threshold only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but adjacent potholes are exactly where embeddings are least sure.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, lightglue (SuperPoint, LightGlue), OpenCV findHomography with RANSAC. Write inliers(img_a, img_b) -> int. Call it when cosine is in [low, high]. Tests: an image vs itself gives many inliers, two unrelated road photos give few, function handles images with no keypoints.
verify: On week-1 borderline pairs, compare wrong merges with and without the geometric check
Record the added latency per borderline pair on your machine

steps.title: Turn scores into merge decisions and pothole clusters
steps.learn: Each report gets a decision: merge into the best candidate, start a new pothole, or send to human review. Clusters should attach to the pothole's canonical record, not chain report to report, or one bad link can join two potholes.

decision.choice: Merge into an open pothole only if distance, cosine and (when borderline) inliers all pass
decision.why: Requiring every signal to agree favors precision, since a wrong merge hides a real hazard. The review band turns hard cases into labels for the next tuning round.

alternatives.name: Single-linkage union-find over all reports
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy, but transitive chains can merge a whole street of potholes.

alternatives.name: Learned classifier over the features
alternatives.tradeoff: Can weigh signals better, but needs more labeled pairs than one commute gives.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, SQLite. Tables: potholes (id, lat, lon, status, representative embedding) and reports (id, pothole_id, time, path). Write ingest(report) applying gate, geo filter, similarity, geometric check and thresholds. Tests: a resend merges, a different pothole 5 m away does not, a review-band case is flagged not merged.
verify: Tune thresholds on week 1 only and record the chosen values
Report merge precision and recall on week 1 to compare with the test later

steps.title: Handle repairs, reopened potholes and bad inputs
steps.learn: A patched pothole can reopen at the same spot, and a fresh report then looks like a duplicate of a closed ticket. Other failure cases: night photos, rain glare, missing GPS and reports from far off the road.

decision.choice: Merge only into potholes whose status is open; a report near a closed pothole creates a new one linked to it
decision.why: Tying merges to ticket status matches how a city works: a closed ticket needs a new job. The link preserves history so a repeat failure at one spot is visible.

alternatives.name: Time window only (merge within N days)
alternatives.tradeoff: No status needed, but an unrepaired pothole older than N days spawns duplicates.

alternatives.name: Ignore status
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but reopened potholes vanish into old closed tickets.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Extend ingest: filter candidates by status open, add a reopened_from link, reject photos below a brightness floor with a retake message. Optionally format an Open311 GeoReport v2 POST body for a new pothole. Tests: report near a closed pothole creates a new linked record, dark image is rejected, missing GPS is rejected.
verify: Simulate closing a week-1 pothole and confirm the next report there creates a linked new record
Confirm 3 night photos get a retake prompt or a correct decision

steps.title: Test it outside on your commute
steps.learn: This is the try-it: report potholes on your commute for the frozen second week, repeating some on purpose from new angles and times. Grading uses the pothole ids you assigned on the spot, never the system's own clusters.

decision.choice: Report every pothole you pass, revisiting each at least twice, and grade against your on-the-spot ids
decision.why: Repeat visits create the true duplicates, and on-the-spot tagging is the only label independent of the merger.

alternatives.name: Have friends report too
alternatives.tradeoff: Different phones and habits make a harder, more realistic test, but tagging needs coordination.

alternatives.name: Report only new potholes
alternatives.tradeoff: Less work, but produces almost no duplicates to measure.

verify: Report merge precision, merge recall and wrong-merge count on week 2 with thresholds unchanged
Compare week-2 numbers with week-1 and explain any drop
List each wrong merge with distance, cosine and inlier values

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The write-up has four parts: the one question, numbers for every claim with the machine and command, why surprising results happened (for example adjacent potholes or GPS drift), and what this does not prove (one commute, one phone, your own labels, a small sample).
verify: Part 1 states the one question
Part 2 gives merge precision and recall with machine, models and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising merges or misses
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including sample size and labeler

projects.title: Ghost bus detector
projects.problem: Transit apps show buses that never come
projects.concepts: Streaming real-time transit feeds (GTFS-realtime), comparing predicted vs actual
projects.tryIt: Log a route for two weeks and publish the most unreliable stops
projects.question: On one bus route over two weeks, how often does a predicted bus never show up at a stop, and which stops are least reliable?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the feeds
steps.learn: A ghost bus is a trip the app predicts at your stop that never arrives. Metrics: ghost rate per stop (predicted trips with no observed arrival), prediction error by how far ahead it was made, and a ranked list of the least reliable stops. Data: the agency's static GTFS plus its GTFS-realtime feeds.

decision.choice: One high-frequency MBTA bus route, 14 days of TripUpdates and VehiclePositions; days 11 to 14 frozen as held-out
decision.why: MBTA publishes standard protobuf feeds with no key needed to fetch, plus the matching static GTFS zip. One route keeps stop-side checks feasible. Freezing the last 4 days before tuning any threshold means the published ranking is scored on data you never tuned on.

alternatives.name: Your own city's agency feed
alternatives.tradeoff: More useful locally, but check it publishes both TripUpdates and VehiclePositions; some agencies need an API key or only publish one.

alternatives.name: Whole network
alternatives.tradeoff: More stops and more ghosts to find, but storage grows a lot and you cannot ground-truth more than a few stops in person.

verify: README states the question, the ghost definition draft, and the 3 metrics before any code runs
Route id, the 14 calendar dates and the 4 held-out dates are written down and committed
Read the MBTA license terms (MassDOT Developers License Agreement) and note what you may publish

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before logging anything
steps.learn: The feeds describe vehicles, not riders, but they carry vehicle and run ids, and your stop-side checks happen in public. Count buses, never people. A 'least reliable stops' list can also be read as official fact, so it must say the agency's own service info is the source of record.

decision.choice: Log only feed fields; stop-side notes record bus number and time, never riders; publish with a caveat
decision.why: Nothing in the project needs data about people, so the safest design collects none. Field notes with only bus label and timestamp are enough to check arrivals. A clear caveat stops riders from planning around your list instead of the agency's alerts.

alternatives.name: Photo or video at the stop as proof
alternatives.tradeoff: Stronger evidence, but captures riders' faces; you would need on-device blurring and still be filming people without consent.

alternatives.name: Crowdsource reports from riders
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers more stops, but collects rider locations and times, which needs consent and a retention policy.

steps.delegate: In Python, write a schema doc and a lint test for the logging tables: assert no column outside an allowlist (feed timestamps, trip_id, route_id, stop_id, stop_sequence, vehicle id and label, position, status, predicted times). Add a field-notes CSV template with columns stop_id, local_time, bus_label, note. Test: inserting an unknown column fails the lint.
verify: The column allowlist exists and the lint test passes before the poller is started
The publish template contains a caveat pointing riders to the agency's official service alerts

steps.title: Load the static schedule and resolve service days
steps.learn: Realtime trips point at static trips by trip_id plus start_date. Which trips run on a date comes from calendar.txt and calendar_dates.txt (exception_type 1 adds, 2 removes). Times are measured from noon minus 12h of the service day and can exceed 24:00:00 for after-midnight trips.

decision.choice: DuckDB over the GTFS CSVs, with a view expanding (service_date, trip_id, stop_sequence, scheduled_ts)
decision.why: DuckDB reads CSVs directly and handles the joins (trips, stop_times, calendar exceptions) in SQL on a laptop. Materializing absolute scheduled timestamps once removes the 25:35:00 and daylight-saving traps from every later query.

alternatives.name: pandas only
alternatives.tradeoff: Familiar, but multi-table joins over stop_times get slow and memory heavy, and logic spreads across notebook cells.

alternatives.name: Load into Postgres
alternatives.tradeoff: Good if you want a long-running service, but more setup than a two-week analysis needs.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 + duckdb. load_gtfs(zip_path, db) creates tables from the static zip. scheduled_stops(route_id, service_date) returns rows with absolute UTC timestamps, computed from noon minus 12h in the agency timezone. Tests: a stop time of 25:10:00 lands on the next calendar day; a date with calendar_dates exception_type 2 returns no trips for that service_id.
verify: Count scheduled trips on your route for a weekday and a Sunday and match them against the agency's printed timetable
Spot-check 3 after-midnight trips have the right absolute timestamp

steps.title: Poll both realtime feeds and archive raw snapshots
steps.learn: Each fetch returns a FeedMessage whose header has a timestamp for when the content was created and FULL_DATASET incrementality, so every snapshot replaces the last. Polling faster than the producer updates only yields duplicates; the header timestamp tells you whether anything changed.

decision.choice: Poll every 30 s, save each new raw .pb gzipped, keyed by header timestamp, then parse into tables
decision.why: Raw snapshots let you re-parse when you fix a bug in day 9, without losing two weeks of data. Deduping on the header timestamp keeps storage small. A 30 s interval is gentle on the server and finer than the arrivals you need to detect; check the agency's guidance and adjust.

alternatives.name: Parse only, discard raw
alternatives.tradeoff: Less storage, but any parsing bug is permanent and you cannot answer new questions later.

alternatives.name: Agency JSON or V3 API
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to read, but the format is agency specific, so your tool will not transfer to another city.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, requests, gtfs-realtime-bindings (from google.transit import gtfs_realtime_pb2). poller.py fetches TripUpdates and VehiclePositions with timeouts and retries, skips a snapshot whose header.timestamp equals the last saved one, writes gzip files and a fetch_log row (fetch_time, http_status, header_ts, n_entities). Run under systemd or launchd. Tests: duplicate header_ts is skipped; HTTP 500 is logged, not fatal.
verify: After 1 hour, fetch_log shows the share of fetches that were duplicates and the median header age at fetch
Kill the poller mid-run and confirm it restarts and the gap shows up in fetch_log

steps.title: Parse predictions and join them to scheduled stops
steps.learn: A StopTimeUpdate links to a stop by stop_sequence or stop_id and gives an absolute time, a delay, or both. Trips can be CANCELED, stops SKIPPED or NO_DATA. A prediction row is one (snapshot time, trip, stop, predicted time), so the same arrival is predicted many times as the bus approaches.

decision.choice: Key everything on (service_date, trip_id, stop_sequence); keep every prediction with its snapshot time
decision.why: stop_sequence disambiguates loops where a stop appears twice in a trip. Keeping every prediction, not just the latest, is what lets you later ask how wrong the app was 10 minutes out versus 2 minutes out.

alternatives.name: Keep only the latest prediction per stop
alternatives.tradeoff: Much smaller tables, but you lose the history needed to measure error by horizon and to see predictions that vanished.

alternatives.name: Key on stop_id only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler joins, but wrong on routes that visit a stop twice per trip.

steps.delegate: Python + duckdb. parse_trip_updates(snapshot) yields rows (header_ts, service_date, trip_id, trip_sched_rel, stop_sequence, stop_id, stop_sched_rel, predicted_ts). Resolve delay-only updates against the scheduled view. Tests: a SKIPPED stop has null predicted_ts and is flagged; a CANCELED trip yields one trip-level row; unknown trip_ids land in an unmatched table, not dropped.
verify: Report the share of realtime trips that match a scheduled trip, and look at 5 unmatched ones by hand
Count CANCELED trips and SKIPPED stops on your route for one day

steps.title: Infer actual arrivals from vehicle positions
steps.learn: Ground truth must not come from the predictions you are grading. VehiclePositions give a position, a timestamp and optionally current_status (INCOMING_AT, STOPPED_AT, IN_TRANSIT_TO) with a stop. Buses that do not stop, or pings that are 30 s apart, mean you often have to infer the pass time.

decision.choice: Use STOPPED_AT when present, else the closest ping within a radius, else interpolate between pings by distance
decision.why: This uses only VehiclePositions, independent of TripUpdates. The three fallbacks cover stops served without a stop event, and recording which rule fired lets you check whether ghosts cluster where inference is weakest.

alternatives.name: STOPPED_AT only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleanest signal, but misses buses that pass a stop with nobody waiting, which would look like ghosts.

alternatives.name: Treat the last prediction as the arrival
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to compute, but it grades the system with its own output, so error is near zero by construction.

steps.delegate: Python, pyproj (Geod for distances), duckdb. observed_arrivals(service_date, route_id) returns (trip_id, stop_sequence, arrival_ts, method, distance_m) using the three-rule cascade. Radius and max ping gap are parameters. Tests on synthetic tracks: a bus passing a stop at constant speed gets an interpolated time within one ping interval; a bus that turns back before a stop gets no arrival.
verify: Report the share of arrivals found by each rule on days 1 to 10
Plot one trip's pings against its stops on a map and check the inferred times look right

steps.title: Mark feed gaps so outages are not counted as ghosts
steps.learn: If your poller or the feed is down, no vehicle is observed and every trip looks like a ghost. A stale header timestamp, a missing vehicle that reappears later, or a whole route going silent are data problems, not bus problems.

decision.choice: Build a coverage table of minutes with fresh data; any stop event inside a gap becomes 'unknown', not 'ghost'
decision.why: Separating unknown from ghost keeps outages from inflating the rate, and the coverage table itself is a reportable number. Freshness is judged from header timestamps and per-vehicle timestamps you already store.

alternatives.name: Drop whole days with any gap
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and conservative, but a single 5-minute outage would throw away a full day.

alternatives.name: Ignore gaps
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra code, but your poller's downtime shows up as the transit agency's failure.

steps.delegate: Python + duckdb. coverage(start, end) builds 1-minute bins with flags: poller_ok, feed_fresh (header age under a threshold), route_has_vehicles. classify_stop_event marks events in bad bins as unknown. Tests: a synthetic 10-minute poller outage turns would-be ghosts into unknown; a fresh feed with no vehicles on the route is flagged separately.
verify: Report percent coverage for days 1 to 10 and list each gap longer than 5 minutes with its cause
Confirm the poller-kill test from earlier shows up as unknown, not ghost

steps.title: Define and classify ghosts, cancellations and late buses
steps.learn: Riders care about one thing: a bus was shown and did not come. But a trip the agency marked CANCELED was honestly announced, and a bus 20 minutes late is not a ghost. Your definition decides the headline number, so fix it on days 1 to 10 and apply it unchanged to the held-out days.

decision.choice: Ghost: predicted at a stop within H minutes, not CANCELED, no observed arrival within a window, coverage OK
decision.why: Tying it to what riders saw (a prediction H minutes out) matches the problem statement. Separate labels for announced cancellations, late arrivals and unknown keep the number honest and explainable.

alternatives.name: Scheduled trip with no vehicle ever seen
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to compute from the schedule alone, but counts trips no app ever displayed, which is a different problem.

alternatives.name: Prediction that vanished from the feed
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures flicker riders notice, but a prediction can disappear because the bus already passed.

steps.delegate: Python + duckdb. classify(service_date) labels each (trip, stop) with ghost, cancelled_announced, late, on_time, unknown, using parameters H, arrival window and late threshold from a config file. Tests with hand-built fixtures for each label, including a trip cancelled after it was first predicted.
verify: Freeze H and the windows in a committed config before computing anything on days 11 to 14
Inspect 10 ghosts from days 1 to 10 on a map and agree each one with your own eyes

steps.title: Measure prediction error by horizon
steps.learn: A prediction made 15 minutes out should be less accurate than one made 1 minute out. Error is observed arrival minus predicted time, grouped by horizon (predicted time minus snapshot time). Use percentiles, not means, because a few huge misses dominate an average.

decision.choice: Horizon buckets (0-2, 2-5, 5-10, 10-20 min); report median and p90 absolute error per bucket and stop
decision.why: Buckets match how riders read the app. Percentiles show both typical error and the bad tail that makes people miss a bus. Ghosts are excluded here and reported separately so the two failure modes do not blur.

alternatives.name: Single mean error per stop
alternatives.tradeoff: One easy number, but early and late errors cancel and the tail disappears.

alternatives.name: Fit a model of delay
alternatives.tradeoff: Could explain causes, but the question is how reliable the app is, not how to forecast better.

steps.delegate: Python + duckdb + matplotlib. error_table(dates) joins predictions to observed arrivals, computes horizon and signed error, and outputs median, p90 absolute error and signed median by bucket and stop. Tests: a fixture with a known 60 s late arrival produces error 60 in every bucket where it was predicted on time.
verify: Plot p90 absolute error vs horizon for days 1 to 10 and check it grows with horizon
Report whether predictions are biased early or late (signed median) per bucket

steps.title: Rank the least reliable stops with uncertainty
steps.learn: A stop with 1 ghost out of 2 predicted trips is not necessarily worse than one with 30 out of 200; small samples produce extreme rates. Ranking by a confidence bound rewards evidence. scipy's binomtest result has proportion_ci with a 'wilson' method.

decision.choice: Rank stops by the lower Wilson bound of ghost rate, with a minimum number of predicted trips
decision.why: The lower bound only puts a stop near the top if the data says its rate is high even after accounting for sample size. That is the right bias for a list you will publish about real places.

alternatives.name: Raw ghost rate
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest to explain, but low-traffic stops with a couple of misses dominate the top.

alternatives.name: Bayesian shrinkage toward the route mean
alternatives.tradeoff: Smooth and principled, but the prior choice needs justifying to readers.

steps.delegate: Python + scipy + duckdb. rank_stops(dates, min_trips) returns stop_id, name, n_predicted, n_ghost, rate, wilson_low, wilson_high via scipy.stats.binomtest(k, n).proportion_ci(method='wilson'). Tests: a stop with 1/2 ranks below one with 30/200 at the same min_trips; stops under min_trips are excluded.
verify: Compute the ranking on days 1 to 10, then once on held-out days 11 to 14 without changing parameters
Report how many of the top 5 stops from days 1 to 10 stay in the top 10 on held-out days

steps.title: Test it outside: two weeks of logs and stop-side checks
steps.learn: The try-it: log a route for two weeks and publish the most unreliable stops. Your inferred arrivals are still a model, so stand at a few stops and record buses by hand to check both arrivals and ghosts against reality.
verify: Do at least 4 stop-side sessions (30 min or more) at 2 stops; record bus label and time for every bus
Report how many hand-seen buses your pipeline matched, and how many of its ghosts you confirmed
Publish the top stops list from held-out days with sample sizes, intervals and the caveat

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example ghosts clustering at one end of the route), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question and the frozen ghost definition
Part 2 gives ghost rate, coverage, error by horizon and stop ranking, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence from the logs or stop-side notes
Part 4 lists assumptions (one route, two weeks, inferred arrivals) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Accessibility mapper
projects.problem: Wheelchair users hit missing curb ramps and broken sidewalks
projects.concepts: Object detection for ramps and stairs, routing that avoids barriers
projects.tryIt: Map a few blocks and test routes with someone who uses a wheelchair or stroller
projects.question: Can phone photos and a small detector map curb ramps and barriers on a few blocks well enough that barrier-avoiding routes hold up in a real wheelchair test?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the test area
steps.learn: Two parts: a detector that finds curb ramps, missing ramps, stairs and obstacles in photos, and a router that avoids what it found. Metrics: detector recall on barriers (a missed barrier strands someone), routes completed without hitting a barrier, and detour length versus the plain shortest path.

decision.choice: Your own phone photos of 6 to 10 blocks; one block's photos labeled and frozen as the test set before training
decision.why: Own photos avoid street imagery licensing questions and match what the app will see. Holding out a whole block, not random photos, stops near-identical shots of the same ramp leaking into both train and test.

alternatives.name: Project Sidewalk labels as the only data
alternatives.tradeoff: CC0, geolocated and validated by other users, but labels were placed on third-party street imagery you may not be allowed to train on; use them as a reference instead.

alternatives.name: Random photo split
alternatives.tradeoff: More training data per block, but the test score is inflated by the same objects appearing on both sides.

verify: README states the question, the 3 metrics and the block boundaries before any photo is taken
The test block is named and its photos stored apart, never used for training or threshold tuning

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting photos
steps.learn: Detect things (ramps, stairs, poles), never people. Street photos capture passers-by, faces, plates and front doors. Routing is a safety claim: a route marked accessible that hits a raised curb can strand someone, so the app must say it is a helper and point to official city information.

decision.choice: Blur faces on the phone before upload, keep only object crops plus location, label routes as advisory
decision.why: On-device face detection means faces never reach your server. Keeping crops of detected features instead of full frames removes most bystander and doorway content. Clear advisory wording and a report button keep the city's official data as the source of record.

alternatives.name: Server-side blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler app, but raw faces are uploaded and briefly stored.

alternatives.name: Blur every person and car box with a COCO detector
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers bodies and plates, not just faces, but costs more compute per photo and still misses small or occluded people.

steps.delegate: Mobile or Python capture tool: run MediaPipe Face Detector with the full-range BlazeFace model on each photo and blur detected boxes before saving; strip EXIF except GPS and heading, kept in a separate field. Tester consent form and a rule that tester GPS traces are deleted after the test. Tests: a photo with a face never reaches storage unblurred; saved files carry no EXIF.
verify: Shoot 10 photos containing people and confirm no stored file shows a recognizable face
Write the advisory note and the official city accessibility or 311 link now, to be shown on the route screen built in step 8

steps.title: Choose the classes and label the photos
steps.learn: The class list decides what the router can avoid. Project Sidewalk's label types include CurbRamp, NoCurbRamp, Obstacle and SurfaceProblem, a vocabulary built for exactly this mapping task. 'Missing ramp' is hard to box: it is the absence of something at a corner.

decision.choice: Classes: curb_ramp, raised_curb_at_crossing, stairs, obstacle, surface_problem; boxes in Label Studio, exported as YOLO
decision.why: Boxing a raised curb where a crossing meets the sidewalk turns 'missing ramp' into something visible. Matching Project Sidewalk names makes the later comparison easy. Label Studio exports YOLO format, one txt file per image with normalized boxes.

alternatives.name: Image-level tags only
alternatives.tradeoff: Much faster labeling, but you cannot tell which corner of the photo has the barrier.

alternatives.name: Segmentation masks
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for sidewalk width and cracks, but labeling takes several times longer.

steps.delegate: Write a Label Studio config with RectangleLabels for the 5 classes and a labeling guide with 2 example photos per class. Script to convert the YOLO export into the Ultralytics folder layout plus data.yaml, keeping the frozen test block separate. Tests: every image has a label file or is listed as background; class ids are zero-indexed and match data.yaml.
verify: Label at least 300 boxes outside the test block and report counts per class
Have a second person relabel 30 photos and report how often you agree on class and box

steps.title: Fine-tune a small pretrained detector
steps.learn: With a few hundred boxes you must start from a pretrained detector and fine-tune. Small models can run on a phone, which also helps privacy. Watch for classes with very few examples; the model will learn to ignore them.

decision.choice: Ultralytics YOLO nano checkpoint (the docs use yolo26n.pt), fine-tuned at imgsz 640
decision.why: The train API is a few lines and handles augmentation, and the nano size suits on-device use. Note the AGPL-3.0 license if you plan to ship a closed app.

alternatives.name: torchvision Faster R-CNN (MobileNetV3 FPN)
alternatives.tradeoff: BSD-licensed and well documented, but more training code to write and slower on a phone.

alternatives.name: Zero-shot VLM per photo
alternatives.tradeoff: No labeling, but slower, costlier, and boxes and recall on small curbs are hard to control.

steps.delegate: Python, ultralytics. train.py loads the pretrained nano checkpoint and calls model.train(data='data.yaml', epochs=..., imgsz=640, seed=0), saving runs with config. Validation is one whole training block, not random photos. Tests: a 1 epoch smoke run on 10 images completes; data.yaml references no test-block path.
verify: Record mAP50 on the validation split and per-class AP, with machine and command
List the class with fewest boxes and its AP; decide whether to label more before moving on

steps.title: Pick a confidence threshold that favors catching barriers
steps.learn: mAP averages over thresholds, but the app needs one. A missed barrier sends someone into a raised curb; a false barrier only causes a detour. So barriers should get a lower threshold than ramps. Score the chosen setting once on the frozen test block.

decision.choice: Per-class thresholds tuned on validation: high recall for barriers, high precision for curb_ramp
decision.why: The cost of errors differs by class: a falsely detected ramp is dangerous (the router trusts it), a falsely detected barrier is only inconvenient. Per-class thresholds encode that asymmetry directly.

alternatives.name: One global threshold
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but forces the same tradeoff on ramps and barriers when their errors cost very different things.

alternatives.name: Human review of every detection
alternatives.tradeoff: Highest accuracy for a few blocks, but does not scale and hides how good the detector really is.

steps.delegate: Python, ultralytics. sweep.py runs model.predict on validation images, matches predictions to labels at IoU 0.5 and prints precision and recall per class over a threshold grid; writes chosen thresholds to config. eval_test.py runs once on the test block with frozen thresholds. Tests: matching code gives recall 1.0 when predictions equal labels.
verify: Report barrier recall and curb_ramp precision on the frozen test block, run once
Look at every missed barrier in the test block and note why it was missed

steps.title: Place detections on the map and merge duplicates
steps.learn: A detection is in pixels; the router needs a node or edge. Phone GPS is often off by several meters, enough to put a ramp on the wrong corner. The same ramp appears in several photos, so detections must be clustered into one feature with a vote.

decision.choice: Snap detections to the crossing node or sidewalk edge the camera faced; cluster within a radius and vote
decision.why: Snapping to the OSM graph turns noisy points into routable features. Using heading picks the corner the camera faced rather than the nearest one. Voting across photos smooths single bad detections.

alternatives.name: Store raw GPS points only
alternatives.tradeoff: No snapping errors, but the router cannot use them without a later matching step.

alternatives.name: Manual placement on a map
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate for a few blocks, but no longer tests whether the pipeline maps anything by itself.

steps.delegate: Python, pyproj, shapely, osmnx. snap(detection, G) projects the point forward along heading, finds candidate crossing nodes and footway edges within a radius, picks the best, returns (osm_id, kind, distance_m). cluster(features) merges same-class snaps within a radius and stores vote counts and photo ids. Tests: two photos of one ramp from opposite sides cluster into one feature.
verify: Walk your blocks and check 20 mapped features against where they really are; report the share on the right corner
Report how many photos per feature on average and how many features rest on a single photo

steps.title: Build the pedestrian graph with accessibility tags
steps.learn: OpenStreetMap already tags some of this: kerb=lowered or flush imply wheelchair=yes, kerb=raised implies no, and ways can carry wheelchair, incline and surface. Coverage varies a lot by city, so your detections fill the gaps. OSM data is ODbL: credit it, and derived data you share must keep that license.

decision.choice: OSMnx graph_from_point with network_type 'walk', adding kerb, barrier, wheelchair, incline and surface tags
decision.why: OSMnx downloads a routable NetworkX graph and its settings choose which node and way tags become attributes. Keeping it in Python means detections and OSM tags merge on the same graph objects.

alternatives.name: OpenTripPlanner
alternatives.tradeoff: Production router with wheelchair settings (maxSlope, stairsReluctance), but adding your own detections means editing OSM input and rebuilding.

alternatives.name: Raw Overpass queries plus your own graph
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control, but you rebuild topology and simplification that OSMnx already handles.

steps.delegate: Python, osmnx, networkx. build_graph(center, dist) sets ox.settings.useful_tags_node and useful_tags_way to include the accessibility tags, downloads the walk network, saves graphml. merge_detections(G, features) writes detected classes onto nodes and edges with a source field (osm or detector). Tests: a node tagged kerb=raised keeps that attribute; merged features never overwrite an OSM tag silently.
verify: Report how many crossing nodes in your area have any kerb tag in OSM before your detections
Report how many of your detected features add information OSM did not have

steps.title: Route around barriers with a cost function
steps.learn: Hard barriers (stairs, raised curb at a crossing) must remove edges; soft problems (rough surface, steep incline, unknown curb) should add cost. NetworkX's dijkstra_path accepts a weight function, and returning None hides an edge. Unknown is not the same as accessible.

decision.choice: Weight function: None for hard barriers, length times a penalty for soft issues and unknown curbs
decision.why: This is the hard-filter-then-soft-score pattern applied to edges. Treating unknown curbs as costly rather than free avoids confidently routing someone into an unmapped corner. Profiles (wheelchair strict, stroller lenient) are just different penalty tables.

alternatives.name: Only remove hard barriers
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but routes freely through unknown corners and rough sidewalks.

alternatives.name: Treat unknown as blocked
alternatives.tradeoff: Safest, but in poorly mapped areas there may be no route at all.

steps.delegate: Python, networkx. make_weight(profile) returns f(u, v, d) using node and edge attributes from both OSM and detector sources, returning None for hard barriers. route(G, a, b, profile) returns the path, length and a list of soft issues on it, or a clear 'no accessible route'. Tests: a stairs edge is never used; when it is the only link, route returns no path.
verify: Pick 10 origin and destination pairs; report detour length vs plain shortest path for each profile
Report how many plain shortest paths cross a known barrier that the accessible route avoids

steps.title: Compare your map with an independent reference
steps.learn: Your detector should not grade its own map. In a Project Sidewalk city, its validated labels are an independent reference; elsewhere, your own walk survey of the test block is. Compare feature by feature after snapping both to the same graph.

decision.choice: Match your features to Project Sidewalk label clusters (or your walk survey) within a radius, per class
decision.why: Label clusters merge multiple labels of the same feature, which mirrors your own clustering. Per-class agreement tells you which barriers the system misses on the street, not just in test photos.

alternatives.name: Compare against OSM tags
alternatives.tradeoff: Available everywhere, but OSM coverage of curbs is patchy, so missing tags look like your false positives.

alternatives.name: Skip the comparison
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves time, but the map's real-world accuracy is never measured.

steps.delegate: Python, requests, geopandas. fetch_reference(bbox) pulls Project Sidewalk label clusters for the area via its API, or reads a survey CSV. match(features, reference, radius) reports per-class true positives, misses and extras. Tests: identical inputs give perfect agreement; a feature just outside the radius counts as a miss and an extra.
verify: Report per-class recall and precision of your map against the reference for the test block
Inspect 5 disagreements on foot and decide who was right

steps.title: Test it outside: routes with a wheelchair or stroller user
steps.learn: The try-it: map a few blocks and test routes with someone who uses a wheelchair or stroller. They are the judge, not your metrics. Compare your accessible route with the plain shortest path on the same trips, and pay them for their time.
verify: Test at least 5 routes with the tester; record barriers hit, places they had to turn back, and minutes taken
Record barriers they found that the map missed, and any marked barrier that was not real
Ask the tester to rate each route and note their reasons in their own words

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a class the detector never learned), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives test-block recall, map agreement, detour lengths and field results, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (few blocks, one tester, one season) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Neighborhood menu search
projects.problem: "Spicy vegetarian under $15, open now"
projects.concepts: Hybrid search with hard filters, the same pattern as your interview task
projects.tryIt: Index menus from 30 local restaurants and try it with friends
projects.question: Can hybrid search with hard filters answer 'spicy vegetarian under $15, open now' correctly for 30 real local restaurants?

steps.title: Frame the menu search question and how you will judge it
steps.learn: One query like 'spicy vegetarian under $15, open now' carries three hard filters (diet, price, opening hours) and one soft-ish preference (spicy). The corpus is yours: 30 local restaurants, so there is no public label set. Success means no top 5 result breaks a hard filter, and friends find something they would order.
verify: Pick the 30 restaurants and record for each the menu source URL or photo and the date collected
Write 20 test queries from real cravings before building, each with at least one hard filter
Define 'success' for a friend session in one sentence before anyone tries it

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app identifies dishes and places, not people. Query logs from friends need consent and no names; round or drop location. Vegetarian tags and any ingredient info are a helper only: anyone with dietary restrictions or allergies must confirm with restaurant staff, and the app must say so.
verify: Confirm logs hold query text, time and item IDs only, with no names, contacts or precise location
Confirm the result screen tells users to confirm diet and allergens with staff
Confirm no allergen-free claim appears anywhere in the UI
Ask permission before publishing any restaurant's digitized menu

steps.title: Digitize 30 menus into item rows
steps.learn: Menus arrive as websites, PDFs and photos. Each item becomes a row: restaurant, section, name, description, price, plus the raw source. Prices are where errors hurt most, because 'under $15' is a hard filter, and OCR misreads digits. The corpus is small enough to review every price by hand.

decision.choice: Vision-language model extraction to a JSON schema, then a human review pass over every price
decision.why: Menus have columns, icons and odd layouts that a VLM reads more robustly than plain OCR; with roughly a thousand items, a full human price review is a one-evening job and removes the riskiest error.

alternatives.name: Classical OCR plus parsing
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs offline and free, but menu layouts make line-to-price pairing fragile.

alternatives.name: Type menus manually
alternatives.tradeoff: Perfectly accurate and fine for 30 menus, but slow to refresh when menus change.

steps.delegate: Python. ingest.py: for each source (image, PDF, URL) call a VLM with a schema MenuItem{restaurant_id, section, name, description, prices: list[{label, amount_cents}], marks: list[str], source_page} and save JSONL plus the source path. Add review.py, a CLI that shows each item next to its source page and lets me fix the price. Tests: schema validation, price parsing ('$12', '12.50'), multi-price items.
verify: Hand-check every extracted price against the source for 5 restaurants and record the error count
Confirm multi-price items (sizes, add-ons) keep all variants
Count items per restaurant and spot-check any menu with suspiciously few

steps.title: Tag diet and spice with provenance, not guesses
steps.learn: 'Vegetarian' is a hard filter, so you need to know whether the menu says it (a V mark, a veg section) or a model inferred it from ingredients. Store each tag as yes, no or unknown plus its source (stated or inferred). Spice can be a level from chili marks or words like 'hot' or 'Sichuan'.

decision.choice: Tri-state tags (yes, no, unknown) with provenance; only stated or high-confidence inferred tags pass the hard filter
decision.why: Diet is a trust problem: a wrong 'vegetarian' answer is worse than a missing one. Provenance lets the UI say 'marked vegetarian on menu' vs 'likely vegetarian', and lets you tighten the filter later.

alternatives.name: Boolean tags inferred by an LLM
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and more coverage, but you cannot tell stated facts from guesses.

alternatives.name: Stated marks only
alternatives.tradeoff: Safest, but many menus mark nothing, so most truly vegetarian dishes disappear.

steps.delegate: Python. tag_items.py: rules for stated marks (V, VG, chili icons, section names) first; LLM fills only missing tags with a schema {vegetarian: yes|no|unknown, spice_level: 0..3|null, confidence}; write provenance per field. Tests: rule tags override LLM, unknown stays unknown when confidence is low, re-running is idempotent.
verify: Compare inferred vegetarian tags with stated marks on restaurants that have both; report disagreements
List 10 items tagged vegetarian by inference only and judge each by hand
Confirm every item has a provenance field for diet and spice

steps.title: Model opening hours so 'open now' is correct
steps.learn: 'Open now' is the hard filter most likely to be wrong. Hours have split shifts, spans past midnight, holiday exceptions and a local time zone. Decide whether 'open' means the door is open or that the kitchen takes orders for at least, say, 20 more minutes.

decision.choice: Weekly interval table per restaurant (overnight spans, date exceptions), evaluated in Python with zoneinfo
decision.why: The whole app stays in one Python codebase with one SQLite file, and 30 restaurants is few enough to enter and test hours by hand. Writing the check yourself forces you to test the tricky cases explicitly.

alternatives.name: OSM opening_hours strings plus opening_hours.js
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles split shifts, overnight spans and holidays with a maintained parser (getState), but it is a JavaScript library, so it adds a second runtime.

alternatives.name: Google Place Details opening hours
alternatives.tradeoff: Fresher hours with less manual entry, but needs an API key, has usage costs and terms.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. hours.py: is_open(intervals, exceptions, tz_name, at, min_minutes_left) and minutes_until_close(...), converting 'at' to the restaurant's zone with zoneinfo.ZoneInfo. Intervals are (weekday, open, close) where close may be past midnight. Tests: split shift, span past midnight, min_minutes_left near closing, a closed-holiday exception, a DST-change day.
verify: Test 'open now' at 10 hand-picked times including just before close and after midnight
Confirm the time zone comes from the restaurant location, not the server clock
Compare stored hours with the restaurant's own site for 10 restaurants and log mismatches

steps.title: Parse the craving into filters plus free text
steps.learn: Turn 'spicy vegetarian under $15, open now' into {diet: vegetarian, max_price: 15.00, open_now: true, spice_min: 1, text: ''}. Decide whether 'under $15' is strict, and which price counts when an item has sizes. Synonyms matter for a small vocabulary: 'veggie', 'meatless', 'hot', 'chili'.

decision.choice: Deterministic regex for price and time words, plus a small LLM call for diet, spice and cuisine
decision.why: Price and 'open now' are high-stakes and easy to parse with rules, so they should not depend on a model. The LLM handles the fuzzy parts where a mistake only costs relevance.

alternatives.name: Rules only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and predictable; feasible with a small vocabulary but misses phrasing friends actually use.

alternatives.name: LLM only
alternatives.tradeoff: Least code, but a misparsed price silently breaks the most important filter.

steps.delegate: Python. parse.py: parse_price(q) and parse_open_now(q) via regex, parse_soft(q) via an LLM with a JSON schema {diet, spice_min, cuisine, text}; merge with rule results taking priority. Synonym table for diet and spice words. Tests: '$15', 'under 15 bucks', 'less than $15.50', 'veggie', no-filter query, LLM failure falls back to rules.
verify: Run all 20 test queries and hand-check every parsed filter
Confirm the regex catches every price phrasing in the 20 queries and no price words leak into the LLM text field
Confirm a query with no filters still returns text-ranked results

steps.title: Index items in SQLite with FTS5 plus a small embedding model
steps.learn: About a thousand short item rows is tiny. Keyword search catches dish names ('paneer', 'mapo tofu'); embeddings catch intent ('something like a burrito bowl'). Fuse both with RRF. Exact cosine over all items is fast enough, so no ANN index is needed.

decision.choice: One SQLite file: FTS5 with bm25() for text, embeddings stored as blobs and scored exactly, fused with RRF
decision.why: Everything (items, hours, tags, index) ships as one file, the hard filters are plain SQL, and the corpus is small enough that exact vector scoring costs little.

alternatives.name: sqlite-vec extension
alternatives.tradeoff: Vector search inside SQL queries; useful if the corpus grows, adds a native extension.

alternatives.name: Qdrant or another vector DB
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong payload filtering and scale, but a server is overkill for 30 restaurants.

steps.delegate: Python. build_index.py: SQLite tables items, restaurants, item_fts (FTS5 over name, description, section); embed item text with a small sentence-transformers model, vectors as blobs. search(text, candidateIds): quote each token and join with OR for MATCH, ORDER BY bm25() ascending, RRF-fuse with cosine. Tests: idempotent rebuild, dish name ranks first, multi-word and punctuation queries, RRF on toy lists.
verify: Confirm a dish name query returns that dish first
Find a paraphrase query that FTS5 misses and the hybrid finds
Time a full query on a phone-class or laptop CPU and record the machine

steps.title: Apply hard filters first and explain empty results
steps.learn: Filter in SQL first (price, diet, open now), then rank only survivors. With a small corpus this is exact and cheap. The common failure is not wrong results but no results: at 10pm few places are open. Relax filters in a fixed, stated order and tell the user what was relaxed.

decision.choice: Strict SQL WHERE on hard filters, then an explicit relaxation ladder (e.g. 'opens in 20 min') with a visible note
decision.why: Friends trust the app only if hard filters always hold; when nothing matches, saying why and offering the nearest option is more useful than silently loosening a filter.

alternatives.name: Post-filter the ranked list
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but can return few or no results, and hides why.

alternatives.name: Soft penalties for filter misses
alternatives.tradeoff: Never empty, but a $17 dish can outrank a $14 one, breaking the user's explicit constraint.

steps.delegate: Python. query.py: build SQL WHERE from parsed filters (min variant price < max_price, vegetarian = yes with allowed provenance, is_open at now), pass candidate IDs to search(). If empty, try a fixed ladder (open within 30 min, then price +10%), returning which step applied. Tests: each filter alone, ladder order, message text matches the applied step.
verify: Confirm no top 5 result for the 20 test queries violates price, diet or hours
Run the main query at a late hour and check the relaxation message is accurate
Log how many test queries return zero results before relaxation

steps.title: Rank survivors with simple features and limit repeats
steps.learn: Among eligible dishes, a useful order mixes text relevance, spice strength when asked, and walking distance. Without a cap, one restaurant with ten curries fills the screen. With little data and no labels, a hand-tuned score is honest; a learned ranker would be fitting noise.

decision.choice: Weighted score of fused relevance, spice match and distance, max 2 items per restaurant
decision.why: Few items and no relevance labels mean simple, explainable weights are the right tool; the per-restaurant cap fixes the most visible problem cheaply.

alternatives.name: Cross-encoder reranker
alternatives.tradeoff: Better text matching on longer descriptions, but menu items are short, so gains may be small.

alternatives.name: Learning to rank
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs many labeled clicks; with a handful of friends it would overfit.

steps.delegate: Python. query.py: compute open restaurant IDs with hours.is_open, then build SQL WHERE from parsed filters (min variant price < max_price, vegetarian = yes with allowed provenance, restaurant_id IN open IDs). If empty, try a fixed ladder (opens within 30 min, then price +10%, never diet), returning which step applied. Tests: each filter alone, ladder order, message matches the applied step.
verify: Confirm no restaurant appears more than twice in the top 5
Check distances against a map for 5 restaurants
Ask 2 friends to rank 5 results by hand and compare with the app order

steps.title: Handle stale prices, wrong hours and reports
steps.learn: Menus and hours change, and a wrong 'open now' sends a hungry friend to a closed door. Show when each price and hours entry was last checked, and let users flag wrong data in one tap so you can fix it.

decision.choice: Store collected_at per menu and hours; show it in results; one-tap 'this is wrong' log
decision.why: With 30 restaurants you can re-verify by hand, but only if you know what is stale and where users found errors.

alternatives.name: Scheduled re-scrape of websites
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps data fresher, but breaks on site changes and many menus are photos.

alternatives.name: Ignore staleness
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but silent wrong answers erode trust quickly.

steps.delegate: Python. Add collected_at and hours_checked_at columns, render 'as of <date>' in results, and an endpoint POST /report {item_id, kind} that appends to a reports table with a timestamp and no user identifiers. Tests: report stored without user data, stale threshold marks entries older than N days.
verify: Confirm every result shows the date its menu was collected
Submit a 'wrong info' report and confirm it is logged with item ID and timestamp only
Re-check 5 restaurants a month later and log what changed

steps.title: Test it outside with friends
steps.learn: Give 5 to 8 friends the app at real meal times with a few scripted queries and their own cravings. Measure what matters here: hard-filter violations in the top 5 (verified against menus or on arrival), sessions where they found something they would order, zero-result queries, and time to a decision.
verify: Report hard-filter violations in the top 5 across sessions, verified against the source, counting relaxed results separately
Report the share of sessions where the friend found a dish they would order
Report zero-result and relaxed-result query counts, and time to decision
Visit or call 3 'open now' results to confirm they were actually open

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: Write the 4-part write-up: the one question, numbers for every claim with machine and command (violations, success rate, latency), why surprising results happened (for example hours errors or late-night empty results), and what this does not prove (30 restaurants, a few friends, one neighborhood).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2 gives a number, machine and command (or session count) for every claim
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a real query
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including stale data and sample size

projects.title: Lost-and-found matcher
projects.problem: Found items rarely get back to owners
projects.concepts: CLIP embeddings to match a found-item photo to lost reports
projects.tryIt: Run it for a campus or office lost-and-found
projects.question: Can CLIP embeddings put the right lost report in the top 5 for a found-item photo, so staff check a handful of reports instead of all of them?

steps.title: Frame the question, metric and data
steps.learn: Success is ranking: for each found photo, is the true lost report in the top 5 (Recall@5), and how high (MRR)? Offline data: Stanford Online Products (120k images of 23k products, several photos per product) stands in for found photo vs owner photo. Text reports you collect and label yourself.
verify: You wrote the one question and the two metrics (Recall@5, MRR) in your README
You downloaded the dataset and counted products with at least two images
You drafted 30 short text lost reports for real objects you can photograph, labeled to their photos

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app matches things, not people. Found photos can include bystanders' faces, and ID cards, phones and letters show personal data. Blur faces before anything is stored, and do not embed photos of documents (CLIP vectors can encode visible text); keep contact data out of the matcher.

decision.choice: Run on-device face detection on upload, blur faces before saving, discard the original
decision.why: If the original is never stored, a later leak or misuse cannot expose bystanders. Blurring before embedding also keeps faces out of the vectors, so the matcher cannot become a face search.

alternatives.name: Ask staff to crop photos manually
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra model, but people forget under time pressure and one missed face is a privacy leak.

alternatives.name: Store originals with restricted access
alternatives.tradeoff: Allows re-processing later, but keeps sensitive images you do not need.

steps.delegate: Python, MediaPipe Tasks FaceDetector with the BlazeFace full-range model (found photos are back-camera shots), Pillow. On upload, detect faces with a low confidence threshold, Gaussian-blur each padded box, save only the blurred image, delete the temp original. Staff flag for ID cards and documents hides the photo from listings and skips embedding it. Retention job deletes closed records after N days. Tests: face image blurred; small distant face blurred; temp file gone; retention works.
verify: No stored image in the database folder contains an unblurred face, checked on 50 test uploads
Embeddings and search code never read the contact table or document text
Closed records older than your retention period are deleted by the scheduled job

steps.title: Design the lost report and found item records
steps.learn: Matching uses two kinds of signal: hard facts (when and roughly where it was lost or found, a coarse category) and soft similarity (what it looks like). Contact details are needed to return the item but never needed for matching, so they live apart from everything the matcher reads.

decision.choice: Structured fields (date window, zone, category) plus a free-text description and an optional owner photo
decision.why: Owners rarely have a photo of a lost umbrella but can describe it, so free text is the main query. Date and zone fields are cheap, reliable filters that shrink the candidate list before any model runs.

alternatives.name: Free text only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest form to fill, but you lose reliable filters and must guess dates and places from prose.

alternatives.name: Strict category dropdowns, no ML
alternatives.tradeoff: Fully predictable and private, but 'black bag' matches dozens of items and staff still check them all.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite via sqlmodel. Tables: lost_report(id, description, category, zone, lost_from, lost_to, photo_path nullable, contact_id), found_item(id, photo_path, category, zone, found_at, status), contact(id, name, email) in a separate table the matcher never queries. Pydantic validation: lost_from <= lost_to, zone from a fixed list. Tests: invalid date windows rejected; matcher module has no import of contact.
verify: You can create a lost report and a found item through the API and read them back
A grep shows the matching code never references the contact table

steps.title: Choose the image and text embedding model
steps.learn: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so matching image and caption pairs land close in one shared space. That lets a found photo be compared directly with a typed description, and with an owner's photo, using the same cosine similarity.

decision.choice: OpenCLIP ViT-B-32 with the laion2b_s34b_b79k weights, run locally on CPU
decision.why: One model covers both photo-to-text and photo-to-photo. It is the example model in the OpenCLIP README, small enough for a laptop or a single office machine, and running locally means photos never leave the site.

alternatives.name: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 via transformers
alternatives.tradeoff: The original OpenAI weights through Hugging Face; similar size, a different training set, so compare both on your eval.

alternatives.name: A larger model from open_clip.list_pretrained()
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick if the eval shows small models miss fine detail; costs more memory and slower embedding.

alternatives.name: Hosted multimodal embedding API
alternatives.tradeoff: No local compute, but every photo goes to a third party, which is hard to justify for personal belongings.

steps.delegate: Python, open_clip_torch, torch, Pillow. Write embed.py with load_model() returning (model, preprocess, tokenizer) for ViT-B-32 / laion2b_s34b_b79k in eval mode, embed_images(paths) and embed_texts(strings), both returning L2-normalized float32 numpy arrays. Tests: output norms are 1 within 1e-5; same input gives the same vector twice; a photo of a mug scores higher with 'a photo of a mug' than 'a photo of a bicycle'.
verify: Embedding 100 photos runs on your machine and you recorded seconds per image
Your mug vs bicycle sanity test passes on your own photos

steps.title: Score a found photo against text and photo reports
