steps.learn: Image-to-text and image-to-image similarities live on different scales, so adding them raw lets one dominate. Short owner descriptions also differ from captions CLIP saw in training, so phrasing like 'a photo of a ...' around the description is something to test, not assume.

decision.choice: Score = image-to-text cosine; when an owner photo exists, combine with image-to-image cosine after per-type z-scoring
decision.why: Text is always present so it is the base score. Z-scoring each similarity type against the current candidate pool puts them on a common scale before combining, so an owner photo helps without swamping the text signal.

alternatives.name: Caption the found photo with a VLM, then match text to text
alternatives.tradeoff: Readable captions staff can check, but adds a slower model and its caption errors become matching errors.

alternatives.name: Max of the two raw cosines
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but the scales differ so the photo score usually wins whenever it exists.

steps.delegate: In match.py write score(found_vec, reports) where each report has a text vector and an optional photo vector. Compute cosines, z-score each type over the candidate pool, and combine with weight w (default 0.5) when a photo exists. Add a prompt_template option for text, e.g. 'a photo of {}'. Tests: identical image beats a random one; a report without a photo still gets a finite score; changing w changes ranks only for reports with photos.
verify: On your 30 labeled text reports, you compared Recall@5 with and without the prompt template
You can show one case where the owner photo moved the correct report up

steps.title: Apply date, zone and category filters before ranking
steps.learn: An item found before it was reported lost, or across campus, is rarely a match. Filtering first shrinks the pool and removes look-alikes. CLIP can also guess a coarse category for the found photo zero-shot by comparing it with prompts for each category name.

decision.choice: Hard filter on date (found within or after the lost window); soft boost for same zone and same zero-shot category
decision.why: Dates are reliable and wrong ones are near impossible matches, so they are safe to filter. Owners often misremember where, and zero-shot categories can be wrong, so those only adjust scores instead of hiding the true report.

alternatives.name: Filter on all fields
alternatives.tradeoff: Smallest pool and fastest, but one wrong zone or category guess hides the right report entirely.

alternatives.name: No filters, similarity only
alternatives.tradeoff: Never wrongly excludes, but look-alike items from other days and places crowd the top 5.

steps.delegate: Extend match.py: candidates(found_item) queries lost reports whose window allows the found date (with a configurable grace in days). Add zero_shot_category(found_vec, category_names) using CLIP text prompts. Apply additive boosts for zone and category matches. Tests: a report lost after the found date is excluded; zone mismatch lowers but does not remove; category list changes are picked up without code edits.
verify: Recall@5 on your labeled set with filters is at least as high as without them
You measured how often the zero-shot category is correct on your own photos

steps.title: Choose how to store and search the vectors
steps.learn: A campus or office lost-and-found holds hundreds to a few thousand open reports, and filtering shrinks that further. At that size an exact scan over a matrix of normalized vectors is fast, and exact search means misses are the model's fault, not the index's.

decision.choice: Exact search: keep vectors in a numpy matrix (persisted in SQLite as blobs) and score with one matrix product
decision.why: The pool is small after filters, so exact search costs little and has no recall loss to debug. It also keeps deployment to a single process with no separate vector service.

alternatives.name: FAISS IndexFlatIP
alternatives.tradeoff: Same exact result with a faster kernel; worth it once a city-wide system holds far more reports.

alternatives.name: HNSW (hnswlib or a vector DB)
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for very large pools; adds approximate misses and index upkeep for a problem this size does not have.

steps.delegate: Write store.py: save and load float32 vectors as SQLite BLOBs keyed by record id; build_matrix(ids) returns an (n, d) numpy array. Score candidates with a single matrix product. Tests: round-trip preserves vectors exactly; scores equal per-row dot products; query over 5,000 vectors finishes under a timing budget you set and record.
verify: You recorded query latency over 5,000 synthetic reports on your target machine
Results match a per-row loop exactly on 100 random queries

steps.title: Evaluate matching offline on a public dataset
steps.learn: Photo-to-photo matching can be measured at scale on Stanford Online Products: use one image of a product as the found photo and another image of the same product as the owner's photo. Text matching is measured on your own labeled reports, since the dataset has no owner-style descriptions.

decision.choice: Simulate pools of 500 owner photos with one true match each, report Recall@1, Recall@5 and MRR
decision.why: A pool of hundreds matches the size of a real campus backlog better than searching all 120k images, so the numbers predict what staff would see.

alternatives.name: Retrieve over the whole dataset
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard for metric-learning papers, but far harder than a real lost-and-found pool and understates usefulness.

alternatives.name: Only your hand-collected photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic images, but too few to tell small differences from noise.

steps.delegate: Write eval.py: sample products with at least two images from the dataset, build pools of 500 with one positive, embed with embed.py, rank with match.score, and print Recall@1, Recall@5, MRR with bootstrap 95 percent intervals over 20 pools. A second mode runs the same metrics on a CSV of your labeled text reports. Fixed seed. Tests: a perfect scorer gets 1.0; a random scorer gets near 5/500 for Recall@5.
verify: You report Recall@5 and MRR with confidence intervals on both the public set and your text set
You kept 10 of your text reports untouched until the final run, to check you did not overfit prompts

steps.title: Handle duplicates, weak matches and no-match cases
steps.learn: The same item may be photographed twice, many items are never reported, and some top matches are weak. A matcher that always shows 5 suggestions wastes staff time on items nobody lost. Perceptual hashes catch re-uploads cheaply; a calibrated score threshold separates 'check these' from 'no likely match'.

decision.choice: Perceptual hash to flag duplicate found photos; show matches only above a threshold chosen from the eval set
decision.why: Duplicates are exact or near-exact images, which hashing detects without the model. A threshold on the raw image-to-text cosine (not the pool z-scored score, which is relative) picked for a target precision on labeled data gives a decision staff can trust.

alternatives.name: Always show the top 5
alternatives.tradeoff: Never hides a real match, but every unreported item still produces 5 false leads.

alternatives.name: Use CLIP similarity for duplicates
alternatives.tradeoff: Already computed, but two different black umbrellas look like duplicates too.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, Pillow. On found-item upload compute a perceptual hash and flag existing items within a Hamming distance you configure. Add calibrate.py that sweeps thresholds on the labeled eval output and prints precision and recall per threshold; store the chosen value in config. Tests: re-saved JPEG of the same photo is flagged; a different object is not; below-threshold items return an explicit no_match status.
verify: You chose a threshold and wrote down its precision and recall on held-out data
Uploading the same photo twice is flagged as a duplicate

steps.title: Keep a human in the loop to confirm and return items
steps.learn: A match is a suggestion. Returning a wallet to the wrong person is worse than not returning it. Staff confirm a candidate, then the claimant proves ownership with a detail that was not visible in any shared photo or listing.

decision.choice: Staff-only review page; claimant must answer an ownership question before handover
decision.why: Photos and descriptions can be seen by anyone browsing, so they cannot prove ownership. A hidden detail checked in person blocks false claims, and staff confirmation catches model mistakes.

alternatives.name: Auto-email the top match
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but a wrong match sends a stranger to claim the item and leaks that it was found.

alternatives.name: Public gallery of found items
alternatives.tradeoff: Owners can self-search, but it invites false claims and exposes photos of personal belongings.

steps.delegate: FastAPI + Jinja templates. Staff page lists a found item with its ranked candidate reports and scores; actions: confirm match, reject, mark returned. Store every action in an audit table with staff id and time. Notifications go only after confirmation. Tests: no notification without a confirm action; non-staff requests get 403; audit row written for each action.
verify: A teammate acting as staff can confirm a match in under a minute from the review page
The audit log shows who confirmed each return and when

steps.title: Test it outside at a campus or office lost-and-found
steps.learn: Real found photos are taken in poor light on cluttered desks, and real reports are vague. Finish the privacy step (face blur, no originals, retention) before any real upload. Then run it alongside the existing process for a few weeks, with permission, and compare against what staff would have done.
verify: You agreed scope and data handling with the lost-and-found owner in writing before starting
You logged, for each returned item, whether the true report was in the top 5 and at what rank
You measured staff minutes per found item with and without the matcher
You counted items returned during the trial versus a comparable earlier period

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Answer whether the top 5 is good enough for staff, with offline and real-world numbers side by side. Ablations (no filters, no owner photo, no prompt template) show which part actually helps.
verify: Part 1: the write-up opens with the one question about top-5 matching for found photos
Part 2: every number states the dataset or trial, the machine, the model weights and the command
Part 3: it explains surprises, such as items that look alike or descriptions CLIP misread
Part 4: it lists assumptions and limits, such as one site, catalog-style public images, small text set

projects.title: Noise map
projects.problem: Which streets are loud, and from what?
projects.concepts: Audio event classification (traffic, construction, music) by time of day
projects.tryIt: Record short clips on walks for a month
projects.question: Which streets on my walks are loudest at which hours, and is the noise traffic, construction or music, judged from a month of short phone clips?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the held-out data
steps.learn: The map answers two things per place and hour: how loud (A-weighted level from the phone) and from what (traffic, construction, music). Offline metric: coarse-tag AUPRC on the SONYC-UST v2 test split. Field metric: agreement with labels you tag while walking, on walks reserved before you tune anything.

decision.choice: SONYC-UST v2 for training and offline scoring, plus your own walks with a held-out set fixed today
decision.why: SONYC-UST is 10 s multi-label clips from NYC street sensors, with coarse tags (engine, machinery-impact, powered-saw, alert-signal, music) that map onto the question. Its 669-clip test split is verified and later in time than training data, so it is frozen by construction.

alternatives.name: UrbanSound8K
alternatives.tradeoff: 8,732 clips of at most 4 s, 10 single-label classes; you must use its 10 predefined folds. Single labels on short clips do not match overlapping street sound.

alternatives.name: ESC-50
alternatives.tradeoff: 2,000 five-second clips in 50 classes and 5 folds; a quick sanity check, but few classes match traffic or construction.

verify: README states the question, both metrics, and the mapping: traffic = engine + alert-signal, construction = machinery-impact + powered-saw, music = music
Before recording, write which walk dates are held out (for example every 4th walk) and never tune on them
Download SONYC-UST and confirm split sizes: 13,538 train, 4,308 validate, 669 test recordings

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before any recording
steps.learn: Street clips capture passers-by talking. The map needs levels and source tags, not audio, so audio should never leave the phone. Recording people may be regulated where you live; check local rules. Map places and sound sources, never people, and do not record on private property.

decision.choice: On the phone, keep only level, tag scores, time and coarse location; on detected speech keep the level, drop tags
decision.why: With no stored audio there is nothing sensitive to leak. YAMNet runs on-device via MediaPipe Audio Classifier and includes Speech among its 521 classes, so a speech gate costs no extra model. Your own labels are tapped in the app while you listen, so no audio is needed later.

alternatives.name: Upload raw audio, process on a server
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier debugging and relabeling, but you hold recordings of strangers' voices and must secure and delete them.

alternatives.name: Keep audio on the phone for labeling, then delete
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets you relabel carefully at home, but a lost phone leaks recordings; needs a hard deletion deadline.

steps.delegate: Android, Kotlin, MediaPipe Tasks Audio Classifier with the YAMNet model. For each 10 s clip: compute level and tag scores in memory, discard the buffer, and write one row (time, rounded lat/lon, level, scores, user tags). If the max Speech score over frames exceeds a threshold, write nothing. Unit tests: no file in app storage contains PCM; coordinates are rounded to the chosen precision.
verify: Record 10 clips while a friend talks near the phone and confirm none produce a stored row
Inspect the export and app storage: no audio files, coordinates only at the coarse precision

steps.title: Set the capture format, audio source and walk routes
steps.learn: Phone audio paths are tuned for voice (gain control, noise suppression), which distorts level and spectrum. Android has AudioSource.UNPROCESSED (API 24+, falls back to DEFAULT if unsupported; check PROPERTY_SUPPORT_AUDIO_SOURCE_UNPROCESSED). On iOS, AVAudioSession mode measurement minimizes system processing.

decision.choice: 10 s clips, 16 kHz mono, unprocessed source, fixed routes walked at several times of day, GPS fix per clip
decision.why: 10 s matches SONYC-UST clips; YAMNet expects 16 kHz mono, so higher rates add nothing. Repeating fixed routes at different hours gives each place samples across times of day, which is what the question compares.

alternatives.name: Continuous recording
alternatives.tradeoff: More coverage per walk, but more battery and processing, and consecutive windows add little independent information.

alternatives.name: Random routes
alternatives.tradeoff: More streets covered, but too few repeat visits per street and hour to compare times of day.

alternatives.name: 48 kHz capture for CLAP
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed if you switch to LAION-CLAP, which expects 48 kHz input; otherwise wasted work.

steps.delegate: Kotlin: AudioRecord at 16 kHz mono PCM float. Use AudioSource.UNPROCESSED when AudioManager.getProperty(PROPERTY_SUPPORT_AUDIO_SOURCE_UNPROCESSED) is true, else VOICE_RECOGNITION, and log which was used per clip. Request a fresh location fix per clip and store getAccuracy(). Tests: clip length is exactly 160,000 samples; source flag is recorded on every row.
verify: Log which audio source your phone actually used and record the phone model
Plan 3 to 5 fixed routes and the hours you will walk each, written before day 1

steps.title: Compute A-weighted level per clip and calibrate the phone
steps.learn: A-weighting (IEC 61672) approximates the ear's lower sensitivity to low frequencies. LAeq (often called Leq) is the level of the mean squared A-weighted signal over the clip. A phone measures dB relative to full scale, not pascals, so absolute dB(A) needs a calibration offset. Average on energy, never on dB values.

decision.choice: LAeq per clip in dBFS plus one offset measured against a sound level meter at a few steady sources
decision.why: One offset turns your phone's numbers into approximate dB(A), so streets can be compared to familiar levels. A cheap Class 2 meter is enough for a hobby map, and logging the offset with the phone model makes the assumption explicit.

alternatives.name: Relative levels only
alternatives.tradeoff: No meter needed and fine for ranking places within your own data, but no absolute dB(A) and not comparable across phones.

alternatives.name: Use an existing sound level meter app
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster start, but its processing is a black box and does not feed your classifier pipeline.

steps.delegate: Python with NumPy and SciPy first, then port. a_weighting_sos(fs) built from the analog A-weighting transfer function via the bilinear transform; laeq(x, fs, offset_db). energy_mean_db(levels) = 10*log10(mean(10**(L/10))). Tests: a 1 kHz sine passes with about 0 dB gain; doubling amplitude adds about 6.02 dB; energy_mean_db([60, 70]) is about 67.4, not 65.
verify: Unit tests pass, including the energy-mean case
Phone vs meter at 3 steady sources: record the offset and the spread between sources

steps.title: Train a source tagger on frozen YAMNet embeddings
steps.learn: YAMNet frames 16 kHz audio into 0.96 s windows with 50% overlap and gives a 1024-d embedding and 521 AudioSet scores per frame. Pool frame embeddings over the 10 s clip and train a small multi-label head on SONYC-UST coarse tags, because traffic and construction often overlap in one clip.

decision.choice: Frozen YAMNet embeddings, mean-pooled per clip, one sigmoid layer over the 8 coarse tags
decision.why: Small enough for the phone, trains in minutes, and multi-label sigmoid outputs allow several sources per clip. Following the SONYC baseline (train on crowd labels in train, select on the few verified labels in validate) keeps results comparable.

alternatives.name: PANNs CNN14
alternatives.tradeoff: A stronger AudioSet tagger per its paper, with a 16 kHz checkpoint, but much heavier to run on a phone.

alternatives.name: LAION-CLAP zero-shot prompts
alternatives.tradeoff: No training and new tags such as 'leaf blower' are just text, but larger, expects 48 kHz audio and is harder to calibrate.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune YAMNet end to end
alternatives.tradeoff: Can adapt features to street audio, but more overfitting risk on about 13.5k crowd-labeled clips.

steps.delegate: Python, TensorFlow with tf-keras (the YAMNet code needs Keras 2), tensorflow_hub. Extract and cache YAMNet embeddings for SONYC-UST train and validate. Train a Dense(8, sigmoid) head with binary cross-entropy on crowd labels; select epochs on verified validate labels. Export backbone + head as one SavedModel as in the YAMNet transfer learning tutorial. Tests: embedding shape (frames, 1024); outputs in [0, 1].
verify: Report macro and micro AUPRC on validate using the baseline repo's evaluation code
Compare mean vs max pooling of frame embeddings on validate and keep the better one

steps.title: Pick per-tag thresholds on validate, then score test once
steps.learn: AUPRC needs no threshold, but the map needs yes or no per tag. Pick thresholds on validate, then run the frozen test split exactly once. SONYC sensors are fixed with identical microphones; your hand-held phone is a different domain, so expect a gap you will measure on your own held-out walks.

decision.choice: Per-tag threshold that maximizes F1 on verified validate labels, applied unchanged everywhere
decision.why: Tags differ in frequency and score scale, so one global cutoff over-fires on some tags and misses others. Choosing on validate and freezing keeps test and your walks honest.

alternatives.name: 0.5 for all tags
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches the challenge's F1@0.5 report and needs no tuning, but rare tags may almost never fire.

alternatives.name: Calibrate scores (Platt or isotonic) on validate
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives probabilities you can average on the map, but needs enough positives per tag to fit reliably.

steps.delegate: Python: choose_thresholds(scores, labels) returning per-tag F1-maximizing cutoffs on validate; evaluate(test_scores, test_labels, thresholds) using the official evaluation code plus per-tag F1. Save thresholds to a versioned JSON that the phone app loads. Tests: thresholds file round-trips; the test evaluation script refuses to run twice without a --force flag.
verify: Record test-split macro and micro AUPRC and per-tag F1, run once, with the command
Note which tags have fewest positives in validate and treat their thresholds as uncertain

steps.title: Reject clips the map should not trust
steps.learn: Field clips fail in predictable ways: wind on the microphone inflates level, clipping caps it, a phone in a pocket muffles it, and a poor GPS fix puts it on the wrong street. Android getAccuracy() is a 68% confidence radius in meters. YAMNet has a 'Wind noise (microphone)' class you can use as a gate.

decision.choice: Gate per clip: GPS accuracy radius, wind-noise score, share of clipped samples, and a minimum level
decision.why: Each gate is cheap, explainable and computed on the phone. Logging the reason for every rejection lets you see whether one gate is throwing away most of a street.

alternatives.name: No gates, rely on averaging
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but wind and pocket clips bias levels in a consistent direction that averaging does not remove.

alternatives.name: Learned outlier detector on embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches failure modes you did not list, but is opaque and needs examples of bad clips to tune.

steps.delegate: Kotlin and a mirrored Python version: gate(clip) returning (keep, reason) using accuracy_m, max wind-noise frame score, fraction of samples at or near full scale, and LAeq floor. Store rejected rows with reason but without tags. Tests with synthetic signals: a full-scale square wave is rejected as clipped; a row with accuracy 80 m is rejected when the limit is 30 m.
verify: Record 5 clips with deliberate wind on the mic and 5 in a pocket; count how many each gate rejects
After the first week, report the rejection rate per reason

steps.title: Aggregate clips into cells and time-of-day buckets
steps.learn: One clip says little; a place and hour needs several visits. Bin clips into hexagonal cells and time buckets, energy-average the levels, and report source share as the fraction of clips with each tag. Few clips mean wide uncertainty, so carry the count and an interval with every value.

decision.choice: H3 resolution 10 cells (about 15,000 m2 average) by 4 time-of-day buckets, minimum clip count per bin
decision.why: H3 cells are uniform enough to compare neighbors and need no road graph. Resolution 10 is roughly street-segment scale, small enough to separate a busy road from a side street on most walks. The minimum count stops one loud clip from painting a street red.

alternatives.name: Snap clips to OpenStreetMap street segments
alternatives.tradeoff: Answers 'which street' directly, but needs map matching and fails at intersections and parks.

alternatives.name: Square lat/lon grid
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to compute, but cell area changes with latitude and diagonal neighbors are farther away.

steps.delegate: Python, h3 v4 (latlng_to_cell), pandas. aggregate(rows, res=10, buckets) returns per (cell, bucket): n, energy-mean LAeq, bootstrap 90% interval, and share of clips per source tag. Mark bins below min_n as insufficient. Tests: energy mean of [60, 70] is about 67.4; a bin with fewer than min_n clips is flagged; the same input always yields the same cell ids.
verify: Report how many cell-bucket bins reach the minimum count after week 1
Check that the bootstrap interval narrows as visits to a bin grow

steps.title: Draw the map with level, source and uncertainty
steps.learn: A noise map misleads if it hides how little data sits behind each colour. Show level by colour, dominant source by icon or pattern, and the clip count, and grey out bins below the minimum. Let the viewer switch time-of-day buckets, since that is half the question.

decision.choice: Static HTML map with folium: one layer per time bucket, popups with n, LAeq interval and source shares
decision.why: folium renders Leaflet maps from Python with no server, which suits a personal project, and layers make the time-of-day comparison one click.

alternatives.name: Map inside the phone app
alternatives.tradeoff: Always with you, but more UI code and harder to share with neighbors or the city.

alternatives.name: Desktop GIS (for example QGIS)
alternatives.tradeoff: Powerful analysis, but not a shareable view and more manual each time data changes.

steps.delegate: Python, folium. render_map(bins, out_html) draws H3 cell polygons (h3 cell_to_boundary) coloured by LAeq, hatched or greyed when insufficient, with a LayerControl per time bucket and popups listing n, interval and tag shares. Test: the HTML contains one feature per non-empty bin and a layer per bucket.
verify: Open the map and confirm grey bins match the insufficient count from the aggregate step
Pick one cell and check its popup numbers by hand from the raw rows

steps.title: Test it outside: a month of walks
steps.learn: The try-it is the real test: record short clips on walks for a month. Score tags only on the held-out walk dates, against the labels you tapped while listening, so the system never grades itself. Then read the map: which streets are loud, when, and from what.
verify: On held-out walks, report per-source precision and recall of tags vs your tapped labels, and the gap to SONYC test
Report clips recorded, share rejected by each gate, and bins reaching the minimum count
Name the 3 loudest cells per time bucket with LAeq interval and dominant source
Revisit one loud cell at the same hour with the sound level meter and compare levels

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the phone, machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a quiet-looking street that tagged as construction), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives SONYC test, held-out walk and calibration numbers, each with phone model, machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence from rows or clips' tag scores
Part 4 lists assumptions (one phone, your routes and hours, calibration offset) and that this is not a regulatory noise measurement

projects.title: Stolen-bike matcher
projects.problem: Stolen bikes reappear on resale sites
projects.concepts: Image re-identification of bikes, search over listing photos
projects.tryIt: Test with friends' bikes photographed in different light and angles
projects.question: Can image re-identification put a stolen bike's resale listing in the owner's top 10 matches despite new light, angles and backgrounds?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen test split
steps.learn: This is retrieval: the query is the owner's photos of one bike, the gallery is listing photos, and success is the right bike ranked high (recall@1, recall@10, MAP@R) with few false alarms. Offline data: the bicycle super class of Stanford Online Products, eBay listings where each class is one product.

decision.choice: SOP bicycle images with the official split (test classes never seen in training), then friends' bikes
decision.why: SOP's test classes are disjoint from training classes, which is the re-identification setting: the stolen bike was never in training. Its train/test split is fixed by the dataset, so the test set is frozen before any tuning.

alternatives.name: Bike Index stolen-bike photos only
alternatives.tradeoff: Real stolen bikes, but no ground-truth resale listings to match against, so no recall can be computed.

alternatives.name: Friends' bikes only
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use, but a few dozen bikes is too small to tune on without overfitting.

verify: README states the question and metrics: recall@1, recall@10, MAP@R, and false alarms per 1,000 gallery bikes
From Ebay_train.txt and Ebay_test.txt keep bicycle_final rows; record image and class counts per split
Hold out a validation slice of train classes for tuning; never tune on test classes

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting any listings
steps.learn: Identify bikes, not people. Listing photos can show sellers, homes and plates. A match is a lead, not proof: the owner should check the official route (a police report and the bike's serial number) and never confront a seller. Only use listings you are permitted to access; many sites forbid scraping.

decision.choice: Keep only bike crops and embeddings, blur faces, show matches privately to the owner with a police path
decision.why: The matcher needs only the bike region, so keeping full photos adds risk and no accuracy. Private, owner-only results avoid publicly accusing innocent sellers, which false positives would otherwise do.

alternatives.name: Store full listing photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier audits and reprocessing, but you hold strangers' faces, homes and contact details.

alternatives.name: Publish matches or alert sellers automatically
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster action, but every false positive becomes a public accusation against an innocent seller.

steps.delegate: Python, MediaPipe Face Detector: blur_faces(img) applied before any image is written; strip EXIF; keep only detector crops and vectors plus listing URL and date. Result screen text: possible match, compare serial number, contact police, do not confront. Tests: an image with a face is stored blurred; stored files have no EXIF; no seller name or phone field exists in the schema.
verify: Run 20 listing-style photos that include people and confirm no stored crop shows a recognizable face
Check the result screen shows the police and serial-number guidance on every match

steps.title: Set up query and gallery sources
steps.learn: Queries come from owners; real stolen reports also exist in the Bike Index registry, whose API v3 search accepts stolenness=proximity with a location and distance and returns manufacturer, frame colors, an is_stock_img flag and photos. A stock photo matches every bike of that model, so it must never be a query.

decision.choice: Owner uploads plus Bike Index stolen records as queries; gallery from manual or permitted listing submissions
decision.why: Bike Index is an open registry with a documented API, so you get real query structure without scraping. Dropping stock images and normalizing manufacturer names makes metadata filters usable later.

alternatives.name: Scrape resale marketplaces
alternatives.tradeoff: Most coverage, but often against site terms, brittle to layout changes, and collects personal data.

alternatives.name: Owner uploads only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fully consented, but tiny volume and no real stolen-report formats to test against.

steps.delegate: Python, httpx. bikeindex.py: search_stolen(location, distance, page) calling /api/v3/search with stolenness=proximity (location and distance are ignored otherwise); store id, manufacturer_name, frame_colors, date_stolen, is_stock_img, large_img. normalize_maker(name) with an alias table. Gallery: a form or CLI to add a listing (image, URL, date, region). Tests with a recorded JSON fixture: stock images are excluded; aliases map to one maker.
verify: Fetch 100 stolen records near you and report how many have is_stock_img true
Check 20 maker names after normalization and count leftover duplicates

steps.title: Detect and crop the bike in every photo
steps.learn: Listing photos contain backgrounds, people and other bikes. If you embed the whole image, the background can dominate: two bikes in the same garage look alike. COCO includes a bicycle category, so a COCO-trained detector gives bike boxes with no training.

decision.choice: torchvision Faster R-CNN (fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn_v2, COCO weights), keep every bicycle box above a score
decision.why: Permissive torchvision code, COCO 'bicycle' class out of the box, and accuracy matters more than speed for a batch job over listings. Keeping all boxes handles photos with several bikes.

alternatives.name: Ultralytics YOLO
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster and easy to use, but AGPL-3.0 unless you buy an enterprise license, which matters if this becomes a service.

alternatives.name: No cropping
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but backgrounds and people drive similarity, causing false matches between bikes shot in the same place.

alternatives.name: torchvision fasterrcnn_mobilenet_v3_large_fpn
alternatives.tradeoff: Much lighter for on-device use, at some cost in accuracy on small or occluded bikes.

steps.delegate: Python, torch, torchvision. crop_bikes(img, min_score) returns crops with a small margin using FasterRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_V2_Weights.DEFAULT and the 'bicycle' label from weights.meta['categories']. Log images with zero detections. Tests: a photo with two bikes yields two crops; a photo with no bike yields none and is logged.
verify: On 50 SOP bicycle images, count missed and wrong crops by eye
Record time per image and the machine

steps.title: Embed crops with a frozen backbone and measure the baseline
steps.learn: Re-identification ranks gallery images by cosine similarity of embeddings. The DINOv2 paper evaluates exactly this non-parametric instance retrieval (Oxford, Paris, Met, AmsterTime) and reports large gains over earlier self-supervised and weakly supervised features. Measure before you train anything.

decision.choice: DINOv2 ViT-B/14 via torch.hub (dinov2_vitb14), CLS embedding, L2-normalized
decision.why: No training, strong instance-level retrieval in its paper, and a fixed baseline every later step must beat. ViT-B is a middle ground; ViT-S/14 and larger variants exist if speed or accuracy needs change.

alternatives.name: CLIP image embeddings (open_clip)
alternatives.tradeoff: Allows text queries like 'red road bike', but trained to match captions, so it may group bikes by type rather than by the exact bike.

alternatives.name: Larger DINOv2 (ViT-L/14 or g/14)
alternatives.tradeoff: Possibly better retrieval, but slower and more memory per crop.

steps.delegate: Python, torch. embed(crops) using torch.hub.load('facebookresearch/dinov2', 'dinov2_vitb14'), resize to a multiple of 14, return normalized vectors. Evaluate on SOP bicycle test with pytorch-metric-learning AccuracyCalculator (precision_at_1, mean_average_precision_at_r) plus recall@10. Tests: vectors have unit norm; the same image twice gives cosine 1.
verify: Record precision@1, recall@10 and MAP@R for DINOv2 on the validation slice of train classes (test is scored once, in step 5)
Run the same evaluation with one open_clip model on the validation slice of train classes and record the difference; do not compare on test

steps.title: Fine-tune with metric learning only if it beats the baseline
steps.learn: Metric learning pulls photos of the same bike together and pushes others apart. 'A Metric Learning Reality Check' found that many claimed gains were marginal under fair comparison, so hold backbone, embedding size and validation protocol fixed and compare on your validation slice only.

decision.choice: Fine-tune the last blocks on SOP bicycle train classes with MultiSimilarityMiner plus TripletMarginLoss
decision.why: pytorch-metric-learning makes mining and losses a few lines, and partial fine-tuning keeps most pretrained features. Selecting on held-out train classes protects the test split and drops the model if it does not help.

alternatives.name: ArcFace or SubCenterArcFace loss
alternatives.tradeoff: Proxy losses train stably with many classes, but add margin and scale knobs to tune.

alternatives.name: No fine-tuning
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero overfitting risk to eBay-style product photos, but leaves bike-specific cues unlearned.

steps.delegate: Python, torch, pytorch-metric-learning. Freeze all but the last 2 DINOv2 blocks; train with miners.MultiSimilarityMiner and losses.TripletMarginLoss on bicycle train classes minus a validation slice; class-balanced batches. Early-stop on validation MAP@R. Tests: a single batch overfits to near-zero loss; validation classes never appear in training batches.
verify: Compare validation MAP@R of fine-tuned vs frozen DINOv2; keep fine-tuning only if it wins
Then evaluate the chosen model once on SOP bicycle test and record it

steps.title: Index listings and combine several photos per bike
steps.learn: Owners have several photos and listings have several photos, so scores must be combined across pairs. Hard filters cut false matches cheaply: a listing posted before the theft date cannot be the stolen bike, and one far away is less likely. Frame color helps but is unreliable under lighting.

decision.choice: FAISS exact inner-product search; bike-to-listing score is the max over photo pairs; date filter hard, distance soft
decision.why: A city's listings are far below the size where approximate search is needed, so exact search removes one source of error. Max over pairs lets the one photo taken from a similar angle carry the match.

alternatives.name: Mean embedding per bike
alternatives.tradeoff: One vector per bike and simpler storage, but averaging across angles blurs distinctive views.

alternatives.name: HNSW index
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed at millions of photos, but adds recall loss and tuning you do not need at city scale.

alternatives.name: Hard color filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Shrinks the gallery, but lighting and repainting cause true matches to be filtered out.

steps.delegate: Python, faiss-cpu. Index normalized crop vectors with IndexFlatIP and a side table (crop_id, listing_id, date, lat, lon). search_bike(query_vecs, date_stolen, home) returns listings ranked by max pair score minus a distance penalty, excluding listings dated before the theft. Tests: an earlier-dated listing never appears; max aggregation returns a listing whose single matching photo is identical to a query photo.
verify: On the validation slice of train classes, compare recall@10 for max vs mean aggregation over a product's images and keep the better one
Record query latency for the full gallery on your machine

steps.title: Re-rank the top candidates with local feature matching
steps.learn: Global embeddings capture overall shape and color; what proves it is the same bike are small details: stickers, scratches, an odd bell. Local feature matching finds corresponding keypoints, and a geometric check (RANSAC) keeps only consistent matches. Use it on the top candidates only, since it is far slower per pair.

decision.choice: LightGlue with DISK or ALIKED features on the top 50, rank by RANSAC-verified match count
decision.why: LightGlue code and weights are Apache-2.0; DISK follows that license and ALIKED is BSD-3. SuperPoint is supported too but under a restrictive license. Verified match counts are also visible evidence you can show the owner.

alternatives.name: SIFT with ratio test (OpenCV)
alternatives.tradeoff: Classic and dependency-light, a good baseline, but needs your own matching and filtering logic.

alternatives.name: No re-ranking
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but look-alike bikes of the same model stay tied with the true match.

steps.delegate: Python, lightglue, OpenCV. rerank(query_crops, candidates, k=50): extract DISK features, match with LightGlue(features='disk'), filter with cv2.findFundamentalMat RANSAC, score = max verified matches over photo pairs, blended with the global score. Save match visualizations. Tests: an image matched with itself yields many inliers; two unrelated images yield few.
verify: On validation-slice queries, record precision@1 before and after re-ranking to decide whether to keep it; score test once at the end
Record added latency per query for k = 20 and k = 50

steps.title: Set the alert threshold and the human review screen
steps.learn: Owners act on alerts, so false alarms are the costly error. Choose a score threshold from false alarms per 1,000 gallery bikes on validation classes. Also handle repeats: the same listing reposted should alert once, which a perceptual hash catches.

decision.choice: Alert only above a validation-chosen threshold; show top 10 with side-by-side match evidence; dedupe reposts by pHash
decision.why: A threshold set from a false alarm budget, not guessed, makes alert volume predictable. Showing verified keypoint matches lets the owner judge quickly and keeps a human in the loop before anyone acts.

alternatives.name: Always show top 10, no alerts
alternatives.tradeoff: Never misses silently, but owners must check noise every day and stop looking.

alternatives.name: Automatic report to police
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but sends unverified leads and errors to people who must act on them.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash. choose_threshold(val_scores, val_labels, max_false_per_1000) returns the cutoff; alert(bike) applies it and suppresses listings whose pHash is within a Hamming distance of an already-alerted listing. Review page renders query and listing crops with LightGlue match lines. Tests: a reposted, resized listing does not alert twice; threshold monotonic in the budget.
verify: Record recall@10 and false alarms per 1,000 at the chosen threshold on validation classes
Repost one gallery listing resized and confirm only one alert

steps.title: Test it outside: friends' bikes in new light and angles
steps.learn: The try-it: friends' bikes photographed in different light and angles. Owners take 'registration' photos; someone else later shoots 'listing' photos indoors, at dusk, at odd angles, mixed into a gallery with look-alike bikes. The grader is the known bike identity, never the system's own score.
verify: Report recall@1 and recall@10 over all friends' bikes, with gallery size and number of look-alike distractors
Report false alarms at the chosen threshold and list each with a reason
Break results down by condition (indoor, dusk, angle) and name the hardest one
Compare with and without re-ranking on the same gallery

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example which look-alikes fooled it and why re-ranking did or did not help), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives SOP test and friends' bike numbers for each stage, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with match images as evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (gallery size, friends' bikes, eBay-style data) and that a match is a lead, not proof of theft

projects.title: Mural collection map
projects.problem: Street art is scattered and undocumented
projects.concepts: Image retrieval to recognize a mural from any angle, a collectible map
projects.tryIt: Photograph every mural in one neighborhood; test recognition at night
projects.question: Can image retrieval recognize every mural in one neighborhood from any angle, and at night, well enough to power a collectible map?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen test set
steps.learn: This is instance retrieval: a query photo must find the one mural it shows, not just 'a mural'. Success from the try-it: photograph every mural in one neighborhood, then measure top-1 accuracy for day queries from new angles, for night queries, and how often a non-mural photo is wrongly accepted.

decision.choice: Own gallery plus queries from a separate walk, frozen before tuning; Revisited Oxford as a public check
decision.why: No public set contains your murals, so the real test must be yours. Queries from a different walk (other day, other angles, some at night) stop you tuning on the test. Revisited Oxford (ROxford5k) is a fixed public landmark benchmark to sanity-check the retrieval code.

alternatives.name: Random split of one walk's photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick, but query and gallery shots share light, weather and angle, so accuracy looks far better than real use.

alternatives.name: Public benchmark only
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible, but says nothing about painted walls, night lighting or your phone camera.

verify: Write the one question and 3 metrics: day top-1, night top-1, false accepts per 100 non-mural photos
Write the split rule: gallery walk, a validation walk for tuning, and a later query walk plus non-mural photos, frozen and never used to pick settings
List the neighborhood boundary and the target number of murals

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before any photos are taken
steps.learn: Collect murals, never people. Street photos catch passers-by, faces and car plates, and night photography in unfamiliar streets has real risks. Murals are also someone's work on someone's wall: credit artists, and do not encourage trespass onto private property to get a shot.

decision.choice: On-device face detection blurs faces before upload; strip EXIF; public-space photos only; artist credit field
decision.why: Running MediaPipe Face Detector on the phone means unblurred faces never reach your server. Stripping EXIF removes device details and exact timestamps you do not need once the mural location is stored. Credit and a takedown contact respect artists and owners.

alternatives.name: Blur faces on the server
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach your server and logs even if briefly.

alternatives.name: Reject any photo with a face
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest guarantee, but busy streets will block many honest captures.

steps.delegate: Client step in TypeScript using MediaPipe Tasks Vision Face Detector: detect faces on the captured image, Gaussian-blur each box with padding, then re-encode the JPEG without EXIF before upload. Tests: a test image with faces produces blurred boxes; output files carry no EXIF; an image with no faces is unchanged except metadata.
verify: Run 10 photos that include people through the client and confirm no clear face survives
Confirm uploaded files contain no EXIF and the app tells users to stay on public ground at night

steps.title: Capture a reference gallery with several views per mural
steps.learn: Recognition from any angle is easier when the gallery already covers several angles. Each mural becomes one record (id, location, artist, photos), and every query is scored against murals, not single photos, so extra views help recall without double-counting.

decision.choice: 3 to 5 day photos per mural (frontal, two obliques, a detail) plus GPS, aggregated per mural at query time
decision.why: Oblique views cover the perspective change a single frontal photo misses. Scoring a mural by its best-matching view keeps the logic simple for tens to hundreds of murals.

alternatives.name: One frontal photo per mural
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest to collect, but steep angles and partial occlusion fail more often.

alternatives.name: Short video sweep per mural
alternatives.tradeoff: Many views for free, but more storage and near-duplicate frames to filter.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Define a murals.csv (mural_id, lat, lon, artist, notes) and a folder per mural of gallery images. Write a loader that validates every mural has at least 3 images and coordinates, and refuses to read the frozen query folder. Tests: missing coordinates fail validation; a query file path raises an error.
verify: Record the mural count and photos per mural for the neighborhood
Plot all mural locations on a map and confirm none sit on private land you entered

steps.title: Choose a global image descriptor for shortlisting
steps.learn: A global descriptor turns a whole image into one vector, so cosine similarity can shortlist candidate murals fast. It must match the same wall across viewpoint and light, not just similar-looking art. Treat it as stage one; geometric checks come next.

decision.choice: DINOv2 ViT-S/14 from PyTorch Hub, L2-normalized embeddings, top-10 shortlist by cosine
decision.why: DINOv2 is self-supervised for general-purpose visual features, small enough for a laptop or modest server, and its code and weights are Apache 2.0. Murals are tens to hundreds of items, so exact search in NumPy is enough.

alternatives.name: CLIP image embeddings (open_clip)
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong on semantics, but tuned to match image to text, so two different murals of a similar subject may sit close.

alternatives.name: Local features only, no shortlist
alternatives.tradeoff: Most precise, but matching every gallery image per query grows slow as the map grows.

steps.delegate: Python, torch, Pillow. Load torch.hub 'facebookresearch/dinov2', 'dinov2_vits14'. embed(path) returns a normalized vector; build_index(gallery) stores vectors with mural_id; shortlist(vec, k) returns mural ids ranked by best view. Script eval_roxford.py runs the same code on Revisited Oxford using the revisitop Python loader. Tests: vectors have unit norm; an image's own gallery copy ranks first.
verify: Report mAP on Revisited Oxford Medium and Hard using the revisitop evaluation code
On a validation walk (not the frozen queries) record recall@1 and recall@10 for the shortlist

steps.title: Use location to narrow candidates, with a fallback
steps.learn: The phone knows roughly where you stand, which can cut the candidate list to nearby murals. But GPS is noisy between buildings and missing indoors or when denied, and the browser reports an accuracy radius you should respect rather than ignore.

decision.choice: Pre-filter murals within max(fixed radius, reported accuracy); fall back to all murals if too few or no location
decision.why: A radius scaled by the reported accuracy avoids dropping the right mural when the fix is poor, and the fallback means bad GPS costs speed, not correctness. At neighborhood scale a haversine scan is fine.

alternatives.name: Ignore location
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and robust to GPS errors, but look-alike murals across town compete for every query.

alternatives.name: Location as a soft score
alternatives.tradeoff: Never hard-drops a candidate, but adds a weight to tune and can still mislead with bad fixes.

steps.delegate: Python: haversine_m(a, b); candidates(lat, lon, accuracy_m, min_radius_m, min_count) returns mural ids, falling back to all murals when location is missing or fewer than min_count are in range. Client sends coords.accuracy from the Geolocation API. Tests: no location returns all; large accuracy widens the radius; a mural at the radius edge is included.
verify: On the validation walk, count queries where the true mural was filtered out; target zero
Record median shortlist size with and without the geo filter

steps.title: Re-rank the shortlist with local features and a homography
steps.learn: Most murals are on flat walls, so the same mural seen from two angles is related by a homography. Matching local keypoints and fitting a homography with RANSAC counts inliers that agree geometrically, which separates the same wall from a merely similar painting.

decision.choice: SIFT keypoints, Lowe ratio test, cv.findHomography with RANSAC; rank shortlist by inlier count
decision.why: SIFT ships in opencv-python as cv.SIFT_create, and the OpenCV tutorial shows the same SIFT, ratio test and RANSAC homography steps (with FLANN). A planar model fits walls well, and the inlier count is an interpretable score for accepting a match.

alternatives.name: ALIKED or DISK with LightGlue
alternatives.tradeoff: Learned matching that may hold up better at night and steep angles, but needs a GPU to be fast; SuperPoint weights carry a restrictive license.

alternatives.name: No verification, global score only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but cannot tell two murals of a similar style or palette apart.

steps.delegate: Python with opencv-python. verify(query, gallery_img) returns inlier count and homography using cv.SIFT_create, BFMatcher knnMatch k=2, ratio test, cv.findHomography(..., cv.RANSAC, 5.0). Cache gallery keypoints on disk. rerank(query, shortlist) scores each mural by its best view. Tests: an image vs a rotated, scaled copy of itself yields many inliers; two unrelated images yield few.
verify: On the validation walk, compare recall@1 before and after re-ranking
Record median query latency for shortlist plus verification on your machine

steps.title: Reject non-murals and flag new murals
steps.learn: Retrieval always returns a best match, even for a photo of a parked car. The app needs an 'unknown' answer, and a new or repainted wall should become a candidate mural instead of being forced onto an old one. Thresholds must be tuned on validation data, never on the frozen queries.

decision.choice: Accept only if inliers clear a floor and beat the runner-up mural by a margin; else 'unknown' or 'new mural?' queue
decision.why: A floor rejects off-topic photos; a margin rejects ambiguous ones between two murals. Unknowns near no gallery mural go to a review queue, so the map grows without letting one user's photo silently create a mural.

alternatives.name: Global similarity threshold only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but cosine scores shift with lighting, so one threshold rarely works day and night.

alternatives.name: Always accept top-1
alternatives.tradeoff: More collections, but wrong awards erode trust in a collecting game.

steps.delegate: Python: decide(scores) returns mural_id, 'unknown' or 'new_candidate' using inlier floor and margin. tune.py grid-searches both on a labeled validation CSV (path, mural_id or 'none') and prints precision of accepted matches and coverage. Tests: equal top-2 scores return unknown; empty shortlist returns unknown.
verify: Add 50 non-mural street photos to validation and record false accepts per 100
Record chosen floor and margin and the precision and coverage they give on validation

steps.title: Make recognition hold up at night
steps.learn: Night photos have noise, motion blur, low contrast and colored streetlight, which cut keypoints and shift global features. You can change the input (contrast normalization), the gallery (add night views) or the matcher. Measure each on validation night shots, one change at a time.

decision.choice: Add 1 to 2 night reference photos per mural, and test CLAHE on the luminance channel before matching
decision.why: Night views in the gallery attack the domain gap directly and cost one evening walk. CLAHE (cv.createCLAHE) is a cheap, local contrast boost that may recover keypoints in dark areas; keep it only if validation shows it helps.

alternatives.name: Learned matcher (LightGlue)
alternatives.tradeoff: May be more robust to lighting changes, but adds GPU cost and a new dependency to the request path.

alternatives.name: Day-only gallery
alternatives.tradeoff: Least collection work, but night queries depend entirely on the features generalizing.

steps.delegate: Python, OpenCV. Add a preprocess option: convert to LAB, apply cv.createCLAHE to L, convert back. Add a 'condition' field (day/night) to gallery images. Ablation script runs validation night queries under: baseline, +CLAHE, +night gallery, both. Tests: CLAHE preserves image shape and dtype; condition field is required.
verify: Report validation night top-1 for all four ablation settings
Record how many murals were too dark to photograph safely and exclude them explicitly

steps.title: Build the collectible map and per-user collection
steps.learn: The product is a map of murals that fill in as you photograph them. The backend runs the pipeline (geo filter, shortlist, verify, decide), records collections idempotently, and serves mural pins. Map tiles have usage rules of their own.

decision.choice: FastAPI backend with SQLite, Leaflet front end, OSM tiles with attribution within the tile usage policy
decision.why: One process and one file database are enough for a neighborhood. Leaflet is a small, standard map library. The OSM tile policy forbids bulk prefetching and requires attribution, so no 'download area offline' feature.

alternatives.name: Self-hosted tiles
alternatives.tradeoff: Allows offline maps and heavy use, but you must build and host the tile data.

alternatives.name: Commercial map SDK
alternatives.tradeoff: Polished and supports offline, but needs keys, quotas and possible cost.

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI + SQLite. Endpoints: POST /recognize (image, lat, lon, accuracy, idempotency key) returns {mural_id|unknown|new_candidate, score}; GET /murals; GET /collection/{user}. Static Leaflet page shows collected vs uncollected pins with OSM attribution. Tests: same idempotency key yields one collection; unknown never adds a collection.
verify: Collect 5 murals end to end on your phone and see pins fill in
Confirm map attribution is visible and no tile prefetching happens

steps.title: Test it outside: every mural, by day and at night
steps.learn: Now run the frozen query set: photos from the second walk, at new angles, by day and at night. Score them once with the final settings. Log every decision with scores so failures can be inspected rather than guessed.
verify: Report day top-1 and night top-1 on the frozen queries, with counts
Report false accepts per 100 non-mural photos and the share of 'unknown' answers
Inspect every night failure and tag a cause (blur, glare, occlusion, repainted)
Record p50 and p95 recognition latency on the server

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example why some murals fail at night), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives day, night, false-accept and latency numbers, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with example images
Part 4 lists assumptions (one neighborhood, one phone, one season) and limits

projects.title: Anonymous queue estimator
projects.problem: Is the dining hall or cafe line long right now?
projects.concepts: On-device people counting with no faces stored, time-series forecasting
projects.tryIt: Count a line at set times for two weeks; predict tomorrow's wait
projects.question: Can an on-device counter that keeps only counts, never images or faces, predict tomorrow's dining hall wait better than a seasonal naive baseline?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the held-out days
steps.learn: Two problems are stacked: counting people in line now, and forecasting the wait at set times tomorrow. Success from the try-it: count the line at set times for two weeks, predict tomorrow's wait, and compare against stopwatch waits. The forecast must beat a simple seasonal naive baseline to be worth it.

decision.choice: Fixed time slots over 14 days; the last 4 days frozen as test; counter checked on MOT17 training sequences
decision.why: Freezing test days by date before collecting prevents tuning on them. MOT17 training sequences have public person boxes, so counter accuracy can be measured without filming anyone. Stopwatch waits give ground truth the system does not grade itself.

alternatives.name: Random held-out slots
alternatives.tradeoff: More test points, but leaks future information into training and overstates forecast skill.

alternatives.name: Skip counter validation
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but count errors and forecast errors become impossible to separate.

verify: Write the one question and metrics: count MAE (people) and wait MAE (minutes) vs seasonal naive
Write the slot schedule and the dates of the 4 frozen test days before collecting anything

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before the camera is mounted
steps.learn: Count people anonymously, on the device, and never store faces or frames. A camera in a dining hall still observes people who did not opt in, so get permission from whoever runs the space, post a clear notice, and design so that even a stolen device holds nothing identifying.

decision.choice: Frames live only in memory; only (timestamp, count) leaves the device; no identities, no tracking IDs stored
decision.why: If images are never written, they cannot leak. Counting does not need identity, so no face recognition and no re-identification, and track IDs (if any) are discarded after each window. Written permission and signage make the deployment legitimate.

alternatives.name: Upload video for server processing
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier debugging and bigger models, but you would be storing and moving footage of people.

alternatives.name: Non-camera sensor (break-beam or manual tally)
alternatives.tradeoff: No images at all, but counts entries rather than line length and is harder to place.

steps.delegate: Write a data contract module in Python: the only persisted record type is {slot_ts, count, n_frames, device_id}. Add a test that scans the output directory and the database after a run and fails if any image, video or array file exists. Add a startup check that the log directory is the only writable path the process uses.
verify: Get written permission from the dining hall and photograph the posted notice (no people in frame)
Run the contract test after a 10-minute run and confirm only count records exist

steps.title: Set up the on-device capture pipeline
steps.learn: A small computer reads the camera, runs a detector a few times per minute, and appends a count. The constraints are heat, power, network outages and clock drift, not peak throughput. Line length changes over minutes, so a low frame rate is enough.

decision.choice: Raspberry Pi 5 with a Pi camera via Picamera2, sampling about one frame every few seconds
decision.why: Picamera2 is the libcamera-based Python library for the Pi camera, and Ultralytics documents running detectors on Pi 4 and 5. Sampling slowly keeps CPU and heat low without missing changes in a queue.

alternatives.name: Old Android phone on a mount
alternatives.tradeoff: Camera, battery and compute in one, but harder to run unattended for two weeks and to lock down.

alternatives.name: Microcontroller camera (ESP32 class)
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and low power, but limited to very small detectors with lower accuracy.

steps.delegate: Python on Raspberry Pi OS. Loop: grab a frame with Picamera2, pass it to count_people(frame) (stub for now), drop the frame, append (utc_ts, count) to a list; every slot window write one row. Use systemd for auto-restart and NTP for time. Tests: with a fake camera, the loop writes one row per window and no frame objects outlive one iteration.
verify: Run 2 hours unattended and record CPU temperature and rows written
Pull power mid-run and confirm the service restarts and resumes logging

steps.title: Pick a person detector that runs on the device
steps.learn: Counting by detection means boxes for each visible person, then a count inside the queue area. Lines are dense and people occlude each other, so recall under overlap matters more than box precision. The model must be small enough for the device.

decision.choice: A small Ultralytics YOLO model exported to NCNN, filtered to the person class
decision.why: Ultralytics documents NCNN as its fastest export on Raspberry Pi, and predict accepts classes=[0] to keep only people. Note its AGPL-3.0 license: fine for a personal project, but commercial use needs their enterprise license.

alternatives.name: MediaPipe Object Detector (EfficientDet-Lite0)
alternatives.tradeoff: Small int8 COCO model with a category allowlist; check its count error on MOT17 before trusting it on dense, occluded lines.

alternatives.name: Density-map crowd counting
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for very dense crowds, but heavier and needs density-annotated training data.

steps.delegate: Python. count_people(frame, roi) with Ultralytics: load the NCNN-exported model, predict with classes=[0] and a conf threshold, count boxes whose bottom-center lies inside the queue polygon (cv.pointPolygonTest). eval_mot17.py compares per-frame counts vs MOT17 train gt on sampled frames, keeping only pedestrian rows with the consider flag set and logging visibility. Tests: empty frame returns 0; a box outside the polygon is not counted.
verify: Report count MAE on sampled MOT17 training frames at 2 confidence thresholds
Record inference time per frame on the Pi

steps.title: Mount the camera, define the queue area, check against hand counts
steps.learn: MOT17 is not your dining hall. Camera height, angle and lighting decide occlusion, and the queue polygon decides who counts as waiting. Hand counts at a few slots give the real error, and a robust summary over several frames smooths out single-frame misses.

decision.choice: Elevated view along the line; slot count = median of per-frame counts in the slot window
decision.why: An elevated angle reduces people hiding behind each other. A median ignores momentary misses or people walking through the frame without joining the line.

alternatives.name: Mean of per-frame counts
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses every frame, but pulled by brief spikes from passers-by.

alternatives.name: Line-crossing counts (in minus out)
alternatives.tradeoff: Measures flow directly, but drift accumulates whenever one crossing is missed.

steps.delegate: Python. Add a config file for the queue polygon set once on the device from a live preview (not saved). Add summarize(counts) returning median, min, max, n_frames per slot. Add a CLI to log hand counts by slot to a separate CSV. Tests: median ignores a single outlier frame; slots with too few frames are flagged.
verify: Hand-count 20 slots across 3 days and record count MAE and bias of the median
Check that people at the counter or walking past are excluded by the polygon

steps.title: Turn a line count into a wait time
steps.learn: People care about minutes, not heads. If the line moves at roughly mu people per minute, joining behind N people means a wait near N divided by mu. Little's law (L = lambda W) is the long-run average version. Service rate changes with staffing and menu, so measure it.

decision.choice: wait = count / service rate per slot, with service rate estimated from stopwatch timings
decision.why: It is simple, explainable, and separates counting error from throughput changes. Stopwatch waits (join to served) are independent ground truth, so the system does not grade itself.

alternatives.name: Regress stopwatch waits on counts
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures nonlinear effects, but needs many timed waits and may overfit two weeks.

alternatives.name: Forecast counts only
alternatives.tradeoff: No timing work, but does not answer the question a student actually asks.

steps.delegate: Python. Log stopwatch timings (slot, join time, served time) to a CSV. estimate_service_rate(timings, counts) gives people per minute per slot type (rush vs quiet). wait_from_count(count, slot) returns minutes. Tests: zero count returns zero wait; known synthetic inputs give the expected rate.
verify: Time at least 15 waits across different slots and record each slot's service rate
Fit the service rate on half the timed waits, then report wait MAE of count/rate on the other half only

steps.title: Start the two-week log and handle gaps honestly
steps.learn: The two-week collection starts now. Real logs have gaps: power cuts, camera covered, holidays, the hall closed. A missing slot is not a zero, and filling it silently will bias both training and evaluation.

decision.choice: SQLite in WAL mode on the device, explicit missing rows, a daily heartbeat and a notes table for closures or events
decision.why: SQLite needs no server and WAL mode lets a reader copy data while the logger writes. Marking gaps and noting closures keeps the forecast honest and lets you exclude abnormal days by rule, not by eye.

alternatives.name: Append to a CSV
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but a crash mid-write can leave a broken last line and concurrent reads are awkward.

alternatives.name: Push to a cloud time-series database
alternatives.tradeoff: Remote dashboards, but depends on network and puts the data off device.

steps.delegate: Python sqlite3. Tables: counts(slot_ts, count, n_frames, status in {'ok','missing','low_frames'}), notes(date, text). Enable WAL mode. A job fills expected slots with 'missing' if no row arrived. A daily heartbeat row proves liveness. Tests: missing slots are written as missing, not zero; restarting does not duplicate rows (unique slot_ts).
verify: After day 3 report the share of slots that are ok, missing or low_frames
Confirm frozen test days are stored but not loaded by any training code

steps.title: Build the baselines the forecast must beat
steps.learn: With 10 training days you only see each weekday once or twice, so fancy models have little to learn from. The seasonal naive forecast (same slot, previous day or same weekday last week) and a per-slot average are the bar any model must clear.

decision.choice: Seasonal naive (same slot yesterday), same slot last week, and per-slot mean on training days
decision.why: These are standard simple methods from FPP3 and cost nothing. If a model cannot beat 'same as yesterday', its extra complexity is not justified. Scale errors against the naive forecast so results are comparable across slots.

alternatives.name: Skip baselines
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves an hour, but you cannot tell whether a model learned anything.

alternatives.name: Only the overall mean
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy, but ignores the daily lunch and dinner rush and sets a bar that is too low.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas. Functions: naive_yesterday, naive_last_week, slot_mean that predict wait per slot for a target date using only data before it. Rolling-origin evaluation over training days only. Report MAE and an error scaled by the yesterday baseline. Tests: no function reads any row at or after the target date.
verify: Report wait MAE of each baseline on rolling origins within the first 10 days
Confirm no baseline reads the frozen test days

steps.title: Fit a small forecast model with calendar features
steps.learn: The wait at a slot depends on time of day, weekday vs weekend, and events (exams, a popular menu). With little data, a model with few parameters and explicit calendar features usually beats one that tries to learn weekly seasonality from two examples.

decision.choice: Per-slot model: slot mean adjusted by a weekday/weekend factor and yesterday's deviation, fit on training days
decision.why: It has a handful of parameters, is easy to explain, and uses the two signals two weeks can support. Compare against baselines with the same rolling origins before touching test days.

alternatives.name: statsforecast AutoETS or MSTL
alternatives.tradeoff: Principled seasonal models, but need more cycles than two weeks provide to estimate weekly patterns well.

alternatives.name: Gradient boosting on calendar features
alternatives.tradeoff: Flexible with event flags, but easy to overfit with a few hundred rows.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas, NumPy. fit(train_df) learns slot means, weekday/weekend factors and a shrinkage weight on yesterday's deviation; predict(date) returns wait per slot. Same rolling-origin harness as the baselines. Tests: predictions use only past data; a constant series gives constant forecasts.
verify: Report rolling-origin wait MAE vs the best baseline on the first 10 days
Write down the final model choice before opening the frozen test days

steps.title: Test it outside: predict tomorrow, check with a stopwatch
steps.learn: On each of the 4 frozen test days, publish the forecast the evening before, then compare against the logged counts and stopwatch waits taken at set slots. This is the try-it: count for two weeks, predict tomorrow's wait.
verify: Report wait MAE for the model and each baseline on the 4 test days
Report count MAE against hand counts taken on test days
List slots where the forecast missed by the most and the cause (event, closure, menu)
Rerun the privacy contract test on the device and confirm only counts exist

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example a slot where yesterday beat the model), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives count MAE, wait MAE vs baselines and Pi inference time, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (one hall, two weeks, one camera) and what it does not prove

projects.title: Real-world "dex" of anything
projects.problem: Turn everyday walks into collecting
projects.concepts: CLIP zero-shot sorting into collectible sets; rarity = how few similar embeddings exist in the database
projects.tryIt: Play with 10 friends for a week; track what gets collected
projects.question: Can CLIP embeddings turn everyday walk photos into a collectible dex where sets are assigned by text prompts and rarity reflects how few similar finds exist?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: The game is two ML calls wrapped in a product: zero-shot set assignment (image vs text prompts) and rarity (how crowded the embedding neighborhood is). Success comes from the try-it: 10 friends play for a week, and you track what gets collected, how often players accept the set, and duplicates.

decision.choice: Offline check on COCO 2017 val images mapped to your sets, then a 10-friend, 7-day live test
decision.why: COCO gives labeled everyday objects for free, so you can measure set-assignment accuracy before anyone plays. The live week then measures what COCO cannot: real walk photos, duplicates, rarity drift and cheating.

alternatives.name: Live test only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest to start, but you cannot tell model errors from bad set design, and you burn your friends' patience debugging thresholds.

alternatives.name: Hand-label 300 of your own walk photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use and worth doing later, but slower to build and biased toward what you happen to photograph.

verify: Write the one question and 3 metrics: set acceptance rate, duplicates missed per 100 captures, captures per player per day
Pick 10 to 20 sets and map at least 5 of them to COCO categories for the offline check

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Collect things, places, plants and animals, never people. Walk photos will include passers-by, faces, house numbers and precise home locations. Also, a game that rewards rare finds can push people onto private property or toward touching wild plants and animals.

decision.choice: On-device face check rejects or blurs before upload; no 'person' sets; coarsen stored location; safety rules in-app
decision.why: Running a face detector (for example MediaPipe Face Detector) on the phone means faces never reach the server, so they are never stored. Coarse location still supports dedup without logging where each player lives.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach your server even if only briefly.

alternatives.name: No face handling
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but you would store bystanders' faces without consent.

steps.delegate: Add an on-device step using MediaPipe Face Detector with the BlazeFace full-range model (rear-camera photos; short-range targets selfie distance): if any face is detected, block the capture with a message, or blur boxes before upload. Server: round lat and lon to about 100 m precision before storing, strip EXIF. Tests: an image with a face never reaches the upload endpoint; stored rows contain no full-precision coordinates.
verify: Upload 10 photos containing people and confirm none are stored with a visible face
Confirm no set prompt targets people, and the app says not to enter private land or handle wildlife

steps.title: Define collectible sets as text prompts for zero-shot sorting
steps.learn: CLIP maps images and text into one space, so a set like 'mailboxes' is just the embedding of prompts such as 'a photo of a mailbox.'. Averaging several templates per set (prompt ensembling, as in the CLIP repo notebook) makes the set vector less sensitive to wording.

decision.choice: open_clip ViT-B-32 (laion2b_s34b_b79k), 3 to 5 prompt templates per set, averaged and L2-normalized
decision.why: No labeled data is needed, so you can add a new set (say 'street murals') by writing text. ViT-B-32 is small enough to run on a cheap server or laptop for 10 players, and open_clip lists many alternative checkpoints if accuracy is too low.

alternatives.name: Fine-tuned image classifier
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher accuracy on fixed sets, but needs labeled photos per set and retraining every time you add a set.

alternatives.name: VLM caption, then map text to sets
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles odd objects and explains itself, but is slower and costlier per capture and its free text still needs mapping.

alternatives.name: Larger CLIP model (ViT-L)
alternatives.tradeoff: Usually better zero-shot accuracy, but more memory and latency per capture; worth it only if the offline check shows B-32 is the bottleneck.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, open_clip, torch, Pillow. Write sets.yaml (set_id, display name, 3-5 prompt templates). Implement build_set_matrix(sets) returning normalized averaged text embeddings, and embed_image(path) returning a normalized vector. Add a CLI that ranks sets for an image. Tests: vectors have unit norm, set order is stable, a known COCO image of a dog ranks a 'dogs' set first.
verify: Run the CLI on 20 COCO val images from mapped categories and record top-1 accuracy
Compare one template vs averaged templates on the same 20 images and note the difference

steps.title: Add an 'unsorted' bucket with a similarity and margin threshold
steps.learn: Zero-shot always returns some top set, even for a photo of your shoe. Real walks are mostly things outside your sets, so the system must be able to say 'not a collectible'. Cosine similarity values are not calibrated probabilities, so thresholds must be tuned on data, not guessed.

decision.choice: Assign only if top-1 similarity is above a floor AND beats top-2 by a margin; otherwise 'unsorted'
decision.why: A floor rejects off-topic photos and a margin rejects photos that sit between two sets (fire hydrant vs bollard). Both are tuned on the COCO check plus a few dozen of your own off-topic photos, which keeps wrong awards rare, the failure players notice most.

alternatives.name: Softmax over sets with a probability cutoff
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to explain, but softmax over a small closed set can be confident on photos that match no set at all.

alternatives.name: Always assign top-1
