alternatives.tradeoff: Maximizes collecting, but wrong sets erode trust fast in a game about getting the right thing.

alternatives.name: Add explicit negative prompts
alternatives.tradeoff: A 'background' or 'random object' set can absorb junk, but its behavior depends heavily on the wording you pick.

steps.delegate: Extend the Python module: assign(image_vec, set_matrix, floor, margin) returns set_id or 'unsorted' plus scores. Write tune_thresholds.py that grid-searches floor and margin on a labeled CSV (path, true_set or 'none') and prints precision of awarded sets and coverage. Tests: an all-equal score vector returns 'unsorted'; floor -1 and margin 0 reproduce plain top-1 except exact ties.
verify: Label 50 of your own off-topic walk photos as 'none' and include them in tuning
Pick thresholds and record precision of awarded sets and the fraction left unsorted

steps.title: Store image embeddings for neighbor queries
steps.learn: Rarity and dedup both ask 'which past captures are near this one?'. With 10 players for a week you have thousands of vectors at most, so exact search is cheap; the real design question is keeping vectors, users and captures consistent in one place.

decision.choice: Postgres with pgvector: one captures table holding user, set, location, time and the vector
decision.why: One database means a capture, its vector and its rarity commit together, and SQL filters (same set, same user, last 24 hours) sit next to pgvector's cosine distance operator. Exact scans are fine at this scale; pgvector also offers HNSW if the game grows.

alternatives.name: FAISS in memory (IndexFlatIP)
alternatives.tradeoff: Very fast exact search, but you must persist and rebuild it yourself and keep it in sync with the database.

alternatives.name: NumPy brute force over a saved array
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest code for a prototype, but concurrency, filtering and persistence become your problem.

alternatives.name: Managed vector database
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales and handles indexing, but adds a second system and cost for a dataset that fits in one table.

steps.delegate: Docker Compose with Postgres plus the pgvector extension. Python with psycopg and pgvector. Schema: users, captures(id, user_id, set_id, embedding vector(512), lat, lon, created_at, model_id, phash). Functions: insert_capture, neighbors(vec, set_id, k), count_within(vec, set_id, max_cosine_distance). Tests: neighbors of a stored vector returns itself first; set_id filter excludes other sets.
verify: Insert 1,000 COCO embeddings and time neighbors() and count_within(); record p50 latency
Check that the embedding dimension in the schema matches the model output

steps.title: Compute rarity from nearest-neighbor counts
steps.learn: Rarity is a density estimate: few captures within a radius means rare. With few items, density estimates are very noisy: on day one everything looks legendary, and one player photographing the same street can make a set look common. Decide whether rarity is frozen at capture time or recomputed.

decision.choice: Same-set neighbor count within a cosine radius, over captures plus a seed corpus; quantile tiers, frozen at award
decision.why: A seed corpus (COCO embeddings per set) acts as a prior so early finds are not all legendary. Counting within a radius is easy to explain to players, quantile tiers keep the tier mix stable as data grows, and freezing avoids taking rewards away.

alternatives.name: Distance to the k-th nearest neighbor
alternatives.tradeoff: No radius to tune and adapts to scale, but very noisy when a set has fewer than k items.

alternatives.name: Kernel density estimate
alternatives.tradeoff: Smoother scores (sklearn KernelDensity), but the bandwidth choice drives everything and is hard to set with little data.

alternatives.name: Rarity by set frequency only
alternatives.tradeoff: Stable and simple, but every mailbox gets the same rarity, ignoring that a blue antique one is unusual.

steps.delegate: Python module rarity.py: rarity_score(vec, set_id) using count_within over captures and seed vectors with per-source weights; tiers from quantiles recomputed nightly and stored in a tiers table. Store awarded tier on the capture row. Tests: with an empty set the seed corpus gives a non-legendary tier for a typical image; adding 20 near-identical vectors lowers the next one's tier.
verify: Simulate a week: replay COCO images in random order and plot tier counts per day
Show 5 'legendary' and 5 'common' results to a friend and record whether they agree

steps.title: Stop the same object being collected twice
steps.learn: Two kinds of duplicate: the same photo re-uploaded (pixel-level near duplicate) and the same physical object shot again from another angle. Perceptual hashes catch the first; embeddings plus place and time catch the second. Two different but identical-looking mailboxes are the hard case.

decision.choice: Per player: pHash Hamming check, then same set + high CLIP similarity + within a small distance of a past capture
decision.why: pHash (imagehash, Hamming distance via hash subtraction) is cheap and robust to resizing and re-encoding, so it catches re-uploads. Requiring location proximity before calling a CLIP match a duplicate avoids blocking two different mailboxes in different streets, which similarity alone cannot tell apart.

alternatives.name: pHash only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but misses the same object photographed from a new angle or distance.

alternatives.name: CLIP similarity only
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches new angles, but merges distinct look-alike objects, blocking honest captures.

alternatives.name: Keypoint matching (ORB or SIFT)
alternatives.tradeoff: Better at 'same physical instance', but heavier per pair and fragile across lighting and season.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, Pillow. Implement is_duplicate(user_id, image, vec, lat, lon) returning (bool, reason). Steps: phash Hamming distance against the player's captures; then pgvector query for same set within a cosine threshold and haversine distance under N meters. Tests: identical file is duplicate; a resized copy is duplicate; same object 2 km away is not.
verify: Photograph 5 objects twice from different angles and confirm all 5 second shots are flagged
Photograph 2 look-alike objects in different places and confirm neither is flagged

steps.title: Build a simple multi-user backend for captures and dexes
steps.learn: The backend owns identity, the capture pipeline (embed, assign, dedup, rarity, store) and each player's dex. For 10 friends the main risks are not scale but correctness: two uploads racing, a slow model call blocking requests, and partial writes.

decision.choice: FastAPI service with server-side embedding, one model loaded at startup, Postgres transaction per capture
decision.why: Server-side embedding keeps one model version for everyone so rarity is comparable across players. Postgres's default READ COMMITTED lets two concurrent transactions both pass the dedup check, so take a per-user advisory lock before checking. 10 players do not need queues; load the model once.

alternatives.name: On-device embedding
alternatives.tradeoff: Better privacy and offline play, but needs a mobile-sized model and every client must run the same version.

alternatives.name: Job queue with workers
alternatives.tradeoff: Smooths bursts and retries, but adds moving parts you do not need at 10 users.

alternatives.name: Backend-as-a-service (auth plus database)
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster auth and storage, but you still need a server process to run the model.

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI app. Endpoints: POST /captures (multipart image plus lat, lon, nonce) returns {set, tier, duplicate, reason}; GET /dex/{user_id}; GET /leaderboard. Token auth per player. Load open_clip once at startup. In one transaction, take pg_advisory_xact_lock(user_id), then run the dedup check and insert. Tests with pytest and httpx: two concurrent identical uploads yield one award; unsorted images are stored but not awarded.
verify: Upload 50 photos from two phones at once and confirm no double awards
Record p50 and p95 upload-to-result latency on your server

steps.title: Add anti-cheat basics
steps.learn: Players will photograph screens, upload web images, share photos between accounts and spoof GPS. You cannot stop a determined cheater, so aim to make cheating harder than playing and to detect the cheap tricks.

decision.choice: In-app camera only, server nonce, cross-player pHash, rate limits, and a 'photo of a screen' prompt check
decision.why: A short-lived, single-use nonce blocks replayed requests; camera-only capture is enforced only by your client, so it stops casual gallery uploads but not a modified client. Cross-player pHash catches shared photos. A zero-shot 'photo of a screen' check flags rephotographed images for review, not auto-bans.

alternatives.name: Platform attestation (Play Integrity, App Attest)
alternatives.tradeoff: Proves a genuine app on a genuine device, but requires native apps and store setup that a friends test may not justify.

alternatives.name: Trust the client
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine among close friends, but rarity data gets polluted by any cheating and you cannot tell later.

alternatives.name: Manual moderation of rare finds
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate for the few legendary awards, but does not scale and delays rewards.

steps.delegate: Extend the FastAPI app: GET /nonce issues a signed, 2-minute nonce bound to the user; POST /captures rejects missing, reused or expired nonces. Add per-user rate limit (captures per minute). Add cross-user pHash lookup and a screen-photo score using open_clip prompts; flag, do not reject. Tests: reused nonce is rejected; 11th capture in a minute is throttled; same image from two users is flagged.
verify: Try 3 cheats yourself (screen photo, shared image, replayed request) and record which are caught
Check flagged captures land in a review list, not silently awarded

steps.title: Handle failures and model upgrades without breaking the dex
steps.learn: Embeddings from different models live in different spaces, so mixing them silently breaks rarity and dedup. Thresholds (set floor and margin, dedup cosine, rarity radius, tier quantiles) are model-specific too and must be retuned. Plan for model swaps, failed uploads and retries from day one.

decision.choice: Store model_id with every vector, re-embed everything on upgrade, keep awarded tiers frozen; idempotent upload key
decision.why: Re-embedding a week of photos is cheap at this scale and keeps one consistent space. Freezing awards means an upgrade never takes a prize away. An idempotency key on uploads makes phone retries on bad signal safe.

alternatives.name: Never upgrade the model
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero migration work, but you are stuck with early mistakes in set assignment.

alternatives.name: Keep old and new vectors side by side
alternatives.tradeoff: No downtime during migration, but every query must pick the right space and storage doubles.

steps.delegate: Add model_id to captures and seed vectors; write reembed.py that streams stored images, writes new vectors under the new model_id, then switches an active_model setting. Add Idempotency-Key header handling to POST /captures. Tests: queries never mix model_ids; a retried request with the same key returns the original result without a second insert.
verify: Switch to a second open_clip checkpoint on a copy of the data and confirm queries only use the active model_id
Kill the server mid-upload and confirm the retry produces exactly one capture

steps.title: Test it outside: 10 friends, one week
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation: play with 10 friends for a week and track what gets collected. Log every capture with its scores so you can replay decisions later, and give players a one-tap 'wrong set' button so you get labels for free.
verify: Report captures per player per day and which sets were collected most and least
Report set acceptance rate (1 minus 'wrong set' taps) and the share left unsorted
Audit 50 random captures for missed duplicates and wrong awards
Plot tier counts per day and check rarity did not collapse as data grew

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example why a set was always 'unsorted' or rarity shifted), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives set accuracy, acceptance, duplicate and latency numbers, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (10 friends, one city, one week) and what this does not prove

projects.title: AI scavenger hunt
projects.problem: Hunts take hours to write
projects.concepts: LLM writes clues from local landmarks; photo matching verifies each find
projects.tryIt: Run one on campus or downtown
projects.question: Can an LLM write true, solvable clues from mapped local landmarks, and can photo matching confirm each find without accepting the wrong place?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: The hunt is two systems: clue writing (judged by human solvers, never by the LLM) and find verification (judged on labeled photos). Success comes from the try-it: run one hunt on campus or downtown and measure finish rate, minutes per clue, wrong finds accepted and right finds rejected.

decision.choice: Freeze a verification test split from Revisited Oxford and Paris now; run the live hunt last
decision.why: rOxford5k and rParis6k pair query photos of specific buildings with curated positives (easy, hard) and junk labels, which is exactly 'is this photo of that landmark?'. Freezing a split before any threshold is tuned keeps the false-accept number honest.

alternatives.name: Google Landmarks v2 subset
alternatives.tradeoff: Far more landmark variety (labels mined from Wikimedia), but a large download and noisier labels; good as a second dev set.

alternatives.name: Only your own photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to the real hunt, but small, and you end up tuning and testing on the same pictures.

verify: Write the one question and 4 metrics: finish rate, median minutes per clue, false accepts per 100 wrong photos, false rejects per 100 right photos
Save the frozen test image list with a checksum and note that no step may tune on it

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Players photograph places, never people, but downtown photos will include passers-by. Faces must not reach the server. Track location only at submission time, not continuously. A race can push players into traffic or onto private land, so the route and rules must prevent that.

decision.choice: On-device face detection blurs or blocks before upload; location only at submit; photos deleted after the hunt
decision.why: Running a face detector such as MediaPipe Face Detector on the phone means bystanders' faces are never stored. Location at submit time is all verification needs, and deleting photos after appeals close removes the remaining risk.

alternatives.name: Server-side blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach the server, even if briefly.

alternatives.name: No face handling
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but stores bystanders' faces without consent.

steps.delegate: Client: MediaPipe Face Detector (full-range model for rear-camera photos) before upload; blur detected boxes or block with a message. Server: strip EXIF, store lat and lon only on submissions, delete photo files N days after the hunt. Tests: an image with a face never reaches the upload endpoint unblurred; no location rows exist outside submissions.
verify: Submit 10 photos containing people and confirm none is stored with a visible face
Walk the route and confirm no stop needs crossing a road away from a crossing or entering private land
Confirm the rules screen says to obey local rules and that stops are public places

steps.title: Pull candidate landmarks for the hunt area from OpenStreetMap
steps.learn: A clue is only as good as the place beneath it. OSM tags such as tourism=artwork, tourism=viewpoint and historic=memorial give names and positions, often with wikipedia or wikidata tags. Overpass is a read-only query API over OSM. Keep things visible from public ground and reachable on foot.

decision.choice: One Overpass query over the hunt polygon, cached to GeoJSON, then the organizer shortlists 8 to 12 stops
decision.why: Free, covers any campus or downtown, and carries the tags needed for facts. A single cached query per hunt stays far inside the main instance's stated usage guidance, and the organizer still decides which stops are safe and fun.

alternatives.name: Commercial places API
alternatives.tradeoff: Richer photos and opening hours, but paid and with its own terms on storing results.

alternatives.name: Hand-written stop list
alternatives.tradeoff: Most accurate, but writing it is the hours of work this project is meant to remove.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, requests, shapely. fetch_candidates(polygon_geojson, tag_filters) builds Overpass QL, posts to the public interpreter with a timeout and descriptive User-Agent, caches raw JSON by query hash, and returns a GeoJSON FeatureCollection (osm_id, name, tags, lat, lon; way centroids). Drop unnamed features and points outside the polygon. Tests: cache hit makes no network call; outside points dropped; unnamed dropped.
verify: Run it on your area and record how many candidates each tag filter returns
Open 10 candidates on the map and confirm each exists and is reachable from public ground

steps.title: Gather grounded facts for each stop before any clue is written
steps.learn: Asked about a small local statue, an LLM may invent a sculptor or a date. Retrieve facts first (OSM tags, plus the Wikipedia page summary when the feature has a wikipedia tag) and give the model only those. A stop with no facts beyond its name gets a purely visual clue.

decision.choice: Per-stop fact sheet: OSM tags plus Wikipedia REST page summary, each fact stored with its source URL
decision.why: Small, checkable inputs make every later clue traceable to a source. Storing the source URL lets you and the code audit any clue in seconds, and it keeps the fact sheet fixed while you iterate on prompts.

alternatives.name: Model's own knowledge
alternatives.tradeoff: No setup, but invented facts about minor local landmarks are likely and hard to spot without checking each one.

alternatives.name: Web search per stop
alternatives.tradeoff: Wider coverage, but more noisy pages to read and verify for every stop.

steps.delegate: Python: build_fact_sheet(feature) returns {stop_id, name, facts: [{fact_id, text, source_url}]}. Facts from selected OSM tags; if a wikipedia tag exists, fetch /page/summary/{title} from the Wikipedia REST API with a descriptive User-Agent and keep the extract. Save one JSON per stop. Tests: no wikipedia tag yields only OSM facts; every fact has a source_url; fact_ids are stable across runs.
verify: Check every fact in 5 fact sheets against its source page by hand
Count stops whose sheet has no fact beyond the name

steps.title: Generate clues as structured output that cites fact ids
steps.learn: Ask for JSON matching a schema: clue text, difficulty and the fact ids used. Then plain code, not the model, can check that every cited fact exists and that the clue does not leak the landmark's name. Several candidates per stop let the organizer choose.

decision.choice: Pydantic schema, 3 candidate clues per stop at rising difficulty, each citing fact ids; code drops leaks
decision.why: A schema makes output parseable and testable. Citing fact ids makes grounding checkable by code, and a fuzzy name filter catches the most common giveaway (the clue naming the answer).

alternatives.name: Free-text clues
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to prompt, but nothing can be checked automatically, so every clue needs a full manual read.

alternatives.name: Fill-in templates, no LLM
alternatives.tradeoff: Always true, but repetitive and dull, which is the problem the project is trying to solve.

steps.delegate: Python, pydantic v2, any LLM SDK that supports JSON-schema output. Model Clue{stop_id, text, difficulty 1-3, fact_ids: list[str], hint}. generate_clues(fact_sheet, n=3): validate, retry once on invalid JSON, drop clues citing unknown fact ids or containing the stop name (case-insensitive, fuzzy ratio threshold). Log every drop reason. Tests with a mocked LLM: bad fact id dropped; name leak dropped; valid clue kept.
verify: Generate clues for all stops and record the share dropped by each filter
Read 10 kept clues and count any claim not found in the fact sheet

steps.title: Check clues are solvable with blind human solvers
steps.learn: A true clue can still be unsolvable or trivially easy. Solvability is measured by people who have not seen the answers, not by the model that wrote the clue. A desk test with a map is cheap and catches most bad clues before anyone walks.

decision.choice: 2 friends who do not know the stops solve each clue from a map; replace clues nobody solves
decision.why: Independent humans are the target users, so their solve rate and time are the real metric. Two solvers is enough to catch clues that are impossible or give the answer away, and it costs an evening.

alternatives.name: LLM-as-judge rates solvability
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and cheap as a pre-filter, but the judge sees the facts and shares the writer's blind spots, so it cannot be the metric.

alternatives.name: Skip the playtest
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves an evening, but a single bad clue can strand a team on the day.

steps.delegate: Small FastAPI page or CLI: shows one clue at a time, never the answer; collects a guess (stop name or map pin) and seconds taken; writes CSV (solver, stop_id, clue_id, guess, correct, seconds). Tests: answer fields never appear in the solver response; timing starts when the clue is shown.
verify: Record solve rate and median seconds per clue for both solvers
Replace or rewrite every clue that no solver got, and note how many that was

steps.title: Verify a find with local feature matching and a geometric check
steps.learn: Global embeddings say 'a statue'; the hunt needs 'this statue'. Match local features to the organizer's 3 to 5 reference photos per stop, filter with Lowe's ratio test, then fit geometry with RANSAC, count inliers. Landmarks are 3D, so use a fundamental-matrix fit; use a homography for flat targets like murals.

decision.choice: OpenCV SIFT, ratio test, RANSAC inlier count against the best reference; accept above a threshold
decision.why: SIFT is in OpenCV's main module since the patent expired in 2020, runs on CPU, and matches specific instances. An inlier count is easy to inspect when a team appeals. References shot the same week from likely approach angles reduce lighting and angle misses.

alternatives.name: SuperPoint/DISK + LightGlue
alternatives.tradeoff: More robust to viewpoint and light, but needs PyTorch and ideally a GPU; SuperPoint weights carry a restrictive license, DISK does not.

alternatives.name: Global embedding similarity (CLIP, DINOv2)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and tolerant of lighting, but can accept a similar-looking different landmark; best as a shortlist before matching.

steps.delegate: Python, opencv-python, numpy. Precompute SIFT keypoints and descriptors per reference into .npz keyed by image hash. verify_find(photo, stop_id) returns {accepted, inliers, best_ref}: downscale, cv2.SIFT_create, BFMatcher knnMatch k=2, ratio test (configurable), cv2.findFundamentalMat with FM_RANSAC, or cv2.findHomography with RANSAC if stop.planar. Tests: a reference matched to itself is accepted; a reference of another stop is rejected.
verify: Shoot 3 to 5 references per stop with no people in frame (reframe or wait), delete any with faces, and confirm each stop has 2 or more angles
Run verify_find on 20 dev pairs and record inlier counts and seconds per call on your machine

steps.title: Tune the accept threshold on dev, then score the frozen set once
steps.learn: Two errors matter: false accepts (wrong place passes, unfair to other teams) and false rejects (right place fails, frustrating). Tune on dev pairs only (rOxford/rParis images outside the frozen split, plus your references), then run the frozen split exactly once.

decision.choice: Lowest inlier threshold that keeps dev false accepts under your target; rejects go to an organizer appeal
decision.why: A false accept cannot be undone without the organizer noticing, while a false reject can be appealed in the app. So the threshold favors few false accepts and the appeal path absorbs the extra rejects.

alternatives.name: Equal error rate point
alternatives.tradeoff: Balances both errors, but treats a wrong accept as no worse than a wrong reject, which is not true in a race.

alternatives.name: Per-stop thresholds
alternatives.tradeoff: Can help stops with little texture, but with 3 to 5 references per stop it overfits quickly.

steps.delegate: Python tune.py: build (query, landmark) pairs from the revisitop ground truth (easy and hard as positives, junk excluded, other landmarks as negatives) for the dev split only; sweep inlier thresholds; print a false-accept and false-reject table; write the chosen value to config.yaml. eval_frozen.py logs the config hash with results. Tests: no frozen image ever appears in a dev pair.
verify: Record the chosen threshold with dev false-accept and false-reject rates
Run the frozen split once and record both rates with the machine and command

steps.title: Add a location check and in-app capture
steps.learn: Photo matching alone can be fooled by a photo of a screen showing the landmark. Combine it with in-app camera capture and a GPS check that accounts for reported accuracy. GPS can be spoofed: Android exposes Location.isMock (API 31) and iOS exposes CLLocationSourceInformation (iOS 15). These are signals, not proof.

decision.choice: Accept only if the image passes AND distance to the stop minus reported accuracy is inside the radius
decision.why: Two independent checks make cheating cost more than walking. Using reported accuracy avoids rejecting honest players in urban canyons, and routing mock-location flags to the organizer avoids silently punishing devices that report them for innocent reasons.

alternatives.name: GPS check only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and fast, but drops the photo task and spoofing apps defeat it.

alternatives.name: Photo check only
alternatives.tradeoff: Works with poor GPS, but a screen photo of a web image may pass the matcher.

steps.delegate: Extend the verify endpoint to take lat, lon, accuracy_m and is_mock. Compute haversine distance to the stop; reject if accuracy_m exceeds a max; send is_mock to review; store each decision with reasons. Client uses the in-app camera only, no gallery picker. Tests: a point just outside the radius is rejected; huge accuracy is rejected; is_mock goes to review; reasons are stored.
verify: Stand at 3 stops and record reported distance and accuracy for each
Photograph a screen showing one stop and record whether the full check rejects it

steps.title: Run the hunt: teams, progress, hints and appeals
steps.learn: Downtown signal is weak and verification is slower than a page load. Make submissions idempotent so a retry never double-counts, run verification in the background so the app stays responsive, and give the organizer an appeal queue for rejects.

decision.choice: FastAPI + SQLite in WAL mode, client-generated submission ids, background verify worker, organizer queue
decision.why: One process and one file is enough for a few teams and easy to back up. WAL lets readers continue while the worker writes. Client-generated ids make retries over a flaky connection safe.

alternatives.name: Hosted backend-as-a-service
alternatives.tradeoff: Less server code and built-in auth, but the Python verifier still needs a server somewhere.

alternatives.name: Spreadsheet plus group chat
alternatives.tradeoff: No code, but the organizer verifies every photo by hand, which does not scale past one or two teams.

steps.delegate: FastAPI, SQLite (WAL), tables hunts, teams, stops, clues, submissions(id uuid from client, team_id, stop_id, status, reasons). POST /submissions stores status pending, idempotent on id; a worker runs verify_find plus the location check and on startup re-queues every pending row. GET /teams/{id}/progress; hints unlock after a set time with a point cost; organizer approves or denies. Tests: repeated id returns one result; pending rows resume after restart; teams progress independently.
verify: Kill the server during a verification and confirm the submission is still processed after restart
Submit the same photo twice with the same id and confirm it counts once

steps.title: Test it outside: one hunt on campus or downtown
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation. Log every submission with inliers, distance, accuracy and decision so you can replay them. Organizer appeal outcomes give you ground truth for verification errors in the field.
verify: Report finish rate and median minutes per clue across teams
Report field false rejects (appeals upheld) and any false accepts found by reviewing all accepted photos
Report clues teams called unfair, and how many hints each stop needed

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example why a stop kept failing the matcher), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives frozen-set and field accept and reject rates, clue solve rates and latency, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (one area, few teams, one day) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Photo territory game
projects.problem: Claim city blocks by photographing them, team vs team
projects.concepts: Anti-cheat with image dedup and location checks; a low-latency game server
projects.tryIt: Play a weekend match across your neighborhood
projects.question: Can image dedup and location checks stop most cheating in a team photo territory game while claims still reach every player quickly?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: Two goals pull against each other: thorough anti-cheat checks and fast claims. Success comes from the try-it, a weekend match across your neighborhood: staged cheat attempts caught, honest claims wrongly blocked, and claim-to-broadcast latency at p50 and p95.

decision.choice: Freeze a DISC21 subset plus a written list of staged cheats now; play the weekend match last
decision.why: DISC21 (the Image Similarity Challenge 2021 data) pairs queries with edited copies of reference images and many distractors, which is the reuse-a-photo cheat. A frozen subset and a fixed cheat script keep the anti-cheat numbers honest.

alternatives.name: Augment your own photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to generate and on-topic, but covers only the edits you thought of.

alternatives.name: Only the live match
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic, but cheats are rare and unlabeled, so you cannot measure catch rate.

verify: Write the question and 3 metrics: cheats caught per staged attempt, honest claims blocked per 100, claim-to-broadcast p50 and p95
Save the frozen DISC21 file list with a checksum and the staged cheat list (re-upload, crop, screenshot, spoofed GPS)

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Players photograph streets and buildings, never people, but faces and homes will appear. Live player positions are sensitive: broadcast cell ownership, never where players are. A race for territory can pull players into traffic or onto private land, so rules and the map must prevent that.

decision.choice: On-device face blur before upload, no player positions broadcast, photos deleted after the match
decision.why: Running a face detector such as MediaPipe Face Detector on the phone means bystanders' faces never reach the server. Only cell ownership needs to be shared, and deleting photos after challenges close limits what is kept.

alternatives.name: Server-side blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach your server, even if briefly.

alternatives.name: Show teammates' live positions
alternatives.tradeoff: Fun for coordination, but it publishes where people are; limit to own team if added at all.

steps.delegate: Client: MediaPipe Face Detector (full-range model for rear-camera photos); blur boxes before upload. Server: strip EXIF; never include lat or lon in broadcasts; delete photos N days after the match; exclude cells over major roads and private land from the play area. Speed check also blocks claims from vehicles. Tests: no broadcast payload contains coordinates; a photo with a face is stored blurred.
verify: Inspect 20 broadcast messages and confirm none contain player coordinates
Upload 10 photos containing people and confirm none is stored with a visible face
Review the cell map and confirm excluded zones cover busy roads and private property

steps.title: Divide the neighborhood into claimable cells and set the rules
steps.learn: Territory needs discrete cells that a GPS point maps to quickly. H3 gives hexagonal cells at fixed resolutions; the H3 resolution table lists average areas (res 9 near 0.1 square km, res 10 near 0.015). Rules decide the game: claim, contest, cooldown and adjacency bonus.

decision.choice: H3 cells at a resolution sized to your blocks; a cell flips only after a cooldown since its last claim
decision.why: Every hexagon has six equidistant neighbors, so adjacency rules are simple, and point-to-cell lookup is one function call. A cooldown stops two teams flipping one cell back and forth every few seconds.

alternatives.name: OSM street-bounded blocks
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches 'city blocks' exactly, but building polygons from streets is messy and block sizes vary a lot.

alternatives.name: Square lat/lon grid
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to code, but diagonal neighbors are farther than edge neighbors and cell area shrinks away from the equator.

steps.delegate: Python, h3 v4, shapely. cells_for_area(polygon, res) via h3.h3shape_to_cells_experimental(LatLngPoly, res, contain='overlap') so edge points are covered; cell_for_point uses latlng_to_cell; neighbors via grid_disk(h, 1); export GeoJSON with cell_to_boundary. Rules module: claim(team, cell, t) with cooldown and scoring. Tests: points sampled in the polygon, edges included, map to game cells; grid_disk(h,1) on a hexagon returns 7 cells; claim in cooldown refused.
verify: Draw the cells over your neighborhood and confirm a cell is roughly one block
Count cells and estimate whether 2 teams can contest most of them in one weekend

steps.title: Check claim locations: in-cell, accuracy, speed and mock flags
steps.learn: GPS spoofing is the cheapest cheat. Combine checks: the fix must sit inside the cell after allowing for reported accuracy, the player cannot move between consecutive fixes faster than a walking or cycling limit, and mock flags (Android Location.isMock, API 31; iOS CLLocationSourceInformation, iOS 15) raise suspicion.

decision.choice: Server-side checks on every claim; failures block the claim, softer signals go to a referee queue
decision.why: The server is the only place a modified client cannot skip. Hard failures (outside the cell) are clear, while mock flags and odd speeds can have innocent causes, so a human looks before a team loses anything.

alternatives.name: Device attestation (Play Integrity)
alternatives.tradeoff: Raises the cost of a modified app, but says nothing about whether the GPS fix is real and adds setup.

alternatives.name: Trust the client
alternatives.tradeoff: No work, but one spoofing app lets a player claim the whole map from a couch.

steps.delegate: Python module location_checks.py: check(claim, history) returns {ok, hard_fail_reasons, soft_flags}. Inside-cell via latlng_to_cell with an accuracy margin; reject if accuracy_m is above a max; speed between consecutive fixes from haversine distance and server timestamps; soft flag on is_mock. Tests: an outside point fails; a jump of 5 km in 1 minute is flagged; is_mock is a soft flag, not a block.
verify: Walk 10 cells and record reported accuracy and whether any honest claim failed
Spoof GPS on a test phone and record which checks fired

steps.title: Reject reused and edited copies of earlier photos
steps.learn: The easiest image cheat is reusing a teammate's photo, maybe cropped. Perceptual hashes catch re-encodes and resizes cheaply; copy-detection descriptors such as SSCD (trained for DISC21) also catch crops and heavier edits. Semantic embeddings are the wrong tool: two honest photos of similar streets look alike.

decision.choice: pHash first pass, then SSCD descriptor search over all photos in the match with a tuned threshold
decision.why: pHash is tiny and fast, so most checks end there. SSCD targets copy detection, so it flags edited copies while leaving different photos of the same kind of street alone. A few thousand match photos fit in an exact in-memory search.

alternatives.name: pHash only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and tiny, but misses crops and heavy edits of the kind DISC21 contains.

alternatives.name: CLIP embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong semantic similarity, but flags honest photos of look-alike streets because it matches content, not copies.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, torch, SSCD TorchScript model (sscd_disc_mixup). On each claim store phash and the normalized descriptor. is_copy(img) checks phash Hamming distance, then cosine over stored descriptors (numpy exact search). tune_dedup.py sweeps the cosine threshold on a DISC21 dev subset; eval runs the frozen subset once. Tests: resized, cropped and re-encoded copies are flagged; two different photos of one street are not.
verify: Record dev precision and recall at the chosen threshold, then frozen-set results once
Record milliseconds per is_copy call on your server with 5,000 stored photos

steps.title: Require fresh in-app captures and flag odd claim patterns
steps.learn: Dedup cannot catch a first-time image from the web or an old photo from someone's gallery. Raise the cost: capture only through the in-app camera, bind each capture to a short-lived server token, and look for patterns no walking player produces, such as bursts of claims or claims far apart in a short time.

decision.choice: In-app capture with a short-lived server token, opponents can challenge any claim, a referee decides
decision.why: The token proves the photo was taken during the match window. Opponents have the strongest incentive to spot a fake, and a referee keeps the decision with a human instead of an automatic rule that could punish honest players.

alternatives.name: VLM scene check per photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Can reject screenshots or indoor shots, but cannot tell which street it is and adds cost and latency per claim.

alternatives.name: Reference photos for every cell
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong evidence via feature matching, but someone must photograph every cell before the match.

steps.delegate: Server issues capture tokens (random, signed, short TTL) over the socket; claims must carry a valid unused token. Challenge endpoint: an opponent marks a claim, it goes to a referee queue with photo, location trail and dedup scores. Rule-based flags: claims per minute above a limit, speed flags from location checks. Tests: expired or reused token rejected; challenged claim appears in the queue with its evidence.
verify: Try to claim with an old gallery photo and record what blocks it
Run the staged cheat list so far and record which cheats each check caught

steps.title: Run an authoritative real-time game server
steps.learn: With an authoritative server, clients only send intents ('claim cell X') and the server decides and broadcasts the result, which is what keeps cheaters from writing their own state. WebSockets give a persistent two-way channel, so ownership changes are pushed instead of polled.

decision.choice: One asyncio process (FastAPI WebSockets) holding match state in memory, append-only claim log in SQLite
decision.why: A weekend match has a few dozen players, so one process is enough and keeps ordering simple: claims are applied in the order the server receives them. The log lets you rebuild state after a crash and replay the match for the write-up.

alternatives.name: Go or Node server
alternatives.tradeoff: Similar design with more headroom, but a second language next to the Python image checks.

alternatives.name: HTTP polling
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest to build, but latency is bounded by the poll interval and idle phones keep sending requests.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, FastAPI WebSockets, SQLite. Messages as JSON with a type field: claim, claim_result, cell_update, snapshot. Server keeps cells and scores in memory, appends every accepted event to a log table, and on startup rebuilds state from the log. Per-match broadcast set of sockets. Tests: two clients claiming the same cell get one winner; state rebuilt from log equals live state.
verify: Connect 2 phones and confirm a claim on one appears on the other
Restart the server mid-match and confirm the map comes back identical

steps.title: Keep claims fast with provisional state and async checks
steps.learn: Image checks are slower than updating a map. If every claim waits for dedup, the slowest check sets the latency. Instead, broadcast a claim as pending at once, run checks in the background, then confirm or revoke. Scores count only confirmed claims.

decision.choice: Pending claim broadcast immediately; location checks inline, image checks async; confirm or revoke
decision.why: Location checks are cheap and stop most spoofing before anything is shown. Image checks run off the event loop so one slow photo does not delay other players, and pending cells are visibly marked so a revoke is not a surprise.

alternatives.name: Block until all checks pass
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and never shows a fake claim, but every claim waits for the slowest check.

alternatives.name: Confirm now, audit after the match
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but a cheater holds cells during the whole match.

steps.delegate: Add a claim state machine: pending, confirmed, revoked. Run is_copy in a worker pool (concurrent.futures or a separate process) so the asyncio loop never blocks; time out to referee review. Record per claim: received, broadcast_pending, checks_done, broadcast_final timestamps. Tests: a duplicate photo ends revoked; scores ignore pending; a slow check does not delay another claim's pending broadcast.
verify: Record p50 and p95 of received to pending broadcast and of received to final state
Inject a 5 second image check and confirm other claims' pending latency is unchanged

steps.title: Survive flaky mobile connections without losing or doubling claims
steps.learn: Phones switch networks and sockets drop silently. A claim sent just before a drop may or may not have arrived. Client-generated claim ids make retries safe, and a per-match sequence number on every server event lets a reconnecting client ask only for what it missed.

decision.choice: Idempotent claim ids, sequence-numbered events, resume from last seen seq or fall back to a snapshot
decision.why: The server stays the single authority, so there is nothing to merge; the client only needs to catch up. Sending missed events keeps reconnects small, and a snapshot covers long absences or a trimmed log.

alternatives.name: Full snapshot on every reconnect
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but larger payloads on weak connections, and clients can miss transitions they would animate.

alternatives.name: CRDT-style offline merging
alternatives.tradeoff: Works offline, but cell ownership with cooldowns needs one authority anyway, so it adds complexity for little gain.

steps.delegate: Server: monotonically increasing seq per match on every event; keep the last N events in memory. Client protocol: hello{last_seq}; server replies with missed events or a snapshot. Claims carry client UUIDs; duplicates return the stored result. Heartbeat ping to detect dead sockets. Tests: drop the socket after sending a claim, reconnect, claim counted once; client with stale seq receives exactly the missing events.
verify: Toggle airplane mode during a claim 10 times and confirm no claim is lost or doubled
Confirm two phones show the same map after one of them reconnects

steps.title: Load-test claim latency before the match
steps.learn: Latency under load is the second half of the question. Use an open model where new claims arrive at a fixed rate whatever the server's speed; a closed model slows its own arrivals when the server slows, hiding the delay (coordinated omission). Measure from the client side.

decision.choice: k6 websockets script, open arrival rate at expected match load and 3x, report p50, p95, p99
decision.why: k6 supports WebSockets and open-model arrival-rate scenarios, so tail latency is not hidden. Testing at 3x the expected load shows how much headroom exists before the weekend.

alternatives.name: Locust
alternatives.tradeoff: Python and easy to extend, but WebSocket clients and an open arrival model need extra code.

alternatives.name: Hand-written asyncio client
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control, but you will rebuild rate control and percentile reporting yourself.

steps.delegate: k6 script using k6/websockets: each virtual player connects, receives a token, sends claims with real test images at a constant arrival rate; measure send to claim_result and to cell_update received by another socket. Scenarios: expected load, 3x. Output percentiles as JSON. Run the server on the match machine. Tests: script fails loudly if any claim result is missing.
verify: Record p50, p95, p99 at 1x and 3x load with machine, server version and k6 command
Record the CPU and memory of the server process during the 3x run

steps.title: Test it outside: a weekend match across your neighborhood
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation. Two teams play for a weekend; one trusted player per team runs the staged cheat list at set times without telling the referee. Log every claim with timestamps, check results and referee decisions.
verify: Report staged cheats caught out of attempted, by cheat type and by which check caught it
Report honest claims blocked or revoked per 100, confirmed by the referee
Report field claim latency p50 and p95 from the logged timestamps
Report cells claimed per team per hour and how often cells changed hands

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example which cheat slipped through and why), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives dedup frozen-set results, cheat catch rate, false blocks and latency, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (staged cheats, 2 teams, one neighborhood) and what this does not prove

projects.title: GeoGuessr for your city
projects.problem: Guess where a local street photo was taken
projects.concepts: Retrieval-based location estimation over your own photo index
projects.tryIt: Have friends upload photos; see if the model beats them
projects.question: Given a street photo from my city, can retrieval over a geotagged photo index place it closer to the true spot than my friends can?

steps.title: Frame the question, pull city metadata and freeze the queries
steps.learn: The metric is distance error: great-circle meters between predicted and true location, reported as median and as the share within 25 m, 100 m and 1 km. Data: Mapillary street-level images for one city area (CC BY-SA). Queries must come from different capture sequences than the database, frozen before any tuning.

decision.choice: Split by Mapillary sequence: hold out whole sequences (and a later capture window) as queries
decision.why: Frames in one sequence are seconds apart and nearly identical, so a random image split lets the model match a query to its own neighbor frame and look far better than it is. Holding out whole sequences forces it to recognize the place, not the shot.

alternatives.name: Random image split
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest, but leaks near-duplicate frames from the same sequence into the database and inflates accuracy.

alternatives.name: Public benchmark only (for example MSLS)
alternatives.tradeoff: Labeled and comparable with papers, but it is not your city, which is the point of the game.

steps.delegate: Python 3: fetch_metadata.py tiles a city bounding box into cells under the API's bbox size limit and calls GET graph.mapillary.com/images with fields id,sequence,captured_at,computed_geometry,geometry,is_pano,thumb_1024_url; retry with backoff on rate-limit errors; write images.parquet. split.py assigns whole sequences to query or database with a fixed seed and writes queries.txt. Tests: no sequence id appears in both sets; split is identical across two runs.
verify: README states the question, the metric (median meters, share within 25 m, 100 m, 1 km) and the city bounding box, written before any model code
Count database images, query images and sequences; confirm zero sequences shared between the two sets
Record the SHA-256 of queries.txt in the README; it must not change for the rest of the project

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The game is about places, never people. Street photos show passers-by, faces, plates and homes. Mapillary blurs faces and plates it detects; its terms forbid trying to unblur or re-identify anyone. Friends' uploads are not blurred unless you add it, and precise GPS of where a friend stood can reveal where they live.

decision.choice: On-device face check blocks or blurs before upload; delete truth GPS after the study; no photos of homes or people
decision.why: Running a face detector (for example MediaPipe Face Detector) on the phone means faces never reach the server. Truth coordinates are only needed for scoring, so they get a deletion date. Rules in the app steer players to public streets.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach your server even if only briefly.

alternatives.name: No face handling
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but you would store bystanders' faces without consent.

steps.delegate: Add an on-device step with MediaPipe Face Detector: if a face is detected, block the upload with a message or blur the boxes first. Server: a scheduled job deletes truth rows after the study end date; never log raw coordinates. Show Mapillary attribution (CC BY-SA) on database thumbnails. Tests: an image with a face never reaches the upload endpoint; truth rows past the end date are gone.
verify: Upload 10 photos containing people and confirm none are stored with a visible face
Confirm the app shows attribution for Mapillary images and tells players to shoot public streets, not homes or people

links.label: Mapillary privacy policy (face and plate blurring)

steps.title: Download database images and handle panoramas and bad locations
steps.learn: Mapillary gives both the uploaded GPS (geometry) and a location refined by its own image processing (computed_geometry). Some images are 360 degree panoramas. The MegaLoc authors suggest cropping a panorama into perspective crops and treating each crop as its own image, since queries are ordinary phone photos.

decision.choice: Prefer computed_geometry, fall back to geometry; cut panoramas into perspective crops sharing the parent location
decision.why: Location labels are the ground truth for everything later, so take the refined one when it exists. Phone queries look like perspective crops, not equirectangular panoramas, so matching crops to crops is fairer to the descriptor.

alternatives.name: Drop panoramas entirely
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but loses coverage in areas captured mostly with 360 cameras.

alternatives.name: Index full panoramas as-is
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer images to store, but the projection distortion makes them look unlike any phone photo.

steps.delegate: Python 3: download.py fetches thumb_1024_url for every database row with a thread pool and resumable progress, saving <id>.jpg plus a CSV of id, lat, lon, source_of_location. pano_crops.py splits is_pano images into N yaw crops with a fixed field of view (use py360convert or equivalent) and records parent id. Tests: every saved file opens with Pillow; each crop row has its parent's coordinates; reruns skip existing files.
verify: Report how many images use computed_geometry versus raw geometry, and how many are panoramas
Plot all database points on a map and confirm coverage gaps you expect (parks, private roads) are visible
Open 20 random crops and confirm none are upside down or heavily distorted

steps.title: Choose the global image descriptor
steps.learn: Visual place recognition turns each image into one vector so that photos of the same place are close even across viewpoint, lighting and season. General models like CLIP group by what is in the picture (a street, a tree); place models are trained so the same corner from a new angle still matches.

decision.choice: MegaLoc via torch.hub as the main descriptor, CLIP image embeddings as the baseline
decision.why: MegaLoc is trained for retrieval of the same location across several datasets and its authors say fine-tuning is usually unnecessary outside cases like caves or underwater. CLIP is the natural off-the-shelf baseline that shows how much place-specific training matters.

alternatives.name: CosPlace (compact descriptors)
alternatives.tradeoff: Much smaller vectors and cheaper to run on CPU, but an older model; the CosPlace README itself points to MegaLoc for state of the art.

alternatives.name: EigenPlaces or SALAD
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong, viewpoint-focused alternatives, all runnable through VPR-methods-evaluation to compare on your own split.

alternatives.name: CLIP only
alternatives.tradeoff: One model for everything, but it matches scene type more than exact place.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + PyTorch: embed.py loads model = torch.hub.load('gmberton/MegaLoc','get_trained_model'), applies the README preprocessing (ToTensor, ImageNet normalize, resize 322x322), batches images under torch.inference_mode(), writes float32 descriptors.npy plus ids.txt. Add a --model clip path using open_clip encode_image(normalize=True). Tests: descriptors are L2-normalized (norms within 1e-3 of 1); the same image embeds identically twice.
verify: Record descriptor dimension, images per second and the device used for both MegaLoc and CLIP
Pick 5 query photos and look at their top-3 database matches for each model; note which model finds the same corner

links.label: MegaLoc: One Retrieval to Place Them All

steps.title: Build the nearest-neighbor index for the city
steps.learn: Memory is images times dimensions times 4 bytes for float32, so high-dimensional descriptors add up fast for a whole city. Because the descriptors are L2-normalized, inner product equals cosine similarity, so an inner-product index ranks exactly by cosine.

decision.choice: Exact Faiss IndexFlatIP first; switch to HNSW or PQ only if memory or latency demands it
decision.why: A city index is small enough that exact search is often affordable, and exact results remove one source of error while you tune everything else. Approximate indexes are a later, measured tradeoff.

alternatives.name: Faiss IndexHNSWFlat
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster queries on large indexes, but uses more memory than flat and returns approximate neighbors.

alternatives.name: PCA then PQ (for example IndexIVFPQ)
alternatives.tradeoff: Large memory savings, but adds quantization error that can drop the correct place out of the top-k.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + faiss-cpu: index.py loads descriptors.npy, builds faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), adds vectors, saves with faiss.write_index; search(q, k) returns ids and scores. Optional --hnsw flag builds IndexHNSWFlat with the inner-product metric. Tests: flat search matches a brute-force numpy dot-product top-10 on 100 random queries; save and reload return identical results.
verify: Report index size on disk and in RAM, and median and p95 query latency for 1,000 queries on your machine
If you try HNSW, report recall@10 against the flat index on the frozen queries

steps.title: Turn the top-k neighbors into one location estimate
steps.learn: The top-1 neighbor's location is the simplest guess, but one lookalike facade can be blocks away. If several of the top-k sit in the same small area, that area is more likely. H3 gives a hexagonal grid where latlng_to_cell buckets each neighbor and grid_disk gathers adjacent cells.

decision.choice: Similarity-weighted vote over H3 cells of the top-k, then the weighted mean of points in the winning cell
decision.why: Voting rewards agreement among neighbors, which is how repeated views of the same corner show up, while the weighted mean keeps precision finer than a cell. k and the H3 resolution are tuned on a validation split carved from the database, never on the frozen queries.

alternatives.name: Top-1 location
alternatives.tradeoff: No parameters and easy to explain, but one confusing lookalike decides the answer.

alternatives.name: Density clustering of top-k (for example DBSCAN in meters)
alternatives.tradeoff: No grid edges, but adds a radius and a min-points knob that are harder to tune.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + h3 (v4 API): locate.py takes top-k ids and scores, maps neighbors with h3.latlng_to_cell(lat, lng, res), sums scores per cell including grid_disk(cell, 1) neighbors, picks the best cell, returns the score-weighted mean lat/lon. Distance via h3.great_circle_distance in meters. Tests: identical neighbors return that point; one outlier among 9 agreeing neighbors does not move the estimate.
verify: Hold whole validation sequences out of the index, then compare top-1 versus voting by median error and share within 100 m
Record the chosen k and H3 resolution and confirm they were not tuned on the frozen queries

steps.title: Re-rank candidates with local feature matching
steps.learn: A global descriptor can confuse two similar storefronts. Matching local keypoints between the query and each top candidate, then counting geometric inliers (matches consistent with one camera geometry via RANSAC), checks that the two photos really show the same structure.

decision.choice: Re-rank the top 20 to 50 by RANSAC inlier count using LightGlue with DISK or ALIKED features
decision.why: Inliers are a strong, explainable signal of same place. LightGlue releases weights for several extractors; its README notes SuperPoint has a restrictive license while DISK and ALIKED do not, which matters for an app friends will use.

alternatives.name: SIFT with ratio test and RANSAC (OpenCV)
alternatives.tradeoff: No GPU and no license questions, but fewer correct matches across big lighting changes.

alternatives.name: No re-ranking
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest and simplest, but leaves lookalike errors uncorrected.

steps.delegate: Python 3: rerank.py uses lightglue (pip from cvg/LightGlue) with DISK(max_num_keypoints=2048) and LightGlue(features='disk'); for each query match against top-N candidates, estimate a fundamental matrix with cv2.findFundamentalMat(RANSAC), score by inlier count, cache features per database image. Tests: an image matched to itself gets the max inliers; two unrelated images get few.
verify: On the validation split, report share within 25 m with and without re-ranking, and the added latency per query
Inspect 10 queries where re-ranking changed the top-1 and count how many it fixed versus broke

links.label: LightGlue: Local Feature Matching at Light Speed

steps.title: Add a confidence score and handle no-coverage photos
steps.learn: Some uploads cannot be placed: indoor shots, close-ups, night photos or streets missing from the index. A confidence score built from signals you already have (top-1 similarity, inlier count, how tightly the top-k cluster) lets the game say 'not sure' or show a radius instead of a confident wrong pin.

decision.choice: Logistic model on similarity, inliers and top-k spread, predicting 'within 100 m', fit on validation data
decision.why: A few interpretable signals are enough, and fitting on validation data keeps the frozen queries clean. The output is a probability the game can show and a threshold for abstaining.

alternatives.name: Fixed threshold on top-1 similarity
alternatives.tradeoff: No training needed, but ignores whether neighbors agree and whether geometry checks out.

alternatives.name: Always answer
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest game logic, but wrong pins with no warning erode trust fast.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + scikit-learn: confidence.py builds features (top-1 cosine, max inliers, median distance of top-k to the estimate), fits LogisticRegression on validation queries labeled within 100 m or not, saves the model, and exposes predict(query) returning lat, lon, p, abstain. Tests: abstain is true exactly when p is below the threshold; saved and reloaded models give identical p; report (not assert) the learned sign of each coefficient.
verify: Plot a reliability curve on validation data and report how many queries fall in each confidence bin
Report coverage (share answered) and share within 100 m among answered queries at your chosen threshold

steps.title: Build the game: upload, hidden truth, guesses and scoring
steps.learn: Ground truth for friends' photos comes from their phone's EXIF GPS, which is also the answer. The truth must be pulled out and stored separately before the model or other players see the image, and the score must be computed by plain distance, not by the model's own confidence.

decision.choice: Server extracts EXIF GPS into a truth table, strips all EXIF from the image, then runs model and human rounds
decision.why: This prevents the model or players from reading the answer out of metadata, and keeps grading independent: distance between each guess and the stored truth, computed the same way for model and humans.

alternatives.name: Players type the location manually
alternatives.tradeoff: No EXIF needed, but labels are noisier and invite mistakes.

alternatives.name: Trust EXIF left in the file
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but the model or a curious friend can read the answer directly.

steps.delegate: Python 3 FastAPI + SQLite: POST /photos reads EXIF GPS with Pillow (Image.getexif), stores lat/lon in a truth table, re-saves pixels only (no EXIF), applies ImageOps.exif_transpose first so orientation survives. POST /guess stores a player's map pin; /score returns meters via great-circle distance for model and players. Tests: saved files contain no EXIF; photos without GPS are rejected; score is symmetric.
verify: Upload a phone photo and confirm with exiftool that the stored copy has no GPS or camera tags
Check that the model's guess is stored before the truth is ever read by any code path except scoring

steps.title: Test it outside: friends versus the model
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation: friends upload street photos taken inside the indexed area, then everyone else guesses on a map and the model guesses too. Fresh phone photos differ from Mapillary captures (camera, season, framing), so expect lower accuracy than on the frozen queries.
verify: Report median error and share within 25 m, 100 m and 1 km for the model and for each friend on the same photos
Report results on the frozen Mapillary queries next to the friend photos to show the domain gap
Ablate on the friend photos: CLIP vs MegaLoc, with and without voting, with and without re-ranking
List the 5 worst model misses with a one-line reason each (indoor, night, no coverage, lookalike)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Use the 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened, for example where re-ranking hurt or the model beat locals, (4) assumptions and what this does not prove, such as other cities, other seasons or areas without coverage.
verify: Part 1 states the question and the distance metric exactly as frozen in step 1
Part 2 gives every number with machine, model, index type and the exact command, plus the queries.txt hash
Part 3 explains at least two surprising results with example images
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits: one city area, Mapillary coverage, friend sample size

projects.title: Sketch-to-find
projects.problem: Draw a shape and find real things that match
projects.concepts: Sketch-based image retrieval with shared embeddings
projects.tryIt: Sketch objects around you and check retrieval accuracy
projects.question: Can one shared sketch and photo embedding let a quick drawing retrieve the matching real objects, even for categories it never trained on?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the held-out categories
steps.learn: Sketch-based image retrieval ranks photos by similarity to a drawing. Data: the Sketchy database, 75,471 sketches of 12,500 photographed objects in 125 categories. Metrics: mAP and precision@10 where a hit is a photo of the sketch's category. Real use means unseen objects, so test on categories never trained or tuned.

decision.choice: Freeze a held-out set of whole Sketchy categories (zero-shot split) plus a validation set of other categories
decision.why: A model tuned on all 125 categories can memorize category-specific features and look strong, then fail on your desk lamp. Holding out whole categories, as the zero-shot SBIR literature does, measures what real sketch-to-find needs.

alternatives.name: Random split of sketches
alternatives.tradeoff: More training data per category, but every test category was seen in training, which overstates real-world accuracy.

alternatives.name: QuickDraw sketches
alternatives.tradeoff: 50 million drawings in 345 categories and closer to doodles, but no paired photos, so you must source photos yourself.

steps.delegate: Python 3: split.py lists Sketchy categories, picks held-out and validation categories with a fixed seed, writes splits.json and the file lists for sketches and photos per split. Tests: no category appears in two splits; every sketch's category exists in the photo list; output identical across runs.
verify: README states the question, metrics (mAP, precision@10) and the held-out category names, written before any training
Record SHA-256 of splits.json; it must not change later
Count sketches and photos per split and confirm no category overlap

links.label: A Zero-Shot Framework for Sketch-based Image Retrieval

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: This finds things, not people. Photos taken around a home can catch faces, screens, mail with addresses and GPS in EXIF. Sketches of people should not search for people. Keep personal photos on the user's device or account, and never use them for training without asking.

decision.choice: On-device face check blocks or blurs; strip EXIF; no person category; photos private to their owner
decision.why: Running a face detector (for example MediaPipe Face Detector) before indexing means faces never enter the index. Stripping EXIF removes home location. Per-user indexes stop one user's sketch from surfacing another user's home photos.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach your server even if only briefly.

alternatives.name: Shared index across users
alternatives.tradeoff: More to search, but anyone could retrieve photos of someone else's home.

steps.delegate: Before indexing, run MediaPipe Face Detector on device; if a face is found, blur boxes or skip the photo. Re-save photos without EXIF. Scope every index query by user id. Tests: a photo with a face is never indexed unblurred; stored files contain no GPS; user A's query never returns user B's photos.
verify: Index 10 photos containing people and confirm no face is visible in any stored or returned image
Run exiftool on stored photos and confirm no GPS tags; query as a second user and confirm zero cross-user results

steps.title: Pick sketch and photo renderings and fix preprocessing
steps.learn: Sketchy ships several renderings. Photos come either non-uniformly scaled to 256x256 or cropped to the object bounding box plus 10%. Sketches come in six variants, including one centered and scaled so its largest side fills 78% of the canvas. Your app's canvas must be normalized the same way as training sketches.

decision.choice: Centered, uniformly scaled sketches (78% fill) and bounding-box photo crops
decision.why: A user's drawing has no paired photo to align to, so the centered rendering is the one the app can reproduce exactly. Bounding-box photo crops focus on the object, like a photo of one thing on your desk.

alternatives.name: Sketch rendered aligned to its paired photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Preserves pose and position cues useful for fine-grained matching, but the app cannot reproduce that alignment for a free drawing.

alternatives.name: Full-frame photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to raw phone photos, but background clutter competes with the object.

steps.delegate: Python 3: preprocess.py loads the chosen Sketchy rendering folders, converts sketches to 3-channel RGB on white, and exposes normalize_strokes(strokes, canvas) that renders app stroke lists to a white canvas, centers them and scales the largest side to 78%. Tests: a rendered square stroke list is centered within 1 pixel; output size and mode match the Sketchy sketches.
verify: Render 10 of your own drawings with normalize_strokes and place them next to Sketchy sketches; check scale and line width look alike
Confirm sketch and photo tensors use the same model preprocessing (size, normalization)

steps.title: Embed sketches and photos with CLIP as a zero-shot baseline
steps.learn: CLIP's image encoder maps both sketches and photos into one vector space without any sketch training, so cosine similarity between a sketch and a photo is an instant baseline. It is a shared embedding by construction, but sketches are line drawings while photos have texture and color, so expect a domain gap.

decision.choice: open_clip ViT-B-32 image encoder for both sketches and photos, cosine similarity
decision.why: No training, runs on a laptop, and gives the number every later step must beat. The Sketch_LVM paper builds its zero-shot SBIR system on CLIP, which makes it a fitting starting point.

alternatives.name: Edge maps of photos (Canny) matched to sketches
alternatives.tradeoff: Puts both in the line domain without a neural model, but is fragile to clutter and texture edges.

alternatives.name: Sketch to text label, then text-to-image search
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to explain, but fails for objects whose name the classifier does not know.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + open_clip: embed.py creates model, _, preprocess = open_clip.create_model_and_transforms('ViT-B-32', pretrained='laion2b_s34b_b79k'), encodes sketches and photos with model.encode_image under torch.no_grad, L2-normalizes, saves .npy. eval.py computes mAP and precision@10 per split. Tests: mAP equals 1.0 on a toy set where each sketch's category photos are its exact copies.
verify: Report mAP and precision@10 on the held-out categories and on validation categories
Show 5 sketches with their top-5 photos and note any pattern in errors (shape versus texture)

links.label: CLIP for All Things Zero-Shot SBIR

steps.title: Fine-tune the shared embedding on seen categories
steps.learn: Metric learning pulls a sketch toward photos of its category and pushes it away from others, closing the sketch to photo gap. The risk is overfitting to seen categories and losing CLIP's generality. The Sketch_LVM code trains CLIP's LayerNorm parameters with learned prompts, leaving most weights frozen.

decision.choice: Freeze CLIP except LayerNorm layers, train with a cross-domain triplet loss on seen categories only
decision.why: Updating only a small set of parameters keeps most of CLIP's general knowledge for unseen categories while still adapting to line drawings. Model selection uses the validation categories, never the held-out ones.

alternatives.name: Full fine-tuning
alternatives.tradeoff: Most capacity to adapt, but tends to forget general features and overfit the seen categories.

alternatives.name: Small linear adapter on frozen features
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest and safest, but may not be able to close a large domain gap.

alternatives.name: Prompt learning as in Sketch_LVM
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong reported results, but more moving parts to implement and tune.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + PyTorch + pytorch-metric-learning: train.py sets requires_grad only for LayerNorm params in the open_clip visual encoder, batches mixed sketches and photos with category labels, uses miners.MultiSimilarityMiner and losses.TripletMarginLoss, keeps only cross-domain triplets, early-stops on validation mAP. Tests: frozen params unchanged after a step; loss decreases on a tiny overfit run.
verify: Report trainable parameter count versus total and training time on your hardware
Plot validation mAP per epoch and record which checkpoint you selected and why

steps.title: Measure on held-out categories and ablate
steps.learn: Now open the frozen held-out categories once for the final comparison. Report seen versus unseen category results side by side: a large gap means the fine-tuning learned category shortcuts rather than sketch-to-photo matching.
verify: Table: mAP and precision@10 for zero-shot CLIP and the fine-tuned model on validation and held-out categories
Report the seen to unseen gap for the fine-tuned model and for CLIP
Confirm in the log that held-out categories were evaluated only after the checkpoint was chosen

steps.title: Index photos of real things around you
steps.learn: Your own photos are cluttered: a mug sits next to a laptop and a plant. Retrieval works on whole-image vectors, so what is in frame decides what the vector represents. Embedding crops of the main object makes a sketch of a mug match the mug, not the desk.

decision.choice: Store one vector for the full photo plus vectors for a few object crops, all linked to the photo
decision.why: Crops let a sketch match the object even in a busy scene, while the full-image vector still helps when the object fills the frame. A personal index is small, so extra vectors per photo cost little.

alternatives.name: Full photo only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but clutter dilutes the object and drops recall.

alternatives.name: Ask the user to crop each photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise crops, but adds friction to every capture.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + faiss-cpu: index_photos.py applies ImageOps.exif_transpose, re-saves without EXIF, skips photos with a detected face, embeds the full photo and crops from an object detector of your choice (log the model name), stores vectors in faiss.IndexFlatIP and rows (vector id, photo id, crop box) in SQLite. Query returns the best score per photo. Tests: stored files have no GPS; own-crop query returns that photo first; deleting a photo removes all its vectors.
verify: Photograph 50 objects at home; report vectors stored per photo and index size
Query with 10 of the photos themselves and confirm each returns itself at rank 1

steps.title: Capture strokes on a canvas and render them like training sketches
steps.learn: The canvas is where train and serve can silently diverge. Line width, canvas size, centering and scale all change the embedding. Keeping the raw strokes (as QuickDraw does, lists of x and y points per stroke) lets you re-render the exact same way as training data.

decision.choice: Record vector strokes in the browser, render server-side with the same normalize_strokes as training
decision.why: One rendering function used in both training checks and serving removes train/serve skew. Vector strokes also allow undo and replay.

alternatives.name: Send a raster PNG from the canvas
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but scale and line width depend on the device and browser.

alternatives.name: Render on the client
alternatives.tradeoff: Lower server load, but now two rendering implementations must stay identical.

steps.delegate: TypeScript + HTML canvas: Draw.tsx records pointer events into strokes [[xs, ys]], supports undo and clear, POSTs JSON to /search. Python FastAPI /search renders with normalize_strokes, embeds, queries the index. Tests: the same stroke JSON yields byte-identical renders; empty or single-dot drawings return a 'draw more' error.
verify: Draw the same shape on a phone and a laptop and confirm the rendered images look the same and the top-5 results match
Confirm empty drawings and extremely long stroke lists are rejected cleanly

steps.title: Rank results, add an optional text hint and a no-match answer
steps.learn: Some drawings are ambiguous: a circle could be a plate, a clock or a ball. An optional typed word gives CLIP's text encoder a second ranked list, and Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines ranks without needing the two scores on one scale. When even the best match is weak, say so.

decision.choice: Sketch-only by default; if a word is typed, fuse sketch and text rankings with RRF; abstain under a tuned score
decision.why: The sketch stays the main signal, which is the point of the project, while text resolves ambiguity cheaply. The abstain threshold is tuned on validation categories so the frozen held-out set stays clean.

alternatives.name: Weighted sum of cosine scores
alternatives.tradeoff: Smooth control over the mix, but needs score calibration between sketch and text similarity.

alternatives.name: Always return top-k
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but shows confident-looking nonsense for drawings with no match in the index.

steps.delegate: Python 3: search.py gets top-50 by sketch and, if text is given, top-50 by open_clip text embedding (model.encode_text on tokenizer output), fuses with RRF score sum 1/(k + rank), returns top-10 or 'no match' when the best sketch cosine is below threshold. Tests: RRF of identical lists keeps order; a blank-canvas embedding triggers no-match.
verify: On validation categories, report precision@10 sketch-only versus sketch plus the category name as text
Report the abstain threshold and the share of validation queries it rejects

links.label: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack et al., SIGIR 2009)

steps.title: Test it outside: sketch objects around you
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation: photograph objects around you, then sketch them from memory and check whether the right object comes back. Label each query with its target photo before searching so the grade does not depend on the system's own output. Include objects from categories not in Sketchy.
verify: Run at least 50 sketch queries; report hit rate at 1 and 5 (target object in top-k) and mean reciprocal rank
