Split results into categories in Sketchy versus not in Sketchy and report both
Compare zero-shot CLIP and the fine-tuned model on the same sketches
Have 3 other people sketch the same targets and report how much accuracy varies by drawer

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Use the 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened, for example where fine-tuning hurt unseen categories, (4) assumptions and what this does not prove, such as other drawing styles or very large photo collections.
verify: Part 1 states the question and the metrics exactly as frozen in step 1
Part 2 gives every number with machine, model, checkpoint and the exact command, plus the splits.json hash
Part 3 explains at least two surprising results with example sketches
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits: Sketchy categories, your own objects, few drawers

projects.title: Change spotter
projects.problem: What changed on this street since last month?
projects.concepts: Image alignment and change detection over time
projects.tryIt: Photograph the same 10 spots monthly
projects.question: Can monthly phone photos of the same 10 street spots be aligned well enough to flag real changes, not lighting, angle or passing cars?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen test sets
steps.learn: Change spotting is two problems in series: align two photos of one spot, then decide which differences matter. Metrics: alignment error on pairs with known geometry, pixel F1 of change masks on a labeled street dataset, and found vs missed changes on your own 10 spots over the months.

decision.choice: Tohoku street change dataset (tune on Kamaishi, test on Takata), HPatches viewpoint sequences, your own monthly photos
decision.why: The Tohoku set has street sequences taken about three months apart with hand-made change masks, close to this project. Splitting by street freezes a test set before tuning. HPatches gives ground-truth homographies to score alignment alone. Your own photos are the real test.

alternatives.name: Own photos only
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use, but a few months of 10 spots gives too few labeled changes to tune thresholds without overfitting.

alternatives.name: Satellite change detection datasets
alternatives.tradeoff: Plenty of labels, but top-down imagery has none of the parallax, angle and occlusion problems of street photos.

verify: README states the question and the 3 metrics, written before any code
Download both datasets; write the Takata test file list and its hash to the README and do not open its masks until the final run
Pick your 10 spots and record why each one is likely to change (shop front, construction, garden)

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Track places, not people. Street photos catch faces, plates and windows into homes. Faces should be removed on the phone before upload and never stored. Stand on public ground, do not photograph into private homes, and do not stop in traffic to line up a shot.

decision.choice: On-device face detection with blur before upload; server also blurs person masks; no person-level results
decision.why: Running MediaPipe Face Detector on the phone means raw faces never reach the server. The server-side person masks from the transient step add a second layer, and results only describe places.

alternatives.name: Server-side blurring only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach and briefly sit on your server.

alternatives.name: Only shoot when the street is empty
alternatives.tradeoff: No faces at all, but limits when you can capture and still misses plates and windows.

steps.delegate: Add on-device face blurring with MediaPipe Face Detector (full-range model for rear-camera photos) before upload; strip EXIF except time. On the server, blur all person masks before storing. Tests: a photo with a face never leaves the device unblurred; stored images contain no EXIF location; a stored image with a person shows them blurred.
verify: Capture 10 photos with people in frame and confirm no stored image shows a recognizable face
Write down where each of the 10 spots is safe to stand and confirm none requires entering private land or the road

steps.title: Design the repeat-capture protocol and spot registry
steps.learn: Alignment is far easier when the second photo is taken from nearly the same place, angle and zoom. Most of the error budget is decided at capture time: viewpoint shift causes parallax, and different hours cause shadows that look like change. A registry ties every photo to a spot id.

decision.choice: Camera screen with a semi-transparent overlay of last month's photo, plus GPS, heading and time stored per capture
decision.why: A ghost overlay lets you line up edges by eye, which cuts viewpoint error more than GPS can (phone GPS is meters off). Storing time lets you prefer captures at a similar hour so shadows match.

alternatives.name: GPS pin only
alternatives.tradeoff: No custom camera UI, but the angle and distance vary month to month and the aligner has to absorb much larger shifts.

alternatives.name: Fixed marks on the ground or a tripod spot
alternatives.tradeoff: Most repeatable viewpoint, but needs physical marks you may not be allowed to leave on public ground.

steps.delegate: Build a small web app (TypeScript, getUserMedia) that shows the live camera with the previous photo of the chosen spot at adjustable opacity. On capture, save the image with spot_id, timestamp, lat, lon and the GPS accuracy value to a SQLite table captures(spot_id, taken_at, lat, lon, acc_m, path). Tests: captures for an unknown spot_id are rejected; the overlay loads the latest photo for the spot.
verify: Take 2 photos of one spot 10 minutes apart with the overlay and 2 without, with no people in frame; compare how far one window corner moves in pixels
Confirm every stored capture has a spot_id, timestamp and location

steps.title: Match local features between the two photos
steps.learn: Alignment starts with keypoints that can be found again in the other photo, described so that lighting and small rotations do not change the descriptor. Lowe's ratio test drops ambiguous matches. Street scenes are hard: repeated windows, moving cars, and foliage that changes by season.

decision.choice: SIFT (OpenCV cv2.SIFT_create) with a ratio test as the baseline, then compare SIFT or DISK features with LightGlue
decision.why: SIFT is in mainline OpenCV, runs on CPU and is well understood, so it is a reproducible baseline. LightGlue is a learned matcher with Apache-2.0 weights for DISK and SIFT features; whether it beats SIFT on your spots is what you measure on the same pairs.

alternatives.name: ORB with Hamming matching
alternatives.tradeoff: Much faster and binary, good on a phone, but less robust to the lighting and scale changes between months.

alternatives.name: SuperPoint with LightGlue
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong learned features, but SuperPoint's weights use a restrictive license, which matters if the app is ever shared.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, opencv-python, numpy, and the cvg/LightGlue package. Write match.py with match_sift(img0, img1, ratio) and match_lightglue(img0, img1, features='disk' or 'sift'), both returning Nx2 point arrays for each image. Tests: an image matched to itself returns many matches with zero offset; a horizontally shifted crop returns matches with the expected shift.
verify: On 10 HPatches viewpoint sequences, record match counts per pair for SIFT and LightGlue
Draw matches for 3 own pairs of one spot shot at different hours or angles, and count obviously wrong matches by eye

steps.title: Fit a robust homography and warp onto last month
steps.learn: A homography maps one plane to another exactly, so it aligns building facades well but leaves parallax for anything at a different depth (poles, parked cars). Robust estimators fit it while ignoring outlier matches. Pixels with no overlap after the warp must be excluded from comparison.

decision.choice: cv2.findHomography with cv2.USAC_MAGSAC, then cv2.warpPerspective plus a valid-pixel mask
decision.why: MAGSAC++ scores models without a hard inlier-outlier cut, so it depends less on the threshold choice, which helps when match quality varies month to month. The warped mask stops black borders from showing up as change.

alternatives.name: Plain RANSAC (cv2.RANSAC)
alternatives.tradeoff: The classic choice and easy to explain, but results depend more on picking the reprojection threshold well.

alternatives.name: Homography then dense optical flow (RAFT)
alternatives.tradeoff: Corrects residual parallax per pixel, but flow can also warp away real changes, hiding what you want to find.

alternatives.name: Full 3D reconstruction (structure from motion)
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles depth properly, but needs many photos per spot each month and far more compute.

steps.delegate: Extend the Python package: align(img_ref, img_new, matcher) returns (H, inlier_count, warped_new, valid_mask). Use cv2.findHomography(src, dst, cv2.USAC_MAGSAC, thresh). Add eval_hpatches.py that projects the 4 image corners with the estimated and ground-truth homographies and reports mean corner error per pair. Tests: identity image gives H close to identity; synthetic warp with 20% outlier matches is recovered.
verify: Report mean corner error and the share of HPatches viewpoint pairs under 3 px for RANSAC vs MAGSAC
On 3 own same-spot pairs shot at different hours, flicker between reference and warped image and note where parallax remains

steps.title: Normalize lighting before comparing
steps.learn: A month apart means different sun angle, white balance, and exposure. Raw pixel differences will flag every shadow. Normalization reduces global color and brightness shifts, but it cannot remove a moved shadow, which is why the comparison method in the next step matters too.

decision.choice: Histogram match the new image to the reference inside the valid mask (skimage.exposure.match_histograms)
decision.why: It removes global exposure and color cast shifts in one call and is easy to inspect. Restricting it to the overlap keeps black warp borders from skewing the histograms.

alternatives.name: CLAHE on both images (cv2.createCLAHE)
alternatives.tradeoff: Equalizes local contrast, helping in shade, but changes both images in ways that can amplify noise and texture.

alternatives.name: No normalization, rely on learned features
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, and deep features are partly lighting invariant, but you lose a cheap fix for exposure jumps.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-image. normalize(ref, warped, valid_mask) applies match_histograms per channel using only valid pixels and returns the corrected image. Tests: an image darkened by 30% comes back with mean intensity within a small tolerance of the original; pixels outside the mask are untouched.
verify: On 5 Kamaishi pairs, report mean absolute pixel difference in unchanged regions before and after normalization
Inspect one shadow-heavy pair and note what normalization did not fix

steps.title: Compute a change map that ignores nuisance differences
steps.learn: The change map scores each location by how different it is between months. Pixel differences react to every small shift and shadow; SSIM compares local structure; deep patch features (from a self-supervised model like DINOv2) compare what is there, which is more tolerant of lighting and small misalignment but coarser.

decision.choice: Cosine distance between DINOv2 ViT-S/14 patch features of the aligned pair, upsampled, with SSIM as a baseline
decision.why: Small residual misalignment and lighting shifts are the main sources of false alarms here, and patch features absorb both better than pixels. Zero-shot work such as ZeroSCD shows pretrained features can detect street changes without training on change labels.

alternatives.name: 1 minus SSIM map (skimage structural_similarity, full=True)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, no GPU and fine-grained, but still fires on shadows and leftover parallax.

alternatives.name: Change network trained on street datasets
alternatives.tradeoff: Can be most accurate in its domain, but needs labeled pairs and may not transfer to your spots and phone.

steps.delegate: Python, torch, scikit-image. change_map_dino(ref, new, valid_mask) loads torch.hub.load('facebookresearch/dinov2', 'dinov2_vits14'), resizes so sides are multiples of 14, takes normalized patch tokens, returns per-patch cosine distance upsampled to image size and masked. change_map_ssim(...) returns 1 minus the SSIM map. Tests: identical images give near zero everywhere; a pasted block gives a peak at that block.
verify: On the Kamaishi tuning pairs, report pixel F1 at the best threshold for SSIM and for DINOv2
View the 3 worst DINOv2 false alarms and label each as shadow, parallax, transient object or other

steps.title: Mask people, cars and other transient objects
steps.learn: A parked car or a pedestrian is a real pixel change but not a change to the street. Detecting these classes in both photos and excluding them removes a large share of false alarms, and also keeps people out of the results.

decision.choice: torchvision maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn (COCO weights): mask person, car, bus, truck, bicycle, motorcycle in both images
decision.why: Instance masks follow object outlines, so less of the scene is thrown away than with boxes. COCO covers the common transient classes on a street, and torchvision keeps the stack in one framework with the change model.

alternatives.name: Box detector, mask whole boxes
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster and simpler, but a box around a bike hides the wall behind it, where a real change could be.

alternatives.name: Semantic segmentation of static classes only
alternatives.tradeoff: Can keep only buildings, signs and vegetation, but needs a street-scene segmentation model and its own label set.

steps.delegate: Python, torchvision. transient_mask(img, classes, score_thresh) runs maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn with MaskRCNN_ResNet50_FPN_Weights.DEFAULT and returns the union of masks for the listed COCO classes, dilated by a few pixels. Combine: comparable = valid_mask and not (mask_ref or mask_new). Tests: an image with no detections returns an empty mask; a street image with a car masks it.
verify: Recompute Kamaishi pixel F1 with and without transient masking and record both
Count how many of the 3 worst false alarms from the last step are now gone

steps.title: Turn the map into change regions with tuned thresholds
steps.learn: People want a few boxes saying 'this changed', not a heat map. Thresholding, morphological cleanup and a minimum area turn the map into regions. The threshold is the precision vs recall knob and must be tuned only on Kamaishi, never on the Takata test set.

decision.choice: Fixed threshold tuned on Kamaishi for best F1, binary opening, remove regions below a minimum area, report top regions
decision.why: A fixed threshold means the same amount of difference always counts the same, so months are comparable. Area filtering removes speckle from leaves and noise.

alternatives.name: Otsu threshold per pair (skimage threshold_otsu)
alternatives.tradeoff: No tuning, but it always splits the map into two classes, so it finds 'changes' even when nothing changed.

alternatives.name: Per-spot learned baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns each spot's normal variation over months (a tree that always sways), but needs several months of history first.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-image. regions(change_map, comparable_mask, thresh, min_area) returns a list of boxes with mean score, using binary_opening and remove_small_objects. tune.py grid-searches thresh and min_area on Kamaishi only and writes the chosen values to config.json. Tests: an all-zero map returns no regions; a single blob above min_area returns one box.
verify: Record the chosen threshold and min_area, tuned on Kamaishi only
Run once on Takata with frozen settings and report pixel F1; no further tuning after this

steps.title: Reject bad alignments and keep a per-spot timeline
steps.learn: When alignment fails (too few inliers, extreme warp, small overlap), every pixel looks changed. Saying 'retake this photo' is better than a wall of false alarms. Each spot's history should compare against the last good capture, not just the previous upload.

decision.choice: Gate on inlier count, overlap fraction and homography sanity; on failure ask for a retake while still on site
decision.why: Checking right after capture means you can retake while standing there, instead of finding a bad month later. Comparing to the last good capture keeps one bad month from breaking the chain.

alternatives.name: Always report, flag low confidence
alternatives.tradeoff: Never blocks the user, but low-confidence maps tend to get trusted anyway.

alternatives.name: Align to a fixed first-month reference
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows cumulative change since day one, but gets harder as the scene drifts (seasons, scaffolding).

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI service: POST /spots/{id}/captures runs align, normalize, transient mask, change map and regions; returns either regions or {retake: reason}. Gates: inlier_count below N, valid overlap below a fraction, or a homography whose corner projection folds or scales extremely. GET /spots/{id}/timeline lists months with region crops. Tests: an unrelated photo triggers retake; an identical photo returns no regions.
verify: Upload 3 deliberately bad captures (wrong spot, big angle change, blurred) and confirm all ask for a retake
Confirm the timeline compares each month to the last capture that passed the gate

steps.title: Test it outside: 10 spots, photographed monthly
steps.learn: The try-it is the real test: photograph the same 10 spots every month. Before looking at the system's output each month, walk the spots and write down what you see changed yourself; that list, not the system, is the ground truth.
verify: For each month, report changes found, missed and false alarms against your own written list
Report the retake rate and the median inlier count per spot
Compare the full pipeline with transient masking switched off on the same months
Note which kinds of change (new sign, removed tree, paint) were found and which were missed

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example parallax false alarms or seasonal foliage), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives HPatches corner error, Takata F1 and monthly found or missed counts, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with example images
Part 4 lists assumptions (one phone, 10 spots, few months, one city) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Live location trivia
projects.problem: Learn about places as you walk past them
projects.concepts: RAG over geotagged Wikipedia articles, a real-time multiplayer server
projects.tryIt: Host a walking trivia night with friends
projects.question: Can a server turn geotagged Wikipedia articles into correct, well-timed trivia for a group walking past those places in real time?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen route
steps.learn: The game asks a question when players walk near a place that has a Wikipedia article. Success: questions are correct per a human check, arrive while players are still near the place, and players enjoy the walk. The test set is a fixed walking route and the article revisions near it.

decision.choice: Freeze one 2 to 3 km route: snapshot nearby article page ids and revision ids before generating anything
decision.why: Wikipedia changes daily, so recording revision ids makes every audit reproducible. Fixing the route before tuning prompts stops you from picking places where the generator happens to look good.

alternatives.name: Random places worldwide
alternatives.tradeoff: Broader coverage of article styles, but you cannot walk them, so timing and GPS behavior go untested.

alternatives.name: Public QA dataset
alternatives.tradeoff: Has gold answers, but its questions are not tied to places and do not test location triggers.

verify: README states the question and metrics: human-checked correctness, trigger distance, entry-to-question latency, player rating
Save the route as GPS points and the snapshot as page id plus lastrevid (from prop=info) with its hash

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Live location is personal data: a stored trace shows where friends live and walk. Keep location only as long as the game needs it. Trivia is a helper: Wikipedia can be wrong, so link the source article. Players should watch the road, not the screen, and never be led onto private property.

decision.choice: Location only while a game runs, held in memory; store only triggered place ids; source link and CC BY-SA attribution
decision.why: Triggers need the current position, not history, so storing traces adds risk with no game benefit. Linking each question to its article lets players check facts and meets Wikipedia's attribution requirement.

alternatives.name: Store full GPS traces for analysis
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful for tuning triggers, but keeps sensitive movement data; if needed, collect it only from yourself with consent.

alternatives.name: Client-side triggers, server sees no location
alternatives.tradeoff: Best privacy, but the group centroid and anti-cheat logic move to clients you do not control.

steps.delegate: Server: keep positions in room memory only, drop them on game end, and log only place ids and timestamps. Serve over HTTPS (browsers require a secure context for geolocation). Client: question card shows article title, link and license note; audio or vibration cue plus an in-app reminder to stop before reading. Tests: after a game ends no coordinates remain in the database or logs.
verify: Grep the database and logs after a test game and confirm no coordinates are stored
Confirm every question shows its source article link and attribution
Confirm no route place is on private land or needs crossing a road without a crossing

steps.title: Ingest geotagged articles for the play area
steps.learn: Wikipedia stores coordinates for articles through the GeoData extension. The list=geosearch API returns pages near a point (radius up to 10,000 m, up to 500 results per call) or within a box. Text comes from TextExtracts as plain text. Reuse requires attribution under CC BY-SA.

decision.choice: Prefetch the play area before the game with geosearch tiles plus TextExtracts, cached locally
decision.why: Fetching once before the walk removes Wikipedia latency from the game loop and respects the API etiquette of modest, serial requests with a descriptive User-Agent. The play area is small, so a few tiled queries cover it.

alternatives.name: Live geosearch during play
alternatives.tradeoff: Always fresh and no prefetch step, but every trigger waits on the network and on API limits.

alternatives.name: geo_tags SQL dump
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers all of English Wikipedia offline, but you must load a MySQL dump and fetch text separately.

alternatives.name: Wikidata coordinates (P625) via SPARQL
alternatives.tradeoff: Structured facts and types, but less prose to write questions from.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with httpx. fetch_area(bbox) tiles the box, calls action=query&list=geosearch with gsradius and gslimit, then prop=extracts&explaintext=1 one page at a time plus prop=info for lastrevid. Store pages(pageid, title, lat, lon, lastrevid, text, url) in Postgres. Send a descriptive User-Agent and make requests serially. Tests: duplicate pages across tiles are stored once; a page without coordinates is skipped.
verify: Fetch the route area and report the number of articles and how many lie within 100 m of the route
Confirm stored lastrevid matches the frozen snapshot; for pages edited since, fetch the frozen revision (action=parse with oldid) or log the drift

steps.title: Index places for fast nearby lookups
steps.learn: Every location update asks 'which places are within r meters that this group has not seen?'. Distance on a sphere is not Euclidean on lat and lon, so use an index that understands geography. Filtering by distance first shrinks retrieval to a handful of candidate articles.

decision.choice: PostGIS geography column with a GiST index, queried with ST_DWithin in meters
decision.why: ST_DWithin on geography takes meters directly, so radius logic stays simple, and the same Postgres holds pages, chunks and game state. A play area has at most thousands of points, well within one database.

alternatives.name: H3 cells in memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Very fast lookups by cell and neighbor rings, but cells approximate circles, so edge cases need an exact distance check.

alternatives.name: SQLite R*Tree
alternatives.tradeoff: No server to run, good for an on-device version, but it indexes boxes, so you add a distance filter yourself.

steps.delegate: Postgres with PostGIS via Docker Compose. Add geog geography(Point,4326) to pages with a GiST index. nearby(lat, lon, r_m, exclude_ids) returns pages ordered by ST_Distance. Tests: a point 50 m from a page returns it at r=100 and not at r=30; excluded ids never come back.
verify: Time nearby() for 100 random route points and record p50 and p95 latency
Check 3 results by measuring the distance on a map yourself

steps.title: Chunk articles and retrieve the passages worth asking about
steps.learn: An article is too long to put into every prompt, and most of it is dull. Retrieval picks passages for the place: geo filter first, then rank chunks within those articles. Good trivia passages hold specific, checkable facts (dates, names, firsts), which keyword and semantic signals both help find.

decision.choice: Section-aware chunks; geo pre-filter; rank by BM25 plus embedding similarity to a 'surprising fact' query
decision.why: Pre-filtering by distance keeps retrieval small and on-topic. BM25 catches concrete tokens like years and names, while embeddings catch passages that read like interesting facts. Combining them is cheap at a few dozen chunks.

alternatives.name: Lead section only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and usually accurate, but questions get repetitive (when was it built) across places.

alternatives.name: Send the whole article to the LLM
alternatives.tradeoff: No retrieval code, but costs more per question and long contexts can bury the facts.

steps.delegate: Python, rank_bm25 (BM25Okapi) and sentence-transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2). chunk(text) splits on section headings into chunks of a few sentences. Store chunk embeddings in Postgres. top_chunks(pageids, k) scores chunks by normalized BM25 plus cosine similarity to a fixed query and returns k. Tests: chunks never cross section boundaries; an article with one section yields chunks; ranking is deterministic.
verify: For 10 snapshot places, read the top 3 chunks and mark which contain a specific checkable fact
Compare that count with lead-section-only chunks on the same places

steps.title: Generate grounded questions with structured output
steps.learn: The LLM writes a multiple-choice question from retrieved chunks. Hallucinated facts are the main risk. Asking for a verbatim supporting quote and checking that quote against the source text catches many invented answers cheaply. Wrong options should be plausible but clearly wrong per the text.

decision.choice: JSON schema output: question, 4 options, answer index, verbatim quote; reject if the quote is not in the chunk
decision.why: Schema-validated output means the server never parses free text. The exact-quote check is deterministic and cheap, and ties every question to a citable article for attribution.

alternatives.name: Template questions from Wikidata facts
alternatives.tradeoff: Facts are structured and correct more often, but questions are formulaic and many places lack rich data.

alternatives.name: Free-form generation, no grounding check
alternatives.tradeoff: More varied questions, but you cannot tell invented facts from real ones without reading the article.

steps.delegate: Python with pydantic: model Question(question, options[4], answer_idx, quote, pageid). generate(chunks) calls the LLM with a prompt that requires answers stated in the text and a JSON response matching the pydantic JSON schema; validate, then check the quote appears in the chunk after whitespace normalization. Tests: invalid JSON is retried once then dropped; a fabricated quote is rejected; duplicate options are rejected.
verify: Generate 50 questions for snapshot places and record the rejection rate and reasons
Read 20 accepted questions against the article and count any whose answer the article does not support

steps.title: Check questions with a judge and pre-generate a bank
steps.learn: A quote check misses questions where the quote exists but the answer does not follow from it. A second LLM pass can filter those, but it is a filter, not the metric: correctness is still graded by a human audit. Generating ahead of time removes LLM latency from the walk.

decision.choice: Second LLM judge filter, then pre-generate a bank per place before the game; live generation only as fallback
decision.why: A judge that sees only the chunk and the question catches unsupported answers the quote check misses. Pre-generation turns a seconds-long LLM call into a database read at trigger time, which matters when players walk on.

alternatives.name: Human review of every question
alternatives.tradeoff: Most accurate, but does not scale past a single route.

alternatives.name: Generate live on trigger
alternatives.tradeoff: Always fresh and no storage, but adds LLM latency and failure risk at the exact moment it matters.

steps.delegate: Python asyncio. judge(question, chunk) returns supported and reason in JSON. prebuild(area) generates N questions per place with bounded concurrency, retries with backoff on rate limits, runs judge, and stores accepted ones with model id and prompt version. Tests: a question whose answer contradicts the chunk is rejected; prebuild resumes without duplicates after a crash.
verify: Report judge rejection rate and the cost and time to prebuild the route
Hand-check 20 judge-rejected and 20 judge-accepted questions and count disagreements with your own reading

steps.title: Decide when to ask: geofences that tolerate GPS error
steps.learn: Phone positions jump around, and the browser reports accuracy as a 95% confidence radius in meters. Trigger too eagerly and questions fire for places across the block; too strictly and players walk past. Hysteresis (enter at r, reset only beyond a larger radius) stops repeat firing at the edge.

decision.choice: Fire when the group centroid is within r of a place for a short dwell, ignoring fixes with poor accuracy
decision.why: Dropping fixes with a large accuracy radius removes most jumps. A short dwell avoids firing on a single noisy fix. Using the group centroid means one question for everyone, which suits a shared game.

alternatives.name: Fire per player on first fix inside r
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest response, but players get different questions at different times and GPS jumps cause false triggers.

alternatives.name: Fixed ordered stops on the route
alternatives.tradeoff: Predictable and easy to test, but loses the 'whatever you happen to pass' feel.

steps.delegate: Browser client: navigator.geolocation.watchPosition with enableHighAccuracy, sending lat, lon, accuracy and timestamp over the socket. Server (Python): Trigger class that drops fixes above an accuracy limit, tracks dwell per place, applies hysteresis and never repeats a place for a room. Tests with replayed GPS traces: a trace passing 20 m from a place fires once; a single outlier fix does not fire.
verify: Walk the route once alone, log fixes, and replay them: report the distance at which each question fired
Count triggers caused by fixes later judged to be GPS jumps

steps.title: Build the real-time multiplayer game server
steps.learn: Players share a room: the server pushes questions, collects answers and broadcasts scores. The server must be authoritative: it decides when a question opened and closed, so clients cannot cheat by changing their clocks. Ordering and duplicate messages need explicit handling.

decision.choice: One authoritative FastAPI WebSocket server, in-memory room state, game events (not locations) persisted to Postgres
decision.why: A walking group is a handful of players per room, so one process handles it easily. Server timestamps decide answer timing, and persisting events lets a crashed server rebuild rooms.

alternatives.name: Socket.IO
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds rooms, acknowledgements, automatic reconnection and a long-polling fallback, at the cost of its own protocol on both ends.

alternatives.name: HTTP polling
alternatives.tradeoff: Works everywhere and is simplest, but adds delay and battery use on phones during a walk.

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI WebSockets. Messages as JSON with type and seq: join, location, question, answer, score. Room holds players, current question, open and close server times. answer(question_id, choice) is accepted once per player and only before close. Tests with pytest and the FastAPI test client: two clients see the same question; a late answer is rejected; a second answer from the same player is ignored.
verify: Run 5 simulated clients against a local server and confirm all receive each question and the same scores
Measure p95 time from trigger to question received across the 5 clients

steps.title: Handle dropped connections and outages mid-walk
steps.learn: Outdoors, phones lose signal, lock their screens and change networks. A player who reconnects must rejoin the same room and see the current question. If the LLM or Wikipedia is down, the game should keep running from the prebuilt bank.

decision.choice: Session token resume with a full state snapshot on reconnect; prebuilt bank as the only path when upstreams fail
decision.why: Sending a snapshot on resume is simpler and safer than replaying missed messages. Keeping the prebuilt bank as the primary source means an upstream outage does not stop play.

alternatives.name: Replay missed events by sequence number
alternatives.tradeoff: Clients see every event in order, but you must buffer events and handle gaps.

alternatives.name: Fresh join on reconnect
alternatives.tradeoff: No resume logic, but players lose their score and the current question.

steps.delegate: Extend the server: join returns a resume token; resume(token) reattaches the socket and sends a snapshot (room, scores, open question, time left). Client reconnects with exponential backoff. If the bank is empty for a place, skip it rather than block. Tests: disconnect and resume within a question keeps the player's score and allows answering; LLM client raising errors never blocks a trigger.
verify: Toggle airplane mode for 20 seconds mid-question and confirm the player resumes with score intact
Kill the LLM API key and confirm a full route replay still serves questions

steps.title: Test it outside: host a walking trivia night
steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation: walk the frozen route with friends. Afterwards, grade every question that was asked against its article yourself; the judge's verdicts do not count as the metric. Ask players to rate each question with one tap during the game.
verify: Report the share of asked questions that were correct per your own post-game check
Report trigger distance and entry-to-question latency (p50, p95) from the game log
Report reconnects, skipped places and average player rating per question
List the 3 lowest-rated questions and why players disliked them

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a judge passing a wrong question or triggers firing late), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives correctness, trigger distance, latency and rating numbers, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with log evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (one route, one city, English Wikipedia, few players) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Cloud shape game
projects.problem: Which animal does that cloud look like?
projects.concepts: CLIP similarity between cloud photos and text prompts, a leaderboard
projects.tryIt: Collect cloud photos for a month; vote on the best matches
projects.question: Can CLIP similarity pick the animal a cloud looks like well enough that its top guesses match what people vote for?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the frozen vote set
steps.learn: No ground truth exists for 'what a cloud looks like', so people are the label. Success: CLIP's top guesses agree with friends' votes over a month. Freeze 40 cloud photos (sky only, EXIF stripped), each labeled by 3+ friends (an animal or 'none') before tuning any prompt.

decision.choice: Frozen 40-photo human-voted test set, plus the CCSN cloud dataset (CC0) as unlabeled background clouds
decision.why: Human labels collected before tuning keep the metric independent of the model. CCSN's 2,543 ground-level cloud photos (10 WMO genera plus contrails) give a large pool of ordinary clouds to calibrate scores against, without needing animal labels.

alternatives.name: Only live votes during the month
alternatives.tradeoff: Less upfront work, but every prompt change shifts the scores people vote on, so you cannot compare versions fairly.

alternatives.name: Label the test set yourself
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but one person's pareidolia is not a consensus, and you will unconsciously label toward what the model says.

verify: README states the one question and the metric: top-3 agreement with the human majority on the frozen 40, plus the 'none' rate
Commit the frozen 40 and a separate 20-photo dev set (photo ids, each friend's label) before any prompt or threshold is chosen
Inter-rater check: report how often at least 2 of 3 friends agree, so you know the ceiling

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The game is about clouds, never people. Sky photos still catch faces at the frame edge, windows and rooftops, and EXIF GPS that reveals where a player lives. Safety: never point the camera at the sun, and never play while driving or crossing a road.

decision.choice: On-device face check blocks the upload; EXIF stripped; only the crop is stored; no location kept
decision.why: A face detector on the phone (for example MediaPipe Face Detector) means faces never reach the server. The game needs no location, so storing none is simplest and safest.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach your server even briefly.

alternatives.name: Keep coarse location for a cloud map
alternatives.tradeoff: A fun feature, but it reveals players' home areas; add only with opt-in and heavy rounding.

steps.delegate: Client: run MediaPipe Face Detector on the full photo before upload; if a face is found, block and ask the player to recrop. Server: store only the crop with EXIF removed and delete the full image after cropping. Show a one-time notice: do not point at the sun, do not play while driving. Tests: a photo with a face never hits /photos; stored files have no EXIF; no table has a location column.
verify: Try uploading 10 sky photos with people in them and confirm none are stored
Inspect the database schema and storage folder: only crops, no GPS, no full frames

steps.title: Capture the photo and isolate the cloud
steps.learn: CLIP sees texture and context, not only outline, so a wide sky shot with rooftops may score 'a photo of a city'. Phone photos also carry EXIF orientation; Pillow's ImageOps.exif_transpose rotates the pixels so the model sees what the player saw.

decision.choice: Player drags a crop box around one cloud; the server applies exif_transpose, then embeds the crop
decision.why: A human crop is cheap, picks the cloud the player means, and removes trees and buildings that would otherwise dominate the embedding. It also makes the game feel like 'my cloud'.

alternatives.name: Automatic cloud segmentation
alternatives.tradeoff: No player effort, but sky segmentation is its own project and fails at sunset or under overcast skies.

alternatives.name: Embed the whole photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but scores are driven by the scene, not the cloud shape.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, Pillow, FastAPI. Endpoint POST /photos takes an image and crop box (x, y, w, h in displayed pixels). Apply ImageOps.exif_transpose, map the box to the transposed image, crop, resize the long side to 512, save as PNG with no EXIF. Tests: a rotated-EXIF test image crops the same region as its upright copy; saved files contain no EXIF; boxes outside the image are rejected with 400.
verify: Photograph one cloud in portrait and landscape and confirm both crops show the same cloud upright
Open a saved crop in an EXIF viewer and confirm no GPS or camera fields remain

steps.title: Decide between the raw photo and a silhouette view
steps.learn: What people see in clouds is mostly outline. An Otsu threshold (skimage.filters.threshold_otsu) picks a brightness cutoff that splits bright cloud from darker sky and gives a black and white silhouette, which removes texture that pulls CLIP toward 'cloud'. Whether that helps is an empirical question.

decision.choice: Embed both the raw crop and an Otsu silhouette; pick per-view by agreement on half of a dev split, not the frozen set
decision.why: You do not know in advance whether texture helps or hurts, so build both and measure. Keeping the frozen 40 out of this choice means the final number is still honest.

alternatives.name: Raw crop only
alternatives.tradeoff: One embedding per photo and less code, but CLIP may answer 'cloud' or 'sky' for everything.

alternatives.name: Edge map (outline only)
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to a line drawing, but soft cloud edges give broken, noisy outlines.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-image, numpy. Write silhouette(img) that converts to grayscale, applies threshold_otsu, returns a white-on-black PIL image, and keeps only the largest connected component (skimage.measure.label). Tests: a synthetic white ellipse on blue returns a mask with one component; an all-blue image returns an empty mask and the caller falls back to the raw view.
verify: Look at silhouettes for 20 of your own photos and count how many keep the shape you saw
On a dev set of 20 voted photos (not the frozen 40), record top-3 agreement for raw vs silhouette

steps.title: Write the animal vocabulary as ensembled prompts
steps.learn: Zero-shot CLIP compares one image vector to text vectors. Each animal becomes several prompts ('a cloud shaped like a rabbit', 'a silhouette of a rabbit') whose embeddings are averaged; the CLIP repo's ImageNet notebook shows this prompt ensembling. A fixed list keeps scores comparable across the month.

decision.choice: open_clip ViT-B-32 (laion2b_s34b_b79k), about 40 animals, 4 to 6 templates each, averaged and L2-normalized
decision.why: No training data exists for 'animal-shaped clouds', so zero-shot is the only realistic start. A small model embeds a crop quickly on a laptop CPU, and open_clip lists larger checkpoints to try if B-32 is the bottleneck.

alternatives.name: Free-text guesses from players only
alternatives.tradeoff: More fun and open-ended, but scores across different guesses are hard to compare without a fixed reference set.

alternatives.name: Ask a vision-language model
alternatives.tradeoff: Can explain its answer, but it is slower per photo and tends to describe the cloud literally.

steps.delegate: Python, open_clip, torch. animals.yaml lists animal ids and templates with a {name} slot for raw and silhouette views. build_text_matrix(view) returns normalized averaged embeddings, cached to disk keyed by model name and file hash. score(image_vec, view) returns cosine similarity per animal. Tests: vectors have unit norm, cache invalidates when the yaml changes, a clear photo of a cat ranks 'cat' in the top 3.
verify: On the 20-photo dev set, compare single template vs ensembled templates and record top-3 agreement
Print the 5 animals that appear most often as top-1 across 200 CCSN clouds and note any 'always wins' animal

steps.title: Calibrate scores against ordinary clouds
steps.learn: Raw cosine scores are not comparable across animals: some prompts score high on every cloud (a 'sheep' prior). Score each animal by its percentile among CCSN background clouds instead, so 'rabbit at the 99th percentile' means this cloud is unusually rabbit-like for a cloud.

decision.choice: Per-animal percentile against CCSN embeddings; show 'just a cloud' when no animal clears a percentile cutoff
decision.why: Percentiles remove per-prompt bias without labels, and the 'just a cloud' answer keeps the game honest on shapeless skies. The cutoff is tuned on the dev split only.

alternatives.name: Softmax over animals
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard zero-shot output, but it always names some animal with high confidence, even for a flat grey sky.

alternatives.name: Raw cosine threshold
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but one threshold cannot fit animals whose base rates differ.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. Precompute CCSN image embeddings for both views. For each animal, store the sorted background scores. percentile(animal, score) uses np.searchsorted. Return top 3 animals by percentile and a none flag if the best is under the cutoff. Tests: a background image scores near the middle on average; percentiles are in [0, 100]; the none flag triggers on a blank sky image.
verify: Plot how often each animal is top-1 on CCSN before and after calibration; the distribution should flatten
Report the 'none' rate on the dev split and on CCSN at your chosen cutoff

steps.title: Handle clouds that have no 'up'
steps.learn: A cloud rabbit may be lying on its side. Scoring rotations and mirror images and taking the max finds it, but taking the max over many views also inflates scores on any cloud (more tries, more lucky matches). So the background must be scored with exactly the same set of views.

decision.choice: 4 rotations plus mirror (8 views), max per animal, and recompute CCSN background percentiles with the same 8 views
decision.why: Matching the augmentation on both sides keeps the percentile meaning intact. Eight views keeps cost per photo bounded on CPU.

alternatives.name: Upright only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest and no inflation, but misses shapes people see sideways.

alternatives.name: Average over views instead of max
alternatives.tradeoff: No inflation, but a shape visible in only one orientation gets washed out.

steps.delegate: Python, Pillow, torch. views(img) returns the 8 rotation and mirror variants. Batch-embed them in one forward pass and take the max per animal. Rebuild the background percentile tables with the same function. Tests: views returns 8 distinct images for an asymmetric input; batching gives the same scores as one-by-one within float tolerance.
verify: On the dev split, record top-3 agreement for 1 view vs 8 views (both with matched backgrounds)
Record mean embedding time per photo for 1 vs 8 views on your machine

steps.title: Collapse burst shots of the same cloud
steps.learn: Players take several shots of one cloud seconds apart; without dedup one cloud floods the leaderboard. Perceptual hashes (imagehash.phash) change little for small edits, and subtracting two hashes gives the number of differing bits, so near-duplicates are hashes within a small distance.

decision.choice: phash plus same player within 10 minutes; keep the best-scoring shot and group the rest under it
decision.why: Clouds change shape quickly, so the time window plus hash distance catches bursts without merging the same sky an hour later, which really is a new cloud.

alternatives.name: CLIP embedding cosine
alternatives.tradeoff: Already computed, but many different clouds look alike to CLIP, so it over-merges.

alternatives.name: No dedup, limit uploads per hour
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but players still upload the same cloud five times.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, SQLite. On upload, compute phash of the crop, look up the same player's photos from the last 10 minutes, and group if the hash distance is under a threshold set in config. Tests: a re-encoded JPEG of the same crop groups; a different cloud from the same minute does not; groups expose one representative.
verify: Take 5 bursts of 3 shots and 5 single shots; report how many bursts merged and how many singles were wrongly merged
Record the hash distance threshold you chose and the distances you saw for both cases

steps.title: Rank matches by votes, not by the model's score
steps.learn: The leaderboard must be graded by people, or the game measures CLIP against itself. Each photo shows its top guess; friends vote 'yes, I see it' or 'no'. Sorting by raw yes-share lets one lucky vote win; the Wilson score lower bound ranks by how sure you are the share is high.

decision.choice: Up/down votes per photo, ranked by Wilson lower bound; no voting on your own photos
decision.why: Wilson handles photos with few votes fairly, which matters in a small friend group where vote counts stay low. Blocking self-votes removes the easiest way to game it.

alternatives.name: Pairwise 'which is better' votes (Elo)
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives a finer ranking, but needs many more comparisons than a small group will make.

alternatives.name: Rank by CLIP percentile
alternatives.tradeoff: No voting needed, but then the leaderboard just repeats the model and tells you nothing about it.

steps.delegate: FastAPI, SQLite. Tables: players, photos, votes(photo_id, voter_id, up bool, unique(photo_id, voter_id)). POST /votes rejects self-votes and duplicates. GET /leaderboard?week= returns photos sorted by Wilson lower bound (95%). Tests: 1 up of 1 ranks below 40 up of 50; duplicate and self votes return 409; ties break by vote count.
verify: Hand-compute the Wilson bound for two photos and match the API output
Confirm the leaderboard query reads only the votes table, never the CLIP score

links.label: How not to sort by average rating

steps.title: Test it outside: a month of clouds and votes
steps.learn: The try-it: collect cloud photos for a month and vote on the best matches. Log each photo's top 3 guesses, percentiles and votes so you can replay decisions later. Score the frozen 40 once at the start and once at the end with the final settings.
verify: Report photos per player per week and the share answered 'just a cloud'
Report top-3 agreement with the human majority on the frozen 40 for the final system and for a raw-softmax baseline
Report the Spearman correlation between CLIP percentile and Wilson score across all voted photos
List the 3 animals with the worst agreement and look at their photos

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example an animal that wins every cloud, or silhouettes helping only some shapes), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives frozen-set agreement, ablations (silhouette, ensembling, rotations, calibration) and latency, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with example photos
Part 4 lists assumptions (a few friends, one sky, one month, one model) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Fridge-to-recipe search
projects.problem: What can I cook with what I have?
projects.concepts: Ingredient detection from a fridge photo, recipe retrieval with hard filters (allergies, time)
projects.tryIt: Use it for your own dinners for two weeks
projects.question: Can a fridge photo plus hard allergy and time filters return a recipe I would actually cook tonight in its top 5?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen test sets
steps.learn: Two parts can fail separately: detection (did it see what is in the fridge) and retrieval (are the top 5 cookable, safe and fast enough). Success from the try-it: use it for your own dinners for two weeks. Freeze two test sets before tuning: hand-labeled fridge photos and a hand-labeled allergen audit sample.

decision.choice: Food.com Recipes and Interactions (Kaggle, 180K+ recipes) plus 25 of your own fridge photos labeled by hand
decision.why: Food.com includes a minutes field and ingredient lists per recipe, exactly what the time filter and ingredient matching need. Your own fridge photos are the only honest detection test, since public fridge datasets do not match your shelves or lighting.

alternatives.name: RecipeNLG or Recipe1M+
alternatives.tradeoff: More recipes, but you would need to check which fields (like cook time) exist before relying on them.

alternatives.name: A recipe API
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean data and images, but rate limits, cost and terms you do not control, and results you cannot audit offline.

verify: README states the question and metrics: ingredient recall and precision on the 25 photos, top-5 'would cook' rate, missed-allergen count
The 25 labeled photos (kept local, no people or papers in frame) and the allergen audit sample are frozen before any threshold or weight is set
Record the dataset version and the machine you will run on

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: A fridge photo shows the inside of a home: family photos and notes on the door, names on prescriptions, sometimes people in the frame. Identify food, never people. For allergies the app is a helper: the person with the allergy must check product labels and official guidance.

decision.choice: Run detection locally, keep only the confirmed ingredient list, delete the photo after scan
decision.why: Nothing in the search needs the photo after detection, so not storing it removes the main privacy risk. Local detection means no third party sees inside your home.

alternatives.name: Keep photos to improve the detector
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful training data, but you then store images of your home; only with explicit opt-in and face blurring.

alternatives.name: Hosted vision API
alternatives.tradeoff: Less setup, but every photo leaves your machine under someone else's retention terms.

steps.delegate: Delete the uploaded image once /scan returns; store only scan id, timestamp and the confirmed list. Add a persistent banner on results: 'Allergy filter is a helper. Always check product labels.' Tests: the uploads folder is empty after a scan; results HTML contains the banner; logs contain no image bytes.
verify: Run 5 scans and confirm no image files remain on disk
Confirm the allergy banner appears on every results page

steps.title: Detect ingredients with an open-vocabulary detector
steps.learn: A fridge has hundreds of possible items and no training set. Open-vocabulary detectors such as OWLv2 take free-text queries ('a carton of eggs', 'a bell pepper') and return boxes with scores, so the vocabulary is just a list you edit. Expect misses for items inside opaque containers or behind others.

decision.choice: OWLv2 (google/owlv2-base-patch16-ensemble via transformers) with a ~150-item ingredient query list, run locally
decision.why: Runs on your own machine, so fridge photos never leave home, and boxes let the UI show what it saw for quick correction. The query list doubles as the normalized vocabulary for search.

alternatives.name: Vision-language model listing items as JSON
alternatives.tradeoff: Often better at packaged and partly hidden items, but slower, may invent items, and a hosted one sends your kitchen photo to a third party.

alternatives.name: CLIP on grid crops
alternatives.tradeoff: Very cheap, but crops cut items in half and it cannot count or localize.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, transformers, torch, Pillow. detect(image, queries) uses Owlv2Processor and Owlv2ForObjectDetection, post_process_grounded_object_detection with a configurable threshold, and returns [{ingredient, score, box}]. Merge duplicates per ingredient keeping the max score. Tests: output schema; threshold 1.0 returns nothing; a stock photo of eggs returns 'egg'.
verify: Run on 10 of your photos (not the frozen 25) and list items it missed and items it invented
Pick the score threshold on those 10 and record precision and recall at 3 thresholds

steps.title: Let the cook confirm the ingredient list
steps.learn: Detection will be wrong sometimes, and a wrong 'I have cream' sends you to a recipe you cannot make. A 10-second confirm screen (tick or untick detected items, add missing ones by typing) turns a noisy detector into a reliable input, and every correction is a free label.

decision.choice: Checklist of detected items above a threshold, plus 'maybe' items below it, plus a typed add box
decision.why: Showing 'maybe' items lets you lower the threshold for recall without spamming the main list. Logged corrections tell you which queries to reword.

alternatives.name: Use detections directly
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer taps, but every false positive becomes a recipe you cannot cook.

alternatives.name: Type ingredients only
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate, but then the photo adds nothing and the project question is moot.

steps.delegate: FastAPI plus a small HTML page. POST /scan returns detections split into likely and maybe; POST /confirm stores the final list and the diff (added, removed) with the scan id. Tests: the diff is computed correctly; confirmed lists only contain vocabulary ids or free-text items flagged as unmatched.
verify: Time yourself confirming 5 scans and record median seconds
Check the stored diffs and list the 3 most-removed and most-added items

steps.title: Normalize recipe ingredients to your vocabulary
steps.learn: Recipe ingredients are free text ('large eggs', 'egg whites', 'boneless skinless chicken breasts'). Matching needs both sides in one vocabulary: map each recipe ingredient string to a canonical id. RapidFuzz scores string similarity (for example fuzz.token_set_ratio) for the long tail after an exact synonym table.

decision.choice: Synonym table for the most frequent ingredient strings, RapidFuzz for the rest, unmatched kept as 'unknown'
decision.why: A few hundred frequent strings cover most ingredient mentions, so hand-checking them is affordable. Keeping 'unknown' explicit (instead of a forced fuzzy match) protects the allergen filter later.

alternatives.name: Text embeddings nearest neighbor
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles paraphrases, but confuses close but different items (butter vs margarine) that matter for allergies.

alternatives.name: LLM normalization with structured output
alternatives.tradeoff: Good on odd strings, but costly over every recipe and must itself be audited.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas, rapidfuzz. Load RAW_recipes.csv, parse the ingredients column with ast.literal_eval, count string frequencies, write top strings to synonyms.csv for review. normalize(s) tries exact synonym, then rapidfuzz.process.extractOne over vocabulary with a score cutoff, else 'unknown'. Tests: 'large eggs' maps to egg; a nonsense string maps to unknown.
verify: Hand-check 100 random normalized strings and report the error rate
Report the share of ingredient mentions left 'unknown'

steps.title: Build an inverted index from ingredient to recipes
steps.learn: Search is a set problem: recipes whose ingredients overlap what you have. An inverted index maps each canonical ingredient to the recipe ids that use it, so candidates are a union of a few posting lists instead of a scan of every recipe.

decision.choice: In-memory dict of ingredient id to sorted recipe id arrays, built once at startup from normalized recipes
decision.why: A few hundred thousand recipes fit comfortably in memory, so a plain index is fast and easy to test. Candidates then go through hard filters and ranking as separate stages.

alternatives.name: SQLite join table (recipe_id, ingredient_id)
alternatives.tradeoff: Persistent and queryable with SQL, with a little more latency and query-tuning work.

alternatives.name: Embedding search over recipe text
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds 'similar' recipes, but cannot guarantee you have the ingredients.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy. build_index(recipes) returns {ingredient_id: np.array of recipe ids}. candidates(have) returns recipe ids with at least one overlap, plus an overlap count per id. Tests: a recipe appears under each of its ingredients; candidates for an empty list are empty; overlap counts match a brute-force scan on 1000 recipes.
verify: Record index build time and memory use on your machine
Record p50 candidate-generation latency for 20 confirmed fridge lists

steps.title: Make the allergy filter a hard, conservative exclusion
steps.learn: FDA lists nine major allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Recipe text rarely says 'milk'; it says butter or parmesan. An allergy must exclude before ranking, not be a score penalty, and the app is only a helper: product labels are the source of truth.

decision.choice: Per-allergen keyword lexicon over raw and normalized strings; exclude matches; also exclude recipes with 'unknown' items
decision.why: False exclusions cost a recipe; false inclusions can hurt someone. Matching raw text as well as canonical ids catches strings normalization missed, and dropping unknowns trades recall for safety.

alternatives.name: Score penalty instead of exclusion
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more results, but an allergen recipe can still rank first.

alternatives.name: LLM allergen tagging per recipe
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles odd phrasing, but must itself be audited and can silently miss.

steps.delegate: Python. allergens.yaml maps each FDA allergen to keywords (butter, cheese, cream for milk; tahini for sesame; soy sauce for soy and wheat). filter_allergens(recipe_ids, allergies) excludes any recipe whose raw or normalized ingredients contain a keyword, or that has unknown items. Tests: a recipe with 'parmesan' is excluded for milk; 'soy sauce' is excluded for both soy and wheat.
verify: On the frozen audit sample (200 recipes hand-labeled for allergens by you, not by the lexicon), report missed allergens per allergen
Confirm the result screen says to check product labels and that the app is a helper only

steps.title: Apply the time limit and audit the minutes field
steps.learn: The time filter is only as good as the minutes field, which is entered by recipe authors. Some values will be zero, missing or implausibly large, and some include marinating or chilling time. Look at the distribution before trusting it as a hard cutoff.

decision.choice: Hard filter minutes <= limit; drop recipes with zero or missing minutes from timed searches
decision.why: A tired cook asking for 30 minutes should never get a 2-hour recipe. Dropping zero or missing values is safer than guessing.

alternatives.name: Estimate time from step count
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovers recipes with bad minutes, but the estimate is a new model you must validate.

alternatives.name: Soft penalty for over-limit recipes
alternatives.tradeoff: More results, but breaks the promise of the filter.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas. Write audit_minutes() that prints counts of zero, missing and very large minutes and a histogram, and filter_time(ids, limit) that keeps recipes with 0 < minutes <= limit. Tests: boundary minutes == limit is kept; zero and missing are excluded; filters compose with the allergen filter in either order with identical results.
verify: Report the minutes distribution and how many recipes the zero or missing rule removes
Time 5 dinners you cook and compare to the listed minutes

steps.title: Rank the safe recipes by what you are missing
steps.learn: After hard filters, order by a few interpretable features: count of missing non-staple ingredients (fewer is better), share of the recipe covered by what you have, and a small popularity signal from ratings in the interactions file. A short staples list (salt, pepper, oil, water) is assumed in stock.

decision.choice: Sort by missing count, then coverage, then a smoothed average rating as tie-breaker
decision.why: Missing items are what actually stop you cooking, so they dominate. Rating smoothing stops a single 5-star review from winning.

alternatives.name: Learned ranker from your picks
alternatives.tradeoff: Fits your taste, but two weeks of dinners is too few labels.

alternatives.name: Coverage only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but favors tiny recipes like 'buttered toast' that use one item.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas. rank(ids, have, staples) computes missing_count, coverage and a Bayesian-smoothed mean rating from RAW_interactions.csv, ignoring rating 0 (a review with no stars), sorts lexicographically and returns top 20 with the missing items listed. Tests: a recipe with 0 missing outranks 1 missing regardless of rating; staples never count as missing; 0 ratings are excluded.
verify: For 5 confirmed fridge lists, label the top 5 as 'would cook tonight' yes or no and report the rate
Compare against coverage-only ranking on the same 5 lists

steps.title: Test it in your kitchen: two weeks of dinners
steps.learn: The try-it: use it for your own dinners for two weeks. Log each scan, the corrections, which result you picked (or none), and the actual cook time. Score detection on the frozen 25 photos once with the final settings.
verify: Report nights used, nights you cooked a suggested recipe, and the rank of the picked recipe
Report ingredient recall and precision on the frozen 25 photos and median confirm time
Report any allergen slip found in the audit sample or in use (target zero)
Report listed vs actual minutes for the recipes you cooked

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example items the detector never sees, or recipes the minutes field mislabels), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives detection, top-5 'would cook', allergen audit and latency numbers, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with examples
Part 4 lists assumptions (one kitchen, one cook, two weeks, Food.com recipes) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Grocery price tracker
projects.problem: Prices for the same item vary across stores and weeks
projects.concepts: Receipt OCR, entity normalization ("2% milk 1gal" = "Milk 2% 128oz")
projects.tryIt: Scan your receipts for a month and find the cheapest store per item
projects.question: From a month of my own receipts, which store is cheapest for each item I buy once products are matched across stores and compared by unit price?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the data
steps.learn: Prices for the same item vary across stores and weeks. The answer only holds if three things work: reading receipts correctly, knowing two lines are the same product, and comparing per unit. Success: after a month, a per-item cheapest-store table you trust, with error rates for each stage.

decision.choice: Your own month of receipts as main data; CORD v2 to test OCR and parsing; Open Prices as a price reference
decision.why: Only your receipts answer your question. CORD v2 (labeled receipts, CC BY 4.0) lets you measure parsing before you have many receipts, though its receipts are Indonesian shop and restaurant receipts, not your stores. Open Prices is an open crowdsourced price dataset (ODbL) to sanity-check prices.

alternatives.name: SROIE (ICDAR 2019) receipts
alternatives.tradeoff: A standard receipt OCR and key-field benchmark, but it labels totals and header fields rather than individual line items.

alternatives.name: Only your receipts
alternatives.tradeoff: Most relevant, but with no labeled set you cannot tell OCR errors from parser errors early on.

verify: Write the one question and the stage metrics: line-item recall, price exact-match rate, product match precision
List the stores you shop at and the 20 items you buy most often

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Receipts identify things and places, but also people: partial card numbers, loyalty IDs, cashier names, and a timestamped log of where you shop. Keep products and stores, drop the rest. Prices are a helper from your past receipts, and shelf prices and store terms are the official source.

decision.choice: Redact payment, loyalty and cashier lines at parse time; keep images local; cloud OCR or LLM only with explicit opt-in
decision.why: The question needs product, store, date and price only. Dropping identifying lines before storage removes most risk, and keeping images local means no cloud service sees anything unless you opt in; Textract opt-in uploads the whole image, so crop off payment lines first.

alternatives.name: Store everything, secure the database
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps full detail for debugging, but any leak exposes payment and shopping-pattern data.

alternatives.name: Delete images after parsing
alternatives.tradeoff: Smallest footprint, but you lose the ability to re-run better OCR later.

steps.delegate: Python. Add redact(lines) before storage: drop lines matching card patterns (masked digits, 'VISA', 'AUTH'), loyalty or member numbers, and cashier name lines per store config. Add a config flag allow_cloud=false that blocks Textract and LLM calls. Tests: fixtures with card and loyalty lines produce no stored digits; with allow_cloud=false no network call is made.
verify: Grep the database for 4-digit card fragments and loyalty numbers and confirm none remain
Confirm the app labels prices as 'from your receipts on DATE' and says to check the shelf

steps.title: Capture receipts so OCR has a fair chance
steps.learn: Most OCR errors start at capture: thermal paper fades, receipts curl, long receipts do not fit one frame, and shadows break binarization. Some stores also offer digital receipts, which skip OCR entirely.

decision.choice: Phone photo with page detection and perspective correction, plus import of digital receipts where available
decision.why: Photos work for every store, and flattening the receipt before OCR fixes skew and curl cheaply. Digital receipts (email or store app) are exact text, so they are a free accuracy win and a ground truth for checking your OCR on the same store's layout.

alternatives.name: Flatbed scanner
alternatives.tradeoff: Best image quality and consistent resolution, but too much friction to keep up for a month.

alternatives.name: Digital receipts only
alternatives.tradeoff: No OCR errors at all, but most stores or payment paths do not provide them, so coverage is partial.

steps.delegate: Python, OpenCV. Write preprocess.py: detect the largest 4-point contour, warp to a top-down view, convert to grayscale, upscale small images, save the original and processed images with a receipt_id. Support long receipts as two overlapping photos per receipt, and drop OCR lines repeated in the overlap when merging. Tests: a rotated synthetic receipt image is deskewed; originals are never overwritten.
verify: Photograph 10 receipts and confirm all 10 are detected and flattened
Keep originals so you can re-run OCR later with a different engine

steps.title: Choose the OCR engine
steps.learn: OCR returns text plus boxes; receipts are hard because of narrow fonts, faded print and columns of prices. Tesseract's docs advise at least 300 DPI, note its built-in Otsu binarization struggles with uneven backgrounds, and say to pick a page segmentation mode (--psm). Measure engines on your receipts.

decision.choice: Local OCR with line boxes (PaddleOCR, or Apple Vision text recognition on iOS), with Tesseract as the baseline
decision.why: Local engines keep receipts off third-party servers and cost nothing per page. Line-level boxes let the parser align item names with prices. Running Tesseract with tuned --psm as a baseline tells you whether the heavier engine is worth it.

alternatives.name: AWS Textract AnalyzeExpense
alternatives.tradeoff: Receipt-aware cloud API that returns line items and fields, but costs per page and sends receipts to a third party.

alternatives.name: VLM reads the image to JSON
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles messy layouts with no parser, but may produce plausible wrong prices; needs checks against the receipt total.

alternatives.name: Donut (OCR-free model)
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns image to structured output end to end, but needs fine-tuning on receipts like yours to beat a tuned pipeline.

steps.delegate: Python. Implement an OCR interface ocr(image) returning lines [{text, bbox, confidence}] with two backends: pytesseract (configurable --psm) and PaddleOCR. Write eval_ocr.py that computes character error rate per receipt against CORD v2 ground truth text and against 10 hand-typed receipts of your own. Tests: both backends return the same schema; empty image returns no lines.
verify: Hand-type 10 of your receipts and record character error rate for each engine
Record which engine gets the price column exactly right more often

steps.title: Parse line items, quantities, discounts and totals
steps.learn: A receipt line is not always an item: there are quantity lines ('2 @ 1.99'), weighed items ('1.32 lb @ 2.49/lb'), coupon lines that belong to the item above, tax flags and subtotals. The receipt total is a free check: items minus discounts should equal the subtotal.

decision.choice: Rule-based parser with per-store patterns, validated by a subtotal checksum; LLM extraction only when the checksum fails
decision.why: Each store's layout repeats, so a few regexes per store are cheap, fast and explainable. The checksum catches OCR and parsing errors automatically. An LLM with a strict JSON schema (for example Pydantic) is a fallback, and its output must pass the same checksum.

alternatives.name: LLM extraction for every receipt
alternatives.tradeoff: Works on unseen layouts with no rules, but costs per receipt and can invent or drop lines.

alternatives.name: Train a layout model on CORD
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns structure from labels, but CORD's layouts differ from your stores, so you would need your own labels.

steps.delegate: Python. parse(lines, store_id) returns {store, date, items:[{raw_text, qty, unit_price, line_total, weight, discount}], subtotal, checksum_ok}. Group OCR boxes into rows by y overlap; per-store regex config in YAML; attach negative lines to the previous item. Fallback: call an LLM with a Pydantic schema when checksum fails. Tests: fixtures for quantity, weight and coupon lines; checksum fails when one price is altered.
verify: On 20 receipts record line-item recall and the share passing the checksum
Hand-check 5 checksum failures and record whether OCR or parsing caused each

steps.title: Normalize sizes and compute unit prices
steps.learn: '2% milk 1gal' and 'Milk 2% 128oz' are the same size: a US gallon is 128 US fluid ounces. Comparing sticker prices across sizes is unfair, so convert to a base unit (ml, g or count) and compare price per unit. Watch for 'oz' meaning weight vs fluid ounces, and sizes missing from the receipt.

decision.choice: Parse size strings to quantities with pint, convert to ml, g or count; fill missing sizes from the product record
decision.why: A units library (pint's UnitRegistry) handles conversions and refuses invalid ones like mass to volume, which catches parsing bugs. Receipts often abbreviate or omit size, so the canonical product (or an Open Food Facts quantity) supplies it.

alternatives.name: Hand-written conversion table
alternatives.tradeoff: No dependency and easy to read, but every new unit and abbreviation is a manual edit and errors are silent.

alternatives.name: Compare sticker prices only
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial, but a 1 gal vs half-gallon comparison gives the wrong cheapest store.

steps.delegate: Python, pint. parse_size(text) handles '1gal', '128oz', '128 fl oz', '12ct', '1.5 lb', '500g'; returns (quantity, dimension) or None. Pre-normalize before pint: 'fl oz' to 'floz'; handle 'ct'/'pk' as count yourself (pint reads 'ct' as carat). Bare 'oz' on liquids (by category) means floz. Tests: 1 gal equals 128 fl oz; '12ct' is count; mass to volume raises; missing size returns None, not 0.
verify: Check 30 real size strings from your receipts and record the share parsed correctly
Confirm 1 gal and 128 fl oz give the same unit price for the same price

steps.title: Define what 'the same item' means and build the catalog
steps.learn: Before matching, decide the comparison level: the exact product (one brand, one size) or a comparable class (any brand of 2% milk, compared per unit). Receipts use store abbreviations ('MLK 2PCT GAL'), so you need a canonical product table plus an alias table per store.

decision.choice: Canonical comparable-product classes (category, attributes, base unit) with per-store alias rows
decision.why: Different stores sell different brands, so exact-product matching would leave few items comparable across stores. A class like 'milk, 2%, per liter' answers your actual question. Aliases learned once per store make later receipts match instantly.

alternatives.name: Exact product by barcode (UPC/EAN)
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise and unambiguous, but receipts usually show store codes or abbreviations, not barcodes.

alternatives.name: Free-form text, no catalog
alternatives.tradeoff: No upfront work, but every comparison needs fresh matching and results drift.

steps.delegate: SQLite schema: products(id, name, category, attributes JSON, base_unit), aliases(store_id, raw_text_normalized, product_id, source in [rule, fuzzy, embedding, llm, human], confidence). Normalizer: lowercase, expand a per-store abbreviation dictionary (YAML), strip sizes and prices. Seed with your 20 most-bought items. Tests: normalizer is idempotent; same raw text at the same store maps to the same product.
verify: Write the class definition for your 20 most-bought items and get the list reviewed by one other person
Record how many receipt lines in week one map via exact alias

steps.title: Match receipt lines to products: rules, fuzzy, embeddings, LLM
steps.learn: Use the cheapest method that is confident, then escalate. Fuzzy string scores handle reordering and typos; embeddings handle synonyms; an LLM handles cryptic abbreviations. Each needs a threshold, and a wrong match is worse than no match because it corrupts price comparisons.

decision.choice: Cascade: alias, RapidFuzz token_set_ratio, sentence-transformers top-k, LLM pick; low confidence to review
decision.why: Most lines repeat, so aliases and fuzzy matching resolve them at near zero cost. Embeddings shortlist candidates for the rest, and the LLM only chooses among that shortlist. Confirmed matches become aliases, so the expensive steps shrink each week.

alternatives.name: LLM for every line
