alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest pipeline, but costs per line, adds latency and may match the same text differently on different days.

alternatives.name: Fuzzy matching only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and fast, but fails on abbreviations that share few characters with the product name.

alternatives.name: Manual matching
alternatives.tradeoff: Perfectly accurate for one person, but tedious enough that you stop after week two.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz, sentence-transformers. match(raw, store_id) returns (product_id or None, method, score). Stages with configurable thresholds; block candidates by category and unit dimension; LLM gets raw text plus top-5 candidates and must answer an id or 'none'. Cache LLM answers as aliases with source='llm'. Tests: alias hit skips later stages; an incompatible unit dimension is never matched.
verify: Label 100 receipt lines by hand and record precision and coverage per stage
Record how many LLM calls were needed in week 1 vs week 4

steps.title: Store price history you can reprocess
steps.learn: Each matched line becomes a price observation: product, store, date, unit price, whether it was on promotion. Parsers and matchers will improve, so keep raw OCR and parse output and record which version produced each observation, so history can be rebuilt instead of hand-fixed.

decision.choice: SQLite with receipts, raw_lines, observations tables; observations derived and versioned, raw data immutable
decision.why: One person's month of receipts is small, and a single file is easy to back up and query. Keeping raw data immutable and observations derived means a matcher fix is a re-run, not a manual edit. Use transactions so a receipt's observations commit together.

alternatives.name: Postgres
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for many users and concurrent writers, but more setup than one person needs.

alternatives.name: Spreadsheet
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to eyeball and edit, but no reprocessing, weak typing and easy to corrupt.

steps.delegate: Python, sqlite3. Tables: stores, receipts(id, store_id, date, image_path), raw_lines(receipt_id, ocr_engine, text, bbox), observations(product_id, store_id, date, unit_price, regular_or_promo, pipeline_version). rebuild_observations(version) re-derives from raw_lines in one transaction. Tests: rebuild is idempotent; deleting a receipt removes its observations; dates parse to ISO.
verify: Change one alias and rebuild; confirm only the affected observations change
Query the unit price history of one item across all stores

steps.title: Compare stores fairly
steps.learn: 'Cheapest' is easy to get wrong: one promotion can win the month, prices move week to week, and an item seen once at a store is not evidence. Separate regular from promotional prices, align by week, require a minimum number of observations, and report coverage alongside the answer.

decision.choice: Per item: median regular unit price per store, items seen at 2+ stores with min observations, promos apart
decision.why: The median resists one-off sales and OCR outliers. Requiring the same item at two or more stores means each comparison is real. Showing promo prices separately answers 'where is it cheap on sale' without hiding the everyday price.

alternatives.name: Lowest price ever seen
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy and exciting, but rewards one-time promotions you may never see again.

alternatives.name: Basket index across stores
alternatives.tradeoff: Answers 'which store overall', but hides per-item differences and needs the same basket at every store.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas. compare(month) returns per product: store, median_regular_unit_price, n_obs, min_promo_price, and a winner only when n_obs meets a threshold at 2+ stores. Output a CSV and a short text table. Tests: a single promo observation cannot make a store the winner; items seen at one store are listed as 'not comparable'.
verify: Report how many of your 20 top items had a valid comparison
For 3 winners, check a shelf price in person and record whether the ranking held

steps.title: Test it outside: a month of real receipts
steps.learn: The try-it: scan every receipt for a month and find the cheapest store per item. Measure each stage so you know which one limits the answer, and log manual fixes as labels.
verify: Report receipts scanned, share passing the checksum, and line-item recall on 10 hand-checked receipts
Report match precision on 100 labeled lines and the share needing review
Produce the cheapest-store table with n_obs per cell and the share of items comparable
Record minutes per week spent on manual fixes

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a store winning only through promos, or a matcher error), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives OCR, parsing, matching and comparison numbers, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (one shopper, one month, your stores) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Hidden-allergen checker
projects.problem: Allergens hide under other names (casein, whey = milk)
projects.concepts: Label OCR, synonym and entity normalization
projects.tryIt: Scan 100 packaged foods at home or in a store
projects.question: Can label OCR plus an ingredient taxonomy catch major allergens hidden under other names (whey, casein mean milk) on real packages without missing any?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen test set
steps.learn: The checker reads a label photo and answers: which of my allergens does this declare, may contain, or cannot be ruled out? The costly error is a miss, so the headline metric is recall per (product, allergen) pair, then precision and how often it abstains. The try-it is scanning 100 packaged foods.

decision.choice: OFF US English ingredient photos (50 dev, 100 frozen test), hand-labeled from the photo, then 100 own scans
decision.why: OFF exports include products with ingredient-label photos, so you can test before visiting a store. Labeling truth yourself from the photo, not from OFF's allergen tags, keeps the grader independent of any tagging logic. Freezing the 100 test products now stops you tuning thresholds on them.

alternatives.name: Use OFF allergens_tags as ground truth
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and large, but those tags are crowd and rule generated and can disagree with the printed text, so you would grade against another system's errors.

alternatives.name: Only your own 100 store scans
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use, but you have nothing to tune on without leaking the test set, and labeling happens under store conditions.

verify: Write the question and 3 metrics: recall per (product, allergen), precision, share of products where the app abstains
Save the 100 test barcodes, photos and your hand labels to a read-only file with a hash, before writing any matcher code
Compare OFF allergens_tags with your hand labels on 10 dev products and note every disagreement

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app looks at packages, not people: no faces, no staff, no location history. It is a reading helper; the official source is the printed label and the manufacturer, which FDA advises contacting when unsure. Anyone with a severe allergy should follow their clinician, not this app.

decision.choice: Discard photos after OCR; store only barcode, verdict and evidence; show 'check the label' on every result
decision.why: The evaluation needs product identity and the text that drove the verdict, not images or where you shopped. A notice on every result, plus never saying 'safe', keeps the tool from being read as a guarantee.

alternatives.name: Keep all photos for debugging
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to analyze OCR failures, but photos can capture people, receipts or locations; keep only opted-in dev photos, cropped to the panel.

alternatives.name: Send photos to a cloud OCR or VLM
alternatives.tradeoff: May read better, but every label photo goes to a third party; require explicit opt-in per scan.

steps.delegate: Python. Add a store_scan() that accepts only barcode, verdicts and evidence spans; images are never written to disk unless dev_capture=true. Add a config allow_cloud=false that blocks any cloud call. Every response includes a fixed disclaimer field. Tests: with defaults no image file appears on disk; with allow_cloud=false no outbound OCR request is made; disclaimer is present on abstain too.
verify: Scan 5 products and confirm no image files remain on the server or phone app storage
Confirm every result screen shows the check-the-label notice and no screen uses the word safe

steps.title: Pin down which allergens and which label rules you cover
steps.learn: FALCPA plus the FASTER Act (sesame, 2023) set 9 US major allergens: milk, egg, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy, sesame. The source must be named in the ingredients, as in 'whey (milk)', or in a 'Contains' line. 'May contain' is voluntary; USDA meat, poultry, egg products are outside FALCPA.

decision.choice: Three outputs per allergen: declared, advisory ('may contain'), or cannot rule out; never 'allergen-free'
decision.why: Declared and advisory mean different things, and the law leaves gaps: highly refined oils are exempt, spices and flavorings may be listed as a class, and a user's non-major allergen (say mustard) can hide there. A third state makes those gaps visible instead of implying safety.

alternatives.name: Binary contains / does not contain
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest UI, but 'does not contain' reads as a safety guarantee the label cannot give.

alternatives.name: Per-region rule packs (EU, UK, Canada)
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for imported or foreign labels, since allergen lists and rules differ by country, but each pack needs its own fact-checked spec and test labels.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Write allergens.yaml with the 9 US major allergens (id, display name) plus a user_custom list, and rules.md citing FALCPA. Implement a dataclass Verdict(allergen, state in {declared, advisory, cannot_rule_out, not_found}, evidence_spans). Tests: no code path returns a state named safe or free; custom allergens round-trip through the YAML loader.
verify: Find 3 dev labels: one with parenthetical declaration, one with a Contains line, one with a 'may contain' line
List which of your test products are USDA-regulated meat, poultry or egg products and mark them out of scope

steps.title: Capture the label photo and use the barcode only as a hint
steps.learn: A barcode lookup gives a product name and maybe an ingredient list fast, but recipes change and crowd data can be stale, so the printed label in your hand is the source of truth. The OFF API asks for a custom User-Agent and limits product reads to 15 requests per minute per IP; bulk work should use the exports.

decision.choice: Scan barcode, show OFF data as a preview, but always OCR a fresh photo of the ingredient panel for the verdict
decision.why: The verdict must reflect the package being bought. The barcode still helps: it names the product, and a mismatch between OFF's ingredient text and your OCR text is a useful signal that the recipe changed or OCR failed.

alternatives.name: Barcode lookup only, no photo
alternatives.tradeoff: Instant and works on bad cameras, but trusts a database row that may be outdated, incomplete, or missing for store brands.

alternatives.name: Photo only, no barcode
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer moving parts, but you lose the cross-check and the product identity used in logs and evaluation.

steps.delegate: Python, FastAPI, httpx. Endpoint POST /scan takes barcode (optional) and an image. Client lookup_off(barcode) calls /api/v2/product/{code}?fields=product_name,ingredients_text_en,allergens_tags,traces_tags with a custom User-Agent, caches results in SQLite, and backs off on HTTP 429 or 503. Phone side: a web page with a camera file input. Tests: cache hit makes no network call; unknown barcode returns a clean 'not found'.
verify: Look up 10 dev barcodes twice and confirm the second lookup is served from the SQLite cache with no network call
Replay 20 dev barcode lookups through the client and confirm it never sends more than 15 product reads per minute

steps.title: Choose the OCR engine for small, curved ingredient text
steps.learn: Ingredient panels are dense small print on glossy, curved packaging. Tesseract's docs say it works best at 300 DPI or more, offer adaptive binarization, and let you set the page segmentation mode (--psm) for blocks of text. Measure engines on your dev photos, not on clean scans.

decision.choice: Tesseract via pytesseract with preprocessing as baseline, compared against ML Kit text recognition v2 on the phone
decision.why: Both run locally and are free, so photos need not leave your devices. ML Kit processes on-device and returns lines with confidence; Tesseract is easy to script in the Python eval harness. Character error rate on the 50 dev photos decides which one feeds the matcher.

alternatives.name: VLM reads the panel to text
alternatives.tradeoff: Often better on glare and curves, but can silently fix or invent words, which is dangerous when one missed word is an allergen; costs per call.

alternatives.name: PaddleOCR
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong open detector plus recognizer for scene text, but a heavier install than Tesseract; worth trying if both baselines fail on curved packs.

steps.delegate: Python. Interface ocr(image) returns lines {text, bbox, confidence}. Backend 1: OpenCV upscale, grayscale, adaptive threshold, then pytesseract.image_to_data with configurable --psm. Backend 2: read ML Kit JSON exported from a small Android test app. eval_ocr.py computes character error rate per photo vs hand-typed dev transcripts. Tests: schema identical across backends; blank image yields no lines.
verify: Hand-type 20 dev ingredient panels and record character error rate per engine
Count how often each engine garbles an allergen-bearing word (milk, whey, wheat, soy) on those 20

steps.title: Find the ingredient list and split it respecting parentheses
steps.learn: OCR text mixes nutrition facts, marketing and addresses. You need three spans: the ingredient list, any 'Contains' statement and any 'may contain' line. Ingredients nest, as in 'chocolate (sugar, cocoa butter, milk)', so splitting on commas alone attaches allergens to the wrong parent.

decision.choice: Rule-based segmenter: anchor on 'ingredients', 'contains', 'may contain' and split with a parenthesis-aware tokenizer
decision.why: US labels use a small set of anchor words, rules are inspectable, and every output span is a substring of the OCR text, so nothing is invented. Failures (no anchor found) become an explicit 'cannot read' instead of a guess.

alternatives.name: OFF ingredient-detection NER model
alternatives.tradeoff: Trained to find ingredient lists in OCR text in several languages; better on odd layouts, but adds a model to host and still needs the Contains parser.

alternatives.name: LLM with structured JSON output
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles messy text, but must be forced to return exact substrings and checked, or it may drop or add items.

steps.delegate: Python. segment(ocr_text) returns {ingredients_span, contains_span, advisory_span, ok}. tokenize_ingredients(span) returns a tree of {name, children} honoring nested () and []. Tests: 'chocolate (sugar, milk), salt' gives milk under chocolate; unbalanced parentheses do not crash and set ok=false; 'Contains: wheat, milk.' parses to two items; every span is a substring of the input.
verify: On 30 dev photos, count segmentations you judge correct and list the failure causes
Confirm the segmenter returns ok=false rather than a partial list on 3 deliberately cropped photos

steps.title: Normalize ingredient names to taxonomy entries, then fuzzy-fix OCR
steps.learn: The hidden-name problem is an entity normalization problem: 'sodium caseinate', 'whey powder' and 'Casein' must map to known entries. The OFF ingredients taxonomy lists synonyms per entry. OCR noise ('wbey', 'caseinatc') needs fuzzy matching, but loose fuzzy matches can also invent allergens or hide them.

decision.choice: Exact synonym lookup first, then RapidFuzz only above a strict score and minimum length, marked fuzzy
decision.why: Exact matches are reliable and explainable. Fuzzy rescue is needed for OCR errors, but short tokens match too much, so a length floor and a tuned score keep it honest. Marking fuzzy matches lets the UI show 'read as whey?' instead of a silent assumption.

alternatives.name: Exact match only
alternatives.tradeoff: No false fixes, but every OCR typo in an allergen word becomes a miss, which is the costly error here.

alternatives.name: Embedding similarity to taxonomy names
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches paraphrases, but similar-looking vectors can link unrelated foods, and scores are harder to threshold and explain.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz. Load OFF ingredients.txt (English synonyms) into a dict mapping normalized synonym to entry id. normalize(token) lowercases, strips percentages and punctuation. match(token) tries exact, then rapidfuzz.process.extractOne with a configurable scorer and cutoff, returning {entry, score, method}. Tests: 'Sodium Caseinate 2%' matches exactly; 'wbey' matches whey only as fuzzy; tokens under 4 characters never fuzzy-match.
verify: Tune the fuzzy cutoff on dev tokens only and record exact, fuzzy and unmatched rates
List the 10 most frequent unmatched dev tokens and decide for each: OCR error, missing synonym, or non-food text

steps.title: Resolve allergens by walking the taxonomy parents
steps.learn: In the OFF ingredients taxonomy, entries name parents with '<' lines and some carry an 'allergens:en:' property. 'Casein' sits under 'milk proteins', which carries en:milk; 'whey' sits under 'dairy', which also carries en:milk. OFF ids are not the US list: semolina resolves to en:gluten, so map ids to your 9 allergens.

decision.choice: Union of the taxonomy ancestor walk and the parsed Contains statement, with disagreements flagged
decision.why: The Contains line is the manufacturer's own declaration; the ancestor walk catches hidden names when there is no Contains line or OCR missed it. When one source says milk and the other does not, flagging it surfaces either an OCR gap or a taxonomy gap for review.

alternatives.name: Trust the Contains statement only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and usually present, but labels may use parentheticals instead, and one OCR miss on that line means a silent miss.

alternatives.name: Hand-written hidden-name list
alternatives.tradeoff: Small and auditable for your own allergens, but you must maintain it and it will miss names you never thought of.

steps.delegate: Python. Parse ingredients.txt into nodes with parents and properties; ancestors(entry) with cycle protection. allergens_for(entry) collects allergens:en values over the node and its ancestors. Map OFF ids to the 9 US allergens in a reviewed table (en:gluten needs the grain to decide wheat). resolve(tree, contains_items) returns Verdicts. Tests: Casein and sodium caseinate resolve to milk; tahini to sesame; semolina to wheat; a Contains-only allergen still appears; a disagreement sets a flag.
verify: Run 20 hidden-name examples you write yourself (whey, casein, semolina, albumen, tahini) and record which resolve correctly
For every miss, check by hand whether the taxonomy lacks the link or your code failed

steps.title: Decide when to say 'cannot confirm, read the label'
steps.learn: A checker that is confidently wrong is worse than none. Abstain when the image is unreadable, when the ingredient span is missing, when many tokens are unmatched, or when class terms like 'spices' or 'natural flavors' could hide a user's non-major allergen. Abstaining trades coverage for fewer silent misses.

decision.choice: Abstain if OCR confidence or matched-token share falls below dev-tuned floors, or if segmentation failed
decision.why: Misses are the expensive error, and they cluster in bad photos and unmatched text. Floors tuned on dev data let you choose an abstain rate you can live with while keeping recall high on what you do answer.

alternatives.name: Always answer
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximum coverage, but a blurry photo can produce 'not found' for every allergen, which looks like a clean bill of health.

alternatives.name: Ask for a retake on low confidence
alternatives.tradeoff: Recovers many bad photos and is worth adding, but a second bad photo still needs the abstain path.

steps.delegate: Python. decide(ocr_lines, segmentation, matches, user_allergens) returns final Verdicts or an Abstain(reason). Thresholds come from config, tuned by tune_abstain.py on the dev set only, reporting recall on answered products vs abstain rate per setting. Tests: empty OCR abstains; 'natural flavors' with a custom mustard allergen yields cannot_rule_out; tune script refuses to load test-set ids.
verify: Plot dev recall on answered products against abstain rate and pick one setting
Confirm the tuning script errors if any frozen test barcode is in its input

steps.title: Score the frozen test set and ablate the taxonomy walk
steps.learn: Now open the frozen 100 once. Grade against your hand labels, not OFF tags or the app's own output. The ablation that answers the project's question: plain string match on allergen words (milk, wheat) vs the full taxonomy walk. The gap is the value of catching hidden names.
verify: Report recall and precision per allergen and overall, plus abstain rate, on the 100 test products
Report the same metrics with the taxonomy walk disabled and count misses that only hidden names explain
List every missed (product, allergen) pair with its cause: photo, OCR, segmentation, matching, or taxonomy

steps.title: Test it outside: scan 100 packaged foods
steps.learn: The try-it: scan 100 packaged foods at home or in a store, photographing the panel as a shopper would (handheld, store lighting). Before looking at the app's answer, write down the allergens you read on the label yourself; that is the ground truth.
verify: Report recall, precision and abstain rate on the 100 scans, next to the frozen offline numbers
Report how many scans needed a retake and the median seconds from barcode to verdict
Count products where OFF data and the printed label disagreed (likely recipe changes or data gaps)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a hidden name missing from the taxonomy, or OCR garbling one allergen word), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives offline and store recall, precision and abstain rate, with the ablation, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising misses or false alarms with the evidence text
Part 4 says this does not prove safety for anyone and lists scope limits (US rules, English labels)

projects.title: Expiry tracker
projects.problem: Food gets forgotten and thrown out
projects.concepts: Date OCR, reminders, simple forecasting of what you'll use
projects.tryIt: Track household food waste before and after
projects.question: Does logging printed dates by photo, with a daily reminder and a simple usage forecast, cut how much food my household throws out?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and a frozen date-photo set
steps.learn: Two questions: can the app read dates, and does using it reduce waste? Waste is the headline (grams thrown out per week, before vs after), measured with a kitchen scale outside the app. Date reading is scored on real package photos. FDA estimates date-label confusion causes about 20 percent of consumer food waste.

decision.choice: Date photos of 130 of your packages (30 dev, 100 frozen test), hand-typed, then a before/after household test
decision.why: There is no single standard public set of expiry-date photos matching your groceries, and your packaging, printers and lighting are what the app will see. Freezing 100 now keeps OCR tuning honest. The household test measures the real outcome the app is meant to change.

alternatives.name: Published expiry-date research datasets
alternatives.tradeoff: Larger and labeled, but packaging and date formats may differ from your shelves, and you must check license and provenance first.

alternatives.name: Skip OCR scoring, only weigh waste
alternatives.tradeoff: Measures the outcome, but if waste does not drop you cannot tell whether date reading or the reminders failed.

verify: Write the question and metrics: grams wasted per week, exact-date accuracy on the test set, share of items needing manual entry
Store the 100 test photos and typed dates read-only with a hash before writing any OCR code
Photograph packages only, with no people, receipts or addresses in frame

links.label: FDA: cut food waste, keep food safe

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app looks at packages, not people, so photos hold only the date area. Household eating patterns are personal; keep them local. Dates are mostly about quality and the app is a helper: it never declares food safe. Follow FDA and USDA guidance, inspect the food, and treat infant formula use-by dates as strict.

decision.choice: Upload only the date crop, delete it once confirmed, keep the database local, link official food-safety guidance
decision.why: The question needs dates and outcomes, not images. Deleting crops after confirmation and keeping data on a home machine removes most risk. Linking to official guidance keeps the app from becoming the authority on whether something is safe to eat.

alternatives.name: Keep photos for retraining OCR
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful for improving the date reader, but only with explicit opt-in and crops that contain nothing but the date.

alternatives.name: Hosted cloud database
alternatives.tradeoff: Shares across phones easily, but places a log of what your household eats on a third-party server.

steps.delegate: Python. Server deletes the crop after the user confirms the date unless dev_capture=true. Bind the server to the home network only. Add a fixed 'quality date, check the food' line and an FDA guidance link to item and digest views. Tests: no crop files remain after confirmation; digest text never says 'safe'; infant formula items show their use-by date without any 'still fine' wording.
verify: Capture 5 items and confirm no image files remain on the server afterward
Confirm the server is unreachable from outside your network

links.label: FDA: cut food waste, keep food safe

steps.title: Model items, date types and outcomes
steps.learn: An item has a product, where it lives (fridge, freezer, pantry), a date, what kind of date it is, where the date came from (printed, estimated, typed), and an outcome (eaten, frozen, thrown out). Opening a package or freezing it changes how long it lasts, so state changes over time matter.

decision.choice: SQLite with an items table plus an append-only events table (added, opened, frozen, eaten, wasted)
decision.why: Events keep history, so the forecast can learn usage rates and the write-up can count what happened to each item. SQLite is a single file on a home server or laptop, enough for one household.

alternatives.name: Single mutable row per item
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler queries, but you lose when things were opened or eaten, which the forecast needs.

alternatives.name: Spreadsheet
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero code and easy to edit by hand, but reminders and forecasts become manual and error-prone.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, SQLite via sqlite3. Schema: items(id, barcode, name, location, date, date_type in {best_if_used_by, use_by, sell_by, other, none}, date_source in {printed, estimated, typed}), events(item_id, kind, at, grams). Repository functions add_item, record_event, active_items(as_of). Tests: active_items excludes eaten and wasted; events are append-only (update raises).
verify: Enter 10 items by hand and confirm active_items returns the right set after eating 3
Confirm every item stores both date_type and date_source

steps.title: Capture: barcode for the name, a framed photo for the date
steps.learn: Two cheap signals make capture fast: a barcode gives the product name, and a photo of just the date area gives OCR a small, simple region. Dates can be printed small or on curved, shiny surfaces, so framing matters more than model choice.

decision.choice: Barcode scan with Open Food Facts lookup for the name, then the user frames the date in an on-screen box
decision.why: A small crop around the date is far easier to OCR than a whole package full of other numbers (lot codes, weights, nutrition). OFF is open and free; its API asks for a custom User-Agent and limits product reads to 15 per minute per IP, plenty for groceries.

alternatives.name: OCR the whole package and search for dates
alternatives.tradeoff: One photo, no framing, but many more number strings to misread as dates.

alternatives.name: Type dates by hand
alternatives.tradeoff: Always correct and works for anything, but slow enough that people stop logging after a week.

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI backend plus a phone web page. Page: barcode via camera, then a capture view with a guide box; send only the cropped region. Backend: lookup_off(barcode) with fields=product_name, custom User-Agent, SQLite cache, back off on 429. Tests: cached barcode makes no network call; unknown barcode prompts for a name; uploaded crop never exceeds the guide box size.
verify: Time 20 captures end to end and record the median seconds per item
Record the share of your groceries whose barcode is found in OFF

steps.title: Choose the OCR setup for short date strings
steps.learn: A date crop is a single short line, so OCR settings change: Tesseract's page segmentation mode 7 treats the image as one text line, and tessedit_char_whitelist can restrict characters. Its docs recommend 300 DPI or more, so upscaling small crops helps. Score on dev photos only.

decision.choice: Tesseract single-line mode on upscaled, binarized crops as baseline, compared with ML Kit text recognition v2 on-device
decision.why: Both are free and local, so photos stay on your devices. The single-line crop plays to Tesseract's strengths; ML Kit processes on-device on the phone and may handle glare and odd fonts better. Exact-date accuracy on the 30 dev photos picks the winner.

alternatives.name: VLM reads the date
alternatives.tradeoff: Often robust to odd print, but can output a plausible date that is not there; needs a confirm step and costs per call.

alternatives.name: Train a small date-digit recognizer
alternatives.tradeoff: Could beat general OCR on dot-style printing, but needs hundreds of labeled crops you do not have yet.

steps.delegate: Python. ocr_date(crop) returns [{text, confidence}]. Backend 1: OpenCV upscale, grayscale, adaptive threshold, pytesseract.image_to_data with --psm 7 and an optional whitelist. Backend 2: read ML Kit JSON exported from the phone. eval_dates.py scores raw-text character error rate and exact date match after parsing on the dev set. Tests: schema identical across backends; blank crop returns no text.
verify: Record character error rate per engine on the 30 dev crops
List the 5 worst dev crops and name the cause (glare, curve, embossing, font)

steps.title: Parse dates safely and confirm ambiguous ones
steps.learn: '03/04/27' is March 4 in the US and 3 April in many other countries. dateparser's DATE_ORDER setting fixes the order (its default for English is MDY), and PREFER_DAY_OF_MONTH decides what a month-only date like 'AUG 2027' becomes. Lot codes and times often sit beside the date and must not win.

decision.choice: dateparser with explicit DATE_ORDER, PREFER_DAY_OF_MONTH='first', a plausibility window, confirm if ambiguous
decision.why: An explicit order avoids silent locale guesses; choosing the first of the month for month-only dates makes reminders early rather than late. A window (not long past, not years ahead) rejects lot codes. Asking the user only for ambiguous cases keeps errors rare without slowing every scan.

alternatives.name: Let dateparser guess with no settings
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but ambiguous day/month dates are parsed by a default order that may not match the label.

alternatives.name: Always ask the user to confirm
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches every error, but adds a tap per item and people start confirming without reading.

steps.delegate: Python, dateparser. parse_candidates(texts, locale) returns [{date, raw, ambiguous}]. Detect keywords (best if used by, use by, sell by, exp) to set date_type. Settings: DATE_ORDER from locale, PREFER_DAY_OF_MONTH='first'. Reject dates outside [today-30d, today+3y]. Mark ambiguous when both day and month are 12 or less and order is not certain. Tests: '03/04/27' is ambiguous; 'AUG 2027' gives Aug 1; 'LOT 230415' is rejected.
verify: Report exact-date accuracy and ambiguous rate on the 30 dev crops after parsing
Write 10 tricky strings by hand (lot codes, times, month-only) and confirm each result

steps.title: Handle date meanings and items with no printed date
steps.learn: Per FDA, apart from infant formula, federal rules do not require quality date labels, and FDA and USDA back 'Best if Used By' as a quality date, not a safety cutoff. Produce, leftovers and deli items often have no date at all, so the app needs an estimate from a trusted storage guide.

decision.choice: Show printed dates with their meaning; for undated items, estimate from USDA FoodKeeper guidance and mark as estimated
decision.why: Reminders should say 'best quality by' rather than 'expires', which is closer to what most dates mean and cuts needless waste. FoodKeeper is USDA storage-time guidance published as open data, so estimates come from an official source rather than invented numbers.

alternatives.name: Treat every date as a hard expiry
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and cautious, but pushes people to throw out food that is still fine, the waste the project is trying to cut.

alternatives.name: Let the user type a shelf life per item
alternatives.tradeoff: Fits your habits, but guesses vary and you lose the link to an official source.

steps.delegate: Python. Download the FoodKeeper JSON from the data.gov catalog into data/. Write map_to_foodkeeper(name) that offers the top 3 entries by fuzzy match for the user to pick, then caches the choice per barcode or name. estimate_date(entry, location, added_at) returns a date and source='estimated'. Tests: estimated items are always labeled estimated; printed dates are never overwritten by estimates.
verify: Map 15 undated items you actually buy and check each estimate against the FoodKeeper entry by hand
Confirm reminder text says 'best quality by' for best-if-used-by items and 'use by' only where printed

links.label: FDA: cut food waste, keep food safe

steps.title: Send one daily digest instead of many alerts
steps.learn: Reminders only cut waste if people keep reading them. One short list a day ('use soon: spinach, yogurt') at a time you cook beats a ping per item. ntfy lets a script send phone notifications by HTTP to a topic; its docs warn that topic names are public, so pick an unguessable one or self-host with auth.

decision.choice: Daily ntfy digest at a fixed hour of items due within 3 days, on an unguessable topic or self-hosted server
decision.why: A digest batches many items into one interruption and fits a dinner-planning moment. ntfy needs no app store release for your own phones. Keeping messages to item names and dates limits what leaks if the topic is found.

alternatives.name: Push per item at fixed lead times
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise timing, but a full fridge produces many alerts and people mute them.

alternatives.name: Calendar events (ICS feed)
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses an app everyone has, but clutters the calendar and is awkward to dismiss when food is eaten.

steps.delegate: Python. digest(as_of) builds the list of active items due within N days, sorted by date, with date meaning. send_digest() POSTs plain text to an ntfy topic URL from config (with optional auth token). Run daily by cron. Tests: no message is sent when nothing is due; eaten items never appear; message contains no location or household names.
verify: Run the digest for 7 simulated days on test items you enter by hand and confirm one message per day, sorted by date, with eaten items absent
Confirm the topic name is random and not used in any public repo or screenshot

steps.title: Forecast what you will not finish in time
steps.learn: Household use is lumpy: you may eat yogurt 3 days, then none for a week. Croston's method forecasts such intermittent demand by smoothing quantity and time between uses separately; FPP3 notes its forecasts are biased and have no intervals, so compare it with simple baselines.

decision.choice: statsforecast CrostonClassic usage rate per product vs a historic average, used only to flag 'unlikely to finish'
decision.why: The forecast drives one nudge (eat first, freeze, or buy less next time), so a simple, explainable model is enough. Comparing with a baseline on rolling-origin splits shows whether Croston earns its place on your sparse data.

alternatives.name: No forecast, dates only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but cannot warn that a large pack will outlast your eating pace before the date.

alternatives.name: Gradient-boosted model across products
alternatives.tradeoff: Shares strength across items, but one household has too little data and the output is harder to explain.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas, statsforecast. Build a daily usage series per product from eaten events. Fit CrostonClassic and HistoricAverage; evaluate MAE with rolling-origin cross-validation over the last weeks. at_risk(item) compares forecast use until the date with remaining quantity. Tests: a product with no history is never flagged; a steady daily user of a 3-day item is not flagged.
verify: Run the evaluation on a synthetic 6-week log (2 steady, 2 lumpy products) and confirm Croston and baseline MAE are both computed per product
Check 10 at-risk flags by hand at the end of the week: how many items really went unfinished

steps.title: Measure waste independently of the app
steps.learn: If the app's own 'wasted' events were the metric, logging habits would grade themselves. Weigh food waste with a kitchen scale into a separate sheet, every time, for the whole test. Also log rough grocery volume per week, since buying less also lowers waste and holidays shift both.

decision.choice: Daily scale weigh-ins into a separate sheet: 3 weeks baseline without the app, then 3 weeks with it
decision.why: A scale reading does not depend on whether an item was logged in the app, so missed captures cannot hide waste. Equal-length periods plus grocery volume let you see whether a drop came from the app or from shopping less.

alternatives.name: Count items thrown away
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier than weighing, but a lettuce and a sauce jar count the same.

alternatives.name: Alternate weeks with and without the app
alternatives.tradeoff: Controls for seasonal drift better, but habits from app weeks spill into off weeks.

verify: Set up the waste sheet with date, grams, item, reason and confirm it is separate from the app database
Weigh a known item to check the scale reading before starting

steps.title: Test it outside: household waste before and after
steps.learn: The try-it: track household food waste before and after. Run the baseline weeks with only the scale, then use the app for the same number of weeks. Score OCR on the frozen 100 once, now, and keep logging grocery volume so you can explain any change.
verify: Report grams wasted per week for both periods, plus grams per unit of groceries bought
Report exact-date accuracy on the frozen 100 and the share of real items entered by hand
Report capture rate: items in the app vs items you remember buying, from receipts

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example waste falling mostly through smaller shops, or dates misread on one brand), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives waste per period, OCR accuracy and forecast MAE, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence from the logs
Part 4 lists assumptions (one household, 6 weeks, self-weighed) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Plant-care advisor
projects.problem: Over- or under-watering houseplants
projects.concepts: Soil sensor data plus leaf photos, a small classifier
projects.tryIt: Run it on your own plants for a season
projects.question: Can a soil sensor plus leaf photos tell me when a houseplant needs water more accurately than a fixed watering schedule?

steps.title: Frame the question, the ground truth and the frozen test block
steps.learn: Each plant gets one answer per day: water, wait, or check (something looks wrong). The advisor must not grade itself, so ground truth comes from the pot's weight on a kitchen scale and the finger test (soil dry about two inches down, per Illinois Extension), logged before reading the advice.

decision.choice: Own plants, own sensor logs and photos; truth from pot weight plus finger test; last 4 weeks frozen as test
decision.why: No public dataset covers watering houseplants in real homes. Weight and finger checks are independent of the sensor and model, so they can grade both. Freezing a later block of weeks as the test set means no threshold is tuned on the days you report.

alternatives.name: PlantVillage leaf images
alternatives.tradeoff: Over 50,000 curated leaf images, but of crop diseases, not houseplant water stress; only good as a pipeline smoke test.

alternatives.name: Use the sensor reading as ground truth
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra daily work, but the sensor then grades itself and calibration drift is invisible.

verify: Write the one question and the metric: share of days where advice matches the weight-plus-finger label, vs a fixed weekly schedule
List at least 3 plants with pot material and size, and write down the dates of the frozen test block

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting any photos
steps.learn: Leaf photos are taken inside your home and can catch people, faces, screens and mail. Photograph plants, never people. Advice can also do harm: some houseplants are toxic to pets, and the app is a helper, so check an official source (for pets, the ASPCA plant list) for any toxicity question.

decision.choice: On-device face check rejects photos with faces, crop to the plant, strip EXIF, store no location
decision.why: Only the leaves matter, so cropping and rejecting frames with faces removes most private content before anything is stored. Stripping EXIF removes GPS and device data the advisor never uses.

alternatives.name: Keep full photos for later relabeling
alternatives.tradeoff: More context when debugging, but stores room interiors and anyone in frame.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler capture code, but raw photos with faces reach the server first.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with Pillow and the MediaPipe Face Detector (Python Tasks API, BlazeFace full-range model). Write ingest_photo(path, plant_id): run face detection and reject the photo if any face is found, crop to a per-plant box saved in config, re-encode pixels only so EXIF is dropped, save as photos/<plant_id>/<date>.jpg. Tests: a photo with a face is rejected; saved files have no EXIF; the database has no location column.
verify: Feed 5 photos with a visible face and confirm none are saved; note that a person with face hidden still passes
Open 5 saved photos in an EXIF viewer and confirm no GPS or device fields remain
If you have pets, look up each plant on the ASPCA list and record the answer as coming from ASPCA, not the app

steps.title: Choose the moisture probe and the board that reads it
steps.learn: A soil probe outputs a voltage that depends on soil water, but also on soil mix, probe depth and how tightly soil packs around it. Over a season, durability matters: DFRobot describes its SEN0193 as capacitive (not resistive) with corrosion-resistant material for long service life.

decision.choice: One capacitive analog probe (for example DFRobot SEN0193) per pot, read by an ESP32 running ESPHome
decision.why: A season-long test rules out probes that corrode. ESPHome builds firmware from a YAML file with an ADC sensor, filters and MQTT, so the agent writes config rather than C, and the ESP32 has Wi-Fi built in.

alternatives.name: Resistive two-prong probe
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest, but exposed electrodes in wet soil are the durability problem capacitive probes are sold to avoid.

alternatives.name: Commercial BLE plant sensor (Xiaomi MiFlora)
alternatives.tradeoff: Packaged and battery powered, and ESPHome can read it, but less control over raw readings and placement.

alternatives.name: Kitchen scale only
alternatives.tradeoff: The most direct water measure, but manual, so you get a few points per day instead of a dry-down curve.

steps.delegate: ESPHome YAML for an ESP32: one adc sensor per probe with attenuation chosen so the probe's 0 to 3.0 V output is not clipped, update_interval 10 min, and an mqtt block publishing to plants/<plant_id>/raw. Add a wiring table per probe. Acceptance test: readings in air and in a glass of water are clearly separated and each is stable over 5 minutes.
verify: Record raw readings in air and in water for each probe and confirm each pair is clearly separated
Leave one probe in an unwatered pot for 24 h and check readings drift slowly, without random jumps

steps.title: Calibrate each probe against pot weight and filter noise
steps.learn: Raw ADC counts are not moisture. DFRobot's calibration example records an air value and a water value per probe; that gives a 0 to 100 scale for the probe, not grams of water. Fitting readings to pot weight turns them into something meaningful for that pot and mix.

decision.choice: Per-probe air and water endpoints, then a per-pot linear fit to water mass from weight; median filter of 5 samples
decision.why: Endpoints differ between probes and soil mix shifts the curve, so a per-pot fit to weight is the honest scale. A median ignores a single bad sample better than a mean, and ESPHome ships median and calibrate_linear filters.

alternatives.name: Use the air-to-water percent directly
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick, but percent of the probe's range is not percent water in soil and differs by mix and pot.

alternatives.name: Exponential moving average
alternatives.tradeoff: Smoother curves, but one spike still leaks in and the value lags right after watering.

steps.delegate: Python: calibrate.py reads a CSV (plant_id, raw, pot_weight_g, dry_pot_weight_g), fits raw to water mass per pot with numpy.polyfit degree 1, saves coefficients to calib.json and prints R squared. Also emit ESPHome filter snippets (median window 5, calibrate_linear endpoints). Tests: a perfectly linear synthetic CSV gives R squared 1; a missing dry weight raises an error.
verify: Weigh each pot at 5 or more points during one dry-down and record R squared of its fit
Insert a fake spike into a logged series and confirm the filtered value barely moves

steps.title: Collect readings through MQTT into SQLite and mark gaps
steps.learn: Readings arrive every few minutes for months. The pipeline must survive Wi-Fi drops, broker restarts and power cuts without inventing data: store each reading with the time it was received and record gaps instead of interpolating across them.

decision.choice: Mosquitto MQTT broker plus a small Python subscriber writing to one SQLite file
decision.why: MQTT is built for small devices publishing to topics and ESPHome speaks it natively. One SQLite file holds a season of readings for a few pots, is easy to back up, and is queried directly from analysis scripts.

alternatives.name: Home Assistant with its recorder
alternatives.tradeoff: Dashboards and automations for free, but your analysis depends on its schema and retention settings.

alternatives.name: A time-series database (InfluxDB)
alternatives.tradeoff: Built for many sensors and downsampling, but one more service to run for a handful of pots.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with paho-mqtt and sqlite3. Subscriber on plants/+/raw inserts (plant_id, received_utc, raw, calibrated) and reconnects with backoff. gaps.py lists gaps longer than 3 update intervals per plant. Tests: non-numeric payloads are rejected and logged; after a broker restart inserts resume; the gap report finds a planted 2-hour hole.
verify: Unplug the ESP32 for an hour and confirm the gap report shows that hour
Restart the broker and confirm inserts resume within a minute with no manual steps

steps.title: Detect waterings and sensor faults before forecasting
steps.learn: Two things break a dry-down curve: watering (a sudden rise) and sensor faults (flat lines, values outside the calibrated range, a probe pulled out of the soil reading like air). Find both first, or the forecast learns from garbage and the advice fires on a broken probe.

decision.choice: Rules: a step-rise threshold for watering; flatline and out-of-range checks for faults
decision.why: These events have clear physical signatures and you can label each one (you know when you watered), so simple rules are easy to test and explain. A learned anomaly model would need many labeled faults that a few pots will never produce.

alternatives.name: Isolation Forest on sliding windows
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds odd patterns you did not anticipate, but its scores are hard to explain and tune with only a few real faults.

alternatives.name: Manual watering log only
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact when you remember, but a missed entry silently corrupts a curve, and faults go unnoticed.

steps.delegate: Python: events.py with detect_waterings(series, min_rise, window) and detect_faults(series, flat_minutes, valid_range) returning typed events with start and end times, stored in an events table. Tests on synthetic series: one step rise gives exactly one watering; a 6-hour constant stretch is a flatline fault; an air-level value is out of range.
verify: Keep a paper watering log for 2 weeks and report detector precision and recall against it
Pull a probe out for 10 minutes and confirm a fault is raised

steps.title: Forecast when each pot will cross its dry threshold
steps.learn: Between waterings, moisture falls at a speed set by the pot, light, temperature and season; Illinois Extension notes unglazed clay pots dry faster than plastic. The useful output is time until this pot crosses its threshold, as a range, updated as readings arrive.

decision.choice: Per-pot fit on the current dry-down segment, using the pot's past segments as a prior and for the error range
decision.why: Each segment is short and smooth, so a simple fit is enough and easy to debug. Past segments cover the first hours after watering, when the current one has too few points, and their residuals give an honest range.

alternatives.name: Prophet or ARIMA on the whole series
alternatives.tradeoff: Model trend and seasonality, but every watering resets the series, which breaks their assumptions unless modeled as events.

alternatives.name: Gradient-boosted model with light and temperature
alternatives.tradeoff: Can learn seasonal effects, but needs extra sensors and many segments per pot.

steps.delegate: Python: forecast.py with forecast_crossing(segment, threshold, past_segments) returning (eta_hours, low, high), fit with numpy, range from past residuals. backtest.py predicts every past segment from its first 24 h and records error at crossing, skipping the frozen test block. Tests: a synthetic linear decline gives the exact crossing; a flat segment returns no crossing.
verify: Backtest on all segments before the frozen test block and report median absolute error in hours
Compare against 'same interval as last time' on the same segments and report which wins

steps.title: Classify the visible leaf state from photos
steps.learn: The photo adds what the probe cannot see: drooping, yellowing, brown tips. These are symptoms, not causes: Illinois Extension notes wilting often means the plant needs water but can be a sign of overwatering. So the classifier reports a visible state and the sensor history decides the cause.

decision.choice: Frozen CLIP image embeddings (open_clip) plus a logistic-regression probe on your labeled photos
decision.why: You will have tens to a few hundred labeled photos, too few to fine-tune a network well. A linear probe on frozen features trains in seconds on a laptop, and the CLIP paper evaluates its representations with exactly this kind of probe.

alternatives.name: Zero-shot CLIP prompts
alternatives.tradeoff: No labels needed, but subtle states like slight drooping may not separate by text prompt; worth measuring as a baseline.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune a small ViT with timm
alternatives.tradeoff: Better with many photos, but overfits a few hundred images and wants a GPU.

steps.delegate: Python: open_clip, torch, scikit-learn. embed.py caches normalized image embeddings per photo. train_probe.py fits LogisticRegression on labels {healthy, drooping, yellowing, brown_tips}, splits by date, excludes the frozen test block, and prints classification_report. Tests: cached embeddings match a fresh run; no test-block date appears in training.
verify: Label each photo before looking at that day's sensor values, then report per-class recall on the dev split
Compare zero-shot prompts against the probe on the same dev split and record both

steps.title: Combine sensor, forecast and leaf state into advice
steps.learn: Advice combines calibrated moisture against the pot's threshold, the forecast and the leaf state. The interesting cases are disagreements: drooping while the soil is wet points to overwatering or drainage, not thirst. Faults must produce 'no data', never a guess.

decision.choice: A small rule table: the sensor decides water or wait, the leaf state can only escalate to check, faults give no_data
decision.why: Rules can state their reason ('soil wet and leaves drooping: check drainage') and are testable against the weight-plus-finger labels. Keeping the photo from triggering watering stops one misclassified photo from drowning a plant.

alternatives.name: A learned model over all signals
alternatives.tradeoff: Could find interactions, but there are few labeled days per plant and its reasons are harder to show.

alternatives.name: Sensor threshold only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, and you need it as an ablation, but it is blind to overwatering symptoms.

steps.delegate: Python: advise.py with advise(plant_id, now) returning {action: water|wait|check|no_data, reasons: [...]} from the latest calibrated moisture, forecast, last leaf state and open faults. Table-driven tests covering every rule, including an open fault returning no_data and wet soil with drooping returning check.
verify: On dev days, report agreement of advise() and of the sensor-only rule with the weight-plus-finger labels
Read 10 advice messages and confirm each states its reason

steps.title: Test it outside: your own plants for a season
steps.learn: The try-it is the evaluation: run it on your own plants for a season. Each day, weigh the pot and do the finger test before reading the advice, then log both. Seasons change light and temperature, so watch whether the forecast and thresholds keep up.
verify: On the frozen test block, report agreement with the weight-plus-finger labels for the advisor, sensor-only and a fixed weekly schedule
Report forecast error in hours on the test block and uptime per probe
Count how many 'check' alerts found a real problem (soggy soil, poor drainage, pests)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a probe that drifted or a leaf state the photo always missed), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives agreement, forecast error and uptime numbers, each with the device, script and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence from the logs
Part 4 lists assumptions (your plants, your home, one season) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Exercise form coach
projects.problem: Bad squat or push-up form causes injuries
projects.concepts: On-device pose estimation, rules or a classifier for common mistakes
projects.tryIt: Record your own sets; compare feedback with a trainer's
projects.question: Can on-device pose estimation flag common squat and push-up form mistakes about as reliably as a human trainer?

steps.title: Frame the question, the mistakes to catch and the sealed test
steps.learn: The coach counts reps and flags per-rep mistakes taken from standard cues (ACE): squat depth, heels lifting, knees not tracking over the toes, back rounding; for push-ups, low back sagging, hips hiking, and partial range. Success is agreement with a trainer on reps never used for tuning.

decision.choice: Dev: your own recorded sets plus Fitness-AQA back squats; test: a trainer-labeled session recorded last and sealed
decision.why: Fitness-AQA has back squat videos annotated by expert trainers for common errors, which tests your rules on other bodies and cameras. The trainer session is the try-it and stays sealed until the end, so no threshold can be fit to it.

alternatives.name: Only your own sets, labeled by you
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but you grade your rules with your own eye, and your form may never show some mistakes.

alternatives.name: QEVD fitness coaching dataset
alternatives.tradeoff: Built for live feedback, but aimed at vision-language models, more than a pose-and-rules pipeline needs.

verify: Write the one question, the mistake list per exercise, and the metric: per-rep agreement and Cohen's kappa with the trainer
Request Fitness-AQA access and note its non-commercial terms
Write down the trainer session date and the rule that its videos are not opened before the test step

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before recording anything
steps.learn: Workout video shows your body, your home and anyone walking past. Keep video on the device and store only pose landmarks. The coach is a helper, not a medical or training authority: stop on pain, and check form with a qualified trainer.

decision.choice: Process frames on-device, discard video by default, store only landmarks, track one person, show a safety notice
decision.why: Landmarks are enough to recompute every angle and rule, and they show no face or room. Pose Landmarker's num_poses defaults to 1, so at most one person is tracked, though it can be the wrong one. Video is kept only by explicit opt-in, for labeling sessions.

alternatives.name: Upload video to a server model
alternatives.tradeoff: Allows bigger models, but sends body and home video off the device.

alternatives.name: Keep all video for relabeling
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier debugging, but stores the most sensitive data by default.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 prototype: capture.py reads the camera with OpenCV, runs MediaPipe Pose Landmarker per frame, and writes only landmarks (x, y, z, visibility, timestamp_ms) to CSV; video is saved only with --keep-video. Show a notice at start: not medical advice, stop on pain. Tests: without the flag no video file exists after a run; every frame row has 33 landmarks.
verify: Run a session without --keep-video and confirm only landmark files exist
Have a second person cross the frame and confirm only one pose is recorded
Confirm the safety notice appears before every session

steps.title: Choose camera views that make each mistake visible
steps.learn: One camera sees a 2D projection, so each mistake is visible only from some angles. Depth, back angle and push-up hip sag show from the side; knees caving inward shows from the front. Assign each mistake a view and record that view.

decision.choice: Phone on a tripod at hip height: side view for depth, back and hips; a separate front-view set for knee tracking
decision.why: Angles measured in the matching view stay close to the real joint angles, so thresholds stay simple and readable. Two short sets per exercise are cheaper than reconstructing 3D.

alternatives.name: One 45-degree view
alternatives.tradeoff: One recording for everything, but every angle is foreshortened, so thresholds must be learned instead of set from the cue.

alternatives.name: 3D world landmarks from one view
alternatives.tradeoff: Pose Landmarker outputs world coordinates, but single-camera depth is estimated, so measure its error first.

alternatives.name: Two synchronized cameras
alternatives.tradeoff: True 3D, but calibration and sync are a project of their own.

steps.delegate: Python: setup_check.py runs Pose Landmarker on 3 seconds of camera and reports whether shoulders, hips, knees, ankles, heels and wrists have visibility above 0.5 and whether the body is fully in frame, printing hints such as 'step back'. Tests on saved landmark files: missing ankles fail the check; a full-body file passes.
verify: Record one set from the side and one from the front and confirm the checker passes both
Write down phone height, distance and frame rate so the trainer session can match them

steps.title: Pick the on-device pose model and its variant
steps.learn: Pose models trade accuracy for speed. You need landmarks for every frame at the camera's rate on a phone, a per-landmark confidence so rules can skip hidden joints, and the specific points your rules use (heels for heel lift).

decision.choice: MediaPipe Pose Landmarker in VIDEO mode; benchmark lite, full and heavy and keep the best that keeps up
decision.why: It gives 33 landmarks including heels and foot index, with visibility scores, in image and world coordinates. It runs on Android, iOS, web and Python, and Google describes it as optimized for on-device, real-time fitness use.

alternatives.name: MoveNet Lightning or Thunder
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, with Lightning for latency and Thunder for accuracy, but its 17 keypoints have no heel or toe points.

alternatives.name: Apple Vision body pose (VNDetectHumanBodyPoseRequest)
alternatives.tradeoff: Built into iOS with no model to ship, but iOS-only and a different joint set to map.

steps.delegate: Python: bench_pose.py runs Pose Landmarker lite, full and heavy with detect_for_video on 3 dev clips, recording ms per frame and the share of frames where hips, knees, ankles and heels have visibility above 0.5. Output a CSV per variant. Tests: timestamps passed are strictly increasing; result count equals frame count.
verify: Report ms per frame and visibility rate per variant on the same clips and machine
Pick the variant that keeps up with your camera's frame rate and record why

steps.title: Smooth landmark jitter without hiding the bottom of the rep
steps.learn: Landmarks jitter from frame to frame, and joint angles amplify the jitter. Smoothing removes it but adds lag; lag matters for live cues, not for per-rep summaries. Frames where a joint has low visibility should become gaps, not be smoothed over.

decision.choice: 1 Euro filter per landmark for live cues; Savitzky-Golay over the whole set for offline per-rep analysis
decision.why: The 1 Euro filter adapts its cutoff to speed, cutting jitter when still and lag when moving, and its authors give a two-step tuning procedure. Offline, savgol_filter can use future frames, so it smooths without shifting the rep bottom.

alternatives.name: Moving average
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but the same lag at every speed and it flattens the bottom of each rep.

alternatives.name: Kalman filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Principled with a motion model, but more parameters to tune than this needs.

steps.delegate: Python: smoothing.py with OneEuroFilter(min_cutoff, beta, d_cutoff) per coordinate and offline_smooth(series, window, order) wrapping scipy.signal.savgol_filter. Low-visibility frames become NaN; gaps longer than a few frames stay NaN. Tests: a constant signal is unchanged; a step input settles; long NaN gaps are preserved.
verify: Plot raw vs smoothed knee angle for one squat set and record the lag at the rep bottom
Tune min_cutoff and beta with the published procedure and record the values

steps.title: Segment the set into reps from a joint-angle signal
steps.learn: Reps are cycles in a joint angle: knee angle for squats, elbow angle for push-ups. Find each rep's bottom and the tops around it; every per-rep check runs on that window. A miscounted rep corrupts every metric downstream.

decision.choice: find_peaks on the smoothed angle with minimum prominence and distance, plus a top-bottom-top check
decision.why: scipy.signal.find_peaks supports prominence and distance, which reject small wobbles and double bottoms. The top-bottom-top check marks reps that never return to the top, which are the partial-range cases you want to flag.

alternatives.name: Fixed angle thresholds with hysteresis
alternatives.tradeoff: Works frame by frame for live use, but thresholds shift with body and camera.

alternatives.name: Learned action segmentation
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles messy sets, but needs labeled rep boundaries you do not have.

steps.delegate: Python: reps.py segment_reps(angle, fps, min_prominence_deg, min_distance_s) returning [(start, bottom, end, partial)] using scipy.signal.find_peaks on the negated angle. Tests: a 10-cycle synthetic sine yields 10 reps; added noise below the prominence adds none; a cycle that stops halfway is marked partial.
verify: Count reps by hand in 5 dev sets per exercise and report the counting errors
Check that each rep window starts and ends near full extension

steps.title: Turn each coaching cue into a per-rep number
steps.learn: Each cue becomes a number per rep: hip and knee angle at the bottom (depth), torso vs shin angle (ACE says they should look parallel at the bottom), heel lift, knee position vs the foot in the front view, and shoulder-hip-ankle line for push-up sag or hiking.

decision.choice: Joint angles from landmark vectors via dot products in the matching view; distances divided by shin length
decision.why: Angles do not change with distance from the camera, so one threshold works near or far. Normalizing distances such as heel lift by a body segment gives the same property.

alternatives.name: Features from world (3D) landmarks
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer view constraints, but estimated depth may add error you have to measure first.

alternatives.name: Raw landmark sequences into a model
alternatives.tradeoff: No hand-made features, but needs far more labeled reps and cannot explain its cue.

steps.delegate: Python: features.py first converts normalized landmarks to pixels (x*width, y*height), then angle(a, b, c) uses numpy dot products; rep_features(landmarks, rep, view) returns min_knee_angle, min_hip_angle, torso_shin_diff, heel_lift_norm, knee_over_foot_ratio (front), body_line_deviation (push-up). Tests: a right angle on a 16:9 frame gives 90 degrees; scaling all landmarks leaves features unchanged; NaN inputs give NaN features, not errors.
verify: Plot features for 20 dev reps you judged good or bad and confirm the bad ones separate on at least one feature
Record features standing 1 m further from the camera and confirm they barely change

steps.title: Build per-mistake detectors that can abstain
steps.learn: Each mistake needs a per-rep decision: flag, ok, or cannot tell (a needed joint was hidden). Tune thresholds on dev reps only. Running the Fitness-AQA squats without retuning shows whether rules tuned on your body transfer to other people and cameras.

decision.choice: One threshold rule per mistake tuned on dev data, abstain on low visibility; logistic regression only where a rule fails
decision.why: A rule maps directly to the cue the user hears ('go lower') and needs few labels. If a mistake does not separate on one feature, logistic regression on the rep features is the next simplest model and still small enough to inspect.

alternatives.name: Gradient-boosted trees on all features
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures interactions, but overfits a few hundred reps easily and is harder to explain.

alternatives.name: Video model trained on Fitness-AQA
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses appearance as well as pose, like the paper, but heavy on a phone and bound by non-commercial terms.

steps.delegate: Python: rules.py with one function per mistake returning flag, ok or abstain plus the feature value and threshold. tune.py grid-searches each threshold for best F1 on dev labels and refuses to read anything under data/test/. Fallback: sklearn LogisticRegression for any mistake whose rule F1 stays low. Tests: abstain when required joints are NaN; tune.py raises if pointed at the test folder.
verify: Report per-mistake precision, recall and abstain rate on your dev reps
Report the same on Fitness-AQA squats without retuning and note the drop

steps.title: Give one timely cue per rep on the device
steps.learn: Feedback helps only if it is timely and rare: one cue per rep, for the most important mistake, right after the rep ends. In live mode results arrive through a callback, so when inference falls behind the app should skip frames rather than queue them.

decision.choice: Pose Landmarker LIVE_STREAM mode, one spoken cue after each rep, mistakes ranked by safety
decision.why: LIVE_STREAM delivers results asynchronously through result_callback, so capture never blocks. Speaking after the rep avoids distracting mid-movement, and a fixed priority (back rounding before depth) avoids a stream of mixed messages.

alternatives.name: Summary after the set only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and no latency pressure, but you cannot correct within the set.

alternatives.name: Continuous on-screen overlay
alternatives.tradeoff: Rich detail, but nobody can read a screen mid push-up.

steps.delegate: Prototype in Python (OpenCV capture, PoseLandmarker LIVE_STREAM with result_callback, pyttsx3 for speech), then port the same rule module to Android or iOS with the MediaPipe Tasks SDK. Log latency per frame and dropped frames. Tests: at most one cue per rep; replaying a saved landmark file produces the same cues as offline analysis.
verify: Measure time from rep end to spoken cue on your device and record it
Do 3 sets with deliberate mistakes and confirm the right cue fires for each

steps.title: Test it outside: your sets compared with a trainer
steps.learn: The try-it: record your own sets and compare feedback with a trainer's. Keep video for this session only (--keep-video) and delete it after labeling. The trainer labels each rep from the video without seeing the app's output, so the app never grades itself.
verify: Report per-mistake agreement and Cohen's kappa between app and trainer on the sealed session
Report rep-count error and abstain rate on the sealed session
List each disagreement and whether the pose, the rule or the camera view caused it

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a mistake hidden in one view, or a rule that failed on Fitness-AQA), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives agreement, kappa, rep-count and latency numbers, each with device and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (one body, one trainer, two exercises) and states it is not injury prevention advice

projects.title: Appliance energy detective
projects.problem: Which appliance is driving the power bill?
projects.concepts: Energy disaggregation on smart-meter time series
projects.tryIt: Toggle appliances and see if the model detects each one
projects.question: From whole-home power readings alone, can a model tell which appliance just switched on and how much of the bill each one drives?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen test house
steps.learn: Energy disaggregation (NILM) splits one mains signal into per-appliance signals. Two metrics answer the question: event detection F1 for the try-it (toggle an appliance, does the model name it?) and per-appliance energy error for the bill. Freeze an unseen test house now, before tuning anything.

decision.choice: UK-DALE 6 s: train on house 1, tune on house 5 (dev), freeze house 2 as the unseen test house; then your own home
decision.why: UK-DALE records whole-house mains plus individual appliances every 6 seconds in 5 homes, so you get ground truth per appliance for free. House 1 has the longest record. Testing on a house never seen in training mimics deploying to your own home.

alternatives.name: REFIT (20 UK houses, 8-second data)
alternatives.tradeoff: More houses, so a better test of generalization, but only nine appliance channels per house and coarser sampling.

alternatives.name: Only your own home
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use, but you have no appliance ground truth until you add plugs, and no way to compare with published work.

alternatives.name: Test on a later week of house 1
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy and gives high scores, but measures memorizing one home, not detecting appliances in a new one.

verify: README states the question, event F1 and per-appliance energy error as metrics, and the frozen split (train house 1, test house 2)
List 4 to 5 target appliances that are submetered in both houses, checked against the dataset metadata
Record the house 2 date range; only the scoring scripts (baselines, seq2point, bill table) read it, never tuning or threshold code

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Second-by-second power reveals when a home is empty, when people sleep and what they do. Treat it like location data. Also: the panel is dangerous, and the model's bill split is an estimate; the utility bill and meter are the official source.

decision.choice: Keep raw readings on the home box, share only daily totals, no cloud upload by default, electrician for any panel work
decision.why: Daily per-appliance totals answer the question without exposing routines. Local storage means nothing about occupancy leaves the house unless the owner opts in.

alternatives.name: Cloud dashboard with raw data
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy remote access, but a third party holds a log of when the home is occupied.

alternatives.name: Delete raw data after 7 days
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller risk, but you lose the ability to retrain or re-score later.

steps.delegate: Add a config flag allow_cloud=false that blocks any outbound HTTP except to the meter and plugs; an export command that outputs only daily per-appliance kWh; a retention job for raw readings with a configurable window. Tests: with allow_cloud=false an outbound request raises; the export file has no sub-daily timestamps.
verify: Run the allow_cloud=false test and confirm any request to a host other than the meter and plugs raises before data collection starts
Write the cost disclaimer text ('estimate; the utility bill and meter are official') in the README for the bill step to display

steps.title: Load, resample and align mains with appliance channels
steps.learn: Mains and appliance monitors are separate sensors with their own clocks and dropouts. Before any model, put them on one time grid, decide how to fill short gaps, and mark long gaps as missing so they never count as 'appliance off'.

decision.choice: NILMTK HDF5 version of UK-DALE, resampled to a common 6 s grid, short gaps forward-filled, long gaps masked
decision.why: NILMTK converts and loads UK-DALE, exposes buildings and meters, and handles resampling and alignment, so you spend your time on the model. Masking long gaps keeps missing data from looking like zero load.

alternatives.name: Raw CSVs with pandas
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control and fewer dependencies, but you rewrite alignment, metadata and appliance naming that NILMTK already provides.

alternatives.name: 1-second mains (houses 1, 2, 5 only)
alternatives.tradeoff: Sharper on/off edges, but appliance channels stay at 6 s, so labels are no finer than before.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with nilmtk (uv install from the GitHub repo as its README says). Write load.py: open ukdale.h5 with nilmtk.DataSet, return aligned pandas DataFrames of mains and the chosen appliances for a building and date range at 6 s, forward-fill gaps under 2 minutes, set longer gaps to NaN plus a mask column. Tests: index is strictly increasing at 6 s; masked rows are excluded from a sum-of-energy helper.
verify: Plot one day of mains with the sum of submetered appliances on top and note the unmetered remainder
Report the percentage of masked time for each house and appliance

steps.title: Run the classical baselines and pick the scoring metrics
steps.learn: Before building anything, get numbers from simple methods. NILMTK ships Mean, combinatorial optimisation (CO), exact factorial HMM (FHMMExact) and Hart85. Its metrics include MAE, NDE, NEP (normalized error in assigned power) and an on/off F1 that thresholds power at 10 W.

decision.choice: Report Mean, CO and FHMMExact on the frozen test house with NEP, MAE and on/off F1 per appliance
decision.why: Mean shows what 'no skill' scores; CO and FHMM are the classic NILM methods the Neural NILM paper compared against. NEP measures assigned-power error relative to true energy (bill share needs total-energy error too); F1 asks 'did it notice the appliance was on'.

alternatives.name: Only RMSE
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to compute, but dominated by big loads and silent about whether a small appliance was ever detected.

alternatives.name: NILMbench fixed tasks
alternatives.tradeoff: Comparable to published leaderboards, but its protocols add setup you do not need for a single-home question.

steps.delegate: Python, nilmtk. Write baselines.py that trains nilmtk.disaggregate Mean, CO and FHMMExact on house 1 and predicts house 2 for the target appliances, then scores with nilmtk.losses (mae, nde, nep, f1score). Save a CSV of appliance x method x metric. Tests: metrics on identical ground truth and prediction give MAE 0 and NEP 0.
verify: Table of NEP and F1 per appliance for all three baselines on house 2
Write one sentence on which appliance every baseline gets wrong and a guess why

steps.title: Detect on/off events as step changes in mains power
steps.learn: Toggling an appliance shows up as a step in mains power that stays at the new level. Noise, motor start-up spikes and cycling loads (fridges) make naive differencing fire constantly. A median filter plus a steady-state check separates real steps from spikes.

decision.choice: Median-filter mains, flag a step when the level change exceeds a threshold and holds for a few samples
