decision.why: It is transparent, needs no labels and runs on a small device. Each event comes with a size (watts up or down), which is the feature you match to appliances next. The threshold is tuned on house 1 only.

alternatives.name: CUSUM change-point detection
alternatives.tradeoff: Better on slow or small changes, but more parameters and harder to explain per event.

alternatives.name: Learned detector (CNN on windows)
alternatives.tradeoff: Can catch subtle events, but needs labeled events and hides why it fired.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy, scipy.signal.medfilt. Implement detect_events(power, kernel, min_delta_w, hold_samples) returning (timestamp, delta_w) rows. Tune min_delta_w on house 1 by matching events to appliance channel on/off transitions within a tolerance window. Tests: a synthetic 0 to 2000 W step yields one +2000 event; a single-sample 3000 W spike yields none.
verify: Precision and recall of detected events vs appliance transitions on one week of the dev house (house 5), with the tolerance window stated
Plot 3 missed events and 3 false events and label the cause of each

steps.title: Name each event by matching it to appliance signatures
steps.learn: Each appliance has a typical step size, and on and off steps pair up (Hart85 in NILMTK does this pairing). Appliances with similar wattage collide, so the matcher must be able to say 'unknown' instead of guessing.

decision.choice: Nearest-signature classifier on step size and duration, with an 'unknown' bucket beyond a distance cutoff
decision.why: Signatures are fit from labeled events: UK-DALE submeters now, then a separate calibration session of plug toggles in your home, never the toggles scored in the try-it. An explicit unknown bucket keeps a 1.5 kW heater from being called a kettle.

alternatives.name: Unsupervised clustering of events
alternatives.tradeoff: No labels needed, but clusters still need names, and similar appliances merge.

alternatives.name: Hart85 from NILMTK as-is
alternatives.tradeoff: Ready-made on/off pairing, but tuned for its own heuristics and does not use your labeled toggles.

steps.delegate: Python, numpy, scikit-learn. Implement Signatures.fit(labeled_events) storing per-appliance mean and spread of delta_w and on-duration, and predict(event) returning (appliance or 'unknown', distance). Pair on/off events greedily by matching magnitude. Tests: an event far from all signatures returns 'unknown'; a perfect copy of a signature returns that appliance.
verify: Confusion matrix on dev-house (house 5) events, not the events used to fit signatures, including the unknown column
Name the two appliances most often confused and their typical step sizes

steps.title: Train a seq2point model for per-appliance energy
steps.learn: Events say what switched; the bill needs energy over time, including cycling and variable loads. Sequence-to-point maps a window of mains to the target appliance's power at the window midpoint, one network per appliance, and its paper evaluated on a house unseen in training.

decision.choice: nilmtk-contrib Seq2PointTorch, one model per target appliance, trained on house 1, scored once on house 2
decision.why: It is a maintained PyTorch implementation of a published method with a standard NILMTK interface, so you compare against the baselines with the same metrics. One model per appliance keeps failures easy to localize.

alternatives.name: Denoising autoencoder (DAE)
alternatives.tradeoff: Outputs whole windows and handles long activations, but you must stitch overlapping window predictions.

alternatives.name: FHMM only
alternatives.tradeoff: No GPU and interpretable states, but struggles as the number of appliances grows.

alternatives.name: BERT-style model in nilmtk-contrib
alternatives.tradeoff: May score higher, but slower to train and harder to debug for a first build.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, nilmtk-contrib[torch]. Write train_s2p.py: for each target appliance build Seq2PointTorch with sequence_length, n_epochs, batch_size, seed set from a config file; train on house 1 (hold out the last 10% of house 1 for early stopping), save checkpoints. Write eval.py that loads them and scores house 2 with the same nilmtk.losses as the baselines. Tests: fixed seed gives identical predictions on a short window.
verify: Add seq2point rows to the baseline table on house 2 and say which appliances improved
Plot predicted vs true power for one day of house 2 for the best and worst appliance

steps.title: Stream your own home's mains power to local storage
steps.learn: Your home becomes a new test house. A whole-home clamp meter exposes live active power; you poll it, timestamp on receipt, and write it to disk on a box in the house. Clock drift, Wi-Fi dropouts and restarts are the failure modes, not throughput.

decision.choice: Shelly Pro EM (Gen2+ RPC) clamp meter polled locally via EM1.GetStatus act_power, stored in SQLite on a home box
decision.why: The local API needs no cloud account, so readings never leave the house. SQLite in WAL mode handles one writer plus readers on a Raspberry Pi. Clamps inside the panel must be fitted by a licensed electrician.

alternatives.name: OpenEnergyMonitor emonPi
alternatives.tradeoff: Open hardware built for home energy logging with its own software stack, but more parts to set up.

alternatives.name: Utility smart-meter data export
alternatives.tradeoff: No installation, but usually far coarser than seconds, which hides individual toggles.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, httpx, sqlite3. Write collector.py: poll http://<meter>/rpc/EM1.GetStatus?id=0 at a fixed interval, store (ts_utc, act_power) in SQLite with WAL, retry with backoff, log gaps as rows with NULL power. Add a resampler that outputs the same 6 s grid as load.py. Tests: a mocked timeout produces a gap row, not a crash; restart resumes without duplicate timestamps.
verify: Run 48 hours and report uptime percentage and the longest gap
Check the 48 h energy from your readings against the utility meter's reading over the same period and record the difference

steps.title: Build a toggle harness with smart plugs as ground truth
steps.learn: The try-it needs ground truth that is independent of the model: when was each appliance really switched, and what did it draw? Smart plugs that report their own power give both, and their logs must never be fed into the detector being graded.

decision.choice: Smart plugs reporting per-appliance power (Switch apower) on safe loads, toggled on a random schedule via Switch.Set
decision.why: Random, logged toggles remove human timing bias and give exact on/off times. Plug power is measured separately from mains, so the grader is not the system's own logic. Keep heaters and kettles manual and attended.

alternatives.name: Manual toggling with a phone button log
alternatives.tradeoff: Works for any appliance, including hard-wired ones, but your timestamps are only as precise as your tap.

alternatives.name: Use the model's own detections as labels
alternatives.tradeoff: Free, but circular: it can never reveal a miss.

steps.delegate: Python, httpx. Write toggle.py: for a list of plug IPs, at random intervals call /rpc/Switch.Set?id=0&on=true|false, log (ts, plug, state) and poll Switch.GetStatus apower into a ground_truth table separate from the meter DB. Add score_live.py matching detected events to toggles within a tolerance window. Tests: matcher counts one detection per toggle at most.
verify: Run 20 random toggles per plugged appliance and confirm every toggle is in the ground_truth table
Confirm score_live.py reads ground truth only from plug logs, never from model output

steps.title: Turn predictions into a bill breakdown with an 'other' share
steps.learn: The user's question is 'which appliance drives the bill'. Integrate predicted power into kWh per appliance per day and multiply by your tariff. Many loads are never modeled, so the gap between mains energy and the sum of predictions must be shown, not spread across known appliances.

decision.choice: Daily kWh and cost per target appliance plus an explicit 'unexplained' bucket, clipped so parts never exceed mains
decision.why: Showing the unexplained share keeps the answer honest when the model only knows 5 appliances. Clipping enforces the physical constraint that appliances cannot draw more than the house.

alternatives.name: Normalize predictions to sum to mains
alternatives.tradeoff: Tidy chart, but silently inflates known appliances with energy from unknown ones.

alternatives.name: Show events only, no energy
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and very accurate for toggles, but does not answer the bill question.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas. Implement attribute(mains, preds, tariff) returning a daily table of kWh and cost per appliance plus unexplained = mains minus sum(clipped preds). Tests: on house 1 with ground-truth inputs the table matches submeter energy; unexplained is never negative.
verify: On house 2, compare predicted vs true monthly kWh share for each target appliance
Report the unexplained share for house 2 and for one week of your home

steps.title: Test it at home: toggle appliances and score detection
steps.learn: The try-it: toggle appliances and see whether the model names each one. Run event detection plus signature matching live, score with the plug ground truth, and note what changes from UK-DALE (different appliances, voltage, background loads).
verify: Per-appliance precision, recall and F1 over at least 20 toggles each, with the tolerance window stated
Detection latency from toggle to label, median and worst case
Count events labeled 'unknown' and list the real appliance for each
Repeat the test at a busy time (other loads running) and report the F1 drop

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example, two appliances with the same step size); assumptions and what this does not prove (one test house, UK appliances, a few weeks of your home).
verify: Part 1 states the one question and the frozen split
Part 2: every number (baselines, seq2point, live F1, bill shares) has the command and machine that produced it
Part 3 explains at least two surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including the unexplained share

projects.title: Thrift price checker
projects.problem: Is this secondhand item a good deal?
projects.concepts: Image search over resale listings, price estimation from similar items
projects.tryIt: Test at thrift stores and garage sales
projects.question: From a photo of a secondhand item, can a system find similar resale listings and give a price range that holds the real price for most items?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen test sets
steps.learn: Two problems hide here: identify the item (image search) and price it from similar items (estimation with uncertainty). Each gets its own metric: recall@K for finding the same product, and interval coverage plus width for the price range. A 'good deal' verdict is only as good as both.

decision.choice: Stanford Online Products test split for image search; Mercari train data with a frozen 10% slice for pricing
decision.why: Stanford Online Products groups photos of the same online product, so recall@K measures 'did we find this item'. Mercari has about 1.48M resale listings with name, condition, category, brand, shipping, description and price, enough to learn prices of used goods.

alternatives.name: Scrape a marketplace yourself
alternatives.tradeoff: Current prices with images, but terms of service, rate limits and no fixed test set to compare runs.

alternatives.name: Only thrift-store items you price by hand
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use, but a few dozen labels cannot tune or test a model reliably.

verify: README states the question, recall@1 and recall@10 for search, and 80% interval coverage plus median width for price
Mercari test slice chosen by hashing train_id, saved to disk, and never used for fitting or tuning
Note that Mercari is a fixed historical snapshot in USD and has no images

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Photograph items, not people: shoppers, staff and sellers at garage sales will be in frames, and photos carry location. The verdict is a helper; it does not check authenticity, safety recalls or condition, and the seller and official recall lists are the sources for those.

decision.choice: On-device face check blocks or blurs before upload; strip EXIF; store only item crop, guess and prices
decision.why: Running a full-range face detector on the phone means most faces are blurred before upload (small or turned faces can be missed). Item crops plus prices answer the question without logging who was nearby or where you were.

alternatives.name: Server-side blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach the server even briefly.

alternatives.name: Store nothing
alternatives.tradeoff: Safest, but you cannot audit wrong verdicts afterwards.

steps.delegate: Build a privacy module for the later app: MediaPipe Face Detector (full-range BlazeFace) that blurs every face box or asks for a retake; an EXIF stripper; a storage policy keeping only item crop, JSON guess and prices; disclaimer text 'Estimate from past listings. Does not check authenticity or recalls.' Tests: on public test photos with faces, every detected box is blurred; output has no EXIF.
verify: Run the face module on 10 public, openly licensed photos with people and confirm every face is blurred in the output
README has the helper disclaimer for the verdict screen and a rule to ask staff before photographing in a store

steps.title: Choose the image embedding that finds the same product
steps.learn: Finding 'the same kind of item' is metric learning: photos of one product should land close together. Pretrained CLIP and DINOv2 features often work without training; Stanford Online Products lets you measure that before fine-tuning anything.

decision.choice: open_clip ViT-B-32 image embeddings as the baseline, DINOv2-small as the challenger, chosen by recall@K
decision.why: CLIP also embeds text, which you can reuse to zero-shot a category from the photo. DINOv2 features are trained without text and are a strong image-only comparison. Picking by measured recall avoids guessing.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune with a metric-learning loss on the SOP train split
alternatives.tradeoff: Usually better on product photos, but needs GPU time and risks overfitting to catalog-style shots.

alternatives.name: Perceptual hashing
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast exact-copy finder, but useless for a different photo of a similar item.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, torch, open_clip, transformers (facebook/dinov2-small). Write embed.py with embed_images(paths, model_name) returning L2-normalized float32 arrays. Write eval_sop.py computing recall@1 and @10 where a hit is another image of the same product id (exclude the query). Pick the model on a val split of held-out SOP train classes; run the test split once. faiss IndexFlatIP. Tests: unit-norm vectors; query never its own hit.
verify: Recall@1 and @10 for both models on the SOP val split (from train classes), then the chosen model once on test, with GPU or CPU recorded
Inspect 10 failures and note whether they are viewpoint, background or truly different products

steps.title: Read brand, type and condition cues from the photo
steps.learn: Mercari has no images, so the bridge from photo to priced listings is text: item type, brand (often on a label or tag), and visible wear. A vision-language model can read labels and describe the item, and a JSON schema keeps its answer machine-readable.

decision.choice: Local VLM (qwen2.5vl via Ollama) returning a JSON schema: item_type, brand or null, visible_text, condition_notes
decision.why: Ollama's format parameter constrains output to a JSON schema, so replies nearly always parse (still validate). Running locally keeps store photos off third-party servers, and a brand read from a tag is a strong price signal.

alternatives.name: Cloud VLM API
alternatives.tradeoff: Often more accurate on small or worn labels, but each photo leaves the device and costs money per call.

alternatives.name: CLIP zero-shot over Mercari category names
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and fast for type, but cannot read a brand name off a tag.

alternatives.name: User types the details
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate when people bother, but slow in a store and skips the vision part.

steps.delegate: Python, ollama, pydantic. Define an ItemGuess pydantic model and call ollama.chat with the image and format=ItemGuess.model_json_schema(); validate with ItemGuess.model_validate_json. Allow brand=null. Tests: a mocked malformed reply raises a validation error that the caller turns into 'ask the user'; a photo of a plain text label returns that text in visible_text.
verify: Photograph 20 items at home with visible brand tags and record how many brands are read exactly
Record median seconds per photo on your machine

steps.title: Map the guess onto the listings' brand and category names
steps.learn: The VLM says 'Levis' while listings say a different spelling; the VLM says 'denim jacket' while listings use a category path. Normalizing both sides onto one vocabulary is what makes 'similar items' filters work.

decision.choice: Fuzzy-match brand to the Mercari brand_name vocabulary with RapidFuzz, with a score cutoff below which brand is unknown
decision.why: Brand names have typos, spacing and punctuation variants, which string similarity handles cheaply. A cutoff avoids forcing a no-name item onto a premium brand, which would inflate the price.

alternatives.name: Exact match after lowercasing
alternatives.tradeoff: Never wrong when it matches, but misses common variants and drops the strongest signal.

alternatives.name: Embedding similarity on brand names
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches looser variants, but can match unrelated brands that share words.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz, pandas. Build brand_vocab from Mercari train rows only (counts per brand). Implement normalize_brand(text) returning (brand or None, score) using rapidfuzz.process.extractOne with processor=rapidfuzz.utils.default_process and a configurable score_cutoff; same for category against category_name values. Tests: case and punctuation variants map to the same brand; a random word returns None.
verify: Hand-label 50 VLM brand outputs and report precision and recall of the mapping at your cutoff
List the 5 most common unmapped strings and decide whether to add aliases

steps.title: Retrieve comparable listings with hybrid search
steps.learn: Comparables are listings of the same kind of item. Keyword search nails exact model names and brands; dense text embeddings catch paraphrases. Fuse both, and restrict to the matched category so a phone case never prices a phone.

decision.choice: bm25s plus all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings over name and brand, fused with RRF, pre-filtered by category
decision.why: BM25 is strong on brand and model tokens; MiniLM is small enough to embed 1.3M training listings on one machine. RRF fuses ranks without calibrating scores. Pre-filtering keeps every candidate in the right category.

alternatives.name: Dense only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but can rank a different model of the same brand above the exact one.

alternatives.name: Post-filter by category
alternatives.tradeoff: One global index, but a strict filter can leave fewer than k results.

steps.delegate: Python, bm25s, sentence-transformers, faiss-cpu. Index only Mercari train rows (never the frozen test slice). Implement comps(query_text, category, k) returning listing ids, BM25 rank, dense rank and RRF score, with per-category sub-indexes or a category mask. Tests: a query copied from a listing name returns that listing first; results all share the filter category.
verify: For 100 validation-split listings, report the share whose top 10 comps share their brand
Assert the comps index contains zero rows from the frozen test slice

steps.title: Estimate price from comparables and item features
steps.learn: Prices are skewed, so model log price. The median of comps is a strong, explainable baseline; a model adds condition, shipping and brand effects. Leakage is the trap: a training row must never see itself among its own comps.

decision.choice: Baseline: median of comps' log price. Model: boosted trees on comp stats plus condition, shipping, brand
decision.why: The comps median is what a careful human does, so it is the bar to beat. HistGradientBoostingRegressor handles mixed features and missing brand natively and supports quantile loss, which the range step needs.

alternatives.name: Text regression on descriptions (TF-IDF plus linear model)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and strong on this kind of data, but blind to the photo pipeline and hard to explain per item.

alternatives.name: Comps median only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fully explainable, but ignores condition and shipping differences.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn, pandas. Features per row: comps (excluding the row itself) median, IQR and count of log price, top comp similarity, item_condition_id, shipping, brand known. Fit sklearn HistGradientBoostingRegressor on log1p(price) using a train/validation split inside train only. Report RMSLE and median absolute percent error vs the comps-median baseline. Tests: leave-self-out holds for every training row.
verify: Table on the frozen test slice: RMSLE and median absolute percent error for comps median vs the model
Show 5 worst errors and say whether comps, brand mapping or the model caused each

steps.title: Turn the estimate into a calibrated price range
steps.learn: A shopper needs a range, not a point. Quantile regression gives lower and upper prices, but its coverage is not guaranteed. Conformalized quantile regression adjusts the band on a held-out calibration set so about 80% of items land inside, under an exchangeability assumption.

decision.choice: Quantile HistGradientBoosting at 10% and 90%, conformalized on a calibration slice of train
decision.why: CQR keeps the adaptive width of quantile models (wide for rare items, narrow for common ones) while restoring coverage. The calibration slice comes from train, so the frozen test slice still grades the result.

alternatives.name: Comps IQR as the range
alternatives.tradeoff: Intuitive, but its coverage is unknown and often too narrow when comps are few.

alternatives.name: Plain split conformal on absolute residuals
alternatives.tradeoff: Guaranteed coverage too, but one width for every item, too wide for common items.

alternatives.name: MAPIE library
alternatives.tradeoff: Packages these methods with tests, but learn the math by writing the few lines yourself first.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn, numpy. Fit HistGradientBoostingRegressor(loss='quantile', quantile=0.1) and quantile=0.9 on log price. On a calibration slice compute conformity scores max(lo - y, y - hi), take the finite-sample adjusted quantile, widen intervals by it. Tests: on synthetic data, coverage on a fresh sample is close to 80%.
verify: On the frozen test slice report coverage and median width, before and after conformalizing
Report coverage separately for brand-known vs brand-unknown items

steps.title: Give a deal verdict, or say 'not sure'
steps.learn: The verdict compares the tag price with the range. When the photo pipeline is unsure (no brand, few comps, low similarity), a confident verdict is worse than none. Show the comps so the shopper can judge.

decision.choice: Good deal if the tag is below the lower bound, fair if inside, pricey if above; abstain when comps are few or weak
decision.why: Rules on a calibrated range are easy to explain at a shelf. Abstaining on weak evidence protects trust, the thing that decides whether someone keeps using the app.

alternatives.name: Show a single point estimate
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest screen, but hides uncertainty and invites false confidence.

alternatives.name: Always give a verdict
alternatives.tradeoff: Never frustrating, but wrong verdicts on unbranded items will be common.

steps.delegate: Python. Implement verdict(tag_price, lo, hi, n_comps, top_sim, brand_known) returning (label, reasons, top 5 comps with name and price). Abstain thresholds come from a config tuned on the validation split. Tests: a tag below lo gives 'good deal'; n_comps under the minimum gives 'not sure' whatever the price.
verify: On the test slice, simulate tag prices and report verdict accuracy and abstain rate
Check that every non-abstained verdict shows at least 3 comps

steps.title: Wire it into a phone-friendly app with a latency budget
steps.learn: In a store you want an answer in seconds on patchy signal. The slow parts are the VLM and the embedding model; search and the price model are fast. Resize photos before upload, load models once, and cache repeated lookups.

decision.choice: FastAPI on a laptop or home server, phone web page uploads a resized photo, models loaded once at startup
decision.why: A web page works on any phone without an app store, and one server keeps one model version for every lookup. If the server is unreachable, the page saves the photo and tag price to check later.

alternatives.name: Fully on-device app
alternatives.tradeoff: Works offline and keeps photos local, but needs small quantized models and a 1.3M-listing index on the phone.

alternatives.name: Serverless functions
alternatives.tradeoff: No server to run, but cold starts with large models can blow the latency budget.

steps.delegate: Python, FastAPI, Pillow. POST /check takes an image and an optional tag price; resize to a max side, strip EXIF with Pillow, run VLM, normalize, comps, price, verdict; return JSON with timings per stage. Static HTML page with camera input. Tests: an image with EXIF GPS returns no GPS in anything stored; per-stage timings sum to under the total.
verify: Record median and p95 end-to-end latency over 20 requests from a phone on mobile data
Identify the slowest stage from the timings

steps.title: Test it at thrift stores and garage sales
steps.learn: The try-it: price real items in real light. Ground truth must come from outside the system: after the trip, look up recent sold prices for each item by hand on a resale site and record them before looking at the app's answer again.
verify: Check at least 30 items; report the share with a verdict vs 'not sure' and median latency in store
Report how often your hand-found sold price falls inside the app's range, vs 80% on Mercari
Report brand read accuracy on the tagged items and list failure causes (glare, worn tags)
Compare range coverage for branded vs unbranded items

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example, coverage dropping in the field); assumptions and what this does not prove (old US listings, no images in price data, a small field sample).
verify: Part 1 states the one question and both frozen test sets
Part 2: recall@K, RMSLE, coverage, latency and field results each have a command and machine
Part 3 explains at least two surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions and limits, including that authenticity is not checked

projects.title: Weather-aware outfit picker
projects.problem: What to wear from what you own
projects.concepts: Clothing embeddings, retrieval with weather and occasion filters
projects.tryIt: Photograph your wardrobe and use it for a month
projects.question: Can retrieval over photos of my own wardrobe, filtered by the day's forecast and occasion, pick outfits I actually wear for a month?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen test set
steps.learn: This is retrieval with hard constraints: from what you own, return a few outfits that suit today's weather and occasion. Success from the try-it: use it for a month and log, per day, whether you wore a suggestion as-is, edited it, or ignored it. Item tagging also needs its own frozen check.

decision.choice: Your own wardrobe with a hand-labeled tag set frozen in week 0, plus a daily accept/edit/ignore log
decision.why: No public dataset holds your clothes or your habits, so the real test must be yours. Labeling warmth, rain-readiness and formality for every item before any model runs gives a fixed answer key for the tagger that you never tune against.

alternatives.name: Public fashion dataset only
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible, but product shots of strangers' clothes say nothing about your closet, your climate or whether you would wear the result.

alternatives.name: Judge suggestions by feel
alternatives.tradeoff: No setup, but a month of vague impressions cannot show whether any change helped.

verify: Write the one question and 3 metrics: daily wear-as-is rate, edit rate, and tag accuracy on the frozen labels
Store the frozen tag labels in a separate file the tuning code never reads
Record the number of items and the month you will run the trial

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before any photos are taken
steps.learn: Photograph clothes, not people. Wardrobe photos taken at home can show family members, mirrors with your face, and EXIF GPS that reveals your address. The forecast is a helper: for storms, heat or ice the official weather service warning is what counts.

decision.choice: Hanger or flat-lay shots, EXIF stripped on device, coordinates rounded to 2 decimals (about 1 km), official-warning link
decision.why: Clothes on a hanger need no person in frame. Stripping EXIF before upload removes the home location. Rounding coordinates for the forecast call gives the same local weather without sending your exact address to a third party.

alternatives.name: Photos of yourself wearing each item
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows fit better, but stores many images of a person, which this app does not need.

alternatives.name: Blur faces on the server
alternatives.tradeoff: Allows casual photos, but raw faces reach the server even if briefly.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 ingest script with Pillow: re-save each wardrobe photo without EXIF, reject images where MediaPipe Face Detector finds a face, and round latitude and longitude to 2 decimals in config. Tests: output files carry no EXIF; a test image with a face is rejected; config rejects coordinates with more than 2 decimals.
verify: Run 5 photos with a visible face through ingest and confirm all are rejected
Confirm stored images have no EXIF and the config holds the link to your official weather warning service

steps.title: Capture each item as a clean, cut-out product shot
steps.learn: Embedding models trained on product photos work best on centered items on plain backgrounds; the FashionCLIP model card notes this bias. Removing the background makes your phone photos look more like that training data, so similarity reflects the garment, not the bed it lies on.

decision.choice: One photo per item, background removed with rembg, stored with category and a slot (top, bottom, shoes, layer)
decision.why: rembg runs locally from Python or the command line, so photos stay on your machine. The slot field lets the outfit builder combine items without guessing structure from pixels.

alternatives.name: Keep raw photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero processing, but background clutter leaks into embeddings and similar items look different.

alternatives.name: Detect and crop with an object detector
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles cluttered piles, but adds a model and still leaves background inside the box.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 using rembg (from rembg import remove) and Pillow: for each photo write a PNG cut-out and a row in items.csv (item_id, slot, category, path). Tests: every item has exactly one slot from the allowed set; output PNGs have an alpha channel; reruns are idempotent.
verify: Inspect 20 random cut-outs and count how many lost part of the garment
Confirm every item in items.csv has a slot and an image file

steps.title: Choose the image embedding model for items
steps.learn: A CLIP-style model maps images and text into one space, so one item vector serves both similarity between items and text prompts like 'a waterproof jacket'. A fashion fine-tune shifts that space toward garment attributes rather than general scenes.

decision.choice: FashionCLIP (patrickjohncyh/fashion-clip) image embeddings, with general open_clip as a comparison
decision.why: FashionCLIP is CLIP fine-tuned on a large set of fashion product images and text, which matches cut-out wardrobe shots. Keeping a general CLIP baseline shows whether the fine-tune earns its place on your clothes.

alternatives.name: General CLIP via open_clip only
alternatives.tradeoff: Broader vocabulary and many checkpoints, but less tuned to fabric, cut and style words.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune on your own labels
alternatives.tradeoff: Could fit your closet best, but a few dozen labeled items risk overfitting the frozen tag set.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with Hugging Face transformers (CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor) loading patrickjohncyh/fashion-clip, plus open_clip for a baseline. Embed every cut-out, L2-normalize, store as a NumPy array keyed by item_id. Tests: vectors have unit norm; embedding the same image twice gives identical vectors; nearest neighbor of an item is itself.
verify: For 10 items, look at the 3 nearest neighbors under each model and note which model groups like with like
Record model name, checkpoint and embedding dimension

steps.title: Tag warmth, rain-readiness and formality
steps.learn: Weather filters need tags such as warmth level and rain-readiness, and occasion filters need formality. Zero-shot tagging scores each item against text prompts per label. Measure it on the frozen labels and let the user correct tags, since a wrong 'waterproof' tag ruins a rainy day.

decision.choice: Zero-shot prompts per tag, auto-applied only above a confidence margin, everything else confirmed by hand
decision.why: A wardrobe is small enough that confirming the uncertain items by hand is cheap, while zero-shot handles the obvious ones. The margin rule keeps the errors you would not notice out of the filter.

alternatives.name: Tag every item by hand
alternatives.tradeoff: Most accurate and simple, but adding new clothes is a chore and nothing is learned.

alternatives.name: Train a small classifier on the embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: Can beat prompts with enough labels, but needs labels beyond the frozen set to avoid tuning on it.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11: for each tag (warmth: light, mid, warm; rain-ready: yes or no; formality: casual, smart, formal) build several text prompts, score items by cosine similarity to prompt embeddings, auto-tag when top-minus-second exceeds a margin, else queue for review. Tests: margin of 0 tags everything; a huge margin tags nothing; output is one tag per field.
verify: Report tag accuracy per field on the frozen labels, and how many items went to manual review
Label 15 to 20 extra items as a tuning set (not frozen); pick margin and prompts there, then list the 3 worst tuning-set mistakes

steps.title: Turn the forecast into constraints for the day
steps.learn: Use the hours you are actually outside, not the daily mean. Open-Meteo's forecast API returns hourly variables such as apparent_temperature, precipitation_probability and wind_speed_10m for given coordinates and timezone, which map onto warmth and rain tags.

decision.choice: Open-Meteo hourly forecast over your out-of-home window, mapped to a required warmth band and a rain-ready flag
decision.why: Open-Meteo needs no API key for non-commercial use, and feels-like temperature plus precipitation probability over your actual hours are what decide a jacket. Thresholds live in config so you can adjust them to how you run hot or cold.

alternatives.name: Current conditions only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but a cool morning hides a hot afternoon, or a dry start hides evening rain.

alternatives.name: Learn thresholds from your feedback
alternatives.tradeoff: Personal, but needs weeks of logs before it beats hand-set thresholds.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with httpx: call the Open-Meteo forecast endpoint with hourly=apparent_temperature,precipitation_probability,wind_speed_10m and timezone, slice to the configured hours, and return {warmth_band, rain_ready}. Cache by date. Tests: a mocked response with rain above threshold sets rain_ready; empty hours raise a clear error; an API failure falls back to yesterday's cached constraints with a warning.
verify: Compare the derived constraints with what you would have chosen on 5 real days
Make the API unreachable and confirm the constraint function returns cached constraints with a visible warning

steps.title: Hard-filter by weather and occasion, then score outfits
steps.learn: Weather and occasion are hard rules: a non-rain-ready jacket on a wet day is wrong regardless of style. Filter items first, then build outfits from the survivors and score them on softer signals such as color and style coherence between pieces.

decision.choice: Filter items per slot, enumerate top, bottom, shoes and optional layer, score by mean pairwise embedding similarity
decision.why: A personal wardrobe gives a small enough product of slots to enumerate after filtering. Pairwise similarity is a simple, explainable coherence signal you can inspect, and the hard filter guarantees no weather mistake gets through.

alternatives.name: Score everything, penalize bad weather
alternatives.tradeoff: One ranking, but a strong style score can outvote a rain rule.

alternatives.name: Learned outfit compatibility model
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures complementary pieces that are not similar, but needs outfit training data you do not have yet.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11: filter items by warmth band, rain flag and formality, enumerate one item per required slot (layer optional), score each outfit by mean pairwise cosine similarity, return top 3 with the tags that let each item pass. Tests: no returned outfit violates a hard rule; an empty slot after filtering returns a clear 'nothing fits' message; results are deterministic.
verify: Run 10 synthetic weather days and confirm zero rule violations
Read 5 top suggestions and note whether the explanation matches why each item passed

steps.title: Add variety and learn from what you actually wear
steps.learn: Pure similarity picks the same outfit every cold day. A recently-worn penalty spreads choices across the wardrobe, and the daily wear/edit/ignore log becomes a feedback signal. Starting with no history is a cold-start problem, so rules lead and feedback adds weight over time.

decision.choice: Recently-worn penalty plus a per-item boost from accepted outfits, both small weights on top of the coherence score
decision.why: Two transparent features are easy to reason about with one user and one month of data, and you can switch them off to measure what each adds.

alternatives.name: No feedback at all
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fully predictable, but repeats favorites and never adapts to your taste.

alternatives.name: Train a ranker on the log
alternatives.tradeoff: More expressive, but a month of one person's choices is too little data to train reliably.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with SQLite: tables wear_log(date, outfit_items, action in {worn, edited, ignored}) and item_stats. Add score terms for days since last worn and acceptance rate per item with config weights. Tests: an item worn yesterday ranks lower than an identical item; zero weights reproduce the previous ranking exactly; edits record which items were swapped.
verify: Log one week and check how many distinct items were suggested versus without the penalty
Confirm setting both weights to 0 reproduces the filter-then-score ranking

steps.title: Test it outside: use it for a month
steps.learn: The try-it is the real test: every morning take the suggestion, edit it, or ignore it, and log the weather. A month spans enough weather changes to see where rules or tags break. Freeze the code and thresholds at the start so the month measures one system.
verify: Record days used, wear-as-is rate, edit rate and ignore rate for the month
List every day you were too hot, too cold or wet, with the forecast numbers that day
Replay weeks 3 to 4 with feedback weights set to 0 and compare how often your worn outfit ranks in the top 3 with and without them

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Use the 4-part write-up: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example, a tag error or a forecast miss); and what this does not prove, such as one wardrobe, one climate and one person's taste.
verify: Write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number has the machine, model checkpoint and command that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with a concrete day or item
An assumptions and limits section lists what a month with one wardrobe cannot show

projects.title: Lecture search
projects.problem: "Where did the professor explain backprop?"
projects.concepts: Speech-to-text, hybrid search over transcripts with timestamps
projects.tryIt: Index a semester of your own lecture recordings
projects.question: Can hybrid search over timestamped transcripts of my own lectures jump me to the moment a topic was explained, within 30 seconds?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen query set
steps.learn: A hit is a result whose timestamp lands near where the explanation actually starts. Success from the try-it: index a semester of your own recordings, then measure recall@5 and MRR on questions like 'where did the professor explain backprop?' written from your notes before any search code exists.

decision.choice: A frozen set of 40 to 60 questions with hand-found start times, a hit meaning within 30 seconds of the answer start
decision.why: No public dataset has your lectures. Writing questions from notes and syllabus, and finding answer times by listening, gives an answer key independent of the transcripts and the system, so the search never grades itself.

alternatives.name: Generate questions from the transcripts with an LLM
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but questions reuse the transcript's exact words and errors, inflating keyword search scores.

alternatives.name: Exact-segment match as the hit rule
alternatives.tradeoff: Stricter, but chunk boundaries become the metric instead of whether you land at the right moment.

verify: Write the one question, the hit window and the metrics: recall@5 and MRR
Split questions: about 15 dev questions for choosing window, k and reranking; freeze the rest in a file the tuning code never reads
Record the number of lectures and total hours to be indexed

steps.title: Privacy and consent check before indexing any recording
steps.learn: Recordings contain the instructor's voice and often classmates' questions. Rules on recording lectures differ by university and place, so check the course policy and ask the instructor. Index for your own study only, keep it local, and do not identify who is speaking.

decision.choice: Only recordings you are permitted to keep, processed and stored locally, no speaker identification, private index
decision.why: Local transcription means audio never leaves your machine. Skipping speaker diarization avoids building a record of which student said what, which this search does not need.

alternatives.name: Cloud speech-to-text API
alternatives.tradeoff: Less setup, but uploads others' voices to a third party; check the policy first.

alternatives.name: Add speaker diarization
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets you filter to the professor, but labels students' voices, which needs their consent.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 config and ingest guard: refuse any audio file not listed in an allowed_recordings.csv (course, date, permission note), and keep audio, transcripts and index under one local data directory excluded from sync. Tests: an unlisted file is rejected; nothing is written outside the data directory.
verify: Confirm the course policy or instructor permission is recorded for every course in allowed_recordings.csv
Confirm the pipeline makes no network calls except model downloads

steps.title: Transcribe with word-level timestamps
steps.learn: Search can only jump to a moment if every word carries a time. Whisper-family models transcribe long lectures robustly; faster-whisper reimplements Whisper on CTranslate2 and returns word timings with word_timestamps=True. Lecture jargon is where errors cluster.

decision.choice: faster-whisper with word_timestamps=True; pick the model size by error rate on a hand-corrected 5 minute sample
decision.why: Runs locally on CPU or GPU with quantized compute types, and word timings feed chunking directly. Choosing size by measured errors on your own professor's speech beats choosing by reputation.

alternatives.name: openai-whisper reference package
alternatives.tradeoff: Same models and simpler provenance, but slower on the same hardware.

alternatives.name: WhisperX
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds alignment for tighter word timings and diarization, but more dependencies and you do not need speakers.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with faster-whisper: WhisperModel(size, device, compute_type) then transcribe(path, word_timestamps=True). Save per lecture a JSON of segments and words with start and end seconds. Tests: word times are non-decreasing and within audio duration; rerunning on the same file gives the same output; a word error rate function matches a hand computed example.
verify: Hand-correct a 5 minute sample and report word error rate for 2 model sizes
List 10 course terms and how often each was transcribed correctly
Record transcription time per lecture hour and the machine

steps.title: Skip silence and catch spurious transcript text
steps.learn: Lectures include breaks, setup and silent demos. A voice activity detector removes non-speech before transcription, saving time and reducing text that was never said. Check the transcript for repeated lines, a common long-form failure.

decision.choice: faster-whisper's built-in Silero VAD (vad_filter=True), plus a repeated-line detector that flags segments for review
decision.why: The VAD is integrated, so it costs one flag. The repetition check is cheap and catches the failure you would otherwise only notice when search returns garbage.

alternatives.name: No VAD
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer moving parts, but silence wastes compute and invites spurious segments.

alternatives.name: Trim silence with a fixed energy threshold
alternatives.tradeoff: No model, but room noise and quiet speakers make one threshold fail in both directions.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11: enable vad_filter=True in faster-whisper; add a check that flags any text repeated 3 or more times in a row and any segment longer than a set duration. Tests: a synthetic transcript with a repeated line is flagged; clean text is not; flags carry lecture id and start time.
verify: Compare transcript length and flagged segments with and without VAD on 2 lectures
Listen to 5 flagged segments and record how many were real errors

steps.title: Chunk transcripts into time windows that keep context
steps.learn: The searchable unit is a short window of speech with a start time. Too short and an explanation is split across chunks; too long and the jump lands minutes early. Overlap keeps an idea that crosses a boundary findable.

decision.choice: Windows of about 45 to 60 seconds built from word timestamps, overlapping by about a third, cut at segment ends
decision.why: Matching the window to the 30 second hit rule keeps the chunk start close to the answer, and cutting at segment ends avoids mid-sentence chunks. Window size is a knob you will sweep, not a fixed fact.

alternatives.name: One chunk per Whisper segment
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise timestamps, but segments are often one sentence, too little context for embeddings.

alternatives.name: Split by slide change
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches the lecture's structure, but needs slide video and OCR, and long slides make huge chunks.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11: build chunks from the words JSON with configurable window and overlap, each with lecture_id, start_s, end_s, text. Tests: every word belongs to at least one chunk; chunk starts are non-decreasing; window and overlap settings change chunk count as expected.
verify: Sweep 3 window sizes, record chunk count per lecture hour and recall@5 on the dev questions only
Read 5 chunks and confirm none starts or ends mid-word

steps.title: Build the keyword index with SQLite FTS5
steps.learn: Course terms like 'backprop' or a theorem name are exact words, which keyword search handles well. SQLite FTS5 builds an inverted index inside SQLite and ranks with bm25(), where better matches get numerically lower values. Transcription errors on rare terms hurt keyword recall.

decision.choice: SQLite FTS5 table over chunk text with the porter tokenizer, ranked by bm25()
decision.why: One local file, no server, and the stemmer matches 'gradients' to 'gradient'. Snippet() gives a highlighted preview for results.

alternatives.name: Tantivy or Elasticsearch
alternatives.tradeoff: More analyzers and scale, but a server or extra dependency for a few hundred hours of text.

alternatives.name: rank_bm25 in memory
alternatives.tradeoff: Tiny code, but rebuilds every run and has no storage or snippets.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 sqlite3: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE chunks USING fts5(text, lecture_id UNINDEXED, start_s UNINDEXED, tokenize='porter'). Query with MATCH and ORDER BY bm25(chunks), escaping user input so punctuation cannot break the query. Tests: a known phrase returns its chunk first; a query with quotes or a hyphen does not raise; empty queries return nothing.
verify: Run the frozen questions through BM25 only and record recall@5 and MRR
List 3 misses caused by transcription errors

steps.title: Add dense embeddings for paraphrased questions
steps.learn: Students ask in their own words ('how do weights get updated') while the professor says 'backpropagation'. Dense embeddings match meaning across that gap. Some models expect different prefixes for queries and passages, and getting that wrong silently lowers quality.

decision.choice: intfloat/e5-base-v2 with 'query: ' and 'passage: ' prefixes, exact cosine search over a NumPy matrix
decision.why: The model card specifies the prefixes, which forces you to handle query and document inputs differently. A semester of chunks fits in memory, so exact search avoids tuning an ANN index.

alternatives.name: Symmetric model without prefixes
alternatives.tradeoff: One code path, but no built-in distinction between short questions and long passages.

alternatives.name: HNSW index (FAISS or hnswlib)
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed at much larger scale, but adds recall loss and knobs you do not need here.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with sentence-transformers loading intfloat/e5-base-v2: embed chunks with 'passage: ' and queries with 'query: ', normalize, store vectors aligned to chunk ids. Tests: missing prefixes raise an error in the wrapper; vectors are unit norm; a chunk's own text as a query ranks it in the top 3.
verify: Run the frozen questions through dense only and record recall@5 and MRR
Run once without prefixes and record the change

steps.title: Fuse keyword and dense results with RRF
steps.learn: Keyword search wins on exact jargon and dense search on paraphrases; fusing them covers both. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines lists by rank, not raw score, so BM25 and cosine values never need to share a scale.

decision.choice: RRF over the top results of each retriever, then merge overlapping chunks that point at nearly the same moment
decision.why: RRF has a single constant and no training. Merging near-duplicate timestamps stops overlapping windows from filling the top 5 with the same moment.

alternatives.name: Weighted sum of normalized scores
alternatives.tradeoff: Can beat RRF when tuned, but tuning the weight on the frozen set overfits it.

alternatives.name: Dense only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but rare course terms and names are often missed.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11: take top 50 from FTS5 and from dense, fuse with RRF (configurable k), then collapse results from the same lecture whose start times are within the hit window, keeping the best rank. Tests: an item first in both lists ranks first; disjoint lists interleave; collapsed results never share a lecture and window.
verify: Report recall@5 and MRR for BM25, dense and hybrid in one table
Count how often collapsing changed the top 5

steps.title: Rerank the shortlist and jump to the moment
steps.learn: A cross-encoder reads the question and chunk together, which ranks more precisely than either retriever but is too slow for the whole index. Use it on the fused shortlist only, then open the recording at the chunk's start time.

decision.choice: cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2 over the top 20 fused results, opening the player a few seconds before start
decision.why: A small cross-encoder adds precision at modest latency on a short list. Starting playback slightly early hides small timestamp errors.

alternatives.name: No reranker
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest and simplest, fine if hybrid already meets the target.

alternatives.name: LLM reranker
alternatives.tradeoff: Better at understanding questions, but adds cost and latency per query.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with sentence-transformers CrossEncoder loading cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2: rerank the top 20 fused chunks and return lecture_id, start time, snippet. A small web page plays the local audio from start minus a few seconds. Tests: reranking a list never adds or drops items; the player URL carries the right offset.
verify: Report recall@5, MRR and median query latency with and without reranking
Click 10 results and confirm playback starts before the answer

steps.title: Test it outside: index a semester of your lectures
steps.learn: The try-it is the real test: index every recording from one semester, then use the search while studying for an exam. Freeze settings first. Questions you actually ask during revision, logged with whether the first result was right, test what the frozen set cannot.
verify: Record lectures indexed, total hours, indexing time and index size on disk
Report final recall@5 and MRR on the frozen questions
Log 20 real revision queries and the rank of the first useful result

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Use the 4-part write-up: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine and command; why surprising results happened (for example, jargon mis-transcribed or chunks too long); and what this does not prove, such as one course, one speaker and your own questions.
verify: Write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number has the machine, model names and command that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with a concrete query
An assumptions and limits section says what one semester of one course cannot show

projects.title: Campus event recommender
projects.problem: Students miss events they'd love
projects.concepts: Ranking, cold-start recommendations, feedback from clicks
projects.tryIt: Share with your dorm or club for a month; track attendance
projects.question: Does ranking events by each student's interests and clicks get more students to events they attend than a plain date-ordered list?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and a frozen test set
steps.learn: Events are items that are always new: each exists for a few days, then expires, so most of the catalog is cold. Success from the try-it: over a month with your dorm or club, attended events per student, compared with a date-ordered list. An offline check on a public click log tests the ranker before anyone uses it.

decision.choice: MIND-small for offline work, its validation set frozen as the test; the live month as the real test
decision.why: MIND is a public news-click log of impressions with clicked and skipped items, and news, like events, is short-lived. Validation is a later day than training, so freeze it as the test, train on days 1 to 5 and tune on day 6.

alternatives.name: Live data only
alternatives.tradeoff: Exactly your setting, but a dorm produces too few clicks early on to compare rankers or catch bugs.

alternatives.name: Synthetic users and clicks
alternatives.tradeoff: Unlimited and controllable, but the results only reflect the assumptions you wrote into the simulator.

verify: README states the question, the live metric (check-ins per student per week) and offline metrics (AUC, MRR, nDCG@5, nDCG@10)
MIND-small validation is stored read-only and the tuning split (last day of training) is written down before any model code
Dataset terms noted: MIND is for non-commercial research use

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before any student signs up
steps.learn: Recommend events, never people. Click and attendance logs reveal interests (faith, politics, health, identity groups) a student may not want linked to their name, and in a dorm-sized group even counts can identify someone. Event details also change: the app is a helper, and the organizer's page is the source of truth.

decision.choice: Opt-in, random pseudonymous IDs, no 'who is going' list, reports only for groups of 5 or more, one-tap delete
decision.why: A random ID is enough to personalize and keeps names out of the logs. Hiding attendee lists removes the most direct way to out someone's interests. A minimum group size for any shared stat and a working delete make the month-long trial something friends can safely say yes to.

alternatives.name: Campus single sign-on with real names
alternatives.tradeoff: Prevents duplicate accounts and eases attendance checks, but ties every click to a real identity.

alternatives.name: No accounts at all
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest privacy, but no history across sessions, so there is nothing to personalize from.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite. Users table holds only a random UUID, chosen interest tags and created_at; no name, email or location columns. Endpoints: POST /signup returns a UUID, DELETE /me removes the user and all impressions, clicks and check-ins. Every event card links to the organizer's source page. Tests: after DELETE /me no row references the UUID; any aggregate query over fewer than 5 users returns nothing.
verify: List every stored field with the reason it is needed; remove any without a reason
Sign up, click 5 events, delete yourself, and confirm zero rows remain for your ID
Confirm no screen shows which individuals clicked or attended an event

steps.title: Ingest club calendars and expand recurring events
steps.learn: Many club and department calendars publish iCalendar (RFC 5545) feeds. Repeating events are stored as one rule (RRULE) with exceptions, so they must be expanded into dated occurrences. The same event is often posted by two clubs with slightly different titles, which would show up twice.

decision.choice: Poll ICS feeds, parse with icalendar, expand with recurring-ical-events, dedupe on normalized title plus start time
decision.why: Feeds are structured and already maintained by organizers. icalendar is an RFC 5545 parser, and recurring-ical-events handles repeats, edits and removed occurrences, which are easy to get wrong by hand. Normalized title plus start time catches most cross-posts.

alternatives.name: Scrape event web pages
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers clubs without feeds, but breaks when layouts change and may conflict with site terms.

alternatives.name: Manual submission form only
alternatives.tradeoff: Clean data you control, but coverage depends on organizers remembering to post.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with icalendar and recurring-ical-events. fetch_feed(url) returns text; expand(text, start, end) uses recurring_ical_events.of(calendar).between(start, end). Event(id, source_uid, title, description, start, end, location, organizer, tags, source_url). dedupe() merges events whose lowercased, punctuation-free titles match fuzzily and starts are equal. Tests: a weekly RRULE gives 2 occurrences in 14 days; an EXDATE occurrence is dropped; a cross-post merges; past events are excluded.
verify: Ingest your real feeds and record events per feed for the next 14 days
Spot check 10 events against their source pages for time and place
Record how many duplicates were merged and inspect 5 merges by hand

steps.title: Represent each event by its content, not its history
steps.learn: A new event has no clicks, so collaborative filtering cannot score it. What exists on day one is its content: title, description, organizer and tags. Embedding that text puts 'open mic' near 'jam session' even without shared words, which is the cold-start answer for items.

decision.choice: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings of title plus description, plus organizer and tag features
decision.why: It maps text to a 384-dimensional vector, runs on a CPU and is Apache 2.0. Inputs over 256 word pieces are truncated, so put the title first. The same code embeds MIND titles and abstracts, so offline and live use one pipeline.

alternatives.name: TF-IDF vectors
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and easy to explain, but misses synonyms and paraphrases between short event blurbs.

alternatives.name: LLM tagging into a fixed category list
alternatives.tradeoff: Readable categories for the UI, but costs per event and labels can drift between runs.

steps.delegate: Python, sentence-transformers. embed(texts) loads 'sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2', encodes 'title. description' with normalize_embeddings=True, caches by SHA-256 of the text in SQLite. Also embed MIND news.tsv title plus abstract. Tests: identical text gives an identical cached vector; vectors have norm 1; empty description still embeds the title.
verify: For 5 real events, print the 3 nearest other events and judge whether they are sensible
Record CPU time to embed 1,000 events and the machine used

steps.title: Give new students a profile on their first visit
steps.learn: New students have no clicks either. A user profile can live in the same vector space as events: start it from interests picked at sign-up, then move it toward events they click. The question is how fast clicks should outweigh what they said.

decision.choice: 3+ interest tags at sign-up; profile = weighted mean of tag and clicked-event vectors, tags fading
decision.why: Three taps is cheap enough that most people finish it, and it personalizes the first list. Fading the stated interests lets behavior take over without throwing away the start when a student has only clicked once or twice.

alternatives.name: Popularity until 5 clicks
alternatives.tradeoff: No questions asked, but everyone sees the same list and small clubs never surface.

alternatives.name: Long interest questionnaire
alternatives.tradeoff: Richer starting profile, but more students abandon sign-up.

steps.delegate: Python. profile(tag_vecs, clicked_vecs, k) returns a normalized vector: weight on tags = k / (k + n_clicks). On MIND, build profiles from the History column with no tags. Evaluate on the tuning split for k in a small grid. Tests: zero clicks equals the tag mean; many clicks approaches the click mean; output norm is 1.
verify: On the MIND tuning split, report MRR bucketed by history length (for example 0 to 2, 3 to 10, over 10) with counts per bucket
Record the chosen k and confirm it was picked on the tuning split, not the frozen validation set

steps.title: Apply hard filters before any scoring
steps.learn: Some rules are not preferences: an event that already started, one inside hours the student blocked, or a members-only event they cannot join must never be shown, however well it scores. Filter first, then rank what is left.

decision.choice: Filter to the next 14 days, outside blocked hours, open to the student; then score
decision.why: Filtering first means a ranking bug cannot surface an impossible event, and it shrinks the list to score. The event count at dorm scale is small, so filtering everything in memory is fine.

alternatives.name: Soft penalties instead of filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps edge cases visible, but a large similarity can outweigh the penalty and show an impossible event.

alternatives.name: Post-filter the top 10
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but can leave fewer than 10 results after filtering.

steps.delegate: Python. candidates(user, events, now) returns events with start > now + 30 min, start < now + 14 days, not overlapping any of the user's blocked weekly hours (timezone aware), and eligible for the user. Tests: a past event is never returned; an event overlapping a blocked hour by 1 minute is excluded; DST boundary handled.
verify: Run 1,000 randomized requests and confirm zero returned events violate a filter, checked by a separate script
Record the median candidate count per request

steps.title: Choose the ranking score and test it on MIND
steps.learn: The score combines interest similarity with things that make an event good to show now: how soon it starts, whether the student follows the organizer, early interest from others. Measure on MIND impressions with standard library metrics, never with your own scoring code.

decision.choice: Hand-weighted linear score first; logistic regression on logged clicks once you have a few hundred
decision.why: A dorm produces little data, and a linear score is easy to debug and explain to users. Logistic regression fits the same features once clicks exist. LambdaMART can wait until there is enough grouped data.

alternatives.name: LightGBM LGBMRanker (lambdarank)
alternatives.tradeoff: Optimizes ranking directly and captures interactions, but needs many grouped impressions to avoid overfitting.

alternatives.name: Neural news recommender trained on MIND
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong on MIND, but heavy to run and tuned to news reading, not event attendance.

steps.delegate: Python, scikit-learn. features(user, event) returns similarity, hours_to_start, follows_organizer, early_clicks. score() is linear with weights in config. eval_mind.py scores each impression, computes AUC with roc_auc_score and nDCG@5/10 with ndcg_score, MRR by hand, averaged per impression. Baselines: random and popularity from training clicks. Tests: a perfect ranking gives nDCG 1; random has AUC near 0.5 on a synthetic set.
verify: Report AUC, MRR, nDCG@5 and nDCG@10 on the frozen MIND validation set for random, popularity and your score
Report what fraction of validation candidate news IDs never appear in the training news.tsv
Record the machine and the exact eval command

steps.title: Learn from clicks without learning position bias
steps.learn: Students click what is on top, so clicks mix interest with position. Joachims et al. reweight each click by the inverse of the chance its position was examined (its propensity). MIND shuffles impression order, so it cannot teach you this: you must log positions yourself.

decision.choice: Log positions; in a few sessions swap rank 1 with a random rank r to estimate propensities; weight clicks 1/propensity
decision.why: Small swaps barely hurt the list but show how clicks change when the same event moves, which is what propensity estimation needs. Weighted training then stops rewarding events just for having been ranked first.

alternatives.name: Train on raw clicks
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but the model learns to keep whatever it already ranked first.

alternatives.name: Train on check-ins only
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to the real goal and less tied to position, but far sparser than clicks.

steps.delegate: Python, SQLite. Log (impression_id, user, event, position, swapped flag, ts) for every card shown, and clicks with impression_id. With probability p per session, swap rank 1 with a random rank r. estimate_propensity() returns p_r/p_1 from click rates on swapped vs unswapped sessions. train() fits a pairwise model (clicked vs unclicked event in the same impression) with each pair weighted by 1/propensity of the click. Tests: every click joins to an impression; swap rate matches p.
verify: Confirm 100% of logged clicks join to an impression with a position
On a simulated log with known position propensities and swaps at share p, confirm estimate_propensity recovers each propensity within 20%
On simulated clicks with known propensities, confirm the weighted model ranks truly relevant events higher than the unweighted one

steps.title: Measure attendance independently and set up a control group
steps.learn: Clicks are not attendance, and the ranker must not grade itself. A short code shown at the event gives an independent check-in signal. A control group that gets the date-ordered list is the only way to know whether ranking, not novelty, changed anything.

decision.choice: Organizer shows a rotating check-in code; users randomly assigned once to ranked or date-ordered list for the month
decision.why: Codes entered in the app record attendance without location tracking. A fixed random split per user avoids users seeing both lists and is simple to analyze at small scale.

alternatives.name: Self-reported attendance
alternatives.tradeoff: No organizer effort, but people over-report and the bias may differ between groups.

alternatives.name: Interleave both rankings in one list
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs fewer users to detect a difference, but measures clicks, not whether more events get attended.

steps.delegate: Python, FastAPI. assign_arm(user) is a seeded random choice stored at sign-up. GET /feed serves ranked or date-ordered by arm. Organizer page shows a 4-digit code that changes daily; POST /checkin(event, code) records attendance once per user per event. Tests: arm never changes for a user; a wrong code fails; double check-in counts once.
verify: Simulate 200 sign-ups and confirm the arm split is within 45 to 55 percent and no user's arm changes on repeat requests
Do a test check-in at a real event and confirm it is counted once

steps.title: Test it outside: one month with your dorm or club
steps.learn: Share the app for a month as the try-it says. Track attendance by check-in codes in both arms, plus clicks and how many different clubs got attendees through the app. With a dorm-sized sample, report raw counts and spread, and say plainly if the difference is within noise.
verify: Report check-ins per user per week in each arm, with user counts
Report click-through and the number of distinct organizers with at least one app-driven check-in
Report how many users were still active in week 4 in each arm

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example an event type that drew clicks but no check-ins), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives MIND metrics and live attendance per arm, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with examples
Part 4 lists assumptions (one dorm, one month, news as a proxy for events) and limits

projects.title: Course schedule planner
projects.problem: Prerequisites, time conflicts and graduation rules are a puzzle
projects.concepts: Constraint satisfaction, ranking plans by preferences
projects.tryIt: Plan next semester for yourself and three friends
projects.question: Can a constraint solver produce valid next-semester schedules (prerequisites, no conflicts, degree rules) that real students rank as their best option?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and frozen test scenarios
steps.learn: A plan must satisfy hard rules (prerequisites, no time overlaps, required section types, credit limits) and then be good by soft preferences. Success from the try-it: plan next semester for you and three friends; every plan valid, and the plan each person would actually register for appears near the top.

decision.choice: UIUC Fall 2026 catalog CSV; 20 test scenarios frozen before solver code, plus 10 separate dev scenarios for debugging
decision.why: It is a real public section-level export with meeting days, times, section types and prerequisite text, so it has the real mess. Scenarios with known feasible or infeasible answers, written first, cannot be bent to fit the solver.

alternatives.name: Your own school's registrar data
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches your friends exactly, but may have no export and its terms may forbid scraping.

alternatives.name: Synthetic catalog
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to control, but hides real quirks like arranged times and half-semester sections.

verify: README states the question, the metrics (violations, solve time, rank of chosen plan) and the dataset term
20 scenarios saved with expected feasible or infeasible labels and a timestamp before solver code exists

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting anyone's courses
steps.learn: Transcripts and grades are education records (FERPA covers them at US schools), and your friends' records are theirs. Degree rules and prerequisites change, and catalog text can be stale: the planner is a helper, and the official degree audit and an advisor are the authority before registering.

decision.choice: Run locally; friends give only course codes completed, no grades or student IDs; delete inputs after the trial
decision.why: Course codes are all the solver needs. Keeping data on your machine and out of a shared server means nothing sensitive is collected that could leak, and deleting afterwards ends the risk.

alternatives.name: Upload and parse transcript PDFs
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves typing, but collects grades, IDs and names you do not need.

alternatives.name: Hosted multi-user app
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to share, but you become the custodian of other students' academic records.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 CLI. Input file student.json holds only completed course codes and preferences; the loader rejects any field named grade, gpa, uin or id. Every printed plan ends with: 'Check against your official degree audit and registration system before registering.' Tests: a file with a grade field is rejected; the notice appears on every output.
verify: Confirm input files contain only course codes and preferences
Confirm every plan output carries the official-source notice
Write down when and how friends' files will be deleted

steps.title: Load sections and meetings into a clean model
steps.learn: Each CSV row is a meeting of a section (CRN), and one CRN can have several rows. Days use letters with R for Thursday. Part of Term is mostly 1 (full term) or A and B (half terms), with a few other values, and many sections are ARRANGED. Schedule Information says which section types to take.

decision.choice: Course, required section types, sections by CRN, meetings as (day, start_min, end_min, part_of_term)
decision.why: Conflicts happen between meetings, not courses, and a lecture plus lab must be chosen together. Minutes since midnight make overlap a simple comparison, and keeping part of term avoids flagging first-half and second-half sections as clashing.

alternatives.name: One row per course, ignore sections
alternatives.tradeoff: Much simpler, but cannot catch lab or discussion conflicts.

alternatives.name: Parse Course Explorer XML directly
alternatives.tradeoff: Freshest data, but more parsing work than a ready CSV.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, csv. load(path) groups rows by CRN into Section(crn, course, type_code, meetings, credit_hours). Parse days string into weekdays (M,T,W,R,F,S), times '09:00 AM' to minutes; ARRANGED meetings have no slots. required_types(course) parsed from Schedule Information, falling back to one section of any type. Tests: 'TR' parses to Tuesday and Thursday; a CRN with 3 rows has 3 meetings; ARRANGED yields no slots; CS 225 needs LBD plus lecture.
verify: Record counts of courses, sections and multi-meeting CRNs loaded
Check 3 random courses against courses.illinois.edu for days and times
Count ARRANGED sections and half-term sections

steps.title: Turn prerequisite text into AND-of-OR rules
steps.learn: Prerequisites are free text, for example CS 225: 'CS 126 or CS 128 or ECE 220; One of CS 173, ... MATH 413.' That is an AND of OR-groups, which maps directly onto boolean constraints. Phrases like concurrent registration or consent of instructor cannot be checked automatically and must be flagged.

decision.choice: Rule-based parser for common patterns, LLM structured output for the rest, and human review for every in-scope course
decision.why: Rules are exact and cheap for the common 'X or Y; one of ...' shape. An LLM with a JSON schema handles odd phrasing, but it can invent a course, so every rule for a course your group might take is reviewed by hand.

alternatives.name: Hand-encode only the 30 or so courses in scope
alternatives.tradeoff: Most accurate for the trial, but does not scale beyond your group.

alternatives.name: LLM for every course, no review
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast coverage, but a silent wrong prerequisite produces invalid plans.

steps.delegate: Python. parse_prereq(text) returns {'all_of': [[course codes any_of], ...], 'flags': ['concurrent', 'consent', ...]} using regexes for 'A or B', 'One of A, B, or C', ';' as AND. Unparsed text goes to an LLM call with a JSON schema; output codes must exist in the catalog or are rejected. Tests: CS 225 text parses to 2 groups exactly; an unknown course code is rejected.
verify: CS 225 parses to exactly the two OR-groups in its catalog text
Record the share of courses parsed by rules alone
Review every in-scope course rule by hand and log corrections

steps.title: Write an independent plan validator before the solver
steps.learn: The solver must not grade itself. A separate checker, written directly from the raw data, confirms each plan: one section of each required type per course, no overlapping meetings on the same day in overlapping parts of term, prerequisites met by completed courses, and credit hours within limits.

decision.choice: Plain Python validator with its own minimal CSV reading, sharing no code with the solver, run on every plan
decision.why: Sharing no constraint code means a modeling bug in the solver shows up as a violation instead of being repeated. Plain loops are slow but plans are small, and the code is easy to read and trust.

alternatives.name: Trust the solver's OPTIMAL status
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra code, but only proves the plan satisfies your model, bugs included.

alternatives.name: Check plans by hand
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches judgment issues, but too slow to run on every plan.

steps.delegate: Python. validate(plan, completed, catalog) returns a list of violations with type and detail. Overlap: same weekday, intervals intersect, parts of term overlap (1, blank and unknown values overlap everything; A and B do not overlap). Tests: two MWF 10:00 sections conflict; an A and a B section at the same time do not; a missing lab is reported; an unmet prerequisite is reported.
verify: Validator passes its unit tests, written from the catalog rules not from solver output
Run it on 5 hand-made plans (3 valid, 2 with one planted violation each) and confirm it reports exactly the planted violations

steps.title: Model sections and conflicts in CP-SAT
