steps.learn: Make one boolean per section and one per course. A course is taken exactly when one section of each required type is picked. Conflicts are pairs of sections that can never both be chosen. Check the status: OPTIMAL is proven, FEASIBLE is not.

decision.choice: OR-Tools CP-SAT; precompute conflicting section pairs and add add_bool_or([~a, ~b]) for each
decision.why: Section times are fixed, so conflicts are known in advance and pairwise clauses are the most direct encoding. CP-SAT handles booleans, linear sums and objectives in one Python API.

alternatives.name: Optional intervals with add_no_overlap per weekday
alternatives.tradeoff: Native scheduling constraint with fewer clauses, but half-term sections need extra handling.

alternatives.name: Integer program with PuLP
alternatives.tradeoff: Familiar linear form, but logical rules like OR-prerequisites need manual linearization.

steps.delegate: Python, ortools. build_model(catalog, wanted, completed) creates new_bool_var per section and course; for each course and required type, sum of its sections == course var; add_bool_or([~a, ~b]) for every conflicting pair (reuse the loader, not the validator); credit sum within [min, max]. solve() with max_time_in_seconds. Tests: two conflicting sections never both chosen; every dev scenario's feasibility matches its label. Do not read the frozen test scenarios.
verify: All 20 frozen scenarios: solver feasibility matches the expected label
Validator reports zero violations on every solver plan
Record solve time per scenario and the machine

steps.title: Add prerequisites and graduation progress
steps.learn: For one semester, prerequisites are checked against completed courses, so ineligible courses are simply fixed to false. Degree rules (required courses, 'choose k from list', credit totals) decide which eligible courses actually move a student toward graduation.

decision.choice: Next semester only: eligibility as hard constraints, degree requirement progress in the objective
decision.why: The try-it asks for next semester, and future section times are unknown, so a multi-term plan would rest on guesses. Counting progress keeps the solver from picking a perfect timetable that does not help a student graduate.

alternatives.name: Multi-semester plan to graduation
alternatives.tradeoff: Answers 'can I finish on time', but needs future offerings you do not have and a larger model.

alternatives.name: Ignore degree rules
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but valid timetables may contain no required courses.

steps.delegate: Python, ortools. eligible(course, completed) evaluates the AND-of-OR rule; flagged rules (consent, concurrent) are reported, not enforced. requirements.json lists groups {name, courses, choose_k}; progress = sum over groups of min(choose_k remaining, chosen in group) via auxiliary int vars. Tests: an ineligible course is never chosen; a group with choose_k = 1 counts at most 1.
verify: Validator confirms prerequisites on all plans
Hand-check requirements.json for your own program against the official catalog page
Report how many plans include flagged courses needing manual approval

steps.title: Rank plans by preferences and offer a few distinct ones
steps.learn: After hard rules, people care about soft things: no early classes, fewer days on campus, short gaps, a class with a friend. One best plan is brittle, since students know things the model does not, so show a small set of good plans that are actually different.

decision.choice: Weighted soft objective; get top 3 by re-solving with a cut forbidding the previous plan's course set
decision.why: Weights make tradeoffs explicit and tunable per student. Cutting on the course set, not sections, avoids three plans that differ only by a discussion slot.

alternatives.name: Lexicographic priorities
alternatives.tradeoff: Clear ordering, but never trades a small loss on a top priority for a big win elsewhere.

alternatives.name: enumerate_all_solutions, then sort
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple to reason about, but the number of valid schedules can explode.

steps.delegate: Python, ortools. Penalty terms: sections starting before a chosen hour, days with any class, gaps between classes per day (aux vars), shared sections with named friends as a bonus, plus requirement progress. top_k(model, k=3): after each solve add add_bool_or of negated chosen course vars. Tests: 3 plans have different course sets; objective is non-decreasing across them.
verify: For your own preferences, explain why plan 1 beats plan 2 from the printed objective terms
Validator reports zero violations on all top-3 plans

steps.title: Explain why no schedule exists
steps.learn: 'Infeasible' alone is useless. Put each user requirement (must take X, no Friday classes, max credits) behind its own literal and pass those as assumptions. If the result is INFEASIBLE, sufficient_assumptions_for_infeasibility returns a subset that cannot all hold together; it is not guaranteed to be minimal.

decision.choice: Assumption literals per user requirement, report the conflicting subset in plain words
decision.why: It names the requirements that clash in one extra solve, which is what a student needs to decide what to drop.

alternatives.name: Drop requirements one at a time and re-solve
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to code and explain, but slow and the order changes the answer.

alternatives.name: Make every requirement soft with a penalty
alternatives.tradeoff: Always returns a plan, but may quietly drop a must-have course.

steps.delegate: Python, ortools. For each user requirement create a bool r, enforce its constraint with only_enforce_if(r), call model.add_assumptions(all r). On INFEASIBLE, map solver.sufficient_assumptions_for_infeasibility() indices back to requirement text. Tests: two required courses with only conflicting sections are reported together; a feasible model reports nothing.
verify: Every infeasible frozen scenario returns a non-empty explanation
For 3 of them, confirm by hand that the named requirements truly clash

steps.title: Test it outside: plan next semester for four students
steps.learn: Plan next semester for yourself and three friends. Each person states preferences, sees the top 3 plans, and says which they would register for and why. With your school's catalog, check plans against the degree audit; with UIUC data, skip that.
verify: Report validator violations across all plans shown (target zero) and solve time per person
Report the rank (1, 2, 3 or none) of each person's chosen plan and edits they made
Record every issue the official degree audit or an advisor found that the planner missed

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with machine and command, (3) why surprising results happened (for example a chosen plan ranked third because of an unmodeled preference), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives violations, solve times and chosen-plan ranks, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results
Part 4 lists assumptions (one term, one catalog, four students, hand-reviewed prerequisites) and limits

projects.title: Volunteer matcher
projects.problem: Nonprofits struggle to find volunteers with the right skills
projects.concepts: Your interview pipeline: hard criteria first, then soft-criteria ranking
projects.tryIt: Pilot with a local food bank or club
projects.question: Can hard filters followed by a soft ranking suggest volunteers a coordinator would invite, without ever breaking a shift's requirements?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen test set
steps.learn: This is the interview-pipeline shape: hard criteria remove anyone who cannot do the shift, then soft criteria rank the rest. Success from the try-it: in a food bank or club pilot, suggestions match who the coordinator would invite, no hard rule is ever broken, and shifts fill with less coordinator time.

decision.choice: Coordinator labels 30 past shifts blind, frozen before tuning; NYC Service opportunities for realistic shift records
decision.why: The coordinator, not your scoring code, decides who is a good fit, so the metric is never graded by the system's own logic. Labels are made before any weights exist. The NYC Service dataset gives real shift records (category, location, dates, volunteers requested) to test the pipeline on.

alternatives.name: Measure fill rate only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to count, but a shift can fill with poorly matched people, and fill rate also moves with season and demand.

alternatives.name: Synthetic volunteers and shifts only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to iterate, but you would be grading your own assumptions about what a good match is.

verify: Write the one question and 3 metrics: precision@3 vs coordinator picks, hard-rule violations (target 0), coordinator minutes per shift
Store the 30 labeled past shifts with volunteer ids, not names or contacts, in a separate file that tuning code never reads
Download the NYC Service dataset and record its row count and the columns you will use

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting volunteer data
steps.learn: Volunteers are people, so collect the minimum needed to match them. Eligibility checks (age, background checks for shifts with minors) are the organisation's responsibility: the app only records the outcome. Never use protected traits as ranking features, and let volunteers see and delete their data.

decision.choice: Minimal profile: postcode, availability, skills, staff-set eligibility flags; consent and deletion
decision.why: A postcode instead of an address is enough for distance, and an 'over 18' or 'check cleared' flag replaces birth dates and documents. Less stored data means less to leak and less to misuse in ranking.

alternatives.name: Copy the full signup spreadsheet
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra work, but you inherit addresses, birth dates and notes you never need.

alternatives.name: Use an existing volunteer platform's data
alternatives.tradeoff: Already consented, but you depend on its export format and may not control deletion.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with SQLite. Define the volunteer table with only: id, display name, contact (opt-in), postcode, availability, skills, eligibility flags, consent timestamp. Add delete_volunteer(id) that removes all rows referencing the volunteer, and an export_my_data(id) function. Tests: delete leaves no rows in any table; schema has no birth date, address or gender column.
verify: List every stored field and the reason it is needed for matching
Run delete_volunteer on a test record and confirm no table still references it
Have the coordinator confirm the consent wording before any real signups

steps.title: Model shifts with hard requirements and soft preferences apart
steps.learn: The whole pipeline depends on the organisation saying which requirements are non-negotiable (a food handler certificate, lifting, a time window) and which are nice to have (Spanish speaker, prior experience). Mixing them in one score lets a high soft score hide a broken rule.

decision.choice: Each shift stores a list of hard requirements and a separate list of weighted soft preferences
decision.why: Coordinators can read and edit both lists, and the code can enforce hard ones as filters and use soft ones only for ordering. It also makes every suggestion explainable.

alternatives.name: One free-text description per shift
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest for coordinators, but every match needs text interpretation and rules become fuzzy.

alternatives.name: All requirements as weighted scores
alternatives.tradeoff: Flexible, but a heavy weight is still not a guarantee, so a rule can be broken.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, pydantic models Shift(id, start, end, location, volunteers_needed, hard: list[Requirement], soft: list[Preference]) and Requirement(kind, value). Loader that imports NYC Service rows into Shift records (category, dates, lat/long, vol_requests). Tests: a shift whose end is before start is rejected; an unknown requirement kind is rejected.
verify: Import at least 200 NYC Service rows and count how many fail validation and why
Ask the coordinator to tag 5 real shifts with hard and soft lists and check the schema holds all of them

steps.title: Normalize free-text skills into a small vocabulary
steps.learn: Volunteers write 'forklift cert', 'can drive a van', 'hablo español'. Matching needs them as the same tags the shifts use. A small organisation-specific vocabulary is easier to check than a large taxonomy, and anything that does not map cleanly should go to a human, not be guessed.

decision.choice: Org-defined tag list; RapidFuzz maps text to tags above a threshold; the rest goes to a review queue
decision.why: Tens of tags cover a food bank's needs, fuzzy matching handles spelling variants cheaply and deterministically, and a review queue keeps wrong tags out of the hard filters.

alternatives.name: ESCO or O*NET skills taxonomy
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard and broad, but far bigger than a food bank needs and still needs mapping from free text.

alternatives.name: LLM extraction to a JSON schema
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles paraphrase and other languages, but costs per signup and needs spot checks for invented tags.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz. normalize_skills(text, vocab, threshold) splits on commas and newlines, uses rapidfuzz.process.extractOne with fuzz.token_set_ratio, returns (tags, unmatched). Synonyms file per tag. Tests: misspellings map to the right tag; an unrelated phrase lands in unmatched; output tags are always in the vocabulary.
verify: Label 50 real or sample skill strings by hand and report precision and recall of the mapping
Record the share of strings sent to the review queue at your chosen threshold

steps.title: Apply hard filters first, with a reason for every removal
steps.learn: Hard filters run before ranking so no score can rescue an ineligible volunteer. Availability is an interval check (the volunteer's window must cover the whole shift), and eligibility flags and certificates are exact checks. Recording which filter removed each person makes empty shortlists debuggable.

decision.choice: Deterministic filter chain in Python, each filter returning kept ids plus removed ids with a reason code
decision.why: Rules stay readable and testable one at a time, and reason counts tell the coordinator why a shift has few candidates. At food bank scale a full scan is fast.

alternatives.name: SQL WHERE clauses only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and simple, but you lose per-filter removal reasons unless you run each clause separately.

alternatives.name: Soft penalties instead of filters
alternatives.tradeoff: Never returns an empty list, but can suggest someone who is not allowed to do the shift.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Implement filters: availability_covers(shift), has_flags(shift.hard), has_certs(shift.hard), not_already_booked(shift). run_filters(volunteers, shift) returns kept and a Counter of reasons. Property test with hypothesis: no kept volunteer violates any hard requirement of the shift.
verify: Run the filters on 20 NYC-derived shifts with sample volunteers and check the property test passes
Pick 3 removed volunteers by hand and confirm their reason codes are correct

steps.title: Decide how travel distance is measured and capped
steps.learn: Distance is both a hard limit (the volunteer's maximum) and a soft signal (closer is better). Straight-line distance between postcode centroids is coarse but private and cheap; travel time by road or transit is more honest for people without cars but needs a routing engine.

decision.choice: Haversine distance from postcode centroid to shift location; cap at each volunteer's stated maximum
decision.why: Coarse location was chosen for privacy, so road routing would add precision the input does not have. Haversine needs no external service and is easy to test.

alternatives.name: Road travel time with OSRM
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for drivers, but needs a self-hosted engine with map data and still ignores transit.

alternatives.name: Transit time from GTFS feeds
alternatives.tradeoff: Fair to volunteers without cars, but needs a transit router and timetable data per city.

steps.delegate: Python. haversine_km(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) and a postcode centroid table. within_range(volunteer, shift) filter and distance_km feature for ranking. Tests: known distance between two fixed coordinates within 1 km; a volunteer just beyond their limit is removed with reason 'too_far'.
verify: Check 5 computed distances against a map tool and note the error from using centroids
Ask the coordinator whether any volunteers rely on transit and note it as a known limit

steps.title: Rank eligible volunteers with a transparent weighted score
steps.learn: Among eligible volunteers, rank by soft fit: overlap with preferred skills, interest in the shift's category, distance, and how recently they were asked (to spread work and avoid burnout). New volunteers have no history, a cold-start case, so the score must not depend only on past shifts.

decision.choice: Linear score of a few named features with weights the coordinator can read; no protected traits
decision.why: With tens of past shifts there is too little data to learn weights, and a readable score lets the coordinator trust and correct it. A recency term prevents always asking the same reliable few.

alternatives.name: Learning to rank from coordinator accepts
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts weights from data, but needs many labeled shifts and is harder to explain.

alternatives.name: Embedding similarity of profile and shift text
alternatives.tradeoff: Captures paraphrase, but hard to explain and can reward wordy profiles.

steps.delegate: Python. score(volunteer, shift, weights) returns total and per-feature contributions: skill_overlap (Jaccard over tags), category_interest (0 or 1), distance_decay, days_since_last_ask. Weights in a YAML file. Tests: identical volunteers except distance rank closer first; per-feature contributions sum to the total.
verify: Tune weights only on shifts outside the frozen 30 and record the final weights
Check top-10 lists for 5 shifts include at least some volunteers with no history

steps.title: Assign volunteers across overlapping shifts with a solver
steps.learn: Ranking each shift alone can put the same top volunteer on three overlapping shifts. Assignment across a week is a constraint problem: each shift needs a number of people, a person cannot be in two overlapping shifts, and each person has a weekly cap.

decision.choice: OR-Tools CP-SAT: boolean x[volunteer, shift], coverage and overlap constraints, maximize total score
decision.why: CP-SAT expresses counts, overlaps and caps directly, and food bank sizes are small. It also reports when a week is infeasible so you can show which shifts cannot be filled.

alternatives.name: Greedy shift by shift
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and fast, but early shifts take the best people and later shifts may go unfilled.

alternatives.name: SciPy linear_sum_assignment
alternatives.tradeoff: Optimal one-to-one matching, but each shift needs slot copies and weekly caps cannot be expressed.

steps.delegate: Python, ortools cp_model. Variables only for pairs that passed hard filters. Constraints: sum over volunteers per shift <= volunteers_needed; at most one of any overlapping shift pair per volunteer; weekly cap. Objective: maximize sum of integer-scaled scores. Return suggestions, not bookings. Tests: no volunteer in two overlapping shifts; caps respected; solver status checked.
verify: Compare filled slots and total score of CP-SAT vs greedy on one real or NYC-derived week
Record solver time for the largest week you have

steps.title: Explain suggestions and handle empty lists and cancellations
steps.learn: Coordinators act on suggestions only if they see why. Each suggestion lists its top features; each short list shows which hard filters removed the most people. Cancellations and no-shows should trigger a re-run for that shift, never an automatic message to volunteers without the coordinator.

decision.choice: Per-suggestion reason lines, blocked-by counts, and explicit coordinator-approved filter relaxation
decision.why: Relaxing a hard rule is a human decision, so the app proposes it and records who approved it. Re-running one shift after a cancellation keeps other assignments stable.

alternatives.name: Silently relax filters when the list is empty
alternatives.tradeoff: Never empty, but breaks the guarantee that hard rules hold.

alternatives.name: Show scores without reasons
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler UI, but coordinators cannot spot a bad weight or a wrong skill tag.

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI endpoint GET /shifts/{id}/suggestions returning ranked volunteers with reason strings and filter removal counts; POST /shifts/{id}/rerun after a cancellation. Tests: an empty result includes non-empty removal counts; a rerun never changes other shifts' suggestions.
verify: Show 5 suggestion pages to the coordinator and record whether each reason line is understandable
Cancel one volunteer in a test week and confirm only that shift is recomputed

steps.title: Test it outside: pilot with a local food bank or club
steps.learn: First score the frozen 30 shifts against the coordinator's blind picks, then run a short live pilot where the coordinator uses the suggestions for real. Compare with the same weeks' workload before the pilot, and run the ranking with and without each feature to see what each adds.
verify: Report precision@3 on the frozen 30 shifts for full ranking, distance only and random order
Count hard-rule violations found by the coordinator during the pilot (target 0)
Record coordinator minutes per filled shift before and during the pilot
Record how many volunteers opted out or asked for data deletion

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened, (4) assumptions and what this does not prove, such as one organisation, a few weeks, and coarse distance.
verify: Write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number names the data split, the machine and the command that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained, such as a feature that did not help
Assumptions and limits are listed, including pilot size and coordinator labels as ground truth

projects.title: Misplaced-book finder
projects.problem: Libraries lose books shelved in the wrong spot
projects.concepts: Spine OCR from a shelf photo, checking call-number order
projects.tryIt: Scan shelves at a library with the staff's permission
projects.question: Can a phone photo of a shelf find books shelved out of call-number order, with few enough false alarms that staff trust it?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen test set
steps.learn: The pipeline reads each spine label, turns it into a sortable call number, and flags books out of order. Success from the try-it: on shelves scanned with staff permission, precision and recall of flagged books against a manual shelf-read, plus the share of labels the app could not read.

decision.choice: Public Library Dataset for OCR development; your own shelf photos with a staff shelf-read as the frozen test
decision.why: The Library Dataset has 285 shelf images and 7,536 annotated books with each spine's library tag, good for testing reading and matching. Order ground truth must come from staff reading the real shelves, done blind to the app and frozen before tuning.

alternatives.name: Plant misplaced books on purpose
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives known positives, but staff must agree and planted errors may be easier than real ones.

alternatives.name: Public dataset only
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible, but it has no order labels and uses one library's labelling scheme.

verify: Write the one question and metrics: flag precision, flag recall, unreadable-label rate, minutes per shelf
Download the Library Dataset annotations and record image and book counts
Agree the frozen test shelves with staff now; photograph them only after the privacy step, before tuning, and store apart from tuning code

links.label: Image-text matching for large-scale book collections (arXiv)

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before any photos are taken
steps.learn: Photograph shelves, never people. Get written staff permission, shoot when aisles are quiet, and skip areas with patron names such as hold shelves. The app is a helper: staff decide whether a flagged book is wrong and where it goes, since some collections use local shelving rules.

decision.choice: On-device face blur before saving, EXIF stripped, hold shelves excluded, flags shown as suggestions only
decision.why: Blurring on the phone means no clear face of a patron is ever stored or uploaded. Treating flags as suggestions avoids moving correctly shelved books that follow a local exception.

alternatives.name: Blur faces on the server
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler phone app, but raw photos with patrons reach your server.

alternatives.name: Reject any photo containing a person
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest guarantee, but busy libraries would block many scans.

steps.delegate: Client step using MediaPipe Tasks Vision Face Detector: detect faces, blur each box with padding, re-encode without EXIF before saving. Tests: an image with faces comes out blurred; saved files carry no EXIF; an image without faces is unchanged apart from metadata.
verify: Run 10 test photos with people through the client and confirm no clear face survives
Get the written permission and a list of excluded areas from staff before the first scan

steps.title: Set a capture protocol for shelf photos
steps.learn: OCR accuracy is set at capture time. Labels are small, so photo distance, angle and lighting matter more than model choice. Order checking also needs to know where one shelf ends and the next photo begins.

decision.choice: One shelf section per still photo, camera parallel to the shelf, overlap with the next photo, shelf id noted
decision.why: Stills give sharper labels than video frames, the overlap lets you join photos without missing a book, and a shelf id per photo keeps order checks within one shelf.

alternatives.name: Video sweep along the shelf
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to capture, but motion blur hurts small text and frames must be deduplicated.

alternatives.name: Fixed rig or cart-mounted camera
alternatives.tradeoff: Consistent images, but needs hardware and permission to move it through aisles.

steps.delegate: Small capture app or a checklist plus a script: capture_session.py takes a folder of photos and a CSV (photo, shelf_id, position), checks each image size and sharpness (variance of the Laplacian with OpenCV) and flags blurry ones for retake. Tests: a blurred image is flagged; a photo without a shelf id is rejected.
verify: Photograph 3 shelves twice each and record how many photos the sharpness check flags
Time how long one shelf takes to capture

steps.title: Locate the call-number label on each spine
steps.learn: Before reading text you need regions: which text belongs to the call-number label and which to the title. Spines are tall and thin and labels sit in a fairly consistent place, so detection boxes plus their x-position give both the label and the book's place on the shelf.

decision.choice: PaddleOCR's text detector for all text, then group lines into labels by position and spacing
decision.why: No training data is needed to start, the detector returns polygons for each text line, and labels with stacked lines can be grouped by column. Revisit if titles get confused with labels too often.

alternatives.name: Train a YOLO oriented-box detector for labels
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise label boxes, but you must annotate hundreds of spines first.

alternatives.name: Segment spines with SAM first (Library Dataset paper)
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives one region per book, but adds a heavy model and still needs OCR inside each spine.

steps.delegate: Python, paddleocr. detect_text(image) returns polygons and texts from PaddleOCR predict (rec_polys, rec_texts, rec_scores). group_labels(lines) clusters lines by x-centre and vertical gap into labels sorted left to right. Tests on 3 hand-annotated photos: grouped label count is within 1 of the true book count; labels are in left-to-right order.
verify: On 10 Library Dataset images compare your label count to the annotated book count
Inspect 20 grouped labels by eye and count title text wrongly merged into labels

steps.title: Choose the OCR engine that reads the labels
steps.learn: Labels are short strings where one wrong character changes the shelf position. Spine text may be rotated, so orientation handling matters. Measure exact-match on whole labels, not character accuracy, because a single error breaks sorting.

decision.choice: PaddleOCR recognition with text line orientation enabled, keeping per-line confidence
decision.why: It runs locally, is Apache 2.0 licensed, handles upside-down text lines, and its confidence scores let you treat low-confidence labels as unreadable instead of wrong.

alternatives.name: Tesseract
alternatives.tradeoff: Mature and light, but its docs stress preprocessing such as rescaling, binarisation and deskew for good results on photos.

alternatives.name: Vision-language model reading the crop
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong on odd fonts, but slower, costs per image, and can return plausible but invented text.

steps.delegate: Python, paddleocr. read_label(crop) returns text and min line score using PaddleOCR(use_textline_orientation=True). eval_tags.py: run on Library Dataset images and compare against the annotated tag per book (exact match after whitespace normalization). Tests: a synthetic label image reads correctly; low score returns status 'unreadable'.
verify: Report exact-match tag accuracy on Library Dataset images for PaddleOCR and one alternative
Record the unreadable rate at your confidence threshold

steps.title: Parse labels into sortable call numbers
steps.learn: Call numbers do not sort as strings: in Library of Congress order QA 9 comes before QA 76, and cutters sort as decimals. Each label must become a normalized sort key for the library's scheme (LC, Dewey, or a local scheme like the Library Dataset's class number plus author letters).

decision.choice: pycallnumber for LC and Dewey, comparing on its for_sort normalization; a small custom key for local schemes
decision.why: pycallnumber parses LC, Dewey, SuDocs and local call numbers and its comparisons use the normalized sort form, so you do not write an LC parser. A local scheme needs only a few lines and tests.

alternatives.name: Plain string sort
alternatives.tradeoff: No code, but gets class numbers and cutters wrong, causing false flags.

alternatives.name: Write your own LC parser
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control, but many edge cases (cutters, dates, volume numbers) that libraries already handle.

steps.delegate: Python, pycallnumber. sort_key(text, scheme) uses pycn.callnumber(text).for_sort() for LC or Dewey, and for the Library Dataset a key of (prefix: digits or letters such as 'N' or 'I**', then author letters) built from its inventory tags. Tests: 'QA 9' sorts before 'QA 76'; a known shelf-list sample sorts into its published order; every inventory tag parses; unparseable text returns None.
verify: Sort 100 call numbers from the Library Dataset inventory or a published shelf list and confirm the order matches
Count labels from your OCR output that fail to parse

steps.title: Correct OCR by matching against the library's shelf list
steps.learn: Most OCR errors produce a call number that does not exist. Matching each reading to the shelf list for that section (exported by staff) turns near misses into real call numbers, and anything without a close match should become unreadable, never a guessed book.

decision.choice: RapidFuzz match within the shelf's call-number range; accept above a threshold, else mark unreadable
decision.why: Restricting candidates to that section's range keeps matches fast and avoids snapping to a similar number elsewhere. Unreadable labels are skipped by the order check instead of creating false flags.

alternatives.name: Use raw OCR text
alternatives.tradeoff: No shelf list needed, but every OCR slip can become a false misplacement.

alternatives.name: Scan barcodes instead of labels
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact identifiers, but needs each barcode visible and one scan per book.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz. snap(reading, candidates, threshold) returns (call_number, score) or None using rapidfuzz.process.extractOne. Candidates come from a CSV shelf list filtered to the shelf's range. Tests: one-character OCR errors snap to the right call number; a random string returns None.
verify: Report tag accuracy on Library Dataset images before and after snapping to its inventory list
Count wrong snaps (snapped to a different tag than the true one) at your threshold on 50 hand-checked labels

steps.title: Build one left-to-right sequence per shelf from overlapping photos
steps.learn: Order checks need the full shelf, but one shelf spans several photos. Books in the overlap appear twice and must be merged once. Shelf ends matter too: the last book of one shelf continues on the next shelf, not the next photo.

decision.choice: Order labels by x-position within a photo, then join photos by matching the same call numbers in the overlap
decision.why: After snapping, call numbers are strong identifiers, so joining on shared ones is simple and testable. Shelf ids from the capture protocol stop joins across shelves.

alternatives.name: Stitch a panorama with a homography
alternatives.tradeoff: One image per shelf, but stitching artefacts on thin spines can split or duplicate labels.

alternatives.name: One photo per whole shelf
alternatives.tradeoff: No merging, but labels become too small to read on long shelves.

steps.delegate: Python. sequence_for_shelf(photos) takes per-photo lists of (x_centre, call_number or None), drops duplicates where consecutive photos share a run of call numbers, and returns one ordered list. Tests: two overlapping lists merge without duplicates; no shared items raises a 'gap' warning instead of guessing.
verify: On 5 shelves compare merged sequence length to the number of books counted by hand
Record how many photo joins produced a gap warning

steps.title: Flag misplaced books with a longest-increasing-subsequence check
steps.learn: Comparing neighbours flags two books for every one misplaced. A better model: the books in correct relative order form the longest non-decreasing subsequence of sort keys, and the rest are the smallest set that, moved, fixes the order. Unreadable books are skipped, not flagged.

decision.choice: Longest non-decreasing subsequence in O(n log n); flag books outside it with their expected neighbours
decision.why: It finds a minimum set to move, so one stray book produces one flag. Showing where each flagged book belongs helps staff check quickly. Ties keep both books since equal call numbers are often copies.

alternatives.name: Flag adjacent inversions
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to code, but flags both neighbours and over-counts.

alternatives.name: Compare to expected position in the shelf list
alternatives.tradeoff: Also finds missing books, but needs a fully current shelf list including checked-out items.

steps.delegate: Python, bisect. misplaced(seq) computes the longest non-decreasing subsequence with bisect_right and parent pointers, returning indices outside it and, for each, the neighbours it should sit between. Tests: a sorted list returns nothing; one moved book returns exactly that book; None entries are ignored.
verify: Run on 5 hand-made sequences with known misplaced books and confirm exact output
On a merged real shelf, check every flag by looking at the actual books

steps.title: Test it outside: scan shelves at a library with permission
steps.learn: Scan agreed shelf sections, then compare flags with the staff shelf-read made without seeing the app's output. Separate errors by stage: unreadable labels, wrong snaps, merge gaps, and order logic, so you know which stage to fix.
verify: Report flag precision and recall on the frozen shelves against the staff shelf-read
Report unreadable-label rate and minutes per shelf versus a manual shelf-read
Attribute each false flag to a stage: OCR, snapping, merging or order check
Rerun without catalog snapping and report how precision changes

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened, (4) assumptions and what this does not prove, such as one library, one labelling scheme, and shelves chosen with staff.
verify: Write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number names the shelves or dataset, the phone, the machine and the command
At least one surprising result is explained, such as which stage caused most false flags
Assumptions and limits are listed, including label scheme, lighting and shelf-list freshness

projects.title: Whiteboard archive search
projects.problem: Whiteboard notes get erased and lost
projects.concepts: OCR plus a vision-language model, search over photos
projects.tryIt: Photograph every whiteboard in your study group for a term
projects.question: Can OCR plus a vision-language model make a term of whiteboard photos searchable, so the group finds the right board for a question?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen query set
steps.learn: The try-it is a term of whiteboard photos from one study group. Success is retrieval: for a question like 'where did we derive the master theorem', the right board appears near the top. Handwriting OCR quality matters only as far as it moves that number, so measure both, but judge the project by search.

decision.choice: Recall@5 and MRR on 50+ member-written queries for held-out weeks fixed now; IAM-line test split for OCR error
decision.why: Queries written by people who did not photograph the board mimic real recall from memory. Fixing the held-out weeks now and freezing their queries before tuning stops you tuning the pipeline to the test. Teklia/IAM-line is a public handwriting line set (MIT license on the card) to sanity-check character error rate.

alternatives.name: Only measure OCR character error rate
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to compute, but a board with messy text can still be found by its title or diagram, so CER alone misjudges search.

alternatives.name: Ask an LLM to write the queries
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to scale, but the queries echo the transcripts the system already sees, so the score is inflated.

verify: Write the one question and the two metrics (recall@5, MRR) plus the secondary OCR metric (CER)
Write down the held-out weeks and the rule: their queries are written blind, saved with board ids, and never read by tuning
Record how many boards and members are in scope for the term

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before any photos are taken
steps.learn: The archive is about boards, not people. Photos catch classmates' faces, and boards can carry names, phone numbers or exam material an instructor did not mean to share. Get the group's consent, keep the archive private to the group, and respect any course rule about recording teaching material.

decision.choice: Blur faces on the phone before upload, strip EXIF, regex-flag phone numbers and emails in transcripts for review
decision.why: On-device face blurring with MediaPipe Face Detector means unblurred faces never reach storage. EXIF carries device and location details you do not need beyond a room tag. Flagging contact details for a human to redact keeps personal data out of the search index.

alternatives.name: Reject photos that contain a face
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest guarantee, but people standing at the board block many honest captures.

alternatives.name: Blur on the server
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach the server and its logs even if briefly.

steps.delegate: TypeScript web client using MediaPipe Tasks Vision Face Detector with the BlazeFace full-range model (back-camera photos): detect faces, Gaussian-blur each padded box, re-encode the JPEG without EXIF, then upload. Python helper flag_pii(text) returning phone and email spans by regex. Tests: a test photo with faces leaves no sharp face; output has no EXIF; flag_pii finds a sample phone number and email.
verify: Run 10 photos with people through the client and confirm no recognizable face survives
Confirm uploaded files have no EXIF and every group member agreed in writing to the archive

steps.title: Capture boards and correct perspective before reading
steps.learn: Boards are shot at angles, so text is skewed and far letters shrink. Finding the four board corners and warping to a front-on rectangle (a homography) makes lines straight for OCR. Glare and partial erasure still remain, so keep the original photo too.

decision.choice: Detect the largest quadrilateral, warp with cv2.getPerspectiveTransform and cv2.warpPerspective, keep the original
decision.why: Whiteboards are usually the largest bright rectangle in frame, so contour-based corner finding works often and is cheap. Keeping the original lets the VLM and the user see context, and gives a fallback when corner detection picks the wrong shape.

alternatives.name: No rectification
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, and a strong VLM may cope, but line-based OCR degrades on skewed text.

alternatives.name: User taps four corners
alternatives.tradeoff: Always correct, but adds friction to every capture and people skip it.

steps.delegate: Python, opencv-python, numpy. rectify(img) finds the largest 4-point contour after edge detection, orders corners, and returns a warped front-on image plus a found flag; if no quad is found it returns the original. Tests: a synthetic rectangle warped by a known homography is restored within a few pixels; a blank image returns found=False.
verify: On 20 of your own photos, count how many are rectified correctly and save failures
Confirm the original and rectified images are both stored with the same board id

steps.title: Group repeat shots of the same board
steps.learn: Several people photograph the same board, and a board is often shot again after more is written. Near-duplicates clutter results. A perceptual hash gives each image a short bit string, and the Hamming distance between hashes (hash1 - hash2 in imagehash) says how alike two photos look.

decision.choice: imagehash phash on rectified images, same session and room, distance threshold tuned on labeled pairs
decision.why: Perceptual hashes are tiny and fast, and restricting comparison to the same session and room avoids merging different boards that look alike. Grouping keeps every photo but shows one representative per board in results.

alternatives.name: CLIP embedding similarity
alternatives.tradeoff: More tolerant of angle changes, but two different boards full of similar handwriting can look close.

alternatives.name: Keep every photo separate
alternatives.tradeoff: No risk of wrong merges, but results fill with copies of one board.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, Pillow. group_shots(images, session) computes phash per rectified image and union-finds pairs under a threshold within a session. Script tune_threshold.py reads a small labeled pairs CSV (same board or not) and prints precision and recall per threshold. Tests: an image and its recompressed copy group together; two distinct boards do not.
verify: Label 100 photo pairs from a non-query session and pick the threshold with the fewest wrong merges
Report how many photos collapse into how many boards for one week

steps.title: Get a line-level OCR baseline with confidences
steps.learn: Classic OCR splits the job into text detection (where are the lines or words) and recognition (what characters). Handwriting is harder than print, and recognizers are trained on specific data. A baseline with boxes and confidences gives you something to check a VLM against later.

decision.choice: docTR for line and word detection, TrOCR (microsoft/trocr-base-handwritten) to read each line crop
decision.why: docTR is Apache 2.0 and returns a nested page, block, line and word structure. TrOCR's handwritten checkpoint is fine-tuned on IAM and is meant for single text-line images, which matches detected line crops. Together they give text plus locations.

alternatives.name: Tesseract
alternatives.tradeoff: Mature and light, but built mainly for printed text, so marker handwriting tends to fail.

alternatives.name: PaddleOCR
alternatives.tradeoff: An all-in-one toolkit with detection and recognition, but you still must check how its models handle handwriting.

steps.delegate: Python, python-doctr, transformers. detect_lines(img) uses doctr ocr_predictor and returns line boxes; read_line(crop) uses TrOCRProcessor and VisionEncoderDecoderModel with microsoft/trocr-base-handwritten. ocr_board(img) returns lines with boxes and text. Script eval_iam.py computes CER with jiwer.cer on the IAM-line test split. Tests: output schema; empty board yields no lines.
verify: Report CER on the IAM-line test split and on 20 of your hand-transcribed board lines
Note which board features (math, arrows, colors) fail most

steps.title: Use a vision-language model for transcript, topic and diagrams
steps.learn: Boards mix text, equations, arrows and sketches that line OCR cannot describe. A VLM can read the whole image and return a transcript, a topic label and a short description of each diagram. Ask for a fixed JSON schema so the output can be indexed and validated.

decision.choice: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct locally, JSON with transcript, equations as LaTeX, topics, diagram descriptions
decision.why: The model card lists Apache 2.0, strong document scores, and structured outputs, and it runs on your own GPU, so group photos are not sent to a third party. max_pixels caps visual tokens per image to control memory and latency.

alternatives.name: Hosted VLM API
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest and no GPU needed, but board photos leave your control and cost per call.

alternatives.name: OCR text only, no VLM
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheaper and fully grounded, but diagrams and equations become unsearchable.

steps.delegate: Python, transformers, Qwen2_5_VLForConditionalGeneration with AutoProcessor, max_pixels set from the model card. describe_board(img) prompts for a JSON object {transcript, equations, topics, diagrams} and validates it with pydantic, retrying once on invalid JSON. Tests: validator rejects missing fields; a fixture response parses; a failure leaves the board indexed with OCR text only.
verify: On 20 hand-transcribed boards, compare CER of VLM transcript vs the OCR baseline
Count boards where the JSON failed validation after the retry

steps.title: Guard against text the VLM invented
steps.learn: A VLM can produce fluent text that is not on the board, which would make the board match queries it should not. OCR is weaker but grounded in boxes. Cross-checking the two, and always showing the photo next to the result, keeps the search honest.

decision.choice: Index VLM words with lower weight unless fuzzy-matched to OCR tokens; show the photo with every hit
decision.why: Words both systems saw are likely real. Words only the VLM saw still help diagram and topic queries, but should not outrank grounded text. The photo is the source of truth for the user.

alternatives.name: Trust the VLM transcript fully
alternatives.tradeoff: Best recall when it is right, but invented terms silently create false matches.

alternatives.name: Drop all VLM-only words
alternatives.tradeoff: Fully grounded, but loses diagram descriptions that OCR can never produce.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz. ground(vlm_text, ocr_tokens) labels each VLM token grounded if a fuzzy ratio above a threshold matches an OCR token; returns grounded and ungrounded text fields for indexing. Tests: an exact shared word is grounded; a word absent from OCR is ungrounded; threshold is a parameter.
verify: Hand-check 50 ungrounded VLM words on 10 boards and count how many are truly on the board
Record what share of indexed words are ungrounded

steps.title: Index text with BM25 and embeddings, fused by RRF
steps.learn: Students search with exact terms ('Dijkstra') and with paraphrases ('shortest path proof'). BM25 catches exact terms, including course jargon; text embeddings catch paraphrase. Reciprocal Rank Fusion combines the two ranked lists using only ranks, so scores need no calibration.

decision.choice: SQLite FTS5 bm25() plus all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings over transcripts, fused by RRF
decision.why: A term of boards is small, so FTS5 in one file and exact cosine search in NumPy are enough. FTS5 bm25() returns numerically smaller values for better matches, so sort ascending. RRF needs no score tuning between the two lists.

alternatives.name: Embeddings only
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles paraphrase, but can miss rare exact terms such as variable names and course codes.

alternatives.name: BM25 only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and transparent, but 'shortest path' will not find a board that says 'Dijkstra'.

steps.delegate: Python, sqlite3 with FTS5, sentence-transformers. Table boards_fts(board_id UNINDEXED, grounded, ungrounded, topics) with column weights in bm25(); embed transcripts with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 in chunks (it truncates past 256 word pieces), max over chunks; search(q, k) returns RRF-fused board ids with k=60. Tests: exact term query ranks its board first; ORDER BY bm25 ascending; fusion matches a hand computed example.
verify: On a dev query set (not the frozen one), report recall@5 for BM25, embeddings and RRF
Confirm grounded text outweighs ungrounded text in the bm25 column weights

steps.title: Add image search and date or course filters
steps.learn: Some memories are visual: 'the board with the big tree diagram' or 'last week in room 204'. CLIP embeds images and text in one space for diagram queries. Date, course and room are exact metadata, best applied as filters before ranking.

decision.choice: open_clip ViT-B-32 image embeddings as a third RRF list; pre-filter by date range and course
decision.why: open_clip exposes create_model_and_transforms with pretrained checkpoints, and image-text similarity covers diagram queries the transcript misses. A term's archive is small, so pre-filtering then exact search never drops valid boards.

alternatives.name: No image embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but sketch-only boards become unfindable.

alternatives.name: Post-filter after top-k
alternatives.tradeoff: Works with any index, but a narrow date filter can leave few or no results.

steps.delegate: Python, open_clip_torch. embed_image(img) and embed_text(q) using create_model_and_transforms('ViT-B-32', pretrained='laion2b_s34b_b79k'); add a CLIP list into RRF; search(q, date_from, date_to, course) filters board ids first. Tests: filter excludes out-of-range boards; a board's own caption ranks it near the top.
verify: On dev queries about diagrams, report recall@5 with and without the CLIP list
Check that a date-filtered query never returns a board outside the range

steps.title: Test it outside: a term of real boards
steps.learn: Now run the frozen queries once on the full term archive. The test is whether people find boards in practice, so also log real searches during the term and whether the user opened the right board. Report each stage's contribution so you know what earned its place.
verify: Report recall@5 and MRR on the frozen queries for OCR-only, VLM-only, hybrid and hybrid plus CLIP
Report median time from query to opening the correct board in 10 live searches
List the 5 worst failures with the photo and the cause (glare, erasure, math, diagram)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine, GPU and command; why surprising results happened (for example where the VLM beat or lost to OCR); assumptions and limits (one group, one term, one handwriting style mix).
verify: The write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number has the machine, GPU, model versions and command used
It explains at least one surprising result and lists what it does not prove

projects.title: Rental listing scam detector
projects.problem: Fake listings reuse stolen photos and unrealistic prices
projects.concepts: Duplicate image search across listings, price outlier detection
projects.tryIt: Run it on listings in your area and check flagged ones
projects.question: Can duplicate-image search and price outlier checks flag scam rental listings in your area with few false alarms?

steps.title: Frame the question, metrics and a frozen labeled set
steps.learn: The FTC describes two common rental scams: hijacked listings that reuse a real listing's photos with new contact details, and fake listings with surprisingly low rent. Your two signals target those. Success (try-it): how many flagged local listings prove suspicious when checked, and how many were missed.

decision.choice: Test set: local listings from a date window fixed now, labeled by written rules after step 2; Inside Airbnb for dev
decision.why: No public dataset labels local rental scams, so ground truth must come from your own checks. Inside Airbnb publishes per-city listings (CC BY 4.0) with picture_url, price, bedrooms and neighbourhood, a real corpus for duplicate-image tests and price spread.

alternatives.name: Only synthetic scams
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible, but real scams differ from your guesses about them.

alternatives.name: Label by your own detector's output
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but the system grades itself and every flag looks correct.

verify: Write the question and metrics: flag precision, recall on labeled suspicious listings, false alarms per 100
Write the label rules and the test date window, and confirm no tuning script will read data/test/
Download one Inside Airbnb city snapshot and record its date

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before collecting listings
steps.learn: A flag is a reason to check, not proof of fraud, and a false accusation harms a real landlord. The tool is a helper: users must still verify the owner, tour the unit and never wire money first, and real scams go to the official channel. Collect listing content only, not poster identities.

decision.choice: Show 'needs checking' with reasons, never 'scam'; link ReportFraud.ftc.gov; store hashes and prices, not contact info
decision.why: Reasons let the user judge. Keeping photo hashes and prices, not names or phone numbers, means the database cannot be used to target people. Respect each site's terms and robots rules: prefer listings the user pastes in over scraping.

alternatives.name: Auto-report flagged listings
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but false positives become complaints against honest people.

alternatives.name: Bulk scrape listing sites
alternatives.tradeoff: More data, but may break site terms and collects personal details you do not need.

steps.delegate: Python. Define a Listing dataclass (source_url, price, period, bedrooms, area, photo_hashes, text, contact_hash) with no name or phone fields; contact_hash is a salted SHA-256 of the normalized phone or email, salt kept local. scrub(text) removes phone numbers and emails before storage. Flag(reasons: list[str], level: 'none'|'check'). Tests: scrub removes sample contacts; no code path emits the word 'scam' to the UI.
verify: Confirm stored records contain no phone numbers, emails or names
Confirm every flag screen shows reasons and a link to report fraud through the official site

steps.title: Ingest listings and normalize price and unit type
steps.learn: Prices only compare when units match: Inside Airbnb's price is a daily price in local currency, while long-term rentals quote per month. Bedrooms, area names and 'studio' vs '0 bedroom' also vary. Normalize before any outlier check, or the detector will just find unit mismatches.

decision.choice: Separate pools by period (nightly vs monthly); map area to a fixed neighbourhood list; studio as 0 bedrooms
decision.why: Mixing nightly and monthly prices makes every monthly listing look expensive and every nightly one cheap. A fixed area list (for example Inside Airbnb's neighbourhoods file for your city) gives stable groups for comparison.

alternatives.name: Convert nightly to monthly
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives one pool, but short stays are priced for a different market, so the conversion misleads.

alternatives.name: Free-text area names
alternatives.tradeoff: No mapping work, but typos split groups and shrink sample sizes.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas. load_insideairbnb(path) reads listings.csv.gz, parses price to float, keeps id, picture_url, price, bedrooms, neighbourhood_cleansed, room_type, period='night'. load_user(csv) reads pasted local listings with period='month'. normalize_area(name) maps to a fixed list. Tests: '$1,200.00' parses to 1200.0; unknown areas map to 'other'; pools never mix periods.
verify: Report counts per area and bedroom group for your local pool and drop groups under a minimum size you set
Spot-check 10 parsed prices against the source pages

steps.title: Fingerprint listing photos with perceptual hashes
steps.learn: Hijacked listings reuse photos, often resized or recompressed. A perceptual hash summarizes an image's coarse structure in a short bit string, so near copies have a small Hamming distance. Exact file hashes fail after any re-encoding.

decision.choice: imagehash phash per photo, Hamming threshold tuned on synthetic edits of Inside Airbnb photos
decision.why: phash is cheap, needs no GPU and survives resizing and recompression well. Tuning on synthetic edits (resize, JPEG quality, small crop, text overlay) of real listing photos gives labeled pairs for free, without touching the frozen set.

alternatives.name: SHA-256 of the file
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero false positives, but any re-save breaks the match.

alternatives.name: dhash or average_hash
alternatives.tradeoff: Also in imagehash and fast; compare them on the same edit set and keep the one with better recall.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, Pillow. hash_photo(img) returns phash as 64 bits. make_edits(img) yields resized, recompressed, 10 percent cropped, mirrored and text-overlay versions. tune.py hashes 1,000 Inside Airbnb photos and their edits plus random non-pairs and prints recall and false match rate per threshold and edit type. Tests: identical image distance 0; edit generator is deterministic with a seed.
verify: Report recall per edit type and false matches per 10,000 random pairs at your chosen threshold
Note which edit types (crop, mirror) break phash

steps.title: Index hashes for fast Hamming search
steps.learn: Every new listing's photos must be checked against all stored photos. Comparing 64-bit hashes is cheap, but a city's listings times several photos adds up. Binary indexes store bit vectors and search by Hamming distance directly.

decision.choice: FAISS IndexBinaryFlat with range_search at the tuned threshold
decision.why: Exact brute force over packed bits is simple and fast at city scale, and returns every photo within the radius instead of a fixed top-k. FAISS binary indexes require dimensions that are a multiple of 8, which 64-bit hashes meet.

alternatives.name: Python loop with imagehash subtraction
alternatives.tradeoff: Clear and fine for a few thousand photos, but slows as the corpus grows.

alternatives.name: FAISS IndexBinaryHNSW or IndexBinaryMultiHash
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster at large scale, but approximate or more parameters to tune.

steps.delegate: Python, faiss-cpu, numpy. build(hashes) packs 64-bit hashes to uint8 rows and adds them to IndexBinaryFlat(64); near(hash, r) calls range_search and returns (photo_id, listing_id, distance). Tests: an inserted hash is found at distance 0; a hash with 3 flipped bits is found with r=4 and not with r=2; results map back to listing ids.
verify: Confirm range_search results match a brute-force Python loop on 1,000 random queries
Record query time per photo for your corpus size and machine

steps.title: Confirm candidate matches with local features
steps.learn: phash breaks on mirrors and heavier crops, and some different rooms look alike (white walls, same furniture chain). Local keypoints matched with a ratio test, then a RANSAC homography, check that two photos really show the same scene geometry.

decision.choice: Second stage on phash candidates and on CLIP-nearest photos: ORB keypoints, ratio test, RANSAC inlier count
decision.why: phash shortlists cheaply; geometric verification removes look-alike false matches and confirms crops. Adding a CLIP-nearest shortlist catches heavier edits phash misses. OpenCV's find_obj.py sample shows ORB, a 0.75 ratio test and findHomography with RANSAC.

alternatives.name: phash only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but misses mirrors and crops and accepts some look-alikes.

alternatives.name: SIFT instead of ORB
alternatives.tradeoff: Often more robust to scale and lighting, but slower than binary ORB descriptors.

steps.delegate: Python, opencv-python. verify_pair(a, b) uses cv2.ORB_create, BFMatcher with NORM_HAMMING and knnMatch k=2, ratio 0.75, then cv2.findHomography(..., cv2.RANSAC, 5.0); returns inlier count. Also flip b horizontally and keep the higher count. Tests: an image vs its 20 percent crop passes; two unrelated photos fail; mirrored copy passes.
verify: On the synthetic edit set, report recall with phash only vs phash plus verification
Hand-check 20 verified matches across different listings and count true reuse

steps.title: Flag prices far below comparable listings
steps.learn: The FTC flags rent far below comparable rentals as a warning sign. Compare a listing with its own group (area, bedrooms, period). Means and standard deviations are pulled by the very outliers you seek; the median and median absolute deviation (MAD) are robust to them.

decision.choice: Modified z-score 0.6745(x - median)/MAD per group; flag low side only; skip groups too small
decision.why: NIST's handbook gives this Iglewicz and Hoaglin score with |M| > 3.5 as a suggested outlier cut. It is explainable to users ('far below the typical price for 2 bedrooms here') and needs no training. Only too-cheap matters for scams.

alternatives.name: scikit-learn IsolationForest
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles many features at once, but scores are harder to explain and need a contamination setting.

alternatives.name: Quantile regression on features
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses size and amenities, but needs more clean local data than a student project usually has.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas, numpy. modified_z(prices) returns 0.6745*(x-median)/MAD, with MAD=0 handled as no flag. price_flag(listing, pool, min_group) finds the group, returns z and a reason string when z < -cutoff. Tests: a known example matches a hand computation; a group under min_group never flags; high prices never flag.
verify: Report per-group sample sizes and the share of listings flagged at your cutoff
Hand-check the 10 lowest-scoring listings outside the frozen set and note true reasons (sublet, room not unit)

steps.title: Combine signals into an explained flag
steps.learn: Signals mean more together: a reused photo under a different contact or address, plus a price far below the group, is a stronger case than either alone. Some reuse is innocent (an agency reposting its own unit). Rules with reasons are easier to audit than a learned score on few labels.

decision.choice: Rules: check if photo reused in a listing with a different address or source, or price z below cutoff; strong if both
decision.why: With a few dozen labels, a learned combiner would overfit. Rules make every flag explainable. Hijacked listings keep the real address but swap the contact, so a same-address match counts as honest only when a salted contact hash also matches.

alternatives.name: Logistic regression on signals
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns weights, but needs many more labeled scams than you will have.

alternatives.name: Flag on any single signal
alternatives.tradeoff: Highest recall, but many false alarms from reposts and genuine bargains.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz. assess(listing, matches, price_z) returns Flag(level, reasons) citing the matched listing id, address similarity, price group and z. A photo match at the same address with the same contact_hash (salted hash of the scrubbed phone or email) adds a note; same address with a different contact_hash is a check (hijack pattern). Tests: table-driven cases for each rule combination, including an honest repost and a hijack.
verify: Run assess on 30 non-frozen listings and read every reason string for accuracy
Confirm a same-address repost is flagged only when its contact hash differs from the original listing

steps.title: Test it outside on listings in your area
steps.learn: Run on current local listings, then check flagged ones by hand as the FTC suggests: search the address with the owner's name, look for conflicting listings, and check the property manager's own site. Also check a random sample of unflagged listings, or you cannot estimate misses.
verify: Report flag precision on flagged listings and the miss rate from a random sample of 50 unflagged ones
Report results on the frozen labeled set once, with the threshold chosen earlier
Record how many flags came from photos, price, or both

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: the one question; numbers for every claim with machine, snapshot dates and command; why surprising results happened (for example honest reposts or sublets driving false alarms); assumptions and limits (one city, small labels, scams that use original photos are invisible to this).
verify: The write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number has the data snapshot date, machine and command used
It explains a surprising result and lists what the detector cannot catch

projects.title: Smart bird feeder
projects.problem: Which birds visit, and when?
projects.concepts: Edge AI on a Pi or ESP32 camera, a distilled model, event logging
projects.tryIt: Mount it outside for a season; publish visit charts
projects.question: Which bird species visit my feeder, and at what times of day and season, measured by a camera that classifies on the device?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the setup
steps.learn: The output is visit events (species, time, confidence), charted by hour and week across a season. Two numbers make it credible: classifier accuracy on your own labeled captures, and the false-trigger rate. Google's birds model card says it is not for counting or population statistics, so report visits, not populations.

decision.choice: Raspberry Pi camera with Picamera2, a pretrained bird classifier, and your own labeled captures as the test set
decision.why: Picamera2 gives Python access to frames plus a low-res stream for cheap motion checks, and pretrained iNaturalist bird models exist in TFLite form. Your own captures are the only honest test: lighting, angle and local species differ from public photos.

alternatives.name: Evaluate only on NABirds or CUB-200-2011
alternatives.tradeoff: Public, labeled and easy, but curated photos look nothing like a feeder cam; CUB also warns its images overlap ImageNet, which can inflate scores.

alternatives.name: Buy a commercial smart feeder
alternatives.tradeoff: Works on day one, but you cannot see or measure the model, the trigger or the data, so you cannot answer the question yourself.

verify: Write the question, the visit-event definition and the two credibility metrics in one paragraph
List 10 to 20 species you expect locally (from eBird data for your area) to compare against the model's label list
Confirm each expected species appears in the classifier's label file, and note those that do not

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The camera identifies birds, not people. Neighbors, passers-by and windows may enter the frame. Do not store faces: drop any frame where the detector sees a person before it is saved or synced, and mask the street out of view. Feeding wildlife has local rules and hygiene guidance; the app is only a helper.

decision.choice: Discard frames with a person detection on the device, mask non-feeder regions, and never upload raw video
decision.why: The detector already runs, so a person filter costs nothing extra, and dropping frames on the device means people never reach the laptop or any published chart. Crops of the perch only are what the project needs.

alternatives.name: Blur people instead of dropping frames
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more bird frames, but blurring can fail and the original still exists in memory or the pre-roll clip.

alternatives.name: Aim the camera so no public space is visible
alternatives.tradeoff: The strongest fix where possible; may limit placement, so combine it with the filter.

steps.delegate: Add a privacy filter: write triggered clips and bursts to a tmpfs (RAM) folder first; run the COCO detector on every frame of them, and if any shows a person above a low threshold, delete the clip and burst and log only a counter (no image). Move to disk only when all frames pass. Add a static mask that blacks out non-feeder regions before saving. Tests: sample images and clips with people never reach disk; counter increments.
verify: Walk past the feeder 10 times and confirm no frame of you was saved or synced, only the counter changed
Check the mask on saved crops: no street, window or neighbor property visible
Check your local wildlife agency's guidance on feeding birds and feeder cleaning, and note the source you used
Confirm published charts make no claims about rare species presence or population (the model card rules this out)

steps.title: Choose the board, camera and mounting
steps.learn: The bird model card says it suits a well-cropped image of a bird, so framing matters more than megapixels: a fixed perch at a fixed distance, plain background, no direct sun into the lens. The board must run a small detector and classifier at a few frames per second.

decision.choice: A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with a Raspberry Pi camera module, in a weatherproof box aimed at one perch
decision.why: It runs Linux, Python, Picamera2 and LiteRT out of the box, so you can iterate on the pipeline in hours. The Picamera2 manual documents lores streams and circular buffers that this project needs for triggering.

alternatives.name: ESP32 camera board (ESP-WHO, ESP-DL)
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and low power, suited to battery, but tight memory and C toolchains; you may only fit trigger plus tiny model and push images elsewhere.

alternatives.name: Raspberry Pi AI Camera (IMX500)
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs the network on the sensor, freeing the CPU, but models must be packaged as RPK files with Sony's tools, which adds a conversion step.

steps.delegate: Write a Python script for Raspberry Pi OS using Picamera2 that captures a still every 10 s for one hour, saves timestamped JPEGs, and logs vcgencmd measure_temp output. Add a mounting-check mode that overlays a target box where the perch should appear. Use a venv created with --system-site-packages (libcamera bindings are not on PyPI).
verify: From a 1-hour test, confirm a bird on the perch fills a sizable part of the frame (measure box width in pixels)
Check images at morning, noon and evening for glare or backlight and adjust the angle
Log SoC temperature inside the closed box on a sunny day; the Pi throttles from 80 C, so stay well below

steps.title: Trigger on motion and keep a pre-roll buffer
steps.learn: Running the model on every frame wastes power. Picamera2's example compares consecutive greyscale frames from a 320x240 lores stream by mean squared error and starts recording past a threshold; CircularOutput keeps seconds of video from before the trigger so the arrival is not lost.

decision.choice: Frame differencing on the lores stream inside a region-of-interest mask around the perch, plus a pre-roll buffer
decision.why: It costs almost nothing per frame, needs no extra hardware, and the mask ignores swaying branches and the street. The pre-roll means the classifier gets frames from the moment the bird lands.

alternatives.name: PIR motion sensor
alternatives.tradeoff: Very low power and lets the board sleep, but it senses heat changes, not pixels; test whether it fires for small birds at your distance.

alternatives.name: Run the detector at a fixed rate (e.g. 1 fps)
alternatives.tradeoff: No tuning of thresholds and catches still birds, but uses far more CPU and energy all day.

steps.delegate: Extend the Picamera2 script: main 1280x720 RGB888 and lores 320x240 YUV420; compute MSE on the Y plane inside a configurable ROI mask, casting to int16 before subtracting (uint8 wraps); on trigger, save a burst of N main frames and a short clip via CircularOutput2 (or CircularOutput); debounce with a cooldown. Log every trigger with its MSE. Unit test the ROI MSE on synthetic arrays, including darker-than-before frames.
verify: On a windy day, count triggers per hour with no bird present and tune the threshold and ROI to cut them
Review one hour of continuous stills and count birds that never triggered (miss rate)
Confirm the saved burst includes the frame where the bird lands (pre-roll works)

steps.title: Detect the bird, crop it, then classify the species
steps.learn: A detector finds a bird box; a fine-grained classifier names the species from the crop. Coral lists a quantized MobileNet V2 trained on iNaturalist 2017 for 900+ birds at 224x224, with CPU and Edge TPU builds. COCO-trained detectors include a bird class. Keep top-3 scores, not just top-1.

decision.choice: Two stages: COCO SSD detector (bird class) on lores, then the iNat bird MobileNet V2 on a main-frame crop
decision.why: The classifier expects a well-cropped bird, and crops from the high-res stream keep detail on small birds. The detector also rejects false triggers (leaves, squirrels) before the classifier, and its person class is what the privacy step uses.

alternatives.name: Classifier only on the whole frame
alternatives.tradeoff: Half the compute and simpler, but birds small in frame get misread, and you lose the person and no-bird filter.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune your own classifier on local species
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer, local classes usually help, but you need hundreds of labeled crops first; plan it after a few weeks of data.

steps.delegate: In Python with ai_edge_litert.interpreter.Interpreter, load a COCO SSD MobileNet TFLite model and the Coral iNat bird TFLite classifier (CPU build) with its label file. Pipeline: detect on lores, keep boxes labeled bird above a score, map to main-frame coordinates, pad 10%, crop, resize to 224, classify, return top-3. Tests: fixed sample images give stable outputs, uint8 vs float input handled from input_details, timings per stage logged.
verify: On 50 saved triggers, check by eye that boxes cover the bird and crops are not clipped
Measure per-stage latency on the device (median of 100 runs) and write it down
Confirm triggers with no bird produce no classification event

steps.title: Decide model size and what runs on device vs laptop
steps.learn: LiteRT post-training quantization: dynamic range (weights only, no calibration data), full integer (needs a representative dataset; CPU, Edge TPU, microcontrollers) and float16. Distillation (Hinton et al.) trains a small student to match a large teacher's outputs, which you can do with your own unlabeled captures.

decision.choice: Device: trigger, int8 models, logging. Laptop: re-label crops with a larger model, train students
decision.why: The feeder must work when the Wi-Fi is down, so every visit gets a label on the device. The laptop has time and compute to re-label low-confidence events and, after a few weeks, distill a smaller local-species student that runs back on the Pi.

alternatives.name: Stream everything to the laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Any model size, no device tuning, but needs reliable Wi-Fi and the laptop on all season; one outage loses data.

alternatives.name: Everything on device, never reprocess
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but errors are frozen in; you cannot improve old events when you get a better model.

alternatives.name: Zero-shot CLIP teacher on the laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Labels species by text prompt with no training, useful as a teacher, but accuracy on fine-grained birds must be checked on your labels.

steps.delegate: Write a laptop-side Python tool: load saved crops, run a larger teacher (a float classifier or CLIP via open_clip) to get soft labels, train a MobileNetV2 student on local species with a distillation loss, convert with tf.lite.TFLiteConverter using full integer quantization and a representative dataset of 200 crops, and compare student vs teacher accuracy on a held-out labeled set.
verify: After labeling in the accuracy step, compare float vs int8 classifier accuracy on the same 200 labeled crops and report the drop
Compare int8 latency on the Pi against float latency on the Pi
Unplug Wi-Fi for an hour and confirm events are still labeled and logged on the device

links.label: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network

steps.title: Turn detections into visit events and log them
steps.learn: A chickadee on the perch for 20 seconds yields many detections but one visit. Group consecutive detections into a visit until no bird is seen for a gap, and store one row per visit with time span, species votes and model version. Store UTC timestamps; convert only for charts.

decision.choice: SQLite on the device in WAL mode, one visits table plus a detections table, crops saved as files referenced by path
decision.why: SQLite is a single file with transactions, so a power cut mid-write does not corrupt the log, and WAL mode lets the sync reader run while the camera loop writes. It is queryable for charts with no server.

alternatives.name: Append-only JSON Lines files
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial and easy to ship, but partial lines after a power loss and no queries without loading everything.

alternatives.name: A time-series database
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for dashboards, but a server process on a small board and overkill for a few hundred rows a day.

steps.delegate: In Python, write a visit aggregator: input detection stream (ts, top-3 species and scores, box, crop path); a visit ends after G seconds with no bird; species is the score-weighted vote across detections. Store visits(uuid, start_utc, end_utc, species, conf, top3_json, model_version, synced) and detections in SQLite with journal_mode=WAL. Tests: synthetic streams with gaps, two birds overlapping, crash mid-visit recovery.
verify: Watch 20 real visits live and confirm each produced exactly one visit row
Pull the power during a visit, reboot, and confirm the database opens and earlier rows are intact
Confirm timestamps are UTC and the board clock was synced (record how you checked)

steps.title: Sync events over flaky Wi-Fi without losing or duplicating
