steps.learn: Outdoor Wi-Fi drops. Treat the device as the source of truth: mark rows unsynced, upload in batches, and mark synced only after the receiver confirms. Because each visit has a UUID, the receiver can upsert, so a retried batch after a timeout creates no duplicates.

decision.choice: An outbox: periodic batch upload of unsynced visits keyed by UUID with retries and backoff; crops copied with rsync
decision.why: Idempotent upserts make at-least-once delivery safe, which is the realistic guarantee over a flaky link. rsync with --partial keeps interrupted files so the next run resumes. Nothing in the camera loop waits on the network.

alternatives.name: MQTT to a broker on the laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Push-based and near real time, but you still need local buffering for outages and a broker running all season.

alternatives.name: Wired PoE instead of Wi-Fi
alternatives.tradeoff: The Pi docs list PoE support on several models with a HAT; one cable fixes both power and network, at the cost of running it outdoors.

steps.delegate: In Python, write a sync worker: every 5 minutes, select up to 500 unsynced visits, POST them as JSON to a small FastAPI receiver on the laptop that upserts by uuid into its own SQLite, mark synced on HTTP 200, exponential backoff with jitter on failure. rsync the crops directory. Tests: receiver gets the same batch twice and stores it once; network cut mid-batch; device offline for a day then catches up.
verify: Kill the network mid-upload and confirm the laptop ends with exactly the device's row count, no duplicates
Leave the device offline for 24 h and measure time to catch up after reconnecting
Track sync lag (now minus newest synced visit) for a week and report the median and max

steps.title: Power it for a whole season
steps.learn: Measure, do not guess: average watts across a day sets the battery or solar size. Raspberry Pi docs say all models need a 5.1 V supply and low-quality supplies can corrupt storage, which in a feeder means a lost log. Heat inside a sealed box causes throttling.

decision.choice: Mains power through an outdoor-rated supply (or PoE), with measured average power logged for a week
decision.why: A Pi running a camera all day is not a small battery load. Mains power removes a whole class of failures so the season of data is complete; the measured watts tell you later whether solar is realistic.

alternatives.name: Battery plus solar panel
alternatives.tradeoff: No cable, but cloudy weeks drain it, and you need measured daily energy plus margin; expect gaps in winter.

alternatives.name: ESP32 with PIR wake from deep sleep
alternatives.tradeoff: Fits battery power, but on-device classification is limited; you may only capture and upload images for the laptop to classify.

steps.delegate: Write a small Python health logger for the Pi: every minute record vcgencmd measure_temp, CPU load, free disk, SQLite size and uptime to the same database, and raise a local flag file when disk is above 80% or temperature is high. Add a daily cleanup that deletes synced crops older than N days.
verify: Measure average power over 24 h with a USB power meter and write down watt-hours per day
Check the board logs for under-voltage or throttling warnings after a week outdoors
Confirm disk use stays flat over a week with the cleanup job running

steps.title: Measure accuracy on your own captures
steps.learn: Label a sample of visits yourself (species or no bird or unsure) using a field guide. Compute top-1 and top-3 accuracy, per-species precision and recall, and a confusion matrix. Frames from one visit are near-duplicates, so split by visit and by date, never by frame.

decision.choice: Hand-label about 300 visits sampled across weeks and times of day, held out by date from any training data
decision.why: Random frame splits leak the same bird into train and test and overstate accuracy. Sampling across weeks covers changing light, plumage and species mix, and keeps the test set honest if you later distill a student.

alternatives.name: Trust model confidence as a proxy
alternatives.tradeoff: No labeling work, but confidence is not accuracy; confident mistakes on lookalike species go unnoticed.

alternatives.name: Score on NABirds instead
alternatives.tradeoff: Large and expert-labeled, but it measures the model on curated photos, not on your feeder; use only as a secondary check.

steps.delegate: Write a labeling tool (Python, a simple local web page or Jupyter widget) that shows a visit's best crop and records species, no bird, or unsure into a labels table. Add an evaluation script that computes top-1, top-3, per-species precision and recall, a confusion matrix, and accuracy by hour of day and by week, using perceptual hashing to drop near-duplicate crops.
verify: Label at least 300 visits and report top-1 and top-3 accuracy with the count per species
List the 3 most confused species pairs and look at 5 examples of each
Confirm no visit appears in both a training set and the test set (check by visit UUID and date)

steps.title: Test it outside for a season and publish visit charts
steps.learn: Run the feeder for a season. Charts are visits per species by hour of day and by week, with confidence filtered and low-confidence events shown as unknown. Track the system too: uptime, triggers per day, false-trigger rate, sync lag. Gaps in uptime must show as gaps, not as zero birds.
verify: Report uptime percent for the season and mark every outage on the charts
Publish charts of visits per species by hour and by week, with the accuracy from your labels next to them
Report false triggers per day at the start and end of the season
Re-label 50 visits from the last month and compare accuracy with the first month

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) numbers for every claim with the device, model version and command; (3) why the surprising results happened, for example a species the model kept confusing or a time of day with many false triggers; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: The write-up states the one question at the top
Every claim has a number with the device, model file and command or script that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with examples (crops, confusion pairs, trigger logs)
An assumptions section says what this does not prove (one feeder, one season, visits not population, label noise)

projects.title: Laundry availability sensor
projects.problem: Walking down to find every machine busy
projects.concepts: Vibration sensor, streaming events, a shared live dashboard
projects.tryIt: Install in your building's laundry room with permission
projects.question: Can a vibration sensor on each machine report free or busy accurately and fast enough that residents stop walking down to a full laundry room?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and a frozen test log
steps.learn: The product is one bit per machine (busy or free) that people trust. Success from the try-it: installed in your building's laundry room with permission, state agrees with what a person sees, start and end are detected quickly, and the board never says 'free' while a machine runs.

decision.choice: Own recordings: a training week of labeled cycles, then a separate test week logged by a human, frozen before tuning
decision.why: No public dataset covers your machines, mounts and floor. A person writing start and end times on paper is ground truth the sensor cannot grade itself on. Freezing the test week before choosing thresholds stops you tuning to it.

alternatives.name: Use the machine's own display as truth
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to read, but shows remaining time, not when the drum actually stops or the door opens; still needs a person.

alternatives.name: Tune and test on the same week
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but thresholds fit that week's loads and the accuracy you report will be optimistic.

verify: Write the question and 4 metrics: state agreement, start delay, end delay, false 'free' minutes per day
Write the test-week protocol: who logs, how often, and that its data is never used for tuning
List each machine (washer or dryer, make, location) the board will cover

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before installing anything
steps.learn: Sense machines, not people. A laundry room is a shared private space, so no cameras or microphones, and no record of who did laundry when. Mounting on appliances in a building you do not own needs written permission, and you must never open a machine or touch mains wiring.

decision.choice: Accelerometer only, stick-on mount outside the cabinet, USB power from an existing outlet, publish machine state only
decision.why: An accelerometer reading of a cabinet carries nothing about residents. Keeping the device outside the machine with no wiring changes avoids electrical and warranty risk. Publishing only states and timestamps means even a leaked log reveals little.

alternatives.name: Camera watching the room
alternatives.tradeoff: Sees doors and lights directly, but records residents in a private space; not acceptable here.

alternatives.name: Clamp current sensor on the supply
alternatives.tradeoff: Measures real power draw, but needs access to the machine's wiring, which raises electrical safety and permission issues.

steps.delegate: Write a one-page README for the building: what each box measures (vibration only), what is sent (machine id, state, time, a vibration level, an online heartbeat), what is never collected (audio, images, user identity), who to contact, and how to unplug it. Also a label template for each device with the same contact. No code tests; a reviewer checklist to rerun once the firmware exists, confirming every published field is listed in the README.
verify: Get written permission from the building manager and keep a copy
Confirm the published payload schema contains no field that could identify a resident
Write the mounting rule (outside the machine, labeled, clear of doors, vents and walkways) and check every device against it at installation

steps.title: Choose the sensor, board and mounting
steps.learn: A running drum shakes the cabinet; a 3-axis accelerometer turns that into numbers. You need a sample rate high enough to see drum and motor vibration, a range that does not clip during spin, and a Wi-Fi microcontroller to send results. Mount rigidity matters as much as the chip.

decision.choice: ESP32 dev board with an ADXL345 breakout over I2C, rigidly fixed to the top or side panel
decision.why: The ADXL345 supports I2C and SPI, selectable ranges from 2 g to 16 g, and adjustable data rates, and Adafruit's maintained library supports it. The ESP32 has Wi-Fi built in. One cheap, identical unit per machine keeps the fleet simple.

alternatives.name: Digital vibration switch module
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest and simplest, but gives only on or off with a pot to tune, so wash pauses and neighbor machines are hard to tell apart.

alternatives.name: One sensor per room plus sound
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer devices, but cannot say which machine is busy and brings back the privacy problem of microphones.

steps.delegate: Arduino-ESP32 sketch using Adafruit_ADXL345_U and Adafruit_Sensor: init over I2C, setRange to 4 g, setDataRate to 100 Hz, read x, y, z with getEvent in a fixed-period loop, and print CSV with a millisecond timestamp over serial. Include a self-check that halts with a clear message if the sensor is not found.
verify: Record 60 s idle and 60 s during spin; confirm no axis sits at the range limit during spin
Confirm the measured sample interval stays within 10 percent of the target

steps.title: Record labeled raw traces for the training week
steps.learn: Before writing any detector, look at full cycles: fill, agitate, soak pauses, drain, spin, and the idle tail. Also record what an idle machine reads while its neighbor spins. These traces are your training data; the frozen test week stays untouched.

decision.choice: Log raw samples to an SD card or a laptop over serial for a week, with hand-written cycle start and end times
decision.why: Raw data lets you try several feature and threshold choices offline. Logging locally avoids debugging Wi-Fi and the detector at the same time.

alternatives.name: Only log on-device summaries
alternatives.tradeoff: Much less data, but you cannot revisit window size or filtering later.

alternatives.name: Stream raw samples to a server
alternatives.tradeoff: Convenient, but Wi-Fi drops create gaps exactly when you need complete cycles.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with pandas and matplotlib: load the CSV logs and a labels.csv (machine, start, end, program), plot each cycle's magnitude with the label span shaded, and save one PNG per cycle. Tests: label times outside the log range raise an error; the loader refuses any file from the test-week folder.
verify: Collect at least 10 labeled cycles per machine type, including different programs
Mark on a plot the longest quiet pause inside a cycle and the strongest crosstalk from a neighbor

steps.title: Turn raw acceleration into one vibration feature
steps.learn: Gravity adds a constant offset, so remove the mean (or high-pass filter) before measuring energy. Then compute RMS of the acceleration magnitude over a short window. Window length trades responsiveness for stability; an FFT shows whether a band-pass helps reject a neighbor's vibration.

decision.choice: Per-window RMS of mean-removed magnitude, 1 to 2 s windows, computed on the ESP32
decision.why: RMS is cheap, interpretable, and enough to separate running from idle in most traces. Computing it on-device sends one number per window instead of a raw stream.

alternatives.name: FFT band energy features
alternatives.tradeoff: Better at rejecting a neighbor's spin at a different frequency, but more tuning and compute.

alternatives.name: Small learned classifier on windows
alternatives.tradeoff: Can learn odd programs, but needs many labeled cycles and is harder to debug than a threshold.

steps.delegate: Python with numpy and scipy.signal: rms_feature(samples, fs, window_s) that subtracts the per-window mean of each axis, takes the magnitude, and returns RMS per window; plus an equivalent C++ function for the ESP32. Tests: a constant 1 g input gives near zero; a sine of known amplitude gives amplitude divided by root 2; Python and C++ agree on a fixture.
verify: Plot idle versus running RMS histograms for each machine and note the gap between them
Compute an FFT of a spin segment and an idle segment during neighbor spin; note the dominant peaks

steps.title: Detect busy and free with hysteresis and hold times
steps.learn: A single threshold flickers near the boundary, and washers go quiet for minutes mid-cycle. Use two thresholds (enter busy above a high one, leave below a low one) and time rules: busy after sustained vibration, free only after a quiet period longer than the longest in-cycle pause.

decision.choice: Per-machine state machine: idle, running, maybe-done, free; thresholds and hold times fit on the training week
decision.why: Hysteresis kills flicker; the maybe-done state covers soak pauses so the board does not say free mid-cycle. Fitting per machine absorbs differences in mounts and models.

alternatives.name: Single threshold with no hold time
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but flickers and shows free during every pause.

alternatives.name: Fixed cycle timer after start
alternatives.tradeoff: Stable display, but wrong for every program longer or shorter than the timer.

steps.delegate: Python module laundry_state.py with a pure function step(state, rms, t, params) returning the new state and an optional event; params loaded from per-machine YAML. Port the same logic to C++ for the ESP32. Tests: replay every labeled training cycle and assert one start and one end event each; a 5 minute quiet gap inside a cycle does not emit free; Python and C++ emit identical events on a fixture.
verify: On training traces, record start and end delay per cycle and any false 'free' events
Write down the final thresholds and hold times for each machine before opening the test week

steps.title: Publish state changes as an event stream over MQTT
steps.learn: Send events (state changed) plus a periodic heartbeat, not raw samples. In MQTT 3.1.1 a retained message is stored by the broker and sent to each new subscriber, so a dashboard that starts late still sees current state. A Will message is published by the broker if the client drops without a clean disconnect.

decision.choice: Mosquitto broker; topic laundry/<machine>/state retained; laundry/<machine>/online with a retained 'offline' Will
decision.why: Retained state answers 'what is it now' for any new viewer; the Will marks a dead sensor without polling. The arduino-mqtt library supports setWill and publish with retained and QoS options on the ESP32.

alternatives.name: HTTP POST to the server
alternatives.tradeoff: No broker to run, but you must build offline detection and last-value storage yourself.

alternatives.name: PubSubClient library
alternatives.tradeoff: Widely used, but its README now says it is unmaintained and it can only publish QoS 0.

steps.delegate: Arduino-ESP32 sketch using the 256dpi arduino-mqtt library: connect Wi-Fi, setWill('laundry/<id>/online', 'offline', retained, QoS 1), publish 'online' retained after connect, publish JSON {state, ts, rms} retained on each state change, and a heartbeat every 60 s. Reconnect with backoff. Test with mosquitto_sub: killing power produces 'offline' within about 1.5 times the keepalive.
verify: Subscribe from a fresh client and confirm current state arrives immediately via the retained message
Pull the power and time how long until 'offline' appears

steps.title: Ingest events and keep a history on a small server
steps.learn: A small service subscribes to the broker, keeps current state per machine in memory, and appends every event to a durable log. History lets you estimate typical cycle length and later compare against the human test log.

decision.choice: Python service with paho-mqtt writing events to SQLite in WAL mode on a Raspberry Pi or home server
decision.why: Events are a few per hour per machine, so one SQLite file is plenty, and WAL mode lets the dashboard read while the subscriber writes. paho-mqtt is the Eclipse Python client.

alternatives.name: Time-series database
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for raw high-rate data, but extra service to run for a few events per hour.

alternatives.name: In-memory only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but loses history on restart, so no cycle statistics or evaluation.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 with paho-mqtt and sqlite3: subscribe to laundry/+/state and laundry/+/online, insert (machine, kind, value, device_ts, received_ts) into an events table, maintain a dict of current state, and expose median cycle duration per machine. Tests: duplicate retained messages after reconnect are not double-counted; malformed JSON is logged and skipped.
verify: Restart the service and confirm current state is restored from retained messages and history is intact
Compare event counts for one day with the number of cycles you saw

steps.title: Build the shared live dashboard
steps.learn: Residents need a page that updates by itself. Server-sent events are one-way, server to browser, over plain HTTP, and the browser's EventSource reconnects on its own. Show each machine as free, busy (with time since start and a typical finish), or unknown.

decision.choice: Server-sent events from the Python service to a single static page using EventSource
decision.why: Data only flows to the browser, so SSE fits and needs no extra protocol. Built-in reconnection matters for phones that sleep. A static page loads fast on a building's guest Wi-Fi.

alternatives.name: WebSockets
alternatives.tradeoff: Two-way and flexible, but more to build and you must handle reconnection yourself.

alternatives.name: Poll a JSON endpoint
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest server, but slower updates or more load, and stale views between polls.

steps.delegate: Add a FastAPI app to the service: GET /state returns current state JSON; GET /events streams state changes as text/event-stream with an initial full snapshot. A static HTML page uses EventSource to render a card per machine and shows 'unknown' for offline or stale machines. Tests: a new client receives the snapshot first; a state change reaches two connected clients.
verify: Open the page on two phones, start a machine, and time how long each takes to show busy
Put a phone to sleep for 5 minutes, wake it, and confirm the page catches up without a refresh

steps.title: Handle offline sensors, stale data and drift
steps.learn: The worst failure is confidently wrong: showing free when a sensor died mid-cycle. Treat missing heartbeats, the Will message, and implausible readings (stuck values, a cycle far longer than any seen) as 'unknown', and say so on the board.

decision.choice: Unknown on Will or missed heartbeats; flag cycles longer than a set multiple of the machine's longest seen
decision.why: Unknown is honest and cheap; people walk down only when they would have anyway. Duration checks catch a loosened mount or a machine left with its door open.

alternatives.name: Keep showing last known state
alternatives.tradeoff: Looks cleaner, but a dead sensor can show free or busy for days.

alternatives.name: Auto-retune thresholds online
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to drift, but can slowly learn the wrong idle level without anyone noticing.

steps.delegate: Extend the service: a watchdog task marks a machine unknown when no heartbeat arrives within 3 intervals or the Will fires; a check flags stuck RMS (zero variance over N windows) and over-long cycles; an admin view lists these with timestamps. Tests with a fake clock: missing heartbeats flip to unknown; recovery returns to the real state.
verify: Unplug one sensor mid-cycle and confirm the board shows unknown, not free, within your heartbeat window
Loosen one mount on purpose and see whether the stuck or over-long checks catch it

steps.title: Test it in the laundry room against the frozen log
steps.learn: Now run the frozen test week: the board runs with settings fixed, a person logs real starts and ends, and the two are compared afterward. Also ask a few residents whether they used it and if it saved a wasted trip.
verify: Report state agreement per minute, median and worst start and end delay, versus the human log
Report false 'free' minutes per day and unknown minutes per day per machine
Report device uptime from heartbeats and count residents who used the board

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the hardware, firmware commit and command used, (3) why surprises happened (neighbor crosstalk, soak pauses, Wi-Fi drops), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove (other buildings, other machines, a longer season).
verify: The write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number names the test week, the hardware and the command or script that produced it
It explains at least one surprising result and lists assumptions and what it does not prove

projects.title: Garden disease time-lapse
projects.problem: Plant disease is caught too late
projects.concepts: Time-lapse images, change detection, leaf classifier
projects.tryIt: Run it on a vegetable bed over a summer
projects.question: Can a fixed garden camera flag leaf disease on a vegetable bed earlier than weekly checks by eye, without drowning you in false alarms?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the frozen sets
steps.learn: Two parts are measured separately: a change detector that says 'this plant looks different', and a leaf classifier that suggests what it might be. From the try-it: run on a vegetable bed over a summer and compare alert dates with symptoms you log by eye.

decision.choice: PlantDoc test split frozen for the classifier; your own dated symptom log as field ground truth
decision.why: PlantDoc has field-style leaf images in 13 species with a fixed train and test split, so the classifier gets an honest public number. Your hand log, written before looking at alerts, is truth the system cannot grade itself on.

alternatives.name: PlantVillage as the test set
alternatives.tradeoff: Large and clean, but lab images on plain backgrounds; the PlantDoc paper reports models trained on it do poorly on real-world images.

alternatives.name: Only judge alerts by looking at them
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick, but you will rate the system by its own output and miss what it never flagged.

verify: Write the question and metrics: days earlier than eye checks, false alerts per week, classifier accuracy
Record the PlantDoc test folder checksum and a rule that it is never used for training or tuning
Set a fixed weekly eye-check routine and log template before the camera goes up

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before the camera runs
steps.learn: Photograph plants, not people. An outdoor camera can see neighbors, a street or a window. And a disease label is a hint, not a diagnosis: treatment decisions should go through a local extension service or plant clinic and the product label of anything you apply.

decision.choice: Crop to the bed on-device, drop any frame where a person is detected, keep images local, alerts say 'check this'
decision.why: Cropping to a fixed bed region removes most of the scene. Running MediaPipe Object Detector (COCO labels include person) on the Pi and discarding those frames means no image of a person is stored. Wording alerts as prompts keeps the human in charge.

alternatives.name: Blur people instead of dropping frames
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more daily frames, but a missed blur leaves a stored image of a person.

alternatives.name: Upload all frames to the cloud
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier processing, but raw images of the surroundings leave your control.

steps.delegate: Python on Raspberry Pi OS with mediapipe and opencv-python: run the MediaPipe Object Detector (EfficientDet-Lite0) on each capture, delete the frame if a person is found above a score threshold, otherwise save only the bed crop defined in config. Tests: a fixture image with a person is deleted; saved files match the crop size; nothing is written outside the data folder.
verify: Aim the camera and confirm the crop excludes any neighbor's window, path or street
Walk through the frame 5 times during capture and confirm no stored frame shows you
Write the alert wording and the local extension contact you will use to confirm a diagnosis

steps.title: Build the camera rig and capture schedule
steps.learn: Change detection works only if the camera, focus and exposure stay the same, so the plant is the only thing that changes. Autofocus and auto exposure make every frame slightly different. Daylight still varies with weather and time of day, so capture at a fixed time.

decision.choice: Raspberry Pi, Camera Module 3, Picamera2: fixed focus, exposure and colour gains; daily captures
decision.why: Picamera2 can set LensPosition in manual autofocus mode and fix ExposureTime, AnalogueGain and ColourGains, so frames are comparable. A few captures around midday each day give a choice when one is blurred or wet.

alternatives.name: Full auto exposure and focus
alternatives.tradeoff: Prettier single images, but brightness and focus shifts look like plant change.

alternatives.name: Old phone running a time-lapse app
alternatives.tradeoff: No hardware build, but harder to control settings, power and storage for a whole summer.

steps.delegate: Python with picamera2: let auto exposure and white balance settle, read ExposureTime, AnalogueGain and ColourGains from metadata, then fix them and set AfMode Manual with a fixed LensPosition; capture 3 stills around noon daily via a systemd timer, saving JPEG plus metadata JSON named by timestamp. Tests: metadata of consecutive frames shows identical exposure and gains; a missing camera exits non-zero.
verify: Capture 5 frames in a row and confirm the stored exposure, gain and lens position are identical
Run one week and report the fraction of scheduled captures that exist

steps.title: Reject bad frames before they reach the pipeline
steps.learn: Rain on the lens, condensation, blown highlights and a bumped camera all create fake change. A cheap quality gate removes them: sharpness from the variance of a Laplacian filter, brightness and clipping from the histogram, and the alignment result from the next step.

decision.choice: Keep the best of each day's captures by sharpness, reject frames failing brightness or clipping limits
decision.why: Choosing the sharpest of a few daily frames is simple and avoids most wet-lens and wind blur. Thresholds are set from the first weeks of frames, not from the symptom log.

alternatives.name: Keep every frame
alternatives.tradeoff: No tuning, but bad frames feed false alerts later.

alternatives.name: Learned image-quality model
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles odd failures, but needs labeled bad frames you do not have yet.

steps.delegate: Python with opencv-python and numpy: quality(img) returns sharpness (variance of cv2.Laplacian on grayscale), mean brightness and fraction of clipped pixels; pick_daily(frames) returns the best passing frame or None. Tests: a Gaussian-blurred copy scores lower sharpness; an all-white image fails clipping; a day with no passing frame is logged, not filled in.
verify: Hand-label 30 frames good or bad and report how many the gate gets right
After the first week, report the fraction of days with a usable frame; repeat it monthly through the season

steps.title: Align each day's frame to a reference
steps.learn: Even a fixed mount moves a little with wind and temperature. Register each frame to a reference before comparing pixels: match local features, fit a homography with RANSAC to ignore bad matches, and warp. Plants grow, so match on static things like bed edges and stakes.

decision.choice: ORB features matched to a reference, cv.findHomography with RANSAC, masked to static regions
decision.why: ORB is fast and free to use in OpenCV; RANSAC rejects matches on moving leaves. Masking to bed frame and stakes keeps growth from pulling the alignment.

alternatives.name: ECC alignment (cv.findTransformECC)
alternatives.tradeoff: Area-based on intensities and good for small drifts, but needs a rough initial alignment for large moves and can fail to converge.

alternatives.name: No alignment, rigid mount only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but a few pixels of shift shows up as change along every leaf edge.

steps.delegate: Python with opencv-python: align(img, ref, static_mask) detects ORB keypoints in the masked regions, matches with BFMatcher Hamming and a ratio test, estimates a homography with cv.RANSAC, warps the image, and returns the inlier count. Reject the frame if inliers fall below a threshold. Tests: a synthetically shifted and rotated reference aligns within 2 px; a random image is rejected.
verify: Flip between 10 aligned frames and confirm stakes and bed edges stay fixed
Report inlier counts over the season and whether any drop below the reject threshold

steps.title: Segment foliage and define one region per plant
steps.learn: Separate living leaves from soil and mulch, then split the bed into one region per plant so an alert names a plant. The excess green index 2g - r - b, on chromatic (sum-normalized) RGB, was shown to separate plants from soil and residue in both sun and shade.

decision.choice: Excess green on chromatic coordinates with an Otsu threshold, plus hand-drawn polygons per plant
decision.why: It needs no training data and normalizing by brightness reduces sensitivity to light. Drawing a polygon per plant once is quick for one bed and makes every number per plant.

alternatives.name: Fixed HSV hue range
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to understand, but yellowing leaves (the symptom you want) may fall out of the range and vanish.

alternatives.name: Learned segmentation model
alternatives.tradeoff: More robust, but needs labeled masks from your own bed.

steps.delegate: Python with numpy and opencv-python: exg(img) computes 2g - r - b on chromatic coordinates; foliage_mask uses cv.threshold with THRESH_OTSU on the rescaled index; a small tool lets you draw and save plant polygons to JSON. Tests: a synthetic image with green squares on brown gives a mask matching the squares; polygons round-trip through JSON.
verify: Overlay masks on 10 frames and estimate by eye how much foliage is missed or soil included
Check that a visibly yellowed leaf is still inside the foliage mask

links.label: Woebbecke et al., color indices for plants

steps.title: Detect unusual change per plant over time
steps.learn: Healthy plants change too: they grow, wilt at noon heat and recover. Track per-plant series such as foliage area and the share of yellow or brown pixels inside the mask, and flag a plant when it departs from its own recent trend, not when it simply differs from yesterday.

decision.choice: Per-plant daily features, robust z-score against a rolling median and MAD, alert after 2 consecutive days
decision.why: Each plant is its own baseline, so tomatoes and lettuce need no separate rules. Median and MAD resist one-off bad frames, and requiring two days cuts weather-driven false alarms.

alternatives.name: Pixel difference against yesterday
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but growth, shadows and wind make every day look changed.

alternatives.name: Forecasting model per plant
alternatives.tradeoff: Can model growth curves, but needs more data than one season gives.

steps.delegate: Python with pandas: features(frame, mask, polygons) returns per-plant foliage area (ExG mask) and the fraction of non-soil pixels in a yellow-brown hue band inside the plant polygon or a dilated mask, so brown lesions excluded by ExG still count; detect(series, window, k, persist) returns alert dates using rolling median and MAD. Tests: steady growth gives no alerts; a step increase in yellow fraction alerts on day 2; brown spots on a leaf raise the fraction; missing days are skipped.
verify: Run on all frames so far and count alerts per week; repeat after the first month, before any symptom appears in your log
Open the before and after crops for every alert and note what caused it

steps.title: Train a leaf classifier on field-style images
steps.learn: Change detection says something is off; a classifier suggests what. Fine-tune a small pretrained CNN on leaf crops. Training data background matters: lab images on plain backgrounds teach the model shortcuts that break outdoors, which is why PlantDoc exists.

decision.choice: Fine-tune timm mobilenetv3_large_100 on the PlantDoc train folder, restricted to the species in your bed
decision.why: MobileNetV3 is small enough to run on a Pi and has ImageNet-pretrained weights in timm. Restricting classes to what you grow avoids wasting capacity and makes errors easier to read. PlantDoc's test folder stays frozen for scoring.

alternatives.name: Train on PlantVillage
alternatives.tradeoff: Far more images, but lab backgrounds; the PlantDoc paper shows weak results on real-world images.

alternatives.name: Zero-shot CLIP with disease names
alternatives.tradeoff: No training, but disease names are fine-grained and rarely described well in captions.

steps.delegate: Python with torch and timm: build the class list from PlantDoc folders filtered to a config of species; hold out 15 percent of train for validation; fine-tune mobilenetv3_large_100 with standard augmentation; save weights and an ONNX export. Tests: no file appears in both train and validation; class order is saved with the weights; the test folder is read only by evaluate.py.
verify: Report top-1 accuracy and per-class recall on the frozen PlantDoc test folder, once
Compare against the majority-class baseline and list the most confused class pairs

steps.title: Run the classifier only on flagged plants, with abstain
steps.learn: Your bed is not PlantDoc: lighting, angle and leaf size differ. Run the classifier only on crops of plants the change detector flagged, and let it abstain when confidence is low or the species does not match what you planted there.

decision.choice: Change detection gates the classifier; show top-2 labels with confidence, or 'unclear' below a threshold
decision.why: Gating keeps compute low and avoids labeling healthy plants as diseased. Top-2 with an unclear option is more honest than one confident label on out-of-domain images.

alternatives.name: Classify every plant every day
alternatives.tradeoff: Could catch what the change detector misses, but many more false disease labels.

alternatives.name: Change alert only, no classifier
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer wrong labels, but you get no hint of what to look for.

steps.delegate: Python with onnxruntime: for each alert, crop the plant polygon's bounding box from the aligned frame, run the ONNX model, keep only classes for that plant's species, and return top-2 with softmax scores or 'unclear' below a threshold. Tests: species filtering removes other crops' classes; a blank crop returns 'unclear'.
verify: Label 30 of your own leaf crops by hand and report classifier accuracy and abstain rate on them
Confirm the threshold was set on validation data, not on your bed's labeled crops

steps.title: Send alerts with before and after images
steps.learn: An alert should let you judge in seconds: the plant name, the first-seen date, side-by-side crops from a week ago and today, and the classifier hint. Log your confirm or dismiss reply to count false alerts, but timing and misses come only from the blind eye-check log.

decision.choice: Daily digest message (email or a chat bot) with crops and confirm or dismiss buttons logged to SQLite
decision.why: One digest per day respects attention and matches the daily capture rhythm. Logging every response creates labeled data without extra effort.

alternatives.name: Instant push per alert
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but many alerts in a bad-weather week train you to ignore them.

alternatives.name: Web gallery only
alternatives.tradeoff: No notification setup, but you have to remember to check it.

steps.delegate: Python: compose a daily digest with per-plant before and after JPEG crops and the classifier output, send via SMTP or a chat bot API from config, and store (alert_id, plant, date, response) in SQLite when the user replies. Tests: no digest is sent on a day without alerts; each alert appears once; responses update the right row.
verify: Receive one digest and confirm each alert can be judged without opening other files
Confirm responses land in the database with the right plant and date

steps.title: Run it on a vegetable bed over a summer
steps.learn: Keep all settings fixed for the season. Your weekly eye-check log, written before reading the digest, is ground truth for when symptoms appeared. Afterward, match each logged symptom to the first alert on that plant.
verify: For each logged symptom, report days between first alert and first eye-check sighting (negative if later)
Report false alerts per week, missed symptoms, and the fraction of days with a usable frame
Report classifier accuracy on field cases whose cause was named independently (eye-check log or extension service), and how many were 'unclear'

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the hardware, model version and command, (3) why surprises happened (heat wilting, rain, lab-to-field gap), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove (other crops, other diseases, other seasons or gardens).
verify: The write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number names the data (PlantDoc test or field log), the hardware and the command
It explains at least one surprise and lists assumptions and what it does not prove

projects.title: Road-quality mapper
projects.problem: Cyclists want smooth routes
projects.concepts: Phone accelerometer, signal processing, crowd-sourced map
projects.tryIt: Ride your usual routes and rank streets by bumpiness
projects.question: Can phone accelerometer data from ordinary rides rank the streets you ride by bumpiness the way a cyclist would rank them?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and a frozen ground truth
steps.learn: The output is a ranking of street segments, so judge it as a ranking: does the app order streets the way a rider does, and does it give the same order on a repeat ride? The rider's ratings are the ground truth, never the app's own score.

decision.choice: Blind rider ratings of 15 to 30 segments, written before any processing, plus a rank correlation metric
decision.why: Rating every segment on a 1 to 5 scale right after each first ride, before seeing any app output, gives an independent truth. Spearman correlation compares orders, which is what the try-it asks for, and ignores scale differences between phones.

alternatives.name: OSM smoothness tags as truth
alternatives.tradeoff: Independent and free where tagged, but coverage is patchy and the scale targets vehicle types, so use it as a second check, not the main one.

alternatives.name: PVS public dataset only
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible labels (good, regular, bad road), but sensors were on a car's front axle, so it cannot tell you about a bike and phone.

verify: Write the one question and 2 metrics: Spearman vs blind ratings, and Spearman between two rides of the same route
Save the segment list and blind ratings in a dated file that later code only reads
Download one PVS dataset and confirm the good, regular and bad road label columns are present

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before any ride is logged
steps.learn: A GPS trace that starts and ends at the same door reveals where someone lives and when they leave. Crowd data adds risk: one rider on a quiet street is identifiable. Riding safety comes first: the app must never need a tap while moving.

decision.choice: Trim each trip's start and end on the phone, upload only per-segment scores, publish a segment only after several riders
decision.why: Dropping the first and last stretch on-device means home and work never leave the phone. Uploading segment scores instead of raw traces shrinks what a breach can expose. A minimum rider count stops one person's routine showing on the public map.

alternatives.name: Upload raw traces, clean on server
alternatives.tradeoff: Easier to reprocess later, but the server now holds full movement histories that must be protected and deleted.

alternatives.name: Strava-style hide start and end only
alternatives.tradeoff: Familiar to users, but it still uploads the full trace behind the setting.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 module privacy.py: trim_trip(points, trim_m) drops every point within trim_m metres straight-line of the trip start or end (a radius zone, as privacy zones use); publishable(segment_stats, min_riders) returns only segments with at least min_riders distinct rider ids. Tests: a short trip inside the zone returns nothing; no output point lies within trim_m of the original endpoints, including on a loop route; a segment with one rider is withheld.
verify: Run trim_trip on one of your own trips and confirm on a map that your home end is gone
Write the rule that logging starts and stops only before or after riding, never needs a tap while moving, and test it when the logger exists

steps.title: Log accelerometer, speed and GPS together from a mounted phone
steps.learn: Vibration lives in the accelerometer; location and speed come from GPS at a much lower rate. Both need shared timestamps so each window of vibration can be tied to a place and a speed. How the phone is mounted changes what it feels, so fix the mount.

decision.choice: A logger that records accelerationIncludingGravity, GPS fix, speed and accuracy with one clock, handlebar-mounted
decision.why: Keeping gravity in the signal lets you recover the vertical axis later whatever the phone's tilt. A rigid handlebar mount is repeatable across rides; a pocket or bag damps and adds body motion.

alternatives.name: phyphox export for the pilot
alternatives.tradeoff: No code to start and exports common formats, but no trimming or upload logic, so only for your own first rides.

alternatives.name: Dedicated IMU board on the frame
alternatives.tradeoff: Fixed, known sample rate and a rigid frame mount like PVS's MPU-9250 setup (100 Hz), but riders will not install hardware, so no crowd.

steps.delegate: Android app in Kotlin: a foreground service (location type, persistent notification) registers SensorManager TYPE_ACCELEROMETER at the fastest allowed rate and FusedLocationProvider updates; write rows (t_ns, ax, ay, az) and (t_ns, lat, lon, speed, accuracy) to CSV in app storage; start and stop from one button before riding. Tests: timestamps strictly increase; a 60 s stationary log has mean magnitude near 9.8 m/s2; logging continues with the screen off.
verify: Record a 60 s stationary log and report the achieved sample rate and its jitter
Ride one known street with a pothole and find the spike in the raw trace at the right GPS point

steps.title: Recover the vertical axis whatever way the phone is tilted
steps.learn: Bumps mostly push the bike up and down, but the phone's axes are tilted. A low-pass filter of accelerationIncludingGravity estimates the gravity direction; projecting each sample onto it gives vertical acceleration, and subtracting gravity leaves the vibration.

decision.choice: Low-pass gravity estimate, then project onto it to get vertical vibration
decision.why: Works on any phone without trusting the OS sensor fusion, and is easy to test with a tilted phone at rest. Using only the vertical component reduces the effect of braking and turning.

alternatives.name: Total acceleration magnitude
alternatives.tradeoff: No orientation math, but braking, pedalling and turns add energy unrelated to the road.

alternatives.name: OS linear-acceleration sensor
alternatives.tradeoff: Gravity already removed, but behaviour differs by phone and you lose the gravity direction you need for the vertical axis.

steps.delegate: Python with NumPy and SciPy: vertical_vibration(t, ax, ay, az, fs) estimating gravity with a low-pass Butterworth filter applied via sosfiltfilt, projecting acceleration onto the unit gravity vector and subtracting its magnitude. Tests: a synthetic tilted constant-gravity input yields near-zero output; a synthetic vertical sine survives at any tilt with the right amplitude.
verify: Lay the phone at two different tilts on a table and confirm vertical vibration is near zero in both
Plot raw magnitude vs vertical vibration for one ride and point to a turn that only the raw signal reacts to

steps.title: Turn vibration into a per-window roughness score
steps.learn: Roughness is vibration energy in the band where the road, not the rider, dominates. Pedalling and slow body sway sit at low frequency, so high-pass the vertical signal, then take the RMS over short windows. Single huge spikes are potholes, a separate signal from steady roughness.

decision.choice: High-pass filter, RMS per window of fixed distance, plus a separate count of spike events
decision.why: Windows of fixed distance rather than fixed time mean every window covers the same length of road whatever the rider's speed, so segments are compared like for like. Separating spikes from RMS lets the map say both 'rough cobbles' and 'one bad pothole'.

alternatives.name: Band power from a Welch spectrum
alternatives.tradeoff: Lets you pick the band from data, but needs longer windows and more choices to tune.

alternatives.name: Learned classifier trained on PVS labels
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses labelled data, but those labels come from a car, so it may not transfer to a bike and phone.

steps.delegate: Python: roughness(vert, fs, cutoff_hz, dist_m, window_m) applying a Butterworth high-pass with sosfiltfilt, cutting into windows by cumulative distance, returning RMS and a spike count above k times the trip's median absolute deviation. Tests: zero signal gives zero RMS; doubling amplitude doubles RMS; one injected spike counts once and barely moves RMS.
verify: Use Welch spectra of a smooth and a cobbled stretch from your rides to justify the cutoff you chose
Run the feature on PVS and check good, regular and bad road windows are ordered by median RMS

steps.title: Separate road roughness from riding speed
steps.learn: The same street shakes more at higher speed, so a fast rider makes every street look worse. Before comparing streets, model how RMS grows with speed on your own data and remove that trend, or compare only within speed bands.

decision.choice: Fit RMS against speed per rider and device, rank streets on the residual
decision.why: Each rider, bike and phone has its own response, so a per-device fit absorbs tyre pressure and mount differences as well as speed. Ranking on residuals keeps only what the road adds.

alternatives.name: Speed bands only
alternatives.tradeoff: No model to trust, but sparse streets may have no data in the chosen band.

alternatives.name: Ignore speed
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but downhill streets and fast commuters skew the ranking.

steps.delegate: Python: fit_speed_model(rms, speed) with a robust linear fit on log RMS vs log speed (scikit-learn HuberRegressor), residual(rms, speed, model). Drop windows below a minimum speed or with GPS accuracy worse than a threshold. Tests: synthetic data with a known speed law yields near-constant residuals; stopped windows are dropped.
verify: Ride one street twice, slowly and quickly, and report RMS and residual for each pass
Plot RMS against speed for all your windows and state the fitted slope

steps.title: Snap windows onto real street segments
steps.learn: Phone GPS wanders between parallel streets and at junctions. Map matching uses the road graph to pick the most plausible path, so each roughness window lands on one OSM way, the unit you will rank and show.

decision.choice: Self-hosted OSRM match service with the bicycle profile, using GPS accuracy as radiuses and annotations=nodes
decision.why: OSRM's match service takes timestamps and per-point radiuses and can return the OSM node IDs along the matched route, which map to ways. Self-hosting keeps traces off third-party servers.

alternatives.name: Valhalla map matching
alternatives.tradeoff: Also open source with a bicycle costing and a trace_attributes endpoint, but a different config and data build to learn.

alternatives.name: H3 cells instead of streets
alternatives.tradeoff: No matching needed, but a cell mixes parallel streets and junctions, so it cannot rank streets.

steps.delegate: Docker Compose for osrm-backend built from a city OSM extract with the bicycle profile; Python client match_trip(points) calling /match with timestamps, radiuses from GPS accuracy, annotations=nodes, gaps=split; map consecutive node pairs to way ids with an OSMnx graph built with simplify=False from the same extract. Tests: a trace along one street returns that way; a trace with a 2 minute gap is split.
verify: Overlay 3 matched rides on a map and count windows assigned to the wrong parallel street
Report the share of windows that could not be matched and why

steps.title: Merge many rides into one robust score per segment
steps.learn: Each segment collects windows from many rides, riders and phones. A robust summary resists one rider hitting a kerb, and a count of rides tells you how much to trust it. Segments with few rides should say 'not enough data' instead of ranking.

decision.choice: Median residual per segment with a bootstrap interval; rank only segments with enough rides
decision.why: The median ignores occasional outliers, and the bootstrap gives an honest interval without assuming a distribution. A ride minimum stops a single pass deciding a street's rank.

alternatives.name: Mean residual
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses all data, but one bad window from a kerb hop moves it a lot.

alternatives.name: Bayesian shrinkage toward a city prior
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles sparse segments gracefully, but adds a prior to explain and tune.

steps.delegate: Python with pandas: aggregate(windows) grouping by way_id, returning median residual, bootstrap 90% interval, ride count, rider count, spike count per km. Store in SQLite with tables windows, segments. Tests: an injected outlier window does not change the median much; a segment with one ride is flagged insufficient.
verify: List the 5 roughest and 5 smoothest segments with ride counts and intervals
Check which ranked segments have overlapping intervals and say which ranks are not distinguishable

steps.title: Publish a ride-safe map of segment roughness
steps.learn: Cyclists use the map to plan, not while moving. Colour segments by rank bands, grey out ones with too little data, and show the date range of the data so old scores are not trusted after resurfacing.

decision.choice: Static GeoJSON of published segments rebuilt nightly, shown on a Leaflet map with OSM tiles
decision.why: A nightly batch from the aggregate table is simple to cache and contains only segment scores that passed the rider minimum, never traces. OSM-based data needs ODbL attribution.

alternatives.name: Live API per map view
alternatives.tradeoff: Always current, but more server work and more chance of leaking fresh, sparse data.

alternatives.name: Feed scores into a routing profile
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives smooth-route directions directly, but needs a custom OSRM profile and rebuild for every update.

steps.delegate: Python job export_geojson(db, min_riders) writing way geometries with fields rank_band, rides, last_ride_date; a static HTML page using Leaflet that colours by rank_band and greys insufficient segments, with OSM attribution. Tests: the export never contains raw points or rider ids; withheld segments do not appear.
verify: Open the map and confirm no segment near your home or trip ends appears
Grep the exported GeoJSON for rider ids and timestamps finer than a day and find none

steps.title: Test it outside: ride your routes and rank streets
steps.learn: The try-it: ride your usual routes and rank streets by bumpiness. Compare the app's ranking with the blind ratings frozen in step 1, check repeat-ride stability, and remove one stage at a time to see what each adds.
verify: Report Spearman between app ranking and blind ratings, with segment count and a bootstrap interval
Report Spearman between two separate rides of the same route
Ablate speed normalisation and vertical projection; report the Spearman change for each
Where OSM smoothness tags exist, report agreement with them as a second independent check

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the phone, mount and command, (3) why surprises happened (a smooth street scored rough, a downhill skew), (4) assumptions and limits: one city, few riders, one bike type, blind ratings by you.
verify: The write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number names the phone model, mount, ride dates and the command that produced it
It explains at least one surprising segment and states what the results do not prove

projects.title: Privacy-first package watcher
projects.problem: Package theft from doorsteps
projects.concepts: On-device event detection that stores events, not video of people
projects.tryIt: Run it on your own doorstep; measure false alarms
projects.question: Can an on-device doorstep watcher report package arrivals and removals with few false alarms while never storing images of people?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and an independent event log
steps.learn: The try-it measures false alarms on your own doorstep. You also need misses: a quiet watcher has zero false alarms. Ground truth must come from outside the system, such as carrier delivery notices and a household log, never from the watcher's own events.

decision.choice: Two weeks of live running scored against carrier notices plus a household pickup log, kept by someone else
decision.why: Carrier notices and a written log exist without any camera, so they grade the watcher fairly and store no images of people. Tuning on week one and freezing settings for week two keeps the final numbers honest.

alternatives.name: Staged test clips with consenting housemates
alternatives.tradeoff: Repeatable and fast, but staged drops look unlike real couriers; delete clips after labelling.

alternatives.name: Public surveillance video sets
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible, but other cameras and scenes, and they are full of people's images you would be processing.

verify: Write the metrics: false alarms per day, missed arrivals and removals, and alert delay in seconds
Write the rule that week two settings are frozen and record the freeze date
Set up the household log sheet with time, event type and who logged it

steps.title: Privacy and safety check before the camera is mounted
steps.learn: A doorstep camera sees couriers, neighbours, children and the street. The design goal is events, not footage: detect that a person is present and a package changed, keep only that. Many places regulate cameras that capture public areas; the app is a helper, check your local rules.

decision.choice: Frames live only in RAM; people become a count; any saved image is a doormat crop taken with no person present
decision.why: If no frame with a person is ever written to disk or sent off the device, a breach or subpoena cannot reveal one. A doormat-only crop is still useful to confirm a package, and gating it on zero detected people avoids saving a passer-by's legs.

alternatives.name: Save clips with faces blurred
alternatives.tradeoff: More context after a theft, but bodies, clothing and gait still identify people and blur can fail.

alternatives.name: Store no images at all
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest privacy, but you cannot check a doubtful alert yourself.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11 module storage_guard.py: the only function allowed to write images, save_mat_crop(frame, roi, person_count), which raises if person_count is not 0 and writes only the ROI crop. Add a CI grep test failing if any other file calls cv2.imwrite or opens video writers. Tests: a person_count of 1 raises; output size equals the ROI.
verify: Aim the camera and confirm the field of view excludes the street and neighbours' doors as far as possible
Read your local guidance on home cameras and note what applies to you
Write the walk-past test to run once detection works: pass 10 times, list every file on disk, confirm none shows you

steps.title: Choose the device and capture loop
steps.learn: Everything runs on a small computer by the door, so frame rate, resolution and model size trade against power and heat. Packages do not move fast; a few frames per second is enough to catch arrival and removal, and lower rates mean cooler, cheaper hardware.

decision.choice: Raspberry Pi with a Pi camera via Picamera2, low-resolution stream for detection, frames kept in memory
decision.why: Picamera2 is the official Python library for Pi cameras and can give a small stream for analysis without encoding video. Local processing means no cloud service ever sees the doorstep.

alternatives.name: Old Android phone as the camera
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and has a screen and battery, but harder to run unattended and to keep from uploading backups.

alternatives.name: IP camera plus a local NVR
alternatives.tradeoff: Better optics and night vision, but most NVR setups record video by design, which this project avoids.

steps.delegate: Python with picamera2: a capture loop yielding (timestamp, numpy frame) from a low-resolution stream at a configurable rate, with no encoder or file output, and a heartbeat file updated each minute. Tests: a fake camera source drives the loop; the loop never creates image or video files; heartbeat updates.
verify: Run 1 hour and record frames per second achieved, CPU temperature and memory use
List the files the process wrote and confirm only logs and the heartbeat exist

steps.title: Define the doormat zone and a cheap motion gate
steps.learn: Most frames show nothing new. A cheap pixel-difference check on a downscaled frame can wake the detector only when something changes, saving power. A fixed doormat region (ROI) narrows where package changes count, so the street and passing cars are ignored.

decision.choice: Frame differencing on a blurred, downscaled image to wake detection; one hand-drawn doormat ROI
decision.why: Differencing is fast and has few knobs. Doorstep scenes have sun, shadows and leaves, so the gate only wakes the detector and never raises an alert itself.

alternatives.name: OpenCV MOG2 background subtractor
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to slow lighting change, but a package left long enough gets absorbed into the background.

alternatives.name: Run the detector on every frame
alternatives.tradeoff: No missed wakes, but more heat and power for no benefit on an empty step.

steps.delegate: Python with OpenCV and NumPy: motion_score(prev, cur) on grayscale, blurred, downscaled frames returning the changed-pixel fraction; a config file with ROI polygon; a gate with a threshold and a minimum wake duration. Tests: identical frames score 0; a synthetic box pasted inside the ROI wakes the gate; a global brightness shift alone scores low after normalisation.
verify: Log gate wake-ups for one day and report how many happened with nobody there
Check the ROI covers the full mat when a large box is placed at its edge

steps.title: Detect and count people on device, then forget them
steps.learn: People matter only as context: a package that disappears while a person is present is a removal, and package checks must wait until the mat is not occluded. A COCO-trained detector restricted to the person class gives a count per frame; nothing else about the person is kept.

decision.choice: MediaPipe Object Detector with EfficientDet-Lite0 int8, category allowlist ['person'], tuned score threshold
decision.why: EfficientDet-Lite0 is MediaPipe's recommended balance of speed and accuracy, trained on COCO which includes a person class. The allowlist and score_threshold options keep only confident person detections, reduced to a count.

alternatives.name: EfficientDet-Lite2
alternatives.tradeoff: More accurate per MediaPipe's docs, but slower and more memory on a Pi.

alternatives.name: Face detection instead of person detection
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller model, but couriers facing away or masked are missed.

steps.delegate: Python with mediapipe Tasks: person_count(frame) using ObjectDetector with EfficientDet-Lite0 int8, category_allowlist ['person'], configurable score_threshold; returns an int only. Tests: a public COCO image with people returns at least 1; an empty doorstep frame returns 0; the function's return type is int and no frame is stored.
verify: Walk through the scene 10 times in day and dusk light and record how many passes were counted
Measure detection time per frame on the device

steps.title: Decide whether a package is on the mat
steps.learn: COCO has no cardboard-box class, so a stock detector will not find packages. With a fixed camera, compare the ROI to a reference of the empty mat: a large, lasting difference means something was left. Only compare when no person is in frame, so a leg is not a package.

decision.choice: SSIM between the current ROI and a rolling empty-mat reference, updated only when the state is empty
decision.why: A fixed camera makes change detection a good fit and needs no training data. structural_similarity in scikit-image is less sensitive to overall brightness than raw pixel difference, and updating the reference only when empty stops a package fading into it.

alternatives.name: OWLv2 open-vocabulary detection ('a cardboard box')
alternatives.tradeoff: Recognises boxes anywhere with no training, but a heavy model for a Pi; run it only to confirm.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune a small detector on your mat
alternatives.tradeoff: Best accuracy for your scene, but you must label many images and repeat it if the mat changes.

steps.delegate: Python with scikit-image and OpenCV: package_score(roi, ref) returning 1 minus SSIM on grayscale crops; RefManager that updates ref by blending only when state is EMPTY and person_count is 0. Tests: identical crops score near 0; a pasted box scores high; a uniform brightness change scores lower than the box; ref never updates while state is OCCUPIED.
verify: Place 5 different packages (small envelope to large box) and record the score for each
Record the empty-mat score at morning, noon, dusk and night to see the lighting noise floor

steps.title: Turn noisy frames into arrival and removal events
steps.learn: Single frames flicker. A small state machine (EMPTY, ARRIVING, OCCUPIED, REMOVING) with hysteresis and minimum durations turns scores into events. Note who was present only as a count: a removal with a person present is the theft-relevant case, but the watcher cannot tell owner from thief.

decision.choice: Explicit state machine with separate on and off thresholds, dwell times, and household snooze from a phone
decision.why: Two thresholds stop flicker near the boundary, and dwell times ignore a shadow passing. No face recognition means it cannot know who took a package, so a snooze while you are home is the honest way to cut removal alerts.

alternatives.name: Alert on any change
alternatives.tradeoff: Never misses, but every shadow and cat becomes a false alarm.

alternatives.name: Recognise household faces
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer alerts on your own pickups, but needs storing face templates, against this project's goal.

steps.delegate: Python: Watcher class consuming (t, person_count, package_score) and emitting events {t, type: arrived|removed, persons_present: bool}; thresholds and dwell times from config; snooze flag. Tests with scripted sequences: brief score spikes emit nothing; a sustained rise emits one arrived; removal with persons emits one removed; snoozed removals are logged but not alerted.
verify: Replay a logged day of scores through the Watcher and count events vs your household log
Try 3 different dwell times on week one only and record false alarms and misses for each

steps.title: Store events, not video, and send alerts locally
steps.learn: The stored record is a row: time, event type, whether people were present, scores, and an optional empty-mat crop. Alerts go out as short text. Events must survive power cuts, and alerts must not be lost when the network blips.

decision.choice: SQLite in WAL mode for events, self-hosted ntfy for push alerts with a retry queue
decision.why: SQLite with WAL is durable and needs no server on a Pi. ntfy can be self-hosted and publishes from a simple HTTP request, so alert text stays inside your network and phone.

alternatives.name: MQTT into a home automation hub
alternatives.tradeoff: Fits an existing smart home, but another broker to run and secure.

alternatives.name: Hosted ntfy.sh or email
alternatives.tradeoff: No server to run, but alert text passes through a third party.

steps.delegate: Python: events.db in SQLite with PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL, table events(id, t, type, persons_present, score, crop_path NULL); notifier posting to a configured ntfy topic URL with exponential backoff from an outbox table. Tests: a killed process loses no committed event; network failure leaves alerts in the outbox and they send on recovery.
verify: Pull the power during a test arrival and confirm the event is in the database after reboot
Inspect the database and the crop folder and confirm no image contains a person

steps.title: Handle night, weather and a dead camera
steps.learn: Night, rain on the lens and low sun break both the detector and the change score. A watcher that silently dies looks the same as a quiet day. Report health as an event too, and lower confidence instead of guessing.

decision.choice: Health events for camera loss and stale heartbeat, plus a low-light mode that marks events uncertain
decision.why: An external check that alerts when the heartbeat stops catches crashes the watcher cannot report itself. Marking low-light events uncertain is more honest than hiding them or treating them as certain.

alternatives.name: IR-sensitive camera with an IR light
alternatives.tradeoff: Real night coverage, but grayscale images change the SSIM noise floor and the detector's accuracy.

alternatives.name: Pause detection at night
alternatives.tradeoff: No night false alarms, but late deliveries go unreported.

steps.delegate: Python: a systemd service with Restart=on-failure for the watcher, a separate timer job that alerts via ntfy if the heartbeat file is older than N minutes, and a brightness check that sets an uncertain flag on events. Tests: an old heartbeat triggers one alert; a dark synthetic frame sets the flag.
verify: Unplug the camera and time how long until you get a health alert
Report false alarms per night vs per day from week one

steps.title: Test it outside: run it on your doorstep for two weeks
steps.learn: The try-it: run it on your own doorstep and measure false alarms. Use week two with frozen settings, scored against carrier notices and the household log, so the watcher never grades itself.
verify: Report false alarms per day, missed arrivals and missed removals for week two, with counts of true events
Report median and worst alert delay from the logged event time
Ablate the person gate on package checks using replayed scores and report the change in false alarms
Confirm, by listing all files, that no image with a person was stored during the two weeks

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the device, camera and command, (3) why surprises happened (shadows, a dark parcel on a dark mat), (4) assumptions and limits: one doorstep, two weeks, it cannot tell owner from thief.
verify: The write-up states the one question in one sentence
Every number names the device, camera, dates and the command or replay that produced it
It explains at least one surprising false alarm or miss and states what the results do not prove

projects.title: Honor-system snack shelf
projects.problem: Club snack shelves lose money
projects.concepts: On-device product recognition, retrieval over a product catalog, tallying
projects.tryIt: Pilot it at a club room or office kitchen
projects.question: Can an on-device camera kiosk recognize each snack taken from an honor-system shelf well enough that the tally matches the stock count?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the test sets
steps.learn: Question: can a tablet at the shelf recognize each snack a person takes well enough that the tally matches the stock count? Metrics: top-1 recognition accuracy, and per-product tally error vs a manual count. Public benchmark: Grocery Store Dataset (one iconic image per class as the catalog, natural photos as queries).
verify: README states the question, both metrics and the pass bar, written before any code
Freeze the Grocery Store test.txt split as the public test set; never tune on it
Photograph each club product on 2 separate days and lightings: freeze one set as the club test set (record sha256), keep the other as validation

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The camera faces people. Recognize products, never people: no faces stored, no per-person tracking, and the tally is anonymous. Snack info from Open Food Facts may be incomplete or outdated, so allergens must be read on the package itself.

decision.choice: Frames kept in memory only; on-device face check before any saved image; no accounts; allergen note
decision.why: Not storing frames removes most risk at once. If you keep failure photos to improve the catalog, a face check (MediaPipe Face Detector) on the device ensures none with a face is saved.

alternatives.name: Store all frames for debugging
alternatives.tradeoff: Helps fix recognition, but stores bystanders' faces and turns the shelf into surveillance.

alternatives.name: Per-person accounts for payment
alternatives.tradeoff: Enables billing, but ties every snack to a person, which the honor system does not need.

steps.delegate: Ensure no camera frame is written to disk by default. Optional 'save failed crop' runs MediaPipe Face Detector on the crop first and discards it if any face is found. Events table has no user field. Add a visible sign text and an in-app line: 'Allergen info: always check the package label.' Tests: a crop with a face is never saved; app storage contains no images after a session.
verify: After 20 test purchases, list app storage and confirm there are no saved frames
Save-failed-crop with a face in view 10 times; confirm none is stored
A notice at the shelf says what the camera does and does not keep

steps.title: Choose how a purchase is captured
steps.learn: An honor shelf loses money when people forget, misremember, or skip paying. The capture design decides how much the camera must see: a person showing the item on purpose, or a camera watching the shelf and inferring what left.

decision.choice: Kiosk flow: the person holds the item up to the tablet camera, confirms on screen, and the item is tallied
decision.why: Recognition runs on a deliberate, centered view of one item, which is far easier than watching a shelf, and the camera never needs to watch people. Confirmation catches mistakes before they reach the tally.

alternatives.name: Passive shelf camera with before/after change detection
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra step for people, but needs alignment, occlusion handling, and a camera pointed at everyone who walks by.

alternatives.name: Weight-sensing shelf (load cells)
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate counts for distinct-weight items, but needs hardware per shelf and confuses items of similar weight.

verify: Write the flow as 4 screens or fewer and time a dry run with a friend: under 15 seconds per item is the target you record
List which failure (forgetting, misrecognition, deliberate skipping) each design addresses

steps.title: Build the product catalog with reference photos
steps.learn: Retrieval is only as good as the catalog. Each product needs an id, the barcode, name, price, and several reference photos (front, back, angled, in hand). Open Food Facts can fill names and ingredients by barcode; the club sets prices.

decision.choice: Own reference photos (5 to 10 per product) plus Open Food Facts metadata looked up by barcode
decision.why: Photos taken with the kiosk camera in the club room match test conditions far better than studio images. Barcode lookup avoids typing product details and gives a stable key for each product.

alternatives.name: Open Food Facts images only
alternatives.tradeoff: No photo work, but images vary in quality and angle and some products have none.

alternatives.name: Manual entry without barcodes
alternatives.tradeoff: Works for unlabeled items like fruit, but names drift and duplicates creep in.

steps.delegate: In Python, write catalog.py: a SQLite table products(id, barcode, name, price_cents, active) and photos(product_id, path). add_product(barcode) fetches https://world.openfoodfacts.org/api/v2/product/{barcode}.json with a custom User-Agent 'SnackShelf/0.1 (contact)' and stores the name; prices are entered by hand. Tests: unknown barcode creates a product with an empty name for manual fill; duplicate barcode is rejected.
verify: Every product on the shelf has a row, a price and at least 5 reference photos
Spot-check 5 Open Food Facts names against the package and fix mismatches

steps.title: Recognize products by nearest neighbor over catalog embeddings
steps.learn: Embed every reference photo once; at purchase time embed the camera crop and return the product whose photos are most similar by cosine similarity. Adding a product means adding photos, with no retraining. Benchmark the approach on the Grocery Store Dataset before using club data.

decision.choice: MediaPipe Image Embedder (MobileNet V3) with cosine similarity, max over each product's photos
decision.why: It runs on Android, web and Python with the same model, so the Python benchmark matches the tablet. A small catalog of club snacks can be searched exactly, no ANN index needed.

alternatives.name: DINOv2 or CLIP embeddings
alternatives.tradeoff: Stronger general features, but heavier models that may be slow on a cheap tablet; worth it if MobileNet accuracy falls short.

alternatives.name: Fine-tuned classifier
alternatives.tradeoff: Can be most accurate on a fixed set, but every new product needs retraining and enough labeled photos.

steps.delegate: In Python, write recognize.py using mediapipe ImageEmbedder (image mode) and ImageEmbedder.cosine_similarity. build_index(catalog) embeds all photos; predict(img) returns top-3 (product_id, score). eval.py runs Grocery Store: iconic images as catalog, test.txt images as queries, prints top-1 and top-3 accuracy. Tests: an image from the catalog returns its own product first.
verify: Report top-1 and top-3 accuracy on the Grocery Store test split (fine-grained labels)
Report top-1 and top-3 on the frozen club test set, using only the club catalog photos

steps.title: Get a clean crop of the item
steps.learn: The embedding sees the whole frame unless you crop: hands, background and other shelf items dilute it. A guide box on screen gives a fixed crop for free; a detector finds the item wherever it is held.

decision.choice: On-screen guide box with a fixed center crop; add a detector only if accuracy on the club test set demands it
decision.why: In the kiosk flow the person is already aiming the item, so a fixed crop is reliable and adds no model. It keeps latency and failure modes small on a low-end tablet.

alternatives.name: Object detector crop (for example MediaPipe Object Detector)
alternatives.tradeoff: Robust to sloppy aiming, but adds a model, and generic detectors may not box unusual packages.

alternatives.name: Whole frame, no crop
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero work, but background and hands push similarity toward the wrong product.

steps.delegate: Add a crop(frame, box) helper used by both the eval and the app, with the guide box as a fraction of the frame. Re-run eval on the club test set with crop vs whole frame and print both accuracies. Test: crop output size is fixed and matches the model's expected input after resizing.
verify: Record club test top-1 with the guide crop vs the whole frame
Try 10 sloppy aims on purpose and count how many still match top-1

steps.title: Abstain when unsure and let people confirm
steps.learn: The catalog is closed but the world is open: people show phones, wrappers, or new snacks. Use the gap between the best and second-best score and an absolute floor. Below threshold, show top-3 and a barcode fallback instead of guessing.

decision.choice: Confident: one-tap confirm of top-1; else top-3 plus barcode scan (ML Kit); thresholds tuned on validation
decision.why: A wrong silent tally corrupts the books, while one extra tap costs little. Barcodes are exact when present, so they make a cheap fallback that does not depend on the embedder.

alternatives.name: Always auto-tally top-1
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest flow, but every misrecognition becomes a wrong charge.

alternatives.name: Barcode scanning only
alternatives.tradeoff: Exact and simple, but slower to aim and fails on loose items without barcodes.
