steps.delegate: Add decide(scores) returning AUTO, CHOOSE or UNKNOWN from top-1 score and top-1 minus top-2 margin. Tune thresholds on a validation split of club photos (not the frozen test set) to hit a target wrong-auto rate. Add ML Kit barcode scanning (EAN-13, UPC-A) mapped through the catalog barcode column. Tests: non-product photos land in UNKNOWN in most cases; barcode path returns the right product.
verify: On the frozen club test set, record the wrong-auto rate and the share of items needing a tap
Show 20 non-product objects and count how many are auto-tallied (target zero)

steps.title: Run it on the tablet, offline
steps.learn: The club room may have weak Wi-Fi and the camera should never stream anywhere. Running the embedder on the tablet keeps frames local and works offline. Catalog embeddings are computed once and stored; only the query is embedded live.

decision.choice: Android app with MediaPipe Image Embedder in live stream mode and catalog embeddings cached in SQLite
decision.why: Same model as the benchmark, no server, no frames leaving the device. A cheap Android tablet mounted at the shelf is easy for a club to buy and lock in kiosk mode.

alternatives.name: Web app with MediaPipe for web
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs on any device with a browser, but camera permissions and kiosk lock are less reliable.

alternatives.name: Server-side recognition
alternatives.tradeoff: Bigger models possible, but frames leave the device and the shelf stops working when the network does.

steps.delegate: Build an Android (Kotlin) app: CameraX preview with the guide box, MediaPipe ImageEmbedder in LIVE_STREAM mode, cached catalog embeddings loaded from SQLite at start, cosine top-3 in memory, decide() logic from the previous step. Frames are never written to disk. Tests: instrumented test that recognizes 3 bundled catalog images; airplane mode run still works.
verify: Measure time from tap to result on the actual tablet over 30 tries; record p50 and worst
Run in airplane mode for a full purchase and confirm the tally is recorded

steps.title: Keep an append-only tally and reconcile with stock counts
steps.learn: The tally is money, so it must be auditable: every event (product, price at the time, how it was recognized, timestamp) is appended, never edited; corrections are new events. Reconcile per product: previous count plus units restocked minus current count gives units taken, which should equal units tallied.

decision.choice: Append-only SQLite event log with correction events; weekly restock and count entered in the app
decision.why: An append-only log makes every number traceable and lets you separate recognition errors from unpaid items during reconciliation. SQLite is local, durable and easy to export.

alternatives.name: Running counters only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but you cannot tell why a count is off or undo a mistaken tap.

alternatives.name: Cloud spreadsheet
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy for treasurers to read, but needs network and puts purchase logs outside the device.

steps.delegate: Add tables events(id, ts, product_id, price_cents, method AUTO|CHOOSE|BARCODE, corrects_event_id NULL) and stock(ts, product_id, restocked, counted). reconcile(from, to) returns per product: restocked, sold_by_count, tallied, gap, gap_value. Export CSV. Tests: a correction event cancels the original in totals; gap math on a hand-built week matches expected.
verify: Hand-build one week of events and counts and confirm reconcile output matches your own calculation
Confirm no code path updates or deletes an existing event row

steps.title: Pilot it in a club room or office kitchen
steps.learn: The pilot answers the question with real use: does the tally match the stock count, and do people use it? Run a baseline period on the old honor box first, then the kiosk, with the same restock and count routine.
verify: Run 2 weeks of baseline and 2 weeks of kiosk; record per-product gap and gap value for each period
Estimate top-1 by hand-checking a random sample of 50 logged events against what was taken (supervised session); report tap and UNKNOWN rates from the log
Log every misrecognition reported by users and classify its cause (lighting, new product, aim)

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Report whether the kiosk closed the gap and why. Separate recognition errors from people skipping the kiosk, using the event log and counts. Be clear that a small pilot in one room does not generalize to every shelf.
verify: Part 1 states the one question and the pass bar
Part 2 gives benchmark and pilot numbers with the device, model and command or app version for each
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result, such as which products were confused and why
Part 4 lists assumptions (one room, honest confirmations, counting errors) and what this does not prove

projects.title: Your first open-source contribution, start to finish
projects.question: How do I go from never having touched a repo I use to a reviewed pull request that maintainers take seriously?

steps.title: Set the goal: one reviewed PR under the repo's own rules
steps.learn: Success is a PR that passes CI and gets a maintainer review; a merge is the goal but depends on them. Every repo sets its own rules: CONTRIBUTING, code of conduct, a CLA (Kubernetes) or DCO sign-off (vLLM), sometimes an AI-assisted contribution policy, and a place maintainers talk.
verify: You can name the files where your candidate repos keep CONTRIBUTING, code of conduct and PR template
You know whether each candidate needs a CLA signature, a DCO Signed-off-by line, or neither
You found whether each candidate has a written policy on AI-assisted contributions

links.label: How to Contribute to Open Source

steps.title: Choose a repo you use that actually merges outside PRs
steps.learn: Pick from tools you already run, then check health: recent commits, how fast outside PRs get a first review, whether newcomer labels exist and have open issues (labels differ: rust-lang/rust uses E-easy, Kubernetes uses good first issue), and a license you can accept.

decision.choice: A mid-sized, active library you use daily, with a live newcomer label and reviews on outside PRs within weeks
decision.why: You already know its behavior from the user side, so bugs and docs gaps are visible to you. Mid-sized means a maintainer can actually review you, and an active newcomer label means they have set aside work for people like you.

alternatives.name: A flagship project (Kubernetes, PyTorch, Rust)
alternatives.tradeoff: Great mentoring and labels, but heavy process (CLA, bots, large CI) and many competing newcomers per easy issue.

alternatives.name: A small single-maintainer tool
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to understand, but reviews depend on one person's free time and the project may go quiet.

alternatives.name: A mailing-list project (Linux kernel)
alternatives.tradeoff: Deep learning payoff, but patches go by email with Signed-off-by and strict style; a steep first contribution.

verify: You listed 3 candidate repos with last commit date, open newcomer issues, and median time to first review on recent outside PRs
Your chosen repo's newcomer label exists in its label list and has open, unassigned issues
You read the chosen repo's LICENSE and know if it needs a CLA or DCO

steps.title: Build the chosen repo from source and run its tests
steps.learn: Follow the repo's own developer docs, not the user install guide. Note the exact toolchain versions CI uses (look in its workflow files) and run the fast test subset first. A clean baseline run tells you which failures are yours later.

decision.choice: The repo's documented developer setup (editable install or its build script) on the OS that CI uses
decision.why: Matching CI's setup means a passing local run predicts a passing CI run, and an editable install lets you edit and rerun without reinstalling.

alternatives.name: The repo's dev container or Docker image
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to CI with least setup, but slower file I/O on some hosts and harder to debug with local tools.

alternatives.name: Full source build with all optional parts
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed if you touch compiled code, but builds can take a long time and need specific compilers or GPUs.

steps.delegate: Read this repo's CONTRIBUTING and CI workflow files and write a setup script for my OS that installs the exact toolchain versions CI uses, does the documented developer install, and runs the fastest test subset. Print the commands before running them. Do not change any repo files.
verify: The fast test subset passes on an unmodified checkout, and you saved the command and its runtime
You recorded tool versions (language, compiler, package manager) and they match a CI job
You can make a one-line local edit and see it take effect without reinstalling

steps.title: Trace one user-facing operation through the source tree
steps.learn: Pick one thing you do as a user (a CLI command, an API call) and follow it from entry point to where the work happens, writing down each file and function. Use code search, a debugger breakpoint or a stack trace to confirm the path rather than guessing from names.
steps.delegate: Help me trace how <operation> runs in this repo. Starting from the entry point, list each file and function on the path in call order with one line on what it does, and cite file paths. Then give me a breakpoint location to confirm it. Do not edit code.
verify: You wrote a call path of at least 5 real files and functions for one operation
You confirmed the path with a breakpoint or stack trace, not just reading
You can point to the test directory that covers that path

steps.title: Learn one subsystem's core idea and commit to it
steps.learn: Contributions land faster when you know one area well: its design doc or paper, its invariants, its tests, and who reviews it (CODEOWNERS or recent reviewers). Read recent merged PRs in that area to learn what reviewers ask for.

decision.choice: The subsystem on your traced path that has open newcomer issues and an active reviewer
decision.why: You already read its code in the trace, so the ramp is shortest, and an active reviewer means your PR will not sit unread.

alternatives.name: The core or hottest subsystem
alternatives.tradeoff: Most impact and learning, but changes there get the strictest review and newcomer PRs often stall.

alternatives.name: Tooling, docs or tests infrastructure
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to land and appreciated, but teaches less about the project's main ideas.

verify: You can explain the subsystem's main invariant in 2 sentences without notes
You read 3 recently merged PRs in that area and listed what reviewers asked to change
You know who reviews this area (CODEOWNERS or recent review history)

steps.title: Land a small docs, test or example change first
steps.learn: A small first PR teaches the mechanics (fork, branch, CLA or sign-off, CI, bots) with little at stake. Some repos reject trivial one-line PRs, so check the policy: a missing test or a docs fix that a real user hit is usually welcome.

decision.choice: Add a missing test or fix a docs gap you hit yourself while building or tracing
decision.why: It is real value the maintainers can verify quickly, it exercises the full PR workflow, and it shows you read the code.

alternatives.name: A typo or formatting fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but several projects treat these as noise or forbid one-off tiny PRs.

alternatives.name: A new example
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful for users, but examples need upkeep, so maintainers may push back on adding more.

steps.delegate: In this repo, write a test for <function> covering <edge case>, following the existing test file layout and naming in <test dir>. Use the repo's test framework and fixtures, keep it fast, and show me the command to run only this test.
verify: Your branch is off an up-to-date default branch in your fork, with commits signed off if the repo requires DCO
The new test fails if you break the code it covers and passes when you restore it
The PR follows the template and CI is green or every red check is explained

links.label: Creating a PR from a fork

steps.title: Pick an open bug and reproduce it with a failing test
steps.learn: Good picks: the newcomer or bug label, recent activity, nobody assigned, and no open PR already linked. Comment before starting. Shrink the report to a minimal reproducible example, then turn it into a failing test in the repo's own test layout.

decision.choice: A labeled, unassigned bug from the last few months in your subsystem, reproduced as a failing test
decision.why: Recent bugs still apply to the current code, a failing test proves the bug and becomes the regression test, and it is in the area you already know.

alternatives.name: An old, highly upvoted bug
alternatives.tradeoff: Clearly wanted, but often old because it is hard or blocked on a design decision.

alternatives.name: A bug you found yourself
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong motivation, but open an issue first so maintainers can confirm it is a bug before you fix it.

verify: You searched open PRs and issue comments and found nobody already working on it
Your minimal example is under 30 lines and fails on the current default branch
The failing test is in the right test directory and fails for the reason the issue describes

steps.title: Fix the bug with the smallest diff that passes the test
steps.learn: Fix the root cause, not the symptom, and touch as little as possible. If you use a coding agent, follow the repo's AI policy (some require disclosure or ban AI PRs) and understand every line, since you must defend it in review.
steps.delegate: Fix <issue summary> in this repo. First run my failing test <path::name> and confirm it fails. Then make the smallest change that fixes the root cause, following the repo's style, linters and test layout. Do not reformat unrelated code. Explain each changed line and why the old code was wrong.
verify: The failing test now passes and the rest of the relevant test subset still passes
You can explain every changed line and the root cause without the agent's notes
The diff touches only files needed for the fix and its test

steps.title: Run the repo's linters, hooks and CI test subset locally
steps.learn: CI is the first reviewer. Find what it runs (workflow files, pre-commit config, Makefile targets) and run the same commands locally. Learn which tests are slow or flaky so you can tell a real failure from noise.
verify: Every formatter and linter CI runs passes locally on your branch
You ran the test subset CI runs for your changed files and saved the command
Any failure you could not fix is explained with evidence it also fails on the default branch

steps.title: Open the PR and work through review to a decision
steps.learn: Fill the PR template, link the issue, state what you tested and how. Reply to every comment, push fixes as new commits unless asked to squash, and rebase when the base moves. If it stalls, ping politely after a week or two or ask in the project's chat.

decision.choice: Open as ready for review once CI passes locally, with a short description and test evidence
decision.why: Reviewers prioritize PRs that are complete and small, and evidence up front saves a round trip.

alternatives.name: Open as a draft early
alternatives.tradeoff: Gets direction on the approach sooner, but some maintainers ignore drafts until marked ready.

alternatives.name: Discuss the design in the issue first
alternatives.tradeoff: Best for larger changes, but adds a wait before any code is reviewed.

verify: The PR description links the issue, says what changed and lists the test commands you ran
Every review comment has a reply or a commit that addresses it
The branch is rebased on the current default branch and CI is green

links.label: Google eng practices: the CL author's guide

steps.title: Write up the contribution and pick the next rung
steps.learn: Record what you learned about the codebase and the process, with links and numbers (time to first review, rounds of review, CI time). Next rungs: a larger bug, a small feature, a performance PR with benchmark evidence, or reviewing other people's PRs.
verify: The write-up links your PR and states its outcome (merged, in review, or closed and why)
It includes numbers: days to first review, review rounds, and test commands run
It names one concrete next contribution in the same repo and why

projects.problem: A repeatable arc for contributing to any project you already depend on: pick well, build, read, reproduce, fix, pass CI, survive review.
projects.proveIt: A PR to a repo you use that passes CI and gets maintainer review (merge if they accept it), plus a short write-up.
projects.license: Varies by repo (read its LICENSE file)
projects.hardware: Depends on the repo; many libraries build on a laptop, GPU or kernel projects need matching hardware

projects.title: verl
projects.question: How do I land a reviewed PR in verl, the HybridFlow RL post-training library, and understand the PPO/GRPO loop I changed?

steps.title: Set the goal and read verl's contribution and AI rules
steps.learn: The repo moved to verl-project/verl. Target: the PPO/GRPO algorithm layer under verl/trainer/ppo. Read CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md (binding for AI-assisted work). PRs need a signed CLA (CLA Assistant, license/cla check); there is no DCO check and no root code of conduct file. Maintainers talk on Slack.
verify: You read AGENTS.md and can state its duplicate check, busywork and disclosure rules
You joined the verl Slack from the README and found the ci-request channel the PR template names
You confirmed the Apache-2.0 LICENSE and read the verl CLA on cla-assistant.io that the license/cla check asks you to sign

steps.title: Set up verl with uv and run the CPU unit tests
steps.learn: verl's environment comes from one uv.lock; you pick extras such as vllm or sglang plus fsdp, megatron or veomni, or cpu alone for GPU-free checks. The uv workflow targets Linux with Python 3.12. CI runs CPU tests as uv run --frozen --all-packages --extra cpu pytest on files named *_on_cpu.py.

decision.choice: uv with the cpu extra for tests, matching cpu_unit_tests.yml
decision.why: The algorithm layer is tested by *_on_cpu.py files, so you can iterate on any Linux machine with the same lockfile and command CI uses, no GPU needed.

alternatives.name: pip install -e .[test,vllm] (CONTRIBUTING)
alternatives.tradeoff: The documented Python-only path, but it does not use the lockfile, so versions can drift from CI.

alternatives.name: The docker/Dockerfile.uv.cu130 image
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for GPU runs and e2e training with all backends, but a large build and requires an NVIDIA GPU host.

steps.delegate: On Linux with uv installed, in a fresh verl clone, write a script that installs pre-commit and hydra-core, runs pre-commit install, then runs the CPU tests in tests/trainer/ppo the way .github/workflows/cpu_unit_tests.yml does (a pytest.ini with python_files = *_on_cpu.py and uv run --frozen --all-packages --extra cpu). Print each command first.
verify: tests/trainer/ppo CPU tests pass on an unmodified checkout and you saved the command and runtime
You can name which extras you used and confirm uv.lock was not modified
pre-commit run --all-files on a clean checkout passes

steps.title: Trace one PPO step from main_ppo.py to update_actor
steps.learn: verl/trainer/main_ppo.py loads ppo_trainer.yaml via Hydra; with trainer.use_v1 (default true) it runs TaskRunnerV1 and PPOTrainerSync on Ray. PPOTrainer._step_once (ppo/v1/trainer_base.py) does gen, reward, old_log_prob, ref, values, adv, update_critic, update_actor; data moves via TransferQueue as KVBatchMeta.
steps.delegate: In verl-project/verl, starting at verl/trainer/main_ppo.py with the default trainer.use_v1=true, list in call order the functions one training step goes through in PPOTrainer.fit and _step_once (verl/trainer/ppo/v1/trainer_base.py), with file paths. For each worker call, name the worker class in verl/workers and how RayWorkerGroup in verl/single_controller/ray/base.py dispatches it. Do not edit code.
verify: You wrote the step path with real file paths for rollout, reward, log prob, advantage and actor update
You found where timing_raw stage names like update_actor are recorded in _step_once in ppo/v1/trainer_base.py
You can explain what runs on the driver vs on Ray workers in one step

steps.title: Read HybridFlow and GRPO, then choose the algorithm layer
steps.learn: HybridFlow pairs a single controller that writes the RL dataflow with multi-controller workers that run training and generation. GRPO drops the critic and normalizes rewards within a group of samples per prompt. In core_algos.py, estimators register with @register_adv_est and policy losses with register_policy_loss.

decision.choice: The algorithm layer: verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py and its CPU tests in tests/trainer/ppo
decision.why: It is pure tensor math you can test on CPU, it maps directly to the papers, and its tests already show the expected style, so you can reproduce and fix bugs without a GPU cluster.

alternatives.name: Rollout backends (verl/workers/rollout)
alternatives.tradeoff: High impact (vllm_rollout, sglang_rollout), but needs GPUs and tracks fast-moving engine versions.

alternatives.name: Training engines (FSDP, Megatron)
alternatives.tradeoff: Core to scale, but bugs often need multi-GPU repros and deep parallelism knowledge.

alternatives.name: Reward functions (verl/utils/reward_score)
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to read and test, but narrower; good if you care about a specific dataset's scoring.

verify: You can explain the group-relative advantage in compute_grpo_outcome_advantage in 3 sentences
You listed the advantage estimators registered in core_algos.py
You named the test file that covers the function you plan to touch

steps.title: Add a missing CPU test for an advantage estimator
steps.learn: AGENTS.md forbids one-off tiny PRs such as a single typo, so a first rung must carry real value. Tests named *_on_cpu.py run in cpu_unit_tests.yml; validate-structure in pre-commit checks the tests layout. Find an estimator or edge case (ties, a group of size 1, masked tokens) no test covers.

decision.choice: A new *_on_cpu.py test in tests/trainer/ppo covering an untested estimator edge case
decision.why: It adds coverage maintainers value, runs in CPU CI, teaches you the estimator API, and fits the AGENTS.md bar for substantive work.

alternatives.name: A docs fix for an algorithm page
alternatives.tradeoff: Welcome if it fixes a real gap users hit, but docs hooks (check-docs-time-info) apply and tiny edits may be rejected as busywork.

alternatives.name: A new example script
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows usage, but needs GPUs to run and must pass check-example-naming; maintainers may not want more examples.

steps.delegate: In verl-project/verl, add tests/trainer/ppo/test_<name>_on_cpu.py testing <estimator> from verl/trainer/ppo/core_algos.py for <edge case>. Follow the style of test_core_algos_on_cpu.py, use small hand-computed tensors with expected values, and start the file with a copyright line from the list in tests/special_sanity/check_license.py plus the Apache-2.0 header. Show the pytest command to run only this file.
verify: The test passes, and fails if you perturb the estimator's normalization
Your hand-computed expected values match a manual calculation you did on paper
pre-commit run --all-files passes, including check-license and validate-structure

steps.title: Pick a verl bug and reproduce it as a failing CPU test
steps.learn: Useful labels that exist: good first issue, call for contribution, bug, help wanted, plus area labels like rollout, fsdp, megatron. Run the AGENTS.md duplicate checks (gh issue view and gh pr list searches) before starting. Reduce the report to a DataProto or tensor input that triggers the bug.

decision.choice: A recent bug or call for contribution issue in the algorithm or reward code, unassigned and without a linked PR
decision.why: These reproduce on CPU, so your failing test can run in cpu_unit_tests.yml, and recent issues still match main.

alternatives.name: A rollout or engine bug
alternatives.tradeoff: Often higher impact, but needs a GPU repro and may depend on a specific vLLM or SGLang version.

alternatives.name: An RFC or roadmap item
alternatives.tradeoff: Larger scope and visibility, but needs design agreement with maintainers first.

verify: You ran the three AGENTS.md duplicate-work commands and found no open PR for the issue
Your minimal input reproduces the bug on current main in a *_on_cpu.py test
You commented on the issue with the repro before writing the fix

steps.title: Fix the bug in core_algos with a test-first agent prompt
steps.learn: AGENTS.md requires that you review every changed line, run the relevant tests, and add attribution trailers such as Co-authored-by for AI tools. Keep the fix minimal and in the layer where the bug lives; if a config field changes, the generated trainer YAMLs must be regenerated.
steps.delegate: Follow AGENTS.md in verl-project/verl. First run my failing test <path> with the cpu extra and confirm it fails. Fix the root cause in <file> with the smallest change, keep ruff and mypy clean, and do not touch unrelated code. If you change a config dataclass or YAML, run scripts/generate_trainer_config.sh. Explain each changed line.
verify: The failing test now passes and all tests/trainer/ppo CPU tests still pass
You can explain the root cause and every changed line without the agent's notes
Your commit has the AI attribution trailer AGENTS.md describes

steps.title: Pass verl's pre-commit hooks and PR title check locally
steps.learn: pre-commit.yml runs .pre-commit-config.yaml: ruff, ruff-format, mypy, autogen-trainer-cfg (regenerates _generated_*.yaml), docstring, license, docs-time, device-API, DataProto, structure, naming and uv checks, compileall. check-pr-title.yml checks the [modules] type: title and that the PR body fills the template.
verify: pre-commit run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure passes on your branch
git status shows no changes to verl/trainer/config/_generated_*.yaml after the autogen hook
Your planned PR title uses an allowed module and type from check_pr_title.py

steps.title: Measure step throughput before and after with verl metrics
steps.learn: verl logs perf/throughput (tokens per second per GPU) and perf/time_per_step from compute_throughout_metrics in metric_utils.py, plus per-stage timings from timing_raw. Docs cover perf tuning and Nsight and torch profiling. Report several steps after warmup, the GPU model and the exact command.

decision.choice: A CPU micro-benchmark of the changed function, plus GSM8K quickstart throughput if you have a 24 GB+ GPU
decision.why: The micro-benchmark isolates your change with low noise; the quickstart shows whether it matters end to end, which reviewers of perf PRs ask for.

alternatives.name: Only end-to-end throughput
alternatives.tradeoff: What users feel, but rollout time dominates and hides small algorithm changes in noise.

alternatives.name: Nsight or torch profiler traces
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows where time goes per kernel, but needs a GPU and is heavier to share in a PR.

verify: You report mean and spread over at least 5 runs or steps, before and after, on the same machine
You recorded hardware, software versions and the exact command
Steps before warmup are excluded and you say how many

steps.title: Open the verl PR with the template and handle review
steps.learn: Use the PR template: a similar-PR search link, a title like [algo] fix: description, test evidence, docs updates. AGENTS.md adds an AI-use statement, tests run, and why it is not a duplicate. Sign the CLA when cla-assistant asks. Post in Slack ci-request when ready for CI. Verify CodeRabbit bot reviews before applying.

decision.choice: One small PR scoped to one module tag, ready for review with test output pasted in
decision.why: A single module tag routes it to the right reviewers, and complete evidence avoids the template warning that reviewers may deprioritize incomplete PRs.

alternatives.name: A draft PR to discuss the approach
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful for a non-obvious fix, but CI and review usually wait until it is marked ready.

alternatives.name: Bundle several related fixes
alternatives.tradeoff: AGENTS.md allows bundling cleanups with substantive work, but bigger diffs take longer to review.

verify: Every template checklist item is filled or explained, including the similar-PR search link
The description states AI assistance, test commands and results, and why it is not a duplicate
Every review comment has a reply, and the branch is rebased on current main

steps.title: Write up the verl contribution and pick the next rung
steps.learn: Summarize what you learned about the HybridFlow dataflow, the estimator you touched, and the review process, with numbers (CPU test runtime, any throughput change, days to review). Next rungs: a new advantage estimator or policy loss via the registries, a reward function, or a GPU rollout bug.
verify: The write-up links the PR and states its outcome and number of review rounds
Every performance number names the hardware and exact command
It names one next contribution in verl with the files it would touch

projects.problem: verl runs RL post-training (PPO, GRPO and more) for LLMs on Ray. Contributing teaches the single-controller dataflow and RL algorithm code.
projects.proveIt: A PR to verl-project/verl that passes CI and gets maintainer review, with a CPU test and a short write-up.
projects.hardware: Linux for CPU tests; NVIDIA GPU with 24 GB+ for the GSM8K quickstart (uv lock uses CUDA 13 torch wheels)
projects.aiPolicy: AGENTS.md: no pure agent PRs; a human must review every line and run tests; PRs must state AI use, tests run and why not duplicate; no tiny busywork PRs. Breaches can mean a ban.

projects.title: NeMo RL
projects.question: How do I go from never touching NeMo RL to a signed-off, CI-tested pull request that NVIDIA maintainers review?

steps.title: Set the goal and read NeMo RL's contribution rules
steps.learn: Aim at environments and rewards, which unit tests cover on few GPUs. Success is a PR that passes CI and gets review. Rules: DCO sign-off on every commit, Conventional Commits PR titles, ruff and pyrefly via pre-commit. Ask in GitHub Discussions or issues. No written AI policy; AGENTS.md is guidance for coding agents.
verify: From CONTRIBUTING.md, write down the sign-off command and what happens to unsigned commits
List the allowed PR title types from .agents/contributor-skills/contributing/SKILL.md
Confirm in docs/ci-cd.md who must comment /ok to test before CI runs on an external PR

steps.title: Set up NeMo RL with uv and run the unit tests
steps.learn: Clone with --recursive (submodules live in 3rdparty), then uv venv, which reads .python-version. Run everything through uv run. Smoke test: uv run examples/run_grpo.py --config examples/configs/grpo_smoke.yaml. Unit tests: uv run --group test bash tests/run_unit.sh; Megatron tests add --extra mcore and --mcore-only.

decision.choice: Work inside the NGC container nvcr.io/nvidia/nemo-rl with your checkout mounted, launching with uv run
decision.why: The README recommends it: it ships CUDA, cuDNN, vLLM and SGLang, so you skip the bare-metal cuDNN header and libibverbs-dev fixes and spend your first day on code instead of drivers.

alternatives.name: Bare-metal uv venv
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewest layers and fast edits, but Megatron needs cuDNN headers and CUDNN_HOME set, and your driver must match the pinned PyTorch.

alternatives.name: Build docker/Dockerfile yourself
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches what CI builds, useful when you change dependencies, but the build is long; docs/docker.md shows docker buildx and SKIP_* build args to trim it.

verify: The grpo_smoke.yaml run finishes its capped steps and you note GPU model, driver and commit SHA
tests/run_unit.sh completes and you record pass, skip and fail counts
git submodule status shows every submodule checked out (no leading minus sign)

steps.title: Trace one GRPO step from run_grpo.py to the loss
steps.learn: examples/run_grpo.py calls setup(), then select_sync_trainer returns grpo_train (nemo_rl/algorithms/grpo.py) while data_plane is off. run_multi_turn_rollout (nemo_rl/experience/rollouts.py) drives nemo_rl/models/generation/vllm and environment rewards. lm_policy.py trains with the loss in nemo_rl/algorithms/loss.

decision.choice: Trace synchronous grpo_train with the default Automodel backend and vLLM generation
decision.why: It is the default path of grpo_math_1B.yaml, runs on one GPU, and touches every stage once: generate, reward, logprobs, train and refit of weights into vLLM.

alternatives.name: async_grpo_train
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick it to learn off-policy replay buffers; more moving parts and harder to step through on a first read.

alternatives.name: Megatron backend path
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick it for parallelism work; requires the mcore extra and puts megatron_policy_worker.py and Megatron-Bridge in the trace.

verify: Write the file:function hop list from run_grpo.py to the loss, each confirmed with a log line or breakpoint
Explain where refit happens, starting from prepare_refit_info in lm_policy.py
Name which Ray worker groups exist during one step and what each holds

steps.title: Learn GRPO's advantages and pick a NeMo RL subsystem
steps.learn: GRPO samples a group of answers per prompt and uses group-relative rewards as advantages inside a clipped policy-gradient loss. grpo_math_1B.yaml uses the grpo estimator with a leave-one-out baseline and normalize_rewards (divide by group std); loss_fn sets ratio_clip_min/max and reference_policy_kl_penalty.

decision.choice: Target environments and reward code: nemo_rl/environments and nemo_rl/algorithms/reward_functions.py
decision.why: Reward bugs silently change training, the code is mostly plain Python, and tests/unit/environments plus tests/unit/algorithms/test_reward_functions.py give nearby test patterns, so a fix plus test fits a first PR.

alternatives.name: Losses and advantage estimators
alternatives.tradeoff: High-impact and covered by golden tests like test_clipped_pg_loss_goldens.py, but reviewers are strict about numerics.

alternatives.name: Generation backends and refit
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for inference systems work; needs multiple GPUs and tracks pinned vLLM and SGLang versions.

alternatives.name: Megatron policy worker
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for large-scale parallelism; needs the mcore extra, multi-GPU tests and Megatron-Bridge knowledge.

verify: Compute leave-one-out, std-normalized advantages by hand for a group of 4 rewards and match advantage_estimator.py
Point to the loss_fn keys in grpo_math_1B.yaml that set clipping and the KL penalty
Read one test in tests/unit/environments and explain what it pins

steps.title: Ship a small test or docs PR to NeMo RL first
steps.learn: A first PR teaches the process (sign-off, title check, waiting for a maintainer to start CI) at low risk. The testing skill says @ray.remote classes need a # pragma: no cover. Docs live in docs/ and build with Sphinx; pre-commit rejects underscores in Markdown filenames.

decision.choice: Add a missing unit test case for an environment or reward function
decision.why: Maintainers ask for tests (the PR template checks for them), the change is small, and it runs with uv run --group test pytest on one file without a multi-node cluster.

alternatives.name: Docs fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest risk and only needs the CI:docs level, but teaches less about the code and must follow the docs guide.

alternatives.name: New recipe YAML
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick if you have GPUs for runs; needs recipe naming rules, a driver script under tests/test_suites and the minimize-check hook.

steps.delegate: In NVIDIA-NeMo/RL, read .agents/contributor-skills/testing/SKILL.md and linting-and-formatting/SKILL.md. Add pytest cases to tests/unit/environments/<file> for <function> in nemo_rl/environments/<module>.py, covering edge cases I list. Follow nearby fixtures, Google-style docstrings and type annotations. Run uv run --group test pytest on that file and show the output. Do not change library code.
verify: Break the target function on purpose and see the new test fail, then revert
The test file passes with uv run --group test pytest and you saved the output
Commit has a Signed-off-by line and a title such as test(environments): ...

steps.title: Pick a NeMo RL issue and reproduce it with a failing test
steps.learn: Labels that exist: good first issue (only a few open, some old), bug, community-request, needs-follow-up. Pick a recent, unassigned issue with no linked PR and comment before starting. Reproduce on the smallest config and record commit SHA, GPU and uv.lock state.

decision.choice: Reproduce as a unit test under tests/unit instead of a full training run
decision.why: A unit test fails in seconds, runs in CI at the L0 level, and becomes the regression test for your fix; training runs are slow and noisy.

alternatives.name: Functional test in tests/functional
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to what the reporter ran, but needs several GPUs and the L1 CI level.

alternatives.name: grpo_smoke.yaml run with a config change
alternatives.tradeoff: End to end and convincing for crashes, but minutes per try and hard to turn into a test.

verify: Your issue comment lists commit SHA, exact command, GPU, and observed vs expected behavior
The failing test fails on main for the reported reason, not for a setup error

steps.title: Fix the NeMo RL bug with an agent, test first
steps.learn: CONTRIBUTING says not to add arbitrary config defaults; AGENTS.md tells reviewers to flag hidden state and dict[str, Any] configs. There is no written AI policy, so the bar is that you can explain and defend every line. New type-checked modules must be added to pyrefly.toml.
steps.delegate: Repo NVIDIA-NeMo/RL (Python 3.13, uv). First read AGENTS.md and SKILL.md files in .agents/contributor-skills (testing, linting-and-formatting, config-conventions, error-handling). Add a failing pytest under tests/unit/<area> reproducing: <issue summary>. Then make the minimal fix in nemo_rl/<module>.py with type annotations, no new config defaults, no refactors. Run uv run --group test pytest on the touched tests and show output. Explain each changed line.
verify: You can explain every changed line without the agent's notes
The new test fails on main and passes with the fix
No new config defaults or unrelated edits appear in git diff

steps.title: Run NeMo RL's pre-commit, pyrefly and test subset
steps.learn: pre-commit runs ruff (lint, import sort, format), taplo for TOML, a no-underscore Markdown filename hook, pyrefly, and a minimize-check on recipe YAMLs. Required checks: lint, at most 10 commits behind, semantic PR title, DCO, secrets detection, Automodel submodule check. PRs run no tests until a CI label is applied.

decision.choice: Run pre-commit plus the touched unit tests locally, then ask for the CI:L0 label
decision.why: L0 runs doctests and unit tests, which is what a small fix to environments or rewards touches, without spending shared GPU time on functional runs.

alternatives.name: CI:L1
alternatives.tradeoff: Adds functional GPU tests; ask for it when your change affects training or generation end to end.

alternatives.name: CI:Lfast
alternatives.tradeoff: Reuses the prebuilt main container so it is faster, but does not build your image, so it is wrong if you change dependencies.

verify: uv run --group dev pre-commit run --all-files reports no failures
Your branch is fewer than 10 commits behind main after git fetch upstream
The touched unit tests pass and you saved the command and output

steps.title: Measure a NeMo RL change with step timing and nsys
steps.learn: NeMo RL reports step time, tokens/sec/GPU and MFU (performance-summary.md). Its performance recipes are multi-node. Nsight profiling targets workers via NRL_NSYS_WORKER_PATTERNS and steps via NRL_NSYS_PROFILE_STEP_RANGE. Step time mixes generation, logprobs, training and refit, so say which stage moved.

decision.choice: Compare per-stage timings on grpo_math_1B over fixed steps, repeated runs, same GPU
decision.why: It runs on one node, uses the timers already logged by grpo_train, and lets you attribute a change to a stage rather than to noise.

alternatives.name: Official performance recipes
alternatives.tradeoff: Comparable to published numbers, but they need many nodes of H100 or GB200 class GPUs.

alternatives.name: nsys trace of one worker type
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds the hotspot inside a stage, but does not prove an end-to-end gain by itself.

verify: Report mean and spread of step time over at least 3 runs before and after
Record GPU model, driver, commit SHA and config overrides with the numbers
An nsys trace for a short step range opens and shows the worker you changed

steps.title: Open the NeMo RL PR and get CI triggered
steps.learn: Fill the PR template: one-line overview, issues closed, usage, test and docs checkboxes. External contributors need an NVIDIA developer to add a CI label and comment /ok to test with your commit SHA. A scheduled workflow closes inactive issues and PRs, so keep it moving and rebase when main moves.
verify: Every commit shows Signed-off-by and the semantic PR title check passes
The PR body links the issue with a closing keyword and shows the failing-then-passing test
You replied to every review comment and pushed fixes as new signed-off commits

steps.title: Write up the NeMo RL contribution and pick the next rung
steps.learn: Summarize what the GRPO path taught you, the bug and its root cause, test and timing numbers with hardware, and how review went. Next rungs: a new environment, a loss or advantage fix with golden tests, or a design doc update, which CONTRIBUTING requires for key features.
verify: The write-up links the PR and states its review or merge status honestly
Every number has the GPU, commit SHA and command that produced it
It names one next rung and the subsystem and tests it would touch

projects.problem: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library (GRPO, DPO, SFT); contributing teaches how RL rollouts, rewards, losses and refit fit together
projects.proveIt: A signed-off PR with a failing-then-passing unit test that passes CI and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up
projects.hardware: Linux with NVIDIA GPUs: 1 GPU runs the 1B GRPO example, the full unit suite needs 2 GPUs

projects.title: slime
projects.question: How do I land a bug fix with tests in slime, Z.ai's Megatron plus SGLang RL framework, within its narrow contribution scope?

steps.title: Set the goal and read slime's collaboration scope
steps.learn: CONTRIBUTING limits outside work to bug fixes and general RL optimizations with benchmarks; refactors, abstraction proposals, unverifiable features and big Megatron changes are out of scope. No DCO, CLA, code of conduct, PR template or AI policy is written. Discussions are off, so talk in issues.
verify: Write which CONTRIBUTING category your planned PR falls in and why it is in scope
Check the good first issue label: when this flow was written it had no open issues
Read the bug report template in .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE and note its required fields

steps.title: Install slime and run its CPU tests
steps.learn: CPU CI installs CPU PyTorch plus test deps, then pip install -e . --no-deps, and runs python tests/<file>.py. GPU work uses the slimerl/slime image with your checkout mounted and pip install -e . --no-deps inside. build_conda.sh builds Megatron and SGLang with patches if you cannot use Docker.

decision.choice: Start with a CPU-only venv that mirrors the cpu-unittest CI job
decision.why: Reward, argument, batching and sample tests run on any Linux box, so you can work before you have GPUs; GPU end-to-end tests need H100-class hosts.

alternatives.name: slimerl/slime Docker image
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for anything touching Megatron or SGLang; requires a Linux x86_64 GPU host with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit.

alternatives.name: build_conda.sh
alternatives.tradeoff: No Docker needed, but it builds Megatron and SGLang from source, writes to /root, and takes much longer.

verify: python tests/test_rm_math.py passes in your CPU venv
In the container, the import check for slime, sglang and megatron.core prints your GPU count
You record the image tag or commit SHA you tested against

steps.title: Trace one rollout and train step through train.py
steps.learn: train.py loops: RolloutManager.generate (slime/ray/rollout.py) runs --rollout-function-path, default slime.rollout.sglang_rollout.generate_rollout; RayTrainGroup.async_train (slime/ray/actor_group.py) runs Megatron in backends/megatron_utils/actor.py and loss.py; update_weights pushes weights to SGLang.

decision.choice: Trace the default synchronous GRPO path without a critic
decision.why: It is the path the README's Code Reading Path follows, and every other mode (critic, fully async, distillation) adds branches on top of it.

alternatives.name: Fully async rollout
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick to study off-policy staleness; adds slime/rollout/fully_async_rollout.py and queue transport to the trace.

alternatives.name: PPO with a critic
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick to study value models; adds critic training and num_critic_only_steps logic in train.py.

verify: Write the file:function hop list from train.py to policy_loss_function in loss.py
Explain which update_weight implementation your config uses and why
Say where rewards are computed: generate_and_rm in sglang_rollout.py

steps.title: Learn slime's GRPO rewards and choose a target
steps.learn: GRPO turns a group of sampled answers into group-relative advantages. In slime, slime/data/batch_builder.py centers rewards per group and divides by the std unless --disable-grpo-std-normalization; get_grpo_returns in slime/utils/ppo_utils.py spreads them over tokens. Rewards: slime/rollout/rm_hub via --rm-type.

decision.choice: Target reward functions in slime/rollout/rm_hub
decision.why: They are pure Python with CPU tests (test_rm_math.py and siblings), a wrong normalization silently flips rewards, and bug fixes with tests are exactly what CONTRIBUTING welcomes.

alternatives.name: Losses and advantages (loss.py, ppo_utils.py)
alternatives.tradeoff: Core and high-impact with CPU tests (test_policy_loss.py, test_cispo_loss.py), but numerics changes also need GPU runs and the precision CI job.

alternatives.name: SGLang deployment (backends/sglang_utils)
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for serving work; needs GPUs and the patched SGLang inside the image.

alternatives.name: Checkpoint conversion (megatron_to_hf)
alternatives.tradeoff: Model-specific and valuable, but testing often needs large models and GPUs.

verify: Compute centered, std-normalized rewards for a group of 4 by hand and match batch_builder.py
Pick one rm_type and explain what its test file pins and what it misses

steps.title: Add a CPU test as your first slime PR
steps.learn: CI runs test files directly, so a pytest file needs a __main__ entry and a top-level NUM_GPUS = 0. To run automatically it must be listed in .github/workflows/pr-test.yml.j2, and the generated pr-test.yml is rebuilt with python .github/workflows/generate_github_workflows.py, never hand-edited.

decision.choice: Add missing edge-case tests for one rm_hub reward function
decision.why: It lands in the welcomed scope, runs in the automatic CPU job, and often exposes a real bug you can fix in the next PR.

alternatives.name: Docs fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy, but docs/en and docs/zh are mirrored and tests/test_docs_consistency.py checks links and paths, so update both.

alternatives.name: New reward function
alternatives.tradeoff: Has a repo skill (add-reward-function), but is a feature and may fall outside the stated scope.

steps.delegate: Repo THUDM/slime. Read .claude/skills/add-tests-and-ci/SKILL.md and tests/test_rm_math.py. Add pytest cases for slime/rollout/rm_hub/<module>.py covering edge cases I list. Keep top-level NUM_GPUS = 0 and the __main__ entry raising SystemExit(pytest.main([__file__])). If it is a new file, register it in cpu-unittest in .github/workflows/pr-test.yml.j2 and run python .github/workflows/generate_github_workflows.py. Run the test and show output.
verify: python tests/<your_test>.py passes, and fails when you break the function on purpose
If you added a file, the template and the regenerated pr-test.yml are both in the diff

steps.title: Find a slime bug and reproduce it on the smallest setup
steps.learn: With good first issue and help wanted empty when checked, read open issues labeled bug: recent, unassigned, no linked PR. Over 100 PRs were open, so check for an existing fix first. For training bugs, the debug guide's --debug-rollout-only, --debug-train-only and saved rollout data split rollout from training.

decision.choice: Reproduce with a CPU unit test when the bug is in pure Python logic
decision.why: It runs in the automatic CPU job, needs no GPU, and becomes the regression test for your fix.

alternatives.name: GPU end-to-end test
alternatives.tradeoff: Use prepare()/execute() with NUM_GPUS; needed for Megatron or SGLang bugs, but needs 4 or more GPUs.

alternatives.name: Replay saved rollout data
alternatives.tradeoff: --load-debug-rollout-data isolates training bugs from sampling noise, but needs a GPU run to capture the data first.

verify: Your issue comment has commit SHA, image tag, command, and observed vs expected output
The failing test fails on main for the reported reason

steps.title: Fix the slime bug with an agent, keeping the diff small
steps.learn: slime syncs with an internal version, so maintainers want small, verifiable diffs with no refactors or new abstractions. No AI policy is written; the repo ships agent skills in .claude/skills, including code review preferences. You must still understand and defend every line.
steps.delegate: Repo THUDM/slime (Python). Read CONTRIBUTING.md and .claude/skills/slime-code-review-preferences/SKILL.md and add-tests-and-ci/SKILL.md. First add a failing CPU test in tests/test_<area>.py with NUM_GPUS = 0 and a pytest __main__ entry reproducing: <issue>. Then make the minimal fix in slime/<module>.py; no refactors or new abstractions. Run python tests/test_<area>.py and pre-commit run --all-files. Explain every changed line.
verify: You can explain every changed line without the agent's notes
The test fails on main and passes with the fix
git diff touches only the fix, the test and any CI registration

steps.title: Pass slime's pre-commit and choose CI labels
steps.learn: pre-commit runs check-yaml, detect-private-key, a large-file check, ruff-check --fix, autoflake, isort (black profile) and black; a workflow runs it on PRs. CPU tests run on every PR. GPU tests run by label: run-ci-changed, run-ci-megatron, run-ci-precision, run-ci-ckpt; maintainers usually apply them.

decision.choice: Request run-ci-changed when your PR adds or edits a test file
decision.why: It runs only the changed test files with their declared NUM_GPUS, which is the cheapest GPU check that still exercises your work.

alternatives.name: run-ci-megatron
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for training, loss or checkpoint changes; runs the full Megatron list and uses much more GPU time.

alternatives.name: run-ci-precision
alternatives.tradeoff: Ask for it when you change numerics; checks consistency across parallel configs.

verify: pre-commit run --all-files --show-diff-on-failure reports no changes
Rerunning generate_github_workflows.py leaves pr-test.yml unchanged

steps.title: Benchmark a slime rollout change with profile_rollout.py
steps.learn: CONTRIBUTING accepts optimizations only with clear benchmarks. The profiling guide parks rollout with --rollout-function-path slime.rollout.sleep_rollout.sleep, lists engines via the router's /workers endpoint, and records traces with tools/profile_rollout.py. Report throughput and variance.

decision.choice: Measure rollout throughput under a fixed request load with the sleep rollout
decision.why: Parking rollout removes training noise, the load is repeatable, and SGLang traces show where time goes before and after your change.

alternatives.name: End-to-end step time from logs
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows the user-visible effect, but mixes rollout, training and weight sync, so variance is higher.

alternatives.name: Precision CI only
alternatives.tradeoff: Proves correctness is unchanged, not speed; pair it with a benchmark, do not replace one.

verify: Report mean and spread over at least 3 runs before and after on the same GPUs
Record GPU model, image tag, SGLang args and commit SHA with the numbers
A trace from tools/profile_rollout.py exists for both runs

steps.title: Open the slime PR and work through review
steps.learn: There is no PR template, so write your own: scope category from CONTRIBUTING, linked issue, root cause, the test command and output, and which CI labels you suggest. No sign-off is required. With many open PRs review can be slow; rebase on main and ask politely on the issue if it stalls.
verify: The PR body states the bug, root cause, test command and output, and links the issue
The diff stays small, with no refactors beyond the fix
You answered every review comment and rebased onto current main

steps.title: Write up the slime contribution and pick the next rung
steps.learn: Summarize how rollout, rewards, training and weight sync connect, the bug and root cause, test and benchmark numbers with hardware, and how review went. Next rungs: a GPU end-to-end test, a loss fix checked by precision CI, or a benchmarked rollout optimization.
verify: The write-up links the PR and states its review or merge status honestly
Every number has the hardware, image tag, commit SHA and command
It names one next rung and why it fits slime's stated scope

projects.problem: THUDM's RL post-training framework joining Megatron training and SGLang rollout; contributing teaches the rollout, reward and train loop
projects.proveIt: A small bug-fix PR with a CPU test that passes CI and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up
projects.hardware: CPU tests on Linux with CPU PyTorch; GPU end-to-end tests need H100/H200-class GPUs, often 4 to 8

projects.title: Miles
projects.question: Can you land a reviewed PR in Miles, the SGLang plus Megatron RL post-training framework, by understanding one rollout-to-train loop?

steps.title: Set your Miles target and read the contribution rules
steps.learn: Success is a PR that passes CI and gets maintainer review; merging is up to maintainers. Miles has no CLA or DCO, uses a Contributor Covenant code of conduct, and talks in #miles-rl on the SGLang Slack. Recent merges come mostly from collaborators and open newcomer issues are few, so plan to find work yourself.
verify: You read docs/developer/contributor-guide.md and CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md and can name the commit-subject convention
You checked the open good first issue and help wanted lists and noted how many are unassigned
You read REVIEW.md and AGENTS.md and know reviews check changes against .claude/rules/*.md
You joined #miles-rl on the SGLang Slack or know it is where quick questions go

steps.title: Install Miles editable and run the CPU suite in tests/fast
steps.learn: Miles pins patched SGLang and Megatron-LM; installing them at the wrong commit is the most common source of bug reports. The image radixark/miles ships them with Miles editable at /root/miles. CPU CI instead puts sglang (branch sglang-miles) and radixark/Megatron-LM (branch miles-main) on PYTHONPATH.

decision.choice: Docker image radixark/miles:dev (the GPU CI default) plus pip install -e . --no-deps, then pytest tests/fast
decision.why: The image matches what GPU CI runs, so failures you see are real, not dependency drift. pytest tests/fast needs no GPU, so you can iterate on CPU-only code paths cheaply before touching GPU tests.

alternatives.name: From source with pip install -r requirements.txt
alternatives.tradeoff: Works without Docker, but you must match the patched SGLang and Megatron-LM commits yourself; the docs warn this is the top bug source.

alternatives.name: Mirror the CPU CI workflow on a laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Clone sglang and radixark/Megatron-LM at the CI branches, set PYTHONPATH, install tests/ci/requirements-ci-cpu.txt. No Docker, but CPU only.

verify: python -c "import miles" succeeds in your environment
pytest tests/fast completes and you recorded pass, skip and fail counts
python3 train.py --help parses without errors

steps.title: Trace one GRPO iteration from train.py to the weight sync
steps.learn: A run is trainer ranks, SGLang servers behind the Miles Router, and a data source, all in Ray. Read train.py, then miles/rollout/sglang_rollout.py (generate_rollout), miles/backends/training_utils/loss/objective.py, miles/router/router.py and miles/backends/training_utils/weight_update/.
verify: You can name the file that turns prompts into samples and the one that computes the loss and advantages
You can say where the rm_type reward dispatch lives (miles/rollout/rm_hub/__init__.py)

steps.title: Learn the rollout and train split and pick a subsystem

projects.title: vLLM
projects.question: Can I land a reviewed vLLM pull request in the V1 scheduler or KV cache manager, with a failing test, benchmark evidence and a DCO sign-off?

steps.title: Frame a scheduler or KV cache PR and read vLLM's rules
steps.learn: Aim at vllm/v1/core (scheduler and KV cache manager). Rules: every commit needs a DCO Signed-off-by, AI use must be disclosed, AGENTS.md warns breaches can lead to bans, outside contributors may have 6 open PRs, and architectural changes over 500 LOC need an RFC issue. Maintainers talk on Slack and the forum.

steps.title: Install vLLM editable on precompiled kernels and run core tests
steps.learn: vLLM supports Python 3.11 to 3.14 but CI uses 3.12. For Python-only work the docs give `VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e .` then `vllm download-kernels`. Kernel work needs PyTorch, requirements/build/cuda.txt and `uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation`. Test deps come from requirements/test/cuda.in.

decision.choice: Python 3.12 venv with `VLLM_USE_PRECOMPILED=1 uv pip install -e .`
decision.why: The scheduler and KV cache manager are Python, so precompiled kernels avoid a long CUDA build while keeping edits live. Matching CI's Python 3.12 reduces environment drift.

alternatives.name: Full source build with --no-build-isolation
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for C++ or CUDA changes; long builds and exact CUDA and PyTorch versions required.

alternatives.name: Incremental compilation workflow
alternatives.tradeoff: Best for iterating on kernels after a first full build, but extra CMake setup for Python-only work.

verify: `python -c "import vllm; print(vllm.__file__)"` points into your clone

steps.title: Trace one request through the vLLM V1 engine core and scheduler
steps.learn: Follow vllm/entrypoints/openai/api_server.py to AsyncLLM (vllm/v1/engine/async_llm.py), over ZMQ via core_client.py to EngineCore.step in core.py, then Scheduler.schedule and update_from_output in v1/core/sched/scheduler.py, KVCacheManager.allocate_slots, and gpu_model_runner.execute_model in v1/worker.

steps.title: Learn PagedAttention and prefix caching, then pick a subsystem
steps.learn: PagedAttention stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks so memory is allocated on demand and shared across requests. Prefix caching hashes full blocks so a new request can reuse earlier KV. In code, BlockPool (vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py) owns blocks and KVCacheManager hands them to the scheduler.

decision.choice: Target the V1 KV cache manager and scheduler (labels `kv-cache-manager`, `scheduler`)
decision.why: It is Python, needs only a precompiled install, has focused tests in tests/v1/core, and benchmark scripts for the block pool and prefix caching, so the full arc fits one GPU.

alternatives.name: Attention backends (vllm/v1/attention/backends)
alternatives.tradeoff: Deeper GPU learning, but often needs specific GPUs and a source build for kernel changes.

alternatives.name: New model support (`new-model` label)
alternatives.tradeoff: Clear scope and a job board, but needs the model weights and enough GPU memory to validate outputs.

alternatives.name: Frontend and OpenAI API server
alternatives.tradeoff: Little GPU dependence, but less about inference systems.

verify: You can explain why fixed-size blocks reduce KV fragmentation

steps.learn: vLLM's AI policy and AGENTS.md reject one-off busywork such as a single typo fix, so the first rung must carry weight. Docs use MkDocs (`mkdocs serve`); tests go in existing files and conftest fixtures where possible, one behavior per test.

decision.choice: Add a missing test in tests/v1/core for a behavior you traced in the scheduler or block pool
decision.why: It deepens what you learned in the trace, maintainers value coverage, and it avoids the busywork pattern the policy forbids.

alternatives.name: A design doc improvement in docs/design
alternatives.tradeoff: Helps readers and needs no GPU, but must be substantive; a docs preview builds only when docs files change.

alternatives.name: An onboarding task from the org project board
alternatives.tradeoff: Curated by maintainers, but tasks may be taken or need hardware you lack.

steps.title: Reproduce a scheduler or KV cache bug as a failing test
steps.learn: Filter open issues by `bug` with `kv-cache-manager`, `scheduler` or `v1`, prefer recent activity and no assignee or linked PR. decision.why: It runs fast, isolates scheduling logic from GPU kernels, and becomes the regression test.

alternatives.name: End-to-end repro with LLM.generate
alternatives.tradeoff: Proves user impact, but slower, needs a GPU and model weights, and is harder to make deterministic.

alternatives.name: Repro via `vllm serve` and HTTP
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for frontend or streaming bugs, but adds async and network noise.

steps.learn: vLLM follows the Google Python style guide, Google-style docstrings, an 88-character line limit and few comments. AGENTS.md says to use uv and .venv/bin/python, not system pip. If an agent helps, add a Co-authored-by trailer and disclose it in the PR; you must defend the change yourself.

steps.title: Pass vLLM pre-commit hooks and understand Buildkite CI
steps.learn: Install hooks via `uv pip install -r requirements/lint.txt` and `pre-commit install`, then run `pre-commit run -a` (ruff, typos, clang-format, mypy, signoff-commit, check-spdx-header). CI pre-commit fails until a PR has a `verified` or `ready` label or you have 4 merged PRs; GPU tests run on Buildkite via `/ci run`.

steps.title: Measure the change with vllm bench and block pool benchmarks
steps.learn: `vllm bench serve`, `vllm bench latency` and `vllm bench throughput` measure end to end; benchmarks/ has benchmark_block_pool.py and benchmark_prefix_caching.py for the KV cache path. Run before and after on the same GPU, repeat runs, report spread, and fix the dataset and request rate.

alternatives.name: Only `vllm bench throughput` offline
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple and repeatable, but hides latency effects of scheduling decisions.

alternatives.name: Parameter sweeps
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers many configs automatically, but takes far more GPU time than a small fix needs.

steps.title: Open a tagged, signed-off PR and handle vLLM review
steps.learn: Titles need bracketed tags such as `[Bugfix][Core]`. The template asks for Overview, Claims, Validation and Details, plus an AI checkbox. Answer each review comment with a change or a reply, then ping for re-review; ping after 7 days without review or ask in #pr-reviews. Allow edits by maintainers.

steps.title: Write up the vLLM fix and pick the next rung

projects.title: SGLang
projects.question: Can you take a change in SGLang's Python runtime from reading the code to a tested PR that Merge Oncalls and Codeowners review?

steps.title: Set your SGLang target and read the merge rules
steps.learn: Aim at the Python runtime in python/sglang/srt. Success is a PR that passes CI and gets Codeowner review. SGLang is Apache-2.0 and its guide mentions no CLA or DCO sign-off. Merges go through Merge Oncalls and CODEOWNERS (MAINTAINER.md). No written AI policy was found. Maintainers talk in Slack.

steps.title: Install SGLang editable and run CPU unit tests

alternatives.name: Dev Docker container from the guide
alternatives.tradeoff: The guide's recommended contributor setup with tools preinstalled; pick it on a GPU host to match CI dependencies, at the cost of a large image.

alternatives.tradeoff: Required only for AOT kernel changes under python/sglang/kernels/aot; long CUDA build and needs a supported NVIDIA GPU.

steps.learn: Under python/sglang/srt: entrypoints/http_server.py takes the request, managers/tokenizer_manager.py tokenizes, managers/scheduler.py batches it (schedule_batch.py, schedule_policy.py), managers/tp_worker.py and model_executor/model_runner.py run the forward, KV lives in mem_cache/, detokenizer_manager.py returns text.

steps.title: Learn RadixAttention and pick an SGLang subsystem
steps.learn: The SGLang paper introduces RadixAttention (KV cache reuse across requests via a radix tree with LRU eviction) and compressed finite state machines for constrained decoding. The default prefix cache is now mem_cache/unified_radix_cache.py (radix_cache.py is the classic one); grammar backends live in srt/constrained/.

alternatives.tradeoff: High impact, but needs specific GPUs (labels such as hopper and blackwell exist) plus accuracy and speed results in the PR.

alternatives.name: Scheduler policy
alternatives.tradeoff: Central to throughput and latency; any change needs GPU benchmarks with bench_serving and careful review from Codeowners.

alternatives.name: New model support
alternatives.tradeoff: Visible and well defined (new-model label), but needs model weights, GPU memory and accuracy evals such as GSM8K or MMLU.

alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest risk and quick to review, but you learn less code; run mint broken-links locally as the guide describes.

alternatives.tradeoff: Shows real usage, but you need a running server and GPU to verify it, and it may need more review discussion.

steps.learn: Filter issues with labels that exist: good first issue, help wanted, bug, and area labels such as function-calling, memory-pool or hicache. decision.why: A CPU repro becomes a fast unit test that CI can run on every PR, and reviewers trust a fix that comes with one. It also keeps the loop on a laptop instead of a rented GPU.

alternatives.tradeoff: Curated for newcomers, but often claimed quickly; check comments and assignees before investing time.

alternatives.name: Hardware-specific bug (amd, npu, xpu labels)
alternatives.tradeoff: Less competition, but you need that exact hardware to reproduce and to show the fix works.

steps.title: Fix the SGLang bug test first with a coding agent
steps.learn: The style guide asks for few CPU-GPU syncs (avoid .item() and .cpu()), caching per-layer checks in __init__, short pure functions, keyword arguments, msgspec.Struct for new containers and no pickle on untrusted data. You must understand every line; Codeowners will ask.

decision.why: Small diffs get reviewed faster in a repo with many open PRs and limited CI, and the test proves the fix. Unrelated cleanups dilute review and make reverts harder.

alternatives.tradeoff: May remove the bug class, but belongs in a separate Refactor PR after discussion with Codeowners.

alternatives.name: Workaround at the call site
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick and low risk, but leaves the root cause for the next caller; acceptable only if maintainers ask for it.

steps.learn: .pre-commit-config.yaml runs isort, ruff, ruff-format, codespell, clang-format, check-registered-tests and Rust hooks (cargo clippy, nightly rustfmt), so install rustup first. steps.learn: The PR template asks for accuracy results when outputs change and speed results when speed changes. bench_serving is the default tool (TTFT, TPOT, ITL, throughput); use num-prompts at least 5x max-concurrency for steady state.
