projects.title: FlashInfer
projects.question: How do you get a reviewed fix into FlashInfer, the CUDA attention and kernel library that vLLM and SGLang call for LLM serving?

steps.title: Frame a FlashInfer contribution and read its rules
steps.learn: Aim at one op family (attention, sampling, GEMM, MoE). Success is a PR that passes CI and gets maintainer review. Rules live in CONTRIBUTING.md: keep the PR template, report perf numbers, understand AI-assisted code. No CLA or DCO was found. Maintainers talk on Slack and GitHub Discussions.
verify: You read CONTRIBUTING.md fully and can state the AI-assisted contribution rule in one sentence
You confirmed the license is Apache-2.0 and found no CLA or sign-off requirement
You joined the Slack or Discussions forum linked from the README

steps.title: Install FlashInfer editable and run one attention test file
steps.learn: Clone with --recursive (cccl, cutlass, nixl and spdlog submodules), then pip install --no-build-isolation -e . -v so pip does not pull a mismatched torch. Kernels are JIT-compiled on first call and cached in ~/.cache/flashinfer, so edits to .cuh files are picked up without reinstalling.

decision.choice: Editable install with JIT compilation, FLASHINFER_CUDA_ARCH_LIST set to your GPU only
decision.why: JIT rebuilds only the kernel variants a test touches and reloads your header edits, which is what a contributor iterating on one op needs. Restricting the arch list keeps compile time down on a single GPU.

alternatives.name: Pre-built flashinfer-jit-cache and flashinfer-cubin
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast startup for users, but they ship compiled kernels, so your source edits are not what runs; fine only for API or docs work.

alternatives.name: The repo devcontainer with sccache
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible toolchain and cached nvcc objects across rebuilds; costs Docker setup and disk, worth it if you rebuild often.

verify: pytest tests/attention/test_batch_decode_kernels.py runs on your GPU and you record pass, skip and fail counts
Touching a .cuh file under include/ triggers a recompile on the next test run (FLASHINFER_JIT_VERBOSE=1 shows it)
python -m flashinfer.collect_env prints your GPU, CUDA and torch versions

steps.title: Trace one paged-KV decode call from Python to the CUDA kernel
steps.learn: BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper in flashinfer/decode.py: plan() builds the schedule, run() launches. gen_batch_decode_module in flashinfer/jit/attention/modules.py compiles csrc/batch_decode.cu, which calls DecodePlan (include/flashinfer/attention/scheduler.cuh) and the kernel in decode.cuh.
verify: You can name the file and function at each hop from plan() and run() down to BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheDispatched
You explain why plan() is separate from run() (work scheduling is done once per batch layout, then reused)
You can say why include/ must stay free of Torch headers and how csrc/ binds kernels to Python through TVM-FFI

steps.title: Learn attention-state merging and pick your target op
steps.learn: FlashInfer splits long KV ranges and merges partial results using the attention state (output plus log-sum-exp), see state.cuh and the recursive attention tutorial. The paper explains the block-sparse KV format and plan/run scheduling. Your target should match the GPU you own.

decision.choice: Target the attention ops (op: attention label) on the GPU you have
decision.why: Attention is the core of the library, has broad tests and a benchmark routine, and most of it runs on SM80 and newer, so you can reproduce and verify on hardware you can rent.

alternatives.name: Sampling kernels
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller, self-contained code with a design blog post; less exposure to paging and scheduling.

alternatives.name: GEMM or MoE (op: gemm, op: moe)
alternatives.tradeoff: High demand from serving engines, but many paths are FP8 or FP4 on Blackwell, which you need to own or rent to test.

verify: You can write the formula for merging two partial attention outputs using their log-sum-exp values
You listed which tests under tests/attention run (not skip) on your GPU

steps.title: Land a small docs or test PR in the attention area
steps.learn: A first PR teaches the review loop without kernel risk. Tests skip unsupported GPUs with helpers in flashinfer.utils such as is_sm90a_supported(). Docs are Sphinx under docs/. Keep the default PR template; the title and description become the squash commit.

decision.choice: Add a missing test case or arch-skip guard for the op you traced
decision.why: Tests are reviewed quickly, exercise the same build and CI path as kernel changes, and show maintainers you understand the op before you touch its kernel.

alternatives.name: API docstring or docs fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Lowest risk and no GPU needed, but teaches little about the code you will later change.

alternatives.name: New benchmark routine option
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful to maintainers but needs agreement on scope first; better after a first merge.

verify: Your new test fails before your change (or on the wrong arch) and passes after it
pre-commit run -a is clean on your branch
The PR description uses the repository template unmodified in structure

steps.title: Claim an attention issue and reproduce it against a PyTorch reference
steps.learn: Useful labels that exist: good first issue (few open, most taken), bug, numerical issue, op: attention, help wanted. Pick one with recent activity and no assignee, then comment !claim to self-assign. Reproduce with a small script comparing output to a plain PyTorch attention reference.

decision.choice: Turn the report into a failing pytest case under tests/attention
decision.why: A pytest case is what the fix PR needs anyway, runs in CI, and pins the exact dtype, head_dim, page size and arch that fail.

alternatives.name: Standalone repro script in the issue
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster to share and good for triage, but you still have to convert it to a test for the PR.

alternatives.name: flashinfer_benchmark.py with --refcheck
alternatives.tradeoff: Quickly cross-checks many shapes between two or more backends, but is not a regression test and cannot catch a bug every backend shares.

verify: The failing case reproduces on your GPU and you attached collect_env output to the issue
The case is minimal: smallest batch, sequence length and page size that still fail
You checked the issue was unassigned before commenting !claim

steps.title: Fix the bug with a failing test first
steps.learn: Fixes go in the right layer: kernel code in include/ (no Torch headers), bindings in csrc/, Python API in flashinfer/, tests in tests/. The repo ships agent instructions (CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills such as debug-cuda-crash). You must understand every line; reviewers may ask you to walk through it.
steps.delegate: In the FlashInfer repo, follow CLAUDE.md. First add a failing pytest case in tests/attention reproducing: <describe bug, dtype, head_dim, page_size, GPU arch>. Compare against a plain PyTorch reference with explicit tolerances. Then make the minimal fix in the correct layer (include/ for kernels, csrc/ for bindings, flashinfer/ for Python). Skip unsupported archs with flashinfer.utils helpers. Do not add Torch headers under include/. Run pre-commit run -a and the touched test file.
verify: The new test fails on main and passes with your fix on your GPU
You can explain each changed line to a reviewer without notes
FLASHINFER_JIT_DEBUG=1 or compute-sanitizer shows no new errors on the test

steps.title: Run pre-commit and the targeted test subset like CI does
steps.learn: pre-commit runs clang-format, ruff check and format, mypy and file hygiene hooks. Public CI never starts on its own: someone comments @flashinfer-bot run (needs label rights or ci-users), and pushes do not re-trigger it. NVIDIA internal CI (/bot run) spans H100 to GB300 and RTX Blackwell, for approved users only.
verify: pre-commit run -a passes with no changes left to commit
The touched test file passes, and you ran it with --full if the change affects parameter coverage
You know a maintainer will likely need to start CI and will ask again after your final push

steps.title: Measure a kernel change with flashinfer_benchmark.py
steps.learn: benchmarks/flashinfer_benchmark.py benchmarks attention, GEMM and MoE routines across backends with --refcheck. Timing uses CUPTI when cupti-python is installed, else CUDA events. A perf PR must give absolute before and after numbers, the GPU and the problem sizes.

decision.choice: CUPTI timing via flashinfer_benchmark.py on fixed shapes, median of repeated runs
decision.why: CUPTI measures kernel time on the GPU without host launch overhead, and the shared script makes your numbers reproducible by reviewers on their own GPUs.

alternatives.name: bench_gpu_time in a custom script
alternatives.tradeoff: Same timer with full control over inputs; use when no routine covers your op, but reviewers must rerun your script.

alternatives.name: Nsight Compute profiling
alternatives.tradeoff: Explains why a kernel is faster (bandwidth, occupancy), but is not the headline number the PR template asks for.

verify: You report absolute times before and after for at least three problem sizes on a named GPU
You ran each configuration several times and report the spread, not one sample
--refcheck passes with your changed backend and at least one other backend listed in --backends

steps.title: Open the FlashInfer PR and work through review
steps.learn: Fill the PR template (Description, Related Issues, pre-commit checklist, Tests; Reviewer Notes optional; leave Experimental Track untouched) and link the issue. Keep the diff to one fix. After review pushes, ask for @flashinfer-bot run again. If it stalls, ask politely in Slack.
verify: The PR links the issue and keeps the template headings
CI has passed on the last commit, since GitHub requires it before merge
Every review comment has a reply or a commit addressing it

steps.title: Write up the FlashInfer fix and choose the next rung
steps.learn: Record what the bug was, which layer held it, how you proved the fix (test, GPU, numbers) and what review changed. Next rungs: a perf PR in the same op, a new backend comparison, or support for another GPU arch.
verify: The write-up states the GPU, CUDA version and commands for every number
It names one thing reviewers changed and why
It names a concrete next issue or op to work on

projects.problem: FlashInfer is a JIT-compiled CUDA kernel library for LLM serving; contributing teaches paged-KV attention, kernel testing and GPU benchmarking.
projects.proveIt: A PR that passes pre-commit and the GPU CI run, gets maintainer review, plus a write-up with before and after numbers if it touches performance
projects.hardware: Linux with an NVIDIA GPU (SM75 Turing or newer); many kernels need Hopper SM90 or Blackwell SM100
projects.aiPolicy: CONTRIBUTING says AI-assisted contributions are supported, but authors must understand and explain their changes; a PR may be rejected if they cannot.

projects.title: FlashAttention
projects.question: How do you get a reviewed change into FlashAttention, where active work is the CuTeDSL FlashAttention-4 kernels for Hopper and Blackwell?

steps.title: Frame a FlashAttention-4 contribution and the unwritten rules
steps.learn: Active work is FA4 in flash_attn/cute (CuTeDSL); FA2 (csrc/) and FA3 (hopper/) are older. There is no CONTRIBUTING file, PR template, CLA, DCO or AI policy; CLAUDE.md is guidance for agents. Talk via Issues and Discussions. Open PRs pile up, so expect slow review.
verify: You read CLAUDE.md and flash_attn/cute/README.md and know which directory each FA generation lives in
You confirmed the license is BSD-3-Clause
You skimmed recent merged PRs to see what size and style of change gets merged

steps.title: Install FA4 in dev mode and run one test file on your GPU
steps.learn: FA4 kernels are Python compiled at runtime by CuTeDSL, so the dev install is pip install -e "flash_attn/cute[dev]" (add cu13 on CUDA 13). FA2 instead needs a long nvcc build with ninja; the README suggests MAX_JOBS to limit RAM. Compilation dominates FA4 test time.

decision.choice: FA4 editable install plus the persistent compile cache for tests
decision.why: No C++ build step, edits to kernel Python take effect on the next run, and FLASH_ATTENTION_CUTE_DSL_CACHE_ENABLED=1 keeps compiled kernels across test runs.

alternatives.name: FA2 source build (pip install --no-build-isolation .)
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed only for FA2 csrc fixes or packaging; slow nvcc build and a large RAM need unless MAX_JOBS is set.

alternatives.name: FA3 build in hopper/
alternatives.tradeoff: For FA3 Hopper fixes only; README marks it beta and it needs H100 and CUDA 12.3+.

verify: pytest tests/cute/test_flash_attn.py -k test_flash_attn_output -x passes on your GPU
A second run is much faster with the disk cache on, and you recorded both times
You noted your GPU arch and CUDA and CuTeDSL versions

steps.title: Trace flash_attn_func through the FA4 forward kernel
steps.learn: flash_attn_func (interface.py) wraps FlashAttnFunc, which calls _flash_attn_fwd. It picks tile sizes, then FlashAttentionForwardSm90 (flash_fwd_sm90.py) or FlashAttentionForwardSm100 (flash_fwd_sm100.py), compiles with cute.compile and caches by dtype, head_dim, masks and arch. softmax.py and mask.py hold shared logic.
verify: You can name the file and class used for your GPU arch and where the compile cache key is built
You can explain what flash_fwd_combine.py does for SplitKV
You can find where score_mod and mask_mod callables are injected

steps.title: Learn tiled online softmax and pick the FA4 area to target
steps.learn: FlashAttention tiles Q, K, V into on-chip memory and keeps a running row max and sum so the full score matrix is never written to HBM. FA2 repartitions work across warps; FA3 adds Hopper asynchrony (warp specialization, TMA) and FP8. FA4 carries this into CuTeDSL for Blackwell.

decision.choice: Target test infrastructure and score_mod or mask_mod paths in flash_attn/cute
decision.why: These touch the real kernels through well-defined hooks and have many test files, so you add value without rewriting a pipelined SM100 kernel. Confirm in an issue that a gap is wanted before you fill it.

alternatives.name: SM100 forward or backward kernel internals
alternatives.tradeoff: Highest impact, but needs a B200, deep knowledge of 2CTA and barriers, and close maintainer contact.

alternatives.name: FA2 build and packaging issues
alternatives.tradeoff: Many users hit them and no new GPU is needed beyond Ampere, but the code is in maintenance mode.

verify: You can write the online softmax update for one new tile (new max, rescaled sum and output)
You can say which FA paper introduced warp specialization and FP8 for Hopper

steps.title: Add one small FA4 test case, and ask before any test refactor
steps.learn: Review is slow and nothing is labeled for newcomers, so a first PR must be small and clearly wanted. CLAUDE.md notes many tests/cute files lack the compile pass, but no issue asks for conversions; propose one in an issue first. Meanwhile a single missing test case is a safe start.

decision.choice: Add one missing test case for the path you traced; propose any compile-pass conversion in an issue first
decision.why: A small added test is easy to review, needs no maintainer buy-in, and teaches the test fixtures and eager reference. A test-file conversion touches many tests, so a maintainer should agree to it in an issue before you start.

alternatives.name: Docs fix in README or CLAUDE.md
alternatives.tradeoff: No GPU needed and quick, but low learning value and small benefit.

alternatives.name: Convert one test file to the compile pass, if agreed
alternatives.tradeoff: Teaches the FakeTensorMode pattern (@maybe_fake_tensor_mode, is_fake_mode), but it is a large diff; do it only after a maintainer agrees in an issue.

verify: Your new test passes on your GPU and fails if you revert the behavior it checks
Any refactor beyond one test was agreed by a maintainer in an issue before you opened the PR
ruff check and ruff format pass on the file

steps.title: Pick an open FA4 issue and write a failing test
steps.learn: Labels exist (bug, good first issue, help wanted) but open issues are effectively unlabeled and good first issue has none open, so search by FA4 terms (cute, sm100, varlen, mask_mod) and recent activity. Pick a report you can reproduce on your GPU.

decision.choice: Reproduce as a pytest case in tests/cute compared to the eager reference
decision.why: tests/cute already has eager_reference.py and parametrized fixtures, so a failing case drops straight into the PR and runs the same way maintainers test.

alternatives.name: Standalone script in agent_space/
alternatives.tradeoff: CLAUDE.md suggests agent_space/ for scratch repros; fast to iterate but must become a test before the PR.

alternatives.name: Reproduce via benchmark_attn.py
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for perf regressions across backends, not for correctness bugs.

verify: The failing case reproduces on your GPU with fixed seed, shapes and dtype
You posted the minimal repro and environment on the issue before writing a fix
You confirmed nobody else has an open PR for the same issue

links.label: Open FA4 (cute) issues by recent activity

steps.title: Fix the FA4 bug with a failing test first
steps.learn: For hangs, illegal addresses or numerical mismatches, CLAUDE.md requires reading AI/DEBUG_METHODOLOGY.md first: falsifiable predictions and a hypothesis log. Tools: cute.printf with thread guards, compute-sanitizer racecheck (TMA false positives are documented), CUTE_DSL_KEEP_PTX=1. Understand every changed line.
steps.delegate: In Dao-AILab/flash-attention, follow CLAUDE.md. Target flash_attn/cute. First add a failing pytest in tests/cute reproducing <bug, dtype, head_dim, seqlens, causal, GPU arch>, compared against tests/cute/eager_reference.py. Support the compile pass with @maybe_fake_tensor_mode and is_fake_mode(). Then make the minimal kernel or interface fix; do not reformat the large excluded files. Run ruff check and ruff format on flash_attn/cute and the touched test file.
verify: The new test fails on main and passes with your fix on your GPU
You can explain the root cause using evidence, not a guess, per DEBUG_METHODOLOGY.md
Neighboring parameter combinations in the same test file still pass

steps.title: Run ruff and GPU tests yourself, since PRs get no GPU CI
steps.learn: The GPU CI workflow (ci.yml) runs on pushes to main on a self-hosted B200, not on pull requests. PRs get only the pre-commit lint workflow, and only for some paths. So the test evidence in your PR is yours: list the commands, GPU and pass counts. Large kernel files are excluded from ruff format.
verify: ruff check and ruff format --check pass on the flash_attn/cute files you touched, using the same excludes as ci.yml
You ran the touched test files and the CI filter tests on your GPU and saved the summary
You recorded GPU model, driver, CUDA and nvidia-cutlass-dsl versions

steps.title: Benchmark an FA4 change with benchmark_attn.py
steps.learn: benchmarks/benchmark_attn.py compares backends (FA2, FA3, FA4 cute, cuDNN when installed) over head dims, sequence lengths, causal and varlen, with --warmup and --rep. Report TFLOPS or time before and after on the same GPU, clocks and shapes.

decision.choice: benchmark_attn.py with fixed shapes, forward and backward separately, several repeats
decision.why: It is the repo's own harness, so maintainers can rerun it, and it compares against FA3 and cuDNN on the same machine, which puts your change in context.

alternatives.name: Nsight Compute on one kernel
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows why throughput changed (tensor core use, stalls); use alongside, not instead of, end to end numbers.

alternatives.name: Custom script with CUDA events
alternatives.tradeoff: Full control over inputs, but harder for reviewers to compare with their own runs.

verify: You report before and after numbers for at least three shapes on a named GPU
You ran each configuration several times and report the spread
The correctness tests for the same shapes still pass

steps.title: Open the FlashAttention PR and keep it reviewable
steps.learn: With no template, write your own: problem, linked issue, root cause, fix, test commands with GPU and results, benchmark numbers if relevant. Keep one change per PR and avoid reformatting. Review queues are long; if it stalls, rebase on main and ask once in the issue thread.
verify: The PR links the issue and lists exact test commands, GPU and results
The diff touches only files needed for the fix
Every review comment has a reply or a commit addressing it

steps.title: Write up the FA4 change and choose the next rung
steps.learn: Record the bug or gap, the evidence that located it, how you tested on which GPU, review changes, and numbers. Next rungs: a test-file conversion a maintainer agreed to, a mask_mod or score_mod feature, or an SM90 tile-size study (AI/SM90_BLOCK_SIZE_TUNING.md).
verify: The write-up gives GPU, CUDA and CuTeDSL versions and commands for every number
It names one thing review changed and why
It names a concrete next rung

projects.problem: FlashAttention is the reference fast exact-attention library; contributing teaches tiled online softmax, CuTeDSL kernels and GPU testing.
projects.proveIt: A PR to flash_attn/cute that passes lint and your own GPU test run, gets maintainer review, plus a write-up with test and benchmark evidence
projects.hardware: Linux with an NVIDIA Hopper (H100) or Blackwell (B200) GPU for FA4; FA2 needs Ampere, Ada or Hopper and CUDA 12.0+

projects.title: Triton
projects.question: Can I take one Triton compiler or frontend bug from a minimal reproducer to a reviewed PR that passes Triton's CI?

steps.title: Set your Triton target and read the contribution rules
steps.learn: Triton (MIT) has a Python frontend, MLIR passes and NVIDIA/AMD backends. Goal: a PR that passes CI and gets review. CONTRIBUTING.md warns maintainers may not review promptly and favors bug fixes with minimized tests. No CLA or DCO file exists. First-time merges are rare.
verify: Read CONTRIBUTING.md and write down which changes it calls uncontroversial and which it calls controversial
Open the checks of a recently merged PR and confirm no CLA or DCO check runs
Read AGENTS.md and the PR template; note the new-contributor checklist items
Join the GPU MODE Discord triton channel linked from the issue template config

steps.title: Build Triton from source and run the no-GPU test suite
steps.learn: The README build is `pip install -r python/requirements.txt` then `pip install -e .`, which downloads a prebuilt LLVM. `make dev-install` also installs test requirements. `make test` needs a GPU; `make test-nogpu` runs lit, C++ unit and frontend tests. TRITON_BUILD_WITH_CCACHE and MAX_JOBS help.

decision.choice: `make dev-install` (editable install against the prebuilt LLVM, with --no-build-isolation)
decision.why: It is the documented developer path, keeps nop rebuilds fast, and gives you triton-opt and the lit tests that most compiler PRs need. You only rebuild LLVM if your change depends on LLVM itself.

alternatives.name: `make dev-install-llvm` (custom LLVM build)
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed when you patch LLVM or debug an LLVM bump at the hash in cmake/llvm-info.json; costs a long LLVM build and disk space.

alternatives.name: `pip install triton` wheel
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine for writing kernels or using the interpreter, but you cannot change or test the compiler.

alternatives.name: triton-dev-containers Dev Container
alternatives.tradeoff: Consistent environment linked from the README, but maintained in a separate Red Hat repo, so it can lag main.

verify: `python -c "import triton; print(triton.__file__)"` points into your checkout
`make test-nogpu` finishes; record wall time and any failures
After touching one .cpp file, `make` rebuilds incrementally; record how long it takes

steps.title: Trace one @triton.jit kernel from Python AST to cubin
steps.learn: JITFunction.run (runtime/jit.py) calls compile() in python/triton/compiler/compiler.py; ast_to_ttir in code_generator.py emits Triton IR. The NVIDIA backend's add_stages (third_party/nvidia/backend/compiler.py) runs make_ttir, make_ttgir, make_llir, make_ptx, make_cubin. Passes: lib/Dialect, lib/Conversion.
steps.delegate: Write a small Python script for a triton-lang/triton source checkout that runs python/tutorials/01-vector-add.py with TRITON_ALWAYS_COMPILE=1, TRITON_KERNEL_DUMP=1 and TRITON_DUMP_DIR=./dump set, then lists the files produced per stage (ttir, ttgir, llir, ptx) with line counts. Also run it once with MLIR_ENABLE_DUMP=1 and MLIR_DUMP_PATH set, and print the ordered list of pass names found in the dump.
verify: Find the stages dict in add_stages and name the five NVIDIA stages in order
From the MLIR dump, name three TritonGPU passes and find each source file in lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms
In the MLIR_ENABLE_DUMP output, find the pass after which #blocked layouts first appear and name it

steps.title: Learn Triton's block model and pick the subsystem to target
steps.learn: Triton programs work on blocks, not threads; the compiler picks layouts and passes such as Coalesce, RemoveLayoutConversions, AccelerateMatmul and the Pipeliner map them to hardware. AGENTS.md says scalars are block-uniform and tests must be valid block programs. Read the MAPL 2019 paper and tutorial 03.

decision.choice: Python frontend and interpreter (python/triton/language, python/triton/runtime/interpreter.py)
decision.why: Python-only changes need no C++ rebuild (AGENTS.md), the interpreter runs with TRITON_INTERPRET=1 on CPU, tests sit in python/test/unit/language, and there is an 'interpreter' label for scoped issues.

alternatives.name: TritonGPU passes (lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms)
alternatives.tradeoff: Core of performance and lit tests run without a GPU, but C++/MLIR is harder and IR or pass design changes count as controversial.

alternatives.name: NVIDIA or AMD backend (third_party/nvidia, amd)
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick if you own matching hardware; CI tests A100, H100, GB200 and AMD gfx90a/gfx942/gfx950, and many bugs only reproduce on one arch.

alternatives.name: Proton profiler (third_party/proton)
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller module with its own maintainer and 'proton' label; less central to the compiler.

verify: Explain in two sentences why a layout conversion can be costly, using a ttgir dump you produced
Run tutorial 03 matmul and state which block size config the autotuner chose (TRITON_PRINT_AUTOTUNING=1)
List three open issues in your chosen subsystem with their labels

steps.title: Choose a first Triton PR that is small but not trivial
steps.learn: The PR template asks new contributors (under 3 merged PRs) to confirm they are not making a trivial change such as a comment typo. Good first rungs: a missing regression test, an undocumented knob from python/triton/knobs.py, or a broken tutorial. The 'documentation' label exists.

decision.choice: Add a missing minimized regression test, or fix a substantive doc gap tied to real behavior
decision.why: CONTRIBUTING values minimized unit tests, and the template rules out trivial edits, so a test or a doc fix that prevents a real mistake is both welcome and small enough to review.

alternatives.name: Fix a tutorial in python/tutorials
alternatives.tradeoff: Visible and useful, but tutorials run on a GPU and some depend on a specific architecture, so verifying takes hardware.

alternatives.name: Typo or comment fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest to write, but the template asks new contributors not to send trivial changes, so it likely wastes a review slot.

verify: Your change passes the 'not a trivial change' item in the PR template, in your own honest judgment
The test runs with `pytest file.py::test_name -s --tb=short`, or `lit -v test/<path>.mlir` from the build dir
You searched open PRs to confirm nobody already sent the same change

steps.title: Reduce a Triton bug to a minimal kernel or lit test
steps.learn: Real labels: bug, needs reproducer, help wanted, interpreter, performance, proton. There is no 'good first issue' label. TRITON_REPRODUCER_PATH captures an MLIR reproducer; `triton-opt file.mlir --run-reproducer` replays it. TRITON_INTERPRET=1 tells semantics bugs from compiler bugs.

decision.choice: An open, unassigned 'bug' or 'needs reproducer' issue with recent activity, reduced to a lit test where possible
decision.why: Lit tests run without a GPU and are what reviewers want for pass bugs; a 'needs reproducer' issue lets you add value even before a fix.

alternatives.name: End-to-end pytest in python/test/unit
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed when the bug only shows at runtime, but requires the right GPU and is slower than lit.

alternatives.name: A bug you hit in your own kernels
alternatives.tradeoff: You understand it best, but search first; check for duplicates (there is a 'duplicate' label).

verify: The reproducer fails on current main for the reason stated in the issue
It is a valid block program with no inline asm or hardware-ID tricks, per AGENTS.md
You posted the minimal repro on the issue before starting the fix

steps.title: Fix the bug test-first in the pass that causes it
steps.learn: Triton has no written AI-contribution policy, but AGENTS.md gives agents its build and lowering rules, and maintainers judge quality, so you must understand every line. Lowerings may inspect only the op they lower; cross-op reasoning belongs in a separate analysis or pass.

decision.choice: Fix where the bad IR is first produced, guarded by a failing lit or pytest test
decision.why: AGENTS.md forbids lowerings that look at other ops, and reviewers reject guards that mask a root cause; a test pinned to the producing pass is minimal and stable.

alternatives.name: Guard or fallback in the lowering
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller diff, but often hides the real bug and conflicts with AGENTS.md lowering rules.

alternatives.name: Python frontend check that rejects the input
alternatives.tradeoff: Right when the program is invalid, wrong when it is valid; it removes the crash but not the bug.

steps.delegate: In triton-lang/triton, fix <bug>. First add a failing test: a lit test in the existing file under test/<Dialect>/ run via `lit -v` from the build dir, or a pytest in an existing python/test/unit file named test_<feature>_<condition>. Then make the smallest fix in the pass that produces the bad IR. Follow AGENTS.md: no side effects in C++ assert, lowerings inspect only their op, no MLIR index type. Rebuild with `make` only for C++ changes. Explain each changed line.
verify: The new test fails before your fix and passes after it

steps.title: Run pre-commit and the matching Triton test subset
steps.learn: .pre-commit-config.yaml runs ruff, yapf, clang-format, mypy and file hygiene hooks. CI (ci.yml) runs pre-commit, NVIDIA (A100, H100, GB200) and AMD integration tests, and a macOS build. Locally use `make test-lit`, `make test-cpp`, or one pytest test.

decision.choice: pre-commit on your range plus the test targets that cover the touched code
decision.why: The PR template requires `pre-commit run --from-ref origin/main --to-ref HEAD`, and the subset (lit for passes, unit pytest for frontend) catches most failures before CI GPU time.

alternatives.name: Full `make test`
alternatives.tradeoff: Most thorough, but needs a GPU and takes a long time; worth it only for broad changes.

alternatives.name: Push and let CI find failures
alternatives.tradeoff: No local GPU needed, but each round costs reviewers attention and shared CI time.

steps.title: Measure a kernel change with triton.testing.do_bench
steps.learn: triton.testing has do_bench (warmup, rep, quantiles), do_bench_cudagraph, perf_report and Benchmark. python/triton_kernels/bench holds matmul and MLP benchmarks; `make test-microbenchmark` runs launch_overhead.py. CONTRIBUTING may reject perf wins whose complexity outweighs the gain.

decision.why: It is the repo's own harness, so reviewers trust and can rerun it; quantiles show variance instead of a single mean.

alternatives.name: do_bench_cudagraph
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for tiny kernels where launch overhead dominates; less representative of eager use.

alternatives.name: Proton profiler
alternatives.tradeoff: Gives per-kernel and hardware-trace breakdowns that explain why, but is heavier to set up than a timing.

steps.title: Open the PR with Triton's new-contributor checklist
steps.learn: Fill the template checklist: non-trivial change, description following the linked commit-message rules, pre-commit run, tests added (/test lit, /unittest C++, /python/test end-to-end), and minimal lit tests. Link the issue. No sign-off is required. If review stalls, rebase on main and ask once on the issue or Discord.

decision.choice: One focused PR with the fix and its minimized test
decision.why: CONTRIBUTING says bug fixes with minimized tests are the changes maintainers commit to accepting; a small diff is easiest to review given limited maintainer time.

alternatives.name: Issue or design discussion first
alternatives.tradeoff: Right for IR, API or pass changes, which are judged case by case; slower but avoids rejected work.

alternatives.name: Several stacked PRs
alternatives.tradeoff: Fits larger features, but each needs its own review and a newcomer rarely gets that bandwidth.

steps.title: Write up the Triton fix and pick the next rung
steps.learn: Write four parts: the one question, numbers for every claim with GPU and command, why the bug or speedup happened at the IR level, and what the change does not cover (other archs, dtypes). projects.problem: Triton is a Python DSL and MLIR compiler for GPU kernels; contributing teaches compiler passes, GPU layouts and lit testing.
projects.proveIt: A PR with a minimized regression test that passes pre-commit and CI and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up.

projects.title: CUTLASS and CuTe
projects.question: Can I find, reproduce and fix a CuTe or CUTLASS bug with a GoogleTest and get it reviewed by NVIDIA maintainers?

steps.title: Set your CUTLASS target and learn how fixes really land
steps.learn: LICENSE.txt is BSD-3-Clause, but python/CuTeDSL is under an NVIDIA EULA (EULA.txt). There is no root CONTRIBUTING.md; the Python docs contribute page says file issues, send PRs, ask in Discussions. No CLA or DCO is documented. Many outside PRs merge directly; some close when the fix already landed internally.
verify: Read LICENSE.txt and name the directory that is under the NVIDIA EULA
Read ten recently closed PRs and count merged vs closed with a maintainer comment
Find the CUTLASS Discord link in the issue template config and the Discussions tab

steps.title: Configure CMake for one GPU arch and run the CuTe core tests
steps.learn: CUTLASS is header-only; CMake builds tests, examples and the profiler. Set CUDACXX to nvcc, then `cmake .. -DCUTLASS_NVCC_ARCHS=<arch>` (90a for Hopper features, 100a for Blackwell SM100). `make test_unit_cute_core` builds host-only layout algebra tests (WITHOUT_CUDA).

decision.choice: A build directory configured for only your GPU's arch, starting with `make test_unit_cute_core`
decision.why: By default CUTLASS builds for many architectures and the full test set takes long; one arch plus the host-only CuTe tests gives a fast loop that most CuTe changes need.

alternatives.name: Full `make test_unit -j`
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers every namespace, but compile time is long; use it before a broad change, not every edit.

alternatives.name: CuTe DSL editable install
alternatives.tradeoff: `pip install -e "python/CuTeDSL[cu13]"` (per cutlass_cicd/README.md) for Python DSL work; EULA-licensed and needs an SM80+ GPU.

alternatives.name: Profiler-only build
alternatives.tradeoff: `-DCUTLASS_ENABLE_TESTS=OFF -DCUTLASS_UNITY_BUILD_ENABLED=ON` from the quickstart; good for perf work, skips tests.

verify: `make test_unit_cute_core` passes; record build and run time
`nvcc --version` and `nvidia-smi` output are saved with your notes
You can explain why 90a rather than 90 is needed for Hopper Tensor Core instructions

steps.title: Trace a Hopper GEMM from collective builder to MMA atom
steps.learn: Example 49 uses the collective builder: adapter (include/cutlass/gemm/device/gemm_universal_adapter.h), kernel (gemm/kernel/sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized*.hpp), collective (gemm/collective/collective_builder.hpp, builders/), then CuTe atoms (cute/atom/mma_atom.hpp) and PTX wrappers (cute/arch/mma_sm90_gmma.hpp).
steps.delegate: In an NVIDIA/cutlass checkout, write a short annotated call map (markdown, not code changes) for examples/49_hopper_gemm_with_collective_builder/49_collective_builder.cu: for its default config, list the template types the CollectiveBuilder resolves to, the kernel header under include/cutlass/gemm/kernel it instantiates, and the MMA atom and PTX wrapper in include/cute it ends at, with file paths and line numbers. Flag any step you could not confirm by reading the code.

Name the kernel schedule file selected and check it exists in include/cutlass/gemm/kernel

steps.title: Learn CuTe layout algebra and pick the area to target
steps.learn: A CuTe Layout is a shape and stride pair mapping coordinates to indices. Composition, complement, logical_divide and logical_product tile and partition data across threads and copies. Read the layout and layout algebra docs, then the CuTe GEMM tutorial and examples/cute/tutorial.

decision.choice: CuTe C++ core (include/cute, tests in test/unit/cute)
decision.why: Layout algebra is precise math with host-only tests, so you can test changes quickly, and it underpins every CUTLASS 3.x kernel, so the knowledge transfers.

alternatives.name: CUTLASS 3.x GEMM collectives and kernels
alternatives.tradeoff: Where most user bugs live, but arch-specific; you need the matching Hopper or Blackwell GPU and long builds.

alternatives.name: CuTe DSL (python/CuTeDSL, examples/python/CuTeDSL)
alternatives.tradeoff: Python, fast compiles and many recent PRs, but python/CuTeDSL is EULA-licensed (examples are BSD-3-Clause) and needs an SM80+ GPU.

alternatives.name: cutlass_profiler and tools
alternatives.tradeoff: Host-side C++ that is easier to read, but fewer issues and less kernel learning.

verify: By hand, compute logical_divide of a small layout and match a case in test/unit/cute/core/logical_divide.cpp

steps.title: Start with a CuTe unit test, example fix or doc correction
steps.learn: Real labels include documentation, CuTe, CuTe DSL, CUTLASS C++, good first issue and help wanted; few good first issues are open at a time. A documentation_request issue template exists. Prefer changes with substance; small outside fixes do merge, but duplicates of internal fixes get closed.

decision.choice: Add missing coverage to test/unit/cute/core or fix a broken example
decision.why: Tests and examples are self-contained, easy to verify on your hardware, and a test that guards a real edge case stays useful even if maintainers re-land it internally.

alternatives.name: Docs fix in media/docs
alternatives.tradeoff: Low risk and no GPU needed, and outside docs fixes do get merged, but you learn little about kernels or the CuTe algebra.

alternatives.name: File a documentation_request issue
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheapest way to report a gap, but you build no code or review experience.

steps.title: Reproduce a CUTLASS bug in a standalone .cu or GoogleTest
steps.learn: Issues get labels like '? - Needs Triage', bug, CuTe, CuTe DSL and CUTLASS C++; a stale bot adds inactive-30d and inactive-90d. Write a minimal .cu that only needs include/, and record nvcc version, arch flag and driver. Check CHANGELOG.md first: the bug may already be fixed in a release.

decision.choice: A triaged bug on an arch you own, with a stated repro and no inactive-90d label
decision.why: Arch-specific CUTLASS bugs cannot be checked without the GPU, and quiet threads may already be fixed internally; a recent, triaged issue is the best bet for review.

alternatives.name: A bug you hit in your own CUTLASS use
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong motivation and context, but confirm it on main first; it may be fixed in the latest release.

alternatives.name: A CuTe DSL bug
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster Python repro, but parts of the DSL stack install as runtime wheels from PyPI, not repo code.

steps.title: Fix the bug test-first in generic CuTe or the arch path
steps.learn: CUTLASS has no written AI-contribution policy. Template-heavy code hides many instantiations, so you must understand every line and know which architectures your change touches. Style is manual: the guidelines forbid automatic formatting and ask for standard C++ idioms.

decision.choice: Fix in the narrowest layer that owns the bug, with a failing gtest first
decision.why: A fix in a generic CuTe header affects every arch and kernel, so keep it narrow unless the bug is in the generic algebra; a gtest proves the exact case.

alternatives.name: Fix in generic CuTe (include/cute)
alternatives.tradeoff: Right when the algebra itself is wrong, but needs tests across several arch targets to show nothing else breaks.

alternatives.name: Arch-specific specialization (sm90/sm100 files)
alternatives.tradeoff: Smaller blast radius, but risks duplicating logic other archs also need.

steps.title: Run the right CUTLASS test targets since CI is maintainer-run
steps.learn: There is no pre-commit or clang-format config. Public GitHub Actions only label and mark stale; blossom-ci.yml runs only when an allowlisted maintainer comments `/bot run`, and recent outside PRs merged with no CI checks. cutlass_cicd/test.py describes the L0 suites and supports --dry-run.

decision.choice: Run the unit test targets for every namespace you touched on your arch, plus a compile for one other arch
decision.why: You get no CI signal until a maintainer runs it, so local evidence is all reviewers see first; a second arch compile catches template breakage elsewhere.

alternatives.name: Full `make test_unit`
alternatives.tradeoff: Strongest local evidence, but long compile; worth it for changes in generic CuTe headers.

alternatives.name: cutlass_cicd/test.py L0 suite
alternatives.tradeoff: Mirrors CI suites (L0_functional, L0_oss_dsl_test), but needs a built package and more setup.

steps.learn: `make cutlass_profiler` builds tools/profiler; filter kernels at configure time with CUTLASS_LIBRARY_KERNELS and at run time with --kernels. It verifies against cuBLAS and supports --warmup-iterations, --profiling-iterations and --output CSV. The methodology doc covers buffer rotation and fixed-clock tests.

steps.title: Open the CUTLASS PR and plan for the release-sync path
steps.learn: There is no PR template, so write your own: issue link, repro, arch, CUDA version, test commands and results. CI rarely runs on outside PRs, so reviewers rely on your evidence. A PR may be closed if the same fix already landed in a versioned update commit. Silent PRs get inactive-30d labels.

decision.choice: One small PR linked to the issue, with the repro and test output in the description
decision.why: Maintainers merge clear outside fixes directly and sometimes fix the same bug internally, so a clear repro and test make your change easy to adopt either way.

alternatives.name: Post the fix on the issue first
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for arch-specific kernels the team may already be changing internally; slower, but avoids duplicate work.

alternatives.name: Draft PR for early feedback
alternatives.tradeoff: Gets eyes on the approach, but a draft without tests is easy to ignore.

steps.learn: Write four parts: the one question, numbers with GPU and command, why the bug happened in layout or template terms, and limits (archs and dtypes not tested). Next rungs: a CuTe DSL example, a Hopper or Blackwell collective fix, or a profiler improvement.

projects.problem: CUTLASS is NVIDIA's header-only CUDA C++ GEMM template library built on CuTe layouts; contributing teaches tiling and Tensor Core kernels.
projects.proveIt: A PR with a failing-then-passing unit test that gets maintainer review and ideally a merge, plus a write-up.

projects.title: PyTorch
projects.question: How do I get a reviewed PR into PyTorch's torch.compile stack (Dynamo and Inductor) as an outside contributor?

steps.title: Frame an Inductor contribution and PyTorch's PR rules
steps.learn: Aim at torch/_inductor. Success is a PR that passes CI and gets review; merge is up to maintainers. Rules: PRs from non-writers must link an issue labeled actionable or name a pre-approving maintainer, or they are closed. EasyCLA runs on every PR. Questions go to discuss.pytorch.org or the PyTorch Slack.
verify: Read the Issue and PR Workflow section of CONTRIBUTING.md and list the five issue triage labels
Read AI_POLICY.md and note how AI-generated content must be disclosed
Find the EasyCLA check on any open PR and sign the CLA for your GitHub account

steps.title: Set up a dev env: nightly checkout or full source build
steps.learn: Inductor and most of Dynamo are Python, so tools/nightly.py can check out a branch with prebuilt nightly binaries. Touching ATen or C++ (including torch/csrc/dynamo) needs python -m pip install --no-build-isolation -v -e . after pip install --group dev; the README warns of 30 to 60 minutes.

decision.choice: ./tools/nightly.py checkout -b my-branch (add --cuda on an NVIDIA box) for Python-only Inductor work
decision.why: Inductor changes live in torch/_inductor Python files, so a nightly checkout gives a working dev tree in minutes instead of a long C++ build, and matches the binaries CI tests against closely enough for Python changes.

alternatives.name: Full editable source build
alternatives.tradeoff: Required once you touch aten, c10 or torch/csrc; costs 30 to 60 minutes and a C++20 compiler (gcc 11.3+ on Linux).

alternatives.name: spin develop
alternatives.tradeoff: Same editable build through the spin CLI, which prefers uv pip; convenient but still a full C++ build.

alternatives.name: CPU-only build with USE_CUDA=0
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster and works without a GPU, but you cannot test Triton GPU codegen.

steps.delegate: Write a bash script that clones pytorch/pytorch, runs ./tools/nightly.py checkout -b inductor-dev (with --cuda if nvidia-smi exists), activates the created venv, installs pytest, and runs pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py -k test_add_const_int -x. Print the torch version and torch.cuda.is_available(). Exit nonzero on any failure.
verify: python -c 'import torch; print(torch.__file__)' points inside your checkout
pytest test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py -k test_add_const_int passes on your machine
Record build method, time taken and GPU model in your notes

steps.title: Trace one torch.compile call from Dynamo to generated Triton
steps.learn: torch/_dynamo/eval_frame.py hooks the frame, convert_frame.py and symbolic_convert.py trace bytecode into an FX graph, then torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py runs AOTAutograd (torch/_functorch/aot_autograd.py) and compiles each graph via graph.py, lowering.py, scheduler.py and codegen/triton.py.
verify: Run a 3-op function under torch.compile with TORCH_LOGS=output_code and save the generated kernel
Set a breakpoint in torch/_inductor/compile_fx.py and confirm it is hit for your function
Write the call chain with one sentence per file in your notes

steps.title: Learn Inductor's loop-level IR and choose a target area
steps.learn: Inductor lowers ATen ops to a define-by-run loop IR (ir.py), the scheduler fuses nodes that share loops to cut memory traffic, and backends emit Triton for GPUs or C++ for CPUs (codegen/cpp.py). Most bugs are a wrong lowering, a bad fusion decision, or a codegen corner case.

decision.choice: Target lowerings and their tests (lowering.py, test/inductor)
decision.why: Lowering bugs are local: one op, one decomposition, a small repro, and an existing test file to extend. They need less context than the scheduler and can often be tested on CPU, which suits a first real contribution.

alternatives.name: Scheduler and fusion heuristics
alternatives.tradeoff: High impact, but changes ripple into performance across many models and need benchmark evidence and deep review.

alternatives.name: Dynamo graph breaks
alternatives.tradeoff: Many reported issues, but requires understanding Python bytecode tracing and guards; good second rung.

alternatives.name: Triton codegen templates
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to GPU kernels, but needs an NVIDIA GPU and Triton knowledge to test well.

verify: Explain in two sentences why fusing a pointwise op into a reduction saves memory bandwidth
Find where one simple op (for example aten.add) is registered in torch/_inductor/lowering.py
Read the TorchInductor design post and note how it handles views and mutation, symbolic shapes, and its define-by-run loop IR

steps.title: Land a first docs or test PR on an actionable issue
steps.learn: PyTorch closes PRs not tied to an actionable issue, so even a docs fix needs one. Labels such as good first issue, module: docs and module: inductor exist. Docstrings use Google style with lines under 80 characters; building docs needs Python below 3.13 and katex.

decision.choice: A docstring or missing-test fix on an issue labeled good first issue or module: docs plus actionable
decision.why: It exercises the whole pipeline (EasyCLA, triage bot, pre-review, CI, @pytorchbot merge) with little code risk, so you learn the process before spending days on a compiler fix.

alternatives.name: Add a regression test only
alternatives.tradeoff: Valuable if the issue asks for it, but a test with no linked actionable issue will be closed.

alternatives.name: Skip straight to a bug fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves a cycle, but process mistakes then cost you a long review on a large diff.

verify: The issue you pick has the actionable label and no assignee
Your docs change renders correctly in a local docs build or the PR docs preview
Your PR description links the issue with Fixes #

steps.title: Reproduce an actionable Inductor bug as a failing test
steps.learn: Filter issues by module: inductor (or oncall: pt2) plus actionable and no assignee. Shrink the repro: compare backend=eager, aot_eager and inductor to see which layer breaks, use TORCH_LOGS (graph_breaks, output_code) and tlparse, and the minifier for large models.

decision.choice: Turn the repro into a test in test/inductor/test_cpu_repro.py or test_cuda_repro.py
decision.why: Repro test files are where Inductor keeps small regression cases, so a reviewer can read your test next to similar ones and CI will guard the fix.

alternatives.name: Add to test_torchinductor.py
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs on several devices from one test, but the file is large and the test must fit its device-generic pattern.

alternatives.name: Standalone script in the issue
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest to share, but nothing prevents a regression after merge.

verify: The repro fails with backend=inductor and passes with backend=eager
The failing test runs in under a few seconds with pytest -k
You commented on the issue with the minimal repro before coding a fix

steps.title: Fix the Inductor bug with the failing test committed first
steps.learn: Fix at the layer that is wrong: a lowering in lowering.py, a decomposition, or codegen. Keep the diff minimal and match nearby style. Per AI_POLICY.md you must read and understand every line, and any agent output in the PR goes under the template's Agent details section.
steps.delegate: In pytorch/pytorch, the test <name> in test/inductor/<file>.py fails because <symptom>. First confirm it fails with pytest -k <name>. Then find the cause in torch/_inductor (lowering.py, decomposition.py or codegen) and make the smallest fix. Follow the existing style, no unrelated refactors. Run the test, the rest of that file and lintrunner -a. Explain the root cause in 3 sentences and list every file you changed.
verify: You can explain the root cause without notes
The new test fails on main and passes with your change

steps.title: Pass lintrunner and the Inductor test subset locally
steps.learn: All linting (ruff, pyrefly, clang-tidy, clang-format and more) runs through lintrunner, configured in .lintrunner.toml; spin lint, spin quicklint and spin fixlint wrap it. Tests run with pytest or test/run_test.py, the orchestrator CI uses. Check HUD to see if a CI failure is already failing on main.

steps.title: Measure a kernel change with PyTorch's benchmark harnesses
steps.learn: The PR template asks for benchmark results on perf PRs. benchmarks/dynamo has torchbench.py, huggingface.py and timm_models.py, and the nightly dashboard runs on an A100. For one op, torch.utils.benchmark.Timer handles warmup and CUDA sync. Report median, spread and the GPU.

decision.choice: torch.utils.benchmark for the op plus a few models via benchmarks/dynamo/huggingface.py
decision.why: The microbenchmark isolates your kernel with proper synchronization, and a handful of real models shows the change does not regress end to end, which is the evidence Inductor reviewers ask for.

alternatives.name: benchmarks/operator_benchmark
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard op-level suite for eager ops; less relevant to compiled Inductor kernels.

alternatives.name: Nightly perf workflow on your branch
alternatives.tradeoff: Full dashboard comparison, but needs repo permissions and takes 4 to 12 hours.

steps.title: Open the PR as a draft and move it through pre-review
steps.learn: Open as a draft, fill the template (linked issue, BC-breaking, human-written summary), then mark ready. A bot triages, reviewers pre-review the direction, automated review and Dr. CI gate ready for review. After approval comment @pytorchbot merge. Ping after a week; PRs idle 60 days go Stale and close 30 days later.

decision.choice: A single small PR from a fork branch, rebased locally on main (or @pytorchbot rebase once allowed) when needed
decision.why: One focused PR is easiest to pre-review in under a minute, which the guide says reviewers aim for; ghstack stacks are for multi-commit series you do not need yet.

alternatives.name: ghstack stacked PRs
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for a series of dependent changes, but more tooling and more review surface for a first fix.

alternatives.name: Use the no-ci title prefix while iterating
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves CI time on drafts, but you must remove it and push again before review.

verify: The PR links an actionable issue with Fixes # or names the supporting maintainer
EasyCLA and lint checks are green
Every reviewer comment has a code change or a reply explaining why not

steps.title: Write up the Inductor fix and pick the next rung
steps.learn: Capture what the bug taught you about Inductor's layers, the review feedback, and any numbers. Next rungs: a Dynamo graph-break fix, a scheduler heuristic with benchmark evidence, or reviewing others' PRs in the same module.
verify: The write-up states the bug, root cause file and the fix in plain terms
Any performance claim lists the GPU, command and spread
