alternatives.tradeoff: Concurrent inserts and vacuum, as in the existing HNSW TAP tests, can surface new bugs; slower and harder to make deterministic.

alternatives.name: Run under Valgrind like CI
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds memory errors invisible in normal runs; needs a Valgrind-enabled Postgres build and runs much slower.

verify: A SQL script reproduces the bug on a fresh database with versions written down
Your new test fails on master for the reported reason
You checked closed issues and the CHANGELOG to make sure it is not already fixed

steps.title: Fix it in C with a test-first agent prompt
steps.learn: Postgres C rules apply: palloc in memory contexts, buffer pins and locks, page changes logged through GenericXLog, and PG_VERSION_NUM guards because Postgres 13 to 20 are tested. SQL object changes go in sql/vector.sql plus an upgrade script. You must understand every line.

decision.choice: A minimal fix that keeps the on-disk index format unchanged
decision.why: Format changes force reindexing or an upgrade path and need the maintainer's buy-in; a local fix is reviewable in one sitting.

alternatives.name: Change the index page layout
alternatives.tradeoff: Sometimes the only real fix; propose it in the issue first because it affects every existing index.

alternatives.name: A SQL-level change with an upgrade script
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed when operators, functions or opclasses change; adds a sql/vector--old--new.sql file and version handling.

steps.delegate: In pgvector/pgvector (C PGXS extension, tabs width 4 per .editorconfig, Postgres style, Postgres 13+ with PG_VERSION_NUM guards), first add a failing test: a pg_regress case in test/sql plus test/expected, or a TAP test in test/t for concurrency or recall. Then make the minimal fix in src/ without changing the on-disk format. Build with CI's PG_CFLAGS from .github/workflows/build.yml (assert, -Wall -Wextra -Werror and its -Wno flags), run make installcheck and the TAP test. Explain every change.
verify: The test fails on master and passes with the fix on an assert build
You can explain every palloc, lock and WAL call in the diff
No new warnings with CI's flags: -Wall -Wextra -Werror -Wno-unused-parameter -Wno-sign-compare (Ubuntu job)

steps.title: Reproduce the build workflow checks before pushing
steps.learn: The build workflow compiles with -DUSE_ASSERT_CHECKING -Wall -Wextra -Werror plus -Wno flags (unused-parameter, sign-compare) on Ubuntu for Postgres 13 to 20, macOS, Windows (nmake, Makefile.win), 32-bit Debian and Valgrind; macOS also runs scan-build --status-bugs.

decision.choice: Run installcheck and prove_installcheck with CI flags on the oldest and newest Postgres you can install
decision.why: Version guards and warnings are the most common cross-matrix failures, and two versions catch most of them before the maintainer sees red CI.

alternatives.name: Push to your fork and let Actions run
alternatives.tradeoff: The workflow runs on every push, so a fork with Actions enabled gets the full matrix; slower feedback per iteration.

alternatives.name: Add scan-build and Valgrind locally
alternatives.tradeoff: Matches the stricter CI jobs and finds memory bugs; needs LLVM and a Valgrind-enabled Postgres and takes longer.

verify: A clean build with the CI warning flags shows zero warnings
installcheck and prove_installcheck pass on two Postgres major versions
Your fork's build workflow is green on every matrix job

steps.title: Benchmark build, vacuum and query cost with the bench flags
steps.learn: PG_CFLAGS="-DHNSW_BENCH -DIVFFLAT_BENCH" makes phase timers print as INFO messages (IVFFlat build phases such as k-means, HNSW vacuum phases); -DHNSW_MEMORY -DIVFFLAT_MEMORY report memory. Speed claims need recall alongside, measured against an exact scan.

decision.choice: Report phase timings plus recall@10 and query latency at fixed index settings, before and after
decision.why: An ANN speedup that silently lowers recall is a regression, and phase timers show which part of build or vacuum your change moved.

alternatives.name: pgbench with a custom script
alternatives.tradeoff: Postgres's own tool measures throughput under concurrency; needs ground truth computed separately for recall.

alternatives.name: EXPLAIN ANALYZE only
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick per-query view, but single runs are noisy and say nothing about recall.

verify: Recall@10 is computed against exact results with the index disabled
At least 3 runs per side with spread, from a warm cache
CPU, Postgres version, shared_buffers and maintenance_work_mem are recorded

steps.title: Open a small PR and respect the maintainer's call
steps.learn: There is no PR template and no sign-off requirement. The default branch is master. Put the reproducer, test and versions in the PR. One maintainer reviews everything; a PR may be closed even when the issue gets fixed another way. If it stalls, one polite follow-up is enough.

decision.choice: One PR with the failing test and the fix, linked to the issue, rebased on master
decision.why: A self-proving diff is the fastest thing for a single maintainer to evaluate, and the test has value even if the fix is rewritten.

alternatives.name: Comment on the issue with the test and analysis
alternatives.tradeoff: Fits a repo where the maintainer writes most code; less credit as a PR, but often the fastest route to a fix.

alternatives.name: Keep a patch in your fork
alternatives.tradeoff: Unblocks your own use, but you carry it across every release.

verify: The PR body has the SQL reproducer, Postgres and pgvector versions, and test commands
The diff touches only the files the fix needs
Every review comment has a reply or a commit

steps.title: Write up the pgvector fix and pick the next rung
steps.learn: Record the bug, the root cause in Postgres terms (pages, locks, WAL, planner), the test that proves it, any numbers with recall, and how review went. Next rungs: iterative scan behavior, IVFFlat, or a distance kernel with benchmark evidence.
verify: The write-up states the bug, the root cause and the PR or issue link
Every number has machine, Postgres version and settings
It names one concrete next contribution and why

projects.problem: pgvector is a Postgres extension in C for vector types and HNSW/IVFFlat indexes; it teaches index access methods, WAL and ANN in a real DB.
projects.proveIt: A PR with a pg_regress or TAP test that passes the build workflow and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up
projects.hardware: Linux or macOS with Postgres 13+ and its server dev files (pg_config); Windows via Visual Studio nmake

projects.title: DuckDB
projects.question: How do you take a reproduced DuckDB bug to a small, sqllogictest-backed C++ fix that passes CI and gets maintainer review?

steps.title: Frame a DuckDB contribution and read the house rules
steps.learn: Aim at the function or execution layer. Success is a PR that passes CI and gets review. MIT licensed, no CLA or DCO in CONTRIBUTING. It asks you to announce the issue you take, keep PRs small and skip typo PRs. There is no good-first-issue label; use 'reproduced'. Talk on GitHub, Discussions or Discord.
verify: You read CONTRIBUTING.md and AI_POLICY.md and noted that CONTRIBUTING also asks for no LLM-generated PRs
You confirmed from the label list that no newcomer label exists and that 'reproduced' and 'needs triage' do
You joined Discussions or Discord and wrote down where maintainers answer questions

steps.title: Build DuckDB in reldebug and run the fast unit tests
steps.learn: The Makefile wraps CMake and uses Ninja automatically if installed (GEN=ninja forces it). 'make reldebug' gives an optimized binary with debug symbols; 'make debug' adds sanitizers and assertions but tests run much slower. ccache is used automatically; CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL caps jobs if memory runs out.

decision.choice: GEN=ninja make reldebug, then run tests with build/reldebug/test/unittest
decision.why: AGENTS.md recommends reldebug and its unittest binary unless there is a good reason for the debug build, which is much slower. You get usable stack traces while keeping test runs short enough to iterate many times a day.

alternatives.name: make debug
alternatives.tradeoff: Sanitizers and assertions catch memory bugs early, but every test run is much slower; switch to it when chasing a crash.

alternatives.name: Plain make (release)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest binary, right for benchmarks, but poor debugging and it hides assertion failures.

alternatives.name: pip install duckdb
alternatives.tradeoff: Instant, but you cannot change or debug the C++ engine at all.

verify: GEN=ninja make reldebug finishes; record wall time, cores and RAM
build/reldebug/test/unittest test/sql/order/test_limit.test passes
build/reldebug/test/unittest (the fast suite) passes on your machine before you change any code

steps.title: Trace one SELECT from parser to pipeline executor
steps.learn: src/main/client_context.cpp parses the query, then runs Planner, Optimizer and PhysicalPlanGenerator. Parsing lives in src/parser (PEG grammar), binding in src/planner, rewrites in src/optimizer, operators in src/execution/operator, and pipelines in src/parallel/executor.cpp and pipeline_executor.cpp.
verify: You ran EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a join plus GROUP BY and mapped each operator to a file under src/execution/operator
In a debugger you stopped in PhysicalPlanGenerator and recorded the call stack back to ClientContext
You named one optimizer pass that changed the plan by comparing EXPLAIN with SET disabled_optimizers

steps.title: Learn vectorized push-based execution and pick a subsystem
steps.learn: Operators process DataChunks of vectors, STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE rows each (2048 by default). Vectors can be flat, constant, dictionary, sequence, FSST or shredded, so code must handle every VectorType. Pipelines run in parallel on morsels of input, following the morsel-driven design.

decision.choice: Target built-in functions under src/function first
decision.why: Function bugs usually reproduce in one SQL line, stay inside one file, and are easy to pin with a sqllogictest. They still force you to handle vector types and NULLs correctly, which is the core concept.

alternatives.name: Optimizer (src/optimizer)
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick it for plan-quality bugs; you must argue semantic equivalence and reviewers look hard at it.

alternatives.name: Storage (src/storage)
alternatives.tradeoff: WAL, checkpoints and compression; on-disk compatibility makes the bar very high for a first change.

alternatives.name: In-tree extensions (extension/)
alternatives.tradeoff: Parquet or JSON readers are self-contained and good for file-format bugs, but need sample files to reproduce.

verify: You can explain why a scalar function must handle CONSTANT_VECTOR and DICTIONARY_VECTOR inputs
You picked one directory under src/function and read two functions in it end to end

steps.title: Land a sqllogictest that pins down untested behavior
steps.learn: CONTRIBUTING strongly prefers sqllogictest .test files over C++ tests, asks for tests across numerics, strings and nested types, and asks you not to send minor typo PRs. A test covering an untested path or an edge case teaches the test format before you touch C++.

decision.choice: A coverage test under test/sql for an edge case of your chosen function
decision.why: It is reviewable in minutes, uses the format every later fix needs, and the coverage report in CI shows whether it exercised new code paths.

alternatives.name: Docs fix in duckdb/duckdb-web
alternatives.tradeoff: Good if you found a doc error; the docs live in a separate repo with its own review.

alternatives.name: C++ test under test/
alternatives.tradeoff: Only when SQL cannot express it, such as concurrent connections; more code to review.

steps.delegate: In duckdb/duckdb, review (do not rewrite) the sqllogictest I wrote under test/sql/function/<area>/ for <function>. Check the '# name', '# description' and '# group' header, list missing cases (NULLs, empty strings, numeric extremes, nested LIST and STRUCT, a 'statement error' with a <REGEX>: message), flag any PRAGMA enable_verification, and say if it should be .test_slow. I run it with build/reldebug/test/unittest <path>.
verify: The new .test passes with build/reldebug/test/unittest and fails if you edit one expected value
Every case has a reason you can state in one sentence
The file has no PRAGMA enable_verification and uses the header format

steps.title: Pick a reproduced issue and turn it into a failing test
steps.learn: Real labels: 'reproduced', 'needs reproducible example', 'needs triage', 'incorrect results', 'fixed on nightly'. Prefer recent activity, no assignee, and no linked PR. Comment that you are working on it, as CONTRIBUTING asks. Shrink the repro to the fewest rows and columns.

decision.choice: A 'reproduced' issue with wrong results or a crash in one function or operator
decision.why: A maintainer already confirmed it, so you are not guessing whether it is a bug, and wrong-result bugs turn directly into a sqllogictest with an expected answer.

alternatives.name: 'needs reproducible example' issues
alternatives.tradeoff: Writing the repro is itself useful work, but the issue may turn out to be expected behavior.

alternatives.name: Feature ideas in Discussions
alternatives.tradeoff: More design freedom, but needs maintainer buy-in first and is much harder to land.

verify: Your failing .test fails on a fresh build of main, not only on an older release
The issue is not labelled 'fixed on nightly' and has no open PR linked
You posted on the issue that you are working on it

steps.title: Fix the bug at the layer where the invariant breaks
steps.learn: Find where the wrong value first appears (binder, optimizer or operator) and fix there. CONTRIBUTING says not to submit AI-generated PRs; AI_POLICY.md allows AI as a tool. So write the patch yourself and use an agent only to explore and review. No autonomous agents.

decision.choice: Smallest fix at the root cause, with the failing test committed first
decision.why: Small PRs are what CONTRIBUTING asks for, and a test that fails before and passes after is the clearest evidence for reviewers.

alternatives.name: Guard or special case downstream
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster to write, but reviewers usually reject symptom patches that leave the invariant broken.

alternatives.name: Refactor the surrounding code
alternatives.tradeoff: Sometimes needed, but split it into a separate PR or it becomes hard to review.

steps.delegate: In duckdb/duckdb (C++), do NOT write the fix. For <issue> and my failing sqllogictest at <path>, explain the root cause and the file and function where the invariant breaks. Then review my hand-written patch against CONTRIBUTING (tabs, 120 columns, unique_ptr, idx_t, enum class, D_ASSERT with a comment, return early) and AGENTS.md's vector API (Values<T>, FlatVector::Writer, no legacy ToUnifiedFormat loops). Check all VectorTypes and NULLs.
verify: The test fails without your change and passes with it
You can explain the root cause and every changed line without notes
The fast suite still passes: build/reldebug/test/unittest

steps.title: Pass format-fix, tidy and the unit suites the way CI does
steps.learn: 'make format-fix' runs clang-format 11.0.1 and black. 'make tidy-check' runs clang-tidy. 'make unit' is the fast suite, 'make allunit' everything (about an hour). AGENTS.md also lists make test_configs and make test_vector. Run CI on your fork first, after pushing upstream tags to it.

decision.choice: format-fix, unit, allunit and test_vector locally, then GitHub Actions on your fork
decision.why: CONTRIBUTING asks you to run CI on your fork before opening a PR and says new pushes move the PR back to Draft, so catching failures before the PR saves review cycles.

alternatives.name: Only make unit
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast, but misses slow tests and vector-type verification that CI will run.

alternatives.name: Rely on upstream CI
alternatives.tradeoff: Less local work, but each failing push costs a Draft cycle and reviewer attention.

verify: make format-check (or format-fix) leaves no diff
make allunit and make test_vector pass; record durations
The Main workflow passes on your fork branch

steps.title: Measure the change with benchmark_runner and the regression script
steps.learn: Build with BUILD_BENCHMARK=1 BUILD_TPCH=1 make. benchmark_runner runs .benchmark files (one warmup plus five timed runs by default, --timed-runs to change). The Regression workflow compares base and PR runners with scripts/regression/test_runner.py --old --new --benchmarks .github/regression/micro.csv.

decision.choice: Run test_runner.py on base and branch release builds with the relevant benchmark list
decision.why: It is what CI's Regression workflow runs, so your local numbers match how maintainers will judge a slowdown, and it compares two binaries on the same machine.

alternatives.name: One .benchmark with --timed-runs 20
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick for a targeted micro case, but you must handle noise and baselines yourself.

alternatives.name: TPC-H or ClickBench lists
alternatives.tradeoff: End-to-end evidence for operator changes; much longer runs and more data to generate.

verify: You report median and spread over at least 10 runs for base and branch
You record CPU model, cores, threads and memory limit used
No benchmark in the list regresses beyond its run-to-run noise

steps.title: Open a ready-for-review PR and work the review loop
steps.learn: No PR template exists: describe the problem, the fix and the linked issue in your own words. Do not open Draft PRs. Pushes move the PR to Draft; mark it Ready for Review once fork CI passes. Labels such as 'Changes Requested', 'Merge Conflict' and 'needs maintainer approval' track state.

decision.choice: Merge main into your branch when it falls behind, as CONTRIBUTING says
decision.why: CONTRIBUTING asks maintainers of branches to merge with main frequently, and it keeps review comments attached to commits.

alternatives.name: Rebase and force-push
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleaner history, but rewrites commits reviewers already saw; do it only if asked.

alternatives.name: Close and reopen a fresh PR
alternatives.tradeoff: Only if the original is unsalvageable; loses review history.

verify: The PR body explains problem, root cause, fix and tests in your own words and links the issue
Every review comment has a human-written reply or a follow-up commit
If it stalls for two weeks, you posted one polite ping on the PR

steps.title: Write up the DuckDB fix and choose the next rung
steps.learn: Record what the bug was, why the layer you fixed owned it, what review changed, and any benchmark numbers with machine and command. Next rungs: a second fix in the same area, an optimizer bug, or a Parquet reader issue.
verify: The write-up states the root cause and links the PR
Every number names the machine and the exact command
It names one concrete next issue or area and why

projects.problem: DuckDB is an in-process analytical SQL database in C++; contributing teaches vectorized execution, query planning and test discipline.
projects.proveIt: A PR to duckdb/duckdb with a sqllogictest that passes CI and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up
projects.hardware: Linux, macOS or Windows with CMake, Python 3 and a C++17 compiler; more cores and RAM shorten builds
projects.aiPolicy: AI_POLICY.md allows AI as a coding tool if you can explain the change yourself; comments must be human-written; no autonomous agents. CONTRIBUTING.md adds: no AI-generated PRs.

projects.title: RocksDB
projects.question: How do you land a tested fix in RocksDB's LSM engine, from an up-for-grabs issue to a reviewed PR with benchmark evidence?

steps.title: Frame a RocksDB contribution and sign Meta's CLA
steps.learn: Aim at table or utility code. Success is a PR that passes CI and gets review. A Meta CLA is required. PRs land through Meta's internal import, so landed PRs show as closed with a 'Merged' label, and many outside PRs close unmerged. Questions go to the Facebook group or Google group.
verify: You signed the Meta CLA and know the 'CLA Signed' label marks it on PRs
You opened a recent PR labelled 'Merged' and saw it closed rather than merged on GitHub
You read CONTRIBUTING.md, CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md and CLAUDE.md

steps.title: Build RocksDB and run one test binary with rocksptest
steps.learn: Make is the build for git clones; CMake covers special cases. Default make builds debug; 'make static_lib' builds release. Objects share paths across flavors, so CLAUDE.md says always use AUTO_CLEAN=1. Tools need gflags, and make check needs clang-format.

decision.choice: build_tools/rocksptest.sh on one test binary, such as db_basic_test
decision.why: It builds with parallel make and AUTO_CLEAN=1 and shards cases with gtest-parallel, so you iterate on one binary in minutes instead of waiting for the full make check.

alternatives.name: AUTO_CLEAN=1 make check
alternatives.tradeoff: The full gate that builds and runs every test; right before a PR, too slow for each edit.

alternatives.name: CMake build
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for Windows and some CI jobs, but the repo's helpers and docs assume Make.

alternatives.name: DEBUG_LEVEL=0 make db_bench
alternatives.tradeoff: Release build for performance work only; not for tests or debugging.

verify: build_tools/rocksptest.sh db_basic_test passes; record time and core count
make static_lib succeeds and you know it is a release build
clang-format and gflags are installed

steps.title: Trace a Put through write thread, WAL, memtable and flush
steps.learn: DBImpl::Put leads to DBImpl::WriteImpl in db/db_impl/db_impl_write.cc. db/write_thread.cc groups writers, db/log_writer.cc appends the WAL, and db/memtable.cc inserts into the skiplist (memtable/skiplistrep.cc). db/flush_job.cc writes an SST via table/block_based; db/version_set.cc records it.
verify: In a db_basic_test case you broke on DBImpl::WriteImpl and recorded the stack from Put
You can say which thread writes the WAL for a batch group and why grouping helps fsync cost
You read docs/components/write_flow and matched two chapters to files

steps.title: Learn LSM compaction tradeoffs and choose a target area
steps.learn: An LSM tree buffers writes in memtables, flushes sorted SST files and merges them by compaction, trading write, read and space amplification. CLAUDE.md says the db core gets the most review scrutiny and calls compaction changes complex and high-risk.

decision.choice: Table, filter and utility code (table/, util/) before the db/ core
decision.why: These areas have focused unit tests such as table_test, smaller blast radius and clearer contracts, so a first fix is reviewable without reasoning about every concurrent write path.

alternatives.name: Compaction (db/compaction)
alternatives.tradeoff: Most interesting LSM logic, but high risk; expect requests for stress tests and long review.

alternatives.name: Java bindings (java/)
alternatives.tradeoff: JNI gaps are often self-contained, but need a JDK and Java build on top of C++.

alternatives.name: Tools such as db_bench
alternatives.tradeoff: Low risk and helps measurement, but teaches less about the engine.

verify: You can explain leveled compaction's write amplification in two sentences
You chose one directory and listed its test binary

steps.title: Add a focused gtest to an existing RocksDB test file
steps.learn: CLAUDE.md: avoid new test files for minor features, never sleep to wait (use sync points), cap tests at 60 seconds, and check every Status, since ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1 make check fails on unchecked ones. A coverage test teaches these conventions cheaply.

decision.choice: One edge-case test added to the existing *_test.cc of your chosen area
decision.why: It follows the repo's test-placement guidance, is small enough to review quickly, and proves you can satisfy sync-point and Status-check rules before you change production code.

alternatives.name: db_bench support for an existing option
alternatives.tradeoff: CLAUDE.md asks perf features to be exposed in db_bench; useful, but touches a large tool file.

alternatives.name: docs/components fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for design notes you found wrong; teaches the code less than a test.

steps.delegate: In facebook/rocksdb (C++20), add a TEST_F to the existing <area>_test.cc covering <edge case>. Use ASSERT_OK on every Status, SyncPoint instead of sleep, Random from util/random.h with a SCOPED_TRACE seed for randomized cases, and keep runtime under 60 seconds. ASCII only. Run build_tools/rocksptest.sh <area>_test --gtest_filter=*<Name>*.
verify: The test passes via rocksptest.sh and fails if you break the asserted behavior
COERCE_CONTEXT_SWITCH=1 build_tools/rockstest.sh <bin> -r100 with your filter shows no flakes
ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1 build_tools/rocksptest.sh <bin> --gtest_filter=*<Name>* passes

steps.title: Pick an up-for-grabs issue and write a failing gtest
steps.learn: Labels include 'up-for-grabs', 'bug', 'crash', 'flaky test', 'waiting' and 'abandoned-or-aged-out'. Most up-for-grabs issues are years old, so check they still reproduce on main. Prefer no assignee. Reproduce with the fewest Options in one test binary, then shrink keys and steps.

decision.choice: An up-for-grabs bug that reproduces in one unit test binary
decision.why: A deterministic gtest is the evidence reviewers want, and one binary keeps your build and run loop short on a laptop-class machine.

alternatives.name: Crash-test failures (db_stress)
alternatives.tradeoff: Real bugs, but need long tools/db_crashtest.py runs and patience to minimize.

alternatives.name: 'flaky test' issues
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for learning sync points; reproducing timing bugs can take many repeated runs.

verify: Your new test fails on current main with a clear assertion message
The repro sets only the Options needed to trigger it
You commented on the issue that you are working on it

steps.title: Fix the bug in the layer that owns the contract
steps.learn: CLAUDE.md's review checklist asks whether each behavior lives in the right layer, whether errors propagate as Status, and whether the change is thread-safe. RocksDB has no AI contribution policy; still, understand every line so you can defend it in review yourself.

decision.choice: Minimal fix where the contract is owned, with the failing test first
decision.why: Reviewers flag caller-specific logic leaking into reusable layers and silent behavior changes; a narrow fix at the owner is easiest to approve.

alternatives.name: New option to toggle the fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Safer rollout for behavior changes, but options carry a deprecation burden and need db_bench and stress coverage.

alternatives.name: Workaround at the caller
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick, but likely flagged as a contract leak in review.

steps.delegate: In facebook/rocksdb (C++20), fix <issue>; start from the failing test <name>. Propagate errors via Status, no new defaulted parameters, no declared 'auto' (auto& ok), use static_cast_with_check or lossless_cast from util/cast_util.h, no dynamic_cast outside tests, ASCII only. New .cc files need the Meta dual-license header and entries in Makefile, CMakeLists.txt and src.mk. Add a one-line note via unreleased_history/add.sh. Explain the root cause first.
verify: The test fails before and passes after your change
You can explain thread-safety and error paths of every changed function
A release note file exists under unreleased_history/bug_fixes if users would notice

steps.title: Pass format, source checks and make check like pr-jobs CI
steps.learn: pr-jobs.yml runs make check-format, check-sources and check-buck-targets, then make check in GCC, ASAN/UBSAN, TSAN and ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED jobs, plus MSVC, MinGW and Clang libc++ builds. Locally: make format-auto, make check-sources, AUTO_CLEAN=1 make check.

decision.choice: format-auto, check-sources, then AUTO_CLEAN=1 ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1 make check
decision.why: These catch the most common outside-PR failures (format, non-ASCII, unchecked Status) on your own machine; CLAUDE.md names both make check runs as the final verification.

alternatives.name: Add an ASAN/UBSAN run
alternatives.tradeoff: COMPILE_WITH_ASAN=1 COMPILE_WITH_UBSAN=1 make check catches memory bugs; worth it for pointer or buffer changes, slower.

alternatives.name: Rely on CI for the matrix
alternatives.tradeoff: MSVC and MinGW breaks only show in CI; expect a round trip if you use POSIX-only code.

verify: make check-format and make check-sources pass with no diff
AUTO_CLEAN=1 ASSERT_STATUS_CHECKED=1 make check passes; record duration and cores
No new POSIX-only header or GCC extension lacks a port:: or OS_WIN guard

steps.title: Measure the change with paired db_bench runs
steps.learn: Build a release binary with AUTO_CLEAN=1 DEBUG_LEVEL=0 make db_bench. Run workloads like --benchmarks=fillrandom,readrandom with --num and --statistics. Reviewers ask for numbers on performance-sensitive changes; CLAUDE.md names db_bench as the tool.

decision.choice: Paired db_bench runs of base and branch release builds on one machine
decision.why: Same hardware, flags and data size isolate your change; alternating runs exposes noise from page cache, compaction timing and CPU frequency.

alternatives.name: tools/benchmark.sh suite
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard multi-phase workloads closer to published reports; takes far longer and more disk.

alternatives.name: microbench/ (make microbench)
alternatives.tradeoff: Google Benchmark cases like db_basic_bench for hot functions; narrower than an end-to-end run.

verify: You report median and spread over at least 5 alternating runs per build
You record CPU, storage device, compression, --num, --threads and value size
You state whether the difference exceeds run-to-run noise

steps.title: Open a RocksDB PR with an evidence-based summary
steps.learn: No PR template exists; claude_md/pull_request_summary_guideline.md asks for why, old and new behavior, implementation, safety and compatibility, and tests with their limits. After CI an automated AI review may comment. A maintainer imports the PR internally to land it.

decision.choice: One focused PR whose summary follows the repo's six-point guideline
decision.why: The guideline is what maintainers use for internal diff summaries, so matching it makes the import and review faster and shows the evidence for each claim.

alternatives.name: Split refactor and fix into two PRs
alternatives.tradeoff: Cleaner review when cleanup is needed; doubles the import and review cycles.

alternatives.name: Open an issue first for design
alternatives.tradeoff: Right for behavior or API changes; slower for a clear bug fix.

verify: The PR states old behavior, new behavior, tests run and what was not tested
The CLA check passes and the issue is linked
If silent for two weeks, you pinged once; you know 'abandoned-or-aged-out' may close it

steps.title: Write up the RocksDB fix and choose the next rung
steps.learn: Record the trigger conditions, which layer owned the bug, what review asked for, and db_bench numbers with machine and command. Next rungs: a flaky-test fix with sync points, a compaction bug, or a db_stress coverage addition.
verify: The write-up names exact trigger conditions and links the PR
Every number names machine, build flags and the db_bench command
It names one concrete next area and why

projects.problem: RocksDB is Meta's embeddable LSM-tree key-value store in C++; contributing teaches write paths, compaction, SST formats and concurrency testing.
projects.proveIt: A PR to facebook/rocksdb with a unit test that passes CI and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up
projects.hardware: Linux or macOS with GCC 11+ or Clang 10+ (C++20); many cores for make check; a quiet SSD machine for db_bench

projects.title: Tokio
projects.question: How do I go from never reading Tokio's source to a reviewed PR that fixes or speeds up one runtime module, with tests?

steps.title: Set the goal and read Tokio's contribution rules
steps.learn: Aim at one module (M-sync, M-time, M-io or M-runtime). Success is a PR that passes CI and gets maintainer review. Tokio has no CLA or DCO, follows the Rust Code of Conduct, talks on Discord, and asks you to comment on an issue before starting work. No AI policy is published.
verify: You read CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/contributing/README.md and can name the five guides it links
You joined the Tokio Discord linked from CONTRIBUTING.md and found where contributors ask questions
You wrote down the module you will target and why, in one sentence

steps.title: Build the Tokio workspace and run its test suite
steps.learn: Tokio is a Cargo workspace (tokio, tokio-util, tokio-stream, tokio-test, tokio-macros). Many APIs sit behind features and cfg flags, so plain cargo test misses code. The docs say to use --all-features, and tokio_unstable tests need RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable".

decision.choice: cargo test --all-features on stable for the whole workspace first, then -p tokio for fast loops
decision.why: It is what docs/contributing/pull-requests.md recommends, and it is a superset of CI's test-workspace-all-features job, which runs cargo nextest with --features full,test-util plus doctests. Once it passes, narrow to one crate and one test file.

alternatives.name: cargo test -p tokio --features full
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster, but skips other crates and unstable-only code paths that your change may touch.

alternatives.name: Add --cfg tokio_unstable via RUSTFLAGS
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for metrics, taskdump and other unstable APIs; forces full rebuilds whenever you toggle the flag.

verify: cargo build --all-features and cargo test --all-features finish at the repo root
You ran one file alone, e.g. cargo test -p tokio --all-features --test sync_mpsc
You recorded the rustc version and wall time of the full test run

steps.title: Trace a TcpStream read through the I/O driver and scheduler
steps.learn: Follow a read from tokio/src/net/tcp/stream.rs into io/poll_evented.rs, then runtime/io/registration.rs and scheduled_io.rs, where readiness and wakers live. runtime/io/driver.rs polls mio; a wake pushes the task onto the queues in runtime/scheduler/multi_thread (worker.rs, queue.rs).
verify: You can point to the line where a pending read registers its waker in scheduled_io.rs
You drew the path from TcpStream to the worker run queue with file names
You found where the I/O driver calls into mio in runtime/io/driver.rs

steps.title: Learn work stealing and wakers, then choose a module
steps.learn: The multi-thread scheduler gives each worker a local run queue, a LIFO slot and a shared inject queue, and idle workers steal. Wakers turn readiness into scheduling. Several tokio::sync primitives build on a batch semaphore and intrusive waiter lists, which is where many subtle bugs live.

decision.choice: Target tokio::sync (M-sync): self-contained, well tested, with loom models in sync/tests
decision.why: Sync primitives are small enough to read in a day, have integration tests per primitive (tests/sync_*.rs) and loom tests, and bugs there are reproducible without network setup.

alternatives.name: M-time (timer wheel)
alternatives.tradeoff: Clear data structure in runtime/time/wheel, but bugs often need paused time and careful reasoning about clock edges.

alternatives.name: M-runtime (scheduler)
alternatives.tradeoff: Most interesting, but changes need loom runs and a strong benchmark case; reviews are slower and stricter.

alternatives.name: tokio-util (codec, sync)
alternatives.tradeoff: Gentler API surface and faster reviews, but you learn less about the runtime core.

verify: You can explain in two sentences why a LIFO slot helps message passing workloads
You read one primitive end to end, e.g. sync/notify.rs, and listed its states
You wrote down the chosen module and the matching M-* label

steps.title: Land a doc test or docs fix as a first PR
steps.learn: Tokio values tiny PRs, even typo fixes. Doc tests are first-class: every API should have one, written from the user's view through the tokio facade. Docs must build with the docs.rs cfg flags on nightly, and cargo spellcheck guards wording via spellcheck.dic.

decision.choice: Add or improve a doc test for an API in your module that lacks a runnable example
decision.why: It is reviewed quickly, exercises the docs build and the doc test runner, and teaches the module's public contract before you touch internals.

alternatives.name: Fix a typo or broken intra-doc link
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest merge, but teaches little about the code.

alternatives.name: Add a missing integration test
alternatives.tradeoff: More learning about internals, but needs agreement that the behavior tested is intended.

steps.delegate: In tokio-rs/tokio, add a doc test to the rustdoc of <API> in tokio/src/<module>. Write it from a user's view via the tokio facade, hide setup lines with '/// #', keep it short. Then run cargo test --doc -p tokio --all-features and RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg docsrs --cfg tokio_unstable" RUSTFLAGS="--cfg docsrs --cfg tokio_unstable" cargo +nightly doc --all-features. Report both outputs.
verify: Your doc test passes under cargo test --doc and fails if you break the example on purpose
The nightly docs build with docsrs flags shows the right feature badge on the API
cargo spellcheck check passes, or new words were added to spellcheck.dic with its first-line count updated

steps.title: Pick an E-help-wanted or E-easy issue and reproduce it
steps.learn: Filter issues by your M-* label plus E-easy or E-help-wanted, skip ones with recent activity or an open PR, and comment before starting. E-needs-mcve marks bugs without a minimal example: writing one is itself a contribution. Tokio prefers integration tests in tokio/tests over unit tests.

decision.choice: Reproduce as a failing integration test in tokio/tests/<module>_*.rs
decision.why: That is where the fix's regression test must live anyway, it runs on the real public API, and it follows the repo's stated preference against unit tests.

alternatives.name: Standalone binary with #[tokio::main]
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick for exploring timing bugs, but must be converted into a test before the PR.

alternatives.name: loom model in src/<module>/tests
alternatives.tradeoff: Required for interleaving bugs in sync or scheduler code; slower to write and run, and needs --cfg loom.

verify: The test fails on master for the reason the issue describes, not a setup error
It fails reliably (e.g. 20 of 20 runs) or you documented the failure rate
You commented on the issue with the minimal example and asked to take it

steps.title: Fix the bug with the failing test committed first
steps.learn: Tokio code is heavily cfg-gated and uses its own loom-aware wrappers for atomics and cells, so a fix must compile under every feature set CI checks. Keep the fix minimal; any change to unsafe code or atomic orderings needs a comment explaining why it is sound.
steps.delegate: Repo tokio-rs/tokio. First commit the failing test in tokio/tests/<file>.rs exactly as written. Then fix <bug> in tokio/src/<path> with the smallest change. Use the crate's loom-aware sync wrappers, not std atomics directly. Justify any ordering or unsafe change in a comment. Run cargo test -p tokio --all-features --test <file>, rustfmt --check --edition 2021 on changed files, and cargo +1.88 clippy --all --tests --all-features. Show all outputs.
verify: You can explain every changed line, including any memory ordering, without the agent
The new test fails before the fix and passes after it
No public API or MSRV change slipped in; if one did, you can justify it to reviewers

steps.title: Run rustfmt, clippy, docs and loom the way CI does
steps.learn: cargo fmt does not work on Tokio; CI runs rustfmt --check --edition 2021 over git ls-files. Clippy is pinned (env.rust_clippy in ci.yml). The basics job gates on clippy, fmt, docs and minrust. Loom jobs run on PRs only when maintainers add R-loom-* labels, so run the relevant loom scope yourself.

decision.choice: Run fmt, pinned clippy, nightly docs and the loom scope for your module locally
decision.why: These are the cheap gate jobs that block everything else in CI, and loom will not run on your PR unless a maintainer labels it, so local loom runs are your evidence.

alternatives.name: Push and let CI find problems
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves local setup, but burns reviewer attention and long CI cycles across many OS and target jobs.

alternatives.name: Also run miri locally
alternatives.tradeoff: Worth it for unsafe changes; needs nightly and is slow, using the MIRIFLAGS from the contributing guide.

verify: rustfmt --check --edition 2021 $(git ls-files '*.rs') prints nothing
Clippy with the toolchain version from ci.yml env.rust_clippy passes with --all-features
The loom command from pull-requests.md passes for your module's scope

steps.title: Measure the change with Tokio's Criterion benches
steps.learn: The benches crate uses Criterion; files like sync_mpsc.rs, sync_semaphore.rs and rt_multi_threaded.rs cover hot paths. Even a bug fix on a hot path should show no regression. Criterion reports confidence intervals, but noise from frequency scaling and other load can still exceed small effects.

decision.choice: Run the bench file for your module on master and on your branch, same machine, quiet system
decision.why: Reviewers of sync and runtime code ask whether a fix costs throughput. A same-machine A/B with Criterion's saved baselines is cheap and directly comparable.

alternatives.name: Skip benchmarks for a docs or cold-path fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine when no hot path changed; say so in the PR instead of posting noise.

alternatives.name: End-to-end app benchmark
alternatives.tradeoff: More realistic, but much noisier, and hard for reviewers to reproduce.

verify: You ran cd benches and cargo bench --bench <file> on both master and your branch
You report the change with Criterion's interval and repeated runs at least twice
You recorded CPU model, core count, OS and rustc version

steps.title: Open the PR with a module-prefixed message and handle review
steps.learn: Title like 'sync: fix ...': lowercase, imperative, prefixed with the module (usually the M-* label). Body: what the code assumes, what goes wrong, the conceptual fix, then 'Fixes: #N'. Once the PR is open do not rebase or squash; push new commits. Expect review from any community member; code owners settle conflicts.
verify: PR title and body follow the commit message guidelines in pull-requests.md
The PR template is filled in and the issue is linked with Fixes:
Every review comment has a reply or a follow-up commit, with no force-push

steps.title: Write up the Tokio fix and choose the next rung
steps.learn: Record the bug, the root cause in runtime terms (waker lost, ordering too weak, state not reset), the test that proves it, benchmark numbers with machine details, and review lessons. Next rung: a loom model for an untested interleaving, an M-runtime issue, or a C-feature-accepted request.
verify: The write-up states the root cause and links the PR and the test
Every number has the machine, command and number of runs
You named one concrete next issue or label to work on

projects.problem: Tokio is Rust's most used async runtime. Contributing teaches schedulers, I/O drivers, wakers and how to test concurrent code with loom.
projects.proveIt: A PR to tokio-rs/tokio that passes CI and gets maintainer review, with a regression test, plus a short write-up.
projects.hardware: Any Linux, macOS or Windows machine with rustup; Linux with a recent kernel for io-uring work

projects.title: etcd
projects.question: How do I go from never reading etcd's source to a reviewed PR that fixes a bug in its server, storage or tests, with a regression test?

steps.title: Set the goal and read etcd's contribution and AI rules
steps.learn: Aim at one area (mvcc, wal, lease, watch or tests). Success is a PR that passes Prow and GitHub checks and gets review. Every commit needs a DCO Signed-off-by line. etcd follows the CNCF Code of Conduct, uses #sig-etcd on Kubernetes Slack and the etcd-dev list, and meets weekly, alternating community and triage calls.
verify: You read CONTRIBUTING.md and the AI Guidance section linked from the PR template
You configured git to sign off commits (git commit -s) with your real name and email
You joined #sig-etcd and noted when the next triage meeting is

steps.title: Build etcd with make build and run the unit pass
steps.learn: etcd is a Go workspace (go.work) with modules for server, client, api, etcdctl, etcdutl, pkg and tests. make build runs scripts/build.sh; tests run through scripts/test.sh with PASSES (unit, integration, e2e). PKG, TESTCASE and TIMEOUT narrow a run. Build tools: make, protoc v3.20.3, yamllint, jq, xz.

decision.choice: Manual setup on a Linux amd64 machine with the Go version from go.mod
decision.why: CONTRIBUTING calls it the most supported option and the only supported architecture is linux-amd64, so local results match Prow. Reports from other environments are generally ignored.

alternatives.name: Devcontainer or Codespaces
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest start with all tools preinstalled (etcd 3.6+), but tied to Docker or a cloud VM and slower for e2e runs.

alternatives.name: macOS or arm64 laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Builds may work, but this is unsupported for development; flaky or different results will not be accepted as evidence.

verify: make build produces bin/etcd and bin/etcdctl
make test-unit passes, and you ran one package alone with PASSES=unit PKG=... ./scripts/test.sh
You started bin/etcd and ran etcdctl put foo bar and get foo against it

steps.title: Trace a Put from clientv3 through Raft into bbolt
steps.learn: kvServer.Put in server/etcdserver/api/v3rpc/key.go calls EtcdServer.Put in v3_server.go, which proposes via raftRequest. raftNode.start in raft.go persists Ready entries with storage.Save (server/storage/wal), then applyAll in server.go applies them through server/etcdserver/apply and txn/put.go into mvcc on bbolt.
verify: You can name the function that waits for the proposal to be applied before replying
You found where entries are written to the WAL before being applied
You drew the path from gRPC handler to backend batch tx with file names

steps.title: Learn Raft and MVCC revisions, then choose a subsystem
steps.learn: Raft itself lives in the separate etcd-io/raft repo; etcd server wires it to storage and apply. Each write bumps a global revision; mvcc keeps a key index (key_index.go) over revisions stored in bbolt, which compaction trims. Watch streams events by revision, and its guarantees are documented.

decision.choice: Target server/storage/mvcc (watch and compaction), with tests already in the package
decision.why: It holds many past correctness bugs listed in the robustness README, has focused unit tests and benchmarks, and does not require changing the Raft library itself.

alternatives.name: server/storage/wal
alternatives.tradeoff: Small and crisp, but durability bugs are hard to reproduce and changes get heavy scrutiny.

alternatives.name: etcdctl or client/v3
alternatives.tradeoff: Gentler first code, quicker review, but you learn little about consensus or storage.

alternatives.name: tests/robustness
alternatives.tradeoff: Great for learning failure modes and linearizability checking, but runs are long and failures need report analysis.

verify: You can explain why a watch must not deliver events below its start revision
You read the KV and watch sections of the API guarantees page
You wrote down the chosen subsystem and its area/* label

steps.title: Start by deflaking a test or fixing a small cleanup
steps.learn: CONTRIBUTING invites help deflaking tests: open issues carry type/flake and history is on testgrid (sig-etcd). The suggested loop is go test -c then golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stress to hammer one test. good first issue and type/cleanup issues are other small entry points.

decision.choice: Take one type/flake issue in your subsystem and reproduce it with stress
decision.why: Flakes block every contributor's PR, so fixes are welcome, and the work teaches the test harness and timing assumptions in the code you will later change.

alternatives.name: good first issue
alternatives.tradeoff: Curated for newcomers, but often few unassigned ones; check the org-wide search too.

alternatives.name: Docs or comments fix
alternatives.tradeoff: Quick to land and teaches the PR flow, but little about the system.

steps.delegate: In etcd-io/etcd, help reproduce flaky test <TestName> in <pkg>. Write the commands to compile it with go test -c -count 1 and run it under golang.org/x/tools/cmd/stress -p=8 with -test.run '^<TestName>$'. Then read the test and list every sleep, timeout or ordering assumption that could explain the failure, with file and line. Do not change code yet.
verify: You reproduced the failure locally and recorded how many runs it took
You can state the race or timing assumption behind the flake in one sentence
If no issue existed, you filed one with the type/flake label

steps.title: Reproduce a bug as a failing unit or integration test
steps.learn: Filter by area/* plus good first issue, help wanted or type/bug; skip assigned issues and ones with linked PRs, and comment first. CONTRIBUTING expects a unit test with every change. Integration tests in tests/integration start in-process clusters; e2e tests in tests/e2e drive real binaries.

decision.choice: Write the narrowest failing test: a unit test in the package, or tests/integration if it needs a cluster
decision.why: Unit tests run in seconds and are what every change must include. Integration tests are needed only when the bug needs multiple members, leaders or network partitions.

alternatives.name: e2e test in tests/e2e
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for etcdctl or process-level behavior; slow and requires make build first.

alternatives.name: Robustness scenario
alternatives.tradeoff: Finds linearizability and watch bugs under faults, but runs are long and failures need report analysis.

verify: The test fails on main for the reason the issue describes
It runs alone with PASSES=unit PKG=... TESTCASE=... ./scripts/test.sh
You posted the minimal reproduction on the issue

steps.title: Fix the bug with the failing test committed first
steps.learn: Fixes in server code often need backports to release branches (backport/v3.x labels), so a small, self-contained diff matters more here. Follow Go Code Review Comments style. Under the Kubernetes AI guidance you must understand every change and disclose AI use in the PR description.
steps.delegate: Repo etcd-io/etcd. First add the failing test in <pkg>/<file>_test.go exactly as written. Then fix <bug> in <pkg> with the smallest change, following Go Code Review Comments style and existing zap logging patterns. Do not change public APIs or protos. Run PASSES=unit PKG=<pkg> TESTCASE=<Test> ./scripts/test.sh and make verify-lint, and show outputs. Do not commit; I will write the commit message and sign off myself.
verify: You can explain every changed line and why the old code was wrong
The test fails before and passes after the fix
The diff is small enough to cherry-pick onto a release branch

steps.title: Pass make verify and the right test passes before Prow
steps.learn: make verify runs static checks (golangci-lint via tools/.golangci.yaml, bom, dep, mod tidy, shellcheck, yamllint, proto checks, go versions). make fix repairs most of them. CI is Kubernetes Prow (presubmits like pull-etcd-verify, unit, e2e) plus GitHub Actions.

decision.choice: Run make verify, make test-unit, and make test-integration if you touched server code
decision.why: These mirror the Prow presubmits that gate review, and running them locally avoids waiting for an org member to /ok-to-test only to fail on lint.

alternatives.name: Only targeted PASSES with PKG
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast loops while coding, but misses cross-package breakage that Prow will catch.

alternatives.name: Full make test including e2e
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to Prow, but takes a long time; reserve it for changes to process or etcdctl behavior.

verify: make verify passes with no changes left in git status
make test-unit passes, and test-integration too if server code changed
Your commits have Signed-off-by lines (git log shows them)

steps.title: Benchmark with the etcd benchmark tool and Go benches
steps.learn: tools/benchmark is the official cluster benchmark (put, range, txn, watch); make bench-put builds and runs it. Packages such as mvcc and wal ship Go benchmarks (kvstore_bench_test.go, wal_bench_test.go). Disk fsync latency dominates writes, so record the storage device.

decision.choice: Run go test -bench for the touched package plus benchmark put on main and on your branch
decision.why: The Go bench isolates the code you changed; the cluster benchmark shows whether it matters end to end, including latency percentiles that reviewers ask about.

alternatives.name: Skip for non-hot-path fixes
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine for logging, cleanup or test fixes; state that no hot path changed.

alternatives.name: Rely on Prow periodic benchmarks
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs only after merge on amd64, so it cannot support your PR's claim.

verify: You ran the same benchmark on main and your branch at least three times each
You report throughput and latency percentiles with run-to-run spread
You recorded CPU, RAM, disk type and filesystem

steps.title: Open the PR, get /ok-to-test, and earn two approvals
steps.learn: Each PR needs a linked issue; prefer small PRs over one over 500 lines. First-time PRs get needs-ok-to-test until an etcd-io member comments /ok-to-test; /retest reruns flakes. Policy asks for two approvals. If a reviewer is silent for 10 days, ping on the PR or Slack. Answer review yourself, not via AI tools.
verify: The PR links its issue, discloses any AI use, and every commit is signed off
All Prow and GitHub checks are green before you request review
Each review comment has a reply or a commit; unrelated flakes have an issue filed

steps.title: Write up the etcd fix and choose the next rung
steps.learn: Record the bug, the root cause in Raft, MVCC or WAL terms, the test that proves the fix, any benchmark numbers with machine and disk, and review lessons. Next rung: a backport to a release branch, a robustness scenario that covers your bug, or a help wanted issue.
verify: The write-up names the root cause and links the PR, issue and test
Every number has machine, disk, command and run count
You named one concrete next issue or rung

projects.problem: etcd is the Raft-replicated key-value store behind Kubernetes. Contributing teaches consensus, MVCC storage, WAL durability and robustness testing.
projects.proveIt: A DCO-signed PR to etcd-io/etcd that passes Prow and GitHub checks and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up.
projects.hardware: Linux amd64 (the only supported dev architecture), or the repo's devcontainer in Codespaces
projects.aiPolicy: PR template asks you to disclose AI use and follow Kubernetes AI guidance: understand every change, no AI co-author trailers or AI commit messages, no large AI PRs, answer review yourself.

projects.title: bpftrace
projects.question: Can I land a reviewed, DCO-signed change in bpftrace's compiler pipeline, from parser to BPF bytecode, with tests that pass the Nix CI?

steps.title: Frame a bpftrace contribution and read its rules
steps.learn: Goal: one PR that passes CI and gets maintainer review (merge is up to maintainers). Rules: every commit needs a DCO Signed-off-by with your real name, big or breaking changes need an RFC issue first. Talk: #bpftrace on OFTC IRC, Discord, GitHub Discussions.
verify: Read the DCO section of CONTRIBUTING.md and set git user.name to your real name
List which kinds of change need an RFC issue and which can go straight to a PR
Read AGENTS.md and note the PR conventions it states (one commit, CHANGELOG, tests)

steps.title: Build bpftrace in the Nix dev shell and run the unit tests
steps.learn: Clone with --recurse-submodules. The guide recommends Nix because CI uses it: nix develop, cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug, make -C build. The binary is build/src/bpftrace. The minimum kernel is 6.1; scripts/check_kernel_features.sh checks the BPF config.

decision.choice: Nix dev shell with a Debug build
decision.why: bpftrace tracks new libbpf and bcc closely, and Nix pins all build and runtime dependencies the same way CI does, so local failures match CI failures. Debug builds also enable the -d dis disassembly stage.

alternatives.name: Distro build with system packages
alternatives.tradeoff: No Nix to learn, but distros that lag (the guide names Debian) may need hand-built bcc and libbpf; the repo Dockerfiles list dependencies.

alternatives.name: Nix shell with another LLVM (nix develop .#bpftrace-llvm21)
alternatives.tradeoff: Use when a bug only shows on one LLVM version; costs a second build tree and download time.

verify: build/src/bpftrace --version prints a version built from your checkout
./build/tests/bpftrace_test runs and passes on a clean master build
sudo build/src/bpftrace -e 'begin { print("hi"); exit(); }' prints hi

steps.title: Trace one script from the parser to an attached probe
steps.learn: AGENTS.md lays out the pipeline: src/parser.cpp builds the AST, passes in src/ast/passes check and rewrite it (type checking lives in src/ast/passes/types), src/ast/passes/codegen_llvm.cpp emits LLVM IR, src/bpfbytecode.cpp holds the BPF programs, and src/bpftrace.cpp with src/attached_probe.cpp attach them.

decision.choice: Watch each stage with the -d debug flag, then read the matching source
decision.why: -d ast prints the AST after every pass, -d codegen and codegen-opt print the IR, and -d verifier prints the kernel verifier log, so you can see which file changes what before reading thousands of lines of C++.

alternatives.name: Step through the Debug build in gdb
alternatives.tradeoff: Shows exact control flow and data, but bpftrace needs root and the pass list is long; slower for a first map.

alternatives.name: Read src/ast/pass_manager.cpp and the passes in order
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for structure, but without running a script you miss how real AST nodes and types look.

verify: Run a one-liner with -d ast and name the pass that first changes the AST
Find where the passes are created and ordered, starting from src/ast/pass_manager.cpp and src/main.cpp
Match one line of -d codegen output to the visitor in codegen_llvm.cpp that emitted it

steps.title: Learn how the BPF verifier constrains codegen and pick a target
steps.learn: bpftrace output must pass the kernel verifier, which rejects programs it cannot prove safe (unbounded loops, unchecked memory access). Many codegen bugs show up as verifier errors, while type checker bugs show up as wrong errors or types and can be unit tested without root.

decision.choice: Target the semantic passes (type checker and related analysers)
decision.why: Their bugs reproduce in GoogleTest unit tests (tests/type_checker.cpp, tests/parser.cpp) without root or a specific kernel, so the fix loop is fast and the CI result is predictable.

alternatives.name: Codegen and IR builder (codegen_llvm.cpp, irbuilderbpf.cpp)
alternatives.tradeoff: Most interesting BPF work, but needs runtime tests as root and can vary by kernel and LLVM version.

alternatives.name: Standard library and tools (src/stdlib, tools)
alternatives.tradeoff: Writes bpftrace code, not C++; must be formatted with bpftrace --fmt and teaches less of the compiler.

verify: Explain in two sentences why the verifier rejects an unchecked pointer read
Run a script that fails verification with -d verifier and point to the rejected instruction
Write down the subsystem you chose and two of its open issues

steps.title: Land a first runtime test or docs fix
steps.learn: Runtime tests live in tests/runtime as suites of directives: NAME, PROG or RUN, EXPECT variants, and TIMEOUT are required. The repo has docs and tests labels. Internal changes such as tests do not need a CHANGELOG entry; user-visible ones do.

decision.choice: Add a missing runtime test case for documented behavior
decision.why: It exercises the full build, the test framework and CI without design debate, and maintainers state every contribution should add tests where relevant.

alternatives.name: Fix docs/language.md or the man page
alternatives.tradeoff: Smallest review cost, but you will not touch the test harness or CI matrix.

alternatives.name: Add a unit test in tests/*.cpp
alternatives.tradeoff: No root needed, but covers one component rather than the whole pipeline.

steps.delegate: In bpftrace (C++20, master branch), add a runtime test case to the suite in tests/runtime/<suite> that covers <documented behavior>. Use the directives in tests/README.md (NAME, PROG, EXPECT or EXPECT_REGEX, TIMEOUT; REQUIRES_FEATURE if a kernel feature is needed). Keep PROG minimal. Show the exact command to run only this test with runtime-tests.sh --filter. Do not change other tests.
verify: sudo --preserve-env=PATH --preserve-env=PYTHONPATH ./build/tests/runtime-tests.sh --filter="^<suite>.<name>" passes
The test fails if you break the behavior it claims to cover
Commit has a Signed-off-by line with your real name

steps.title: Pick a labeled issue and reproduce it as a failing test
steps.learn: Filter open issues by good first issue, difficulty: easy or help wanted; skip ones labeled waiting-for-feedback, RFC or with an assignee or recent PR. Comment before starting. Record uname -r, bpftrace --info and LLVM version, since behavior can vary by kernel and LLVM.

decision.choice: Turn the one-liner into a failing GoogleTest case when it is a frontend bug
decision.why: Unit tests run in seconds with --gtest_filter, need no root, and become the regression test the PR template asks for.

alternatives.name: Failing runtime test in tests/runtime
alternatives.tradeoff: Required when the bug is in attachment or output; needs root and may need MIN_KERNEL or REQUIRES gates.

alternatives.name: Self test with a test: probe in tests/self
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for stdlib behavior written in bpftrace itself; less useful for C++ pass bugs.

verify: The issue reproduces on current master with your exact command and kernel recorded
./build/tests/bpftrace_test --gtest_filter='<Suite>.<Name>' fails for the reported reason
You left a comment on the issue saying you are working on it

steps.title: Fix the bug in the pass where it starts
steps.learn: Fix the root cause in the pass that produces the wrong state, not a later symptom. Conventions from AGENTS.md: C++20, 80 columns, snake_case, trailing underscore on private members, Result or std::optional instead of exceptions, LOG levels. You must understand every line an agent writes.

decision.choice: Minimal fix in the originating pass plus the failing test
decision.why: bpftrace design principles prefer boring, removable code, and reviewers can check a small diff against the test in one sitting.

alternatives.name: Guard against the bad state in codegen
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster to write, but hides the real bug and maintainers may ask for the upstream fix.

alternatives.name: Refactor the pass while fixing
alternatives.tradeoff: Only if the refactor is required; mixing it in makes review slower and may need an RFC.

steps.delegate: Repo: bpftrace (C++20). The failing test <name> in tests/<file>.cpp reproduces <bug>. First confirm it fails, then fix the root cause in src/ast/passes/<pass>.cpp. Follow AGENTS.md: snake_case, trailing underscore for private members, no exceptions for recoverable errors, LOG macros, C++ style comments, 80 columns. Run git clang-format upstream/master. Do not touch unrelated files. Explain each changed line. Follow the repo's AI guidance in AGENTS.md.
verify: The new test fails before the change and passes after it
The full ./build/tests/bpftrace_test suite still passes
You can explain why the bug happened without reading the agent's notes

steps.title: Pass clang-format, clang-tidy and the Nix CI matrix
steps.learn: ci.yml runs git clang-format --diff against origin/master in nix develop and builds and tests across LLVM versions on NixOS via .github/include/ci.py, some runtime tests in vmtest. clang-tidy.yml and shellcheck.yml run on PRs. Format every commit.

decision.choice: Enable GitHub Actions on your fork and open a PR within the fork to run the CI workflows
decision.why: The guide recommends it: you see the full LLVM matrix and vmtest kernels without spending maintainer attention on red CI.

alternatives.name: Reproduce one CI job locally with ci.py
alternatives.tradeoff: Use when a single job fails; set NIX_TARGET and the job env shown in the Actions UI, at the cost of a long local build.

alternatives.name: Rely only on local tests
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but misses other LLVM versions and kernels, so PR CI may fail.

verify: git clang-format upstream/master leaves no changes
./scripts/clang_tidy.sh reports nothing new in files you touched
Each build_test job in a PR on your fork passed (they are continue-on-error, so check every job, not the workflow badge)

steps.title: Measure compile time and probe cost with bpftrace bench modes
steps.learn: The guide says BPF program and runtime performance is on the critical path. --mode compiler-bench times each compiler pass; bench probes run with --mode bench (or --bench) report average time per probe.

decision.choice: Benchmark a Release build before and after with --mode bench
decision.why: Debug builds and assertions distort timings; BENCH probes measure the generated BPF code directly, which is what users pay for at every event.

alternatives.name: --mode compiler-bench
alternatives.tradeoff: Right when the change touches passes or startup time; says nothing about per-event probe cost.

alternatives.name: Time --mode codegen over ./tools for both builds
alternatives.tradeoff: Covers compile time of every shipped tool, like the old compare_tool_speed.sh; says nothing about per-event probe cost and that script needs updating first.

verify: Report median and spread over at least 5 runs for base and patched builds
Record CPU model, kernel version, LLVM version and build type
State if the difference is within run to run noise

steps.title: Open a one-commit PR and work through review
steps.learn: The PR template checklist asks for docs updates (docs/language.md, docs/stdlib.md or the man page), a CHANGELOG.md entry for user-visible changes (it includes the PR number, so add it after opening) and test coverage. PRs are squashed and rebased into one commit.

decision.choice: One signed-off commit with a changelog-worthy title
decision.why: Maintainers squash and rebase so each master commit maps to one changelog line; a single clean commit makes that trivial.

alternatives.name: Several well-structured commits
alternatives.tradeoff: Accepted for complicated changes with rebase and merge, but every commit must be formatted and titled for the changelog.

alternatives.name: Draft PR for early feedback
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful if design is unclear, but substantial changes should start as an RFC issue instead.

verify: Every PR template checklist item is checked or explained
git log shows one commit with Signed-off-by and a rebased base on current master
Each review comment has a reply or a pushed change; if review goes quiet, ping politely on the PR or on IRC or Discord

steps.title: Write up the bpftrace contribution and choose the next rung
steps.learn: Record the question, what you changed and why, numbers with machine and command, what surprised you in the pipeline or verifier, and what the change does not cover. Next rungs: a codegen bug, a new builtin through the RFC process, or reviewing others' PRs.
verify: The write-up links the PR and states its review or merge status
Every number names the build type, kernel, LLVM version and command
It lists one concrete next contribution and the subsystem it touches

projects.problem: bpftrace compiles a tracing language through LLVM into BPF programs; contributing teaches compiler passes, BPF verification and Linux tracing.
projects.proveIt: A single-commit, signed-off PR with a new unit or runtime test that passes CI and gets maintainer review, plus a write-up
projects.hardware: A Linux machine or VM (kernel 6.1 or newer with BPF options) and root for runtime tests; Nix recommended
projects.aiPolicy: AGENTS.md (also CLAUDE.md) gives AI agents the build, test, formatting and PR conventions; no separate rule on disclosing AI use was found.

projects.title: PostgreSQL
projects.question: Can I get a PostgreSQL patch through pgsql-hackers and the CommitFest, with regression tests, green cfbot CI and real reviewer feedback?

steps.title: Frame a PostgreSQL patch and the mailing list workflow
steps.learn: The GitHub repo is a read-only mirror: no PRs or issues. Patches go by email to pgsql-hackers, tracked in the CommitFest app; the Hacking Discord is for chat. No CLA or DCO: posting grants PGDG the right to distribute it. Expect 3+ versions.
verify: Read Submitting a Patch and the Code of Conduct on postgresql.org
Subscribe to pgsql-hackers and read a few recent patch threads end to end
Note the review offset: each CommitFest submitter is expected to review another patch

steps.title: Build PostgreSQL with assertions and run make check
steps.learn: Clone https://git.postgresql.org/git/postgresql.git. Review guidance asks for --enable-cassert and --enable-debug; --enable-tap-tests runs the Perl tests. make check runs core regression tests on a temporary install; make check-world runs every suite. Meson (meson setup, ninja, meson test) also works.

decision.choice: Autoconf: ./configure --enable-debug --enable-cassert --enable-tap-tests, then make
decision.why: The docs still call Meson experimental outside Windows, and the wiki review and pgindent instructions are written for make, so you can follow them exactly.

alternatives.name: Meson with --buildtype=debug -Dcassert=true
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster incremental builds and the same system CI uses for many jobs; some wiki pages need translating to meson test.

alternatives.name: Optimized build without cassert
alternatives.tradeoff: Only for timing performance; assertions slow the server and would hide or distort results.

verify: make check passes on an unmodified master checkout
make check-world completes and you note how long it took
SELECT version() on your build reports the master development version

steps.title: Trace one SELECT through exec_simple_query
steps.learn: In src/backend/tcop/postgres.c, exec_simple_query calls pg_parse_query (grammar in parser/gram.y), pg_analyze_and_rewrite_fixedparams (parser/analyze.c, rewrite/rewriteHandler.c), pg_plan_queries (standard_planner in optimizer/plan/planner.c), then PortalRun in tcop/pquery.c, which drives executor/execMain.c.

decision.choice: Attach gdb to one backend and break on each stage
decision.why: A debug build lets you inspect Query, Plan and executor state at each boundary, which teaches the node structures faster than reading alone.

alternatives.name: debug_print_parse, _rewritten and _plan settings
alternatives.tradeoff: No debugger needed, prints trees to the log; verbose and does not show control flow.

alternatives.name: Read the optimizer and executor READMEs first
alternatives.tradeoff: Best for design intent, but you do not see live data structures.

verify: Hit breakpoints in pg_parse_query, standard_planner and standard_ExecutorRun for one query
Match EXPLAIN output for that query to the Plan nodes you saw in gdb
Name the file that turns raw parse trees into Query nodes

steps.title: Learn the planner and MVCC model, then choose a subsystem
steps.learn: The planner builds Paths, costs them and turns the cheapest into a Plan (optimizer README). Heap tuples carry MVCC visibility info; a HOT update skips new index entries when no indexed column changes and the new version fits on the same page.

decision.choice: Target the executor and EXPLAIN output
decision.why: Changes show up in SQL regression tests, behavior is easy to observe, and changes to src/backend/commands/explain.c are directly visible in EXPLAIN output.

alternatives.name: Heap, MVCC and vacuum
alternatives.tradeoff: Core and fascinating, but concurrency bugs need isolation tests and reviewers are cautious about data-safety risk.

alternatives.name: Client programs (src/bin/psql, pgbench)
alternatives.tradeoff: Lower risk and quicker review, but teaches less about server internals.

verify: Explain how a Path differs from a Plan in your own words
Explain when an UPDATE can be HOT, using README.HOT
Write down the subsystem you chose and the README you read for it

steps.title: Review a CommitFest patch before sending your own
steps.learn: There is no good first issue label. The wiki suggests new contributors start by reviewing: apply a patch, build with cassert, test it and reply on its thread. Reviewing a Patch lists phases: submission, usability, feature test, performance, coding, architecture.

decision.choice: Review a small patch in the Open CommitFest
decision.why: Review is the project's documented on-ramp, it builds credit for the offset you will owe, and it teaches the checklist your own patch will face.

alternatives.name: Send a documentation patch (doc/src/sgml)
alternatives.tradeoff: Concrete output, but still needs a hackers thread and a CF entry; less learning about review.

alternatives.name: Add a missing regression test
alternatives.tradeoff: Useful and low risk, but reviewers may question value without a linked bug or discussion.

verify: You applied a patch with git am or patch and built it with --enable-cassert
Your review reply covers apply, build, tests and at least one usability point
You replied on the original thread, keeping threading intact

steps.title: Find a bug on the lists and reproduce it as a regression test
steps.learn: With no issue tracker, look at pgsql-bugs archives and recent hackers threads; the Todo wiki warns items may be stale and need discussion first. Check nobody posted a patch. Reduce the report to a SQL script, then a regression test in src/test/regress/sql with expected output.

decision.choice: A pg_regress test in src/test/regress
decision.why: Most SQL-visible bugs fit here, it runs under make check, and a patch without regression tests is treated as WIP.

alternatives.name: Isolation test in src/test/isolation
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for concurrency and locking bugs; specs are harder to write and read.

steps.learn: Blend in with adjacent code: no #ifdef to toggle your change, comments explain why, no unrelated reformatting. Include docs in doc/src/sgml when behavior changes. No AI-specific policy was found, but you must defend every line on the list yourself.

projects.title: scikit-learn
projects.question: Can I land a tested, well-scoped fix in scikit-learn's estimator code that two core developers are willing to approve?

steps.title: Read scikit-learn's rules before choosing a module
steps.learn: Goal: one PR tied to an issue that is ready for work, passing CI and reviewed. Merging needs two core developer approvals. There is no CLA or DCO; you must have the right to license under BSD-3-Clause. Maintainers talk on GitHub and Discord. A strict AI policy applies and the repo ships an AGENTS.md.

steps.title: Build scikit-learn with Meson and run one module's tests
steps.learn: scikit-learn builds Cython extensions through meson-python, so you need a compiler with OpenMP (on macOS, conda compilers plus llvm-openmp, or Homebrew libomp). An editable install recompiles on import, so editing a .pyx file only needs a fresh import, not a manual rebuild.

decision.choice: Conda-forge env plus pip install --editable . --no-build-isolation (the same as make dev)
decision.why: The development setup guide lists the exact conda-forge packages (numpy, scipy, cython, meson-python, ninja, pytest, ruff, pyrefly, pre-commit). Conda adds an OpenMP-capable compiler on macOS and Linux; on Windows you still install Visual Studio Build Tools first.

alternatives.name: venv plus pip
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine on Linux with system gcc; on macOS you also need the Xcode command line tools and Homebrew libomp, one more piece to keep working for OpenMP.

alternatives.name: Dev container in .devcontainer
alternatives.tradeoff: Reproducible Linux environment with no local compiler setup, at the cost of running inside a container or Codespace.

verify: python -c "import sklearn; sklearn.show_versions()" shows an sklearn version ending in .dev0

steps.title: Trace LogisticRegression.fit from validation to solver
steps.learn: fit in sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py is wrapped by _fit_context (sklearn/base.py), which checks hyperparameters against _parameter_constraints. validate_data (sklearn/utils/validation.py) checks X and y, then _logistic_regression_path builds a LinearModelLoss (_linear_loss.py) and calls the solver.

steps.title: Learn the estimator contract and pick a target module
steps.learn: Every estimator follows one contract: __init__ only stores parameters, fit learns attributes ending in an underscore and returns self, and get_params/set_params enable clone. check_estimator and parametrize_with_checks (utils/estimator_checks.py) enforce it; sklearn/tests/test_common.py runs them.

decision.choice: Target one module you use, such as linear_model or preprocessing, via its module: label
decision.why: Labels like module:linear_model and module:preprocessing let you filter issues to code you already understand as a user, which the contributing guide recommends. Pure Python modules keep the first fix away from Cython.

alternatives.name: Cython-heavy modules (tree, cluster, neighbors)
alternatives.tradeoff: Rich performance work, but you need Cython and memory view fluency, and reviews are slower.

alternatives.name: utils and validation
alternatives.tradeoff: Touches every estimator, so a small change can break many common tests; better as a second or third PR.

steps.title: Start with a docstring or example fix you can doctest
steps.learn: Docs live in three places: docstrings in sklearn/, the user guide in doc/modules/, and gallery examples in examples/. Docstrings are doctested: pytest sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py runs them. Typo-only PRs are allowed without an issue; anything larger needs an issue ready for work.

decision.choice: Fix an incorrect or unclear docstring in your target module, backed by an issue
decision.why: It exercises fork, build, doctest, sphinx-lint and CircleCI doc preview with low risk, and docstring accuracy issues are real problems users file. It also builds a track record before a code PR.

alternatives.name: Improve a gallery example
alternatives.tradeoff: More visible and teaches sphinx-gallery, but CI rebuilds the example and reviewers care about runtime and plots.

alternatives.name: Add a missing test
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to code and valued, but you must show it covers an untested path, not duplicate existing tests.

steps.learn: pre-commit runs ruff check and format, pyrefly, cython-lint, sphinx-lint and codespell. steps.learn: Performance PRs must include a benchmark script and profiling output. asv_benchmarks/ covers linear_model, ensemble, cluster, svm and more; asv continuous -b LogisticRegression upstream/main HEAD compares commits. Profile first (%prun, line_profiler) per the performance guide.
